### Description of all ancient Christian

*Pamphilus of Caesarea* <note>Eusebius (c. 260–339 AD) is known as the "Father of Church History." # THE PRINTER TO
## THE CHRISTIAN READER.

Honorable dear Reader, since I have come into possession of the *Church History of Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the first major historian of the Christian church.</note>, and also the *Ecclesiastical History* <note>original: "Historie Ecclesiastica"</note> which is called the *Tripartita* <term>Tripartita: A "three-part" history created by merging the works of three 5th-century historians: Socrates Scholasticus, Sozomen, and Theodoret.</term>, translated into Dutch by good men of the Church, and seeing that there are now many various chronicles and histories printed and sold that do not specifically recount the affairs of the Church as these do. Furthermore, because there is today a great question and struggle as to who stands closest to the ancient Christian church and remains in agreement with it, and since these historians specifically recount the beginning and progress of said church—from the revelation of Christ in the flesh until around the year 400—they present to us, as if in a chest, all the treasures of ecclesiastical matters. In our current time, this is highly useful for all those whom God has placed in any form of government, whether spiritual or worldly, as well as for those outside of it.

In view of this, I have spared no expense nor shirked any labor so that this work might come forth for honor and profit, and for the service of our Dutch Nation, having been printed and widely sold for so long in various other languages. I hope to have done the kind Reader a convenient service here; if you buy and read this History instead of other fictionalized histories <note>The printer is likely contrasting factual church history with popular medieval romances or unverified legends.</note>, you shall easily understand and find, through the struggle of the **Martyrs** who fought for the truth described herein (alongside other churchly matters), the footsteps that the **Apostles** and **Apostolic Men** have walked. And you shall neither be unaware nor ignorant of how, when, and for what reason every error made its incursion. I have also newly added here at the end, for the service of the Christian Reader, that which has happened to the Church of God in various Provinces, but principally in **France** <note>This refers to the contemporary struggles of the Huguenots in the French Wars of Religion.</note>, in order to have good knowledge of Church matters. This is most necessary for a Christian: to seek that which is Heavenly (as in Colossians 3) <note>Referring to Colossians 3:1-2: "Set your hearts on things above, where Christ is..."</note> and to align himself with the understanding of the first and oldest Christian Churches. May God preserve us therein, and let us always enjoy the comfort of said Church, the **Holy Spirit**, through Christ, the giver of the same Holy Spirit.

->AMEN,<-

Dated Dordrecht, 1613.

<margin>Eusebius also wrote many other books</margin>
For Eusebius, a Prince and the most prominent of all Church historians, has acquitted and applied himself exceptionally well to present these things to us. # THE PRINTER TO
## THE CHRISTIAN READER.

Honored and dear Reader, since the *Church History* of Eusebius has come into my hands, as well as the *Ecclesiastical History* which is called the *Tripartite History* <note>original: "Historie Ecclesiastica... Tripartita." This is a famous 6th-century compilation of three earlier Greek historians: Socrates Scholasticus, Sozomen, and Theodoret.</note>, translated into Dutch by good men of the Church, and seeing that there are now many different chronicles and histories printed and sold which do not specifically recount church matters as these do. Furthermore, because there is such great dispute and conflict today regarding who stands closest to the ancient Christian church and who is in agreement with it, these history writers specifically recount the beginning and progress of that same church—from the revelation of Christ in the flesh until around the year 400—and present to us, as if in a chest, all the treasures of ecclesiastical matters. These are now, in our own time, highly useful for all those whom God has placed in any position of government, whether spiritual or worldly, as well as for those outside of it.

Considering this, I have spared no expense nor shied away from any effort so that this work might be brought forth for honor and use, and for the service of our Dutch Nation, having been printed and widely sold for so long in various other languages. I hope to have done a convenient service to the kind-hearted reader herein; for if you purchase and read this history instead of other fictional stories <note>The printer is likely contrasting factual church history with popular medieval romances or folk tales.</note>, you shall easily understand and find the footsteps that the Apostles and Apostolic Men <note>The "Apostolic Men" were early Christian leaders believed to have been direct disciples of the original Apostles.</note> walked, through the struggle of the Martyrs who fought for the truth as described here, alongside other ecclesiastical matters. And it shall not be unknown or hidden from you how, when, and for what reason all errors made their intrusion. For the service of the Christian Reader, I have also newly added at the end that which has befallen the Church of God in various provinces, but principally in France <note>This refers to the contemporary struggles of the Huguenots (French Protestants) during the French Wars of Religion.</note>, in order to have good knowledge of church affairs. This is most necessary for a Christian: to seek that which is Heavenly (Colossians 3) and to join himself to the understanding of the first and oldest Christian Church. May God preserve us therein, and always let us enjoy the comfort of that same Church—the Holy Spirit—through Christ, the giver of that same Holy Spirit.

->AMEN.<-

->Given at Dordrecht, 1613.<-

# PREFACE to the Christian
## Reader, on the usefulness of these Histories.

<margin>The argument for reading history</margin>
Just as all histories, chronicles, deeds, actions, and events, dear Reader, are always read with great desire and longing, and always to some use or profit: so much more will the reading of this *Ecclesiastical History* <note>original: "Historie Ecclesiastica"</note> of Eusebius, Ruffinus, and the other *Tripartite Ecclesiastical History* be of benefit to those who have found any discernment in the Holy Scriptures. Such a person will easily come to know what was done and handled in the Christian Church by the Apostles and Apostolic Men after the time of Christ.

<margin>Eusebius also wrote many other books.</margin>
For Eusebius, a prince and the foremost of all writers of Church History, acquitted and exerted himself singularly in presenting these things to us. In this, he lacked neither learning, wisdom, nor eloquence, nor even memory. For he does not merely bring forward the most ancient Fathers, one after another, along with the old stories and their deeds; he also tells us vividly—and allows us to judge—the things as they occurred and happened continuously, one after another, in the Church, drawing from the books, acts, letters, councils, and synods of the oldest Fathers. And although this History is disregarded and rejected by many—who would rather read lying, fictional things—they shall be corrected here, being reminded of the truth. For what is more necessary for a human to know than what has happened and occurred in the Church of Christ since the manifestation of our Lord?

<margin>The teaching of history is necessary for a good Christian life.</margin>
For if all histories bring us some benefit, how much more so this church history: which instructs people in the eternal, Divine Religion, and points us toward the first, oldest Fathers and how they served God, so that we might in some way be joined with them to God. And truly, if histories did not bring to our memory all worldly and spiritual dealings—and especially what concerns Religion—then the negligence and imagination of men would devise and darken all the glory and beauty of Divine and human laws. This happens especially among the Atheists <note>original: "Atheos"</note> and those commonly called Epicureans <note>In this period, "Epicurean" was a derogatory term for someone who lived for worldly pleasure and denied the immortality of the soul or divine providence.</note>, who hold no more regard for God than for themselves. Otherwise, what would we know of the creation of the World, of Adam, Seth, Noah, or the Deluge <note>original: "Diluvie," referring to the Great Flood.</note>, <margin>Genesis 7. Exodus 1. Acts 7. Psalm 105.</margin> of the Patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and their seed? Or of King Pharaoh in Egypt, under whom the Hebrew people first began to multiply, and the leader Moses, the rising of other Kingdoms, and the planting of the promised land according to the Prophecies?

Further, what would we know of Alexander the Great, who greatly troubled <note>original catchword: "quelde," meaning to plague or torment.</note> this people?

It specifically highlights Eusebius as the preeminent historian who used primary sources like synodal records and letters.</summary>

Likewise, what would we know of the mighty Emperor Octavian <note>The Emperor Augustus, under whose reign Jesus was born.</note>, under whose broad Empire Christ the Prince of Peace was born, and His people—who, born like drops of the morning dew, serve Him and are dedicated to Him? How should we know (I say) how to speak of this people, or of any Reformation in church matters, were it not that these Histories, their deeds, facts, works, and dealings made them known to us? For these are good masters who teach us with kindness, without rod or staff. For if we give credit to the Author of these Histories, he has—with great understanding and diligence (such as no one before him has done)—gathered the stories into a little bundle and a History. He has drawn these from all the records and proofs left from former times, and from what he saw and heard in his own time, just as one pulls little flowers from a great meadow. He shows us all customs and abuses, which truly gives us great enlightenment amidst all error and despair.

<margin>History writers are watchers and mountain-beacons.</margin>
As we may pluck and read from the flowers, which are presented to us as a sustenance and gathered for our benefit, they shall also serve us like certain reflections which, being placed in dark places, are lit from afar; it is as if a cry comes from a high tower to avoid the wandering of the path and to walk the right way.

Such a beautiful and glorious treasure does this History have hidden within it; therefore, the praise and honor mentioned in this place (by the discerning Reader) shall rightly hold the first place in one's consideration.

<margin>Nothing is higher than man’s salvation.</margin>

# PREFACE.

<margin>Reformation without agreeing with the Fathers, yet falling short of the elders and displacing the ancient boundary stones. Deuteronomy 27:17, Proverbs 22:28.</margin>
...displaced or moved the former boundary stones <note>A biblical metaphor for established laws or doctrinal truths that should not be altered.</note>, which shall all be measured with the plumb-line of the first Fathers. For this reason, Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), often called the "Father of Church History."</note> so diligently describes both those who were the displacers and killers, and those who—to protect the true Reformation and the boundaries of the true elders—poured out their blood to the last drop, so that by following the service of the ancient fathers’ faith, they might bring it to us pure and unblemished.

And if we do not wish to be accused of ingratitude, or be found in willful error, we must accept these things which they, as fathers, have left to their children as a Testament, confirmed and made binding by their blood.

<margin>Christian Reformation is not a new teaching, but a reuniting with the teaching of the ancient church.</margin>
Therefore, we have good reason to search through this History and see the footsteps our fathers walked, which we may follow with profit. We must also take care here that we do not choose as our "true fathers" the wanton Ham, the crafty Ishmael, or the Esauites <note>References to biblical figures who were part of the holy lineage but turned away or were rejected: Ham (son of Noah), Ishmael (son of Abraham), and Esau (son of Isaac).</note> along with the Israelites in whom **GOD** had no pleasure. These also were "Fathers" and belonged to the Church once, and still do. Therefore, let this example and more stand here at the entrance of this History (which writes of the true Church): let everyone see to it in time that he does not come like the Wild Esau

<margin>Genesis 27:38; Hebrews 12:17; Genesis 21:9; Matthew 7.</margin>
seeking to receive the blessing, only to find that Jacob has already taken it and that he is told: *Cast out the bondwoman with her seed*, Genesis 16. For she shall not inherit with the free children, Galatians 4. And it shall also be fulfilled that many shall cry **LORD, LORD**, and shall not enter into the Kingdom of Heaven.

Thirdly, whoever wishes to make this History useful for himself should begin with Eusebius and learn the beginning and life of our Lord Jesus Christ, which the four Evangelists have described.

Also, the church history of Luke, called the Acts of the Apostles. All the Epistles of the other Apostles, and Apostolic Men <note>The generation of leaders and writers who personally knew the Apostles.</note>, and all the Martyrs and holy men of God—all of whom directed and measured their lives and deeds according to this carpenter’s square <note>original: "winckel haeck." A metaphor for a standard of truth or a rule of conduct.</note>.

<margin>In reforming, one shall improve both teaching and life. Hebrews 13.</margin>
To this end, the words of Paul previously mentioned apply: remember your predecessors who taught you the Word of truth, and follow their example.

<margin>The Apostles allowed themselves to be martyred for the teaching of Christ.</margin>
Now you see in this book how they arranged their outward life and being; how they ate and drank; how they watched and prayed; how they loved the true **GOD** and obeyed His service. You see how they set themselves against all superstition and false idolatry, and did so only for our only Savior **JESUS CHRIST**, who is the eternal truth. They did this with such fire and steadfastness that they desired present death for the sake of the incorruptible Religion, viewing it as the beginning of eternal life which **GOD** bore witness to them in the present. This was done with such a multitude and such desire that they feared the day would be too short for them to depart from this world into such glory and the fellowship of the Heavenly spirits. Thus **GOD** also brings forth to them the ancient thoughts from Isaiah, saying: *O Jacob my servant, fear not; and Israel whom I have chosen, be not dismayed; for if you go into the water, I am with you, so that the stream shall not drown you; if you go into the fire, I do not leave you; you are mine, I strengthen you, etc.* Isaiah 41 and 43. Thus being comforted in their pain...

<margin>The Providence of God</margin>
We must also take note here of God’s singular providence <term>providence: God’s divine guidance and care for the world</term> and care for His Bride and Church. So that she would not perish in the gruesome devastation and persecution that occurred under Nero, Trajan, and other tyrants, He wonderfully preserved the Bible along with many other ancient fathers. From this, one may take what serves to assure our faith—all of which proves and teaches for our own good that the Christian Reformation must be shaped and fashioned according to the evidence of the Holy Divine Scripture. When approaching this Scripture, one shall pray for the Holy Spirit as its only true interpreter, and then look upon the wonderful grace of God shown to our first Fathers, and upon their good lives and teachings. See how they set themselves against all Heathens and un-Christians. These fathers are not to be despised, yet they remain in their own rank as fallible men, and their words are not to be compared to the eternal Word of God. Likewise, they did not base their holiness on their own being, but on Him who had shed His blood for them—for whose sake they now also shed their blood to confirm that which they had received from Him.

# PREFACE.

<margin>Matthew 13</margin> ...by which the cunning and assault of Satan and the Antichrist is driven away and broken.

If there is a question about the Church—who she is and her standing—we must look to this time. For who are closer to the Apostles than the Apostolic men and those who followed them? Shortly after this time, as well as before it, the Church became sluggish, and the Devil sowed his weeds therein. <margin>Matthew 13</margin>

And from this immediately sprang unspeakable errors. Just as mentioned in <margin>2 Samuel 7</margin> <note>Specifically 2 Samuel 7:14: "I will chasten him with the rod of men."</note>, even under the pious Emperors who brought in the <term>support of religion<note>patronage and legal recognition of the Church</note></term>, there arose great complacency, negligence, pride, and a fondness for disputes, etc. But God, <margin>Eusebius, Book 8, Chapter 2</margin> chastising his Church with the rods of men, afterward allowed Tyrants to rule over them. As Eusebius himself explains with these words, saying: "The Lord <margin>Irenaeus 2</margin> has allowed the glory of Israel to be tarnished and all her walls to be destroyed." That is to say, through the Tyrants who devastated the Christian churches and created many thousands of martyrs.

But there is also much to learn and observe from this history and other histories at the outset, according to ecclesiastical custom: how God has punished the tyrants and persecutors of the Church both temporally (through their own cunning) and eternally. I consider it necessary to relate this here for the terror of tyrants and the comfort of Christians, to see the miserable end and the horrible vengeance of God against such persecutors of the Christian Church. I leave here a summary and a living example for posterity, so that they might see the shape of the coming work and not encounter empty words while reading, but rather look upon these and similar ends.

<margin>In the year of Christ 57. A tyrant who killed his mother, master, and wife, set Rome on fire, and laid the blame on the Christians.</margin> Nero <note>The text says "Nero Domitianus," likely conflating the two emperors or using a combined name, though the description refers specifically to the Emperor Nero</note>, under whom—among many others—Paul was beheaded along with many other disciples, finally became mad and insane, and was miserably torn and bitten by wild animals. Some believe that in such madness he stabbed himself and took his own life. In the 32nd year of his age and the 14th year of his reign, of which Orosius <note>original: "Horosius"</note> writes in Book 7, Chapter 12.

<margin>In the year of Christ 84. Had it proclaimed that he should be called God.</margin> Domitian, the second persecutor of the Christians, was stabbed by his own servants in his bedchamber, and his body was torn and eaten by bats and other creatures. His body was carried away in pieces and buried in the 35th year of his age and the 15th year of his reign.

<margin>In the year 101. The Roman Empire was then at its height.</margin> Trajan, the third persecutor of the Christians—who, although he was warned by Pliny the Younger <note>original: "Phileni Secundi"</note> with advisory writings to cease his tyranny against the Christians—yet God would not let him go unpunished. For he died of dysentery <note>original: "buyckloop"</note>; some believe he was killed by his own people. <margin>He reigned 19 years and 6 months.</margin>

<margin>In the year of Christ 164. Reigned 18 years.</margin> Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Verus, the fourth persecutor of the Christians, was also punished along with many thousands of people. For during the height of the persecution of Christians, such a terrible pestilence and other sicknesses arrived that in Italy some lands, cities, and villages died out completely. In such a miserable state, he forgot his tyranny against the Christians. And he, the tyrant, died himself in great sorrow and misery.

<margin>In the year of Christ 196. A tyrant of all people who reigned 18 years.</margin> Septimius Severus, the fifth persecutor of the Church, was horribly punished by God and was attacked with constant rebellion and wars, as well as other adversities, so that he consequently forgot the persecution of the Christians.

# PREFACE.

<margin>In the year of Christ 238. Reigned 3 years.</margin>
Julianus Maximinus <note>Gaius Julius Verus Maximinus, also known as Maximinus Thrax</note>, the sixth persecutor of the Christians, was killed by his own people along with his son. His head was sent to Rome to be put on public display, which made the people so joyful that they spoke this proverb about him: because of his evil nature, "one should not let even a rabid dog live."

<margin>In the year of Christ 254. Many Christians, as numerous as the sand of the sea, were killed. Reigned 2 years.</margin>
Decius, the seventh persecutor of the Christians. In the battle against the Goths, his son was killed, and he himself fell into a pit and physically sank into Hell with the Devil.

<margin>In the year of Christ 257. Under this man, the entire Roman Empire was corrupted and attacked by thirty tyrants who called themselves Caesars or Emperors. Reigned 6 years.</margin>
Valerianus, the eighth persecutor of the Christians, who operated in Italy. At the height of his persecution, he was driven into Mesopotamia by the Germans and defeated in Persia by King Sapor <note>Shapur I of the Sasanian Empire</note>. He was captured and had both his eyes put out. The King kept him as his footstool; whenever the King wished to mount his horse, Valerius had to crouch down, and so the King stepped from his back onto the horse. He died in such misery and wretchedness.

<margin>In the year of Christ 257 and 6 months.</margin>
Aurelianus, the ninth persecutor of the Christians. This man was terrified by a bolt of lightning from Heaven; yet, as he did not cease his tyrannical persecution, he was stabbed to death by his own servants (just as Joash was for the sake of Zechariah <note>Refers to the biblical account in 2 Chronicles 24 where King Joash was assassinated for killing the prophet Zechariah</note>) and thus received his earned reward.

<margin>He had intended much more evil, but God prevented this.</margin>
Diocletianus, the tenth persecutor of the Christians. This man’s entire body became swollen and burst open; he was consumed internally and externally by gruesome pain, and so died in great agony and misery.

<margin>In the year of Christ 228; 18,000 Christians suffered under him in one month. Reigned 20 years.</margin>
Maximinus <note>Maximinus II Daia</note>, his companion and the eleventh persecutor of the Christians, came to a miserable end with similar punishment. After mistreating the Christians, he received his reward from God just like his companions.

<margin>In the year 308. Reigned with Maximinus and divided the lands. Reigned 4 years.</margin>
Constantius <note>Constantius II</note> and Anastasius, who gave the <term>Arian heretics<note>Followers of Arius who believed Jesus was not fully divine; they were the primary rivals to the Orthodox Church at the time.</note></term> cause for the twelfth persecution of the Christians. But they also did not go unpunished, for Anastasius was burned by Heavenly Fire and fell into great madness. And Constantius died of <term>intestinal colic<note>original: "darm-gichte"</note></term>.

<margin>Opened the pagan temples; forced the Christians to offer sacrifices to idols.</margin>
Julian the Apostate succeeded them. However, in battle against the Persians, he was shot through so that his blood flew upward; when he saw this, he said: "You have conquered at last, O Galilean," <note>original Latin: "tu vicisti tandem Galilee". According to legend, these were Julian's final words, acknowledging the triumph of Christ (the Galilean).</note> which is to say, the Galilean has won.

<margin>In the year 576. Maxentius reigned in 310 for 2 years; he was against the Christians and favored the Arians. Tripartite History, Book 9, Chapter 15.</margin>
Valens and Maxentius, the thirteenth persecutors of the Christians. Valens and all his people were ambushed in the battle against the Goths, and he was burned in a house along with some of his followers. And Maxentius, with many of his servants, drowned miserably in the Tiber.

Through Genseric and Huneric, Kings of the Goths and Vandals, the fourteenth persecution of the Christians occurred. This had its beginning under the Emperors Constantius, Anastasius, and Valens around the year 376, and continued under the brothers Arcadius and Honorius, and Theodosius. And because these were mostly Arian Christians who had been banished and driven out by the <term>Orthodox<note>The mainstream church following the Nicene Creed</note></term>, this persecution was carried out in the most gruesome manner. For these people, leaving their land due to famine, arrived in Thrace, Africa, Illyricum, Noricum, Pannonia (which is Hungary), Italy, and there

What misery the Christians suffered there—of devastation, burning, plundering, capturing, hanging, and strangling—can be read at length in other writers and is too oppressive to recount here. For in their murdering and killing, they spared no gender or age, whether woman or man, young or old. The Priests and Ministers of God's Word were put to death in shameful ways: the places where God's Word was preached were devastated and trampled. Against this wild horror and Antichrist, Augustine wrote an entire book and named it **The City of God** <note>original: *De Civitate Dei*</note>, which referred to the Christians who suffered much from the city of the godless, or Antichrists. In this work, he laments greatly over these robbers who, after they had devastated other lands and cities, also conquered Carthage and the Church of Cirta. And Hippo, after it was besieged for fourteen months by water and by land, was burned a short time after Augustine’s death. Thus the entire land of Africa was lost, and the other aforementioned lands were most horribly devastated with sword and fire by these Huns, Goths, and Vandals, who were all Arian Christians <note>Arians were a group who followed the teachings of Arius, holding that Jesus was created by God and not co-eternal with Him; they were considered heretics by the Orthodox/Catholic church of the time.</note>. And this persecution exceeded all others in cruelty and duration. For under Emperor Honorius, around the year of Christ 407, having chosen a King, this rule remained in their hands for about 150 years, until Justinian II <note>The author likely means Justinian I, whose general Belisarius reclaimed Africa in 534 AD, or is using a different chronological system.</note>, that is 690 years, who avenged the entire land of Africa after it had been occupied for 96 years by these Arian Christians, drove them out, and made them subject to the entire Roman Empire: and he paid them back in the same measure as they had done. For just as they had called out <margin>Matthew 7. Therefore God plagued and punished them, and they also received their reward. God punished and stilled such things miraculously: for becoming at odds with one another, they destroyed each other to the death like dogs, and so at last, as has been said, they became a prey to their enemies. And thus God removed the sorrow from His Christians, avenged it in His own time, and exacted that innocent blood from their hands, just as the histories mention before and after.

<margin>Three enemies of the Christian church.</margin>
Which are commonly always three in number, and enemies of the church: namely, the proud, the powerful, and the rich, of whom few are called to the Kingdom of God <note>referencing 1 Corinthians 1:26</note>, but who mostly resist it, either secretly or openly.

<margin>Luke 1:52. Psalm 138:6. Proverbs 10:16 and 11:5, 6 and 13. Esther 9:16. 1 Samuel 15:28.</margin>
Therefore Mary, in her Song of Praise <note>The Magnificat, a song of Mary recorded in the Gospel of Luke.</note>, sings of this punishment, both in general and in particular: *He has cast down the mighty* <note>original: "Deposuit potentes"</note>, that is, He has thrust down the powerful, the proud, and the rich, and has exalted the humble, Luke 1:52. Just as in this History, their fate and received reward are shown.

Thus you will also find here an entrance into the Church under the New Testament; how it began and was spread abroad. Of the persecution and peace of that same Church. Likewise of the right doctrine, of the punishment for sin, of <term>penance<note>Voluntary self-punishment or acts of devotion to express sorrow for sin.</note></term> and <term>Discipline<note>The practice of maintaining order and correcting behavior within the church community.</note></term>, and of the Apostolic ban <note>Excommunication or being cast out from the church community.</note>. Of the changes in the right doctrine, and of the <term>Ceremonies<note>Formal religious acts or rituals.</note></term> and customs of the Church. Likewise of the government of the Church, what form and appearance it had at each time: of the discord, of the <term>Councils<note>Formal meetings of church leaders to decide on matters of doctrine or administration.</note></term>, of the persons of the <term>Heretics<note>Those holding beliefs that contradict established church doctrine.</note></term>, of the miracles, and of the wondrous signs. Likewise of other Churches and Religions alongside the <term>Orthodox<note>From the Greek meaning "right-believing"; those who follow the traditional and established faith.</note></term>: of the worldly state of the Jews. Likewise of the changes of the <term>Regimes<note>The various ruling governments or political systems under which the church existed.</note></term>, under which the Church did not perish but was wonderfully preserved by God. Thus you find described here all the seasons of the years and many different things set out at length, which gives a delight to reading. But it requires a sharp and practiced mind to bring all these matters together and to make a distinction between right and wrong Faith, between right customs and abuses. And so that the Christian Reader may not wander in this, nor burden their senses, and might read this History profitably, we shall for that purpose set down some further points of learning.

<margin>Instruction regarding Christian Doctrine.</margin>
Namely, first, to take good heed in this History of the right Doctrine and faith, and to make a summary of what manner [of worship] existed at each time, and also of the similarity and difference of Ceremonies in all places, and why these and others were established.

<margin>Of the form of government.</margin>
Secondly, to take good heed of the form, nature, and manner of the Government used by the Ministers of the Church, whereby the agreement with the articles of faith is pointed out to us, just as Paul says: *No one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid* <note>original: "Gheen ander fondament en can niemant legghen dan daer gheleyt en is"</note>, 1 Corinthians 3:11.

<margin>The persons.</margin>
Thirdly, the persons are described at length, through whom the government is seen and the faith is described against the Heretics; this shows the most weighty dealings, the clear light, and drives away the dark clouds of the misty air. So that one may know all things which otherwise would have been as dead and forgotten to us, and see what, when, where, and in what manner, with which, and by whom those things occurred, if we are not negligent in reading this History.

<margin>Church History.</margin>
Fourthly, this History is an indication of the origin of all error and

# PREFACE.

<margin>Points to the beginning of error.</margin>
...and falsification; and beside the right foundation of doctrine, it shows the deceit of the world, which through misunderstanding receives poison for medicine and accepts false doctrine for truth. Therefore, it is essential to have good judgment in the dealings of the church.

<margin>Points the wanderer to the right path.</margin>
Fifthly, these histories teach how to understand and judge <term>heretics<note>Individuals whose religious opinions or practices differ from the official teachings of the church.</note></term>, and they bring led-astray consciences back to the right path. This is achieved as they see therein the testimony of the ancients, by which they find error refuted and condemned. Likewise, as God carries His Kingdom among the pagans and non-Christians and seeks and gathers His little sheep (Ezekiel 34), so do they also find that same Shepherd.

Sixthly, they also find here the path which the ancients walked, as this example testifies: *I will put enmity between you* (Genesis 3:15) <note>original: "Ick sal vpantschap tusschen u setten"</note>. That is, that the true church has commonly been subject to the <term>cross<note>A common metaphor in this period for the suffering and trials endured by the faithful.</note></term> and persecution.

<margin>Distinguishing right shepherds from the tyrannical ones.</margin>
Seventhly, they set down the signs by which one shall distinguish heretics and false teachers from the right teachers of the church and from tyrants. Likewise, one sees here the devil’s seat and dwelling in the church of heretics, in which he wonderfully shows off with titles and appearances, and misleads and blinds many people with pagan idolatry, through violence, coercion, and success. Thus, no one should look at the great crowds, but should instead pay close attention to the truth.

<margin>Prophets and martyrs who cry out against false doctrine and tyranny.</margin>
Eighthly, one sees here that when doctrine began to perish and fall in the church, God—as in the time of the Prophets—raised up heroes and brave men who called out and spoke against falsehood, disregarding tyranny, scorn, shame, or persecution. They applied the <term>plumb line<note>original: "rechtsnoer," a tool used by builders to ensure a wall is perfectly vertical, here used as a metaphor for the standard of truth.</note></term> to help set things right, so that right doctrine and God’s honor would not come to shame; many were warned by this and kept safe from false doctrine.

<margin>Gives examples of God’s vengeance against the wicked.</margin>
Ninthly, church history teaches us the punishment suffered by those who introduced false doctrine and practiced hypocrisy, and it provides an example for those who persecute both secretly and openly. Likewise, these histories are also worthy of praise—even if they are not equal to the <term>Apostolic writings<note>The books of the New Testament, held to be the ultimate authority.</note></term>—because they have preserved and brought down to us many memorable and incidental things, although many improper matters have been gathered and mingled among them.

Tenthly, they also teach the weakness and error of the most prominent people, showing that falsification was sometimes found even in them. This is so that one might know how to make a distinction between the Prophetic and Apostolic writings and the individuals themselves, and so that one (as commonly happens) does not exalt great persons too high above the Apostles nor their doctrine.
<margin>Proverbs 8:12. Psalm 37:25 <note>The original text cites "Spr. 37. 25." While "Spr." usually refers to Proverbs (Spreuken), Proverbs only has 31 chapters; this is likely a reference to Psalm 37:25 regarding the experience of the righteous.</note></margin>

<margin>Church history: a treasury of all church matters.</margin>
Eleventhly, they teach us to understand rightly and clearly the writings of the Fathers related here, and open the prophecies to us. From these, one can easily guess and learn what will serve people for good or ill, both now and in the time to come. Just as Solomon wisely says: *I, wisdom, dwell with the prudent, and know how to give good counsel* (Proverbs 8) <note>original: "Ick wijsheyt woone by den verstandighen/ ende weet goeden raet te gheven"</note>. And again: many are wise through experience; they advise and hit the mark.

Twelfthly, this history is like a <term>treasury<note>original: "schatcamer," literally a "treasure chamber" or storehouse of valuables.</note></term> of all church matters and dealings. Whoever wishes to have knowledge of them may enter here and take from it. Whoever considers this fruit and benefit of little value is no Christian and is worthy of being deceived, for he cannot, with all the saints of God, pluck the lilies and roses from among the thorns.

<meta>This page concludes the "Preface" (Voor-reden) of the work. It transitions from the numbered points of benefit found on the previous page to a concluding exhortation on the necessity of studying ancient Church history as a foundation for the Reformation.</meta>

<sig>** iij</sig>

# PREFACE.

<margin>That ancient and true work praised here is worthy of all honor.</margin>
We relate these things so that one might see and observe how great a benefit it is, and how necessary it is, to diligently read <term>Church Histories<note>Accounts of the development, trials, and doctrines of the Christian Church from its beginnings.</note></term>, even though the children of this world neither see nor value such things. Instead, they would rather read useless, worldly, and fabricated fables. Therefore, seeing and noting this glorious work, as well as the comfort and benefit that the <term>godly<note>Specifically, those who are devout or "God-fearing."</note></term> reader can learn from it, we have spared no labor nor shied away from any expense so that this *Ecclesiastical History* <note>original: "Eccleſiaſtica Hiſtoria"</note> might be brought forth to honor and use, and be widely read. We hope this will satisfy the simple reader, and that they might be able to judge the ancient Christian Church a little better than those who are entirely ignorant of ancient things. Such people now wish to judge and measure everything according to the opinions and customs currently received by men, just as if human wit pleased God. For appearance and fame have nothing to stand against ancient tradition; for it is the oldest and truest, says <term>Tertullian<note>An early and influential Christian author (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) from Carthage.</note></term>. So then, let us cast and keep our eyes upon the first Fathers. In the fear of God, let us seek to compare and improve our lives and teachings in the <term>reformation<note>The 16th-century religious movement aimed at reforming the beliefs and practices of the Roman Catholic Church.</note></term> of all matters, and found ourselves upon that which is ancient. Let us ensure it agrees with and contains the truth in which all the Prophets, <term>Apostolic Men<note>Early Christian leaders who were contemporaries of the original Apostles or were taught directly by them.</note></term>, and Martyrs rested, died, and fell asleep in the Lord. If you look upon and hold to this, you will have the understanding of this Church history and the *universal Catholic Faith* <note>original: "univerſale Fidem Catholicam"</note>, which is the oldest universal faith. To this I commit myself, and I pray the Lord will gather and preserve His Church in true prosperity and unity of faith, through Him who lives and reigns—with the comfort of His Church, the Holy Spirit—from eternity to eternity, AMEN.

->Farewell.<-

<summary>This concluding section of the preface argues that studying ancient Church history is vital for the Reformation, as it provides the "oldest and truest" foundation for faith over modern human opinions. The author exhorts readers to look to the early Church Fathers and Martyrs as the standard for universal Christian belief.</summary>

<keywords>Church History, Reformation, Tertullian, Apostolic Men, Martyrs, Universal Faith, Catholic Faith, early Church Fathers</keywords>

# Churches, called the Ecclesiastical History
# of Eusebius.

### Preface of Eusebius Pamphilus of Caesarea.

<margin>
Matthew 7.

<note>A decorative drop cap initial 'A' features elaborate floral scrollwork and a small human face centered within the letter's counter, typical of early modern printed books.</note>
**A**s I have intended to describe the successions of the holy Apostles, and the times that have passed from the time of our Savior until our own time; which and what kind of things have occurred during that same time within the assembly of Christians; and who the most excellent men have been in the most famous places; and what leaders have presided to stand for the assembly of God; and what each one in his time has written and taught for the confirmation and instruction of the word of God; and also who they were, how many, and at what time the new teachings <note>original: "niewer Leeringhē", referring to doctrines considered heretical by the early Church</note> came forth against Christianity, which have fallen into the deepest abyss of error, because they were diligent and bold in strife and discord, being teachers and masters of false knowledge <note>original: "valscher wetenschopt"; this is a reference to the "knowledge falsely so called" mentioned in 1 Timothy 6:20, often associated with Gnosticism</note>; and have thus gradually torn apart the assemblies of Christ like ravening wolves. And also I wish to examine what evil has come upon the Jews, because they were cunning against our Lord and Savior; and furthermore, in what manner and how many times the word of God was fought against by the Heathens <note>original: "Heydenen", referring to the pagan world</note>, and how many honorable people in these times, with steadfast hearts, have fought for the truth of the Word of God even unto the pain of martyrdom; and moreover, I wish to tell of all the martyrdoms that have occurred in our time, and what merciful help and assistance everyone received from our Lord and Savior Christ.

<margin>
The beginning of the physical presence of Jesus Christ.
</margin>
So I shall take no other beginning than from the time that our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ was physically here on Earth. But I pray that I will not be judged harshly, for I confess that in this work we have begun more than we are capable of with our own strength, to tell faithfully and rightly all that has happened

<column-break/>

there; and that we dare to go so boldly on this path, which is yet unpaved and which no one of our own has yet trodden.

<margin>
Eusebius’s Guide is God.
</margin>
Thus we must have God as our Guide <note>original: "Leptsman", an archaic form of the Dutch word "leidsman", meaning leader or guide</note>, and also be certain that the help of our Lord and Savior will stand by us, but no human help on which we may rely; nor do we see any footsteps that have gone before us, except only that which is scattered to us—the proofs and left-behind memories of past times and histories, from which we have as much help as one placed in a dark place who sees lights kindled from afar; then as if called from a high tower, by which we are warned through their voice to avoid the error of the path. Therefore, choosing everything that has been left to us that we believe to be suitable for this History, and plucking the little flowers of the Teachers as if from a meadow, we have begun to gather the histories into a small bundle, and suspect that it is sufficient and suitable—even if one cannot tell it all—to nevertheless gather and set in order the principal followers of our Savior and the Apostles, to whom the most prominent assemblies of the holy Church were delivered. It seems to me that I have undertaken a very necessary work, and most of all because, as I have said before, I perceive that no writer of the holy Church has prepared himself to tell the same to posterity.

<margin>
Histories are messengers of antiquity and the life of memory.
</margin>
From which I also hope that from this our labor, and from the knowledge of past things, much usefulness shall come to those who are diligent to know the same. Even though we have also gathered some things very briefly into Chronicles (as in the Book we have written concerning the times <note>This refers to Eusebius’s earlier work, the "Chronicon," which provided a chronological timeline of world history</note>), we shall nevertheless [continue] more broadly and fully in this book...

# The Chronicle of Eusebius Pamphilus

<margin>A</margin>
All [histories] tell and reveal past events. Therefore, our first discourse shall be a beginning—as we have promised—concerning our Lord Christ. And because we have undertaken to describe the history of the Christians, it is first necessary to know from where such a race of people have their origin and beginning, and what that name signifies, and from whom such a people received their name; thus it is necessary that we recount the same from a slightly higher point in time, in order to make it more clearly known.

### That God the Lord is a Creator and Ruler of all things, just as it is written in the Law and in the Prophets.

->¶ What the argument of the promises may be.<-

## The First Chapter.

<margin>Proposition.</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
Since Christ exists in a twofold manner, and holds within himself the fullness of the Divine and Human nature—and that the "head" is held to be the Divine substance, and the "feet" for the human nature which he took upon himself for our salvation—our narrative is more perfectly arranged if we begin from the "head." <margin>Christ.</margin> That is to say, if we begin from the Word of his Divinity, through which the antiquity <margin>Nobility of the Christians</margin> and also the nobility of the Christian people (whom some suspect to be a people of a new name) is shown. No reason can express nor reveal the generation of Christ, nor his substance and nature; for the Divine Word proclaims of him, saying: "Who shall tell of his generation?" <margin>Isaiah 53.</margin> And also in another place, with nothing less than a Heavenly voice, it is said of him: "No one knows the Son but the Father, nor <margin>Luke 10:22</margin> does anyone know the Father, but the Son." <margin>F</margin> Therefore, only the Father who begot him knows the Son. Therefore, in the Holy Scripture—which was written through the Holy Spirit—he is proclaimed and named the <margin>Known from old.</margin> eternal Light that has always been from

<margin>Adam and Eve were driven out of Paradise.</margin>
**A.** Having lived in a state of salvation, Adam and Eve corrupted God’s commandment through negligence and fell into this mortal and frail life. Because of the Divine curse, they exchanged the delights of Paradise for a dwelling upon the cursed earth. Being thus cast out into the world, those born of such parents—

<margin>The people lived wildly.</margin>
**B.** —for the most part wandered astray like wild and fierce beasts. They possessed no cities for the sake of decency, nor any laws for the righteousness of life. No art or learning was found among them, nor did they know anything of scholarship; rather, they were like wild and savage people, having no permanent dwelling place and living thus in desert lands. Although there was naturally within them—by the mercy of the Creator—some good seed, they allowed it to remain uncultivated and desolate. They gave themselves over instead to the habit of wickedness, a path toward which mortal man is more inclined. From this it happened that they committed wicked sins among themselves and became so corrupted that they even struck one another dead; indeed, their cruelty grew so great that they devoured one another. 

<margin>They gave themselves over to evil.</margin>
**C.** Because of these men, the fables of the world have arisen, telling of how the gods and the great Giants fought with one another <note>Eusebius is likely referring to the *Gigantomachy*, the Greek myth of the battle between gods and giants, interpreting it as a distorted memory of the lawlessness before the Flood.</note>. This continued until the Divine vengeance opposed these bold transgressors, first with the Deluge <term>Deluge: the great flood of Noah</term> and also with the rain of fire, thereby restraining the horror of their sins with diverse and varied vengeance and punishment. And since it now pleased the Creator—

<margin>Theomachie. Gigantomachie. The battle of the gods and Giants.</margin>
**D.** —to improve the human race, which had been stained and corrupted by the sickness of malice, rather than to utterly destroy them, He took pity on their hearts, which had been darkened by wickedness. He—who was in the beginning with God, and who was the Word and the Wisdom of the Father—then sent and employed His angels and the ministers of His power. Sometimes, in His unspeakable dignity, He even revealed Himself, yet found very few who were mindful of God’s righteousness. 

<margin>Through Christ the human race is renewed.</margin>
**E.** Nevertheless, it pleased Him (as was fitting for God) to repair and recall the human race through His divine revelations, blessed warnings, and instruction out of the darkness. This He did in no other form than that of a human, in which form alone mankind could be taught, instructed, and helped.

<column-break/>

<margin>Hebrews.</margin>
**S.** Thus, He gradually converted an upright people, who are called Hebrews, to His service and honor. All of these things signified something higher in the spirit. He impressed upon them these and other legal commandments—

<margin>Ceremonies of the Old Law.</margin>
**T.** —as the basic elements of the holy instruction that was to come. This Law, like a beginning of light, shone upon the world, and through its sweet fragrance, it filled the sea and the earth far and wide. Thus, in various places of the world, the wise men, lawgivers, and philosophers perceived its scent: the fitting and honorable commandments, and the likeness of decency and justice. So they gradually began to instruct and teach their subjects and listeners, drawing them away from the wild and savage manners of men toward suitable and honorable institutions. And at that time—

<note>An ornamental floral woodcut serves as a decorative transition between the historical narrative of the Law and the announcement of the Incarnation.</note>

**V.** —they taught that men should maintain friendship, harmony, and covenants among one another, and that people should be helpful to one another and share the use of things. This continued until the human heart became somewhat—

<margin>The Old Law as a preparation for the wickedness of man, which Christ would provide.</margin>
**W.** —more teachable toward Divine institutions, and they became more patient with one another. Being thus accustomed and practiced in such habits, they would be capable and ready for the Divine institutions and able to comprehend the wisdom of God and the Father of all things. In this state, the Master of all virtues—the Word, Reason, and Wisdom of God Himself, who in the beginning had created Man with the Father—this same one, I say, took upon Himself the substance of human nature. He took on the appearance and form of a servant—

<margin>The Son who is God became man, so that the human race might be redeemed.</margin>
**X.** —and became entirely as we are in all things, not being different in time. When it pleased Him that the Roman Empire should rise to its great breadth, He came into the world and was born among us. However, He did not reveal this to the learned [of that world], but fulfilled and suffered everything that the Prophets had spoken of Him beforehand.

# Eusebius Pamphilus's Chronicle

¶ In these [times] one was raised in the manner and life of robbers, and later had great fellowship with Hyrcanus, the High Priest <note>The Dutch text uses "oversten Bisschop" (Highest Bishop) to refer to the High Priest of Jerusalem, a common terminology in early modern translations.</note> of the Jews; from him this Herod was born, who lived in the times of our Savior. This is described by Africanus <note>Julius Africanus (c. 160 – c. 240 AD), an early Christian traveler and historian whose works served as a source for Eusebius.</note>.

¶ How in Herod's time the succession of the Jewish Kings failed, according to the prophecy of the Prophet Daniel.

### Chapter 5.

<margin>Genesis 49.</margin>
Therefore, when the kingdom of the Jews had come to a man of a foreign race, the Prophecy was undoubtedly at hand: that the expectation of the Gentiles should come, seeing that they lacked the Scepter of the Princes and the descent of the Kings which had lasted from the time of Moses. For before they were led into the captivity of Babylon, they were first ruled by Kings, Saul and then David. For before the Kings, they were governed by Judges, who held the dominion of the people after the times of Moses and his successor Joshua <note>original: "Jesus synus navolgers"</note>. After the return from Babylon, there was no lack of good rulers who instructed the people with good teaching.
<margin>High Priests Rule.</margin>
Thus the Jewish people were ruled by High Priests until the time that Pompey, a Senator of the Romans, came to Jerusalem and fought for and won the city with Roman arms. He defiled the Sanctuary and the holy things of the Temple, so that the enemies even entered into the secret places <margin>Aristobulus, the last King of the Jews. Pompey.</margin> of the Temple. The same man who at that time ruled in the kingdom and the high priesthood according to the descent of his ancestors was named Aristobulus; he was led to Rome as a prisoner by Pompey along with his children, and he left the high priesthood to his brother Hyrcanus. At that same time, the Jewish people became subject to the Roman Empire and <margin>Hyrcanus, the last High Priest of the Jews.</margin> paid tribute. And Hyrcanus, in whom the last authority and high priesthood of the Jews had come, was captured by the Parthians. And so Herod, as <margin>Herod.</margin> previously mentioned—a foreigner appointed by the Roman senate while Augustus reigned—obtained the Kingdom of the Jewish People. It was under his reign that the coming of our Savior was at hand, as was the salvation and the expectation of the calling of the

<column-break/>

Gentiles, which according to the prophets, just as the Prophets had prophesied, <margin>Deuteronomy.</margin> was fulfilled. From that time on, the hereditary succession of the leaders and Princes who had descended from the tribe of Judah was suspended, as if by persecution; and thus the ordinance which had always followed its course from the ancestors was suddenly destroyed. Of this we have a fitting <margin>Antiquities Book 18. Chapter 6.</margin> testimony from the same Josephus, who proves that this same Herod, after he had received the kingdom from the Romans, did not appoint High Priests according to the ordinance of the lineages; but he admitted <margin>Unfit men.</margin> some unfit and ignoble men into the Priesthood. His successor Archelaus did the same in the ordinance of the Priests; and the same Josephus says that after him, the Romans themselves took the kingdom of the Jews for themselves. He also says that Herod kept the Holy Vestment <note>The sacred regalia of the High Priest, including the breastplate and ephod, which were historically required for certain rituals.</note> of the High Priest locked and guarded with his seal, and that he never gave the High Priests the power to use that garment. <margin>Archelaus's deeds.</margin> His successor Archelaus did the same. This custom and dishonor of the High Priest was also maintained by the Romans later on. I have said all this to testify to the truth of the prophecies which were fulfilled in the coming of our Savior. Likewise, the number of weeks was openly proven by the Prophet Daniel, which would be fulfilled and would endure until the time of Christ, which we have written of in other places. After the fulfillment of these weeks, the anointing and the "Christendom" <note>Here referring to the messianic office or the "anointed" status of the Jewish nation/priesthood.</note> would be destroyed—that which, as the Prophet testifies, was esteemed and held by the Jews as the most holy. This was openly proven to be fulfilled at the same time our Lord Jesus Christ came. It was necessary to describe this first, to reveal the truth of the time.

<margin>

B The descent of nature is held to be that which comes from the truth of the seed or blood. <margin>

</margin>
C Thus the two manners of birth are described by different Evangelists, so that one describes the one who biologically fathered him, and the other describes the one under whose name he was born. And thus it is that neither Gospel is a lie, since one follows the descent of nature, and the other follows the rule of the law.

D The lineage is joined together, so that one is counted through Solomon, and the other through Nathan, through the legal institutions which occurred for those who died without children; so that through that second marriage, in which one and the same person was born of different parents, a child born of one appears to be of another.

<margin>Natural and legal succession.</margin>
Among the people of Israel, he says, the names of the generations were sometimes reckoned according to nature and sometimes according to the ordinance of the Law. The descent of nature was held to be that which comes from the truth of the seed or blood. But the descent of the Law was used when a child was born through another, and was established and born in the name of a brother who died without children <note>This refers to "Levirate marriage," a Jewish custom (Deuteronomy 25:5-6) where a man was obligated to father a child with his deceased brother's widow to carry on the brother's name.</note>.

And although the hope of the resurrection was not yet fully received among those people, they nevertheless followed such a figure of the resurrection so that the name of the lineage would not perish through infertility. In this manner, such an ordinance of birth was maintained among them, so that some were born of others, yet were reckoned by the benefit and command of the Law.

<margin>Matthew and Luke describe the lineage according to the Law; Luke describes what are called the "legal ones," who are born to brothers from widowed wives.</margin>
Thus, the two ways of birth are described by different Evangelists; for one describes the one who naturally fathered him, and the other describes the one under whose name he was born. And thus, no Gospel is a lie, since one follows the descent of nature and the other follows the rule of the Law. The lineage is joined together with one another, so that one is counted through Solomon and the other through Nathan, by the legal institutions which occurred for those who died without children; thus, through that second marriage—in which one and the same person was born of different parents—a child appears to be born of others.

<margin>Herod is tormented.</margin>
**D** Herod (he says) was tormented daily with a bitter sickness, demanding vengeance for the crimes he had cruelly committed before. A watery and foul-smelling fluid ran down by his swollen feet, and in the lower part of his body, he was strained by inflammation. His private parts became putrid, and because of the stench, they began to crawl with worms. Due to an unceasing breathlessness, his private parts were most hideously afflicted. **F** In addition to all these pains, he had a horrific stench which came from his limbs—

### ¶ How there were four High Priests between Annas and Caiaphas.

#### The 15th Chapter.

<margin>The Emperor's officials sell the High Priesthood among the Jews according to their pleasure.</margin>
Holy Scripture proves that our Lord fulfilled the entire time of His teaching during the tenure of the High Priests <note>The original Dutch uses "overste bisschoppen" (chief bishops), a term early modern translators often used to describe the Jewish High Priests of the Temple.</note> Annas and Caiaphas. During the time when Annas held the High Priesthood <note>original: "Bisdom"</note>, He began to teach, and this lasted until the beginning of the High Priesthood of Caiaphas. Within this period, not even four full years were concluded. For in those days, the legal Commandments were brought to nothing through violence and ambition; the honor of the High Priesthood was no longer given based on the merit of one’s life or according to lineage, but through the power of the Romans. Thus, the authority of the Priesthood was given now to one and then to another, so that they were changed yearly. 

The same Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian whose works provide essential context for the New Testament era.</note> describes how there were four in succession who enjoyed the High Priesthood from the time of Annas to the time of Caiaphas, writing thus: Valerius Gratus deprived Annas of his Priesthood and installed Ishmael, a son of Fabi; and a little while later he rejected him and placed in the High Priesthood Eleazar, a son of Annas the High Priest. After one year, he also rejected him from his office and delivered the High Priesthood to Simon, a son of Camithus. He also enjoyed the office for no more than a year, and his successor was Joseph, who was also named Caiaphas. The entire time that our Lord and Savior taught upon the earth is contained within a four-year period, during which these High Priests whom Josephus records were described, and they hardly served a year each. Thus, this is in agreement with what Josephus also describes: that Caiaphas was High Priest in the same year that our Savior suffered, just as the Gospel Scripture also proves.

The histories which we promised to describe regarding Thaddeus happened in this way. When the divinity of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ became known and honored in all places because of his wonderful powers and works, many people from the surrounding lands, and even strangers from far-off countries, were moved and invited <margin>B</margin> to seek the remedy of health, especially those who suffered from particular or unusual infirmities. There was a certain King named Agbarus <note>Also known as Abgar V of Edessa.</note> who held dominion over certain peoples located beyond the river Euphrates. He suffered from an incurable sickness—at least, incurable by any human power. When he heard of the name of our Lord Jesus and of the wonderful works of his power, he prayed to him most heartily through a letter, which he sent by a messenger, <margin>C</margin> asking that he would please heal the great illness that he suffered daily. At that time, the Lord did not grant him bodily health immediately <note>Literally "prolonged" or "deferred" his health.</note>; nevertheless, the King was deemed worthy to receive an answer to his letter from our Savior, in which it was also promised that he would soon after obtain the fulfillment of his desire. For after <margin>D</margin> the resurrection and ascension of our Lord into <margin>Thomas.</margin> Heaven, Thomas the Apostle, by divine inspiration, sent out one of the seventy disciples named Thaddeus <margin>Thaddeus.</margin> to preach and proclaim the Word of God in the city of Edessa, in order to fulfill that which had been promised by the Lord. ### Eusebius Pamphili’s Chronicle

<margin>King Abgar is sick.</margin>
¶ And that this should be the same one of whom Jesus had written to him, saying: "When I am taken up, I will send you one of my disciples, who shall heal your sickness." And he summoned Tobias to him, with whom Thaddeus was staying, and said to him: "I have heard that a powerful man has come into your house; bring him to me." When Tobias came to Thaddeus, he said to him: "Abgar the ruler has summoned me to him and told me that I should lead you to him, so that you might heal him." And Thaddeus said: "I will come, for I am sent primarily for his sake." The next morning, early, Tobias took Thaddeus with him and came to Abgar.

¶ And as he came into the presence of the Ruler, it seemed to Abgar that upon the entrance of the disciple Thaddeus, a certain radiance <note>original: "claerheyt", meaning a divine brightness or aura</note> shone upon his face. As Abgar saw this, he worshipped Thaddeus. And all those who were with the King were astonished, for they did not see the radiance; it was shown only to Abgar, who began to say to Thaddeus: "You are truly a disciple of Jesus the Son of God, who said to me: 'I will send you one of my disciples who shall heal you and give you life.'" And Thaddeus answered: "Since you have believed greatly in him who sent me, I am therefore sent to you. And if it be that you remain in his faith and trust, then all the desires of your heart shall be given to you."

¶ Then Abgar said to him: "I have believed in him so much that I would have liked to kill the Jews who crucified him, if I had such a host of people, were it not that the authority of the Roman Empire prevented me." 

¶ And Thaddeus answered and said to him: "Our Lord has fulfilled the will of his Father, and when he had fulfilled the same, he was taken up again to the Father." 

¶ Abgar said to him: "And I know and believe in him and in his Father." 

<margin>Thaddeus heals King Abgar.</margin>
¶ And Thaddeus spoke: "Therefore I lay my hand upon you in his name." And when he had done that, he was immediately healed of all the sicknesses and infirmities that he had. Abgar wondered that just as he had heard the words and fame of Jesus, he found it to be so in reality through his works, that it was ful-
<meta>catchword: filled</meta>

<column-break/>

<margin>Abdon is healed of gout.</margin>
filled through his disciple Thaddeus, who healed him without medicines or herbs: not only him, but also another named Abdon, a son of Abdias, who had swelling in his feet <note>The Dutch "boeten" is an archaic spelling of "voeten" (feet). Abdon is described as having "podagra," or gout.</note>; and when Thaddeus came to him, he healed him through the laying on of his hands. He also healed many other citizens of the same city who were tormented with various sicknesses. And thus doing great and wonderful works, he proclaimed the word of God. 

¶ After that, Abgar said to Thaddeus: "You do all these things through the power of God, and we who see it are astonished; therefore I pray you, tell us of the coming of our Lord, how it happened, and of his Power, in which he did all that I have heard of him." 

<margin>Of Christ</margin>
¶ And Thaddeus answered: "Now I shall be silent, but because I am sent to proclaim the Word of God to all people, gather all your citizens tomorrow, and before them all I will proclaim it, and I will sow among them the word of Life, and the coming of our Lord Jesus, how it was, and why, and for what cause he was sent by his Father, and of the powers of his works, and of the secrets <note>original: "heymelijckheden", referring to divine mysteries or hidden truths</note> which he spoke in this world, and in whose power he did his works. And also of his new proclamation, and how small and humble he was, and how he humbled himself, and laid down his Majesty, and thought little of his Divinity, so that he was nailed to the cross and descended into hell, and broke the barrier of the enclosure <note>original: "den tuyne dat letsel", likely referring to breaking the gates of hell or the prison of death</note> which no one in all the world could break, so that he might raise the dead—he who descended alone, but ascended with great glory to his Father."

¶ Thus Abgar commanded that all his citizens should come together early in the morning to hear Thaddeus’s preaching; and afterward, he commanded that they should give him silver and gold, but he did not receive it, saying: "If we have forsaken our own, how shall we take that which belongs to others?" This happened in the 43rd year. <note>Likely referring to the year 43 AD, or the 43rd year of the local era in Edessa.</note>

¶ These things (so I believe) are not improperly translated by us from the Syrian language <note>Eusebius notes that he translated these records from the official archives of Edessa, which were written in Syriac.</note> and shall also have a place in our History.

# The Second Book of the Chronicles of the ancient Christian Churches, written by Eusebius Pamphilus of Caesarea.

### PREFACE TO THE SECOND BOOK.

In the first book, enough has been said—as much as was necessary and could be contained in a brief form—regarding the Divinity of our Savior Jesus Christ, and the antiquity of the Christian faith and teaching, showing that these are no new things. Also mentioned was the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, his passion, and the fulfillment of his mission, as well as the election of the Apostles. Now we shall describe what followed after his ascension into Heaven, based on the testimony of the Holy Divine Scripture, and partly from other books, faithfully written for the benefit and service of posterity.

---

### ¶ Of the lives and institution of the Apostles after the ascension of our Lord.

#### ¶ The First Chapter.

<margin>Sons of Zebedee.</margin>
The first who was appointed to the Apostleship by lot in place of Judas the traitor was Matthias, who was one of the disciples of our Lord, as has been shown above. 

<margin>Stephen chosen as a Deacon: the first martyr of Christ.</margin>
There were also ordained seven Deacons, through the prayers and the laying on of hands of the Apostles, for the service of the widows. Among whom was Stephen, who was the first after the Lord (precious after his election) 
<margin>Was stoned.</margin>
to be stoned by those who were the very ones to whom the Lord was rightfully given by Christ. 
<margin>Stephen, called a Crown.</margin>
Stephen—that is, a Crown. <note>The name Stephen is derived from the Greek word *Stephanos*, meaning a crown or wreath, which the author notes as a symbol of his martyrdom.</note>

Thereafter James, who was named a "Brother of the Lord" because he was the son of Joseph (who was held to have 

<column-break/>

been Christ's father, for the Virgin Mary was betrothed to him), who, before she came together with him, was found with child, having conceived by the Holy Spirit, as the Evangelist testifies. This James was also called "the Just" by the ancients, because of the virtues and privileges of his singular life. The histories testify that he was the first to occupy the Seat of the Holy Church in Jerusalem, 
<margin>James the Just, Bishop at Jerusalem.</margin>
just as Clement describes in the sixth book of his *Dispositions* <note>original: "dispositien", referring to Clement of Alexandria’s *Hypotyposes* or *Outlines*, a lost work of early church history</note>, saying: "Peter, James, and John, after the ascension of our Savior, although they were the leaders, did not claim for themselves the honor of the leadership, but appointed James, who was called the Just, as a Bishop of the Apostles." And also he writes in his seventh book of this same man: "The Lord (he says) after his resurrection gave all wisdom to James, who was called the Just, and to John and Peter; and they delivered it to the other Apostles, and they to the seventy, of whom Barnabas was one."

<margin>Scattering of the Apostles.</margin>
In the meantime, the first persecution against the assembly of God in Jerusalem occurred under the first martyr, Stephen, and it scattered all the disciples or—as the Holy Scripture proves—sowed them throughout that entire Jewish land and Samaria, except for the twelve Apostles.

<margin>Preached only to the Jews.</margin>
From which disciples some came to Phoenicia, and to Cyprus, and into Antioch; these had not yet dared to proclaim the mysteries of the faith to the Heathen <note>original: "Heydenen" - refers to non-Jewish Gentiles.</note>, yet they revealed it to the Jews.

<margin>Paul.</margin>
At that same time, Paul was still persecuting God’s assembly, going into houses and dragging out men and women, delivering them into prison.

<margin>Philip a deacon</margin>
And Philip, who was ordained as one of the seven Deacons with Stephen, traveled down into Samaria; being filled with the power of God, he was the very first to proclaim the Word of God to the Samaritan people. In him was such power of Divine grace that he also cast down Simon Magus through his preaching, who at that time was held in great fame and honor by that Samaritan people, so much so that they considered him to be the great power of God.

<margin>Feigned Catechumens <note>original: "Ghebijnst Catechumēnos" - refers to those who pretend to be students of the faith for ulterior motives.</note>.</margin>
When this Simon saw the signs and miracles that occurred through the powers of Divine grace from Philip, he was greatly terrified and was also amazed, and he feigned <note>original: "bevinst" - to pretend or simulate.</note> belief in Christ, so that he also received baptism. It is indeed a wonder that even to this day, the same thing happens among those who have received from him—as if an inherited hypocrisy—the most impure of sects; they enter the Holy assembly under such deceit, and steal baptism, and defile our ho-

-linesses, like a spreading disease. For their poisonous words creep forward like the mange <note>original: "schorfte" - a skin disease in livestock, used here as a metaphor for heresy.</note> among the sheep; and with secret and careless gnawing of the words, they thrust their deadly poison into them, until their harmful darkness is investigated through the diligence of the Shepherd and is thus brought into the light. So also was this Simon, who was caught by the wisdom of Peter.

As the proclamation of the Divine Word increased daily, there was—through God's foresight—from the lands of Ethiopia, a high official of a Queen of that same people (it is still a custom in that land to this day that they are governed by women) so that he might fulfill his vow at Jerusalem.
<margin>Official of Candace.</margin>

It is said that when he had returned to his country, he proclaimed to the people of the land the wisdom of the supreme God and the knowledge of the salvation of our Lord, just as it had been taught to him.

<margin>The Senate.</margin> When the report was spread throughout all that land, it was announced to the Emperor Tiberius. Also concerning his other wonderful works, and that after his death, when he had risen, it was believed by many that he was God. Tiberius, having learned of such things, brought the matter before the Senate. And it is said that the Senate rejected it, because such evidence was not first brought for a decision 

<margin>The authority of God is sufficient in itself.</margin> and because the opinion and sentence of the communities had preceded their own authority. For of old a Law was ordained, that no one should be considered a God by the Romans unless it was first confirmed by the decree and sentence of the Senate. And therefore it happened in this way, so that one should not suspect that Divine power required any human authority or confirmation. Although the Senate rejected it for the reasons we have stated above, nevertheless 

<margin>How Emperor Tiberius responded. Tertullian.</margin> Emperor Tiberius held to his own opinion, so that he did not allow himself to be moved to persecute the teaching of Christ. This is also described by Tertullian, a man who was very learned in the Law and in Roman Rights, and is also illustrious among our writers; he writes in his *Apology* <note>original: "Apologetico" — Tertullian's famous defense of Christianity written around 197 AD.</note>, which he wrote against the Heathen <note>original: "Heydenen" — refers to the non-Christian practitioners of Roman religion.</note> for the confirmation of our Faith, in this manner. "In order that we" (says he) "may also recount such an origin of the Laws: It was of old a settled Right that no God should be hallowed or consecrated by the Emperor unless the same was first approved and permitted by the Senate. Just as Marcus Aemilius did regarding his God Alburnus. This serves to excuse our case: that among you heathens, Divinity shall be judged by human opinion and suspicion; and unless such a God should be pleasing to men, he would not be a God, and men must be merciful to such a God." <note>Tertullian uses irony here to argue that if God's status depends on a human vote, then humans are effectively superior to their gods.</note>

The Emperor Tiberius, in whose time the Christian name was spread in the world, was notified from Syria, located in Palestine, by which things the truth of the Divinity was revealed; and he brought the same to the Senate and made his desire known. And since the Senate did not approve it, they rejected it. The Emperor nevertheless remained in his opinion and threatened the accusers of the Christians with dangers. This is what Tertullian describes.
