### The 4th Chapter.

Meanwhile, when Emperor Tiberius had reigned about twenty-two years, he died. After whom Caius <note>Caius Caesar, better known to history by his nickname Caligula.</note> received the empire, and he delivered the whole Jewish <margin>Caius Caligula the Emperor.</margin> kingdom to King Agrippa, and also the parts of the Kingdom that Philip and Lysanias had; and shortly thereafter, he also gave him Herod’s portion. This same Herod <note>Herod Antipas, the tetrarch of Galilee.</note>, who had caused John <note>John the Baptist.</note> to be killed, and who was also involved in strengthening the suffering of our Lord, the Emperor tormented in many ways and banished him eternally, as Josephus writes in his books which we have recounted above.

->How Philo performed his embassy for the Jews before Emperor Caius.<-

### The 5th Chapter.

In these times, <margin>Philo.</margin> Philo was in great esteem; an illustrious historian who was highly regarded among the learned, not only in our own matters but also in the Philosophy of the Greeks. He was a Hebrew man by the lineage of his ancestors, and was among the most illustrious and noble in Alexandria. How great and how learned he was in Divine and Ancestral Institutions and Laws is known to us from the legacy of the Books that have

<column-break/>

come to us. Who could express enough how great his teaching was in the liberal writings and in Philosophy, and most especially in the Platonic and Pythagorean doctrine, so that he surpassed nearly all those who were in his time and those who had been before him? Now this historian describes in five books what evil happened to the Jews in Caius’s time. <margin>5 Books on the misery of the Jews.</margin> And he also describes Caius’s madness: that he was puffed up with such pride that he wished to be called God. In the same books where he describes the misery of the Jews, he also writes of his mission and the command he undertook to come before [the Emperor] for the Jews, his friends. And when he had fulfilled his mission before Caius for the ancestral laws, he brought back nothing but mockery, and he was also in peril of his life.

And Josephus also writes thus in his eighteenth book of *Antiquities* <note>original: "outheden" — referring to Josephus’s "Jewish Antiquities," a massive history of the Jewish people.</note>, saying: When a riot had arisen in the city of Alexandria between the Jews and Greeks, three envoys were sent from each side to the Emperor Caius, among whom there was one on the side of the Greeks named Appion: <margin>Appion.</margin> who, while he accused the Jews in many other things, and especially above all, [charged] that they did not show the Emperor such honor as is customary to do for all those who are subject to the majesty of the Romans; and they further said that they made no altars nor Temples in honor of Caius, nor any other such thing in which Divine honor was shown to him by his other subjects, but that they alone are those who do not set up statues for him, nor observe the Sacrament of his Name <note>original: "Sacrament sijns Naems" — This refers to the oath of allegiance and the religious cult of the Emperor.</note>. When Appion alleged these and many other heavier things, by which he intended to kindle Emperor Caius to anger, Philo—who was an envoy of the Jews, a man great in all deeds, a brother of Alexander the Alabarch <note>The "Alabarch" was a high-ranking official or tax-collector in Alexandria, often the head of the Jewish community.</note>, and learned in Philosophy—very strongly defended and cleared these same accusations. But Caius rejected him and commanded that he should quickly depart from his sight; and being filled with anger, he considered within himself what evil he might do to the Jews. When <margin>Divine help instead of human.</margin> Philo went out with such injustice, he said to the Jews who stood by him: "We must still have good courage, for Divine help is necessary where human help ceases." For which reason Emperor Caius became angry with him. This is described by Josephus.

<margin>Philo's book on the Embassy to the Emperor.</margin>
And this same Philo recounts himself in his book that he wrote concerning his embassy <note>Philo of Alexandria’s "Legatio ad Gaium" (Embassy to Gaius), which describes a Jewish delegation to Emperor Caligula.</note> what happened to him. From which I shall recount only those things which will sufficiently prove to the reader that among the Jews, divine vengeance was present because of the crime they had boldly committed against Christ.

### What great tribulations befell the Jews after they had crucified our LORD.

## The 6th Chapter.

<margin>Julianus wishes to kill the Jews.</margin>
In the early times of Emperor Tiberius (he says), there was in the city of Rome one named Julianus <note>The text likely refers to Lucius Aelius Sejanus, the powerful Praetorian Prefect under Tiberius, whom Philo identifies as a primary antagonist of the Jews in Rome.</note>, who was highly esteemed by the Emperor: this man was inclined with all his power to kill all the people and the race of the Jews.

<margin>Pilate.</margin>
Likewise Pilate in the Jewish land (under whom the crime against our Savior was accomplished), while the Temple in Jerusalem still remained undefiled, he tempted the people to defile it, and often began to do so with very great rioting.

<margin>Philo's words concerning Emperor Caius.</margin>
And he also says that after Tiberius' death, the successor in the Roman Empire was Caius <note>Caius Caesar, better known as Caligula.</note>: who also with many other tribulations was very bitter and cruel to the Jewish people. This is openly perceived from the words of the same writer, where he says: Much wickedness of mind was in Caius, which he demonstrated against all people, and especially against the Jewish people; for those same places that were consecrated and sanctified for prayer, those he commanded to be defiled against the manner and religion of the same people, beginning in Alexandria, where he filled the same places with his statues, images, and arms.

<margin>Temple of the holy city of Jerusalem</margin>
The Temple of the holy city, which alone had remained undefiled from the unseemly filth, and was always held by the ancients to be free, he boldly changed into a temple of his own name, so that it should be called the House of Jove <note>Jupiter.</note>, of the most noble and new God Caius. And many other unspeakable plagues, and beyond all sorrow that one may describe, befell the Jews in Alexandria under Emperor Caius, which is also recounted by the aforementioned Philo, in his second book, which he wrote, "On the Virtues."
<margin>Philo's book on the Virtues.</margin>

<column-break/>

And Josephus also writes similar things that happened in Pilate's times: for because of the crime against our Savior, so did all this evil happen to the entire Jewish people. Hear what he also laments in his second book of the Jewish War. These (he says) who were sent into the Jewish land by Tiberius, he commands the Judge Pilate that one should secretly by night bring into Jerusalem the images of the Emperor, and the same were set up there.

<margin>The Emperor's image brought into the Temple.</margin>
When the day had dawned, this awakened a great disturbance among the Jewish people, being astonished and disturbed by the sight of such new things. He suspected from this that their laws were therefore despised and downtrodden, and all the ordinances of their ancestors, for whom it was not permitted to have such things within the walls of the city: But it was only because the swift vengeance of their evil confession condemned them, because all the people (just as the Gospel testifies) cried out together: "We have no king but the Emperor."

This same historian also recounts another vengeance that happened to them, saying: After this, another disturbance fell among them, because the holy treasury, which is called in their language *Corbonas* <note>original: "Corbonas" — from the Hebrew *Korban*, meaning a dedicated offering or the sacred treasury.</note>, was given out for the common need of a watercourse <note>An aqueduct used to bring water into the city.</note>, which was not permitted; this watercourse was also led some three hundred stadia <note>A stadium was approximately 185 meters; 300 stadia is roughly 35 miles.</note> far, by which the people were moved with great indignity.
<margin>Corbonas, God's treasury</margin>
And when Pilate was in Jerusalem, they went boldly to him, and were troublesome to him with great shouting. And Pilate, seeing beforehand the coming riot, had mixed his horsemen among the commonalty, and being armed, they were covered with citizens' clothing, and he had commanded them that they should use no swords among the rioting people, but only clubs. Therefore when it was time, a sign was given from the judge's seat, and some began to beat one another, to pull down, and to wound.
<margin>Punishment of the Jews in flight and of the...</margin>
Many fell in the flight and perished through their own trampling. The others were scattered and terrified by their own dead, and suppressed that violence of sorrow with silence. Still many other plagues befell the people of Jerusalem, and they were always rioting in new things, which the same historian describes, proving that from the time of the permitted crime, never [was peace] from him...

<margin>A</margin> ...pertaining to [this history], as seen from the accounts. <margin>B</margin> Furthermore, they also cast aside all the anxieties of this life and go out of the city into small gardens or fields, avoiding such company as does not share their purpose and intent, and whose lives are different, knowing that such things are a hindrance to those who wish to walk this strict path of virtue. Such an ordinance and life, being kindled with the heat of faith—which was first believed—it is evident that they maintained, as we openly read in the Acts <margin>Acts 4</margin> of the Apostles; for all those who believed under the Apostles sold their goods and lands, and laid the value at the feet of the Apostles,

<margin>C</margin> and it was distributed to each according to their need, so that no one among them was in want. And because this Philo writes that these people were disposed in the same way as the believers in the City of Alexandria—just as it had been disposed in Jerusalem by those who believed there—it is certainly beyond doubt that it was all the same work, the same institution, and the same faith.

<margin>D</margin> Furthermore, in the beginning of the same book <margin>In the beginning of Philo's book, concerning the Apostolic men, which he calls *vita contemplativa supplicum*: That is, heavenly, and always praying to God, as Jerome says. <note>original: "vita contemplativa supplicum" - The Contemplative Life of Suppliants</note></margin> which we mentioned before, he gave such a beginning. "In many places of the world," he says, "this race of men is found. For many had to partake in the perfection of this night <note>Likely a reference to the "watch" or vigil of the soul</note>, such as in Greece and the Barbarian lands. And there is still a greater multitude in Egypt around the cities, and especially by Alexandria. For from all places, the very best came there, just as a hasty farmer runs toward a fruitful field of the land."

<margin>E</margin> And that same land is most suited to Philosophy, more than the fruits located in the valley called Maria <note>Lake Mareotis</note>; it is pleasantly and delightfully elevated with some small hills, and possesses a secret and temperate quality of the air.

<margin>F</margin> After having described their dwellings, and what they are like, and their situation, he describes their assemblies, and says thus: "There is in every place a house that is dedicated to prayer, which is called *Semeneyon*, or *Monasterion* <margin>*Semenois* <note>Semneion</note>: a place of honor and holiness.</margin> which signifies in our language a Gathering of the Honorable or a Cloister, in which," he says, "they go and celebrate the mysteries of an honorable and secluded

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin> life; and they bring nothing there that is fit for food or drink, or any service of the human and natural body, but only the books of the Law and the Prophets, and psalms, and other such things. Being instructed in these teachings and exercises, they acquire through daily diligence a burning desire for that perfect and blessed life."

<margin>H</margin> And a little later he says again: "From the rising of the sun until evening, all the time is spent in diligent exercises, with which they are instructed through the Holy Scripture in Divine Philosophy, interpreting the ancestral laws in a spiritual sense. For they suspect that beneath the <margin>Under the Letter.</margin> appearance and image of such things as are written in the letter of the Law, a deeper and special Divine mystery is hidden within."

<margin>I</margin> They also have certain disputations and interpretations of the Ancient Men, who were teachers of their institutions, who evidently left behind many memorials of their writings; these they follow as guides of their ways, imitating the institutions and manners of those same teachers.

<margin>K</margin> It is certain that this aforementioned Philo spoke this regarding the Evangelical and Apostolic books, in which it is practiced and taught how one ought to understand the Law and the Prophets spiritually.

☛
Who can now doubt whether this Philo describes our own institutions? And if it should be that anyone still doubts this, we shall also add other things which he says, which are attributed to no one else but our people alone, so that even the most unbelieving person must confess it.

<margin>Women. Virgins.</margin>
The women (he says) of whom we have spoken are also women among whom are many elderly virgins, who maintain the purity of their bodies not through any compulsion, but out of devotion,
<margin>Origin of the Nuns.</margin>
who give themselves to the study of wisdom; not only do they hold to the spirit, but they also believe that the body ought to be sanctified, deeming it improper that a vessel prepared to receive wisdom should serve the desires of the flesh, and that they should give themselves to those from whom are desired the immortal and holy equipment of the Divine Word, from which a progeny is left behind that is not attached to perishable mortality. Should anyone think this is but a small thing, hear what he writes further.

<margin>The manner of explaining the Holy Scripture.</margin>
The handling of the Holy Scriptures, he says, is such that they mostly use the spiritual sense; and these men think that the whole Law is like a body, and that its body is the letter, and everything that is shown through
<margin>The Letter is the body; the soul is the spiritual understanding. Allegorical explanation.</margin>
the same Letter: but the soul is the spiritual and immortal sense which is hidden under the letter, which they learn from their Teachers as something higher and noble to behold, as if through a mirror; so that they also bring forth from the names a wonderful form of understanding. <note>Philo was famous for his allegorical method, which Eusebius argues was the precursor to Christian biblical interpretation.</note>

That Paul proclaimed the Gospel to the Gentiles from Jerusalem and the surrounding regions as far as Illyricum <note>A Roman province in the western Balkans.</note> is proven by his own words, and also by what Luke writes in the Acts of the Apostles. And also that Peter proclaimed Christ in the same provinces to those of the circumcision <note>original: "besnijdenisse"; referring to the Jewish people.</note>, and addressed them by their own names in the same Epistle which is proven beyond doubt to be his, in which he writes to those who were scattered—doubtless the Hebrews, for they are called "The Scattered," as those driven from their own places and set in dispersion—as he says, in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. And also Luke, in the Acts of the Apostles, mentions many of his companions who shared in his preaching, such as Timothy and Titus, of whom one was Bishop at Ephesus, and the other was appointed by him to instruct the congregations in Crete. And also Luke himself was of that race from Antioch, a master of the art of medicine, and a companion of Paul and also of the other Apostles, to whom he was of service. This man, from the teaching of medicine which he had received from the company of the Apostles and their doctrine, has left us two "medicine books" in which not the bodies, but the souls are made healthy: namely, the Gospel, in which his prologue begins: "Even as they delivered them unto us" (he says) "which from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word of God, whom I have followed from the beginning." <note>Luke 1:1-3. Yet no one was spared, nor did they fail to snatch the small sustenance of life from the very teeth of the children. Nor was the weeping and miserable food they consumed hidden; rather, the robbers were quickly upon them. If they saw any doors closed, they suspected that there were people inside eating, and in haste, they kicked the doors open and fell upon the houses. If they found that food had been consumed, it was forced back up out of their throats, and they snatched it from the people's mouths. The old men were beaten if they held onto any food of their own.

The women were dragged by the hair if they tried to hide any food, or if by chance any was found in their hands. There was no reverence for the elderly because of their gray hair, nor any mercy for the young children; instead, they threw the young children to the ground to take a small piece of bread from them, while the children clung to their necks. Against those who anticipated the robbers and had already consumed their food, the robbers acted with great fury and devised cruel pains, stopping the unfortunate victims' natural digestion and passage <note>A reference to the physical torture of blocking bodily functions to extract information about hidden supplies.</note>, and some others they pierced with sharp awls in their private parts (I shudder as I tell these histories) and forced the wretched through such pains to confess to having some bread or flour.

And these same robbers and tormentors suffered no hunger (for it would have been more tolerable had they seemed to do such things out of necessity), but they did it so that they might gather food for themselves for the coming time, or so that their cruelty might be strengthened through the practice of such works. Those who had even crawled through the camp of the enemies to secretly gather some herbs were met by these men, who—despite the victims rejoicing that they had escaped the hands of the enemy—took everything they had brought with them. Even when they begged and called upon the terrible name of God so that they might keep some portion of what they had obtained at the peril of their lives, they gave nothing back; rather, it was considered an act of mercy if, when they were caught alive, they were not also robbed of their lives.

**Of the Ancient Christian Churches. The Third Book.**

Josephus’s book on how the mind holds mastery.

¶ It is sufficiently clear how honorably we treat our own Scriptures. For although such a long time has passed, no one has been so bold as to take anything away from them, nor to add to or change them. Instead, such faith is deeply rooted and innate in all the people of our nation that we surely believe these Writings to be from God; we cling to them always and (if the time requires it) would gladly give our lives for them. It is perhaps not improper to include here another part of the work of these historical fathers. It is known that Josephus also composed another noble book: *That the Mind holds the Mastery within us.* <note>This refers to the work "On the Rule of Reason," also known as 4 Maccabees, which was historically attributed to Josephus.</note> Some have called this the book of the Maccabees because it contains the wars and struggles undertaken by the Maccabean brothers. Furthermore, at the end of the 20th book of his *Antiquities*, this same author writes that he intended to describe in four books the faith of the ancestral religion: concerning God and His substance, His laws, and why some things are permitted by Him and others are not.

<margin>
He promised 4 more books.
</margin>

He mentions that yet other books were made by him. Also, at the end of the aforementioned *Antiquities*, he rebukes a man named Justus of Tiberias <note>Justus of Tiberias was a rival Jewish historian whose account of the Jewish War often contradicted Josephus's own version.</note> for falsehood, because Justus had attacked the work Josephus had written. Josephus addressed him with these words: "I have not followed you in these things which I have written, for I presented my books to the Emperor, and the events were still almost before our eyes when it happened. For I am certain that I have maintained the truth in all things. Nor has this opinion been deceived according to the testimony of the gods. Rather, I have allowed many others to see it, many of whom were also present in the same war, such as King Agrippa and some of his closest kin."

<margin>
Unjustly following him.
</margin>

And the Emperor Titus so greatly approved of these writings that he deemed it proper that these books, and the knowledge of these histories, should come to all men; he even signed them with his own hand to signify that they ought to be read publicly before all people. King Agrippa also testified to the truth of our books with 62 letters, two of which I have included. Of these things, enough has now been said; let us now return to the order of our history.

It is said that he was a very near cousin of our Lord according to the flesh, for Clopas was the brother of Joseph, as Hegesippus <note>Hegesippus was an early Christian chronicler whose works are mostly lost but were extensively quoted by Eusebius.</note> testifies.

## ¶ Concerning Clement.

## ¶ Concerning the Epistle of Clement.

### The 16th Chapter.

<margin>The Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians.</margin>
This Clement wrote a letter to the Corinthians which is very singular and wonderful. He wrote it in the name of the Roman Church when discord had arisen in Corinth. This Letter was commonly and publicly read in many congregations in former times, and also in our own day. But regarding the riot that occurred there in Corinth and the discord among the people, <margin>Hegesippus</margin> Hegesippus <note>An early Christian chronicler (c. 110–180 AD) whose works are mostly lost except for fragments preserved by Eusebius.</note> is a very faithful witness, who proves it in this manner, saying:

## ¶ Concerning the discord that occurred under Domitian.

### The 17th Chapter.

<margin>Domitian, a persecutor of the Christians.</margin>
Now Emperor Domitian <note>Roman Emperor from 81 to 96 AD; Christian tradition views his reign as a period of significant persecution.</note> exercised and demonstrated great cruelty against many. In the city of Rome, he had many noble and illustrious men put to death without right or reason, and he also cast uncountably many into misery, and for such reasons appraised and seized their goods. He finally became a follower of Nero, in that he godlessly took up <margin>Theomachy. Fighting against God.</margin> <term>Theomachy</term> <note>From the Greek 'theos' (God) and 'mache' (battle), meaning a war against the divine.</note> against the Divine honor.

This Domitian was the second under whom persecution of our people occurred; nevertheless, his father Vespasian never did our people any wrong.

## ¶ Concerning the Apostle John and his Revelation.

### The 18th Chapter.

<margin>At what time John was sent to Patmos.</margin>
At which time the Apostle and Evangelist John, for the proclamation of the Divine Word and the testimony of the truth, was sent to the Island of Patmos. And Irenaeus, writing an account of the name of the Antichrist—which is contained in the revelation called the Revelation of John—writes thus of this John in the fifth book *Against Heresies*: "If one should (he says) more openly proclaim this name in this time, its power would be better revealed by the same man who saw this very Revelation. For it was not revealed long ago, but in our own time, and it was published toward the end of the reign of Emperor Domitian."

<column-break/>

In that same time, the institutions of our faith flourished so greatly that even some historians who had no knowledge of our Christianity left a memory of it to posterity, recording the persecution of that time and also the <term>martyrologies</term> <note>Original: "martelisarien"—records or accounts of the lives and deaths of martyrs.</note>. Those who diligently investigated the time prove that it happened in the 15th year of the reign of Domitian, because he <margin>Flavia Domitilla. The [relatives] of Flavius Clemens were taken away to the Island of Pontia.</margin> took Flavia Domitilla (the daughter of his sister and wife of Flavius Clemens) along with many others, and because of the testimony they gave of Jesus Christ, they were brought to an island called Pontia.

## ¶ Domitian commands David's descendants to be killed.

### The 19th Chapter.

<margin>The descendants of David were killed.</margin>
When Domitian had commanded that all those of the lineage of David and of the Royal tribe should be killed, we are taught from of old that some were brought there who had their descent from Jude, who were considered brothers of our Lord according to the flesh. These same were oppressed with a double hatred: as those who were of the lineage of David, and also because they were the closest kin of Christ. This, <margin>Hegesippus.</margin> Hegesippus relates orderly with these words.

## ¶ Concerning the lineage of our Savior.

### The 20th Chapter.

<margin>The grandsons of Jude were denounced by Revocatus as being of the lineage of David.</margin>
There yet lived (he says) some of the lineage of our Lord according to the flesh, the grandchildren of Jude, who was called a brother of the LORD according to the flesh. When these were accused by some as being those who had come from the lineage of David, they were brought before the EMPEROR Domitian.

# The Chronicle of Eusebius Pamphilus
### Folio 48.
<header>The Chronicle of Eusebius Pamphilus</header>

The same writer testifies concerning this as follows: the assembly (he says) which is at Ephesus was founded by Paul and built up by John <note>original: "Joanne"; referring to the Apostle John.</note>, who remained there until the time of Trajan <note>Roman Emperor from 98–117 AD.</note>. Here you have a faithful witness who testifies of the Apostle's times. Receive now also what Clement says (whose testimony we also promised); he describes a necessary history, which we shall set down here, and we believe it will be beneficial to those who read it.

<margin>A fable and yet not a fable.</margin>
He describes it thus: Hear (he says) a fable, and yet it is no fable, but a thing that actually happened concerning John the Apostle, and it is known to all men. When he had returned to Ephesus from Patmos after the death of the tyrant <note>Referring to Emperor Domitian, who had exiled John to the island of Patmos.</note>, he was asked to visit the surrounding provinces to found assemblies in places where there were none, and to provide for and instruct the places where they already were with Priests and Ministers, just as the Holy Spirit directed him.

<margin>History of a youth brought to a better life by John.</margin>
When he had come to a city not far from there, and had fully performed all the services of the assemblies, he saw a youth, strong of body, fair of face, and very courageous of spirit. Looking upon the Bishop whom he had recently ordained, he said: “I entrust this youth to you with all diligence, under the witness of Christ and the whole assembly.” The Bishop received the youth and promised to do all he could with diligence, as he was commanded. And John, repeating the same command many times, very earnestly entrusted the youth to him, and then traveled back to Ephesus. Thus, the Bishop took the youth who was entrusted to him into his house, and raised and cared for him with all diligence; and finally, he also gave him the grace of baptism <note>original: "doopsels".</note>.

<margin>What it means: he baptized him.</margin>
After this, now trusting in the grace with which he was admonished, the youth began to be a little more gentle.

But when the youth in his unripe age began to use his freedom, he was soon taught by his companions—who were idle and unchaste—to love sin and the way of a shameful life. First, he was deceived by improper banqueting, and later they took him along as a companion to thieves and made him a partner

<column-break/>

in stealing by night. Thereafter they also drew him into greater crimes; for the youth was daily taught and instructed in more evil. Because he was sharp of understanding and like a strong, unbridled horse that bites cruelly, he left the line of the right path and despised his Master. Thus, with a hasty pace, following one crime after another, he finally became desperate and hopeless of obtaining salvation from God.

Now, he thought little of committing small crimes, and worked ever harder to perform greater and more evil deeds. He gave himself over entirely as a lost child, and could not bear to be lesser than any other in crime.

And above all this, those who were previously his masters in crime, he made into his disciples. From these, he formed and established a band of robbers and murderers, over which he became a powerful leader and Prince, and with them, he committed every cruelty.

When some time had passed (and necessity required it), John was invited to come again to that same city. When he had ordered all the things for which he had come, he said: “O Bishop, produce that which was entrusted to you, which I and also Christ so notably commanded you, as the assembly you govern testifies.” The Bishop was astonished, thinking at first that some money was being demanded from him which he had not received. But he realized that John could not be deceived, nor would he demand what he had not given. So, in doubt, he stood amazed.

<margin>John’s address to the elder.</margin>
Then John, seeing him hesitate, said: “I demand the youth back from you, and the soul of your brother.”

Then the Elder sighed very heavily and was moved to tears, saying: “He is dead.” Then John said: “In what manner, or by what death?” The Elder answered: “He is dead to God, and has become the most wicked and criminal of all, and has finally given himself over to murder; he has now taken over a mountain with the help of many robbers.”

When the Apostle heard this, he immediately tore the garment he was wearing and, beating his head with great sighs, said: “I left you as a good guardian of your brother’s soul! But get me a horse now, and a guide for the way.”

<margin>The Gospel of John.</margin>
Well then, we shall now also declare the writings of this Apostle, which are those held in authority and value. <margin>I</margin>
The venerable and truly God-worthy Apostles of Christ, being pure of life and having all the strength of their minds, did not hold the decoration of words in great esteem; but trusting in such Divine powers as the soul is adorned with, and also in the grace of the drawing

<margin>The Apostles' rich speaking.</margin>
which was granted to them by our Lord Jesus Christ, they did not set the words of their supreme and glorious proclamations in the clever words of worldly wisdom. <margin>The Apostles have written little.</margin>
many books. Thus, this assurance of the proclamation is not in human words or instruction but requires more the promise of Divine powers. Therefore, they ought not to be placed among the books about which there is doubt, but should be entirely rejected as foreign and contrary to the rule of Christianity. ### Concerning Menander the Sorcerer.

### The XXVI Chapter.

<margin>Menander.</margin>
After Simon Magus followed Menander, a pupil of the devil <note>original: "eẽ schult des duyvels"</note>, who

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin>
was no less [wicked] than the first, and he was also a Samaritan by birth. In the devil's arts, his equal was not found; he was not merely the same as his master, but surpassed him in malice. He exalted himself even more, calling himself a Savior <note>original: "Salichmaker"</note> and claiming he was sent from the invisible and heavenly world for the salvation of mankind. He said that no one could overcome the Angels of the world unless they first received from him the orderly teaching of his devilish art, and that through the baptism given by him, one became immortal and eternal, even in this life. Anyone who desires to know this will easily understand it from the books of Irenaeus and also Justin <note>Justin Martyr</note>; where he writes of Simon Magus, he also describes certain things about this man: how this Menander, a Samaritan from the village of Capparattbea and a disciple of Simon, came to Antioch through the prompting of the Devil. We know that through his arts he deceived many people, also teaching his followers that they would not die. Even today, there are some who believe such things, which is a thought of the Devil—that men who defile themselves with devilish arts boast of a Christian name, so that through such means they might defile the holy and worthy mysteries of our Religion. Yet they mock and despise Christian teaching, such as the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of the dead. Those who follow such teachers have fallen away from the hope of salvation and life.

### Concerning the Sect of the Ebionites.

# The Chronicles of Eusebius Pamphilus

<margin>Paul.</margin>
There are some among them, however, who flee from this wickedness—namely, the idea that he [Christ] was born of a man and a woman. These maintain that he was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary; nonetheless, they do not believe or confess that he was always God, or the Word and Wisdom of God. They observe the physical requirements of the Law. At the same time, they despise all the Epistles of the Apostle [Paul] and call him an apostate and a destroyer of the Law. They use a single Gospel, which is called the Hebrew Gospel <note>The Gospel of the Hebrews, a text used by Jewish-Christian groups, now lost to history</note>, and they regard all other writings as nothing. They observe the Sabbath with the Jews according to the Law, and with us, they observe Sunday in honor of the Lord’s resurrection. For this reason, they are called by their rightful name, Ebionites, because of the poverty <note>The name Ebionite is derived from the Hebrew word *ebyon*, meaning 'poor,' which Eusebius interprets as a "poverty of understanding."</note> of their understanding.
<margin>Poor in understanding.</margin>

->¶ Concerning Cerinthus, a Bishop of false teaching.<-

### Chapter XXVIII.

<margin>Cerinthus. Gaius, a church writer.</margin>
In these same times, there also arose a prince of heretics named Cerinthus. Regarding him, Gaius (whom we mentioned previously) wrote the following in his *Dialogue*. "And Cerinthus also," he says, "through certain revelations which he presumed were written by a great Apostle—revelations supposedly shown to him by Angels—has told us of some such abominable things, saying: That after the resurrection, a worldly Kingdom of Christ is coming to Jerusalem, and that men will again be bound in the flesh to serve lusts and sins, and will conduct their lives in that manner. And contrary to the faith of the Scriptures, he mentions a period of a thousand years, in which he says there will be many perishable works and wedding feasts, in order to deceive those who are inclined toward unchastity."
<margin>Dionysius, Bishop of Corinth.</margin>
And also Dionysius, when he was speaking of the Revelation of John and of certain things handed down from of old by the Assembly <note>The early church community</note>, makes mention of this man with these words: The Cerinthian heresy had its origin in one who was diligent, through his fabrications, to seek the authority of a great name; he was driven by a base understanding of these Scriptures, which contained this heresy: that Christ's Kingdom would be an earthly Kingdom coming into this world.
<margin>Cerinthus's wicked understanding of Christ's Kingdom.</margin>
And

<column-break/>

since he was inclined toward the pleasure and gluttony of his belly, he taught that the future would be exactly as his own desires demanded. He taught that one should fulfill all the cravings of the belly—everything the belly desires in eating, drinking, and marriage feasts. And so that he might seem to say something good or holy, he taught that the legal festivals should be observed again, and that fleshly sacrifices should be performed once more.

<margin>Irenaeus.</margin>
Irenaeus has also revealed the secrets of this heretic in the first book of his work. If anyone desires to know this more fully, they may learn to understand it in that same book.

->¶ Concerning Nicolaus and his followers.<-

### Chapter XXIX.

<margin>The Nicolaitan heresy.</margin>
But there was yet another heresy, called the Nicolaitans, which grew for a short time, and which is mentioned in the Revelation of John.
<margin>Their origin.</margin>
These heretics boasted that they had a Teacher and founder of their sect, Nicolaus, who was one of the seven Deacons chosen by the Apostles along with Stephen. But Clement of Alexandria, in his third book called *Stromata* <note>original: "Stromaton." This refers to Clement's work 'Miscellanies,' a foundational text of early Christian philosophy.</note>, writes thus of him: Nicolaus (he says) had a very beautiful wife, and when, after the ascension of our Lord and Savior, he was rebuked by the Apostles for being jealous, he wished to clear himself. He brought his wife forward and gave his consent if anyone wished to have relations with her.
<margin>Their shameful life.</margin>
From this cause, these heretics think to follow his example, believing that because of this word and deed of Nicolaus, anyone may abuse the flesh according to their own lusts. And though this deed or word was intended simply and innocently <note>Clement argues Nicolaus was trying to prove his lack of worldly attachment, not encourage immorality.</note>, they have now adopted his name to excuse their own pleasure, mingling with one another without any reverence. It is known to me that this Nicolaus knew no other woman than his own wife, whom he had taken in marriage; his children, who were daughters, remained in their virginal purity until extreme old age, and his son also preserved the holiness of his undefiled body.

### How Symeon, the Bishop of Jerusalem, was martyred.

### The XXXII. Chapter.

<margin>Symeon, son of Cleophas, Bishop of Jerusalem.</margin>
After Nero and Domitian, under whom (in the time of which we have spoken) through the unrest of the people, a persecution of our people occurred in all cities. In this time also Symeon, the son of Cleophas—who was ordained, as we have previously shown, as the second Bishop of Jerusalem—was released from the bonds of the flesh through martyrdom.

<margin>The words of Hegesippus.</margin>
Hegesippus <note>Hegesippus (c. 110–180 AD) was a Christian chronicler whose works are now mostly lost, surviving primarily through these quotes in Eusebius.</note> testifies to this, whom we have brought forward as a witness in many matters. He relates that this aforementioned Symeon was accused by certain heretics of also being a Christian; and when he was frequently tortured with many kinds of pain, so that even the Judge himself and his friends were amazed at his endurance, the Judge finally commanded that he should be killed by the same passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the method of suffering and death, specifically crucifixion.</note> that the Lord had suffered.

It is also pleasant to hear the very words that Hegesippus uses in his testimony. He says thus, where he is writing about the heretics: "From these same people there were also some who accused Symeon, the son of Cleophas, as one who was of David’s lineage <note>The Roman authorities were often suspicious of those claiming descent from the royal house of King David, fearing they might lead a Jewish revolt.</note> and also a Christian."

<margin>His death.</margin>
And so he became a martyr when he was 120 years old, under Emperor Trajan and Atticus the Governor.

The same writer also describes how his accusers—since in those times a search was being conducted for those who were of David’s lineage and royal descent—were also captured among their people. That this Symeon was also one who had heard our Lord may be proven by his great age, or by the faith of the Gospels, where it is also told that his mother Maria was the wife of Cleophas.

<margin>John 19:25. The grandchildren of Jude, the brother of the Lord.</margin>
And Hegesippus tells of yet some others, besides those we have spoken of before, who were the grandchildren of Jude, who was one of the brothers of our Lord; they were found in that time to be of Christ's lineage, and they became martyrs in the times of Domitian, writing in this manner:

<column-break/>

<margin>¶</margin>
There also came some who were leaders of the Assembly <note>The "Assembly" refers to the early Christian Church (Greek: *Ekklesia*).</note>, as witnesses and close friends of our Lord. And while the Lord's Assembly was in peace, they remained until the time of Emperor Trajan, until the time that the cousin of our Lord, Symeon—of whom we have spoken before, the son of Cleophas—was accused by heretics of being a Christian and was thus handed over to the Governor. And after he was tortured for a long time with many kinds of pain, he fulfilled his martyrdom, so that all who were present, and even the Judge, wondered how an old man of 120 years could endure the pain of the cross.

<margin>Symeon, 120 years old, is killed.</margin>
Thereafter, the same Hegesippus describes that in those times, the Christian Church still remained as a pure and undefiled virgin, and that there were no corrupters of the truth, nor any arrogant men who defiled the Divine Word; and even if there were any such by chance, they were hidden in secret in certain places.

<margin>*</margin>
<margin>While the Apostles and disciples of the Lord lived, the heretics dared not act.</margin>
But when that company of the Apostles, and all those who had heard His living voice from the Lord, had passed from this life, then the evil error of false teaching raised itself up as if in an empty house where there was now no protector nor guardian of the Divine treasure; and as the common saying goes, with "bare heads" <note>The margin explains this as a "proverb meaning without shame and openly." The original Latin phrase *nudo capite* implies acting with bold audacity.</margin> they took up the weapons of falsehood and positioned themselves to fight against the Apostolic truth. And this was the internal struggle with which the assembly was burdened.

<margin>A proverb: that is, without shame and openly.</margin>
But the Church was also oppressed externally with the weight of persecution, and such a great, unspeakable multitude of martyrs were killed daily that the other official, Pliny <note>Pliny the Younger, a Roman governor whose famous letter to Trajan provides early non-Christian evidence of Christian practices.</note>, who governed a province at that time, being moved by the great multitude being put to death, wrote to Emperor Trajan that many thousands of people were being beheaded daily. In these people, it was not found that they had committed any crime or anything contrary to the Roman mandates, except that they sang songs of praise early in the morning to Christ their Lord, who is called God.

<margin>Pliny II. Trajan.</margin>
And he reported that they forbade adultery and all such crimes, from which they turned themselves entirely away, and that in all other things they did nothing else but what the common institutions and laws command.

<margin>Z</margin> And while it is impossible for us to recount each one individually—who they were that, after the times of the Apostles, were successors among the Congregations in all the world, whether they were Leaders, or Evangelists, or Shepherds—it shall be enough for us alone to mention those whose memory has come to our knowledge from the books of faith and of preaching, just as Clement and Ignatius, and the others of whom we have made mention before.

### ¶ Of Clement's Epistle, and of his other writings.

### Chapter 38.

Clement, in his Letter which he writes to the Corinthians, cites Paul’s Letter to the Hebrews and makes use of its testimonies. From this it appears that the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> must have sent it to the Hebrews, and that he wrote it in his native tongue <note>original: "vaderlijcke sprake" - referring to Hebrew or Aramaic.</note>. And as some say, Luke translated it, and some others say it was this Clement, which is more likely to be true; for the style of Clement's Epistle is like this one, and the sense of both these writings is entirely and wholly identical. There is also mention of another Letter that Clement is said to have written, of which we have no knowledge, and many other of his books, which some say they still possess, such as the Dispute of Peter and Appion, which was not in use among the Ancients. The reason for this is that it is found that the rule of the Apostolic faith did not remain pure and uncorrupted therein.

# ¶ Of the Evangelists who were in the Same time.

## The 37th Chapter.

<margin>Heros succeeded Ignatius at Antioch.</margin>
<margin>N</margin> After this Ignatius, Heros ruled the assembly of the city of Antioch. And while it is impossible for us to tell of each one individually, who <margin>Z</margin> they were that were the successors of the Apostles' times among the Assemblies in all the world—whether they were Overseers <note>original: "Oversten"; often referring to Bishops or Elders.</note>, or Evangelists, or Shepherds—it shall be enough for us only to mention those whose memory has come to our knowledge from the Books of the faith and of the proclamation, such as Clement and Ignatius, and the others of whom we have made mention before.

### ¶ Who were the Bishops of Rome and Alexandria under Trajan.

#### The first Chapter.

<margin>Cerdon, Bishop at Alexandria, dies.</margin>
<margin>Primus succeeds him at Alexandria; Alexander follows Evaristus.</margin>
<margin>The Jews are rebellious.</margin>
<margin>Lupus, a commander of the Roman Army.</margin>
In the twelfth year of the reign of Emperor Trajan, Cerdon (whom we have said before governed the Church in Alexandria) died; after whom the priesthood <note>original: "Priesterdom" — here referring to the episcopal office or bishopric.</note> was received by the fourth after the Apostles, named Primus. At the same time, when Evaristus had served the priesthood in Rome for eight years, Alexander received it, the fifth successor after Peter and Paul. And at that time, the institution of our Savior and the progress of the Christian Church was growing daily: But the Jews were tormented with heavy plagues.

For they were ignited in Alexandria, and in Egypt, and in Cyrene with such a cruel, rebellious spirit, that they first began to fight with their neighbors, and the people who were located nearest to them. And thereafter, as the rebellion was gradually growing, in the following year they waged open war—which was not small—against the Roman Governor in the lands of Egypt, named Lupus. In the first battle, victory followed the Jews. And the Heathens <note>original: "Heydenen" — meaning the non-Jewish Roman or local population, often referred to as gentiles.</note> who had fled from the battle, coming to Alexandria, captured and killed all the Jews they still found within the city. And the other Jews who were in Cyrene

<margin>B</margin>

As the fuel for this war grew excessively, in the 18th year of the same Emperor’s reign <note>roughly 134-135 AD</note>, Bethera <note>modern Bittir, near Jerusalem</note>, a very strong city located near Jerusalem, was besieged by the Romans. ### A Letter from the Emperor Antoninus to those of Asia, concerning our profession.

### The 13th Chapter.

->The Emperor Marcus Aurelius, Antoninus Augustus, Armanicus the High Priest <note>original: "overste Bisschop," translating the Latin title *Pontifex Maximus*.</note>, Tribune for the fifteenth time, and Consul for the third time, to all the people of Asia, Greetings.<-

<margin>Letter of the Emperor Antoninus for the Christians in Asia.</margin>
I do not doubt that the Gods desire and wish that evildoers and criminals do not remain hidden. And it belongs even more to them to punish those who do not wish to offer sacrifices to them, than it befits you. But you confirm the sentence and the opinion of those whom you are persecuting, by saying that they are criminals and godless. From this it follows that they would rather offer up their souls for their God, and lovely and willingly receive death, than to be such as you are and be subject to your Religion. Regarding the earthquake that has happened there, or may yet happen, it is not improper to comfort your sorrow with an honest warning; for I understand that out of hatred and envy, you blame them for such things and common occurrences. By these things, they gain more trust from their God. And you, at all times when such things are unknown <margin>The Heathens blame the Christians in order to make them hated.</margin> to you, you neglect the other gods and the entire service of the immortal God whom the Christians honor; you drive them away, cast them out, and persecute the servants of Religion unto death. Regarding these things, many Governors of the Provinces have also written to our worthy Father, and he answered them that they should do no burden or trouble to such a manner of people, unless it were evident that they had been convicted of doing something against the State of the Roman Emperor. And many Governors have also written to me concerning this, to whom I—following the opinion and sentence of my father—have also answered in such a manner. And if it happens that there is still someone who begins any stir against such people under the guise of some other crime, then the one who is accused for the sake of that name shall be set free, even if it were found that he is such as they have charged...

¶ Even those who had come to capture him felt regret that they had been ordered to lead such an honorable and God-fearing man, in such advanced old age, to his death. And afterwards, in the same Epistle, it is written as follows.

¶ After he had finished his prayer, having remembered all those known to him, from the greatest to the least, from the noble to the common, and all the Christian assembly spread throughout the world. And as the hour approached, he went out, and sitting upon a donkey, he was led into the city <margin>The Great Day of the Sabbath</margin> on a day of a great festival. <note>The "Great Sabbath" usually refers to the Saturday before Easter, or a Sabbath that coincides with a feast day.</note>

¶ And before he arrived there, he was met by the official, or Prefect of the Peace <note>original: "Prefect vanden Payse", referring to the Irenarch, a police official responsible for maintaining order.</note>, named Herod <margin>Herod the peacemaker. Nicetas.</margin> the Tetrarch, and his father Nicetas, who made him sit in their carriage and spoke to him harmfully by every means, saying: "What harm is there in saying that the Emperor is God, and to offer sacrifice to him, and thereby live in peace and safety?" At first, he heard these things and remained silent <margin>Silent.</margin>. But as they persisted, he said to them: "What need is there to say much? For I shall not do what you tell me." And when they perceived that they could achieve nothing with their counsel, they were incensed with wrath and thrust him out of the carriage with such indignity and haste that he injured one of his feet as he fell to the ground. But he disregarded this as nothing and was well content, and with all cheerfulness hastened to the place where he was ordered to be brought. And when he came to that place, a very great uproar arose among the people at his arrival, and <margin>A voice from heaven.</margin> a voice descended from Heaven, saying: "O Polycarp, be strong, and act manfully." And there were many who heard the voice, but no one saw who spoke. Meanwhile, there was a riot among the people when they saw Polycarp brought in, and he was asked from afar by the Judge if he were Polycarp; and he confessed it. Thereupon the Judge spoke to him: "Have reverence; have mercy on your old age and spare your elder days, and <margin>Swearing by the fortune of the Emperor.</margin> swear by the Fortune of the Emperor; repent of your past errors and cry out as the others do: 'Away with the godless thieves!'" <note>original: "geestelicke dieven" (spiritual thieves); this refers to the common Roman accusation that Christians were "atheists" because they denied the traditional gods.</note> Then Polycarp, looking upon the crowd with a grave countenance who were in that place to watch, and lifting his right hand toward Heaven, cried out with a loud voice as he sighed: "Away with the godless thieves!" But as the magistrate

<column-break/>

wanted more and said: <margin>Swear by the Fortune of the Emperor.</margin> "Swear by the Fortune of the Emperor, and speak blasphemy against Christ, and I will set you free." <margin>It has been 86 years.</margin> Polycarp answered: "Eighty-six years have I served Him, and He has never done me any wrong; how then could I curse and blaspheme my King who has given me salvation?" And when he was forced again to swear by the Fortune of the Emperor, <margin>P</margin> <note>The letter P in the margin likely stands for Polycarp, marking his speech.</note> he spoke: "If you seek this glory, that I should swear by the Fortune of the Emperor, and you pretend not to know who I am, I speak freely and confess that I am a Christian. And if you wish me to give an account of my Christian religion, appoint a day and I will answer." Then the magistrate spoke: "Persuade the people." Polycarp answered: "I have answered you, <margin>Instruction; how far one should listen and be subject.</margin> for we are taught that we should honor the Princes and Officials who are from God, in such things that are not contrary to our religion; but to satisfy that raging crowd is not my duty." The magistrate said: <margin>X</margin> "I have the beasts ready to devour you, unless you quickly repent." And Polycarp answered: "Let them come, for I am steadfast in my conviction, nor may we be sorrowful to change from good to evil; it would be better for those to be changed to good who remain steadfast in evil." Then the magistrate said: "I will have you consumed by fire, since you do not despise the beasts nor repent of your purpose." <margin>P</margin> Then Polycarp answered: "Do you threaten me with the fire that is quickly kindled and shortly thereafter extinguished? But you are ignorant of the eternal fire of the coming Judgment, which is prepared to punish the evildoers forever. But for what do you wait? Do to me what you will."

¶ Saying these and many similar words, Polycarp was filled with confidence and joy, so that the cheerfulness of his countenance and the steadfastness of his answers amazed the magistrate with great wonder. <margin>Z</margin> So he sent one of the officers to the people and commanded that he should protest with a loud voice that Polycarp had several times confessed that he was a Christian. When the people heard this, the whole multitude of the Heathens and the Jews of the city of Smyrna cried out with unspeakable madness: "This is the Teacher of all Asia..."

Even if he reads our scriptures / and does not understand the power <note>original: "brachte"; referring to the inner meaning or fruit of the text</note> thereof / or if he does understand / so he proves himself / so that he is not held suspect in such / he is still much more wicked and base to judge / who to obtain the favor of the unlearned common people / becomes an enemy and a traitor of the truth and of religion / which he himself well knows to be good. What I say / is true / and I also suspect that the disputations of our question / which we have had among one another / have come into your hands and to your knowledge. These are the words of the blessed Justin / by which it is noted / as he had said before / that his martyrdom was accomplished / through the snare-laying of Crescens. And Tatian, a very learned man / who in his youth learned most wonderfully the art of eloquence / through which he came to great honor / who afterwards converted to our Scripture / and also left behind costly books against the Heathens / in which he mentions Justin with these words: And also (he says) the wonderful man Justin / has also rightly pursued men like these / saying / that they are thieves. And a little thereafter, when he said some things about the Philosophers / he also said this: Crescens, who had his dwelling in the great city <note>Rome</note> surpassed all others in sins against nature / and was no less greedy in the desire for money. And he did not agree with others that one should despise death / and he himself had an evil opinion of death / so that he brought Justin to death / just as to that last evil because he proclaimed the truth / and punished the deceptive Philosophers.

Fol. 72.
# Eusebius Pamphilus’s Chronicle

<margin>Urbicius the Judge</margin>
Since Ptolemy was a lover of the truth, as is testified, he did not hide the honor and glory of his confession and confessed that he was a Christian. This man the Centurion then captured and threw into prison, and held him there for a long time, where he became emaciated due to the great misery and wretchedness of the Church, and finally presented him to the Judge Urbicius. From whom likewise only this was asked of Ptolemy: whether he was a Christian? And he publicly confessed a second time that he was a Christian, and that he had also learned the Christian life. For whoever forsakes that which is so [true], undoubtedly judges that which he forsakes to be evil. And as soon as he had confessed that, Urbicius the Judge commanded that he should be led to his death.

<margin>Lucius, a Christian</margin>
When Lucius, also a Christian, saw this—that the sentence was given so recklessly—he spoke to Urbicius: "I pray you, tell me, for what reason do you judge this man so hastily, and let him be led to death, only for the sake of a single word he says, confessing himself to be a Christian? While if there is another who is confessing all sorts of other sins—of homicide, of adultery, of murder and robbery, or of any other crimes—would you do it so hastily? This is unseemly. O Urbicius, a good Emperor, and a wise young man, the Emperor's son, nor also the Senators ought to act thus." <note>Lucius is addressing the judge but appealing to the virtues expected of the Roman leadership, including Marcus Aurelius and his son.</note> Then Urbicius said to Lucius: "It seems to me that you are also a Christian," and when Lucius answered, "It is true, I am," Urbicius commanded that he should also be led to death. Then Lucius said: "I thank you that you deliver me from these evil masters, and send me back to the good and best Father: the King of all things, our God." And yet another who likewise freely confessed to being a Christian was also killed by the same sentence.

What follows further in Justin <note>original: "Justino"</note> is that which I have said before. "I am a hope," says he, "of those who have stood for the truth, and I lie waiting to endure their persecution."

### ¶ What writings of Justin have come down to us.

### The XVIII. Chapter.

<margin>The books of Justin</margin>
This same Justin has left us many memorials of his noble, good books, through which one may 

<column-break/>

recognize his learning, and how skilled he was in divine teaching, from which those may gain much profit who have love and desire for the teaching of wisdom. 

<margin>Justin’s Apology for the Christians, to Emperor Antoninus Pius</margin>
And first of all, his book is still with us, of which we have spoken before, which is written for our religion, to the Emperor Antoninus, and to his son and his council. 

<margin>The second book of the Apology, to Emperor Antoninus Verus</margin>
He also wrote that other book likewise, in defense of our faith, to the successor of the aforementioned Emperor, named Antoninus Verus, from whose times we have now begun to describe. 

<margin>A book against the Heathens</margin>
And he also wrote another book against the Heathens, in which he writes very abundantly of our [philosophers] and of the Greek philosophers. There he also writes of the nature of demons, which is too long to include here. 

<margin>On the Monarchy</margin>
And he wrote yet another book against the Heathens, which is named *Rebuking* <note>original: "Beschaminge"; likely referring to the *Cohortatio ad Graecos* or "Exhortation to the Greeks"</note>. And another book, named *Monarchia* <note>original: "Monarchia"; referring to Justin's work on the sole government of God</note>, which he compiled not only from our books, but also from the books of the Greeks. 

<margin>Psaltes. On the Soul.</margin>
And another that is named *Psaltes* <note>original: "Psaltes"; the Harper</note>. Yet another *On the Soul*, written in a manner as if it were signed by him, in which he lays down many opinions of the philosophers, against whom he promises to write, and in that same book will bring forth his feeling and judgment of the philosophers. 

<margin>Dialogue held with Trypho</margin>
He also describes a dialogue <note>original: "tweesprake"</note>, as with the Jews, which he himself had at Ephesus with a Jew named Trypho <note>original: "Triphon"</note>, who was very learned among the Hebrews. In which book he proves by what manner he was brought to divine grace, to the knowledge of the true faith, and how he first did all his diligence to know the teaching of the philosophers, in order to investigate the truth. 

<margin>The hatred of the Jews against the Christians</margin>
He also writes of the Jews, that they are very cruel persecutors of the Christians, and he rebukes this Trypho with it, saying: "For you alone have no repentance for those things which have been evilly done by you; but you have also chosen men from Jerusalem, being fit for such a task, and have sent them into all lands to publish and to say that a wicked sect of Christians had arisen, and have thus defamed us with false lies of crimes, so that those who knew nothing of Christianity would be terrified, and thus avoid our company; in which you have not only brought shame upon us, but upon others, to whom you are a cause of death..."

Fol. 73b
The Fourth Book

->...of the ancient Christian church.<-

<margin>The gift of prophecy in the Church until Justin’s time.</margin>
...you have been dead, because of your lying speech. He also writes that the grace of prophecy was present in the gathering [of the church] until his own time, and also that the *Revelation* <note>Original: "Apocalypsis"</note> was written by John the Apostle. He uses many prophetic writings against Trypho <note>Trypho was a Jewish philosopher with whom Justin Martyr held a famous recorded dialogue regarding the fulfillment of the Law in Christ.</note> and overcomes him therein, noting that the Jews had removed and cut out many such passages <note>Original: "allegatie"</note> from the Scriptures. There are still many more other books which may be found by many of our brothers, which were judged worthy by the ancients and approved. <margin>Irenaeus uses Justin’s testimony.</margin> Thus, Irenaeus also cites from his writings, and in the fourth book *Against Heresies* he writes as follows: "Well has Justin expressed it in the same book that he wrote against Marcion, saying: 'I would not believe our Lord if he said that there were another God than the creator of all creatures.'" And also in the fifth book of his works, he says: "Justin also affirms that before the coming of our Lord, the devil never dared to be so bold as to blaspheme God, because he did not yet fully know his own condemnation at that time."

We have wished to declare these things regarding Justin’s books, in order to encourage all good Christians to examine them.

### ¶ Which Bishops were in Rome and Alexandria during the same time.

### Chapter 19.

<margin>Soter, bishop at Rome; Agrippinus at Alexandria.</margin>
In the eighth year of the aforementioned Emperor Verus <note>Lucius Verus, who co-ruled with Marcus Aurelius.</note>, when Anicetus had held the Bishopric at Rome for eleven years, he died, and Soter succeeded him. And when Celadion had served the priesthood at Alexandria for fourteen years, Agrippinus became his successor.

### ¶ Which Bishops were at Antioch.

### Chapter 20.

<margin>Theophilus at Antioch. Cornelius. Heros.</margin>
At the same time, Theophilus was the sixth from the Apostles who served the Bishopric at Antioch; the fourth was Cornelius. After whom, in the fifth position, Heros followed.

<column-break/>

### ¶ Of those who were Historians of the Church in those times.

### Chapter 21.

<margin>Hegesippus</margin>
There was Hegesippus, of whom we have spoken before, held in great esteem; and Dionysius, the Bishop of Corinth; and also Pinytus, very excellent among the Bishops. Likewise Philip and Apollinaris, and Melito, and Musanus, and Modestus, and especially Irenaeus; the writings of all these contain upright and Apostolic teaching, and they still exist in our times.

### ¶ Of Hegesippus, and what he describes.

### Chapter 22.

<margin>Uniformity in doctrine.</margin>
Among these, Hegesippus, in the fifth book of his *Commentaries*—wherein he very richly proves the sentiment and conviction of his faith with many instructions—says that when he was traveling to the city of Rome, he visited many places and many Bishops with whom he spoke amiably. He found them all to be teachers and preachers of one and the same faith. Likewise, he mentions the Epistle of Clement which he wrote to the Corinthians, so that it seems necessary to me to place the same admonition in this work. "And the gathering of the Corinthians," he says, "remained righteous in their proclamation until the time of <margin>Primus, Bishop at Corinth.</margin> Primus the Bishop, whom I saw when he traveled over the sea to Rome; and I stayed a long time with him in Corinth, because of the delight I had in the purity of his faith. And when I arrived in Rome, I stayed there so long that Soter followed after Anicetus, and Soter’s successor was <margin>The first heretic.</margin> Eleutherus. And in all these successions <note>Original: "ordinancien"</note> and in all other things that I saw in various cities, all things were maintained just as the Law had taught of old, and as the Prophets had instructed, and as the LORD has ordained."

He also writes of the heretics who had their origin in his time, and says thus: "After James, who was named 'the Just,' was martyred for the testimony of the truth, just as our <margin>Election.</margin> Savior had been, then by Divine election, Simeon, a son of Cleophas..."

# Chronicles of Eusebius Pamphilus / of the

<margin>¶ Cleophas</margin> Cleophas was ordained Bishop and chosen by all because he was the Lord’s cousin <note>Original: "Susterling," literally a sister's child or nephew; Hegesippus records that Symeon, son of Clopas, was a cousin of Jesus.</note>. And in those times
<margin>The Church a virgin.</margin> the Holy Church was still called a Virgin, for she was not yet defiled by the adulterous teachings of heretics. For
<margin>Theobutes, a heretic out of ambition.</margin> Theobutes, because he was considered unworthy to be a Bishop, first began to disturb and corrupt all things. He was one of the seven heresies sown among the people, among whom was also Simon, from whom came
<margin>Simon. Cleobius. Dositheus. Gortheus. Masbutheus. Menand.</margin> the Simonians; and from Cleobius, the Cleobians; and from Dositheus, the Dositheans; and from Gortheus, the Gorthenians; and from Masbutheus, the Masbuthenians; and from Menander, the Menandrians; from whom also sprang the Marcionites, and Carpocratians, and Valentinians, and Basilidians, and Saturnians. Each of these was distinct, corrupting and fighting against the true teaching of the Gospel, and each had his own sect and his own followers. From these have further sprouted the false Christians, and the false prophets, and the false apostles, who have wandered through many different lands, destroying the unity of the brothers, and have thus, through false teaching, defiled the most pure bridal chamber of the Holy Assembly, and have spoken abominable things against God and against the Lord Jesus Christ His Son.

<margin>Essenes, Galileans, Hemerobaptists, Samaritans, Sadducees, Pharisees.</margin> This same author also tells of many heresies that were among the Jews, which and what kind they were, and says thus: There were various opinions among the children of Israel that were very contrary to the tribe of Judah, from which Jesus Christ was born: For there were Essenes <note>Original: "Iessei"</note>, Galileans, Hemerobaptists <note>A sect that practiced daily ritual washing for purification.</note>, Masbutheans, Samaritans, Sadducees, and Pharisees. He writes many other things, of which we have already made mention in part due to the suitability of the context. He also speaks of that Hebrew and Syriac Gospel, and he disputes much regarding the Hebrew language and Jewish teachings, through all of which he demonstrates that he came from the Hebrews to the Christian faith.

This same man, along with Irenaeus and all the Ancients, says that the book called
<margin>The ancients' judgment on the Proverbs of Solomon.</margin> Wisdom is Solomon’s book, as is also the book of Proverbs, and several others.

When he was speaking against certain heretics, he proved that many writings had also been falsified and corrupted in the books of the Apocrypha.

Fol. 71.
# of the ancient Christian churches. The IV. Book.

<margin>A</margin> concerning marriage, and concerning purity <note>Original: "reynich-heydt," referring to chastity or celibacy.</note>, and also that a person who has fallen into any sin whatsoever, even if it were heresy, should be received back again if they repent of that sin.

<margin>Epistle to the Knossians. Note this, you Bishops.</margin>
<margin>B</margin> And there is yet another Epistle of the same teacher to the Knossians <note>The Dutch text says "Gnosten/Gnostos," but historical records of Dionysius indicate this was addressed to the church at Knossos.</note>, in which he exhorts and prays their Bishop, Pinytus, that he should not weigh down his subjects with any heavy burdens, and that he should not teach that forced purity is necessary, in which the weakness of some might be in danger. To which letter Pinytus answered the same Dionysius, that his opinion is the very best counsel, and prays him earnestly that since he had written before, he would henceforth send somewhat stronger and more powerful food <note>A reference to Hebrews 5:12-14, where "milk" is basic teaching and "solid food" is advanced doctrine.</note>, by which his people of the Assembly might always be nourished toward better progress, so that they <margin>C</margin> would not always be fed like young children with milk when they were older in the faith. In this same letter, this Pinytus clearly demonstrates the signs of his true faith, and the diligence he had for his people, and the power that was in him for teaching and wisdom, so that he has left that to us as a living image in a mirror.

<margin>The letter of Dionysius to the Romans.</margin>
<margin>D</margin> Dionysius wrote yet another letter to the Romans, which was given to Bishop Soter, in which he proves that he gladly receives the teachings that have been taught of old in the Roman Assembly, with words such as these. In the beginning (says he) it has been a <margin>An old custom of the Roman churches.</margin> custom to be helpful to all the brothers with good deeds, and to provide in various lands and many assemblies all that was needed there, and to comfort everyone in their need, and that one should also send what was required for the necessity of the brothers who were condemned to the mines to work in the metals <note>Original: "berchwerck," referring to the Roman punishment 'ad metalla' (condemnation to the mines) often given to Christians.</note>. <margin>E</margin> To do such things was from the first a manner among the Romans, which teaching was left to them by their fathers, and has always been fully maintained. <margin>The praise of Soter, the Roman Bishop.</margin> And also your Holy Bishop Soter has not only maintained what the fathers had taught, but he has also improved and increased it; he not only shared with the Saints what physical necessity required, but also comforted the brothers who came to him with lovely and kind speech, and he gave himself to all foreign brothers who came to him as a kind <margin>F</margin> and Spiritual Father.

In this same letter, he also makes mention of Clement’s Epistle which he wrote to the Co-

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin> rinthians, proving that it has always been an old custom and institution that this letter was always read in the Assembly; and he says thus: <margin>The letter of Clement at Corinth.</margin> We have passed this present Sunday lovably, in which we have read your letter, which we always read for our exhortation, just like Clement’s Epistle, which was written by us previously. The same also writes that his <margin>The Epistle of Dionysius is falsified.</margin> Epistles have been falsified by some, speaking thus: I have written some letters at the request of the brothers, which certain deceitful apostles <note>Original: "duppelsche Apostelen," literally 'double apostles,' referring to false teachers or those with divided loyalties.</note> have filled with weeds, removing some things and adding others, for which I commit them to the judgment of God. What wonder is it that they have falsified the words of the Holy Scriptures, since they have corrupted our writings, which are base and of no esteem? In common speech, it is said that it was Tatian who first brought forth this heresy, and that he was the same man we spoke of before, of whom the blessed Justin gave testimony, and whose disciple he is said to have been.

<margin>Read Irenaeus on the continent ones, book 1, chapter 30.</margin>

### ¶ Of the Sect of the Tatians.

#### The 29th Chapter.

They also speak against the salvation of the first man <note>Meaning Adam.</note>. And this has now been brought forward by him of whom Tatian was a chief teacher, and he taught such blasphemies, having previously been a disciple of Justin: but as long as he was with him, he did not reveal himself to hold such views. But afterwards, when Justin had become a martyr, he separated himself from the assemblies and, being puffed up with pride because he had had such a master—deeming himself better than others—he preferred to follow his own style of teaching rather than the old way. And he taught some things that had not been heard of for many a time, such as the fables of Valentinus, and he considered Marriage to be the same as fornication and unchastity, confirming such views also with Marcion and Saturninus. He also brought into doubt with new questions whether Adam was also saved. And thereafter, this same Irenaeus says thus:

Fol. 79.
Older Christian Churches. The 5th Book.
G iiii

## Preface to the Fifth Book.

<margin>Eleutherus, Bishop of Rome.</margin>
After Soter had served the priesthood in Rome for eight years, Eleutherus—the twelfth in succession from the Apostles—followed him in this office, in the seventeenth year of the reign of Emperor Antoninus Verus <note>original: "Antonini Veri"; historically refers to Marcus Aurelius, who reigned from 161–180 AD.</note>. During this time, in many provinces of the Roman Empire, very severe and cruel persecutions occurred due to the outcries and riots of the common people, so that in many lands many thousands of martyrs were tormented. This is easily understood from the writings we have seen, which were written at that time to preserve the memory of such events.
<margin>Eusebius says this of his book, which he wrote concerning the ancient martyrs.</margin>
And although we have written much more extensively, making special mention of the martyrs in another book—the content of which provides necessary instruction in doctrine and knowledge—it nevertheless seems good and appropriate to us to recount and set down in this our book some brief histories from the many that appear in that same volume. And just as other historians recount wars, triumphs, victories, and the brave deeds of their captains, and also how many citizens and enemies were slain, likewise concerning women and children and the destruction of cities and lands in various ways: so it is not unjust that we also describe the history of things pertaining to God,
<margin>The Christian struggle of the martyrs.</margin>
the struggle that the flesh endured for the salvation of the soul, and what struggle the soul had so that they might obtain the heavenly Fatherland, and what wars were accomplished for the truth of the faith. In these, the fight was not against powerful horsemen <note>original: "Ruyteren"; a term used for cavalry or knights, here contrasting physical soldiers with spiritual enemies.</note>, but against the spiritual devil; not for the bravery of the flesh, but for the bravery of the spirit. And thus we shall not describe wars of how lands and provinces were won, but what happened to gain the knowledge of the Kingdom of Heaven—those who did not seek the power of an earthly kingdom, but sought to receive the glory of all triumphs from the immortal King and God of all things.
