The servants of Christ living at Lyons and Vienne, cities of Gaul <note>original: "Walschen Landes"</note>, to all the brothers throughout Asia and Phrygia who share the same faith and hope of redemption with us through our Lord Jesus Christ: peace, grace, and glory from God the Father and from our Lord Jesus Christ.

<margin>B
A letter from the Christians at Vienne and Lyons concerning the martyrs.</margin>
Following the preface of the letter, they recounted it thus, setting in order the great tribulations we have suffered, and the madness of the heathens which they exercised against the holy martyrs. It is impossible to speak of it with the mouth—even if we were there—nor is it in our power to describe these things. For the enemy of the human race has set himself against us with all his strength, marking the beginning of his coming with harsh persecutions, and has thus instructed and taught his servants against the servants of God, to fulfill and practice every service of wickedness and cruelty. Thus, it was first forbidden to us to live in our own houses.

<margin>P
1. The living in houses.
2. The bathhouses.
3. The going out.
4. Always hidden.</margin>
Second, we were forbidden to bathe. Third, we were not allowed to appear in public. Fourth, we were not to be seen in any place, whether at home or outside, nor even in the city. But God’s grace was present, delivering some of our weak ones from their hands, and offering up certain strong men who were more steadfast and firm than any pillar <note>original: "Calomne"</note>. Through their patience, they did not only endure the attacks the enemy could devise, but always desired more, willingly surrendering themselves to all the reproach and pain of the torments.

<margin>Q
Men stronger than walls.</margin>
<margin>R</margin>

He used such cruelty upon them that it is impossible to speak of all the thoughts of his cruelty. There was one of our brothers named Vettius Pagathus <note>historically Vettius Epagathus</note>, who had a perfect love for God and was upright toward all men. His life (though he was still a young man) was so pleasing and well-regarded by all people that he even surpassed many elders. <margin>X

<margin>Y</margin>
This same man, being filled with the fervent and divine love of the Spirit, seeing the cruel torments being inflicted upon the servants of God, and that they devised such inhuman pain against right and reason to be done to human limbs, could no longer endure such injustice. He requested that he be given a hearing to speak in defense of the good citizens, in whom it could not be proven that they had committed any crime. He was highly esteemed in the city and very learned. Since the stubbornness of the Judge would not receive nor hear his defense, the Judge only asked him if he also was a Christian. # The Chronicles of Eusebius Pamphilus / The
<page-num>Fol. 82.</page-num>

One named [Sanctus] <note>The previous page established that this refers to Sanctus, a deacon from Vienne.</note> also suffered more than can be expressed in words, and more than is fitting for human nature to endure. The servants of the Devil devised and carried out unspeakable torments to hear something from him and to torture some improper confession out of him; thus he suffered all manner of new tortures that far exceed the state of human nature.

<margin>
Saint Sanctus, the Deacon, mocks the Tyrants.
</margin>
But this same good champion, being filled with God's grace, so greatly mocked their cruelties and the beastly savagery of their lashes that he would never tell them from what country he came, nor of what lineage, nor from what house, nor even his own name.

<margin>
He declares himself to be a Christian.
</margin>
And being questioned on all these things, he answered nothing in all his torments but: **"I am a Christian."** <note>original: "Ich ben een Christen"</note> That is my name, that is my lineage, and that is my fatherland; I am entirely nothing else but a Christian. Therefore the servants were ignited with an unspeakable rage because he was being destroyed by such manifold types of pain, yet they could not force or torture him into stating or confessing his own name.

Finally, they took glowing plates of copper and pressed them against his tenderest parts, near his genitals, and heated them again and again, holding them against his most sensitive limbs, so that his flesh was scorched and falling away from the heat of his body. But he remained immovable, un-terrified, and undaunted, for the flame of the fire was tempered by the heavenly and eternal fountains that flow from the body of our LORD Jesus Christ. Thus he was pained and martyred in all his limbs, so that his entire body was nothing but one wound, and the likeness of a human form had so vanished from him that not only was he unrecognizable, but one could not even tell what he was, so greatly was he tormented by the cruelty of the tortures.

But Christ alone knew him through the glory of his martyrdom, which by his patience destroyed all the power of the Adversary; and He strengthens His knights through that example of patience, openly proving to all people that there is nothing gruesome where the Father is loved, nor any sorrow where the faith of Christ exists. But the wicked craftsmen were not ashamed of the strength of the Martyrs. A short time later, noticing

<column-break/>

that the wounds were still fresh—such that even a light touch of the hand would be enough to renew the pains and torments, and to once again plague the limbs that were nearly all rotted—they hoped that one of two things would happen: either that he would fulfill the will of the Tyrants, or that if he gave himself up to all torments until death, the cruelty of his pains would serve as a fear and terror to the others. But it happened quite differently than the evil criminals had intended. For it came to pass (which the unbelievers can hardly believe) that his body was renewed in its original form and strength through the second round of torments. And the strength and use of the limbs, which the first cruelty had taken away, was healed by the second, so that these second torments were not a pain to him, but a medicine and a healing.

<margin>
Blandina is brought back to the tortures and accused by the Heathens of eating people in their gatherings.
</margin>
In the same way, Blandina (whom we spoke of before) was also brought back to the tortures a second time as an example to others. While she was still nearly half-alive and very close to death, because they struck and tormented her again so severely, she suddenly raised herself up as if she had jumped out of a sleep. Mindful of the eternal salvation to come, she spoke with a strong voice, as if she were speaking to the people from a high place, saying: "Men, you are greatly mistaken <note>original: "doleve" - delusional or erring</note> to think that these children eat human limbs; they do not even eat the flesh of mute beasts." <note>This is a refutation of the "Thyestean feasts" accusation—a common Roman slander that Christians practiced ritual cannibalism.</note> And remaining thus steadfast in her suffering, she was returned to the number of the Martyrs.

### The Fourth Book,
### Of the Ancient Christian Churches.

<margin>Dying in the dungeon.</margin>
After all manner of torments that the cruelty of the raging tyrants could devise, they were thrown into a stinking, dark place and left to die there. In this way, many were killed in the prison, whose spirits God has received; He did not withdraw His divine help from them in that wretched place. There were some among them who had suffered the most cruel torments,
<margin>Pothinus, the Bishop of Lyon.</margin>
and although they were not permitted any human remedy, they began to heal in a wonderful manner through the power of the Lord. They obtained a singular joy of heart, and even where there was no more hope for the body, they began to grow so strong that by their exhortations they also strengthened the others to patience. For those who were newly imprisoned, and whose bodies were not yet hardened by torments, were more terrified than the others; these same people died from the horrible and foul stench of the dark dungeon. Furthermore, it would be unfitting to remain silent regarding the glorious confession of the martyr Pothinus <note>original: "Photinus"; historically known as Pothinus, the first Bishop of Lyon.</note>, who was the Bishop of Lyon. As he was more than 90 years old and very weak of body due to his age, being nearly dead, he lived only for the desire of martyrdom. Thus he was led, or rather dragged, to the tribunal; for he was very frail from age and illness, and his life was preserved at that time only so that Christ might triumph greatly in that brittle body. As the old man stood at the tribunal before the Judge, the community—that raging mob—began to shriek and cry out: "This is Christ himself!" When he was asked by the Judge who the God of the Christians was, he answered: "If you are worthy of it, you shall know." <note>This bold answer implies that divine knowledge is only granted to the righteous, not to those actively persecuting the faith.</note> Because of this answer, the common people were ignited with such unspeakable rage and fury that those standing nearby struck him with their fists, and others kicked him with their feet, being unmoved by his dignity or age. And those who were far from him threw whatever came to the hands of the furious men; each one thought it a great crime if they had not done some evil or spite to the old man.
<margin>Pothinus</margin>
For they believed that by such abuse, they were avenging their gods. When they had thrown him, thus half-dead, into the dungeon, he

<column-break/>

shortly thereafter offered up his spirit to God.
<margin>Strengthened in the dungeon.</margin>
At that same time, the goodness of God quickly sent, through His grace and mercy, a singular event which had never before happened under any tyrants: for all those who had previously denied the faith <note>Known as "lapsi," or those who fell away under pressure.</note> and were released for that reason, were captured again and thrown into the dungeon. Their shame was now so much greater, for they were not imprisoned as Christians, but as murderers and for improper unchastity, and they suffered double pain. For the other Christians
<margin>The traitors are imprisoned in the dungeon as murderers, and not as Christians.</margin>
who were tormented there remained moderate and had their solace in the crown of martyrdom; the love of Christ and the grace of the Holy Spirit refreshed the wretched. But these others were tormented with much heavier torments and chains—that is, with the gnawing of their consciences—so that one could easily distinguish them from the others by the appearance of their faces. For the true Christians were led out joyfully from the torments, and one saw in their faces
<margin>From the face one sees how the heart is disposed.</margin>
a singular divine loveliness; for they regarded the bonds with which they were bound as precious jewels. Thus, through the stench of the prison, they became a sweet fragrance to our Lord Christ, so that they did not think of themselves as being locked in a stinking prison, but in a fragrant place of precious spices. But the others were sad, dejected, and horrible to look upon, more deformed than any ugliness. They were also mocked by the heathens as bastards and listless people who had lost their faith and had not found a [new] name, and those who lacked the Christian name nonetheless did not escape the penalty of murderers. When the other Christians saw this, they were unspeakably strengthened, so that from the moment they were captured, they confessed themselves to be Christians without any evasion or hidden words.

And after many other accounts described in this Letter, it is written thereafter: "And after that, through various types of martyrdom, our Lord Christ has made a crown, like a wreath of roses decorated with many kinds of flowers, and has offered it to His Father, so that they might receive the gift of eternal life as winners of a great battle." ¶ A short time thereafter, they were brought into the middle of a place where an unspeakably large multitude of people had gathered to watch. Once more, Maturus and Sanctus were tortured with every kind of blow and torment, as if they had never been tortured before. The executioners and servants did this, incited by the cruel voices of the people, to break and destroy their endurance and to rob them of the crown which, in a manner of speaking, was already upon their heads. But the hope of the coming glory, which was so near that they felt they were reaching out and grasping it with their hands, strengthened their courage more and more.

<margin>n</margin>
After they had used every kind of torment, and the time ordained for the torture had nearly passed, and when they could not bring the martyrs to change their convictions or intent in any way, they were placed in iron chairs under which a great fire was stoked, so that the flesh which had been torn by the blows was then roasted by the fire. When they saw at last that their spirits were immovable, they struck off their heads.

<margin>o</margin>
After that, Blandina was bound to a stake and raised up in the shape of a cross, prepared to be food for the beasts. While she hung thus upon the wood, she poured out her prayer to God with a cheerful and undaunted face, praying that she might remain steadfast, and for her other companions who were fighting in the same struggle. She hoped that her prayer would be heard for the sake of the others, whom she now helped not only with her prayers but with her example; she also taught that it is certain that all who are partakers of Christ’s suffering <note>original: "deelachtich zijn des lijdens Christi"</note> shall also be partakers of His glory.

<margin>p</margin>

<margin>q</margin>

### The 3rd Chapter.

<margin>Attalus.</margin>
Afterward, there was a great outcry from the common people that Attalus should be brought forward. For he was very noble, and—what is noble above all—he was a man of good conscience; because of his faith in our LORD Jesus Christ, he was steadfast in all persecutions. As he was led around the scaffold <note>original: "Schavot"</note> with his title carried before him, in which was written, "Attalus, a Christian," the fury of the common people began to rage against him beyond measure. But when it was told to the Governor <note>original: "President"</note> that he was a citizen of Rome, he commanded that he be led back to the dungeon with the others, and he wrote to the Emperor to know what his pleasure was that should be done with him. In the meantime,
<margin>The Christians in the dungeon.</margin>
while they were thus in the dungeon awaiting the answer, they did not spend their time unprofitably; rather, through the joy of their spirit and the bravery of their faith, they strengthened those who seemed weaker. Those who were not yet martyrs gave good courage to many other martyrs through their exhortations. For this reason, the mother of the Gatherings <note>The Church.</note> was filled with great joy, seeing her children—who had seemed to fall into death—being led back to life through these combatants. Many who had denied the faith and become as outcasts were reborn through their exhortations and Christ was renewed in them; for they were taught by these that God does not desire the death of sinners, but that they convert and live.
<margin>Ezekiel 18.</margin>
When the answer from the Emperor arrived, it stated that all who remained steadfast in the faith should be executed, but those who denied it should be released.

<margin>z</margin>
<margin>The Fair.</margin>
At a great festival, to which people come together from all lands—as the market <note>The Great Fair of the Three Gauls, held annually in August.</note> used to be held with us in Lyons—when the greatest multitude was gathered, the Governor went to his judgment seat and commanded that the Christians be brought to him. He ordered that they be tortured with the greatest torments in the presence of the people, and again racks and other instruments prepared for torture were brought forth. And all those among them who were citizens of Rome, he commanded to be beheaded; the others, he ordered to be thrown to the beasts to be devoured. Nevertheless, in all this, Christ was greatly praised and blessed.

# Among Christian Churches. The Fifth Book,

A ...especially because those who had previously denied their faith—and were not released even then—now found that although they had once wished to recant, mercy and freedom were being offered to those who remained steadfast. They stayed firm in their resolution and were thus called back from damnation, being added to the number of the martyrs. Now, as the Judge was conducting his examination and inquiry <note>The Dutch "Inquisitie" here refers to the Roman legal examination or "cognitio" rather than the later medieval Inquisition.</note> into these matters, there was a certain physician born in Phrygia named Alexander. He was an upright and wise man, well-liked and beloved by all people because of his honorable and virtuous life.

<margin>Alexander.</margin>
B This man, moved by the love of God, stood by as the prisoners were brought into the Tribunal <note>original: "Vyerschare," a traditional Dutch term for a court of justice.</note> before the Judge to determine if they remained steadfast or wished to recant. He encouraged the prisoners with outward signs and gestures not to deny their faith, so that it became known to all the bystanders, and his own heart and convictions were made plain.

C When the common people noticed this, they became very angry, especially because those who had first recanted were now withdrawing their recantation and suffering while confessing themselves to be Christians. They cried out loudly against Alexander, claiming that this change of heart happened because of his prompting. Therefore, the Judge commanded that he be brought before him in the middle of the court, and he asked him who he was. With a free confession, he testified that he was a Christian. At that same moment, the Judge condemned him to be thrown to the beasts to be devoured.

D The next day, he was brought forth with Attalus. The Judge, wishing to please the people, also commanded—contrary to the Emperor's decree—that Attalus be thrown to the beasts as well. But when the cruel beasts would not touch the bodies of the Saints, they were beaten and tortured with every manner of torment. Finally, the Judge commanded that they be thrown into the middle of that place before all the people.

E This blessed Alexander, in all the torments he suffered, never spoke a word; rather, from the beginning to the end, he was always speaking within himself to God, praying and offering thanks. And when Attalus was placed on the iron chair, under which hot coals were stoked, and the smell of his roasting flesh reached the nostrils of the people standing nearby, he cried out with a loud voice to the

<column-break/>

G people: "Behold, this which you are doing now is truly eating human flesh! Why do you investigate us as if we did this crime in secret, when you are doing it in the open? We do not eat human flesh, nor do we do any evil." And when he was asked what name his God had, he answered: "Those who are many are distinguished by names, but He who is the only One needs no name."
<margin>The Christians were accused by the Heathens of eating human flesh.</margin>

H When this had concluded, on the last day of the market-festival, Blandina was brought forth again with a child of fifteen years from Pontus named Ponticus. By the Judge's command, they had been forced to stand by whenever others were being tortured and martyred, so that they might be terrified by seeing the torments of the others.
<margin>Blandina, a child from Pontus. H</margin>

I When they were placed in the middle of the arena before the Judge, they were commanded to swear by the gods. They replied again that those things they were being forced to swear by were not gods. And as they spoke many other words blaspheming <note>In this context, "blaspheming" refers to the Christians' refusal to acknowledge the divinity of the Roman gods, which Romans considered a form of atheism or impious speech.</note> the gods of the Heathens, the multitude of people grew more enraged. They showed no mercy for the youth of the child, nor for the fragile nature of the woman. They tortured them with every manner of torment prepared there, so that they were tested by all the cruelties that malice could invent.
<margin>I</margin>
As Ponticus received a great strength of patience through his mother's <note>Though likely not his biological mother, Blandina acted as a spiritual mother to the young Ponticus during their ordeal.</note> encouragement, he remained steadfast in the confession of the faith and offered up his unspotted spirit to God. Finally, the glorious Blandina—like a noble mother who had sent her children before her to the crown of martyrdom—being very eager and hasty to follow, was joyful and glad, like a bride invited to come to the bedchamber of her dear Bridegroom.
<margin>K</margin>
Therefore, she was dancing joyfully amidst her blows, and as she was roasted upon the grill, she was glad, appearing as cheerful as if she were at a royal banquet. Afterward, she was thrown before the beasts, which did not harm her.
<margin>L</margin>

Finally, the Judge ordered that her throat be cut with a sword / whereby those wicked people were greatly amazed / and said / that there had never been a woman / who had been able to suffer such torments and so many. But their cruelty could not yet find its fill / for being ignited with the venom of the old Serpent <note>The "old Serpent" is a traditional biblical reference to the Devil, seen here as the driving force behind the Roman persecutors.</note> / and not yet satisfied by their cruel and fierce ways / for through the patience of the holy Martyrs / their raging madness was always more hideously ignited. Thus, as there were many various ways of mocking among them / so there was great distress among us / and especially for this reason / because we were not permitted to bury the bodies / for at night it was also not suitable to do such things / nor could the servants be softened by any prayers or gifts / so diligently did they ensure that we could not bury our remains.

<margin>Their belief in the resurrection was mocked.</margin>
After some days during which they had not permitted any burial / they burned all the bones of the Martyrs to powder / and they threw those ashes into the river Rhone <note>original: "Rodanum," the Latin name for the Rhone river in France.</note> / so that no trace might remain anywhere / and in doing so / they said / that they were taking vengeance for their gods / and that by this / the hope of resurrection was taken away from them. And they also said: "These Christians think that they shall yet rise again from their graves / and therefore they surrender themselves through some boldness or superstition so joyfully to all torments and suffering / let us see now if they shall rise again / and if their God may stand by them and deliver them from our hands."

<margin>D</margin>
This happened in the same times / just as the letter from the brothers of Lyons has made known to us. From which one may consider / what also occurred in other lands.

<margin>A</margin> insults and torments which they were suffering. They were humble among the brothers, but proud among the persecutors; and gentle toward their brothers, and fierce toward the tyrants. They were obedient to Christ, but rebellious against the Devil. They humbled themselves under the mighty hand of GOD, by which they are now highly exalted. They were pleasing to all people, and accused 
<margin>B</margin> no one; they released everyone <note>Meaning they forgave those who had faltered in their faith.</note>, and burdened no one. They also prayed for their persecutors, speaking the same 
<margin>Acts 7</margin> words of the first holy martyr Stephen: "Lord, do not hold these sins against them." <margin>F</margin> deprived of the grace of Christ. In the same letter, another story is told, which seems to me worthy to be included here. There was among the number of those imprisoned for the confession of Christ, one named Alcibiades.

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin> This man lived very strictly and would not receive any food except salted bread and water. When he wished to maintain this severity of life even in the prison, it was revealed to Attalus—after his first confession which he had made before the tribunal—that Alcibiades was not doing right by not using God's creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to all created things, including food and wine, which were seen as gifts from God.</note>, and that he would leave behind for others an example of offense <note>Original: "schandalisatie" (scandal). The concern was that his extreme asceticism might make other Christians feel guilty for eating normally.</note>. When Alcibiades was 
<margin>H</margin> told this, he received all other food with gratitude; for that same Spirit that revealed he should learn this was also advising him to follow this counsel. Regarding this, enough has been said.

<margin>I</margin> same time many other powers and graces occurred in various Assemblies through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, it is also easily believed that the spirit of prophecy might have been given to these men. <margin>Martyrs, guardians of the right faith.</margin> <margin>K</margin> faith, citing the letters of the martyrs who had been martyred among them, which they had sent while writing in the prison to the brothers who were there in Asia and Phrygia, and also to Eleutherus the Bishop of Rome, exhorting him regarding the peace of the Assembly. ¶ We well know that the status of an office alone does not make anyone righteous, though one may use it justly in his priesthood; rather, we commend him more for his upright life. ## How under the Emperor Marcus Aurelius, through the hearing of our prayers, God granted rain upon the Earth.

### The 5th Chapter.

<margin>Marcus Aurelius.</margin>
In the times of the Emperor Antoninus <note>This refers to Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, who reigned from 161–180 AD.</note> when these aforementioned things occurred, the histories show that the Emperor Marcus Aurelius went to war with his brother against the Germans and Sarmatians <note>The original Dutch text identifies the ancient Sarmatians with the Polish people (Polonen) of the translator's era.</note>. When the army was in great need and peril because they had no water and did not know what to do from thirst, some Christian riders were found in a Legion. These men (as is the custom among our people) bowed their knees and prayed, and God heard their prayers. Thus, an abundant rain suddenly came, so that the soldiers who were in great peril—for whom the Christians had prayed—had their thirst quenched; and the enemy bands that were nearby were driven away by many fiery lightning bolts.
<margin>The prayer of the Christian servants obtained water.</margin>

This history is described by the historians of the heathens, but they do not describe it as having happened through the prayers of the Christians, nor do they believe the other miracles that occurred among our people. But among our own historians, Tertullian testifies to this same event; and among the Greeks, Apollinaris, who writes that this same Legion was named the "Thundering Legion" <note>original: "fulminea Legio"</note> in memory of the Emperor’s deed. And Tertullian says that there are still letters from the Emperor Marcus that openly prove this. It is now proper that we return to the order of our History.
<margin>The Thundering Legion.</margin>

<column-break/>

When Pothinus, being more than 90 years old, had finished his struggle with the other martyrs of the land of Gaul <note>original: "Walschen landes." This refers to the region of modern-day France.</note>, Irenaeus received the priesthood of the Christian Church of the city of Lyons. We find that this Irenaeus was, in his youth, a disciple of Polycarp. He writes in his third book against the heretics that he wrote that same book in the time of Eleutherius, the Bishop of Rome—the time of which we are now speaking—and he proves it with these words:

## The number of Bishops who have been in Rome.

### The 6th Chapter.

<margin>Linus at Rome.</margin>
Now that the congregation at Rome was founded, the Holy Apostles entrusted the office of the Bishopric to Linus. Paul makes mention of him in his letter which he wrote to Timothy. After him followed Anacletus, and the third in the Bishopric was Clement. He had shared his life with the Holy Apostles and had read for a long time, being himself taught by the Apostles; he always had the form of their teaching before his eyes and in his memory.
<margin>Read Irenaeus against the heretics, book 3, chapter 3.</margin>

<margin>Clement, a representative of the Roman church, wrote to the rebellious Corinthians.</margin>
In the time of this Clement, a very great uprising arose at Corinth among the brothers, so that Clement himself wrote a necessary letter on behalf of the Roman Congregation to the Corinthians. In this letter, he exhorted them to peace and renewed their faith, which had somewhat faltered, writing therein the teaching of the Apostles which he had recently received from them. And thereafter Irenaeus says: After this Clement followed Evaristus, and after Evaristus, Alexander; and after him was ordained the sixth from the Apostles, Sixtus. After whom came Telesphorus, who was martyred. Thereafter came Hyginus, and then Pius, after whom came Anicetus. After him followed Soter, who is now the 11th in the Bishopric from the time of the Apostles; and he has kept that same teaching of the Divine faith which the Apostles taught entirely pure and undefiled.

# The older Christian churches. Book 5, fol. 89.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>A remaining Divine power in the church in the time of Irenaeus.</margin>
Irenaeus describes this in his aforementioned books. And he also writes in his second book that in his times there were still many in the Gathering <note>The Dutch "Vergaderinghe" (Gathering) is used here to translate the Greek 'ecclesia', referring to the congregation or the Church.</note> who possessed a singular Divine power, and he writes in this manner:

<margin>B</margin>
It is very different from them <note>Referring to heretics who cannot perform true miracles.</note>, that they do not raise the dead as the Lord raised them, and as many Brothers have often done in many Gatherings; so much so that when the whole local Church was gathered together, and after they had fasted and prayed, calling upon God's mercy, the spirit of the dead person returned into his body, and he was made living again through the prayers of the Saints. And after this he says further: If it be the case that they wish to say that the Lord Jesus Christ performed such Miracles through fantasy <note original: "fantasije">In this context, it refers to an illusion or magical trickery rather than reality.</note>, then let us go to the Prophets, who prophesied beforehand that such things would happen through him; these also prove and confirm that he is the Son of God. Wherefore the Disciples, receiving such grace from him, do such things in his Name to help the salvation of men, just as God has appointed to each person. Some others drive out Devils, and they cleanse them so thoroughly that sometimes those who are healed remain in the Gathering, believing. Some others have knowledge of future things and see Prophetic visions. And others lay their hands on the sick, and they are healed. And sometimes the dead have also been raised by these means, and have lived among us thereafter for many years. And to speak of everything, it is not possible to recount all the powers that occur throughout the whole world in God's gatherings through the grace and Name of OUR LORD Jesus Christ, who was crucified under the Judge Pontius Pilate. And although these miracles happen daily, they do not happen for any sale or reward, but just as the grace of the Lord is received for free, so they share the same grace for free.

<margin>F</margin>
And Irenaeus writes again in another place concerning this as follows: We have (he says) many brothers in the Gathering who have heard the grace of Prophecies, and have the gifts of the Holy Spirit, so that they spoke with many tongues, who also

<margin>The 70 Translators.</margin>
But hear now what he says of the 70 Translators <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible traditionally attributed to seventy or seventy-two Jewish scholars in the 3rd century BCE.</note> of the Holy Scriptures. "God," he says, "became man, and the same Lord has saved us, who has given us that sign which is written of the Virgin, and not as some of them say, who now boldly cause the Scripture to be interpreted otherwise, saying: 'Behold, a young woman shall conceive in her womb, and shall bear a son.'"

<margin>P</margin>
Thus have Theodotion of Ephesus and Aquila of Pontus interpreted it, both being new Jews <note original: "niewe Jode">This likely refers to proselytes or converts to Judaism who produced Greek translations of the Old Testament that differed from the Christian-favored Septuagint, particularly regarding Messianic prophecies.</note>, whose interpretation the Jews have followed, who say there that Christ was born of Joseph.

<margin>Q</margin>
And thereafter he says: "Before the power of the Romans was strengthened, while yet the Macedonians ruled Asia, Ptolemy Lagus's son was a King of Egypt; and desiring to adorn his library, which he made at Alexandria, with all kinds of books of the ancient Greeks, he also desired from those of Jerusalem that he might obtain their Hebrew scripture translated into the Greek language."

<margin>R</margin>
"And because they were then subject and subordinate to those of Macedonia, they sent the most learned and expert men, 70 Priests, very learned in both languages, unto Ptolemy; through whom, nonetheless, the will and counsel of God was fulfilled."

"Thus the King, being desirous to receive an individual teaching, and fearing that they might by chance hide some interpretation or sense which is contained in the truth of the Holy books, he commanded that each of them should be separated from one another; and being thus separated, he had each one translate or render the text, and willed that such a translation should be maintained in all the books; and he later let them all be called together, to see what each one had translated."

<margin>S</margin>
And then was God greatly praised, and it was known that the Holy Scripture was truly Divine. For they had all together written the same words, the same names, and the same sense, from the beginning to the end, so that even the Heathens who were present there acknowledged that the translation of the Scriptures had happened through

<column-break/>

<margin>T</margin>
<margin>Scripture is the Divine word.</margin>
God's inspiration. And it is no wonder, though Divine providence has ordained it so. For previously, in the captivity that happened to the people under King Nebuchadnezzar, the Scripture was entirely corrupted. And after 70 years, when the Jews returned again into their Land, in the time of the King of the Persians called Artaxerxes, <margin>Esdras brought back the light of the law.</margin> so God inspired a Priest named Esdras <note>Ezra the Scribe.</note>, of the lineage of Levi, that he should restore all the books and words of the first Prophets, and give back to the people the Law which <margin>V</margin> was given through Moses. This Irenaeus describes.

# Eusebius Pamphilus’s Chronicle

<margin>
Rhodon wrote against Marcion.
</margin>

$\P$ This same man <note>Rhodon, a Christian writer from Asia Minor and a student of Tatian.</note> has written many books, and specifically against the heresy of **Marcion**, which **Tatian** proves is divided into many different opinions and views. And who they were, and for what reason they are so divided in their opinions, he proves with these words:

<margin>
His words regarding the Marcionite sects.
</margin>

"Therefore," (he says) "they are at odds with one another, because they wish to maintain and confirm what is impossible. For there is one of their company named **Appelles**, who lives in great old age and abstinence, and was professing that there has been but one principle of all things; but the Prophets, he said, were taught otherwise by a spirit, following the counsel of a Virgin named **Philumena**, who was possessed by a devilish spirit."

<margin>
Appelles.
</margin>

$\P$ Some others, like their leader **Marcion**, established two principles <note>Dualism: the belief in two opposing gods or forces, such as a god of the Old Testament and a god of the New Testament.</note>, among whom are **Potitus** and **Basiliscus**. These same were followed by **Potitus Lupus**. But being confused in their teaching, as **Marcion** himself was, they turned to that which they suspected to be easiest, and taught that there are two principles, and this they assert without any proof.

<margin>
Syenus.
</margin>

$\P$ Some others are even more confused, saying and asserting that there are three principles and three natures. Their superior and leader is **Syenus**, as the defenders of their teaching say. And he also writes himself that he disputed with **Appelles**, saying: "I have spoken with the aged **Appelles**, and he was defeated, showing that he was teaching many things wrongly."

$\P$ And finally he spoke, saying that it is not necessary to examine the reasons for faith, but that each person ought to remain in that which he believes, and that those who hope in **Christ** shall be saved, provided they are found in good works; and yet he openly confessed concerning God (as we have said before) just as we say, that there has been but one principle. And after this he explains all their opinions, and he also brings forth his own sense, saying: "I asked **Appelles**, with what will you prove the reasons for one principle? Or teach us how it may be." Then he answered: "The Prophets rebuke one another, for they are not true, because they are discordant among themselves; for whatever is contrary to another is false." And how there was only one principle, he could not know, but it nonetheless seemed to him to be so. And when he was sworn by me that

<column-break/>

he should tell me the truth, he confirmed with his oath that he could not understand how there is one single unborn God, but that he only believed it. Then I noticed that he was a Teacher of that which he confessed not to understand.

<margin>
Calistion, a disciple of Tatian.
</margin>

$\P$ In the same book it is also told that there was in Rome one of **Tatian's** disciples named **Calistion**, who writes that **Tatian** composed a book of *Problemata* <note>original: "Problemata"; refers to "Problems" or "Inquiries."</note> and questions, in which he explains all that is dark and difficult to understand in Holy Scripture. And also this same Rhodon promises in his books that he would also write against that same heresy. Where he writes upon the *Hexameron* <note>original: "Hexameron"; a treatise on the six days of creation described in Genesis.</note>, he says that **Appelles** has written very many evil things against the Law of **Moses**, and he blasphemes greatly against the whole Law, which, refuting it as it seemed to him, destroys all that is written.

<margin>
Book of the Propositions and Questions of Tatian.

**But there has also been another writer of the Christian Church, named Apollonius, who also wrote a book against this heresy, in which he openly proves that their prophecies are false, and rebukes them in all their words, and likewise the lives and manners of those who were teachers and founders of this heresy, and says thus.**

<margin>Apollonius wrote against Montanus.</margin>

Let us see (he says) who this new master is, and let us first see if his teaching and his works agree with the LORD’S teaching and judgment. This is the one who taught that one should not keep marriage <note>The Montanists practiced extreme asceticism, often demanding that married followers separate to lead "pure" lives.</note>, and who was the very first to establish laws for fasting, and named the two small towns of Pepuza and Thimium, located in Phrygia, "Jerusalem" <note>Montanus claimed these obscure towns were the site of the New Jerusalem descending from heaven.</note>.

<margin>Fast day established by Montanus.</margin>
In which he ordained that all his disciples should gather; and there he appointed collectors of money who, under the name and thought of offerings, cleverly obtained gifts and favors, and he provided for those who preached his word, so that being compelled by such means, they might teach his doctrine more freely. This he says of Montanus.

Then concerning his women <note>Referring to the prophetesses Prisca (Priscilla) and Maximilla.</note>, he writes afterward thus.

We prove first of all that after these prophetesses were filled and possessed by their spirit, they left their husbands.

<margin>Prisca.</margin>
Why then do they lie that Prisca was a virgin? And afterward he says again: Do you not know that Holy Scripture has forbidden prophets to receive money, or gifts, or favors? If I now see someone who says he is a prophet and takes gold, silver, and costly clothes, how shall I suspect him to be a prophet?

<margin>Themisus.</margin>
And afterward he is still saying: And also Themisus, who was exalted and puffed up among them solely by the name of professing their teaching; but he lacked the fruits of true confession. <margin>Alexander, one of the Montanist sect.</margin>
Is this man not condemned as guilty of murder and other wicked criminal works? We do not say it alone, but the public records make it known. Which of the two is it who forgives the other's sin—is the prophetess forgiving the martyr his murder, or the martyr the prophetess her greed and robbery? For our Lord has said

<margin>Matthew 10</margin>
> Do not possess gold, nor money, nor two tunics,

and these do the contrary in all things; for they obtain and gather that which the Lord commanded even those who possess it to cast away. Let us then test those who are called prophets or martyrs among them, who have gathered money not only from the rich, but also from the poor, from widows and orphans. Or if they have confidence in their good life, let them come forward and present themselves to dispute with us, so that when they are defeated, they may henceforth refrain from practicing such dealings.

For one must also recognize and test the prophet, as the Lord said, by his fruits,

<margin>Matthew 7.</margin>
> for the tree is known by its fruits,

...to write and to correctly revise, seeing as the copy has been handed down to us with such great diligence by the Holy Men. <note>The author is emphasizing the importance of accurate manuscript transmission in preserving the original teachings of the Church Fathers.</note>

And in the book that Irenaeus wrote to Florinus <note>Florinus was a Roman presbyter who had fallen into heresy, likely Gnosticism; Irenaeus wrote to him to pull him back to the faith.</note>, of whom we have spoken above, he makes mention of Polycarp, with whom he also had his conversation, and proves it with these words: "This teaching, O Florinus, which you write, I say for certain is not upright; for these teachings are not in harmony with the Christian faith, nor can the heretics who have departed from the assembly protect this teaching. For when I was still a child, I saw you in Asia with Polycarp, where you were then flourishing <note>original: "bloeyede"</note> while you were still living in the Palace, and were diligent to please Polycarp. And much more are the things that happened at that time in my memory and remembrance than those that are present; for the things that one learns in youth are imprinted in the memory, so that they are not easily forgotten."

### Of Apollonius who was martyred at Rome.

#### The 21st Chapter.

<margin>H</margin>
<margin>I</margin>
In the time when Commodus <note>Emperor Commodus (reigned 180–192 AD). While historically viewed as a tyrant, the Church enjoyed a period of relative peace during his reign compared to his father, Marcus Aurelius.</note> ruled the Roman Empire, the Christian Church had peace in all the world, and the Word of the Lord gathered the souls from all races of men to the knowledge and loveliness of the most high God. So much so that even in the City of Rome, very many of the most noble and very rich men, with their wives and children, and with all their kin and household, converted to the faith. But the old enemy of human salvation <note>A common historical reference to the Devil.</note> could not suffer this, and he sought out many and diverse ways to fight against the Christians.

<margin>K</margin>
<margin>Apollonius, a renowned man, becomes a witness for Christ.</margin>
So he first dragged to the judge in the City of Rome a man very illustrious and learned in our faith, and in Philosophy, named Apollonius; and he stirred up against him a wretched accuser, who was a desperate man. And because the Roman Law commanded that the accused Christian should be judged, but that the accuser should first be punished <note>original: "corrigeren"</note>, the Judge Perennius first gave a sentence over the accuser: that his legs should be broken. <note>In some periods of Roman law, if a capital accusation failed or was deemed malicious, the accuser suffered a severe penalty.</note>

<margin>L</margin>
Thereafter the blessed martyr Apollonius was exhorted to give in writing the defense of his faith, which was read openly and clearly before the Senators and all the people. And thereafter, by the counsel of the Senators, he was beheaded. For from of old, such an evil Law had been concluded in Rome. <note>Refers to the standing imperial decrees that made being a Christian a capital offense if the person refused to recant, despite the punishment of the specific accuser.</note>

During the reign of this same Emperor Commodus <note>Reigned 180–192 AD; he was the son of Marcus Aurelius.</note>, after Eleutherus had served the Bishopric <note>original: "Priesterschap"</note> in Rome for twelve years, he was succeeded by Victor. And at Antioch, the eighth bishop in succession from the Apostles became Serapion, of whom we have made mention above. At that time, Theophilus was in Caesarea in Palestine, and Narcissus was in Jerusalem, both of whom oversaw the congregations. At Corinth was Bacchylus, and at Ephesus was Polycrates, both worthy Bishops. Indeed, in those times many venerable bishops were found in many places: but we make mention only of those whose faith and wisdom were made manifest through the evidence of their own works.

### ¶ Concerning the dispute over the high feast of Easter.

#### The 23rd Chapter.

<margin>The opinion of the Asians regarding the Easter feast.</margin>
In the same time that these Bishops governed the Churches, a great dispute arose in Asia concerning the high feast of Easter. This was because they observed the feast according to the ancient custom of the fourteenth day of the Moon <note>This practice is known as Quartodecimanism, from the Latin for "fourteenth."</note>, as it was commanded to the Jews when they offered the Lamb. They deemed this necessary regardless of which day of the week the fourteenth day of the Moon fell upon, and they held that one did not need to fast beyond that. Because such a custom had never been observed in any other Churches in this way, many Bishops gathered for this reason, and Councils were called together in various Provinces. Writing letters to one another, they all from their various places confirmed the teaching of the assemblies: that it was not proper to celebrate the high feast of Easter on any day other than Sunday, the day on which the Lord rose from the dead, and that the fast should cease on that day.

<margin>The decree of the church regarding the Easter feast.</margin>
¶ <margin>Council at Caesarea.</margin> Even to this day, there exists the Decree of the Council held at Caesarea in Palestine, at which the foremost were Theophilus, the Bishop of Caesarea, and Narcissus, the Priest <note>Here referring to the Bishop</note> of Jerusalem. Likewise, another decree of the Council was ordained at Rome, over which the leader was Victor, the Bishop of Rome, and Palmas of the Province of Pontus.

¶ <margin>Council at Rome.</margin> <margin>France.</margin> And in Gaul <note>original: "Walschlandt," referring to the French-speaking or Celtic territories</note>, the Council of Priests was called by Irenaeus the bishop. And in Achaia, by Bacchylus, the bishop of Corinth. All of these, from various places, brought forth the consensus and sentence of their judgment.

<margin>Irenaeus means as much as "peace," from which comes the name Irenaeus the "peace-maker." <note>The Greek name *Eirenaios* is derived from *eirēnē*, meaning peace; a fitting name for his role in this dispute.</note></margin>
Neither could Polycarp persuade Anicetus to abandon that which he said his ancestors had maintained. And when they had dealt with one another in this way for a long time, they finally established communion with one another, so that Anicetus permitted Polycarp—who was worthy to use the priestly office <note>Original: "Priesterlijck officie," here referring to the privilege of presiding over the Eucharist as a guest.</note>—out of venerable contemplation; and so they departed from one another with a perfect faith and a firm love, so that all the congregations, whether they were maintaining Easter in this way or that, nevertheless always wished to maintain harmony among one another. In such a manner Irenaeus writes to reconcile and make peace within God’s congregation. And he does not write only to Victor, but he has written through all his letters to many various rulers of the Christian Churches, stating that it is not proper for any question or matter to cause discord within God’s congregation.

¶ From this passage of Irenaeus, it is manifest that if a Bishop came to Rome, the Roman Bishop grandly arranged for him, as a guest, the Sacrament called the Eucharist <term>Eucharistia: the Holy Communion or Lord's Supper, from the Greek for "thanksgiving"</term>, which also happened by chance from the other Bishops, and was undoubtedly taken up from that Apostolic custom: Since the Eucharist is a Sacrament of communion, Irenaeus rightly concludes from this that those to whom the Eucharist has been sent should not be held as heretics.

Fol. 100. Eusebius Pamphili's Chronicle / the 10th book <note>original: "den x. boeck". Although the heading says Book 10, this content actually corresponds to Book 5 of Eusebius's *Ecclesiastical History*.</note>

¶ Polycarp could not persuade Anicetus to abandon the custom which he said he had observed with his ancestors. Thus they departed from each other with a complete faith and a firm love, so that all the Churches—whether they observed Easter in this way or that—nevertheless desired to maintain harmony among themselves.

<margin>Irenaeus means "peaceful," from which comes the name Irenaeus: peacemaker.</margin>
In such a manner Irenaeus writes to reconcile and make peace within God's Church. And he did not write only to Victor <note>Victor I was the Bishop of Rome who had attempted to excommunicate the Asian churches over the Easter date.</note>, but he also wrote through all his letters to many different governors of the Christian Churches, stating that it is not proper for there to be any question or cause of discord within God's Assembly.

¶ From this passage of Irenaeus, it is evident that if a Bishop came to Rome, the Roman Bishop would honorably offer him the Sacrament called the Eucharist as a guest. This also happened by chance with other Bishops, and was undoubtedly taken up from the Apostolic custom. Since the Eucharist is a Sacrament of communion, Irenaeus rightly concludes from this that those to whom the Eucharist was sent should not be considered heretics.

# The sixth book of Eusebius Pamphilus of Caesarea, translated from the Greek into Latin by Rufinus of Aquileia.

## ¶ Concerning the persecution of the Churches under the Emperor Severus.

### The first chapter.

<margin>Severus Augustus</margin>
But while the Emperor Severus <note>Septimius Severus, Roman Emperor from 193 to 211 AD, whose reign saw localized but intense persecutions of Christians.</note> was still harassing the Assembly of Christians with persecution, there were many Knights of Christ who remained steadfast in the Faith, suffering many torments and pains; and especially in the city of Alexandria, where they were brought from all over Egypt and the Thebaid <note>The region of Upper Egypt, centered around Thebes.</note> as if to a place of battle, like valiant champions, having obtained from God the crown of immortality through their patient endurance of the torments of death.

## ¶ Concerning the martyrdom of Leonides, Origen’s father, and how Origen was raised in his youth.

### The second chapter.

<margin>Leonides, the father of Origen, a martyr.</margin>
Among these was also Leonides, the father of Origen, who was beheaded for the Confession of Christ and left behind this son of his while he was still young. And it does not seem to me improper to say a little about the courage and spirit with which this young Origen grew in his diligence and zeal for the Divine Law, especially since a great fame of him has been spread among many people.

And were someone to describe the whole of this man’s life, it is certainly of such a nature and so great that to tell it—

<column-break/>

—would require a book of its own. Nevertheless, in this present history, we shall set down in this book, with as much brevity as possible, a few things out of many, which we have learned from his own letters that have been preserved until our time, or from certain other histories. These events, as time required, are worthy to come to the knowledge of posterity, even from the time of his youth when he was taken from the cradle.

<margin>The Emperor Severus. Laetus, Prefect over Egypt. Demetrius, bishop at Alexandria.</margin>
In the tenth year of the reign of Emperor Severus, at that same time, Laetus was the presiding Governor over Alexandria and Egypt; and in that same land, Demetrius received the Bishopric after Julianus. And as the fire of persecution was ignited beyond measure, and many were being crowned with the crown of martyrdom at that time, Origen—being still a child—was so burned and ignited with such zeal to be a martyr that he willingly gave himself up to dangers.

<margin>Origen, while still young, is desirous of Martyrdom.</margin>
And when he saw that others were fighting for the faith, he quickly went to them and presented himself, so that it seemed he pursued death and wished to seize it by force. This he would have undoubtedly obtained, had he not been preserved by Divine Providence (as is well to believe) for the benefit of many people and for the edification of the entire assembly, through the carefulness of his mother, who prevented his glorious death.

<margin>He is prevented by his Mother’s carefulness.</margin>
She, at first pleading with him with motherly prayers that he should consider well and spare his mother’s heart, only caused him to be ignited all the more with the love of martyrdom, especially because it had become known to him that his father was imprisoned; he hurried greatly to be a companion to his father’s bonds and his Martyrdom, but he was prevented by the shrewdness of his mother in this way—

For they are always improving and correcting / because that which they have just corrected always displeases them soon after. And they are always seeking something new / and when they practice the same / then it seems to them to be false. What presumption lies in doing this / I suspect is not unknown even to themselves. Either they do not believe that the Holy Scripture was written by the Holy Spirit / and thus they are unbelieving: or they deem themselves to be wiser than the Holy Spirit.

And what else are they proving herewith / than that they are driven by the devil? For sometimes one still finds in their books the correction in their own hand / and they themselves confess that they have learned such from their masters and Teachers / and from such manners of falsified Scripture / they have also received such a distorted understanding of interpretation thereof.

Some of them have not even deigned to do so much as to corrupt the Scripture / but have rejected it entirely / namely the Law and the Prophets <note>Referring to the Old Testament.</note>.

<margin>They reject the law and the Prophets.</margin>
Through such ungodly and horrible rejection / they have at last fallen into the deepest stream of damnation. Concerning which enough has now been written for this History.

# The sixth book of Eusebius Pamphilus of Caesarea / translated from the Greek into Latin / by Rufinus of Aquileia.

## ¶ Of the persecution of the Churches / under Severus the Emperor.

### The first chapter.

<margin>Severus Augustus <note>Septimius Severus, Roman Emperor from 193 to 211 AD, whose reign saw localized but intense persecutions of Christians.</note>.</margin>
<note>A square woodcut decorative initial 'N' depicting a seated man in classical robes, possibly a scholar or ruler, within an architectural frame.</note>
When Emperor Severus was still harassing the assembly of Christians with persecution / there were many soldiers of Christ / who for the sake of the Faith steadfastly suffered many torments and pains / and especially in the city of Alexandria / where they, as if in a place of combat / were brought as valiant champions from all over Egypt and the Thebaid <note>The region of Upper Egypt, centered around the ancient city of Thebes.</note> / who through these torments and their patient endurance of death for God's sake, obtained the crown of immortality.

## ¶ Of the martyrdom of Leonides, the father of Origen / and how Origen was raised in his youth.

### The second chapter.

<margin>Leonides the father of Origen / a martyr.</margin>
<note>A square woodcut decorative initial 'O' featuring stylized foliage and vine patterns.</note>
Among whom was also Leonides / the father of Origen / who was beheaded for the Confession of Christ / and left behind this son of his while he was still young. And it does not seem inappropriate to me / to say a little / with what courage and spirit this young Origen grew / in the diligence and fervor of the Divine law / and this especially because a great fame of him has been spread among many people.

And were anyone to describe all of this man's life / surely his deeds are so numerous and so great / that to tell them

<column-break/>

would require a dedicated Book. Nevertheless, we shall set down in this present history with as much brevity as possible / a little out of many things in this Book / which we recognize from his own letters that have been preserved until our time / or from certain other histories. These accounts / when the time requires it / are worthy to come into the knowledge of posterity / even from his younger time since he was taken from the cradle. In the 10th year of the reign <margin>Emperor Severus. Laetus / Governor over Alexandria and Egypt. Demetrius Bishop at Alexandria.</margin> of Severus / at that same time Laetus was the high Governor over Alexandria and Egypt: and in the same land Demetrius received the Bishopric after Julian / and when the fire of persecution was kindled beyond measure / and when many were crowned with the crown of martyrdom at that same time / Origen, though still a child / was so burned / and was kindled with such fervor to be a martyr / that he willingly gave himself up to dangers.

<margin>Origen, still a boy, was eager for Martyrdom.</margin>
And when he saw that the others were fighting for the faith / he quickly went there / and presented himself / so that it seemed he pursued death / and wished to seize it by force: which he would have undoubtedly obtained / had he not been preserved by Divine providence (as is well to believe) for the profit of many people / for the edification of the entire assembly / through the care of his mother / who prevented his glorious death. <margin>Is prevented by the mother's care.</margin> Who / when she first pleaded with him with motherly prayers / that he should take good counsel / and spare his mother’s grief / he was thereby all the more kindled to the love of martyrdom, and especially for this reason / because it had now become known to him that his father was imprisoned / and he hastened greatly to be a companion of his bonds and his Martyrdom / but he was thus prevented by his mother’s cleverness <note>According to tradition, Origen’s mother hid all his clothes so that he could not leave the house to turn himself in to the authorities.</note>.

prevented. When she <note>Origen's mother.</note> had learned one evening and sensed that he intended to rise very early the next morning before daybreak, wishing to give himself up willingly to the struggle of the martyrs, she went during the night into her son’s bedroom where he was sleeping. There she secretly took all his clothes, without which he could not appear in public, so that he would be forced by necessity to remain at home. These were the first inquiries and the prelude of his youth; these were the first proofs of Origen’s piety and goodness, by which one may know what fervent love he had for God. Thereafter, he began to read and study the books of Holy Scripture, and to exercise himself diligently in the teachings of the Divine faith, in which his father had begun to instruct him. Along with the secular books <note>Original: "weerlijcke boecken" — referring to classical Greek and Roman literature, philosophy, and grammar.</note> in which he was taught in his youth, his father had also occasionally given him some Holy Scripture to read, exhorting him to value these Scriptures more than what he was learning in the schools.

<margin>How Origen was raised by his father.</margin>
And finally, the father read to him daily and entrusted these things to the child's memory, which was not unwilling; indeed, he was always more eagerly ignited to learn.

<margin>His natural talent <note>original: "Ingenium"</note> quickly showed itself in Origen.</margin>
For when he read the Scriptures, he was not satisfied with a simple understanding, but he would ask his father for the deeper meaning and sense of the Scriptures, inquiring of him how he understood that which is said: that the Holy Scripture is inspired by the Holy Spirit, and the Divine wisdom that lay behind the simplicity of the words. And the father feigned as if he were punishing him, telling him to beware of inquiring into things beyond his age. Nevertheless, he was inexpressibly joyful within himself, thanking Almighty God who had granted him to be the father of such a child.

<column-break/>

And it is said that the careful father, often while the child was sleeping, would uncover the boy's chest. Looking upon his breast, he honored it as a temple in which the Spirit of God was enclosed; and when he had kissed it with loving kisses, he went away and thanked God for the salvation granted to him through such a child. These and many similar things are said of Origen’s youth. When his father had completed his martyrdom, Origen (being seventeen years old) remained with his widowed mother and six younger brothers in great poverty, because his father’s estate—which was considerable—was recorded for confiscation and forfeited for the sake of the faith.

<margin>His property confiscated.</margin>
But the providence of Almighty God did not forsake them. Because of the sharpness of his intellect and the diligence of his piety, he was supported by a very rich and noble woman <note>A wealthy "matron" or patroness of the Christian community in Alexandria.</note>.

<margin>Supported by a matron.</margin>
She, however, had at that time chosen a man in her house to be like a son, named Paul, born in Antioch, who was a famous follower and enthusiast of an old heresy.

<margin>Paul of Antioch.</margin>
While Origen was still a youth, because he was obliged to stay with this woman, he demonstrated the Christian and faithful teaching that he had learned in his childhood. For although this aforementioned man—as a master and famous teacher—daily gathered an inexpressibly large multitude of people, not only heretics but also many of our own <note>referring to orthodox Christians</note> (because he was esteemed by all to be very learned), Origen could in no way be changed or moved, for the sake of honor or necessity, to dispute with him or speak of such things in his company. So highly did he prize the maintenance of the Christian rule in his youth, and so greatly did he abhor the company of heretics, just as he himself teaches in a book where he says that the teaching of heretics is abominable.

<margin>Origen will have no fellowship with Paul.</margin>
Nevertheless, he was also always diligent in common secular writings, in which his father had set him to learn; but he practiced himself therein much more diligently after his father had passed away. He was so learned in the arts of Grammar and Rhetoric that he kept a school to teach others, by which his father’s household was supported with what they needed.

# The Sixth Book. Folio 105.

### ¶ How Origen in his youth proclaimed the Word of GOD, and how, being a schoolmaster, through the good example of his life, he drew many to martyrdom.

## The Third Chapter.

<margin>Origen taught a good conscience.</margin>
**B** Now while Origen was maintaining the school of Grammar <note>In this context, "Grammar" refers to a classical education in literature, rhetoric, and language, which Origen taught to support his mother and six younger brothers.</note> (as he himself testifies in his own writings), there was no teacher in Alexandria among God's Assembly <note>Original: "Gods Vergaderinghe"—referring to the Christian Church or congregation.</note>, because they had all been cast out and had fled away due to the cruelties and threats of the persecutors. Thus, some of the Heathens <note>Non-Christians, specifically those practicing traditional Roman or Greek religion.</note> still came to him to learn Grammar from him, and also to hear the word of our faith and Religion. These he not only converted from unbelief to the faith, but he also <margin>Brought the Heathens to the Christian faith.</margin> taught and instructed them in the institutes of the perfect life. Among these, the first was Plutarch, who was converted by him to our faith; he not only maintained the institutes of the perfect life but (which is the ultimate salvation) finally obtained the crown of martyrdom. The other was <margin>Heraclas.</margin> Plutarch’s natural brother, named Heraclas, who, after he was taught in our faith and wisdom by Origen and had also perfectly received from him an instruction in the pure life, was chosen as Bishop of Alexandria after Demetrius. And at that same time, while Aquila was a Governor in Alexandria and <margin>Aquila, Governor of Egypt. Origen's fame. His office toward the martyrs.</margin> in Egypt, the raging persecution was increasing, when Origen was eighteen years old. In which time, gradually, his name became very famous among both believers and unbelievers, both outside and inside the house. And he was especially noted because he not only strengthened all the Saints who were imprisoned for the confession of the faith toward martyrdom through the Word and through the exhortation of perfect and spiritual teaching, but he was also helpful to the poor Christians who were perishing from want in the painfulness of the dungeon for the sake of the faith. For he was also often in the courtrooms of the Judges, and stood by the Martyrs even in their pains, and was compassionate with them in his heart, and stood firm against the improper questions and interrogations of the Judges,

<column-break/>

proving this well with his countenance and all kinds of signs, so far as it was possible to say, so that they were thereby strengthened in their answers. And when they had then received their sentence, he practiced the same faithfulness and placed himself in all dangers; nor did he shrink away even though the persecutors looked upon him horribily, and in the end, he even greeted the martyrs with a kiss. Because of this, the Heathens raised an outcry against him, but being protected by the Divine right hand, he escaped to the wonder of all people. It is not easy to tell nor to speak of what great dangers the Divine power of God delivered him many times and often—yea, daily—as he was always diligent without any weariness to proclaim God's Word. And how often they laid snares for him, those who would secretly kill him, and yet he escaped. And because he was so established in God's work, he so incensed the rage of the unbelievers that there were servants ordained for the purpose of besetting the house in which it was suspected he was living; nonetheless, he was so preserved by Divine protection that no one could seize or capture him. The hearts of men were so greatly enraged against him alone because they saw that daily many were converted through him from their unbelief to our faith. And daily such persecution was carried out against him that the great city of Alexandria could not hide him; but he was always hunted from house to house, since they saw that in all places great multitudes were converted to the faith through him. For he maintained that his perfect teaching was not only in word, but he also fulfilled it with deeds, giving an example of his spoken teaching. And it was said of him: "This is he who, as his word is, so also is his life; and such a life as he lives, such a word he also speaks." For that which he teaches, he does; and that which he does, he teaches. Divine grace was openly with him at all times, through which unspeakably many people were drawn to follow him in God's faith. When Demetrius the Bishop noticed that especially through the grace of his teachings and the proclamation of the Divine word, great multitudes came to him, he gave him the office of being a master in the assembly to interpret the word of God. This office was the first after the Apostles to be signified in Alexandria.

<margin>Is in great danger among the Heathens.</margin>
<margin>This is he who does as he teaches.</margin>
<margin>Origen becomes schoolmaster of the youth in Alexandria.</margin>

## ¶ How Origen in his youth preached the Word of GOD / and how, while being a Schoolmaster / through the good Example of his life / he drew many to martyrdom.

### The 3rd Chapter.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Origen taught a good conscience.</margin>
Now, while Origen was maintaining the school of Grammar <note>In this context, "Grammatica" refers to the comprehensive study of classical literature and language, which was the standard education of the time.</note> (as he himself testifies in his own writings), there was no master among God’s Assembly <note>The early Christian church or congregation in Alexandria.</note> in Alexandria, for they had all been cast out and had fled because of the cruelties and threats of the persecutors.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Heraclas.</margin>
The second was Plutarch’s natural brother, named Heraclas. When he had been taught in our faith and wisdom by Origen, and had also perfectly received the regulation of a pure life from him, he was later chosen as the Bishop of Alexandria after Demetrius.

<margin>Aquila, Governor of Egypt.</margin>

<margin>Origen’s fame.</margin>
This was especially because he not only strengthened all the Saints <note>Refers to the Christian faithful being held for their beliefs.</note> who were imprisoned for the confession of the faith, encouraging them toward martyrdom through the word and the exhortation of perfect and spiritual teaching; but he also assisted the poor Christians who were perishing from lack and poverty within the painful misery of the dungeons.

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>His duty toward the martyrs.</margin>
For he was also often in the tribunals <note>original: "vperscharen" (vierschaar) — the four benches that formed a traditional court of justice.</note> of the Judges, and stood by the Martyrs in their pains. proving with his countenance and all kinds of signs—as much as it was possible to say—that they were strengthened thereby in their answers. And when they had received their sentence, he practiced the same faithfulness and placed himself in all perils. Nor did he shrink back though the persecutors looked upon him with horror; he even greeted the martyrs at the end with a kiss, so that the Pagans raised a great outcry against him for it.

<margin>H</margin>
But being protected by the Divine right hand, he escaped to the wonder of all people. It is not easy to tell or to express from what great perils the Divine power of God delivered him many times and often—indeed, daily—as he was always diligent without any delay in preaching God’s Word. And how often they laid snares for him, intending to kill him secretly, yet he still escaped.

<margin>I</margin>
<margin>He is in great danger among the Pagans.</margin>
And because he was so established in God's work, he so unsettled the rage of the unbelievers that servants were ordained for the purpose of besieging the house in which he was suspected to be living. Nevertheless, he was so preserved by Divine protection that no one could seize or capture him.

<margin>K</margin>
The hearts of men were so greatly enraged against him alone because they saw that many were daily converted by him from their unbelief to our faith. And daily such persecution was carried out against him that the great city of Alexandria could not hide him; instead, he was always hunted from house to house, as they saw that in all places great multitudes were converted to the faith through him.

<margin>L</margin>
For he maintained that his perfect teaching was not in word alone, but he also fulfilled it with deeds, giving an example of his spoken teaching. And it was said of him:

<margin>This is he who does as he teaches.</margin>
"This is he whose life is just as his word is; and such a life as he lives, such a word he also speaks: for what he teaches, he does, and what he does, he teaches." Divine grace was always openly with him, through which unutterably many people were inclined to follow him in God’s faith.

<margin>M</margin>
<margin>Origen became a schoolmaster of the youth in Alexandria.</margin>
When Demetrius the Bishop noticed that, especially through the grace of his teachings and the preaching of the Divine word, great multitudes came to him, he gave him the office of being a master in the assembly to explain the word of God. This office he was the first to serve in Alexandria after the Apostles.

When he had learned one evening, and felt that he wished to rise very early in the morning before daybreak, and wanted to give himself up willingly to the struggle of martyrdom, his mother went into the bedroom during the night where her son was sleeping, and secretly took all his clothes—without which he could not appear in public—so that he would be forced by necessity to stay home. **O** These are the first inquiries and the prelude of his youth; these were the first proofs of Origen’s piety and goodness, through which one may know what a fiery love he had for God. **X** learned), Origen could in no way be moved or changed for the sake of honor or necessity to ever dispute with him or speak of such things in his company. <margin>Teaches Grammar.</margin>
