# Folio 106. Eusebius Pamphilus’ Chronicle

<margin>Judas on the weeks of Daniel.</margin>
¶ Pantænus was the first, the second was Clement, and the third was Origen, a disciple of the same Clement. Origen, in his book *Stromata* <note>original: "Stromaton" (Greek for "Miscellanies"), a collection of varied notes on Christian life and philosophy.</note>, noted in the prologue the time in which he wrote his books, which lasted until the end of the reign of Emperor Commodus. From this, it is known that the events we are now considering occurred during the time of Severus. At that same time, another writer named Judas produced an interpretation of the "weeks" written by the prophet Daniel <note>Referring to the prophecy in Daniel 9:24-27 regarding the timeline of the Messiah's coming.</note>. This Judas was writing during the tenth year of the Emperor Severus. Because of the great severity of the persecution, he suspected and even proclaimed that the Antichrist was already present, which caused many Christians to be terrified. When Origen was appointed by Bishop Demetrius to the office of the catechetical school <note>original: "schole der Vergaderinghe" — the famous School of Alexandria where new converts were instructed.</note>, he no longer cared for the teaching of worldly arts. Instead, he devoted himself more fully to the Word of God. He was prudent and diligent, and did not behave like a child. He sold his books of Pagan wisdom to a faithful friend on the condition that the friend would give him four pennies every day. He did this so that he would not be a burden to anyone, nor be troubled with providing for the necessities of his body, and so that he would not appear to be gathering money at home. He lived in this manner for a long time and was regarded by all as a "Christian Philosopher" — in his life, his manners, and all his practices. To restrain the lusts and desires of his youth and to make progress in his wisdom, he restrained himself day and night with strict abstinence. He practiced the Holy Scriptures without ceasing, living in great sobriety, fasting, and keeping vigils. When the needs of nature demanded sleep, he did not rest on a bed or anything similar, but lay down upon the bare earth. Above all things, he upheld the Gospel commandments, saying that one should fulfill the commands of our Savior with all love and diligence; for He commands that one should not have two coats, nor use shoes, nor worry about tomorrow. He worked to fulfill all these things with diligence and faith beyond his strength and his age, enduring cold and nakedness, just as the Apostle Paul exhorted. Thus, he gave all his disciples an example of blessed poverty, so that they might forsake all they possessed. And

<margin>Origen teaches Egistium.</margin>
<margin>He sells his library of Heathen books.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 10:10</margin>
<margin>He fulfills the Gospel command.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 6.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 4:11.</margin>

<column-break/>

for this reason, he was loved and welcomed by all people. He had no strife or quarreling with anyone, except for those he angered because they desired to share some of their own goods with him to provide for his needs; he refused these gifts and would take nothing, wishing to strictly maintain the commandment of poverty. This was so even though he might well have taken payment for his labor in preaching the Word of God, for which everyone thought him worthy, as the Apostle says, not only of double honor but of many kinds of honor <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 5:17, which states that elders who preach and teach are worthy of "double honor."</note>. But he considered his highest honor to be the contempt for temporal things. It is said that for many years he went barefoot without shoes and never used wine or anything similar, taking nothing more than what the bare necessities of life required, until a disease of the chest put his life in peril and forced him to change his ways. With such examples of his life, he instructed those whom he converted from worldly philosophy to the true "life-wisdom" of Christ and His true Philosophy. He did not only teach them to maintain the faith in the innermost secrets of their souls—which he himself did outwardly—but he also worked and exhorted them through such daily practice to the love of martyrdom. Some of these disciples were indeed imprisoned during the persecution and obtained the crown of martyrdom.

<margin>1 Timothy 5:17.</margin>

<margin>Origen emasculated himself.</margin>
¶ God. And he did this not only to maintain his purity, but to remove any evil suspicion and the occasion for gossip that might arise from it: thus he fulfilled the Lord’s voice <note>A reference to Matthew 19:12, which Origen famously interpreted literally in his youth.</note> through his own actions, especially since during the time of persecution he preached the Word of God both in secret and in public to women as well as to men. And although he wished to keep this act secret and did not seek the praise of men, it could not remain hidden, but came to the knowledge of Demetrius the Bishop. At first, Demetrius was greatly amazed at the bold strength of Origen's spirit and praised the greatness and fervor of his faith and such a great undertaking in the work of God.

¶ He then said to Origen: "Continue steadfastly in the work of teaching and preaching, for the persecutors now have no cause to suspect evil of you." Such was his opinion of Origen at that time, before his mind was turned against him.

<margin>Origen. The Priesthood.</margin>
¶ When he later saw that this young man’s fame had greatly increased, and that he was held in higher esteem daily within the City, he began—pricked by envy—to disparage what he had previously highly praised. For when worthy and singular men, the excellent Bishops of Palestine—namely Alexander, the Bishop of Jerusalem, and Theoctistus, the Bishop of Caesarea—saw his divine understanding of the Word of God, they wished to ordain him a Priest. They even deemed him worthy of the high priesthood <note>Likely referring to the office of bishop or a high ranking within the presbytery.</note>, and everyone said he was worthy of the honor because of his wisdom and the virtues within him. This was greatly envied by Demetrius; finding no fault in him regarding any misconduct, he brought forth as a "misuse" that which he had previously praised <note>Meaning Origen’s act of self-mutilation, which technically disqualified a man from the priesthood under canon law.</note>, laying the blame on those who had ordained him. But these events happened long afterward.

<margin>Demetrius, the hater of Origen.</margin>
¶ Thus Origen, being a Teacher of the Assembly in Alexandria, was highly esteemed among all those who had cause to come there by his fame and to hear him preaching the Word of God. As the Apostle says, he taught in every way he could, day and night, secretly and openly, being unhindered by all things that might have obstructed him; and being present there, he fulfilled his office with all

<column-break/>

<margin>Antoninus / Severus the Emperor.</margin>
¶ confidence. When Severus had held the empire for eighteen years, his son Antoninus <note>Better known to history as Emperor Caracalla.</note> became Emperor after him. In this time, there were very many who sought the glory of God in their confession; nevertheless, they were preserved and sustained through God's providence.

# Of Alexander and Narcissus, Bishops of Jerusalem.

## The 7th Chapter.

<margin>Alexander, Bishop of Jerusalem.</margin>
Among these was Alexander, of whom we have spoken before; he was chosen as Bishop of Jerusalem while Narcissus, who had previously held the Bishopric, was still living. <margin>Narcissus.</margin> But since we have now mentioned Narcissus, it seems fitting to relate something of his history, of which many things are kept in the memory of the inhabitants of that land. We will tell only one of his stories, from which one may easily believe the other accounts told of him.

<margin>The solemn day of the Easter Vigil.</margin>
It happened on an Easter Vigil <note>original: "Paesch-avondt" — the night before Easter Sunday.</note> that there was no oil <term>olpe|lamp oil</term> in the lamps, and when this became known through the servants, the people were grieved. But Narcissus, full of confidence and strong in faith, commanded the servants to draw water and bring it to him. When they had brought the water, <margin>Water into oil.</margin> he prayed and blessed the water, and commanded that it be poured into the lamps. And suddenly, through a wonderful power of God, the nature of the water was changed into the richness of oil, and it gave off a clearer light than was usual. For the greater belief in this history, the oil that was changed from water was still preserved by many Brothers of that place, so that the knowledge and proof of the miracle has even come down to us. Thus was the proof of his faith examined; but how great the strength of his spirit was shall also be proven by one of his deeds.

As this Narcissus, among all his other good virtues, was very steadfast in spirit and immovable in that which was righteous, there were some wicked men who were evildoers. Fearing that if they were punished for their sins, they would not be able to escape the penalty, they went and conspired together against him

D In the book *Stromata*, he cites Holy Scripture, not only for the strengthening of our faith, but also the writings of the ancient Greek Teachers; for it seemed fitting to him that in this book he should compare the teachings both together with one another, and prove our faith not only with the Holy Scripture, but also with the ancient writings of the old, wise Greeks, and also with such writings as the other Heathens consider to be good. # The Chronicle of Eusebius Pamphilus
## [of the Church]

<margin>The Gospel of John.</margin>
¶ ...was proclaimed. When Peter later learned of this, even though he had not commanded it, he nevertheless praised it. <margin>Alexander of Jerusalem to Origen.</margin>
¶ Alexander, of whom we spoke above, writing to Origen, makes mention of Clement and Pantenus, as those who were known to him in the flesh. And he writes thus: "It has been the will of God, as you well know, that the friendship which I have held from the fathers shall remain unblemished, and that it always be increased more fervently and strongly. We know that the Fathers who were before us are blessed, to whom we also shall come after a short time: I mean Pantenus, my Lord truly blessed, and the holy man my Lord Clement, who both taught and instructed me in many things; but also all the others who are such, through whom I also have knowledge of you, whom I regard as a worthy man, and as my Lord and my brother." These are the words of the aforementioned Clement <note>The text likely refers to the letter written by Alexander mentioning Clement, preserved by Eusebius.</note>.

<margin>Adamantius</margin>
<margin>Origen visits the ancient Roman church.</margin>
¶ While Zephyrinus <note>The Dutch text reads "Severinus," but historical records and Eusebius's original text identify the Bishop of Rome at this time (c. 211–217 AD) as Zephyrinus.</note> was Bishop of the Roman Church during this time, Origen—who was also named Adamantius <note>A nickname meaning "man of steel" or "unconquerable," referring to his tireless work ethic.</note>—came to Rome, as he himself writes in a certain place, because he desired to see the ancient Roman congregation. And staying there no long time, he hastily returned again to Alexandria to his office of teaching. There he fulfilled his accepted work with all diligence and care, not only through the admonition and support of Demetrius, who was then Bishop, but he also took it upon himself so that the hearers would not lack the instruction of the Divine teachings.

### ¶ Concerning Heraclas, whom Origen took into his office.

->The 12th Chapter.<-

As Origen now saw that he was not capable of doing everything—such as investigating deep questions and explaining the Holy Scripture, and also daily instructing every person in the faith who—

<column-break/>

—came to him and had newly become Christians. He was so encumbered by these people that he did not have one hour of free time, and was always called from one thing to another, so that from early morning until dark evening, his place was never empty; some were arriving and others were not leaving, because they were bound together by the sweetness of the Word of God. Thus it seemed more appropriate to him that he should separate from himself those who were just beginning in the faith, and he entrusted that same office to one of his disciples, who was very well and perfectly learned, and proven in all virtues, <margin>Heraclas the Assistant <note>original: "Hypodiāculus"; a term for a helper or sub-teacher.</note> or helper, teaching the school of the beginning, and Origen [teaching] the school of the perfect.</margin> named Heraclas, whom he made a partner in his office and labor. This same man was very eloquent in speech, and also very learned in all philosophical teachings. To him he handed over the office of teaching those who had newly become Christians, laying the foundation of the faith, while keeping for himself the instruction of the perfect <note>In this context, the "perfect" refers to advanced students or those fully initiated into the deeper mysteries of theology.</note>.

### ¶ What diligence Origen applied to the Holy Scripture, and how he also learned the Hebrew language.

->The 13th Chapter.<-

<margin>Learns the Hebrew language</margin>
Among other diligent works that Origen performed to better understand the Holy Scripture, he also investigated and learned the power of the Hebrew language, so that he might know the truth found in the literal letter of that same language, and what difference there is between those who have translated the Scripture—including the 70 Translators <note><term>Septuagint</term>: The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally attributed to seventy scholars.</note>, as well as Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, and some others who are not common. <margin>The copies of the Old Testament varied.</margin> And he found such [copies] in secret places where the name of the translator was not mentioned. He says only of these that he found another translation in the city of Actia near Nicopolis, and another in Jericho, and still others in some other places. For these reasons, he was the first to find the method by which he wrote the translations of various translators side-by-side, so that he first wrote the Bible in Hebrew, with Hebrew... <note>This refers to the creation of the *Hexapla*, a massive six-columned comparison of the Old Testament.</note>

Fol. 113.
# The Sixth Book.

<margin>The sixth and seventh editions.</margin>
...Hebrew letters; secondly, he wrote the Hebrew words in Greek letters; thirdly, he added the translation of Aquila; fourthly, [that of] Symmachus; fifthly, the Seventy Translators <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, which is our [version]; the sixth, Theodotion’s translation. For which reasons he called these books *Hexapla*, that is, "six-fold." In the Psalter and some other books, he added something from other translations that had no name, which he called the seventh translation.

### ¶ Concerning Symmachus the Translator.

#### The 14th Chapter.

<margin>Symmachus an Ebionite.</margin>
However, one should know that one of these translators, named Symmachus, was an Ebionite <note>An early Jewish-Christian sect that maintained Jewish law and saw Jesus as a human prophet rather than divine.</note>, which is a heresy that says Christ was born of Joseph and Mary and was a mere human, and that the Law should be kept in the Jewish manner, as we have said above.

This Symmachus also wrote commentaries on Matthew, in which he seeks to confirm the authority of his heresies.

Origen himself writes this, stating that he found them with a woman named Juliana, who said she had received the books from Symmachus himself.

### ¶ How Ambrosius and many others were converted by Origen: And whether it is appropriate for laypeople to dispute in the Church when the Bishop is present.

#### The 15th Chapter.

<margin>Ambrosius turns away from the error of the Valentinians.</margin>
Among these was a man named Ambrosius, very renowned in lineage and also in learning, who was tainted with the Valentinian <note>Followers of Valentinus, a major Gnostic teacher who held complex views on the nature of the divine and the material world.</note> heresy, and was overcome by Origen, so that he was enlightened with the radiance of the true light, leaving behind the dark errors and converting to the light and radiance of the Holy Assembly <note>original: "H. Vergaderinghe"; refers to the Church.</note>. And many other learned men, well-examined in wisdom, when they heard of the great fame of Origen

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin>
in all lands, they came to him, some to dispute with him; others, who had better intentions, to hear the truth and live according to it. Countless disciples who were highly regarded came, were won over, and having repentance, left their error. And also the great philosophers, who were highly esteemed, confessed that Origen had no equal, both in their wisdom and in ours.

<margin>H Origen instructed the youths in philosophy.</margin>
He had a custom, when he saw intelligent youths inclined toward learning, to also give them to learn the same things that philosophers are first allowed to learn: a part of geometry, or arithmetic, and all that serves for instruction in disputation. When necessity sometimes required that he should explain some books of the philosophers, he was also heard by the most learned men in that same art with such wonder that he was held by them as the supreme [teacher], and as one of the ancient and first philosophers. <margin>J</margin>

<margin>I Admonishes his followers to the liberal arts of learning.</margin>
He exhorted the laypeople and the unlearned to study, saying that learning is a great help to understanding the scripture, both in the liberal arts <note>original: "vrye Consten"; the traditional academic subjects of the medieval and ancient world.</note> and in philosophy. For he said that our Christian faith is the true philosophy, and that Greek philosophy is a part of it. And therefore, he said, truth does not lose its part because falsehood, coming before, has claimed it. Of his teachings, there are many witnesses, even among the philosophers, some of whom wrote their books to him, and some brought their books to him to be approved according to his judgment.

<margin>K L Porphyry, a mocker of the Christians.</margin>
When Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who was one of the most famous pagan opponents of Christianity.</note> in Sicily, who wrote many books against us in which he blasphemes the Divine Scripture—coming to the interpreters of that same scripture, he could find nothing in Origen’s books that he could punish <note>find fault with</note>, so he turned to speaking ill of him, and mocking him, and shaming him for that which makes him worthy of all honor to us; in some things speaking the truth, but in others, as he is accustomed to do, falsely fabricating. And sometimes he regards him as a great philosopher, at other times he despises him again as a Christian. And listen to what he says of him:

<margin>M The words of Porphyry from the 3rd book against the Christians.</margin>
"These Christians (he says), who adhere to the Scripture of the Jews, and finding therein no certain understanding or interpretation, turn to improper and unfit narratives, which were written more so that they would be pleasing and agreeable to the reader..."

...would be, rather than for some instruction in the same Scriptures which are dark to understand. <margin>Origen the student of Ammonius the philosopher</margin>
¶ And thereafter he says again: The beginning of this improper and unheard-of exposition has its origin from a man whom I saw when I was still very young, who was the superior in all learning, as still shown by the books he left behind; this was Origen, who is the foremost among all their Masters; he was a disciple of Ammonius, who was the most excellent philosopher of his time. But regarding learning, Origen followed his master Ammonius so closely that it seems all the Wisdom of the master was entirely poured out into the disciple. But in life and purpose, he went another, contrary way than his master. For while Ammonius was a Christian in his youth and born of Christian parents, yet upon reaching maturity of understanding and entering the gate of Philosophy, he quickly turned himself back to the proper manner of life <note>Porphyry implies here that Ammonius returned to paganism, a claim Eusebius disputes later on this page.</note>.

<margin>Porphyry calls the Christians a foreign religion</margin>
¶ But Origen did entirely the opposite, who was born a Heathen of Father and mother, and was also learned in Greek Wisdom, yet he turned himself to that life of a foreign Religion; and devoting himself to it, he thus defiled and corrupted all his precious understanding that was adorned with Philosophical wisdom; for taking on that life, he acted as a Christian and as an evil person, and thus darkened that precious light of the teaching and Wisdom of the Greeks with his improper and unfit fables. For he had obtained all that wisdom, all the secrets of Plato, and he was learned in the books of Numenius and Chronius, and in Apollophanes and Longinus, and also in Moderatus and Nicomachus; and the foremost sect of Pythagoras was not hidden from him, but he had searched all commentaries

<column-break/>

of their most learned. He had also diligently read through the books of Chaeremon the Stoic and Cornutus, from which he took all the secret and hidden wisdom of the Greeks and mixed them with this foreign sect and with Jewish superstitions, and thus turned the glory of the philosophers to foreign and strange teachings. These are the words of Porphyry in the third book that he wrote against the Christians, in one part telling the truth, and in the other lying: For regarding the great learning and understanding of the aforementioned man, he has said nothing other than what is true: But that he says that he [Origen] came from Heathenism to a Christian life, and that Ammonius fell from Christianity to the error of the Heathens, is obviously false

<margin>Ammonius remained a Christian, born of believing parents.</margin>
and a lie; for Origen's grandfather and great-grandfather were Christians, and his father (as we have said before) was martyred. In so doing, we follow the example of the Apostolic man Pantenus, our predecessor, who was very learned in Greek wisdom and in Philosophy, and also Heraclas, who is now a Priest in Alexandria, whom I found with the Master of the Philosophers, who for some years...

And so that he might avoid all slander, he set aside his common clothing <note>Original: *habijt*, referring to the everyday dress of a citizen.</note> which he used to wear, and took up the philosopher’s garb, which he still wears to this day; nor does he cease reading the books of the philosophers, but still studies them daily with all his might. Origen wrote this in response to those who complained about him.

At this same time, while he was thus diligently exercising himself in the Word of God at Alexandria, a messenger <note>Original: *Kupterman*, likely a transcription error for *Kourier-man* (courier).</note> arrived, bringing a letter for him, one for Bishop Demetrius, and one for the Governor of Egypt. In those times, Origen also began to write commentaries on the Holy Scripture, being compelled thereto by the many prayers and entreaties of Ambrosius. This Ambrosius applied such diligence to the task that he abundantly provided everything necessary for this work. He provided Origen with seven notaries <note>Shorthand writers who recorded dictation in real-time.</note> who were to be taught by him and remain with him without ceasing, following one after another, for Origen dictated without stopping. He also provided seven other writers <note>Copyists or scribes who produced the final clean manuscripts.</note>, and as many young maidens who were also well-instructed and learned in writing. In this manner, Ambrosius abundantly furnished him with everything he required, urging him daily to complete the work of the Word of God. But Ambrosius was also very diligent in the Word of God himself, for which reason he was worthy that Origen should perform such service for him in return, revealing to him what was secret and hidden in the Holy Scripture.

### ¶ Concerning the persecution of Maximinus.

->The 20th Chapter.<-

<margin>Maximinus the emperor.</margin>
Now when Emperor Alexander <note>Alexander Severus, reigned 222–235 AD.</note> had ruled the Empire for thirteen years, he died, and after him came Emperor Maximinus. He was very envious of the household of Alexander, his predecessor, and he commanded a new persecution against the leaders of the Christian teachings, ordering them to be killed as they were the cause of such a sect being maintained.

<margin>Origen writes a book to Ambrose concerning martyrdom.</margin>
During this same time, Origen wrote a book on martyrdom to Ambrose, which came into many hands; some were so strengthened in the faith by it that they willingly gave themselves over to martyrdom. Thus, many were martyred in those years during which Maximinus carried out the persecution.

<margin>Gordian the emperor.</margin>
<margin>Anterus, Bishop.</margin>

### ¶ How Beryllus was overcome by Origen.

## The 23rd Chapter.

Beryllus, of whom we have spoken before, was a Bishop of the city called Bostra, <margin>The godless teaching of Beryllus.</margin> situated in the land of Arabia. He was diligent in corrupting and violating the true and Apostolic Teaching. He began to teach strange things which were far from the truth, saying: That our Lord and Savior Christ was I not present before the birth of his body, and that he properly had no Divine essence, but that only the Father’s Divinity dwelt in him. For this reason, many Bishops gathered and held great disputes with him. But among them all, Origen was most heartily prayed and exhorted that he should dispute against this Beryllus. K And thus Origen went there; and first, by disputing with him gradually, he diligently examined Beryllus's views. And when he had done so, he quickly showed him what lack of understanding and misuse he had conceived, and what evil and error must L result from such an opinion. He advised him <margin>Beryllus is reformed by Origen.</margin> to reject his proposed error and return to the true and blessed teaching. <margin>By teaching, he healed the master of these errors.</margin> This event is M unheard of in such matters: for he so drove out the error from the congregation of God that he also healed and converted the master of those very errors.

It is also said that this dispute between Origen and Beryllus is still recorded in writing, which is itself a clear proof of his most excellent learning.

It is said that he gladly received that which was commanded of him by the Priest, and that the Divine fear was in him, and he approved and praised our faith with words and deeds.

### Concerning the converted teaching of the Arabs, and how Origen overcame them.

#### The 27th chapter.

AT that same time, a new heresy arose in the land of Arabia, so that there were some who said that the Souls of men were corrupted together with the bodies and were perishable, and that the souls in the time of the resurrection would be awakened again with the bodies <note>This specific heresy is known as "thnetopsychism," the belief that the soul dies with the body and is resurrected later.</note>. <margin>Origen brings to naught the heresy of the Elcesaites.</margin>
**T**here was yet another heresy at the same time, which was named the Elcesaites <note>The Elcesaites were a Jewish-Christian baptismal sect that emerged in the 2nd century; they were known for their syncretic beliefs and for teaching that one could outwardly deny the faith during persecution while remaining a believer in one's heart.</note>; as soon as it arose, he [Origen] obscured it and brought it to nothing.

They teach this same thing, and carry a book with them everywhere, which they say came down from Heaven; and they claim that whoever hears it read shall receive forgiveness of sins, and that it is another forgiveness than that which Christ has given.

# Eusebius Pamphilus’s Chronicle / of the

<margin>A</margin>
This persecution did not take its beginning among us from the Emperor’s Mandate <note>Refers to the official edict of Emperor Decius around 249–250 AD; Eusebius is noting that mob violence started earlier.</note>, but the servant of the Devils began it, a year before that Mandate was published. This servant was called the "divine man" in our city, because he incited the common, wild people against us. By him, the multitude of people was so inflamed that they dared nothing else but to thirst for the blood of the righteous. And first, they caught a good old man named <margin>Metranes</margin> Metranus, and commanded him to speak evil words against our faith. And when he refused to do so, they beat him with sticks all over his body, and they pierced his face and eyes with sharp reeds; and having been thus tortured, they cast him out of the city, and while there was still a little breath left in him, they drove it out with stones.

<margin>C Quinta.</margin>
After that, they took a noblewoman named Cointha <note>Also known in other traditions as Quinta.</note>, and led and forced her to worship the idols. And when she refused to do so—indeed, rather blaspheming their gods—they took a rope and bound it to her feet, and dragged her through all the streets of the city, and thus killed her with a horrific and shameful manner of pain. After that, they all together with one accord fell upon the houses of the servants of God, robbing and breaking their goods, and destroying everything with a hostile cruelty, so that they took away the most precious goods; and the remainder, which was not worth much, they gathered together in the streets and burned it.

<margin>Hebrews 11. D</margin>
But our people (as the Apostle said) received the plundering of their goods with joy. <note>original: "de beroovinge van haren goeden met blijdschap ontfanghen" - a reference to Hebrews 10:34/11 regarding the endurance of early Christians.</note>

<margin>Apollonia. S</margin>
And when they had also captured an old virgin named Apollonia, they first pulled out all her teeth. After that, they made a great fire of wood and threatened her with it, saying they would burn her alive therein unless she would renounce God together with them. And when she saw her fire burning, she was thinking within herself for a short while, but suddenly she withdrew herself from the hands of the wicked servants, and thus willingly leaped into the fire with which they had threatened her; so that even the servants of wickedness were terrified that she was more ready to die than they were to kill.

<margin>T Serapion.</margin>
And when they had bound Serapion in his home, they inflicted many cruel pains upon him: and first they nearly dismembered him entirely, and finally threw him out of a window. There was not one person of our people who was present on the road, nor was it permitted for us to walk in the streets; and there was no freedom by day or night to go out without peril. <margin>The Christians were forbidden from walking in the streets during the time of persecution.</margin> For if anyone of ours appeared in public, there was immediately an uproar and a shrieking among the common people, so that whoever was seized by the people was dragged by the feet or burned in the fire. <margin>V</margin> As such evil increased daily, a raging riot was suddenly kindled among the persecutors, and through discord they fought one another in the city; and by this, we had a little rest. <margin>X</margin> But it did not last long. For suddenly the most bitter mandates of the Emperor were sent, through which such unspeakable devastation was committed against us, so that the word was fulfilled which was spoken before by the Lord: <margin>Matthew 24.</margin> if it were possible, even the elect would be offended. <note>The translator uses "geschandaliseert" (offended/scandalized), here meaning to be tripped up or led into sin/apostasy.</note> <margin>Mandate against the Christians.</margin> Because of this Mandate, they were almost all so terrified that some of the nobles who were Christians gave themselves up voluntarily, without being called, to renounce the faith.

<margin>Y Apostates</margin>
Some others were only summoned and appeared before the Judge, and some were also reported and accused by their own household and neighbors; they hurried toward the horrific sacrifices and unclean offerings. Some others went all trembling and entirely pale in color, so that it appeared more that they themselves were to be sacrificed than that they would sacrifice to the idols; so much so that some of the common people mocked them, because they seemed to be in such agony and fear both to sacrifice and to die. Some others leaped so shamelessly to the altars that they wished to reassure everyone they had never been Christian. <margin>Z Matthew 19. 23 Matthew 9.</margin> These were they of whom the Lord had spoken before: That they shall hardly be saved. <note>Refers to the difficulty of the rich or the unfaithful entering the kingdom of heaven.</note> Others followed these stubbornly, or they ran away. Some of those were captured and thrown into the prison, and some, as soon as they came before the Judge, renounced the faith; and when some began to be tortured even a little, they also fell away from the faith. But those who [were] blessed...

### Of the Older Christian Churches. The Sixth Book.

<margin>Cathari.</margin>
**A** Cathari / which is as much as to say in Greek / **The pure and unstained**. <note>original: "De suyvere ende onbesmette"; from the Greek 'Katharoi'. This group believed the Church should not readmit those who had denied their faith under persecution.</note> Because of this matter, sixty Bishops and sixty Priests, along with very many Deacons, gathered in the city of Rome and held a Council there. And furthermore, letters were written to other Bishops in various provinces, so that they might also make known their advice and opinion on what should be done in this proceeding.

<margin>Council at Rome.</margin>
**B** Thus it was ordained there, that Novatus <note>Though the text calls him Novatus, this refers to Novatian, a Roman priest who made himself a rival Pope; he is often confused in early modern texts with Novatus of Carthage.</note>—along with all those who followed him out of the arrogance and pride of their hearts, turning toward this inhumane opinion against brotherly love—should be <margin>Cut off.</margin> cut off from the Assembly. And it was decided that those who had fallen during the struggle <note>Referring to the 'Lapsi', Christians who renounced their faith during the Decian persecution.</note> should be healed again through brotherly mercy and the nourishment of repentance.

<margin>Letter from Cornelius, Bishop of Rome, to Fabian regarding Novatus.</margin>
**C** Regarding these matters, Cornelius, the Bishop of Rome, wrote to the Assembly of Antioch, informing Fabian <note>historically Fabius</note>, the Bishop of that same city, what the Council gathered at Rome had ordained, as well as the judgment of the Italians, the Africans, and the other Western provinces. Concerning this, <margin>Cyprian</margin> Cyprian, a Bishop of Carthage, wrote a magnificent book: in which he admonishes all those who have fallen to repent; and all those who are against this or speak against it, he concludes and writes that they are strangers and cut off from the Body of Christ.

**D** There is yet another Letter, which Cornelius the Bishop of Rome wrote to Fabian the Bishop of Antioch, in which he writes who and what kind of man this Novatus was in life and manners, and in what way he had departed from the Assembly of God:

**E** And he says that he fell into all of this because of a certain desire to be a Bishop, which desire he secretly carried in his heart; and he was especially puffed up because, in his beginning, he had won over to his opinion and received as companions some upright men who had confessed the name of Christ during the persecution.

**F** Among these was <margin>Maximus, Urbanus, Sidonius, Celerinus.</margin> Maximus, a Priest of the Roman Assembly, and Urbanus, who had twice confessed the Name of Christ during the persecution, and also Sidonius and Celerinus, who were also very famous

<column-break/>

**G** among the confessors, because they had fought steadfastly and had suffered and overcome all manners of Torments. But these men saw that Novatus was doing all his deeds with deceit, and with lies and false oaths, and that he only feigned goodness so that he might deceive simple and unlearned people; so they left him behind and shunned him,

<margin>Public confession of sins.</margin>
**H** and they returned to the Assembly with great repentance. In the presence of the Bishops and Priests, and also before laymen, they first confessed their wandering, and thereafter revealed the aforementioned deceit of Novatus: how he used to always swear to the Brethren that he in no way desired any Bishopric,

**I** yet he quickly undertook to be a Bishop. He ordained statutes and certain teachings, and thus he received that Bishopric arrogantly, but not from God. For he was brought to it by three simple Bishops and plain men to whom these things were not known—men from the furthest reaches of Italy—whom he had brought there through subtle and deceptive persuasions to consecrate him, not in the customary manner, but mostly in a written manner <note>Likely referring to a non-canonical or fraudulent appointment.</note>.

<margin>They turn toward the Judge and confess openly to being Christians.</margin>
Among the torments / so that they were raising their hands / and stood with various signs of their bodies so as to strengthen the courage of him who was in suffering / so that the unbelievers / who were gathered there / perceived it / and it brought some of them to the same opinion they themselves held: Who, before the common people had called out over them / so they leaped forward into the middle before the Judge / and confessed that they were Christians. <margin>A</margin>
What shall I say of the teaching that recently began in the lands of Pentapolis? <note>Pentapolis refers to a region in North Africa (modern Libya) where the Sabellian heresy—which denied the distinct persons of the Trinity—first gained a foothold.</note> This teaching is full of blasphemies against God the Father and our Lord JESUS CHRIST, denying and saying that he is not the true Son of the Father; furthermore, they deny the understanding and grace of the Holy Spirit.

I investigated the matter in the presence of the brothers to the best of my ability and my small understanding, and I later committed this to writing, explaining and distinguishing certain authorities of the Holy Scriptures, which may be found in the books I have sent to you.

<margin>Dionysius proves from the 5th book on baptism to Sixtus.</margin>
There was a brother among us who had been a believer from of old, even before I or my predecessor Heraclas <note>Heraclas was the Bishop of Alexandria from 232 to 248 AD, preceding Dionysius.</note> were ordained Bishop. When this man was present among those who were being baptized, and heard what was being asked of them and what they answered, he came to me weeping. He fell down at my feet and began to confess that the baptism he had received from the heretics was entirely different. Because he saw that the baptism administered by us was different, he considered his own to be no baptism at all, as all their confessions were filled with blasphemies and godless slanders. He said that he felt such remorse for this error that he did not dare to lift his eyes to God.

## ¶ Of Emperor Valerian, who was first good, and thereafter persecuted the Christian Church.

### The 9th Chapter.

<margin>Valerian and Gallienus, emperors.</margin>
<margin>Dionysius of Alexandria, to Hermammon regarding Emperor Valerian. Revelation 13:5.</margin>
But when Gallus had served as Emperor for barely two years, he died. After him, Valerian received the Empire, along with his son Gallienus. Concerning him, Dionysius writes again to Hermammon in this manner, which also stands in the Revelation of John, saying: "And there was given unto him a mouth speaking great things and blasphemies; and power was given unto him to continue forty and two months." <note>Dionysius interprets the "Beast" from Revelation 13 as a prophecy for Valerian’s reign of persecution.</note> Both of these were fulfilled in this Emperor Valerian.
<margin>Read more here about the imprisonment.</margin>
For it is quite wonderful to consider how kind and mild he was in the beginning toward the servants of God—more so than all the Emperors who came before him—so that he seemed to show favor even to those who were called Christians in name only. He honored the servants of the Lord so greatly that his entire household was like a church of the Lord. But afterwards, he was corrupted and turned away from the truth by a teacher, a wicked master and prince of all the sorcerers from Egypt <note>historical: "doctor... van alle Toovenaers upt Egypten" — likely referring to the official Macrianus, who was said to have influenced Valerian toward magic and anti-Christian sentiment.</note>. Thus, he commanded that holy and righteous men should be persecuted and killed, as they were the ones who opposed the sorcery with which he was defiled.

There were at that same time—and are even now—those who, through their faith, were well able to extinguish the Devil’s cunning and deceit. This Emperor commanded that young children be killed to perform his unclean ceremonies and hideous sacrifices. He robbed parents of their children and searched through their tender limbs for human veins, seeking a voice where he had driven out the life. He writes many other such evil things concerning Valerian, and that he was—

<column-break/>

<margin>His eyes were put out.</margin>
captured by the Barbarians, where his eyes were put out <note>Valerian was the first Roman Emperor to be taken captive in battle, falling to the Persian King Shapur I in 260 AD. Tradition states he was treated with great cruelty.</note>, and he left his children as followers of his wickedness and impurity.

## ¶ What Dionysius suffered in the persecution.

### The 10th Chapter.

<margin>Germanus the Bishop.</margin>
<margin>Dionysius is led away into exile.</margin>
<margin>Paraetonium, a place in Egypt.</margin>
<margin>Maximus, Dionysius, and Demetrius. Lucius. Faustinus, Aquila.</margin>
What this same Dionysius suffered in this persecution, and what martyrdom they inflicted upon him for the name of the Lord, he wrote to a Bishop named Germanus. This man appears to have been his detractor <note>original: "achterclapper" — a slanderer or backbiter.</note>, and to him Dionysius wrote the account of his confession, which took place before Aemilianus the judge. In this account, as Dionysius said that one ought to worship only the one single God who made Heaven and Earth, and that the others were not gods nor should they be worshipped, he was sent away and confined in misery in the desert, at a stronghold called Cephro. This was done because the people of that land were entirely inclined toward idolatry, so that they received Dionysius with a cruel spirit and a perverse mind. But afterwards, when he sowed the word of God among the people through the grace of God alone, the greater part of those coarse and cruel people were converted to the Almighty God and turned away from their idolatry, becoming subjects of Christ. When this was discovered, they removed him again from the castle and brought him near Alexandria to a desolate place where no man lived. Since our people visited him there (because the place was situated so near the city) and received him like a sweet scent of the Good Shepherd, the common people were strengthened by him toward martyrdom. So they again sent a captain with horsemen and bound this Dionysius, and with him Gaius and Peter, with chains. They inflicted many kinds of pain upon them and led them into the desert of Libya, and there left them bound in a desolate, dark, and abandoned place. They left them there, three days' journey from Paraetonium in the lands of Egypt, without any help from men. The aforementioned man wrote this in his various letters, in which he also relates that Maximus the priest and Dioscorus, Demetrius and Lucius, and also Faustinus and Aquila, became very famous confessors. And some of the deacons died in the islands after they had steadfastly confessed their faith.

### ¶ Of the Martyrs who were martyred at Caesarea in Palestine.

<margin>

During the time when Valerian persecuted at Caesarea in Palestine, many suffered various kinds of martyrdom there. Among these, three youths were particularly notable: one named Priscus, the second Malchus, and the third Alexander.

As these men lived in the suburbs of Caesarea, they were ignited with a divine fire of faith and rebuked one another for their lukewarmness and sluggishness. A woman martyr.

### ¶ Concerning Asterius the martyr.

### Chapter 13.

<margin>Asterius the martyr.</margin>
Among these there was also, above all others, an illustrious nobleman, a Senator in the City of Rome, very wealthy and of royal descent, named Asterius. He was present when Marinus was beheaded, and took the dead body upon his shoulders, covering it with his own garment. Because of this honor which he showed the martyr, he himself shortly thereafter became a martyr. He performed many other pious Christian works in the faith of Christ, as those who knew him in the flesh have told us. Among these, this also happened through him:

<margin>Caesarea Philippi, called Paneas.</margin>
At Caesarea Philippi, on a certain day, some sorcery-idolatry <note>original: "wighels-afgoderije"</note> took place at the foot of a mountain called Panium, from which the Jordan has its source where it first begins to flow. It was a custom in this place, following ancient pagan errors, that on a festival day a sacrifice was offered to the gods, which by the devil’s art and deceit always quickly vanished, so that it was seen no more. This was then regarded as a great miracle, so that those who witnessed it were made to believe that the sacrifice was invisibly taken up into Heaven.

<margin>The wondrous work regarding the sacrifice, which could be seen nowhere.</margin>
While this was happening, Asterius was present; and noticing that all the people were held in their idolatry by this wonder at the miracle, he was dismayed and felt pity for this great delusion of the people. He turned his eyes and also his hands, sighing toward Heaven, and called upon Christ—who is God above all—with total trust and tears, that He might punish the deception and sorcery of the deceitful devil,

<column-break/>

and reveal to the wretched people the secret of this error. When he had prayed thus while weeping, it was quickly seen how the sacrifice—which they had suspected was invisibly taken to heaven—[floated] upon the water, so that afterward such error no longer occurred in that place. Thus, through the prayer of a Christian, such an ancient fraud, which had been carried out for so long by the Devil and his servants, was destroyed.

### ¶ Concerning the miracles that occurred
### through the power of the Savior 
### Christ, at Paneas.

### Chapter 14.

<margin>The woman who was healed of the issue of blood was a citizen of Caesarea Philippi. Matthew 9:20.</margin>
<margin>This cast work representing the miracle shown to this woman was destroyed by Julian the Emperor.</margin>
<margin>The wondrous work of the herb, as it grows up to the hem of the garment.</margin>
And since we have mentioned this city, it is not improper to include in this history that the woman who was delivered from the issue of blood by our Savior—as the Evangelists testify to us—was a citizen of this city of Caesarea, and her house is still shown there to this day. Above the door of her house, one sees upon high pillars a likeness of a woman cast in bronze, slightly bending her knees and stretching out her hands in supplication. And the other cast image is a likeness and figure of a man <note>Representing Jesus Christ.</note>, clothed in a dignified garment, stretching out his right hand toward the woman. At the foot of this image on the pillar grew a remarkable herb of a new kind. When it sprouts, it grows no higher than the hem of the cast image; and when it climbs and has grown so high that it touches the hem, it acquires the power to heal all kinds of sicknesses and infirmities, whatever bodily disease it may be, if one takes a little of the juice of this herb. But before it has touched the height of the hem, it has no such power.

This image (it is said) was made in the likeness of Jesus's face, which has remained until our times, as we have seen with our own eyes. It is no wonder if some of the believing Gentiles had this made, because of the benefit they had received from our Savior; and it seems they regarded this as a gift made to His honor, since we still see even in these days...

# of the Ancient Christian Churches. The 7th Book.

<page-num>Fol. 135.</page-num>
<header>of the Ancient Christian Churches. The 7th Book.</header>

<margin>Portraits of the Apostles Peter and Paul seen by Eusebius.</margin>
Since the likenesses of the Apostles Peter and Paul have been made on small tablets, and are still shown to us by some who have preserved their figures and images from ancient times, it seems to me that this is maintained out of a pagan custom, <note>original: "Heydensche ghewoonte"; Eusebius suggests that the practice of painting portraits of holy men was a carry-over from Greco-Roman traditions of honoring secular heroes or philosophers.</note> in that they were accustomed to honor in such a manner those whom they deemed worthy of honor. For that the likenesses of the ancients are still preserved in the memory of posterity is a proof for some that they are honored thereby, and for others a proof of love.

### ¶ Concerning the chair of James the Apostle, the Bishop.

### Chapter 15.

<margin>James’s chair.</margin>
In like manner, the chair <note>original: "stoel"; referring to the *cathedra* or episcopal throne, symbolizing the authority of the bishop.</note> of James—who was the first Bishop upon the earth, chosen in Jerusalem by our Savior and by the Apostles, and whom Holy Scripture has named a brother of the Lord—is also there. This chair is still preserved there at this time, and in it sit all those who have served the Bishopric at Jerusalem until this day. And the chair is held worthy and preserved there as a memorial of the elders and of their good life, or so that one shall also be mindful to maintain that first life of the priesthood.

### ¶ Concerning the peace which the holy Church had under Gallienus the Emperor.

### Chapter 16.

<margin>Gallienus becomes kind toward the Christians.</margin>
When the Emperor Gallienus, son of Valerian, was holding the Empire alone, he acted more kindly toward our people than his father had, and issued Mandates that they should cease to persecute the Christians, but that every individual should be left to his own judgment to act in all divine matters. <note>This refers to the "Edict of Gallienus" (c. 260 AD), which effectively ended the Valerianic persecution and began a period known as the "Little Peace of the Church."</note>

### ¶ Which Bishops existed in that same time.

### Chapter 17.

In the same time, while Sixtus was still Bishop at Rome, and Demetrianus

<column-break/>

<margin>Gregory and Theodore, brothers.</margin>
at Antioch, and Firmilianus at Caesarea and Cappadocia, Gregory—a disciple of Origen, previously named Theodore—was in Pontus with his brother Athenodorus. And at Caesarea in Palestine, after Theoctistus, Domnus received the Bishopric and died shortly thereafter; and after him, in our times, Theotecnus, a disciple of Origen, became Bishop. And at Jerusalem, after Mazabbanes, Hymeneus received the priesthood. All these governed their congregations and churches in peace.

### ¶ How those at Alexandria destroyed themselves through rebellion.

### Chapter 18.

<margin>Alexandria is rebellious.</margin>
Although there was now no outward persecution at Alexandria, yet the citizens, through faction and rebellion, began such discord against one another that the city, which was so rich in inhabitants that there was scarcely room to walk in the streets, was brought to such a state by faction and discord that it was very rare to see a man on the street. Indeed, all ways and streets were wet and splashed with the blood of the citizens and dead bodies. There was no one there who buried them, and from that great stench of the rotted bodies, a horrible pestilence arose; thus, what the sword had not been able to do, the sickness of the plague accomplished.

<margin>Dionysius recounts that Alexandria was devastated by her own citizens.</margin>

### ¶ Concerning Asterius the martyr.

#### The 13th Chapter.

<margin>Asterius the martyr.</margin>
Among these there was also, above all others, an illustrious nobleman, a Senator in the City of Rome, very wealthy and of royal descent, named Asterius. He was present when Marinus was beheaded and took the dead body upon his shoulders, covering it with his own fine garment. And through this honor which he performed for the martyr, he himself shortly thereafter became a martyr as well. ### ¶ Concerning the faithful love of the Christians during the sickness at Antioch.

## The 20th Chapter.

<margin>The love of Christians: visiting the sick even unto death, etc.</margin>
Thereafter, our persecutors turned their hands and weapons against themselves; nonetheless, even that did not disturb or sadden our festival. After that followed the pestilential sickness and a horrible plague, which was much more terrifying and heavy for them, seeing as they had no hope for the future life. But for us, all these things were like exercises of virtue and trials of faith. Even though the mortality was heavier and more gruesome against the Heathens <note>Non-Christians/Pagans</note>, nonetheless, it did not entirely spare our own people.

And a little later he writes, saying: Many of our brothers, who out of great love and without any hesitation visited the sick, and also served and performed the works which our Lord commanded, were likewise ignited by the sickness and died with those whom they desired to serve; they had a desire to share in their sorrow, and they accounted this temporal life as nothing. And also many of our own, who were particularly excellent men—among whom were some Priests and Deacons, and many others of the people—who, with a zealous and steadfast faith, just as in the time of persecution,

<column-break/>

showed mercy to the sick and did not spare themselves, suspecting through the work of mercy and by faith that they were not different from the martyrs. And as they were diligent in healing the sick and carrying their bodies to the earth, they also followed those whom they were carrying on their shoulders toward the grave.

The Heathens were exactly the opposite; for as soon as they began to grow sick, the parents abandoned their dear children, the husband separated from his wife, and the children deserted their parents. When they saw and noticed that the limbs began to tremble because of the sickness and that the lips turned pale, they thrust them out of the house and threw them half-dead onto the streets, leaving the bodies to lie there unburied, thinking thus to escape the power of death, which overtook them doubly: for to this raging sickness was added the great stench of the unburied bodies.

#### Eusebius Pamphili’s Chronicles / of the

<margin>Coracion renounces the teaching of Nepos.</margin>
¶ When they were further heard, the proof and demonstration of their words was not based on human persuasion or advice, nor through any beautiful reasons or words; but it had its foundation and proceeded from the truth of the Divine Scriptures. Thus, our proof and demonstration were so powerful and manifest that one of their greatest Doctors <note>In this context, "Doctor" refers to a high-ranking teacher or theologian of the church.</note>, who was the most excellent in life, standing up in the midst of them all—after they had all heard his words—cried out and testified that no further mention should be made of this teaching, and that it was enough that they had wandered in error for so long. Furthermore, he declared that they should not only no longer maintain or follow this teaching, but also no longer even remember such things, since the Divine Scripture was so clearly and openly against it. All the other brothers were filled in their hearts with great joy and gladness, and they greatly thanked and praised our LORD for the correction and enlightenment of their understanding.

### Of John’s Revelation.

## The 24th Chapter.

<margin>The opinion of Dionysius of Alexandria regarding John’s Revelation.</margin>
<margin>Cerinthus, as some believe, is the author of this book.</margin>
Coming then to John’s Revelation <note>original: "Joannis Openbaringe"; also referred to as the Apocalypse.</note>, he writes thus: Some of our ancestors have suspected that the Book of Revelation should be entirely rejected from the Scriptures, and they rebuked every chapter of the same book, saying that the title or inscription of the same book is not true but very strange. They claim that only the name of John was placed therein, and that it is not possible to prove that this book is John’s Revelation, which is covered with such a veil of ignorance. They also say that there is nothing singular in it that may be attributed to Apostolic dignity. Moreover, they say there has been no one among the Teachers of the holy Church who has said that this very book is Holy Scripture. Rather, they claim the writer of this book was one named Cerinthus <note>A gnostic heretic of the late 1st century who was a contemporary of the Apostle John.</note>, a founder of the heresy of the Cerinthians, who wished to confirm the faith of his teaching with the authority of an Apostolic name, which was written by him. Furthermore, they say that Cerinthus’s teaching maintains that Christ’s Kingdom is to come upon the earth.

<column-break/>

<margin>Lust seeks its rest in this time.</margin>
And because carnal lust was very pleasing to him, he suspected and also felt that one should give the Saints such things in the promises of the future Kingdom as the lusts of his mind desired: namely, the works of the belly and of lust—the satiety of food, and abundance of drink, weddings, and all such things—would also be maintained in those times, and that they would then again renew the Festivals and Sacrifices of the Jews, and the offerings of the Law. But regarding my own feeling, I do not dare in any way to reject the Scripture of this book, and especially because many of the brothers feel the same as I do. But this is my judgment of the same book: that what is written therein surpasses the manner of human understanding, and therein is a wonderful, secret, and hidden sense, which I marvel at and honor, even if I do not understand it. And I hold such a feeling: that certain Divine mysteries are covered with human words, which I cannot distinguish with my understanding as well as I believe them. Therefore, I will not reject that which I do not understand, but the less I understand it, the more it is a wonder to me.

<margin>I marvel, honor, and revere: Yes, even if I do not understand it, I trust it, so I do not reject it.</margin>
¶ Thereafter, when Dionysius comes to relate the entire body of this book, and particularly examining each part and clearly proving that it is in no way possible that a worthy understanding should appear therein according to the letter <note>Dionysius argues for an allegorical or spiritual meaning rather than a literal, physical one.</note>, he speaks. And he writes even more, saying: When he had finished all his prophecy, he writes: "Blessed is he who keeps the word of the prophecies of this book, and I, John, who hear and see these things." Thus, I do not deny that this Scripture is written by one named John. It is, without doubt, written by a holy man through God’s Spirit, even if it was not John the Apostle, son of Zebedee, brother of James, whose Gospel and Christian Epistle are written in his name.

This Dionysius uses many proofs that this Revelation was undoubtedly given by God, and that the writer is named John, yet not the same John who wrote the Gospel: for that John makes no mention of his name anywhere. But he who wrote this Revelation mentions his name many times. And also there is a distinction in

The Council was held at Antioch against Paul of Samosata.

Paul of Samosata is rebuked by the fathers.

All these aforementioned men often gathered and came together, placing Paul of Samosata in their midst to uncover his heresy and blasphemy—which he sometimes hid and sometimes feigned—rebuking him with manifold disputation and instruction. Nevertheless, they could not bring the matter to an end by holding a council once or twice, but they were continually meeting and departing without any fruit.

Gregory, who was previously named Theodorus, a bishop in Pontus, that is, at Neocaesarea.

In the land of Pontus there was a body of water very abundant in fish, from which great profit and gain came to those who owned it. The possession of this fishery came to two brothers through inheritance; but the greed for money, which conquers the hearts of all men, also corrupted and tainted their brotherly friendship. For at the time when the fish were usually caught, the two brothers came—not so much to catch fish as to catch men—for they warred and struck one another, and <margin>A bloody war of two brothers over a fishery.</margin> human blood was shed for the sake of the fish. But through God's providence, Gregory arrived there and saw the battle and the slaughter of men, and those two raging brothers. He asked and investigated why the brothers were so inflamed against one another to their mutual destruction, and he learned it was for nothing else than the fishery. And when both parties, because of the dignity of his person, ceased and were silent, he said: "My dear children, do not defile your rational souls for the sake of dumb beasts, nor dissolve brotherly love and unity for the greed of gain, nor so stubbornly abandon the Law of God and nature. Come both with me to the shore of this harmful water: I shall now, through the power of the Lord, deliver you both from this bloody strife." **O**ne single God, father of the living word, of the essential wisdom, and of his power and likeness; a perfect producer of the perfect, a Father of the only Son. One Lord, one alone out of one alone, a Figure and Image of the Divinity; an active word, a wisdom comprising all things, and a power through which all creatures might be created. To Dionysius and Maximus, and to all the priests and bishops, along with the elders and deacons, and all the congregations under heaven: Hellenus and Hymeneus, Theophilus, Theotecnus, Maximus, Proculus, Nicomas, Helianus, Paul, Bolasus, Protogenes, Hierax, Eutychius, Theodore, Malchion, Lucius, priests, and all those gathered with us from the neighboring cities and lands—bishops, priests, and deacons—our dear brothers in the Lord, greetings.

And shortly thereafter they wrote: We send you this letter and pray that if anyone has been led astray by the teaching of Paul, they may be healed by you. Just as Dionysius in Alexandria and Firmilianus in Cappadocia <note>Dionysius was the Bishop of Alexandria, and Firmilianus was the Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia; both were leading figures in the mid-3rd century Church.</note> previously deigned to warn the church of Antioch, they also wrote personally to Paul, who first devised this heresy. And Firmilianus, of blessed memory, twice visited this Paul himself and rebuked him in person, as we all know and as those who came with him can testify. But because Paul promised he would correct his error, Firmilianus believed him, hoping that it might still be possible for the dispute to be resolved for the better without any scandal to Christendom. But Paul, acting with deceit, has deceived man and forsaken God, and has blasphemed his own faith in which he was reborn. and as the blessed Firmilianus was traveling again toward Antioch, and having arrived at Tarsus, while we were all waiting together for his arrival at Antioch, word was brought to us that he had departed from this world. <margin>
By what means P. Samosatenus came to his riches.
</margin>

It is not quite possible to recount Paul’s conduct; for as soon as he turned from good teaching to error, having always been poor before and having received no inheritance from his parents, he suddenly became very rich from the goods of the Church, which he obtained through deceit and from those whom he coerced into selling their paternal inheritance, claiming he would distribute it faithfully—thinking that "godliness is in gain." <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 6:5. Paul of Samosata was accused of using his ecclesiastical office for financial extortion.</note> His pride was unbearable, for he preferred to be greeted and regarded as a Captain <note>original: "Hooftman," referring to a secular military or civil official; Paul held the high-ranking civil office of *Ducenarius*.</note> rather than as

<column-break/>

a Bishop. He displayed great pomp and ambition in the streets, reading and writing letters before everyone. And wherever he went, he had his notaries and scribes around him, before and after. So much so that everyone who saw it complained that the Divine Religion was being blasphemed by his unspeakable pride. Within the Church, he had a high seat prepared for himself, much higher than those before him; and he commanded that a throne be built above it, and he also had a secret chamber prepared there, just as the judges of this world are accustomed to have. When he spoke to the people, he threw his right hand high and slapped his hand against his side, and leaped up with his feet, and made a noise with his footstool. From the people, he desired not only favor and honor, but also that the priestly vestments (called *Oraria*) <note>original: "Oraria." These are stoles or liturgical scarves. The text suggests he used them theatrically.</note> should be waved for him like stage actors, and that a voice sounding like it came from a cellar <note>Likely referring to a deep, dramatic, or artificial tone of voice intended to sound authoritative or mystical.</note> should be given to him. These things were despised not only by the men but also by the women. And if anyone among his followers (who was somewhat more modest) refrained from shouting loudly, they were punished by him as being undisciplined. Furthermore, he scolded and blasphemed certain ancient Teachers who had died, shamelessly praising himself. He preferred to be praised as a Rhetorician <note>original: "Rhetor." A professional public speaker or orator.</note> or an eloquent man, rather than as a Teacher of the Church.

Psalms that used to be sung are left out.
</margin>

The Psalms that used to be sung to our LORD Jesus Christ, he has left out, as being new and recently devised. And certain songs composed by him, he had sung in the middle of the Church on Easter days by women whom he had previously trained for that purpose in his own manner, so that one who heard it might be terrified.

<margin>
P. Samosatenus made a Psalm in which he was praised as an Angel from heaven.
</margin>

For after he denied that the Son of God had descended from Heaven, but instead had his first beginning from Mary on earth, he then composed Psalms to be sung by the people in which he himself was praised as an Angel who had descended from Heaven. He even stood by to hear such singing and did not forbid it, but with great arrogance, he took delight in hearing it.

<margin>
Praised by foolish women.
</margin>

By the women who lived with him, whom the people of Antioch call *Sy-nisactas* <note>original: "Sy-nisactas," from the Greek *syneisaktoi*, meaning "spiritual sisters" or "house-companions." Synisactas.

**B** * + This matter has been strangely corrupted, not only in the printed copies but also in those written by hand, as is noted from Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD) was an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his preaching and his critiques of clerical misconduct.</note>, regarding how in those times there were some who kept women in their houses, not for the sake of evil lusts or to procreate children, but gave this reason: since some daughters had neither mother, nor father, nor brother, nor any such kin, it was necessary **C** that someone should take them in and protect them against malicious people. **G** in such a conclusion: Therefore, since this man has resisted God and renounced the true faith, we have considered it necessary to provide another Bishop for the Christian congregation at Antioch, namely, the virtuous man Domnus, a son of Demetrianus of blessed memory, who served the bishopric of this same church blamelessly. And we have also let you know this, so that it may be known to you that you ought to write to him, and likewise **H** receive letters back from him. And this Paul, who is not deemed worthy to be among the Christian assembly, shall be written off as cursed, and the followers of his heresy shall be placed under the ban of excommunication.

<margin>Domnus becomes Bishop of Antioch in Paul’s place.</margin> **I** Now when Domnus was chosen as a Bishop, and Paul was cut off from the congregation and from his priesthood, and he would not vacate the house of the church, they sought recourse with the Emperor Aurelian <note>Emperor Aurelian ruled from 270–275 AD; though a pagan, he was asked to arbitrate a property dispute within the Church.</note>, who gave such a **J** sentence: that the house of the church should be given to those to whom the priests of Italy and the bishop of Rome should write. And thus, to the aforementioned evil of this Paul, damage and dishonor were also added, as he was publicly driven from the church by the power of justice. Such was Aurelian against us at that time, but after that <margin>Emperor Aurelian.</margin> **K** time he entirely changed his good intentions, and was so turned by evil counsel that he took it upon himself to persecute the Divine Assembly, so that it is said the letters were already written, only they were not yet **L** signed. But God the Lord hindered such a thing and punished him with a sudden death—he who intended to kill good men. In which God makes known to us that we are not punished or persecuted whenever it pleases the tyrant, but when God wishes to test us, then **L** we are punished.

**M** When Aurelian had reigned for 6 years, Probus received the empire after him; and when he had also reigned for as long, Carus came after him, with his sons Carinus and Numerian, by whom the realm was served for not a full **N** 3 years. Then Diocletian became Emperor, and he allowed great persecution and destruction to occur within the Church. <margin>Diocletian is the persecutor of the Christians.</margin>

A short time before Diocletian received the Empire, Dionysius died in Rome after he had served the Bishopric for nine years, and Felix received his seat. At this time there was a man whose name sounds like "madness," <note>original: "Manes"; the author is playing on the Greek word *mania*, meaning madness, to describe the founder of Manichaeism.</note> called Mani. This Mani, through the inspiration of the Devil, taught a horrible heresy; he was born in Persia and was a barbarian in his life and manner. He was so clever in his understanding that it seemed he was possessed by the devil or raving, for sometimes he wanted to prove that he had taken on the form of Christ, and sometimes he said that he himself was the Holy Spirit. He was puffed up with madness, choosing twelve disciples just as Christ did, and sent them out to preach. Having gathered together all kinds of foolish and evil heresies that had previously been destroyed, he poured out his venom in our times.

When they were besieged by enemies and lacked fruit and grain, so that hunger was more troublesome there than the enemy, the people were divided into discord among two factions. A third part was separate from them, living contentedly under the Romans, among whom was the aforementioned Anatolius, without any involvement in the fighting. Thus, he went into the camp to the chief commander of the Romans and told him of the great necessity of hunger that the besieged citizens were suffering, so that he obtained mercy from the commander for those citizens, which he put into effect in this manner:

Both of the discordant parties took this advice thankfully and opened the gates of the city, letting out those who were unfit for war. Taking this opportunity, those who were non-combatants also went out, along with nearly everyone who was suffering from hunger—and especially our people, who had no desire for fighting and war. Anatolius received them all and, like a father and a master, he fed and refreshed them. Thus, by means of the food, he helped the great multitude of people, and the other few who remained...
