# The Seventh Book
<meta>catchword: good</meta>

...older Christian churches.

Considering their small number, and out of fear of the war, they sought peace. Thus, with his wise counsel, he delivered the great city of Alexandria from hunger and war. <note>Anatolius is credited here with negotiating during the Roman siege of the Pyruchium quarter in Alexandria (c. 263 AD), allowing non-combatants to leave and saving them from starvation.</note>

This man was the second person from Alexandria to be chosen as Bishop of the city of Laodicea, following the events of the war as previously stated. Many books by this Anatolius have come to our knowledge, and it seems fitting to me to recount his views concerning Easter.

<margin>Anatolius on Easter</margin>
In the first year (he says), which begins the first month—which follows the nineteen-year cycle <note>This refers to the Metonic cycle, used to align the solar year with the lunar months to determine the date of Easter.</note> according to the reckoning of the Egyptians—it is the 26th day of the month Famenoth. According to the reckoning of the Macedonians, it is the 22nd of the month Dystri; and according to the custom of the Romans, it is the 16th before the Kalends of April <note>March 17th.</note>. On this day, it is found not only that the sun has ascended into its first degree, but also that it holds the fourth part on that same day—namely, in the first of the twelve parts.

<margin>The beginning of the months.</margin>
This part is the first of the twelve parts <note>The twelve signs of the Zodiac.</note>, the beginning of the months, the head of the cycle, and the end of the course of the seven stars called "planets" <note>original: "dwalende" (wandering stars); in antiquity, the sun, moon, and five visible planets.</note>, as well as the end of the twelfth part and the entire circle. Therefore, we say that all those who wish to celebrate Easter before the beginning of the New Year are greatly mistaken.

<margin>All authorities.</margin>
We have not invented this calculation recently, but it is proven and confirmed by the reckoning of the ancient Jews, and was observed before the birth of Christ. This is clearly demonstrated by Philo and Josephus, and even before them by Agathobolus, and also his disciple Aristobulus of Paneas. Aristobulus was one of the seventy scholars <note>The "Septuagint" translators.</note> sent by the high priests to King Ptolemy of Egypt to translate the Hebrew books into the Greek language. When the King investigated many things and asked about the teachings and commandments of Moses, they answered his questions.

<margin>The time of the growing season.</margin>
When these same men were explaining the questions and inquiries from the book of Exodus <note>original: "Erodo," likely an error for "Exodo."</note>, they stated that the Passover lamb should not be sacrificed before the "growing time" <note>The Spring Equinox.</note> had passed, when the days and nights are of equal length. And Aristobulus further adds that at the time of the equality of day and night when Easter is observed, not only must the sun have passed the Vernal Equinox <note>original: "Equinoctium Vernale"</note>, but the moon must also have passed it.

<column-break/>

For there are two times of the year when the days and nights are of equal length: the "growing time" <note>Spring</note> and the "fading time" <note>Autumn</note>, which were created as equals to one another. Thus, on the 14th day of the first month toward evening, the feast of Easter is ordained, when the moon is found to be standing directly opposite the sun. As one may see with their own eyes, the sun will be in a portion of the Vernal Equinox—at the equality of day and night in the growing season—and the moon, conversely, will be in the Autumnal Equinox <note>original: "Equinoctij Autumnale"</note>, the fading season.
<margin>Two seasons of the year.</margin>

I have read many strong proofs in their books which clearly enough demonstrate that Easter should be observed after the Equinox, as previously stated. This Anatolius wrote many other books, through which his blessed learning may be recognized. Theotecnus, Bishop of Caesarea, chose him as Bishop during his own lifetime and laid hands upon him so that he would be his successor. Thus, for a short time, he served the Church of Caesarea alongside Theotecnus.

## Of the Bishops, Martyrs, and Teachers of the same time.

### The 30th Chapter.

<margin>How Anatolius became Bishop of Laodicea.</margin>
While Anatolius was traveling to Antioch for the Council against Paul of Samosata, and Eusebius the Bishop of Laodicea had died, the congregation of the Laodiceans took him by force and chose him to be their Bishop.

<margin>Stephanus.</margin>
After him, Stephanus was Bishop in Laodicea. He was no less learned or eloquent than his predecessors, but he was very different in the strength of his faith, which the fire of persecution tested. For in the time of suffering, he showed little of his learning; however, because of his weakness, God's poverty <note>Possibly a reference to the "weakness of God" being stronger than men, or a comment on the lack of spiritual wealth during his lapse.</note> was not displayed.

<margin>Theodotus.</margin>
For after he had fallen, God provided His Church with a Bishop named Theodotus, a man who was adorned not only with words, but with deeds and power.

By profession, he was a master physician, but he was appointed by the LORD to heal souls. He was very great in faith, merciful, diligent, and careful, and also of great discernment in all things.

# The Eighth Book of Eusebius
## Pamphili’s Chronicle <note>original: "Pamphili Chronica"</note> / of the ancient Christian Churches.

### The First Chapter.

<margin>Concerning the prosperity of the Christians, through which they became negligent in the service of God.</margin>
<note>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'H' depicts a male figure standing in a landscape with buildings in the background.</note>
Although it is not possible to recount how wonderfully and powerfully the Word of Christ was proclaimed throughout all the world, and how prosperous the teaching of the godly has been.

So it is well known that some of the Roman Princes held the Christians in such high esteem that they gave them power to rule lands and to administer justice.

<margin>One could be a Christian openly.</margin>
It was also permitted to their wives, children, servants, and the entire household not only to believe in Christ, but also to freely confess and live according to it: so much so that they regarded the Christians as faithful people and held their company with them: for they were certain that, because they believed in Christ, they would not act unfaithfully or wickedly,

<margin>Dorotheus the Chamberlain <term>Chamberlain</term> <note>original: "Camerinck"; a high-ranking official in charge of the royal household or treasury.</note></margin>
such as Dorotheus, a Chamberlain to the King, who was considered very faithful in all things because of the Lord's faith, for which reason he was honored and praised by all men.

<margin>Gorgonius the Chamberlain.</margin>
With whom was also Gorgonius, and many other Christians with them, who were in great honor in the Palace, and who, on account of their faithfulness, were chosen to be governors <note>original: "Obersten"</note> of lands and cities.

<column-break/>

<margin>The number of Christians has increased greatly.</margin>
Furthermore, the multitude of people who came together in the churches, and especially on the feast days from all places, is not easily spoken of; for the old houses that were ordained for praying to GOD therein became too small, and they were multiplied daily, so that their enclosures seemed to be like small towns.

So it was that many times the state of the Christian Church was increased in such prosperity that its glory and honor seemed to surpass all that is on earth, and began to approach Heaven; for the people were protected by the right hand of God, so that the hatred, envy, and cunning of the wicked devil could do no harm, because of the sweetness and the maintenance of righteousness.

<margin>Note how, through the prosperity of the Christians, negligence, mockery, and indulgence <note>original: "getenheydt"; likely referring to a lack of discipline or spiritual hunger.</note> entered into the service of God.</margin>
But just as GOD is forgotten in luck and prosperity, and also brotherly love, so also, because of these great freedoms, manners were changed and stained, and Christian teaching became corrupted, as we began to hate one another, and to reproach and accuse one another, and have fought against ourselves, as we wounded the hearts of our neighbors with the poisonous arrows of words, and stirred up discord and war, the Princes against each other, and one people against another; for there was feigned holiness in the face, and deceit in the heart, and also in words; and that evil began to multiply on all sides, so that Divine Providence, seeing that His people were harmful and hindered by the great peace and freedom, looked down: and He began first to restrain those who had fallen among the soldiery <term>Soldiery</term> <note>original: "Ridderschap"; referring to Christians serving in the Roman military.</note>,

AFTER we have covered the successors of the Apostles in seven books / it seemed good to us and not inappropriate / that we should describe in the 8th Book, for an eternal memory and remembrance for those who come after us / that which also happened in our own times: concerning the persecution under Diocletian / Maximian / and Maximinus / the Emperors.

# The eighth Book of Eusebius Pamphilus’s Chronicle / of the ancient Christian Churches.

### ¶ Concerning the prosperity of the Christians / through which they became negligent in the service of God.

### The first Chapter.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial letter ‘H’ depicts a figure sitting in a landscape with a house and mountains in the background.</note> ALTHOUGH it is not possible to tell how wonderfully and powerfully Christ's Word was proclaimed in all the world / and how prosperous the Teaching of the Godly has been.

<margin>One might openly be a Christian.</margin> So it is known that some of the Roman Princes <note>The "Princes" refers to the Roman Emperors who preceded the persecution, such as Gallienus, who issued edicts of tolerance.</note> held the Christians in such high esteem / that they gave them power to rule lands / and to judge. It was also permitted to their wives / children / servants / and all their households / not only to believe in Christ / but also freely to confess that faith / and to live according to it: So much so that they regarded the Christians as those who were faithful / and they kept their company with them: for they were certain / because they believed in Christ / that they would not act unfaithfully or wickedly. Such was the case with <margin>Dorotheus the Chamberlain.</margin> Dorotheus, a Chamberlain <note>A "Chamberlain" (Camerlinck) was a high-ranking official in charge of the royal household or treasury.</note> of the King / who because of his faith in the Lord was considered very faithful in all things / for which reason he was honored and praised by all men. <margin>Gorgonius the Chamberlain.</margin> With whom Gorgonius was also / and many other Christians with them / who were in great honor in the Palace / and who on account of their faithfulness were honored to be Governors of lands and Cities.

Thus the state of the Christian Church was increased in such prosperity / that its glory and honor surely seemed to exceed all that is on earth / and began to reach toward Heaven / for the people were protected by the right hand of God / so that the hatred and envy / and cunning of the evil devil could do no harm / because of the loveliness and the maintenance of righteousness. <margin>Note / how through the prosperity of the Christians / negligence and forgetfulness in the service of God has come.</margin> But just as in luck and prosperity GOD is forgotten / and also brotherly love / so also / because of these great freedoms, their manners were changed and stained / and the Christian Teaching became corrupted / as we began to hate one another / and to reproach and accuse one another / and we fought against ourselves / as we wounded the hearts of our neighbors with the poisonous arrows of words / and stirred up discord and war / the leaders against one another / and one people against another / for there was feigned holiness in the face / and deceit in the heart / and also in words / and as that evil began to multiply on all sides / so Divine providence / because His people were harmful and a hindrance to the great peace and freedom / set them down : And he first began to restrain those who had fallen / among the military service /

IT would not be possible for us to write what great shame and dishonor happened to the Priests of God. Nor is it our intention to recount all the great discord and madness that was ignited among our own people. But it has pleased us only to reveal in this History that we have felt the Divine hand against us / out of the righteous judgment of God / and out of necessary punishment. It is not necessary to know for whose sake the tempest of persecution has come / or which / or what kind of people were drowned in the waves of unbelief: but I shall only relate that which may teach and edify ourselves who speak / and others who hear. Thus, we shall begin to describe here the Divine martyrdoms and struggles of the most blessed martyrs / as precious as it is possible for us.

### ### How it was commanded by the Emperor Diocletian / that the Churches should be destroyed.

### ### The 2nd Chapter.

<margin>
Mandate of Diocletian.
</margin>
In the 19th Year of the reign of Diocletian, in the month of March / as the high feast of Easter was approaching / the Mandates of the Emperor were issued and proclaimed in all lands / that all the churches / in whatever lands they might be / should be torn down to the ground and destroyed, and that the Holy Scripture should be entirely burned. And whoever among the Christians held any office / or was in any position of honor / it should be taken from them / and they should be stripped of their status. And whoever was in servitude or property / and remained a Christian / they should never be able to obtain their freedom. All these things were contained in the first Mandate that was issued against us.

### The 5th Chapter.

In Nicomedia <note>The capital of the eastern part of the Roman Empire under Diocletian.</note> there was a nobleman who was in great worldly honor / when he saw that horrible Edict <note>original: "Mandament." Referring to the first edict of Diocletian (303 AD) ordering the destruction of churches and scriptures.</note> posted in the Marketplace against the servants of God / he was inflamed by the fervor of his faith / and in the presence of the people, he openly took that book of the wicked Edict with his hand / and tore it into pieces. At that same time, Maximian Caesar / and Augustus with him / that is / Diocletian the Emperor / were both in that same city. When the deeds of the nobleman were announced to them / they raged against him with all manners of cruelty / yet with all their torments they could not achieve so much that anyone saw him sorrowful in his pain / but he was always joyful and cheerful of countenance / and though his limbs failed him in the torments / yet his spirit rejoiced in his countenance. This was difficult for the tormentors to endure / that with all their tortures they could not make this man grieve.
<margin>
Here you see openly / that Augustus and Caesar are different / how the Emperor under Augustus is: the Roman Kings are called Caesar, Augustus is called Imperator, that is / the Emperor.

<margin>Vinegar, salt, fire, and a gridiron for the martyrdom.</margin>
As he was speaking freely, lamenting with great sadness and pain that the others had been martyred, it was commanded that he too should be brought forward and forced to offer sacrifice to the Idols. When he refused, it was ordered that he should be hung up and his entire body torn with iron scourges <note>These were likely the *ungulae*, claw-like metal instruments used to rake the flesh.</note>, so that through these torments he might be made willing to do what was commanded of him. As this Peter remained entirely unmoved, even when his whole body was torn and his skin stripped away, it was ordered that vinegar and salt be poured over his body. And as he also bore this pain manfully and steadfastly, a gridiron <term>gridiron|A metal frame used for roasting, repurposed here as a horrific tool of execution.</term> with coals was placed in the middle, and his wounded and raw body was laid upon it. They kindled the fire under the gridiron—not quickly, but gradually—so that the pain might last longer.

As the servants turned his body back and forth to renew his pain, suspecting and hoping that they might obtain some consent from him through such means, he remained steadfast in the faith. When his flesh was consumed by the fire, he joyfully offered up his spirit to God in the faith. Therefore, his rightful name was Peter <note>original: "Petrus"</note>, seeing as he was foremost in faith and in name <note>A play on the name Peter, meaning "rock," and his role as a foundational witness to the faith.</note>.

<margin>Gorgonius.</margin>
This Peter had been instructed in the Divine teachings by his master of office in the palace, named Dorotheus, a chief among the Emperor’s chamberlains. His companion was Gorgonius, who was his equal in the greatness of his faith. Through the instruction of these two, all the chamberlains were taught in the faith and remained constant in it.

Now, when Dorotheus and Gorgonius saw this Peter being tormented with such inhuman cruelty, they spoke steadfastly and freely to the Emperor: "O Emperor, why do you punish in Peter the conviction which is powerful and crying out in all of us? Why do you wish to consider as a crime in him that which we all confess and acknowledge? This is our faith and our service to God, and we are of one mind and one feeling." When the Emperor had commanded that they be brought forward, they were tormented with the same tortures as the others, and finally, he ordered that they should be hanged and strangled.

At that same time, there was also beheaded—

<column-break/>

<margin>Anthimus, Bishop of Nicomedia.</margin>
—Anthimus, a Bishop of that same city, because he had remained steadfast in the confession of our Lord Jesus Christ. He went before them like a good Shepherd on the path of martyrdom, and all his sheep and subjects followed him. The cause of this was that at the same time, a part of the Palace at Nicomedia burned down. The Emperor suspected, with a false opinion, that this had been done by our people. Because of this, he was kindled with an inexpressible and raging anger, and he commanded that all Christians should be captured; that some should be beheaded with the sword, and others thrown into the fire and burned. But in the Christians, the fire of faith was kindled much more through Divine grace. When each person was brought by the servants and asked if they would offer to the gods to be set free, both the women and the men could not bear to be asked such things, but freely stepped into the fire or offered their necks to the swords.

<margin>The fire at the Town Hall in Nicomedia is blamed on the Christians.</margin>
<margin>Cruelty against the Christians at Nicomedia.</margin>
When this handling of cruelty grew so great that it was terrifying even to those who beheld it, the servants threw a portion of the people into ships and sailed with them into the depths of the sea; and there, as all remained steadfast in the faith, they drowned them. Such cruelty and madness were kindled among them that the royal servants had the bodies of those who (as previously mentioned) had been martyred and buried—including Peter and Gorgonius—dug up again and thrown into the sea. They said: "Lest perhaps these should become gods to the Christians, and those who will not worship our gods should begin to worship our servants." For they suspected that we would show the martyrs divine honor.

<margin>By the royal servants, these Peter and Gorgonius, the Emperor’s chamberlains [were treated].</margin>
<margin>Melitene, Syria.</margin>
At the same time as these things happened in Nicomedia, where the evil and cruel tyrant hungered for the flesh of the righteous, it also began and occurred in the same manner in the lands of Melitene <note>A region in eastern Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey.</note> and Syria. For through that Imperial Mandate, they obtained permission to throw all the leaders of the churches into the dungeon; and with these, men and women of the congregation, noble and common, were captured. It was a ghastly thing to see. For suddenly a silence fell upon the city, while a clamor rose from the prisons, and on the streets, one could hardly see a soul.

<margin>Prisons filled with Christians.</margin>
In the prisons, there was no empty space, so that it seemed as if not only—

### A proof of how the martyrs in Egypt and Tyre were killed and martyred.

#### The VII. Chapter.

<margin>The martyrdom in Africa, Mauritania, Thebaida, and Egypt.</margin>
**W**HO can tell or express the great multitude of Martyrs who were martyred in various lands and provinces, and especially in Africa and Mauritania, and also in <term>Thebaida|A region in Upper Egypt centered around the city of Thebes, famous for its early monastic and Christian communities.</term> and in Egypt? Likewise, we cannot tell enough of the knightly struggle of the martyrs, which we ourselves have seen in Palestine or in Tyre, which is the largest city in Phoenicia.

<margin>Steadfastness, a power of God. Matthew 28.</margin>
With such powerful steadfastness the Martyrs suffered the torments for the sake of righteousness, so that it is not possible to believe—for one who does not know—that the strength of the martyrs is God's strength, which was always with them, as our Lord spoke, saying: "Behold, I am with you always until the end of the world." Therefore, as we have said before, we do not wish to speak from hearsay, but we wish to tell of what we ourselves have seen with our own eyes.

<margin>The martyrs' flesh was raked by the executioner through scourging, and thrown before the beasts.</margin>
All manners of torments were brought forth one after another. First, the martyrs of God were raked through their whole bodies with iron scourges, and thereafter they were thrown before wild beasts, such as Lions, Bears,

<column-break/>

Leopards, and all kinds of cruel and horrible beasts, also wild Swine and Bulls, which were made even fiercer with fire and iron. All these were prepared against the servants of God, and all the cruelty of men, beasts, and the elements were armed against the martyrs. Thereafter, the servants of God were stripped naked and placed in the middle of a sandy area <note>The arena of the amphitheater.</note>, and they [the handlers] provoked the wild beasts in their dens with special arts to a fury until they were snarling, and then they let them out; and suddenly they filled the place where the Assembly of martyrs stood in the middle. And as the wild animals often ran around and back again, they [the animals] felt a Divine protection and assistance in the martyrs and withdrew from their bodies. What happened? The fury that was restrained in the wild animals passed instead into the men. No one thought that Divine power was present there; no one believed that Divine help assisted the friends of God, but there were found those who were skilled and clever enough to provoke the beasts and drive them onto us, whom the Divine right hand protected.

<margin>That the beasts recoiled from the Christians.</margin>
But so that it might be manifest to all people that the cruelty was not taken away from the beasts, but that Divine help preserved His servants, the wild animals—those very ones sent to provoke them—tore and devoured [the handlers] with unspeakable haste. And when no one of the servants or handlers dared to approach, the Holy martyrs were commanded to provoke the beasts against themselves with the sound of their hands: but even so, it did not happen. And if any of the beasts, being provoked, came near to them, it immediately came to itself and was called back <note>original: "gheropen" - literally 'called back', suggesting the beasts retreated as if summoned away.</note>.

Then there was an unspeakable wonder and fear over all those who saw it, as they beheld the naked men standing there (among whom were many youths) in the midst of so many wild beasts, and they were all together unafraid and not terrified, lifting their hands to Heaven, and with their eyes and hearts entirely united with God; they not only despised these temporal things but even held their own flesh in low regard. And while their Judges were trembling with terror, they remained standing pleasantly in the midst of the wild animals with a cheerful and joyful countenance.

O stubborn and cruel hearts of men! The cruelty of the beasts was made gentle through the power of God, and...

¶ Human madness was not pacified by the example of wild beasts.

After this, God was further tested by men. It was ordered that some criminals should be thrown before the beasts; and as soon as that was done, they were quickly torn apart by the wild animals—one by a lion, another by a leopard, the third by a wild boar, and the fourth was tossed into the air by a bull. And so they were all destroyed in the blink of an eye. But these beasts, though thus provoked, did not harm or hinder the servants of God; instead, the Divine Spirit surrounded them like a strong wall, for He is truthful who spoke: <margin>Matthew 18:19</margin> <note>While the margin cites Matthew 18:19, the quoted text refers to Matthew 18:20: "Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them."</note> Where two or three of you are gathered, there I am in the midst. When human cruelty still could not prevail, it was ordered that the wild beasts be changed; the first were driven back into their dens and others were let out. When these, like the first, did no harm to the servants of God, they were also driven away, and they sent men there who <margin>The people are more cruel than the beasts.</margin> exceeded the wild beasts in cruelty and horribleness; and what they could not accomplish with the wild beasts, they accomplished themselves with the sword. And so that they might prove in every way that they were more evil than the beasts, they forbade their bodies from being buried in the earth, ordering instead that they be thrown into the water. This struggle was endured by the beloved martyrs in the city of Tyre, who had come there from the lands of Egypt.

¶ How the Martyrs in Egypt were killed.

### The VIII. Chapter.

<margin>Martyrs in Egypt.</margin> IN Egypt there were also unspeakably many men, women, children, and old people who, counting this life as nothing, gave it up for the faith of our LORD JESUS Christ, and obtained the salvation of the coming glory. Some of these, after many blows and bonds, after being scourged and torn with <term>hooks|Iron instruments (ungulae) used to scrape the flesh from the ribs of the accused during torture.</term>, and after various other horrific manners of torment, were at last thrown into the fire; some others were drowned in the sea; and some others were beheaded, willingly and joyfully stretching out their necks; some others were killed by hunger in the dungeon; and some...

<column-break/>

...were hanged on gallows, among whom were some who were hung with their feet upward and their heads downward.

¶ Of the horrific and manifold torments with which the Martyrs in the <term>Thebaid|A region of Upper Egypt, named after the city of Thebes, which became a stronghold of early Christian monasticism.</term>, in Egypt, were tormented, and what Martyrs Eusebius himself saw there.

### The IX. Chapter.

<margin>Martyrs in the Thebaid</margin> THE cruelty that occurred in the Thebaid is impossible to tell. The tormentors took there, in place of [iron] claws, potsherds or glass shards, with which they so shredded the bodies of the martyrs that absolutely no skin could be found remaining on their bodies. They took the women naked, so that their modesty was not covered, and using a certain instrument, they pulled up one foot and let the head hang toward the earth—a horrific sight—and left them hanging thus for an entire day. Some other women were led to where two trees stood near each other, and from both trees <margin>The martyrs were torn apart by the bending of the trees.</margin> they bent down the high branches and tied one foot of the martyr to each branch; then they suddenly released the branches which they had forcibly bent, and thus the martyrs were torn asunder. And this did not happen for a short time or a few days, but daily for several years, such that every day people were killed by such manners of pain—men, women, and also children—at least ten and sometimes as many as a hundred in a single day.

During the time when we were traveling in the land of Egypt, we ourselves saw with our own eyes that the cruel and evil judge, sitting in the <term>judgment seat|A formal tribunal or bench where a Roman magistrate presided over legal cases.</term>, had brought before him <margin>What Eusebius himself saw during his journey in Egypt.</margin> an unspeakably large multitude of the faithful people, all of whom he questioned individually; and when they confessed that they were Christians, he gave the sentence that they should be beheaded. And as the Christians thus willingly confessed and surrendered themselves to the sword, the cruel and inhuman tyrant was not moved by the great multitude or the great strength of the Christians, but he had them led away and ordered that they all be beheaded together.

Fol 155
[History] of the older Christian churches. The Eighth Book,

**A** There the Christians went together out into a field situated outside the city; they were not bound by the hands of the executioner, but they were bound together by the bonds of faith. No one was missing from their number, though no one stood guard over them; all together they willingly stretched out their necks, and each one desired to go before the other, so that the hands of the executioner grew weary one after another, and the sharpness of their swords became blunt.

**B** I saw there that the executioners were tired and rested themselves, and took up other swords; and even the day was too short for them to complete their office. Yet there was not one among them all, no, not even a small child, who could be frightened by death.

**C** Instead, the faithful Christians worried more that the day would fall too short, and that they would thus be hindered and separated from the company of the martyrs. Thus, out of the steadfastness of faith, they desired this present death with cheerfulness and joy, as the beginning of eternal life.

<margin>Singing psalms and songs of praise.</margin>
**D** When the first were thus killed, the others were not sleepy or sluggish, but sang psalms and songs of praise to God the Lord, and each one awaited his time when he was called to the martyrdom: and in so doing, they gave up their final spirit in gratitude to God.

# Of the Martyr Phileas, and how he writes to the Thmuitans of the new ways of torment, which the cruelty of the tyrants has devised.

## The 5th Chapter.

<margin>O true nobility.</margin>
**E** **O** Wonderful and most worthy company of martyrs, a host of strong men, and a noble crown of the reflection of Christ’s glory, which is more precious than all noble gemstones. A leader went before this host, as an illustrious guide and shepherd, named Phileas, who was Bishop in that same city,

**F** <margin>Thmuis.</margin> <note>Thmuis was an ancient city in Lower Egypt, a center of early Christian learning.</note> which was called Thmuis. This Phileas possessed the nobility of his primary lineage from heaven according to the strength of his spirit, and also according to the world he was noble; for he was in great honor in the public service of the Romans, and he was very learned in all natural arts belonging to virtue, and in this last <term>Philosophy</term> <note>In the early Church, "Philosophy" was often used to describe Christian theology as the "true" or "ultimate" wisdom, surpassing Greek thought.</note> (which is the first of all) which

<column-break/>

**G** is Christian teaching; he received it in such a way that he also surpassed all those who had been Bishops there before him. And since he had many friends of his kin, noble men, in that same city, he was often led before the Judge, who advised him that he should surely consent without further warnings, seeing as so many of his closest friends prayed for him; and that he should surely consider his wife and remember his children, so that he would not remain so stubborn in his purpose and intent.

**H** Phileas completely despised their chatter and remained immovable, like a hard cliff <margin>Matthew 7.</margin> <note>A reference to the house built on the rock in Matthew 7:24–25.</note> against which the water beats; he lifted his heart to heaven, having God before his eyes, and held the Holy Martyrs and Apostles as his closest friends.

**I** <margin>Philozomus.</margin> <note>Historically known as Philoromus, a high-ranking Roman official (tribune) in Alexandria who was martyred alongside Phileas.</note> At the same time, a captain of the Roman soldiers named Philozomus was present. He, when he saw that Phileas was being testified to by the tears of his friends and was being tormented by the cleverness of the Judge, and that he could in no way be moved or bent, cried out, saying:

> Why do you test the steadfastness of this man in vain? Why do you wish to make him, who is a believer in God, an unbeliever? Why do you force him to forsake God so that he may consent to men? Do you not see that his eyes do not hear your words, and **K** that his eyes do not see your tears? How can he be moved by earthly tears, whose eyes see and behold the heavenly glory?

When he had spoken such things, the anger of everyone was moved against Philozomus, and they demanded that he likewise should receive the same sentence as Phileas.

**L** To which the Judge consented, and commanded that they should both be beheaded. And since we have made mention of this Phileas, and have praised his understanding and teaching, it seems good to me that we should also place in this history [excerpts] from his books, where he writes of the martyrdom of the martyrs to the Thmuitans, saying thus: "The holy martyrs who have fought with us have left us good examples, just as they were taught from the Divine Scripture; they fixed the eyes of their hearts on GOD and willingly embraced death without any fear for the sake of the truth. For always, without ceasing, they remembered that our LORD Jesus Christ became Man for our sake..."

**M** <margin>Thus writes Phileas to the Thmuitans regarding the pains of the martyrs.</margin>

<margin>
New ways of martyrdom against Christians, which everyone was permitted to perform.
</margin>
The strength, patience, and steadfastness of these martyrs is impossible for me to express, and is scarcely even believable, except to those who have seen it with their own eyes. For they were placed outside [the protection of law], and anyone, according to his will and lust, could inflict every insult upon the martyrs and torture them as he pleased: and if anyone could devise a new manner of torment and bring it there, he was allowed to perform the torture himself. Some were beaten with sticks, others with rods, some with whips, others with leather thongs that were tied with knots and bound to sticks. And every person was diligent to bring forth some new manner of torment. Some had their hands bound behind their backs and were stretched out upon wheels, and thus their limbs were gradually torn apart. To be mangled with claws or hooks was considered an old method and no longer esteemed. And when this manner of torment was assigned to any martyr, they did not only dig through the sides with hooks (as they used to torture murderers and killers), but they tore through the abdominal ribs and shins of our people, even down to the nails, with their scrapers and hooks. And neither the face nor the forehead could be free from the torments. Above all these things, when their entire bodies were thus torn without any mercy, their naked bodies were thrown into the streets—not only naked of clothes, but also of skin—and they left them lying there as a gruesome sight for those who passed by. Some they bound to pillars with their hands behind their backs and left them so. And the martyrs who were hung before the judge did not only remain hanging for the duration that they were questioned and examined, but remained for the entire day on the <term>Eculeis<note>original: "Eculeis." The *equuleus* was a wooden rack shaped like a horse, used to stretch the victim's body until the joints were dislocated.</note></term>, which are torture-racks, while other

<column-break/>

matters were being handled by the Judge, in order to investigate whether there might be any among the martyrs who, because of the great torments they suffered without ceasing, had changed his purpose and intent. While such cruelty was in the persecutors—and human reason was so completely taken from them that they had torn and mangled the whole body with torments and blows—the martyrs were then tied by the feet with a cord and thus dragged naked back into the prison, and their bodies, so freshly wounded, were thrown upon the ground, which was strewn with shards of stone pots, and their feet were locked together in a stock. Many there were who remained strong and bravely steadfast unto death, and thus put the wicked torturers to shame. Some who had recovered [from their wounds] called upon the torturers to begin again. Because the torturers were ashamed to torture them again—since the martyrs were still so bold—they commanded that they should be beheaded. These are the words of the true Divine Philosopher and blessed martyr Phileas, which he wrote from the prison where he lay captive to his congregation, which was committed to him, so that he might make them partakers with him of the heavenly reward.

### Of the city of Phrygia, in which all the Christians were burned for the confession of Christ.

### The 11th Chapter.

<margin>
A city in Phrygia burned with all its Christians.
</margin>
In Phrygia, a singular event occurred, through which common human law and the Roman law itself were violated and defiled. There was a Christian city in which all the people—the mayors and all the leading men together with the community—confessed that they were Christians and would not sacrifice to the gods. So the Romans commanded that they should besiege the city, so that neither women nor men, young nor old, could run away, and that they should then consume the city with fire: which was done, so that no one escaped. Such they did to their own citizens, which would have been a great cruelty to do even to their enemies. The <margin>Adauctus the martyr, the Emperor's treasurer.</margin> leader of all these blessed Martyrs was Adauctus, the noble and brave lover of truth, being born in Italy. He held many high-stewardship offices in the Emperor's palace, and...

## ¶ Concerning the multitude of Martyrs, who were at Alexandria and at Antioch, and how they were roasted upon a Gridiron.

### The xii. Chapter.

<margin>A terrible martyrdom at Alexandria.</margin>
How could I recount that which occurred in Alexandria, which even exceeds all the fables of the ancient Poets? For they cut off the ears of the Christians, and split their noses, chopped off their hands and some other limbs, and let them go in that wretched state.

<margin>The Christians roasted on the fire at Antioch.</margin>
At Antioch, they were laid upon a gridiron with glowing coals beneath it, and thus roasted. Among these were two youths, who did that which is worthy to be told. When these two were captured and men sought to force them to sacrifice to the Gods, they said: "Lead us to the Altars." And when they were brought there, they thrust their hands into the burning fire and said: "When we pull these hands out, then believe that we have sacrificed." And they held their hands still in the fire for so long,

<column-break/>

until the flesh was entirely burnt away.

<margin>G</margin>
Some others, when they were sought <margin>Some, throwing themselves from above, ended their lives.</margin> out to perform sacrifices, shunning such loathsome blasphemy, ended their lives by falling or leaping down from above; in these, the confidence to suffer patiently was less, but there was a greater cunning <note>The author uses "cunning" (liſtiehept) here to mean a clever or desperate resolve to escape sin through death.</note> to preserve their faith. Among these was also a noble and honorable woman, adorned with beauty and purity, and very abundant in goods. She had two <margin>H</margin> daughters, whom she had raised according to the Divine commandment in the fear of God <margin>Deuteronomy 6:7</margin> and they were very honorable and beautiful. And because of these natural and Divine gifts, they were envied by wicked men, and were sought after with all diligence. Thus they were warned, so that the storm and the pursuit might pass over. But such great diligence was applied, and they were so industriously sought, that the servants found them and forced them to return to Antioch. As they were thus forced and sitting upon a wagon, the virtuous mother spoke to her daughters: "You know, my dearest daughters, how I have raised you in the fear of God in your youth, and that God has been your father, your instructor and teacher, and that the virtue of purity has so pleased me in you, that your eye has not even been defiled by an impure sight. What is it that we <margin>I</margin> do now? You see well that all the <margin>K</margin> violence they do to us is nothing other than to separate us from God, or to cause us to lose our purity. Thus they shall surrender our bodies to public brothels, bodies which are scarcely known even to the common air. I pray you, my dear daughters, that <margin>L</margin> our faith be not so small that we fear death, or that we value our purity so little that we should desire to live once we had lost it. But if it happens that it pleases you to follow your mother's example, as you have done for so long, then let us forestall the executioner's impure hands, and take away the occasion <margin>The mother with her two daughters, out of honor, drown themselves in the river.</margin> of these impure men, and let us overcome this world, which forces and pulls us toward an impure life, with a pure death." When the mother saw that through such admonition, the daughters were also inflamed with the same purpose, they came while traveling to a river. And as they requested <margin>M</margin> to climb down for the necessity of nature <note>A euphemism for needing to relieve themselves.</note>, and the servants withdrew a little out of natural reverence, they fastened their clothes tightly and threw themselves thus into the flowing river.

->¶ Concerning the various martyrdoms that occurred in Pontus, among men and women.<-

### The xiij. Chapter.

<margin>Various martyrdoms in Pontus.</margin>
In the lands of Pontus, even more gruesome martyrdoms took place. They took sharp reeds and thrust them between the fingernails of the fingers of some; and over the backs of others, they poured molten lead until it reached their private parts. Also, they thrust glowing irons into the private parts and secret members of the women without any shame or mercy. But what can I do? Words fail me with which one might describe what crude, gruesome, and unheard-of blasphemies the unbelievers inflicted upon the Christians. Nevertheless, the strongest and most beloved martyrs suffered and overcame such things, while the Judges used all their diligence to find new methods of torment. But when they were finally sated with this unspeakable cruelty—not through reason or mercy, but because they began to notice that the cities were being robbed of their best citizens, and that the fields and lands lacked laborers, and that fathers were deprived of their children and children of their parents—they began to act somewhat more humanely and issued such a Mandate.

### The Punishment of the Christians.

<margin>Gouging out the right eye.</margin>
"Since it is not proper that so many citizens who remain so stubborn in their faith should be killed, it pleases us that such a class of people shall not be put to death. Instead, all those who hold to this form of confession <note>The public declaration of Christian faith.</note> shall have their right eye gouged out with an iron, and the same branded with a cautery mark; and also the left knee shall be crippled with the same branding iron, and they shall then be sent through the lands to labor in

<column-break/>

<margin>†</margin>
iron and mountain mines, or be assigned to other labor or work."

<margin>✠</margin>
This was the "Imperial mercy" which the Princes exercised over the Christians. They fashioned everything according to their own ways as it seemed good to them. But for the righteous and holy, the Crown of Patience was prepared by our Lord and Savior, and the faith of the believers was tested therein. And although it is impossible for me to recount all those who honored God through the suffering of their flesh, it nevertheless seems improper to me to remain entirely silent and make no mention of anyone. Thus, we shall tell of a few, especially those who were leaders of the Church.

->¶ Concerning the Bishops and leaders of the Church, and how they were martyred.<-

### The xiiij. Chapter.

<margin>☩</margin>
The first in the memory of the righteous was Anthimus, a Bishop in Nicomedia, who was beheaded; he who preached Christ in Nicomedia through his teaching and life. After him, Lucian of Antioch, who at that time preached Christ in word and deed. In the city of Tyre was the noble martyr Tyrannio <note>original: "Tyramio"</note>, who from his youth was raised in the teaching of Christ and was Bishop in that same city. Zenobius of Sidon, a Priest; and Silvanus <margin>p</margin>, the Bishop of the church of the Emesenes <note>The people of Emesa, modern-day Homs, Syria.</note>, who was thrown to the wild beasts in his city and thus fulfilled his martyrdom. In Palestine, Silvanus was the first, a Bishop at Gaza, along with many other Clergy. In Phaino <note>original: "Fano"; a mining district in Palestine famous for convict labor.</note>, forty were beheaded at once. Peleus and Nilus were burned with many Clergy. In this number also belongs the most precious flower of the churches and the Heavenly fruit, Pamphilus of Caesarea. In Alexandria, and in all Egypt or in <margin>z</margin> Thebais <note>original: "Thebaida"; the region of Upper Egypt.</note>, the first martyr—like a shining star—was the venerable Peter, Bishop of Alexandria; and with him Faustus, Dius, and Ammonius, Priests; and Phileas, Hesychius, Pachomius, and Theodosius, bishops of the cities of Egypt; and unspeakably many others were martyred with these same Bishops. To write of each martyrdom individually would be too long for us; thus I leave it to their fellow citizens who were present there to tell such things to posterity.

### How God avenged Himself upon the Tyrants.

### The xv. Chapter.

<margin>Diocletian. Maximian.</margin>
In the meantime, the state of Christendom became very distressed and disturbed due to the great cruelty and tyranny, which was not hidden from the eternal God. And while the Lord wished to allow His family to be chastened in a few, and as the bloody servants of cruelty raged against many, immediately the avenging right hand of God was ready against the Tyrants. And those who first, when they kept the Church in peace, governed the Empire in all prosperity, God changed their fortune so that Diocletian himself, being so distressed and confused, laid down the Royal Scepter along with his companion Maximian and lived only with common folk. <note>This refers to the unprecedented joint abdication of Diocletian and Maximian in 305 AD.</note> And Maximian, who was next in honor and subsequently the leader and standard-bearer of our persecution, was plagued with so many various diseases and filths of the body, and came to such madness, that after long and incurable illnesses, he shamefully killed himself. But this happened later.

### Concerning the cruelties of Constantius, Constantine, Licinius, and Maxentius.

<margin>Constantius. Herculius.</margin>

Because of this, a great famine <term>diere tijt; literally "dear time," a period of extreme food scarcity and high prices</term> arose in the city of Rome and the surrounding lands, so that there was very little support for life.

# Of the cruelty of Emperor Maximinus, and of Dorothea and Sophronia.

## The XVII Chapter.

<margin>The second dog of Emperor Maximinus.</margin>
<margin>Maximinus surpassing his companion in sorcery.</margin>
In Egypt and in all the lands situated toward the East, Maximinus likewise reigned in such cruelty and fury, so that it seemed the one followed the other in wickedness; and they were such equal companions in their tyranny that it was not possible [to distinguish them]. Nevertheless, Maximinus surpassed his companion in the blasphemy of sorcery. For he ordained and also desired that the masters of sorcery and the evil arts should be given the greatest and most public honors.

Likewise, he was also very inclined toward the service of idols, so that he did not rest for a single moment without augury and divination.
Where

<column-break/>

<margin>He commanded the idolatrous temples to be erected and placed noblemen there as priests.</margin>
he was a more [cruel] persecutor than the first Emperors had been. He commanded that the idolatrous temples, which had previously been abandoned by their servants, should be renewed again, and he ordained priests and bishops there from among his noblemen, and also those who were previously in great command and office; and the knights were their servants, and he ordained properties for them so that they might maintain their status. And the greatest augurs, diviners, and sorcerers he made the governors of provinces or captains and leaders of the people.

<margin>V</margin>
To accomplish all these vain services and wickednesses, much money needed to be gathered. For this reason, it happened that all the provinces and lands were robbed of money in various ways, through the manifold taxation and burdens with which they were weighed down. He knew how to charge the wealthy with some invented crime or injustice, and thereby seize [their wealth], so that he condemned some and banished some from the country, and always took all their goods and their paternal inheritance. For which reason he gathered much money and property, and shared it with his sorcerers and soldiers. At the table, when he held his meals, he was so dissolute and wanton that one might suspect, through the fullness of the wine, that he had been insane; and being thus drunk, he commanded some things that he did not remember the next day—namely, that he had commanded them.

<margin>He invents a crime for the wealthy to confiscate their property.</margin>
<margin>X</margin>
Thus he lived very dissolutely in all manners of improper pleasures, and gave his servants and knights a bad example. So it was that all the injustice and wantonness that occurred there by the superiors who governed the lands went unpunished, because of the Emperor’s example, who did such things himself. He was also very diligent among other evils he committed, that he had left neither city nor scarcely a village where he did not fulfill his adultery with some noble women, or violate some virgins. How could such an open enemy of justice and honor, and of all good things, not also be an enemy of the Christians? Against whom he used such cruelty that he surpassed his predecessors therein, with all manners of torments, with fire and glowing plates and irons, with wild beasts, and also by throwing them into the depths of the sea, with the hacking off of limbs,

# of the Ancient Christian Church. The 8th Book. Fol. 157.

<margin>A [The tyrant] takes pleasure in torturing every limb.</margin>
A ...and the lifting up of his eyes, he took such pleasure in it that he wished he could inflict a particular pain upon every single limb. Nevertheless, the Christians proved much stronger and were found more steadfast in suffering than he was clever and subtle in devising such manifold martyrdoms. Many a time he was also defeated by women, who were so inflamed by the fervor of their faith in the Word of God that although they were captured as women, they were crowned in the struggle as strong men. They much preferred to suffer death—indeed, they desired it—rather than be defiled by any impurity.

<margin>B Dorothea, a noble maiden of Alexandria</margin>
B So it happened at that time in Alexandria to a young noblewoman, very rich, named Dorothea. She was of high birth, very diligent, well-educated in all the arts, and exceedingly beautiful. Valuing the purity of her soul more than that of her body, she preferred to offer herself to God rather than submit to human use, so that, being sanctified to God, she wished to remain a virgin. But the tyrant <note>referring to Maximinus Daza</note>, who was inflamed with lewdness as well as cruelty, became aware of her beauty. Desiring her more for her looks than for her good manners and virtues, he set his mind on defiling and violating this noble maiden. When he learned she was a Christian, and that according to his own edicts she deserved to be punished rather than enjoyed through his lust, he was torn as to which of the two he should subject her to first.

<margin>C</margin>
But when lewdness overcame his wavering mind, he approached the maiden—who was daily expecting to suffer martyrdom—through secret messengers, urging her to consent to his impurity. To these she answered that it was improper for her to defile the temple of her body, which she had offered to God, with idolatry and the filth of lewdness.

<margin>E</margin>
Thus she preferred and was readier to die than to consent to any such things. She also stated it was not fitting for such a cruel tyrant to speak of anything lovely or pleasant, as his heart was so filled with cruelty; he was not worthy that his cruel spirit, which he revealed daily by shedding Christian blood, should receive any recreation <note>original: "recreatie"; meaning pleasure or relief</note> from her. By this answer, the tyrant was further inflamed to lust, so that

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin>
he resolved that if he could not obtain her through friendship or cunning, he would take her by force. Therefore, this pure maiden fled secretly by night with some of her servant-maidens and another virgin, leaving behind all her goods, house, and estate, thus leaving the insane tyrant in his rage. He wished to dishonor many other noble women and maidens like her, but they much preferred to suffer death than to be obedient to his impure mind.

<margin>H Sophronia of Rome.</margin>
All of these received death very joyfully and bravely, believing that two types of crowns were prepared for them by the Lord: not only for their confession of faith, but also for their purity. Similarly, there was in Rome a noblewoman named Sophronia, whose husband was a prefect and judge under the tyrant Maxentius. This Maxentius noticed the beauty of this woman and sent his ministers of lewdness, as was his custom, commanding that the woman be brought to him. She told this to her husband. After the husband had thought and deliberated for a long time, he finally said with a heavy sigh: "What shall we do in this? We must either suffer or die." When the wife saw that her husband, out of fear of death, was willing to surrender and deliver his wife's honor, she said to those who had been sent to fetch her: "Wait a little while, until I am properly dressed and adorned."

<margin>I</margin>
Afterward, she went into her bedroom, and after she had first

<margin>K Stabs herself</margin>
prayed on bended knees, offering her purity to God, she pierced her breast and body with a sword. She then sent her maid, who had been guarding her, to announce this message to the tyrant, saying: "Let such Christian women be more pleasing to the tyrant."

<margin>L</margin>
In this manner, both these tyrants—the one in the East and the other in the West—raged as if armed with the same devilish spirit. Nonetheless, through their tyranny, the strength of the Christians was tested, and through the steadfastness of their faith, they became greater and more widely known.

# The Chronicle of Eusebius Pamphilus

¶ ...those who served God were put to death. And as the desire of this tyrant was continually ignited toward greater cruelty and lust, without any counsel or satiety of blood being able to change him, Almighty God, through His providence, chose to come to the aid of His servants. Those whom He had tested through fire, He now led back to refreshment. For Divine vengeance struck at the very source of the crime: suddenly, he who had walked proudly with joyful and healthy flesh was himself struck down, with all his limbs swelling, bloating, and stretching. Deep within his breast arose a swelling <note>likely a tumor or severe inflammation</note> which devoured his internal organs like a serpent. Thereafter, he developed fistulas <note>painful, abnormal passages or sores</note> deep within his flesh, so that, amidst the internal rotting, an unspeakable multitude of worms crawled within his body. The stench was so unbearable that no physicians could even approach him.

<margin>Galerius Maximianus begins to fall ill.</margin>
<margin>He stinks unbearably.</margin>
Because his flesh had been so delicately and luxuriously nourished, the stench of its corruption was all the more horrifying. And because the physicians could not endure being near him, he sometimes commanded that they be put to death. Among them was one who, suspecting he would be killed rather than be able to cure him, spoke through God’s inspiration: "O Emperor, you are greatly mistaken to think that men can heal what God has sent. This sickness is not natural, nor can it be cured by any physicians. But remember what you have done against God’s servants, and how impiously and arrogantly you have acted against the Divine Religion; then you shall understand and know from whence you may obtain help and remedy. For though he <note>the doctor</note> may die with the others, you nonetheless shall not be healed by any physician."

<margin>The Mandate <note>The Edict of Toleration, 311 AD</note></margin>
The Emperor Galerius Maximianus, Unconquered, Augustus, Supreme Priest <note>original: "overste Bisschop", translating the Latin *Pontifex Maximus*</note>, Conqueror of the Germans, Conqueror of Egypt, Conqueror of Thebes, five times Conqueror of the Sarmatians, twice Conqueror of the Persians, six times Conqueror of the Carpians, Conqueror of the Armenians, Victor of the Medes and the Adiabenians, holder of Tribunician power twenty times, Emperor nineteen times, Consul eight times, Father of the Country; And the Emperor Flavius Valerius Constantinus, Pious, Fortunate, Unconquered, Augustus, Supreme Priest, holder of Tribunician power five times, Consul four times, Father of the Country:

Among all the things we have ordained for the benefit and utility of the common good, we first desired to bring all things back into accordance with the ancient discipline of the Roman Laws. To this end, we had previously ordained that the Christians, who had abandoned the religion of their ancestors, should be compelled to return to it. But noting that they are so stubborn in their resolve that they will in no way return to the manner of the ancient religion established by our ancestors—instead, each has made a law for himself according to his own will and gathered various peoples in different places—therefore, when a Mandate was published by us that they should return to their ancestral laws established of old, there were many who preferred to cast themselves into great peril...

...things, so that they were forced by wonder to confess that He is the great, only, and true God whom the Christians serve.

And those of ours who had remained faithful and brave during the martyrdoms lived peacefully in all joy and confidence. And those who had acted weakly and sluggishly <note>referring to those who had lapsed or recanted their faith under the pressure of persecution</note> desired with all humility and prayer the medicine and help of those who had remained steadfast, praying that through their prayers they might obtain mercy from the Almighty God. And those who were released from the metal mines came humbly into all the cities and gladdened the Assembly of God with an unspeakable joy. Traveling along the way, in villages and in the streets of the cities, they proceeded while singing Psalms and hymns of praise, so that people wondered and praised God; for they saw those whom they had previously seen bound with chains and enslaved in the mines now returning home with great joy and cheerfulness. Even those who were previously troublesome to us and persecuted us were delighted by this sudden change. When all such things happened in the cities, the villages, and the countryside, and the people rejoiced with a fitting joy over this peace for the Christians, the tyrant <note>Maximinus Daia</note> could not bear it, for he was an enemy of all good. With his innate cunning, he did his best to turn this peace and joy into sorrow.

### <margin>R</margin> Concerning the Tyranny of Maximinus against the Christians, that they were not allowed to dwell in their own houses, nor to assemble.

#### The 2nd Chapter.

<margin>S</margin>
<margin>Christians were first forbidden to assemble in the churchyards.</margin>
And while Maximinus—as said above—reigned in the East and in the land of Egypt, he did not leave the Christians in peace for more than six months, but quickly did his best to disturb this. Thus he sought out various causes, and first he forbade our people from assembling in the churchyards <note>cemeteries or burial grounds of martyrs, which were traditional gathering places</note>. And after that, he incited and awakened certain wicked men in the city of Antioch to send an embassy and a petition against us, desiring that the Christians should not be per-

<column-break/>

<margin>T</margin>
<margin>Embassy against the Christians.</margin>
-mitted or allowed to live in their own houses and estates. He initiated this embassy through a steward of the city of Antioch named Theotecnus, who was a man of wicked character and intent.

In the same way, this Maximinus had also incited and arranged for certain crafty and vile citizens in other cities to carry out such a crime, so that from all those provinces such an embassy or message should be sent forth.

<margin>V</margin>
Many other things he handled against us with a singular hatred and stubborn quarreling, until in every way he renewed the wicked treatment that had recently ceased. That evil heart and fierce mood were set as if he were suffering hunger and thirst, unless he saw the flesh of the citizens torn apart and their blood shed.

### <margin>X</margin> Concerning the Idol Philius, which was costly consecrated at Antioch.

#### The 3rd Chapter.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Jupiter Philius, that is, a God of friendship.</margin>
Thereafter, it seemed to him that he had found the very best cause; for in Antioch, an image was costly consecrated named Jupiter Philius <note>original: "Jupiter Philius"; Philius is the Latin form of the Greek "Philios," meaning "friendly" or "of friendship."</note>, that is, a God of friendship. This image was so enchanted with certain sorceries and impure consecrations that it even deceived the eyes of those who looked upon it; it was thought to perform wonderful things, to tell of future events, and also to warn beforehand and give answers. This was so believable to the common people, and the Emperors considered it to be so. Finally, it was believed by all men, and it was said that this idol had given a warning that the Christians should not be allowed to live in the cities or in the places located near the cities, but that they should be driven as far away as possible. When this became public, all those situated under the Tyrant's Rule, in all cities and provinces—knowing that it was pleasing to their Prince—held such a similar feeling and suspicion toward the Christians. And they thus sent their messages or embassies to the Emperor, and obtained that which was first plotted by him: that they should request such things.

<margin>A</margin> ¶ How Maximinus honored the priests of the Idols.

### The iiij. Chapter.

<margin>B</margin> <margin>The Temple-priests are endowed with honors.</margin> **T**hen a great rage of persecution was once again renewed against us, and Maximinus, with all his diligence, appointed and ordained priests and bishops of the Idols in every city and province, endowing them with many gifts and honors. He handled everything with great care so that they might prosper through his favors, and consequently be more inclined to hate and kill the Christians. He achieved this the more effectively because he held those in the highest favor whom he found to be the most cruel toward the Christians.

And if there was anyone who wished to give a piece of bread / they were so terrified that upon seeing it and desiring to stretch out their hand to take it / the strength of their body failed them / and they fell down dead before the feet of the one who was giving it. And if there was anyone among those who were very rich and wished to share some food with the needy out of compassion / he was hindered by the crush of the great multitude / among whom there was no one whom he could rightfully refuse / and he could not complete that work of mercy / because of the violence of those who had been made shameless by hunger. Thus all the streets and alleys were filled with dead bodies / and there was no one who would bring them to the earth / because those who still seemed to be alive / were as powerless from sickness / as those who were about to die immediately: which was a gruesome thing to behold / for many bodies were devoured by the dogs.

<margin>This is the fruit of this bloody Mandate of Maximinus.</margin>
Thus two gruesome plagues came among the people / namely famine and pestilence. For the poor who sought their daily food through the labor of their hands / were destroyed by the hunger / and the rich who had plenty to live on / by the pestilence. So that one saw / that a noble generation died out in a short time.

<margin>Hunger and pestilence, two strong war-bears.</margin>
In such various ways hunger and pestilence waged war / but the end was always death, which destroyed cities and lands. This was the repayment for the Law and the pride and the puffed-up arrogance of Maximinus / and a vengeance of the judgment that had gone out against the Christians. This was his "divine service" / and the majesty of his religion / of which he boasted / that it had been given to him from Heaven.

<margin>The Pagans called upon the Christians for help.</margin>
In all these things / while the dead bodies lay unburied in the streets / and in the houses / having died of hunger and of the pestilence / and while those who still lived were distressed by hunger / then all the Pagans <note>original: "Heydenen"</note> earnestly begged the Christians for mercy / and assistance / whom they had shortly before driven out of their houses and dwellings and out of the land / asking that they might, according to their usual manner, give help with food to the living / and bury the dead who were unburied / because mercy and love were found only among them: for the Pagans were forced to confess / that there was no religion nor life so holy and perfect as to be helpful to all men / and to advise and serve one's neighbor:

and also that there is no other God than the God of the Christians.

<margin>Mark 5.</margin>

<margin>Triple service of the Christians toward the Pagans.</margin>

And those who were sick with the pestilence / whom none of the Pagans, not even their nearest friends, dared to approach / these they sought out and helped / and were themselves not infected with that sickness / for they were preserved by God’s grace / and they also buried their dead without any fear. ## ¶ Concerning Constantine’s victory against Maxentius, and concerning the command of Constantine and Licinius, how one shall honor Christ.

### The ninth chapter.

<margin>Constantine Augustus against Maxentius</margin>
**A**s now the most godly Emperor Constantine, a son of the pious Emperor Constantius, was preparing himself for war against Maxentius the tyrant at Rome, and as he came with his army, he was already hospitable toward the Christians and honored the true God; however, he had not yet received (as is the custom among us) that sign of the Lord’s passion <note>This likely refers to baptism or the public profession of faith symbolized by the cross.</note>.

<margin>Truly, how one formerly received the Christians.</margin>
As he was now traveling, and on the way often pondering the burden and necessity of the upcoming war, and often raising his eyes to heaven, desiring Divine help, he saw in a dream <note>or vision</note> toward the East in the Heaven a sign of the cross, like a burning fire. As he was terrified by such a sight and greatly amazed, it seemed to him that angels stood by him, saying:
<margin>In this, conquer. <note>original Latin: "In hoc vince"</note></margin>
> O Constantine, in this conquer.

And being joyful because of this vision, and now being assured of victory by means of that sign he had seen in the Heaven, he marked himself therewith upon his forehead. Thus was he invited by Heaven to the faith: and it does not seem a wonder to me, just as it was also spoken from Heaven: 
<margin>Acts 9:4 and 22:7.</margin>
> Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? I am Jesus of Nazareth. 

There is only this much difference here: that this man did not persecute, but was a lover of the faith. Thereafter, Constantine had that sign which had been shown to him in Heaven made upon his banners, and thus adorned with the weapons and banners of our Religion, he set forth to fight against his enemy. 
<margin>Labarum is the name of the banner. <note>The Labarum was a military standard used by Roman emperors, which Constantine modified to include the Chi-Rho symbol.</note></margin> 
And it is said that he also had the sign of the Cross made of gold, and held that in his right hand. 

But it seems to me quite necessary that we relate and tell somewhat more broadly what intention and meaning this godly prince had. As Constantine, through the help of Divine power, was now certain of victory, he reflected that he was named Roman Emperor, *Pater Patriae* <note>original Latin: "Father of the Fatherland"</note>, and desired to surpass in kindness and peace all those who had reigned before him, as far as it was possible; and that he was now forced to wage war, not only against the land, but against the city of Rome, which is the head of the Empire,

<column-break/>

and that he could not obtain nor liberate the common land without an assault upon the territory which the tyrants possessed. Thus he was distressed in this, and prayed to God day and night that He would not defile his right hand, which was armed with that blessed sign, with Roman blood. As he always prayed for this, Divine providence also granted it to him. For when he was positioned with his people not far from the bridge called Mulvius <note>The Milvian Bridge</note>, Maxentius was incited by Divine power, and thus hastily rushed out of Rome to meet the Emperor Constantine, and ordered that the rest of the army should follow him; and he thus rode ahead armed with few people. He had previously commanded that they should break the same Bridge, and that they should lay planks upon piles, deceitfully like a mouse-trap, and cover them to make them look like the bridge. And as he now rode hastily ahead on horseback, not thinking of the work that he himself had caused to be made, he rode with a few horsemen upon the bridge, and the boats <note>supporting the trap</note> gave way, and he thus fell into the Tiber and drowned.
<margin>Maxentius drowns in the Tiber</margin>

Thus all the war and bloodshed was brought to nothing by the tyrant's death, and Constantine’s right hand was preserved undefiled by the blood of the citizens. Then it was seen that what happened through Moses to the children of Israel could also rightfully be said: 
<margin>Exodus 14 and 15.</margin>
> He has cast Pharaoh's chariot and all his forces into the Sea, and his best horsemen and soldiers are drowned in the Red Sea. 

For this Maxentius and the horsemen who were with him also drowned in the depths, and were overturned with the Bridge which he had prepared for the Emperor Constantine, so that one may also rightfully say of him: 
<margin>Psalm 7:16, Ezekiel 7:19, Proverbs 27:29</margin>
> He has opened and dug a pit, and has himself fallen into the pit which he made. His sorrow shall return upon his head, and his malice shall descend upon the crown of his head.

This is aptly applied to wicked men.

But to the Emperor Constantine, as a servant of God, one may rightfully attribute what Moses sang after the victory, when his enemies were destroyed, saying: 
<margin>Exodus 15:1, 21.</margin>
> Let us sing to the LORD, for He has done a glorious deed: horse and rider He has thrown into the sea. He is my helper and protector and has become my salvation. Who is like unto Thee, O Lord, among the gods? Who is like Thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders...

# The Chronicle of Eusebius Pamphilus

<margin>
Constantine comes in triumph to Rome.
</margin>

Although these things did not occur through human words alone, Constantine nevertheless sang such gratitude in his heart to the supreme God—who had helped him to victory—and thus rode triumphantly into the city of Rome. Then all the people, the mothers with their children, the Senators, and all the common Roman people rejoiced, being delivered from such subjection and the burden of the cruel tyrant; they received Constantine as the author of their salvation and the restorer of their liberty. But he was not changed by the praiseworthy shouts of the common people or the joy of such a city, nor did he attribute the victory to himself, but rather to the divine gift. And when the Senators had ordained his statue, as was customary in the manner of a triumph, he commanded that a banner of the cross of our Lord be placed in its right hand, and that they should inscribe beneath it: 

> Through this singular sign, which is a sign of true power, the city of Rome, the Senators, and all the common people are delivered from the burden of the tyrant's rule, and restored to their former freedom and nobility.

<margin>
Licinius Emperor.
</margin>

At the same time, Licinius also held agreement with Emperor Constantine (for he had not yet fallen into the madness <note>This refers to the later persecutions initiated by Licinius when he eventually turned against Constantine and the Christians.</note> that he came to hereafter), knowing and confessing that God was the cause of all this prosperity and victory; they established with one hand and mind a Law <note>The Edict of Milan, 313 AD.</note>, in which they honored the God of the Christians with full praise, confessing therein that the cause of this victory and of all other works was the same God, and that for this reason all men should thank and honor God. They also sent this Law or Mandate to Maximinus, who at that time reigned in the East, and who desired the friendship of them both.

<margin>
The Law commanded by the Emperors Constantine and Licinius on how one shall honor Christ.
</margin>

This Maximinus, being dismayed by the prosperity and victory of these Emperors—and although everything being written was contrary to him—nevertheless dared not set himself against it; it shamed him that he should give way through compulsion and the power of others. Thus, through fear and shame, he took counsel with his wretched advisors to issue a Law or Mandate by his own authority, as if it were also his own will, expressing similar sentiments for the Christians. In this, he would recount and relate how it had seemed good to his ancestors, the Emperors, that the Christian people—as those who were contrary to the service of the gods—should be utterly destroyed,

<column-break/>

<margin>
Freedom of choice.
</margin>

and that he himself for a long time was of the same opinion, to strengthen and execute such a sentence. But seeing that the more such people were hindered and forbidden, the more they grew and increased: "Therefore it is my will, that if anyone consents to the service of the gods through kind and loving words, they shall be received; but no one shall be unwillingly forced thereto. Instead, it shall stand in the free will of every individual by what service and manner they wish to honor and serve God, and that for this matter no disturbance or destruction should be allowed to happen in the Provinces."

<margin>
Sabinus the official.
</margin>

Maximinus wrote this to Sabinus, the chief judge. Nevertheless, it was known to all men that this did not come from a good heart, but was a feigned friendship. Thus, there was no one among our people who dared to hold gatherings or do anything in public regarding our faith—such as rebuilding the churches or the like, as our status required and as the Mandate sent to him by the Emperors contained. But the evil tyrant, cruel of mind, only permitted this out of fear, and he did not change his desires until divine vengeance punished him. Because he had unjustly and out of the audacity of his mind assumed the name "Augustus" or the empire, and because he was a man in whom there was no wisdom, sobriety, or moderation, but was haughty and puffed up with pride, he also raised himself against his fellow rulers of the Empire, in whom royal piety was shining. He declared himself to be the highest and first of them both, and shortly thereafter broke the treaty or truce, waging war and fighting against Licinius; in a short time, he devastated everything and became a burden and trouble to the cities and the armies.

<margin>
The decree of Maximinus, who pretends as if he held it as his own.

Maximinus's battle against Licinius.
