But victory fled from him who was unpleasing and hateful before God and men, and went to his adversary. When his soldiers and cavalry were mostly slain, those few who remained surrendered themselves to the opponent. When Maximinus now saw that he was deceived by his gods and abandoned by men, he...

### A MANDATE OF THE EMPEROR GALERIUS MAXIMINUS, for the Christians.

->**The Emperor Galerius Maximinus Germanicus, Sarmaticus Pius, blessed and invincible, Augustus.**<- <note>Galerius Maximinus, also known as Maximinus Daza, was a Roman Emperor who initially persecuted Christians but changed his policy on his deathbed.</note>

<margin>F</margin> Inasmuch as we constantly provide care for our subjects, and would gladly counsel for their benefit and the common profit and welfare, and would not entirely abandon that which might be pleasing and dear to many. Thus, because it is manifest to all men how it was commanded by our ancestors, the divine emperors Diocletian and Maximian, that it should not be permitted for Christians to gather together, and that therefore much robbery and violence has been committed by the Officers, and daily to the great disadvantage and harm of our subjects (for whom we have a special concern), so that they were nearly robbed of all their goods and ancestral

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

recognitions. There-
<margin>G</margin> fore, in the past year, we wrote a Law that if anyone wished to adhere to this people or faith, such a will and intention should be hindered by no one, but they should follow their own mind in it, and that it be permitted for them to do as they please without any fear or suspicion. It has nevertheless become known to us that some of the Officers have forbidden our subjects to be troubled,

<margin>H</margin> yet others torment them in the name of our authority, so that they might be more hesitant in the Religion they love. And so that hereafter all fear and doubt may be removed, we command by this our Mandate, and wish it to be public to everyone, that it is permitted to all those who adhere to the Christian faith (through this our kind generosity) that each may serve this Religion and its glory as they please and as fits their mind. We also permit that they may again rebuild their houses of prayer, their *Cathedrals*, according to their pleasure.

<margin>I</margin><margin>Note "Dominica oratoria" (Houses of the Lord).</margin> And that it may be known that this our permission is increased in all things, we also command by this decree: If any houses, fields, or any other goods, by order of our ancestors, have come to confiscation from the Christians' property, or if anyone has subtracted or diminished anything, or given it to another through a gift—all these we command shall be returned to the Christians according to their ancient right, and to each what belongs to him, so that all men may perceive the benefit of our kind generosity.

<margin>L</margin> * The first Christians had built their Churches in honor of Christ and called them *DOM*, in which they came together to pray, to read the Holy Scripture, and to receive the Eucharist. And the word *Domini*, which is "of the Lord," was more commonly used than the name "Christian," following Apostolic custom and the use of the Gospel Histories. Since they always had the Lord in their mouths, they also called the place in which they gathered in the Lord's Name *Dominica*, that is, *Dom*. For this reason, the Germans have called the Episcopal Churches, which are the most prominent and oldest, *Dom* <note>original: "Dom-kercken"</note>, and their Canons "Dom-heeren" [Cathedral Lords], just as some Templars take their name from the Temple.

<margin>M</margin> There is also still seen near Molsheim an old little church where some Roman antiquities are found; it is called by the farming folk *Dompieter*, which is *Dominicum Petri* <note>The Lord's House of Peter</note>. Maximinus reinstated such an ordinance, he who the year before had caused a decree of punishment against us to be engraved upon tablets of copper, as if it were to endure forever. In those tablets, he commanded that we should be hunted and banished from the cities, villages, and the countryside as the most wretched of criminals. Yet even this conversion was not from a sincere heart, but rather as if he intended to settle a debt with God by way of compensation. Because the hope he placed in his gods had deceived him in the first war, his intention in this was to change his protector and helper so that he might begin the war anew. But the wretched man did not know that God cannot be persuaded toward a poorly conceived work by the bribes or payments of men.

# How Maximinus died, and of the conduct of the early Christians, of their singing and preaching, and of other ceremonies, and of Licinius’s mandate against the Christians.

## The 10th Chapter.

<margin>Maximinus dies.</margin>
<margin>They are publicly ashamed.</margin>
Now, when Maximinus had prepared himself with all his power for an unjust war, he was beset by internal pains in his loins and was so greatly tormented that he could neither rest nor lie still. Jumping from his bed, he frequently fell to the earth; and he, who was previously a glutton for food and a great drunkard, could now taste neither food nor drink. Thus, his flesh was utterly wasted away by illness. Nevertheless, this sickness brought the wretched man to such a point that, at the final end of his life, he acknowledged and confessed the righteous vengeance of God and the guilt of his own crimes. Finally, he became blind through his illness, and then he saw most clearly what madness he had committed against Christ; and so he died. When he—who had at times been unspeakably enraged against us and at other times slightly more merciful out of fear—was dead, the other righteous Princes <note>Likely referring to Constantine and Licinius, who were co-emperors at the time.</note> permitted this transition without any suspicion or fear. Thus, the affairs of the Christians were established much more clearly than before, and the Word of God and

<column-break/>

Christ’s teaching were proclaimed much more gloriously and freely. Then our enemies, because of the great cruelty and tyranny they had used against us, were ashamed, so much so that they did not dare to lift their eyes or look at anyone. For Maximinus was declared by imperial decree to be a tyrant and a criminal, hateful to God and men. It was ordered that his painted tablets and copper statues should be destroyed and cast down, and some were smeared over with black paint. <note>This refers to the Roman practice of *damnatio memoriae*, where a fallen ruler's name and image were systematically erased from public records and monuments.</note> Thus, a very hasty and unforeseen change occurred, so that even the name of Maximinus, who had intended an eternal punishment against the Christians, was removed from human memory or preserved only in shame.

<margin>Peucedius</margin>
The righteous Princes also commanded that Maximinus’s officers and judges should be put to death, as they were participants in his crimes and cruelty. Among these, the leader in all manner of cruelty was Peucedius, who had been made a Councilor three times by Maximinus and was the High Judge. And likewise,
<margin>Quintianus.</margin>
Quintianus, who had raged in Egypt with unspeakable tyranny, spilling the blood of the Christians. And many others through whom Maximinus’s wickedness had taken its nourishment and growth.
<margin>Theotecnus.</margin>
Among these was also Theotecnus, who finally learned that God is an avenger and a rewarder of evil deeds. Because he had consecrated and dedicated an idol in Antioch, Maximinus had granted him the office of judge. But when Licinius came to Antioch and commanded that all the sorcerers be captured and put to death, these priests
<margin>The miracle of the idol by which they were captured.</margin>
and sorcerers of the new idol, along with their companions and masters, were also captured. When they were asked in what manner the idol gave its answers or warnings, or how such miraculous things seemed to happen, they at first refused to speak. But when they were finally questioned more diligently <note>A common euphemism in historical texts for questioning under torture.</note>, they revealed and confessed the whole matter: how it had been orchestrated and how it was all put together and staged by the art of Theotecnus. Thus, because Theotecnus was the cause of such
<margin>Maximinus’s children, along with the sorcerers and soothsayers, were killed.</margin>
great deception, Licinius commanded that he, along with the other servants, sorcerers, priests, and soothsayers of this new devil, should be put to death. Likewise, the children of Maximinus were also killed—those whom he had designated and chosen as heirs to the Empire—as well as his closest friends, who had been a burden to the citizens and the common people.

# Among Christian Churches. The Second Book.

**Column 1**

<margin>Psalm 146</margin>
Those who had been troublesome and burdensome were also put to death. It must have been a foolishly raging people who did not hear the warning of the Holy Scriptures, which say: "Put not your trust in princes, nor in the children of men, in whom there is no salvation: For their spirit shall go forth and return to the earth, and then all their thoughts shall perish." <note>A quotation from Psalm 146:3-4, emphasizing the transience of human power compared to God.</note> But we, whose hope and salvation is in the Almighty God alone, and in our Savior Christ—a King of all things and redeemer of our souls—willingly accept punishment from him, and likewise expect peace and grace from him again.

As now that wicked generation of men, who were pleasing neither to God nor to men, was so quickly melted away, then was rightfully fulfilled what the Holy Spirit had spoken before:
<margin>Psalm 37</margin>
> I have seen the wicked exalted and lifted up like the cedar tree of Lebanon, and I passed by, and behold, he was not; and I sought his place, and found it not.

Thus the dark cloud was driven away, and a clear and joyful day shone brighter upon the earth than before; the shining Sun cast its light into Christ’s Assembly, and there was no one who could see otherwise, except for the hateful eye. But all people rejoiced that the atrocities of the cruel tyrants were over; even those who were not believers nevertheless confessed with favor that the true God is a helper to mortal men, and that the hope of those who hope in Christ is sure and firm.

Therefore, a great joy came among all people as a gift of God, and especially when one saw the places that had previously been destroyed by the tyrants now being rebuilt much more magnificently and costlier than before. For the favor of the Christian Princes was very helpful to us, and with their Christian mandates they greatly strengthened the courage of our people, as they were also frequently writing to the Bishops, honoring the Priests with great dignity, and also performing their assistance very generously.
<margin>Dedications, or consecrations of the Churches.</margin>

In these times, our people held many high celebrations with all joy and gladness in cities and lands, with all peace and gratitude. The Priests gathered together, and no one who lived far from one another felt it a burden to come together. One people came to the other, and as true members of one body of Christ, they were

<column-break/>

joyfully joined together with one another.

So it was that in them was well fulfilled the prophetic figure <note>The author refers to a "figure," a theological term where an Old Testament event foreshadows a New Testament reality.</note> announced in mystery, saying: "That one bone shall be gathered to the other, and one limb to the other," in which also one spirit was poured into all the members, which might rightly be called one soul: for in them all is one faith, and the one God is honored by them all, and with one mouth they all praise the Lord together. Among the Priests and in everything that belonged to the service of God, a great loveliness and grace was seen to shine.
<margin>Ezekiel 37:7</margin>
<margin>The Choir of Psalm-singers</margin>

Nearby stood the choirs of those who sang Psalms; the young men and the maidens, the elders with the youths praised the Name of the Lord.
<margin>Service of exaltation.</margin>

Here the spiritual and hidden Services were maintained with good order. There sat the Bishops and Priests, shining through their venerable old age. And if someone there, being stirred by the grace of God, began to preach before the people, they listened diligently with all silence, turning their mouths and eyes toward him, and waited as if something from Heaven were being messaged and announced to them through him.
<margin>The Preachers to the people.</margin>

Such reverence and dignity was there among those who listened, and such good order was kept among the Priests, so that now one, then the other—and not only two or three spoke (as the Apostle says) and the others examined—but all those into whose mouths the word was given were speaking, just as Moses had said:
<margin>Prophecy in the churches. 1 Corinthians 14.</margin>
<margin>Numbers 11:29</margin>
> Would to God that all the Lord’s assemblies prophesied, and that God gave up His spirit to them.

There was neither hate nor envy; the gifts of God were served to the people, and each one, according to what is written, was diligent to be in abundance for the edification of the Assemblies. And all these things happened in great love, and they held one another in great honor, each considering the other better than himself. The simple and humble people, wondering, honored those who taught the people through the wisdom of the Word. And the wise and learned men more highly esteemed those to whom God gave a greater trust through their pure and unadulterated simplicity.
<margin>The Bishops and Priests likewise</margin>
<margin>Philippians 2:3</margin>

To offer offerings; and to these was much entrusted and the office commanded to offer the sacrifice <note>This likely refers to the celebration of the Eucharist or the "sacrifice of praise" during the dedication of new church buildings.</note> to God, who was preserving the common simplicity of life in the purity of the heart. Thus they considered with all diligence how they might honor and prefer one another.

Folio 170.
### Eusebius Pamphilus’s Chronicle

**Column 1**

<margin>Constantine Augustus dearly loves the church.</margin>
☼ Now that the glory of the Churches was appearing before God and men with such simplicity, being nothing other than a heavenly likeness and image here on earth, it was most significant that the Emperor Constantine rejoiced in this. Growing daily in faith and the Christian religion, he was filled with an unspeakable joy over the prosperity and welfare of the Christian Churches. He was also of the opinion that he should not consider the priests as his equals, but that they should be held much higher, as those who bore the image of the Divine presence.

☼ As he was now regarded by everyone—not only as an Emperor but as a father—the wretched one <note>Referring to Licinius, Constantine's co-ruler in the East.</note> could not endure that our people proceeded with such happy prosperity, or that Constantine's favor toward us should remain unhindered. For Licinius at first, because of his agreeable manners, upright life, and virtues, was not only received and accepted by Constantine to be a partner in his Empire, but Constantine also gave him his sister in marriage. When Licinius saw that Constantine reigned over all people, not so much through fear and violence as through love and godliness, and that he was held in great honor and dignity by all men, and especially by the Christians, he became entangled in human pride. He was seized by the inhuman crime of envy and first prepared to deceive the pious Prince with secret treachery, especially through his servants who were very close to him. But Constantine, suspecting no evil from his deceit—for he placed his total trust in God—armed himself in all things with that sign that had been shown to him from Heaven, so that no treachery could be harmful to him. <note>original: "dat teecken dat hem vanden Hemel ghewesen was" – This refers to the Vision of the Cross or the Chi-Rho symbol which Constantine adopted after his vision before the Battle of the Milvian Bridge.</note>

☼ When Licinius was not restrained from the cruelty of his intentions, neither by the memory of past favors nor by his kinship as the Emperor’s brother-in-law, and when all his secret treachery profited him nothing, he suspected that the Emperor Constantine was helped and preserved through the prayers of the Christians. Because Constantine was protected by these, Licinius was ignited with a foolish rage and openly defied the Emperor, thus acting against his own honor and oath. He held a particular hatred against our people, and in this he
<margin>Licinius against Constantine</margin>

<column-break/>

complained that the Christians, in their festivals and prayers, did not pray to our God for him as much as they did for Constantine. Thus he was now entirely changed—that same man who had previously spoken sternly on his own behalf against those who, in the time of the tyrants, had acted cruelly against the Christians, now turned his own arrows against us and consecrated his cruel tyranny with Christian blood.

<margin>¶</margin>
<margin>Licinius’s mandate against the Christians.</margin>
¶ First, he commanded and ordered that if anyone were a Christian, they should leave his Court and depart from all his knighthood and soldiery. <note>term: "Ridderschap" – In this context, it refers to the administrative and military service classes of the Roman imperial bureaucracy.</note> And after that, he issued a Mandate <note>A formal legal decree or edict.</note> that all those who confessed to be Christians should be cast into prison. Then he quickly devised a cruelty in which he surpassed his predecessors: he ordered that no one should bring either food or drink to those who were imprisoned, saying: that it was improper and unjust to show mercy to anyone, or to give any assistance to those whom he had condemned by his law.

<margin>¶</margin>
<margin>Licinius disturbs the church government.</margin>
¶ Thus, a great multitude were thrown into prison and killed by hunger, and he thought that by this he would keep his tyranny hidden. But as the cruelty of his mind grew, that did not suffice; he soon displayed his raging cruelty against the bishops and priests of God. He first targeted the most learned and those most skilled in wisdom and teaching; these he attacked with a cunning cleverness, causing them to be accused not of their faith, but of other fabricated crimes and injuries. Without any further investigation, he ordered that they should be put to death.

<margin>¶</margin>
<margin>Hanging the Christians and chopping them into food for the fishes.</margin>
¶ Thus, this man practiced a manner of cruelty that had never been heard of before. For those who would not offer sacrifice to the idols, he did not merely order (as the other tyrants, his predecessors, had) that they should be tortured; he delivered them to the butchers to be hung up by their feet like pigs, and then split open and hacked apart, and thereafter chopped into small pieces and thrown into the sea as food for the fishes. And the churches, which he had helped build together with Constantine’s mandate, he caused to be destroyed again. He was very diligent in this, seeking to surpass in cruelty all the tyrants who had come before him.

# The Tenth Book of the History of the Ancient Christian Churches / written by Rufinus / a Priest in Aquileia.

---

**Column 1**

## ¶ Concerning the Heresy of Arius.

### The First Chapter.

<margin>Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria.</margin>
When, at Alexandria, after Achillas (who was chosen after Peter the Martyr), Alexander had received the priesthood <note>Original: "Priesterdom" — here referring to the office of the Bishop.</note> / and because everything with us was peaceful and without persecution / and the glory of the Christian churches rejoiced / because of the magnificent confessors who had confessed Christ during the persecution / so was our prosperity disturbed by our own strife and envy.
<margin>B</margin>
For there was a priest at Alexandria / named Arius / who in outward appearance and form was more godly than in power or in deed: and he was very ambitious and improperly curious.
<margin>Arius, Priest of Alexandria.</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
This man began to bring forward many wicked and disorderly things concerning the Faith of Christ / and things that had never been dared / he began to make doubtful / and he presumed to cut off and separate the Son of God from the eternal and unspeakable substance and nature of God the Father. Which greatly disturbed many in the church.
<margin>D</margin>
And when Alexander the Bishop / a man lovely and quiet of nature / with diligent and daily warnings / desired to draw this Arius away from his evil purpose and assertions / his punishment and good warnings bore no fruit in Arius /
<margin>E</margin>
for he had at that time already infected some with his venom and poison / and not only at Alexandria / but he had also scattered the same in other cities and lands / and was of the opinion / that it would be harmful / if he did not bring such things forward.
<margin>F</margin>
And he also revealed this opinion of his to many other priests. So that at last this question came to the ears of the Emperor Constantine / who with all diligence and labor / was taking up the Christian cause.
<margin>G</margin>
And he thus, through the instruction of the priests, called together and gathered in the city of Nicaea / a Bishoply Council / and commanded that Arius should present himself before the 318 Bishops / and that he should be judged concerning his opinion and view.

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

<margin>The Council of Nicaea.</margin>
<margin>H</margin>
## ¶ How Constantine exhorted the Bishops in the Council of Nicaea / to unity.

### The Second Chapter.

<margin>The private matters among the bishops to be treated alongside the common cause.</margin>
<margin>I</margin>
What a wonderful work the Emperor did in this Council / is not to be kept silent:
<margin>K</margin>
For when the Bishops from all lands had come together and gathered / and when they (as it was accustomed to happen) had some bickering and strife among themselves concerning various matters /
<margin>L</margin>
so that the Emperor was often addressed because of it / and some presented Libels <note>Original: "Libellen" — from the Latin 'libellus', these were formal written petitions or grievances, often containing accusations against fellow clergy.</note> or letters concerning each other's faults / and each was more diligent in his own matters than they were in the cause for which they had come and gathered.
<margin>M</margin>
When the Emperor noticed and saw / that because of this bickering the Chief Article <note>The "Chief Article" refers to the core theological dispute regarding the divinity of Christ and the Arian controversy.</note> was being hindered / he ordained a certain day / on which every Bishop / if it seemed to him that he had any complaint against anyone / should bring it forward.
<margin>N</margin>
And when the appointed day had come / he sat / and received Libels from everyone: and these he kept all together with him / and

That Word or Wisdom, which we call a Son, has had mercy on human error, and was born of a virgin, and has through the passion of His death delivered us from eternal death, and through His resurrection He has shared with us that eternal life, which we expect as a future Judge of all things we have done.

# Church History /

<margin>The "Dominicum," or "Lord's House," refers to the ancient Christian church, which we today commonly call "churches," as we have previously demonstrated.</margin>
<margin>The "sign of faith" refers to the cross; for by this, people are first made Christians.</margin>
the Cathedral <note>original: "Dom-kercke," from the Latin *Domus Dei* or House of God.</note>, and receives the **sign of faith**. And the Philosopher turned to his disciples and to those who had come there to listen, and spoke: "Listen, you learned men: As long as I was dealt with using words, I gave words for words, and whatever was spoken, I countered through the art of speech. But when a power came forth from the mouth of the speaker instead of mere words, the words of the [human] powers could not resist it, nor can man prevail against God. Therefore, if any of you has been able to feel from these spoken words what I feel, let him also believe in Christ and follow this old man, in whom God has spoken." Thus this Philosopher became a Christian, and rejoiced greatly that he had been defeated.

### Chapter 4.

<margin>Paphnutius.</margin>
In this Council there was also Paphnutius, a man of God and a Bishop from Egypt. He was a **confessor** <note>In the early church, a "confessor" was someone who suffered torture or imprisonment for their faith but was not killed.</note> among those whose right eye was gouged out by Maximian <note>Maximian was a Roman Emperor who presided over a period of intense Christian persecution.</note>, and who was hamstrung in the left knee and condemned to the mines to work in the metals. In this man was such a grace of power that through him such signs occurred as had previously occurred through the Apostles. For he drove out devils by his word, and the sick he healed through his prayer alone; and it is said that he gave sight to the blind and restored the strength of the body to those with gout.

<margin>Constantine's love for those scarred for Christ's sake.</margin>
Constantine held this Paphnutius in such honor and esteem that he often called him to the Palace, and received him, and with great devotion he kissed the eye that had been gouged out for the sake of his confession of Christ.

### Chapter 5.

<margin>Spyridon</margin>
Among their number was also Spyridon, a bishop in Cy-

<column-break/>

prus, a man also numbered among the Prophets, as much as we have been able to learn from those who have seen him. And even though this Spyridon was a Bishop, he nevertheless remained a shepherd of sheep, as he had been before. So it happened one night that thieves came to the sheepfold; and as they stretched out their wicked hands to take the sheep, they were bound with invisible bonds and remained there until morning, as if they had been caught like oxen. When the old Spyridon went to lead his little sheep to the pasture in the morning, he saw these young fellows fastened in the sheepfold without any human bonds. When he learned of their crime, he untied them by his word—those who had been bound by his [spiritual] worthiness. And so that they would not have been there through the night in vain, he said: "O you young fellows, take a ram with you, so that you do not appear to have come for nothing; but it would have been more fitting for you to have obtained it through a request than through theft."

Another much more wonderful work is told of him. He had a daughter named Irene, which daughter, after she had served him well, died as a maiden. After her death, someone came and said that he had given her something to keep safe. And the father did not know of this, and they searched the whole house for what was missing, but nothing was found. The other man insisted that he had entrusted it to her, and began weeping and complaining that his life would be ruined unless he had back what he had given her. The old man was moved by his tears and went quickly to his daughter’s grave and called her by her name. Then she spoke from the grave: "What do you want, my father?" So he spoke: "Where have you laid that which you were entrusted to keep?" She answered: "It is buried in such-and-such a place; there you shall find it." And he returned home, and just as his daughter had answered him from the grave, he found it and delivered it to the claimant. Many other miraculous things are said to have happened through this Spyridon, which are common and well-known in that land.

In those times, there were many such men in the Lord's Assembly, many of whom were also in this Council. And also Athanasius, who at that time was a Deacon of Alexandria, and was a great help to the old man, his Bishop

# Church History, described by Rufinus. The 10th Book.

Thus they met daily, and did not dare to ordain anything regarding such matters presumptuously or lightly. Arius was frequently called into the Council, and his assertions and proofs were examined daily; with all diligence, they sought what should be decreed against them.

<margin>B Arius is condemned.</margin>
At last, after much and manifold handling, it pleased them all—as if they had all spoken with one mouth and one heart with a powerful voice—that one should write **Homousion** <note>original: "Homousion," a Greek term meaning "of the same substance." It was the central point of debate, asserting that Jesus is of the exact same essence as God the Father.</note>, which is to say, that the Son is of one being with the Father; and this was established by the sentence of them all. It is said that there were no more than seventeen who were pleased by the faith of Arius,

<margin>C</margin>
which was that the Son of God was created, and not born from the same Divinity as his Father. The sentence of that Priestly Council was brought to the Emperor. He received it and honored it as if it had come from God. And he decreed upon it that whoever wished to go against this confession

<margin>D The sentence of exile, and not with the beast.</margin> <note>The marginal note "n3 met het dyer" likely means "not with the beast," implying that the punishment was exile rather than the "beasts" of the arena or capital punishment.</note>
would be doing wrong, as if against Divine institutions, and would also be driven away. Thus, there were only two who held with Arius and were exiled with him. The other eleven held a counsel with one another and consented to sign with their hands alone, but not with their hearts.

<margin>E Eusebius, Bishop of Nicomedia.</margin>
The particular cause of this hypocrisy was Eusebius, the Bishop of Nicomedia. And in this manner was that Council closed, after they had ordained various statutes, which some signed truthfully and some hypocritically, as was afterwards revealed.

1. They further ordain that it shall be maintained in the Assemblies that no one among those who have castrated themselves, due to the intolerance of unchastity, shall be received into the clergy.

<margin>I</margin>
2. That no one who has been recently received from the Heathens and baptized shall become a cleric before he has been well examined.

<margin>K</margin>

4. That every Bishop (if it were possible) should be ordained by all the Bishops of the same Province. And he who is right, let the same be confirmed by all.

6. That those at Alexandria, and those of Rome, shall maintain the old custom: that he of Alexandria shall have his diligent care over the Churches which are in Egypt, and he of Rome over the Churches situated thereabouts.

# Church History /

...than the other Bishops, and especially that of the Metropolitan, shall be stronger. <note>This refers to the voting power and authority of the Metropolitan bishop in episcopal elections.</note>

<margin>Prerogative of the Bishop of Jerusalem.</margin>
8. That the singular honor which has been given of old to the Bishop of Jerusalem shall be maintained, without prejudice to the Metropolitan Bishop of that same province.

9. Regarding the Cathars <note>original: "Catharen," from the Greek for "the pure." This refers to the Novatians, a group that was very strict about not readmitting people who had abandoned the faith during persecutions.</note> (who are the Novatians among us), if it happens that they repent and return to the church, following the teaching of the Christian Church, such Clergy shall be allowed to remain in their orders and be received, yet they should be re-ordained. And if their Bishops come to our Bishops, he shall sit in the place of the Priests. And the title of Bishop shall remain only with the one who has always held the Christian faith, unless the [Catholic] bishop wishes to honor the other with such a title; or, if it pleases him, he may place him in a vacant Bishop’s seat.

10. That in one city there shall not be two Bishops.

11. If anyone is imprudently ordained as a Bishop, and it is later discovered that he has committed some crime, or he is convicted by others, he shall be deposed. And if there were someone among those who had fallen [from the faith] who was ordained through ignorance, and it later becomes known, he shall be deposed.

12. If it happens that some have fallen [from the faith] during the persecution without being tortured, and they have repentance in their hearts, they shall stay for 3 years among the Catechumens <note>original: "Catechumenes," students or "Christian scholars" who were being instructed in the faith but were not yet full members.</note>, and thereafter they shall be placed with the believers for 2 years, only in prayer, and then they shall be received back into the Assembly.

13. Those who formerly had cast off their military service <note>original: "Ridderschap," referring to the profession of arms.</note> for the sake of their confession, and then returned to it, must remain in repentance for 13 years, and thereafter be received if they repent with their whole heart. However, it is in the power of the Bishop to moderate this, according to the fruits of repentance he sees.

14. Those who are still in repentance and die, they shall be received beforehand <note>This means they are given communion on their deathbed so they do not die outside the church.</note>. But if he remains alive after being received by the Assembly, he shall be obliged to complete the set time, or as the Bishop may moderate it.

15. The Catechumens who have fallen shall be separated for 3 years from the prayer of the Catechumens, and thereafter they shall be received again.

16. That no one, whether Bishop or Cleric, shall presume to thrust themselves from one church to another.

<column-break/>

17. That no Cleric who has left his church without a necessary cause, and goes about as a vagabond among other Assemblies, shall be received into communion.

18. That no one shall ordain a Cleric from another assembly without the consent of the one under whom he is situated.

19. That no Cleric shall receive usury <note>original: "woecker," or excessive interest.</note>, nor take any profit from wheat or from wine, as they are accustomed to giving the new for the old, or taking a sixth part profit, or even double; and if anyone does such things, he shall be cast out as one who receives base and improper profit.

20. That the Deacons shall not be esteemed above the Priests, nor shall they sit in the place of the Priests, nor shall they distribute the Eucharist <note>original: "Eucharistia," the sacrament of the Lord's Supper.</note> in their presence; rather, when the Priests do so, they shall only serve. But if it happens that no Priest is present, then they may distribute it in the Assembly; and if they do otherwise, they shall be cast out.

21. That the Paulianists <note>original: "Paulianisten," followers of Paul of Samosata, whose views on the nature of Christ were considered heretical.</note>, who are also called Photinians, shall be re-baptized.

22. And the Deaconesses, because they do not receive the laying on of hands, belong among the laity.

When they had thus ordained and concluded these things, so that the dignity of the Divine Laws was ascending, and also the ancient rule of the keeping of Easter <note>original: "Paesschen." The Council of Nicaea standardized the date of Easter for all Christians.</note>, through which no further change might arise, and all things being well-ordered, they delivered the same to the Assemblies; and in all lands, East and West, the peace of the churches and one faith were maintained.

## The 8th Chapter.

<margin>
Prayer of Macarius to God.
</margin>
**O** LORD, who have deigned to grant salvation to the human race through your only Son, and that through the passion of the cross; and now in these final times have given it into the heart of your handmaid to seek that blessed wood upon which our salvation hung: Deign to reveal to us which of these three was for the glory of our LORD, and which for the punishment of crimes, through this woman who lies here half-dead, so that as soon as the blessed wood touches her, she may be called back from

the gates of death to life. And when <margin>G</margin> he had prayed such things, he first laid one of them upon her, and it did nothing; nor did the second likewise. In the division of the world held by the Apostles by the casting of lots, in order to proclaim the word of God in all lands, the land of Parthia fell to the lot of the Apostle Thomas; Ethiopia to Matthew; and the neighboring India <note>In late antiquity, "India" often referred broadly to regions surrounding the Red Sea, including the Kingdom of Axum in present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea.</note> fell by lot to Bartholomew. This India is situated in great heat and is inhabited by many people of various languages. In this land, because it is situated so far away, no Apostle had preached. But in the time of Constantine, this land first received the seed of the Christian faith through the following cause.

There was formerly a philosopher named Metrodorus; he traveled to various places to see the world, and it is said that he reached the great and farthest India. One of these, who was the younger, was named Edesius, and the other Frumentius. "But this is the only gift that we may give back to the same—if we honor as God him (namely Christ) who made me healthy when I was calling upon him." The King was very slow to believe such things and wished to wait further; nevertheless, he was often exhorted by his Wife <note>The Queen of Iberia, known in tradition as Nana.</note>, until it happened at one time that he was hunting in the woods with his company, and the day was darkened with very thick darkness, so that through the darkness the path became unrecognizable. Thus his company wandered away from one another, and he was surrounded alone by a great darkness, and he knew not what he should do or where he would turn; and being in this desperation for his life, such a thought suddenly came to him: "If it be the case that this Christ is the true God of whom my Wife speaks, let him deliver me now out of these darknesses, so that, leaving all other things behind, I may serve him." As he had barely [uttered] this with his mouth, but believed it with his heart, it became a beautiful day again, and the King came safely back to his City, and as soon as he had arrived, he told the events to his wife. Thus he had the captive Woman called and desired to know the manner in which he should honor her GOD, and that henceforth he would serve or honor none of the other gods, but only the God Christ.

<margin>The King becomes a Christian.</margin>
Thus the captive woman taught him there how Christ is God, and the manner in which he ought to be prayed to and honored, and she taught and revealed as much as was fitting for a woman to teach. Nevertheless, she exhorted them that they should build a church, and she described the form of it. Thus the King called all his people together and told them all the events that had happened to him and his wife from the beginning, and he taught the faith, and thus became the Apostle of his people before he was even baptized. The men became believers through the counsel of the King, and the women through their Queen.

Thus, by the consent of them all, the church was quickly built, and when the circuit of the walls was finished, it had come so far that they should set the pillars. When the first and second pillars were erected, and they were to erect the third also with various instruments and through the strength of oxen and human help—even so, when it was half-way erected, it could not with any kind of instru-

<column-break/>

ment or help be raised further; and though they often sought it with all their might, they could not move the pillar at all. The people were greatly astonished, and the King’s spirit was sorrowful, and no one could think what this might signify. But when the night was approaching, and everyone had gone away, and all human help had ceased, the captive woman remained there alone through the night in her prayers. And when the King with his people came back early in the morning, full of concern, he saw the pillar fully upright—the very one that so many instruments and the strength of men and beasts could not move—and it was thus hanging above in the air, a foot higher than the place where it belonged. When all the people saw that, they greatly thanked God and praised the King's faith, and the piety of the captive woman was established with the testimony of this present miracle. And while they were all thus wondering, the pillar, before all their eyes and without anyone's help, slowly lowered itself onto the foundation that was made for it. Thereafter, the other pillars were so easily erected that they were all set on the same day. And now that the Church was magnificently finished, and the people were very eager for the Christian faith, Embassies were sent by the counsel of the captive woman to the Emperor Constantine; they told him all the stories and requested that Priests be sent there who might complete the divine work begun there. Which the Emperor sent over with all joy, being more gladdened by this than if he had brought many unknown Lands and Kingdoms under the Roman Empire.

<margin>Bacarius, a King of the Iberians, a commander and leader of the Palestinian circle.</margin>
That these things happened thus was told to us by that faithful Man Bacarius <note>original: "Bacarius"</note>, a King of that same people and a fellow-citizen among us, who has a singular diligence for religion and truth; he was a Captain of the Palestinian Circle <note>The *Limes Palaestinae*, a military district of the Roman Empire.</note> in Jerusalem and lived with us honorably. But now we wish to return to our subject.

### described by Rufinus. The Fifth Book. Folio 18.

### The 11th Chapter.

<margin>Constantia, a sister of Constantine Augustus.</margin>
But after Helena, the mother of Emperor Constantine, had departed from this world, Constantia, the widow of Licinius, enjoyed the company and consolation of her brother Constantine. And it happened that a priest came into her acquaintance who was secretly favorable to Arius <note>Arius was a priest whose teachings—Arianism—claimed that Jesus Christ was not co-eternal with God the Father, a view declared heretical at the Council of Nicaea.</note>, and he initially behaved with deception toward the Emperor’s sister and did not reveal his true leanings.

**B** And when he later became very familiar and intimate with the Princess, he gradually began to reveal his views, saying: That Arius was treated out of hatred and not because of any wrongdoing, and had come to his current state through the secret envy of his Bishop <note>Bishop Alexander of Alexandria, Arius's primary opponent.</note>, because he was well-regarded and beloved by the common people.

**C** These and similar stories he often recounted, and thus brought Constantia, the Emperor’s sister, over to his opinion. When she had now fallen ill and lay dying, she was visited by her brother, who spoke to her in a lovely and Christian manner: and she, in her final moments (so it is said), requested of her brother that he would please receive this priest into his company, and that he should hear the counsel he would give him concerning his salvation; and that she, now dying, had no other concern than that his Empire might fall into disturbance and peril because of the guilt of [wronging] the innocent.

**D** The Emperor received this admonition from his sister, suspecting that his sister’s concern for him was faithful. He gave the priest an audience, and shortly thereafter he commanded that Arius should be recalled from exile, and that he should declare what he believed regarding the faith.

<margin>Arius is called from his exile by Constantine.</margin>
**E** And when Arius had returned, he gave his confession of faith to the Emperor in writing, which had a semblance of the same words [as the orthodox faith], but not the same meaning. The Emperor, reading this, was greatly astonished, and it seemed to him that it was the same sentiment and meaning as had been ordained in the previous Council <note>The Council of Nicaea (325 AD), which established the orthodox creed.</note>.

**F** Nevertheless, he did not change his purpose but sent him again to be examined by the Council, for many Bishops were to gather from far-off lands in Jerusalem for the church dedication <note>The dedication of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.</note>. He wrote concerning Arius as follows: If they heard the explanation and confession of his faith, and if he were not overwhelmed by accusations—as he complained—then, since he was now reformed from his error, [he should be received] lovingly 

<margin>Church dedication in Jerusalem.</margin>

<column-break/>

**G** and meekly, and they should not send him away; for the Council had not rejected his person, but his incorrect teaching, provided that his Bishop Alexander consented. Thus Arius was easily received by those who were initially favorable to him and who had hypocritically signed [the previous decrees].

**H** Thus he was also sent to Alexandria, but he achieved nothing there: for although ignorant people are easily deceived, one cannot so quickly deceive those who know the truth.

<margin>Constantine dies.</margin>
**I** As these things were happening in Alexandria, the venerable Emperor Augustus Constantine died in the suburb of Nicomedia, in the 31st year of his Reign, leaving by Testament his children as heirs of the Roman Empire. At which time Constantius his son, to whom he had entrusted the Eastern Empire, was not present. It is said that the Emperor Constantine secretly called the aforementioned priest—who had been recommended to him by his sister—to himself and delivered to him his testament which he had written. He made him swear an oath that he would give the same into no one else’s hand but only to Constantius when he arrived.

<margin>This his Testament to the Priest.</margin>
**K** And since this same priest was also favored by the Emperor’s chamberlains <note>High-ranking court officials who managed the imperial household.</note>, they kept the death of the Emperor secret and quiet until the time that Constantius had arrived; they suppressed some who wanted to start innovations, so that all things remained as they were. When Constantius had now arrived, the priest delivered the testament of the Emperor to him.

<margin>Constantius.</margin>
**L** For which service Emperor Constantius, who was eager for the Empire, was so lovingly minded toward the priest that he—who was attempting to govern all things—was now governed by the priest himself. When the priest had thus entangled the Emperor, he began to advise him that Arius should be restored to his place, and that all the priests who would not consent to it should be forced to do so.

<margin>Eusebius of Nicomedia.</margin>
¶ Now we have this from the writings of Athanasius. But Eusebius, the Bishop of Nicomedia—of whose craftiness in signing the creed we have spoken before—having now found an opportunity through the priest who was a close companion to the Emperor, worked to revoke all the proceedings that had been handled at the Council <note>Original: "Conciliū". This refers to the First Council of Nicaea (325 AD), which condemned Arianism.</note>. He summoned Arius, who was then in Alexandria, and by an Imperial Mandate called for a Council once more in Constantinople. To this Council came especially those who favored Arius and Eusebius; they frequently urged Alexander, the Bishop <note>The text says "Bishop of Alexandria," but historical accounts identify this as Alexander of Constantinople, where the event took place.</note>, to receive Arius back into the church. And when they did not prevail upon him, they finally spoke to him with reproachful words and announced a set day for him, that he might consider receiving Arius back in the meantime. They threatened that if he would not do so, he would be driven from his Bishopric and sent into misery, and another would be put in his place. Then Alexander went at night, as the set day approached, to lie before the altar, and stayed awake all night in his prayer, sighing with tears, and commended the Lord’s Church to Him. Early in the morning, while Alexander was still in his prayer, Eusebius came with his followers, like a captain of the heretical war. He arrived very early at the house where Arius was staying and told him that he must quickly come into the Church; and if it should happen that Alexander, being present, would not receive him, they would drive him out.

## ¶ How Arius died from an evacuation of the bowels.

### The 13th Chapter.

<margin>Arius dies while defecating.</margin>
Thus everyone had a great desire to see whether Alexander would remain steadfast and whether Eusebius and Arius’s purpose would falter. While everyone was in doubt about this matter, Arius went toward the Church, surrounded by a great multitude of people and bishops. He then stepped away from them to relieve his natural needs <term>ghevoegh: an early modern Dutch euphemism for a bowel movement</term>. And while he was sitting in such a place, all his entrails fell out of his belly into the privy; and thus that blaspheming and stinking heart died in such a place and with such a death as it was

<column-break/>

worthy of. When this was reported to Eusebius in the church, and also to the others who tormented the holy and innocent man Alexander to make him receive Arius back, they were put to shame and went away. Then the word of the Lord was fulfilled to His glory, which Alexander had uttered in his prayer, saying: "O Lord, please judge between me and Eusebius’s threats, and Arius’s violence." Thus the heretics gathered together and were afraid that the events, exactly as they had happened, would come before the Emperor Constantius <note>The text likely means Constantine the Great, though his son Constantius II was also a major figure in the Arian conflict.</note>; and they feared not only that he might turn away from the unbelief in which he was entangled, but that he would take revenge on those who were the cause of his deception. Thus they spoke with the Emperor’s chamberlains, who were also of the same unbelief, asking them to inform the Emperor as much as possible about Arius’s death in a way that he should by no means hear that God’s vengeance was demonstrated therein. When this had occurred, they proceeded with the matters of faith as they had begun.

<margin>Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria.</margin>
When Alexander had died at Alexandria, Athanasius received that Bishopric. It was by his counsel and investigation that the deception of the heretics was openly uncovered. As soon as they learned that he had become Bishop, fearing that their dealings would not easily proceed because of his diligent care, they sought all manners of ways against him and prepared to deceive. It does not seem out of place to me to tell a little of this man's origin and what he was like in his youth, just as we have heard it from those who were raised with him. ### The 17th Chapter.

<margin>Arsenius, a reader of Athanasius.</margin>
This Arsenius, whose arm they claimed had been cut off, had previously been a reader <note term="Lector">A "reader" or lector was one of the minor orders of the early Christian clergy, responsible for reading the Scriptures during the liturgy.</note> for Athanasius; fearing some disgrace or punishment, he had fled. And certain crafty men who were against Athanasius had this Arsenius kept in hiding by some who were well aware of their plot, so that they might carry out their venture according to their own whims. Nevertheless, it became known to this Arsenius, in the place where he was hidden, what horror they were planning against Athanasius on his account. And whether he was moved by a heartfelt compassion or by Divine providence, he escaped secretly by night from their hands and traveled by ship to the city of Tyre. On the day before the Priests and Judges were to gather to deliberate on this matter, and as the final day set for Athanasius approached, he presented himself before Athanasius and revealed their entire plot to him. Athanasius commanded him to remain inside the house and to make his presence known to no one.

Thus the Council was gathered together, in which were some who were also aware of this plot, and who had all assembled to condemn Athanasius.

At this same time, Paphnutius the Confessor, of whom we have previously spo-

<column-break/>

ken, was also present there; he knew well that Athanasius was innocent in this matter.

<margin>Marinus, the bishop at Jerusalem, is warned by Paphnutius.</margin>
When Paphnutius saw Marinus, the Bishop of Jerusalem—who had also been a Confessor with him, having had an eye gouged out and a kneecap cut off <note>These were common mutilations suffered by Christians during the Great Persecution under Emperor Maximinus Daia.</note>—and who was a simple man, not suspecting that the Priests would devise such a horror, sitting in the midst of those who were part of this plot, Paphnutius went into the middle of the assembly to him and said: "O Marinus, you who received with me the prize of confession, it is not fitting, nor can you suffer it, that you should sit in the council of the wicked and enter in with transgressors." And he took Marinus by the hand and led him out from their company, and instructed him in all things, and joined with him in an eternal covenant and fellowship with Athanasius.

<margin>The first accusation.</margin>
When this had occurred, the proceedings and accusations against Athanasius began. The first complaint was from a woman who said that she had previously given lodging to Athanasius, and that during the night, when she suspected no evil, she had suffered violence from him and been violated. In response to this complaint, Athanasius was summoned, and he entered with Timotheus his Priest. Athanasius had instructed Timotheus that once the woman had stated her complaint, Athanasius himself would remain silent; he commanded the Priest to give the answer to the complaint and the reasoning of this woman. When the woman had poured out her entire complaint as she had been commanded, Timotheus turned to her and answered: "Tell me, woman, have I previously lodged with you, and have I done such violence and outrage to you as you say?" Then the woman (as such shameless women are wont to do) began to scold and rage at Timotheus, saying: "Yes, you! You are the same one who did me violence, and in such a place defiled my purity!" And she turned herself to the Judges and began to swear, taking the Divine faith as her witness that she was speaking the truth. Then they were all put to shame, and some mocked the situation, for Athanasius, by remaining silent, had proved his innocence, and the deception of the fabricated crime was made manifest. Nevertheless, the Judges were not permitted to question the woman as to why she had said such things, or by whose advice she had been prepared to say them; for some who sat there as Judges were the same ones who...

The second accusation concerned the arm of Arsenius, as they said: "O Athanasius, this severed arm accuses and complains against you. This is the right arm of Arsenius; tell us why and for what purpose you have cut off this arm?" Then Athanasius answered: "Who among you all knows Arsenius, seeing as you say,

'This is the right arm of Arsenius'?" Then some stood up and said that they knew Arsenius very well—among whom were some who were unaware of this cunning plot. Then Athanasius requested of the Judge that he would grant him leave to bring in a certain man whom he urgently required and demanded for his case. When Arsenius was then brought forward and showed himself, Athanasius spoke to those who sat in the Council,

and to the Judges: "This is Arsenius." And when he had raised Arsenius’s right hand, he spoke: "See, this is his right arm, and that is his left arm. Then it became like night and darkness in the eyes of the accusers, and they knew not what to do, or where they should turn or go. For that this was truly Arsenius was testified by those who had previously said they knew him well. But

<margin>D</margin>
because the Council was not gathered to judge rightly, but rather to suppress Athanasius and his cause, they made a great uproar among themselves and said that Athanasius was a sorcerer <note term="Toovenaer">The charge of sorcery or "black magic" was frequently leveled against Athanasius by his Arian opponents to explain his survival or his ability to produce "miraculous" evidence like the living Arsenius.</note> and that he had bewitched the eyes of the people, and that it was not proper that such a man should be allowed to live; and in their furious uprising, they wanted to tear him apart with their hands.

<margin>Archelaus, an Eastern count, presided in the Council.</margin>
¶ But Archelaus, a Count who was also in the Council by the Emperor’s command, delivered him from the hands of those who wished to tear him to pieces; he brought him away secretly and warned and advised him that he should flee as far as he possibly could. Nevertheless, that Council met again as if they had not found all things to be contrary to the truth, and they condemned Athanasius as if he had confessed to the alleged crime. And thus they sent these fabricated lies to all the ends of the world and, through the Emperor’s compulsion, forced other Bishops to consent to the condemnation of Athanasius.

and was persecuted in all places.

## The XVIII. Chapter.

<margin>Athanasius, unjustly condemned, was forced to flee.</margin>
<margin>Sought everywhere.</margin>

Thus this good Athanasius became a fugitive in all lands, and there was no place where he might be free to remain. The Tribunes, Provosts, Counts, and all the soldiery had orders through Imperial Mandates to search for him; and a great sum of money and reward was placed on Athanasius's head for whoever brought him alive, or failing that, for whoever should bring his head. Nevertheless, though they sought him with all the Emperor's power, they did so in vain, for God was with him.

<margin>I</margin>
<margin>For 6 years Athanasius lay hidden in Trier in a cistern.</margin>
During this time, he remained hidden and secret for six whole years in a dry cistern <note term="Cisterne">A cistern is an underground reservoir for rainwater. In this period of Christian history, hiding in such places was common for those escaping persecution.</note> where there was no water, so that during that time he did not see the sun. When he was eventually betrayed by the servant girl—who was the only one who knew where Athanasius lay hidden and who served him by her master's command (who had granted him that hole)—he was warned by God's inspiration on the same night they came to capture him, and he moved to another place. Thus those who wished to capture him were deceived; they drove away the man who had supported him, and the girl was also punished as one who had falsely informed on him.

# Church History

<margin>Constans writes to his brother Constantius on behalf of Athanasius</margin>
**A** Thus he wrote to his brother Constantius, stating how he had found in truth that Athanasius, a priest of the most high God, had been unjustly driven out and hunted. Therefore, he would be doing what is right if he restored the same Athanasius to his place without any further trouble. And if he was unwilling to do this, then he himself would take thought of the matter and come personally into his kingdom, to significantly punish those who were the cause of such a crime. When Constantius received these writings, he was terrified, for he knew that his brother was well able to fulfill that which he had threatened. Thus he became well-disposed and commanded that Athanasius should come to him; and after a short delay, the Emperor presented him with the opportunity to travel joyfully back to his Church. Yet the Emperor was nonetheless advised by his wicked council that he should request this of Athanasius, saying: "It is a small thing, O Athanasius, that the Bishops demand of you: that you should grant to their people, who are of their faith, one church out of the many churches that are in Alexandria, for those who wish to have no communion with you and yours." <note>This was a strategic move by the Arian faction to establish a legal foothold in the orthodox stronghold of Alexandria.</note>

<margin>Note: a church in Alexandria.</margin>
**M** Athanasius answered through God’s inspiration, saying: "What is it, O Emperor, that I could refuse of your request, you who have the power to command all things? But I also have a request which I would dearly wish you to consent to." When the Emperor answered that he would not refuse him, even if it were difficult to do, provided that he willingly allowed that one thing, Athanasius said: "This is what I pray for: since there is also a people here in this city of Antioch who wish to have no communion with these others, please also consent that they may have a church of their own." <note>Athanasius used the Emperor's own logic against him: if the Arians deserved a church in Alexandria, then the Nicene Christians (Athanasius's supporters) deserved their own church in the Arian stronghold of Antioch.</note>

<margin>A church in Antioch.</margin>
**E** The Emperor answered joyfully that it was indeed fitting and right, and that such a thing should happen. But when the Emperor told of the matter to those whose advice he followed, they said that they no longer desired to have a church in Alexandria, nor did they wish to allow Athanasius’s party a church in Antioch; for they were more concerned with those who were present there than those who were far away.

<margin>Athanasius’s wisdom.</margin>
**A** Thus the Emperor marveled at Athanasius’s wisdom and commanded him to travel hastily to receive his church again. But when, through the cruel crime of Magnentius <note>Magnentius was a commander who usurped the throne and murdered Emperor Constans in 350 AD.</note>, the Emperor Constans was robbed of his kingdom and his life, Athanasius’s old enemies again pushed and stirred up their hatred with the Emperor Constantius. They drove him from his church once more and sent in his place a man named George, who was a companion of their wicked opinion.

<column-break/>

<margin>The flight of Athanasius begins again. George is placed in Athanasius’s stead. Constantius comes into the Western lands.</margin>
Then Athanasius had to flee again and remain hidden, because the Emperor’s mandates against him were published everywhere, and many gifts and rewards were promised to those who could capture him. And when the Emperor Constantius was prepared to avenge his brother’s death, he destroyed the tyrant Magnentius and took possession of the Western Empire, becoming the sole Lord over both Empires. Then he began to torment the Western Bishops and sought to force them through schemes to consent to the Arian heresy <note>Arianism: the belief that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father, which the Council of Nicaea had condemned.</note>, having already condemned Athanasius once more, who was always a strong obstacle to him.

# The Fifth Book,

->written by Rufinus.<-

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>A subtle question.</margin>
The Eastern Greek Priests concluded there that they had come to an agreement with one another at Seleucia, and they easily deceived the simple and unlearned Western Priests in this manner, asking: Whom would they rather worship and honor, the Consubstantial <note>original: "Homousion"</note> or Christ? And since they did not know the power of the word "Consubstantial," nor what its meaning was, they confessed that they believed in Christ and not in the "Consubstantial." Thus many—with very few exceptions who knew better—fell and were deceived, acting against what the Fathers at Nicaea had ordained and concluded. They blasphemed and mocked that word "Consubstantial," arguing that it should not remain in the explanation of the faith, and thus they defiled their communion with the company of the Arian heretics. At this time, the face of the Church was very ugly and foul, for she was not being corrupted by strangers as before, but was being devastated by her own people. One drove the other out, and the other was driven out, and both were of the Church. Nowhere was there an altar or sacrifice, but rather transgression and exile were found among many. It was a similar punishment, but an unequal victory. They were tormented in a similar way, but they were not glorified equally. For the Christian Church grieved over those who were driving others to their downfall.

Liberius, who was Bishop of Rome after Julius (who followed Silvester), was driven out by the Arians and sent into exile. In his place, the heretics ordained his deacon, named Felix; he was not only tainted by a diversity of opinions but was united with all their communion and ordinances.

<margin>A stronger/ Eunomius.</margin>
Eunomius was a man who was leprous in both body and soul, corrupted from within and without, yet he was very skillful and adept in the <term>Sophistry</term> <note>A method of clever but often misleading reasoning or argument.</note> which is called **Dialectics**.

This same man wrote much against our faith and left behind certain rules for debating to his disciples. From him, the heresy is now called that of the <margin>Eunomians.</margin> **Eunomians**. There was <margin>Macedonians.</margin> also another man named **Macedonius**, whom they appointed and ordained as Bishop of Constantinople after our own people had been driven out and killed. And although he acknowledged that the Son is like the Father (though he also blasphemed against the Holy Spirit just as they did), he was nevertheless driven out by them because he preached and taught that the Son was like the Father. And he was not joined to our side, because he held different views than us regarding the Holy Spirit.

<margin>Eunomians. Arians.</margin>
Thus has this venomous beast—which first raised its head, like that of hell, through **Arius**—divided into three parties: the **Eunomians**, who say that the Son is unlike the Father, for a creature can in no way be like the creator; the **Arians**, who say that the Son may indeed be like the Father in the abundance of grace, but not by the property of nature—that is, only so <margin>Macedonians.</margin> far as a creature may be compared to the creator; and the **Macedonians**, who say that the Son is like the Father in all things, but that the Holy Spirit has nothing in common with the Father or the Son.

These things were done by them, just as it is written of such people: *They are torn apart, and have not taken it to heart.* <note>A reference to the internal fracturing of heretical groups as a sign of their lack of divine truth.</note> But many who were esteemed for a righteous life, and many monasteries in Constantinople and all the surrounding lands, and many honorable Bishops, for the most part followed the error of **Macedonius**.

<margin>Julian.</margin>
When **Julian** succeeded him, he rightfully received the Empire which he had first moderately accepted as **Augustus**, and he alone held the Empire. Since this Julian wished to destroy and nullify all of Constantius's ordinances, he also commanded that the Bishops who had been condemned to exile should be allowed to return. And after that, he became a hindrance and a burden to us with all his might. Thus the Bishops returned, and **Liberius**, the Bishop of Rome, had already returned while Constantius was still alive. But whether he had done the Emperor's will and had co-signed <note>Referring to the signing of Arian creeds under pressure.</note>, or whether he was petitioned for by the common people of Rome, is unknown. <margin>Liberius returns from his exile.</margin>

# The Fifth Book.

## written by Rufinus. <note>Rufinus of Aquileia (c. 345–410 AD) was a monk and historian who translated and expanded upon Eusebius’s Church History.</note>

<margin>The assembly of confessors at Alexandria.</margin>
**A** Being upright and great in faith and merit, they investigated with all diligence and took counsel on how the Christian Church might return to rest after this great tempest and storm of the heretics. To some who were zealous in the faith, it seemed good that no one should be received into the priesthood who was in any way defiled by fellowship with the heretics, and that only such men should be received who followed the Apostle Paul and sought not their own profit, but the profit of many—those who followed Christ, <margin>Philippians 2:7–8</margin> who, although He was the life of us all, humbled Himself for the salvation of us all and descended even unto death, so that He might find life even among the dead.

<margin>Two opinions on receiving those back from heresy.</margin>
**B** Others said it would be better to humble oneself a little and bend, in order to raise up again those who had fallen; and that no one should boast or imagine that the Kingdom of Heaven is granted to them alone because of the purity of their lives, but rather that it is much more honorable and glorious to enter therein with many others. Therefore, it seemed good to them that only those who were the cause of the unbelief should be cut off and separated, and that the other priests should be allowed to choose if they wished to renounce the error of their unbelief and return to the true faith and the institutions of the Fathers. They argued that no one should be hindered from returning, but rather that all should rejoice in their improvement and conversion, <margin>Luke 15.</margin> just as it is written in the Gospel concerning the younger son, who had uselessly consumed his father’s goods; when he came to his senses, he was not only received, but deemed worthy of his father’s embrace and received again the ring of faith and was clothed with the mantle. By this, all the priestly proofs were signified. They noted that the elder son was not acceptable to his father because he envied that his brother was received, and he himself was not certain that he would not fall—he who accused his brother and would not forgive.

<margin>F</margin>
## ¶ Of Asterius, Eusebius, and of the articles that were concluded and ordained in the same Council.

### The 29th Chapter.

<column-break/>

<margin>Asterius was sent to the Eastern lands. Eusebius to the Western lands.</margin>
**G** When they had brought forward such Evangelical words, the Bishops approved them and ordained that Asterius and those with him should be provident and careful toward the East, and Eusebius toward the West.

<margin>Decree concerning the Holy Spirit.</margin>
In this Council, it was also ordained after much disputation concerning the Holy Spirit, that one shall believe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance and being, and are not created within the Trinity. 

<margin><term>Ousia</term> <note>original: "Vsia"</note>, a being or essence. <term>Hypostasis</term> <note>original: "Hipostasis"</note>, substance, subsistence, or the state of being.</margin>
**H** Also concerning the distinction of substances and subsistences—which the Greeks call <term>Hypostases</term> <note>The underlying reality or distinct personhood of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note>—they spoke from the Scriptures, saying that substance and subsistence were one thing; and as we do not say that there are three substances in God, so one shall not say that there are three subsistences in God.

<margin><term>Homoousion</term>, of the same being. <term>Homousion</term>, one being. <term>Heteroousion</term>, of a different being.</margin>
**I** Others thought that substance and subsistence were different things; they said that substance indicates the nature and being of a thing in which it exists, but subsistence indicates the person who is essential. Therefore, because of the heresy of **Sabellius** <note>Sabellianism was the belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not distinct persons but just three "modes" or masks of one God.</note>, it must be acknowledged that there are three subsistences, so that we do not fall into his error and be suspected of his heresy, for he acknowledges only three names and not three subsistences.

<margin>The Humanity of Christ.</margin>
**K** And concerning the Humanity of Christ, they confessed that the body which the Lord took from Mary had a soul and an intellect. <note>This was a refutation of Apollinarianism, which argued Christ had a human body but a divine mind instead of a human soul.</note> When they had thus ordained and diligently arranged all things, each person traveled back on his way in peace.

For when he had traveled from there to the Council, he had promised them that he would act in the Council in such a way that they would ordain such a Bishop that both sides would be satisfied and at peace. Those who followed Meletius—who, for the sake of the true faith (as previously mentioned), had been driven from his church by the <term>Arians</term><note>Arians were followers of Arius, who taught that Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father, a view declared heretical at the Council of Nicaea.</note>—did not join or have communion with Bishop Eustathius (from whose group Paulinus also came), but instead held their own assembly and identity separately. When Eusebius had wished to unite these parties, but was hindered by Lucifer and could not accomplish it, he departed from that place.

When Meletius had returned from his exile, and the majority of the people were favorable toward him, he retained the Church at Antioch and held his own <term>Synod</term><note>A synod is a local council of church leaders gathered to decide on matters of doctrine or administration.</note> and assembly with the Eastern Bishops; nevertheless, he did not join himself to Athanasius. This greatly vexed Lucifer, because Eusebius would not receive the Bishop whom he had ordained at Antioch. Lucifer thought that Eusebius would also not accept what the Bishops ordained at Alexandria, but he was bound by the agreements of his deacon, whom he had sent to the Council in his stead and who had signed in his name; thus, he could not reject those who had acted with his own authority. He also realized that if he were to accept this, his entire plan would be hindered. After he had deliberated on this for a long time, doubting which of these two things he should do, he finally chose to accept that his deacon's signature at the Council was valid and good, but that in other matters he held a different opinion which seemed pleasing and good to him. Thereafter, he traveled to the lands of Sardinia, and was so hindered by a sudden death that he had no time to gather his followers; for reckless things are often corrected over a longer time. But it is unknown to me if his views were deeply rooted in him. Nonetheless, the sect of the <term>Luciferians</term><note>A rigorist schismatic group named after Lucifer of Cagliari, who refused to readmit bishops who had previously wavered toward Arianism.</note> takes its origin from him, though they are known to very few people today.

<margin>
The Luciferian sect.
Eusebius, a teacher and a Priest.
</margin>
Now that Eusebius had traveled through the East and also through Italy, performing the office of both a priest and a physician <note>This likely refers to his work "healing" the spiritual rifts in the fragmented churches.</note>, he called upon all the churches to reject their unbelief and to receive and return to the true Christian faith.

In the same manner did Bishop Hilary act, who had also been driven out with the other Bishops and had now returned to Italy. As Eusebius had commanded him, he began ear-

<column-break/>

nestly to act, in order to repair the churches and bring them back to the true faith, just as the Fathers had ordained.

### ¶ Of Hilary.

### The 21st Chapter.

<margin>Hilary.</margin>
This Hilary <note>Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), often called the "Hammer of the Arians" and the "Athanasius of the West."</note> was a gentle and amiable man by nature, as well as learned and very skilled in giving counsel, so that he diligently and appropriately visited and accomplished all things. He also wrote very precious books concerning our faith, in which he completely revealed the cunning deceits of the heretics, by which the common Christian people were deceived, and also the simple innocence of the people who quickly accept a false faith. Thus, he corrected those who were not present—whom he could not teach with a living voice—through his writings and good instruction. These two men shone like two great lights of the world in Illyricum, Italy, and Gaul, so that they drove all the darkness of the heretics out of every nook and corner.

# Church History /

...that envoys were sent from the Persians, seeking peace. They requested that provisions of food be arranged for their soldiers, who had suffered great hunger, and they expressed a willingness to reform their previous arrogance toward our people with total goodwill. And when they had established a peace for twenty-nine years, and had returned again under the Roman Empire, a clear light appeared and rose for our people from the lands of the East. Emperor Jovian, with all diligence and discretion, sought to restore the common good after great misfortune and calamity. He did not forget the care of the churches, nor did he act as foolishly as Constantius <note>Constantius II, who reigned 337–361 AD, was known for his interference in church doctrine and his support of Arianism.</note>; rather, the fall of his predecessor served as a warning to him. Therefore, he summoned Athanasius with honorable and friendly letters, requesting and receiving from him a plan for how the churches might be governed in the true faith. But these joyful and godly beginnings were disrupted by an untimely death. For eight months after he had received the Empire, he died near Cilicia.
