another Macarius <note>The text likely refers to Macarius of Egypt (the Elder) and Macarius of Alexandria (the Younger), two prominent figures in early monasticism.</note>, and also Heraclides and Pambus, disciples of Anthony <note>Saint Anthony the Great, often considered the "Father of All Monks."</note> who were living in Egypt, and most especially in the desert named Nitria <note>The Nitrian Desert was one of the three most important centers of Christian monasticism in 4th-century Egypt.</note>. <margin>
A lame man is made healthy.
</margin>

A short time before that, there was a blind man who desired to be led to Macarius's little cell, **E** which was in the desert, a journey of three days. When this blind man, through the great labor of those who led him, arrived there, he did not find Macarius in his cell. Thus the blind man became very distressed and could in no way moderate his grief, because he had not obtained any comfort for his health. Being very fervent in faith, he said to those who had led him there: "I pray you, please lead me to the very side of the wall where the Elder used to rest." And when he was brought there, **F** he took a little dry earth with which the wall had been plastered and smeared, and took it in his hand, and prayed that they would draw some water for him from the well from which the Elder 

<column-break/>

was accustomed to drink. **G** With this water he moistened the earth and smeared his eyes with that same mud, and washed them with the water. <margin>A blind man is healed</margin> He immediately regained his sight, so that he needed no one's help to return home. And he was not ungrateful, like the lepers of whom one reads in the Gospel, but he returned there with all his household and thanked God, and told everything just as it had happened.

This Macarius had near his cell a cave of a wolf, <margin>Other sources: Lioness. * Lions.</margin> which at one time brought her young wolf-cubs, who were blind, to the feet **H** of the old man. When he perceived that the beast was pleading because her young were blind, he prayed to the Lord, and the young ones received their sight and followed their mother back to the cave. <margin>The miracle of the Lioness.</margin> And shortly thereafter, the wolf returned there with her young and brought a whole sheepskin with wool to the old man as a token of gratitude; she dropped it from her mouth **I** and laid it down before the door, and went away.

If we were to tell all the miraculous stories, we would have to abandon the brevity of our narrative, for these histories would require a book of their own.

In all this, Lucius was not ashamed, nor did he show any reverence because of the miraculous works; instead, **K** he commanded that these same Fathers should be secretly taken away from their sheep <note>Referring to their monastic followers or "flock."</note> and carried to an island in Egypt. ### ¶ On the persecution that occurred in the city of Edessa.

## The v. Chapter.

<margin>Edessa, a city in Mesopotamia</margin>
There is a city in Mesopotamia named Edessa, which is a city of faithful people and is adorned with the relic of the Apostle Thomas. When the Emperor himself <note>Emperor Valens (reigned 364–378), a supporter of Arianism.</note> had seen (after he had forbidden the people from the churches) that they held their gatherings in the fields, he was incited with such anger that he struck his High Judge with his fist, saying: "Why have the people not been driven from there and dispersed, as I commanded?" Although this Judge was a heathen, he had suffered the contempt of the Emperor, and though he was to ride out the next day

to destroy the Christians, he nevertheless, through human mercy, secretly warned the citizens and let it be known so that they might take heed and not be found in that same place. When he had risen early in the morning, he caused his servants and attendants to make much more noise and commotion than usual, all for the purpose that no one, or very few, should put themselves in peril as far as was possible. Nonetheless, he saw that the people were hurrying to that same place much more than they were accustomed to do, and they ran with great speed, as if they sought to be the ones left behind to be killed.

<margin>A woman who hurries to be with the Christians so that she may die with them.</margin>
And he also saw a woman who hurried so much that she left her door unlocked and had not covered herself as is becoming for women; and as best as she could, she took a young child with her and ran hastily, pushing through the ranks and past the Officer’s servants. The Judge could endure it no longer and said: "Seize that woman and bring her to me." And when she had been brought to him, he said: "O wretched woman, why do you hurry so greatly?" She answered: "To the field where the Christian people are gathered." He spoke again: "Have you not heard that the High Judge travels there to kill all the people he shall find?" Then she spoke: "Yes, I have heard it, and for that reason I hurry, so that I also may be found there to die." Then he said again: "Where are you going with that small child?" She answered: "So that it may become a martyr."

After these things had been quickly read to him, he reflected upon them in his understanding and memory, so much so that he did not merely hear what was read, but wrote it in the "Book of his heart." In a short time, through the help of God who was his teacher, he came to such wisdom and knowledge of the Holy Scriptures and human teachings that he was chosen as a Doctor <note>In this context, "Doctor" refers to a "Doctor of the Church," a title given to an eminent teacher of doctrine.</note> and a Teacher of the Christian school. <margin>Didymus becomes a schoolmaster in Alexandria.</margin> He was ordained to this position by Bishop Athanasius and other learned men. He was also so skilled in the arts of Dialectic, Geometry, Astronomy, and Arithmetic that none of the philosophers could surprise or confuse him in these arts; as soon as he heard their answers, they had to admit he was the master of them all. They also had his arguments, common disputations, and answers recorded by Notaries, which are still held in great value today. Nevertheless, we who have heard some things from his own mouth, and have read what others recorded of his speech, find them even more powerful. <margin>The power of living words.</margin> There is a certain divinity, beyond nature, in the living words that flowed from his mouth. When Saint Anthony <note>Saint Anthony the Great, often considered the father of Christian monasticism.</note> came from Thebaid to Alexandria to give testimony to the faith of Athanasius against the Arians, he comforted Didymus with <margin>Comfort through physical blindness.</margin> excellent words, saying: "O Didymus, do not let it grieve you that you are deprived of eyes of the flesh, for even gnats, flies, and lizards have such eyes. Instead, rejoice, for you have the same eyes that the Angels have, through which God is seen, and through which a great light of knowledge is kindled within you."

### ¶ How many holy people and lights lived in Egypt and in the deserts, through whom God performed signs.

### Chapter 8.

During this time, Egypt possessed not only men learned in Divine Philosophy, but also men who led a simple life in the wild desert with purity of heart, who also performed Apostolic signs and miracles. Among these are those whom we ourselves have seen, and who <margin>Blessing</margin> blessed us with their own hands:

¶ Macarius of the upper desert, and another Macarius of the lower desert, Isidore in Scetis <note>original: "Septen," likely referring to the monastic community of Scetis.</note>, Pambo in Cellia, Moses and Benjamin in Nitria, Spion and Elias and Paul at Apeliotes, and the other Paul in Pherne, Poemen and Joseph in Pispir (which is called Anthony's mountain). At this same time, Mesopotamia also had learned and zealous Christian men. Some of these we saw at Edessa and in the land of Carrhae.

### ¶ Concerning Gregory Nazianzen, and Basil the Great, and where they learned the understanding of the Holy Scriptures.

### Chapter 9.

<margin>Gregory Nazianzen and Basil the Great in Cappadocia.</margin>
Cappadocia was no less fruitful, for she brought forth many holy men for us, and notably Gregory and Basil. These were two shining lights, both of very noble birth. While they were both studying in Athens, they were requested to teach Rhetoric; Basil fulfilled this greatly, but Gregory despised it even more. When they had given themselves entirely to the service of God, Gregory, out of great love, was so bold with his dear companion that he took Basil by the hand while he sat in the teacher's chair and led him away to the monastery. There they left all pagan books behind and for seven years (so it is said) they occupied themselves with the Divine Scriptures. They did not take their understanding of the <margin>To desire the understanding of Holy Scripture.</margin> Holy Scriptures from their own presumption, but followed the writings and authority of the elders, who had received the rule of understanding from the successors of the Apostles. They searched their commentaries and explanations, especially in the Prophets, and sought therein—as if in earthen vessels—the hidden treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

He was greatly troubled, for some were against him and had begun to write unwise things against him, hoping that he would return to his own land and that another Bishop would be ordained in his place. 

As no one dared to say such a thing to him directly, he perceived for himself that they were murmuring against him. <margin>Books of Basil and Gregory translated by Rufinus.</margin>
These two have left behind many precious books and proofs of their understanding and learning, which were read and taught daily in the church. From these, we have also translated about ten orations <note>Sermons or formal speeches.</note> each from Greek into Latin. 

<margin>Institutions of the Monks made by Basil.</margin>

<margin>Valentinian in the western lands.</margin>
In the Western lands, Valentinian reigned and kept the Christian faith unspotted; according to the ancient institutions of the Roman Empire, he governed the common good.

### ¶ Of Bishop Damasus, and the presumption of Ursinus.

### The 10th Chapter.

<margin>Damasus, Bishop at Rome.</margin>
After Liberius, Damasus received the priesthood in Rome. One Ursinus, a deacon of the same church, could not endure that Damasus should be his 

<column-break/>

superior. He fell into such a frenzy that he convinced an unlearned and coarse bishop to support his presumption. He gathered a force of wild and riotous people and came into the church called Sicininus, where he violently attempted to be Bishop, contrary to all the ordinances and institutions of the fathers. Through this event, such a riot arose that they fought one another, for the people wished to protect their respective sides, so that the places of prayer were filled with blood.

<margin>Ursinus also caused a great alarm for the sake of the Bishop's office.</margin>
The judge Maximinus, who was a cruel man, turned this into an occasion for envy against the good and innocent priests, so that he imprisoned and tortured the clergy. But the protector of the innocent, our God, was present there, and the penalty was turned back upon the heads of those who had begun the riot.

<margin>Maximinus the Judge.</margin>

### ¶ Of the death of Auxentius, the heretical Bishop of Milan, and how Ambrose, being an officer, became Bishop.

### The 11th Chapter.

<margin>Auxentius</margin>
When Auxentius <note>original: "Aurentius"</note>, the bishop who was a leader of the heretics <note>Referring to the Arians, who disagreed with the Nicene Creed regarding the nature of Christ.</note>, died in Milan, the people were divided into two factions, and the different teachings were very vehemently opposed to each other. A great and dangerous riot and discord arose, threatening the destruction of the entire city, for both parties were divided and each wished to maintain their own purpose.

<margin>Ambrose, an officer.</margin>
At that same time, Ambrose was there, an officer and governor of that province. When he saw that the destruction of the city was imminent, he went hastily into the church by virtue of his office to still the riot of the people. After he had spoken his reasons to the congregation for a long time, recounting much from the true and common teaching for the sake of peace and unity, a cry and a great shouting suddenly arose from these discordant and partisan people. With one voice, they cried out together, desiring that Ambrose should be their Bishop. And those who were baptized cried out—for Ambrose was still a **Catechumen** <note>A "Catechumen" is someone receiving instruction in the faith but who has not yet been baptized. It was highly irregular for a non-baptized person to be elected Bishop.</note>—that they desired to have him as a Bishop, and that otherwise there would be no united people or one single faith.

### ¶ Of the death of Emperor Valentinian.

## The XII. Chapter.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Emperor Valentinian dies.</margin>
During this time, the Emperor Valentinian traveled from Gaul <note>original: "Vranckrijck"</note> to Illyricum <note>A region in the western Balkans.</note> to fight the Sarmatians <note>Ancient Iranian nomadic peoples.</note>. Hardly had he begun the war when he was overcome by a sudden illness and died. He made his sons his heirs and left them the Empire; one was named Gratianus Augustus and the other Valentinian, who was still very young and had not yet received the royal insignia. Nevertheless, necessity compelled it, because there were some who wished to seize the Empire as if it were vacant; so Probus the Governor was forced to clothe this young Valentinian in the purple robe, even in his brother’s absence, which he did faithfully.

### ¶ How the Goths devastated the land of Thrace, and how Valens the Emperor was killed.

## The XIII. Chapter.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>The Goths come into Thrace, which is in the landscape of Europe in Greece, in Macedonia, and where Constantinople lies.</margin>

Then Valens <note>The Eastern Roman Emperor known for his support of Arianism.</note> ceased fighting against God’s congregation; the same power with which he had contested the Christian church, he now turned and took up to resist the enemies.

This war was afterwards the beginning of the destruction of the Roman Empire.

And being in Milan, she began to disturb the state of the Christian churches. She threatened the Priests that she would drive them out and send them into misery unless they renounced the faith of the fathers and instead accepted the Decrees and confessions concluded at the Council of Ariminum <note>original: "Concilium tot Arimino"; a council in 359 AD where Arianism was temporarily favored over the orthodox Nicene Creed.</note>, where the faith of the fathers had remained uncorrupted until then.

<margin>B</margin>

But although this woman, armed with the spirit of Jezebel <note>A reference to the biblical Queen Jezebel who persecuted the prophets of Israel.</note>, fought fiercely, Ambrose—filled with the power and grace of Elijah—resolutely set himself against her and fought back. She ranted and chattered within God's Assembly, inciting the people and stirring them to discord and defiance. And the youth <note>The young Emperor Valentinian II.</note>, inflamed with anger that any contempt should be shown to his mother (which she falsely invented), sent a troop of armed men into the church. ### ¶ Concerning the crime of Theodosius against the Thessalonians, and how he was punished by the Priests: and concerning his public penance which he performed.

### The xviii. Chapter.

<margin>23</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
In this same time, through the instigation of the devil, a foul crime was committed by the God-fearing Emperor Theodosius. For when a riot had arisen in Thessalonica and one of his soldiers was struck down by the mob of the raging people, the Emperor, hearing this, was ignited with cruel wrath. He commanded that the people should be invited to gather to behold the swordplay or fencing matches, and then suddenly and unexpectedly had the people surrounded by horsemen and ordered them to strike down everyone at hand. Thus, he did not avenge a crime, but rather the rage of the people. When he was subsequently punished for this by the Italian Priests <note>This refers primarily to Saint Ambrose, the Bishop of Milan, who famously excommunicated the Emperor until he repented.</note>, he acknowledged his guilt with sighing and tears, and performed public **penance** in the sight of the entire assembly. He patiently fulfilled the appointed time of repentance, and did not make use of the status of his Imperial highness. And above all this—which is truly to be wondered at—he established and confirmed a law that the Sentences of Emperors and Princes, when they are passed in matters of punishment, should be extended and held back by those who carry out the execution for thirty days. This was done so that mercy and the opportunity for repentance (if the case were such) might take place.

# Ecclesiastical History

<margin>Apollinarians are condemned.</margin>
This error <note>The Apollinarian heresy, named after Apollinaris of Laodicea, who taught that Jesus had a human body and soul but a divine mind, rather than a human mind.</note> was first driven out and condemned in the city of Rome by Damasus, the Bishop of that same city, and by Peter, the Bishop of Alexandria, who had gathered a Council. They condemned it in this manner, declaring: That whosoever says the Son of God (who, just as He is truly God, is also truly man) has any diminishment in His humanity or His divinity, shall be regarded as a stranger to the Church. This sentence was also confirmed in Alexandria and concluded in the Council held at Constantinople. <note>The First Council of Constantinople in 381 AD, which expanded the Nicene Creed and specifically condemned Apollinarianism.</note>

<margin>Apollinarians separate themselves.</margin>
From this time forward, the Apollinarians departed from the Church and appointed bishops of their own sect, protecting their teachings and their own churches.

### Concerning the Bishops who were in the East.

### The xxi. Chapter.

<margin>Siricius</margin>
<margin>Timothy</margin>
<margin>Theophilus</margin>
<margin>Cyril</margin>
<margin>John</margin>
<margin>Flavian</margin>
<margin>Paulinus</margin>
<margin>Meletius</margin>
In the city of Rome, after Damasus, Siricius received the priesthood. And in Alexandria, after Peter had died, Timothy succeeded him, and after him, Theophilus. In Jerusalem, after Cyril, came John; these two reformed this Apostolic see once again. In Antioch, when Meletius had died, Flavian succeeded him. But because Paulinus was still alive—who had always remained in the company of the faithful—this often caused great discord there. Nevertheless, no true peace was obtained there, for when one side had established its seat, it was overturned by another, so that no manner of peace could be maintained; and yet it was well known that there was no dispute regarding the faith itself. <note>This refers to the "Meletian Schism," a complicated succession dispute in Antioch where multiple bishops claimed the see despite agreeing on the Nicene faith.</note>

<margin>Theodore at Tyre.</margin>
The same also occurred at Tyre; for when a Christian—a lovely man of the old Christians, who had been tested and approved through much suffering and was made Bishop of the confessors by the testimony of Athanasius—was there, his loveliness and modesty were despised, and they ordained another from the party of Meletius. And also in many other churches to the East, this discord among the priests brought great confusion. In Constantinople, a Judge of the city named Nectarius was chosen; he was instructed in the faith and had recently received <term>baptism</term><note>The rite of initiation into the Christian church involving water.</note> when he became a Priest there.

<column-break/>

### Concerning the riot that occurred in Alexandria against the Christians.

### The xxij. Chapter.

<margin>A riot arises against the Christians in Alexandria under Bishop Theophilus.</margin>
In the meantime, a new riot, and larger than any before, rose against the Christian church in Alexandria from this cause: There was an old church building which lay desolate and as if forgotten; it was said that the Emperor Constantius had given it to the bishops who preached and understood his unbelief. <note>Constantius II was known for supporting Arianism, which the author here labels as "unbelief."</note> This church had nothing good left but the walls, because it was so dilapidated. So the Bishop who was there at that time <note>Theophilus of Alexandria.</note> thought it good to request this church from the Emperor, because as the number of faithful people increased, the place of prayer should also grow. When he had received this church and wished to repair it, secret caverns in the earth were found in those places, which were more fit for the dens of their <term>blasphemy</term><note>Here referring to secret pagan rituals or "mysteries" viewed as insulting to God.</note> than for Divine service. Therefore, when the Heathens saw this, they thought that their murders and villainies—the wickedness of their knavery which they had obscured and covered for so many years—could no longer remain hidden. They became as enraged and frantic as if they had drunk dragons' blood; and this not only with a noise of shouting or an uproar as they were accustomed, but they began to fight our people with force and weapons. Thus, both parties fought one another openly in the streets. Our people were greater in number and stronger in power, but because of the modesty of our Religion, they were not as cruel as the others.

<margin>Suffering, murder, and killing of the Christians.</margin>
Wherefore many of ours were often wounded and some even struck dead; and the Heathens fled to the Temple as if to a fortress and dragged the captured Christians there. After lighting the idolatrous sacrifices, they forced those same prisoners to offer sacrifice. And when the Christians refused this, they were tormented and thus killed by new and unheard-of manners of pain. Some they crucified, and some they broke the legs of, and thus cast them into the caverns and pits which had been made of old to receive the blood of their sacrifices and other impurities of the Temple.

After this letter from the Emperor was read, our people were of the mind to destroy the famous Temple of the Idol Serapis, which was in Alexandria and was a cause of many errors. The site of this Temple was not high by nature, but was raised through great labor, so that one had to ascend at least 100 steps. The first and innermost covering of the statue consisted of gold plates, and above that it was covered with silver plates, and finally with copper, which served as a protection for the primary and most precious deception. <meta>This page continues the account of the destruction of the pagan temples in Alexandria, specifically detailing the fall of the Great Temple of Serapis and the dismantling of its colossal statue.</meta>

# Ecclesiastical History / Fol. 206.

<margin>The nature of the lodestone.</margin> To greet Serapis, the priests carefully observed their timing, so that when the image was brought in, the rays and radiance of the sun—shining through a small window—would illuminate Serapis's mouth and lips. This appeared to the common people as if Serapis were being greeted by the Sun with a kiss.

There was yet another method of deception, which was this: It is said that a lodestone <note>original: "zeylsteen"; a naturally magnetized mineral</note> possesses such power that it draws iron toward itself. Thus, a likeness of the Sun was very skillfully and subtly crafted from iron, and the lodestone—whose nature is to attract iron—was fixed high in the vaulted ceiling. The image of the Sun was placed exactly beneath it, and through the power of the stone, the iron likeness of the Sun was drawn upward, so that it appeared to the people to be rising and hanging there in the air. And so that this trickery would not be discovered by any sudden fall, the ministers of this deceit would say: "The Sun has risen to greet Serapis, only to return again to its place." Many other such things were made by the ancients in that place to deceive the people, which would take too long to recount in full.

Thus, as we had begun to say, when the Emperor's decrees were read, our people were ready to destroy the source of such delusions. Nevertheless, a rumor had been spread by the Pagans among the common folk that if any human hand touched the image, the earth would sink and the Heavens would fall. Because of this rumor, the people still felt some fear. And behold, one of the soldiers <note>The original Dutch uses "kupters," likely a corruption referring to the soldiers or brave men; historical accounts often identify this man as a Roman soldier</note> who was armed more with faith than with any other weapon, drew his double-edged sword and struck the face of the wicked image with all his might. <margin>The Image of Serapis is cast down, broken, and dragged through the streets by the Christians.</margin> Then a great cry was raised by both sides of the people; yet the Heavens did not fall, nor did the earth sink. So he struck again and again, casting down the dark and smoky spirit of the old, rotten wood. Afterward, some iron was brought to it, and it burned more easily than dry wood.

Thereafter, they pulled down the neck and the head, and hacked all

<column-break/>

the limbs of the Image to pieces with axes, bound them with ropes, and dragged them away to various places. And thus was this ugly, old, and deceitful idol shamefully burned here and there in the presence of the people of Alexandria who had once worshipped it. Finally, the remaining block of the image was burned in the marketplace. This was the end of the idle unbelief and the ancient errors of the Idol Serapis. <margin>The end of Serapis.</margin> Regarding the origin of this idol, there are various opinions among the Pagans. Some suspect that it was Jupiter, because a bushel <note>original: "Mudde"; likely referring to the *calathus*, a basket-shaped crown symbolizing the underworld or fertility</note> was set upon his head, which was proof that he ordered all things with moderation, or that he gave life to man through the abundance of fruits. Others suspect that it signified the power of the river Nile, by whose fertility the entire land of Egypt is fed and made very fruitful. <margin>Jupiter.</margin>

Others said that this image was made in honor of our Joseph, the son of the Patriarch Jacob, because of the measuring of the wheat through which he helped the land of Egypt during the famine. Still others said they had found in the ancient History of the Greeks that an honorable nobleman or King had lived at Memphis who was named Apis. When there was a shortage of wheat in Alexandria during a time of famine, he gradually sustained his citizens with his own wheat and provisions. When he died, the Egyptians built a Temple at Memphis in his honor, in which an Ox <note>The sacred Apis bull</note> was always fed—having various colors as a sign of a good husbandman—which Ox was named Apis in memory of his name. And they carried Apis's sepulcher <note>tomb</note> where his body lay to Alexandria; this was called in their language *Soros* <note>Greek for a coffin or funerary urn</note>, meaning a grave, and thereafter over time it became *Sorapis*, and finally, through corruption, *Serapis*. But whether these things be so or not, we leave that to God the Creator. Now we wish to return to our begun work. <margin>Apis.</margin> <margin>Memphis.</margin>

## The 24th Chapter.

<margin>All images in Alexandria were broken and cast out.</margin>
<margin>A</margin> Now that the head of idolatry has been overthrown and destroyed, all the villainies and abominations of the Idols throughout all Alexandria have likewise been revealed with shame through the diligent earnestness of Bishop Theophilus. My spirit shrinks from speaking out <margin>B</margin> about what snares were prepared by the devil for miserable, mortal men, and what murder and blasphemy lay hidden and concealed in the place called the <term>Adyta</term> <note>original: "Adyta"; from the Greek for "not to be entered," referring to the innermost secret chambers of a temple where only priests were permitted.</note>. <margin>Adyta.</margin>
<margin>Children's heads.</margin>
<margin>C</margin> When these things came to light in this manner and were brought into the open, the Heathens were ashamed and fled away. Because of this, there were many who, once they understood and condemned the fraud and the crime, accepted the Christian faith and the true service of God. ## The 25th Chapter.

<margin>Tyrannus, a priest of Saturn.</margin>
<margin>F</margin> There was a priest of the idol Saturn named Tyrannus. This man, as if his idol had commanded it, spoke to some of the highest and noblest men who used to come to the Temple to worship—and whose wives pleased him most for his own lust—saying that the god Saturn had commanded that such a woman should spend the night in the temple. And whoever of these men heard such things, thinking that the idol

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin> took pleasure in his wife, rejoiced greatly that his spouse was esteemed so worthy. He would adorn her in the finest clothes and send her there with gifts and jewels, so that she would not be rejected by coming empty-handed. And when Tyrannus the Priest, in the presence of everyone, had locked the woman in the temple and closed the doors, he handed over the keys and went away. <margin>H</margin> Afterward, when all had become quiet, this priest of Saturn made his way through secret and hidden passages beneath the earth into the image of Saturn. For this idol was hollow, carved out in the back, and was skillfully joined to the wall. In the temple, many lights were burning. Now, while the woman was busy praying, the Priest suddenly let a voice out from him through the hollow image, so that this unhappy woman was startled by both fear and joy that she should be worthy enough for such a god to speak with her. <margin>I</margin> After this unchaste god had spoken with the woman to frighten her further and to incite her to lewdness, he used an instrument he had made so that all the burning lights were covered with linen cloths and were thus quickly extinguished. <margin>Tyrannus commits unchastity with the women.</margin> And then this Priest came out of the image of Saturn and fulfilled his unchaste will with the frightened and terrified woman. <margin>K</margin> When this practice had continued for a long time, one after the other, it happened that there was a woman of honorable heart who was very terrified by such a crime. Observing all these proceedings diligently, <margin>The wickedness of Tyrannus is noticed.</margin> she recognized the voice of Tyrannus. Upon coming home, she told her husband and informed him of the deceit and the crime. <margin>L</margin> This man, being inflamed by the shame of his <margin>He was captured.</margin> wife—or rather, the great injury to himself—had the Priest seized and brought to be tortured. And when he was overcome by this villainy and had confessed and suffered for it all, and when all that deceit had become public, a great shame fell upon all the houses of the Heathens; for the mothers were harlots, the fathers were scoundrels, and the children were bastards and dishonorable. <margin>M</margin> Thus was the idol quickly destroyed along with the Temple, and the crimes were punished.

## The 26th Chapter.

Who could now recount the horrible abuses of the priests of Canopus, where the veil of the priestly letters <note>original: "Prieſterlijcke letteren"; the translator refers to Egyptian hieroglyphics, which were often viewed by early Christians as a secretive script for magical or pagan lore.</note> (for so the ancient writings of the Egyptians were named) served as an open school of sorcery? This place was held by the Heathens to be the great fountain of all idolatry, so much so that it was considered far more famous and worthy than Alexandria itself. It seems fitting to me to reveal the origin of these errors in a few words. It is said that the Chaldeans in former times held Fire to be their God; carrying it about into all lands, they fought against all the other gods of various provinces, on the condition that whoever was the victor should be regarded by all people as the supreme God. But since the gods of the other provinces were made of copper, gold, silver, wood, stone, or other materials—all of which were corrupted and overcome by fire—the fire maintained the victory over them all. When the Priest of the idol Canopus heard of this, he devised a cunning cleverness. In the land of Egypt, large earthenware jars are made which have very tiny holes on all sides, used to make murky and thick waters pure for drinking. The priest took such a jar and stopped up all the holes with wax; he then had it painted with various colors and filled it with water. He set it up as a God, taking the head of an ancient idol—said to be that of King Menelaus—and joined that head quite subtly and skillfully onto the jar.

<margin>The God of the Chaldeans is fire</margin>
The Chaldeans arrived and wished to fight this God as well; they kindled a fire around the jar. However, due to the heat of the fire, the wax melted, and the water leaked out little by little, so that the fire was extinguished.

<margin>The God Canopus overcomes the God of the Chaldeans.</margin>
Thus, through the deception of the Priest, Canopus gained the victory over the Chaldeans. This is why the image of Canopus is made with very small feet, a short neck, and a swollen belly, being rounded at the back like a jar. For this reason, Canopus was honored as a God who held victory over all other gods. These things might by chance have been profitable to the Chaldeans. But when the Priest of God, Theophilus, arrived,

<column-break/>

neither sweetness nor any deception of wax could help them. Instead, all the idols were destroyed and cast to the ground.
<margin>Canopus is destroyed.</margin>

### ¶ Of the Churches that were built in the place of the Idol Temples.

## The 27th Chapter.

<margin>The Chapel of the Martyrs.</margin>
This did not happen merely to leave the places desolate; rather, the dens and graves of crimes and the old images of the idols were cast down, and high Churches—Temples of the true God—were built there. For after the Heathen houses at the tomb of Serapis <note>The Serapeum of Alexandria, the most grand temple in the city, dedicated to the syncretic god Serapis.</note> were destroyed, the <term>Martyrium</term> <note>A chapel or shrine built over the relics of a martyr or at the site of their death.</note>—that is, the Chapel of the Martyrs—was built on one side, and the church on the other. But for what reason the Chapel of the Martyrs was founded, I think is worthy to be told.

### ¶ How the grave of John the Baptist was destroyed, and of the Relics that are kept in Alexandria.

## The 28th Chapter.

<margin>The grave of John the Baptist in Sebaste, Palestine, was treated without mercy.</margin>
In the time of Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (reigned 361–363 AD), the last pagan Roman Emperor who attempted to roll back Christian influence.</note>, the madness of the Heathens was entirely unbridled and let loose toward every cruelty. So it happened that in the city of Sebaste, located in Palestine, with bloody hands and raging minds, they laid hold of the grave of John the Baptist. They first scattered the bones, then gathered them again and burned them in the fire; the ashes, mixed with dust, they scattered over the fields and meadows. But through God's providence, it happened that some from the Monastery of Philip—a man of God from Jerusalem—had come to Sebaste at that same time to pray. When they saw what was happening there, they mingled themselves among those who intended to scatter the bones. With great diligence and reverence, they secretly obtained some of those bones and brought the worthy Relics to Philip, their Father.

<margin>The Monastery of Philip near Jerusalem.</margin>
He felt it was inappropriate that he should keep such a treasure alone, and so he sent the relics to Athanasius <note>Athanasius the Great, Bishop of Alexandria and a central figure in early Church history.</note>, who was the presiding Bishop at that time, via Julian his Deacon, who later also became a Bishop in Palestine. ### ¶ How the measure of the flood of the River Nile was carried into the churches of the Christians.

### The 30th Chapter.

<margin>H</margin>
<margin>I The Nile Cubit in the temple of the Christians.</margin>
It was also a custom in Egypt that the measure of the flood of the River Nile <note>The *Cubitus Nili*, a standard measuring rod used to track the river's annual rise, essential for predicting the harvest.</note> was brought into the temple of Serapis, as if to one who was the cause and master of the rising and flowing waters. Now, when his image was burned, there were many who thought that Serapis would remember the contempt shown to him and would henceforth not give enough water. But so that God might show that Serapis—who came long after the Nile—was not the one who makes the waters rise, there was such a flooding of the river as had never been heard of before. Therefore, the water-measure was carried to the Lord of the waters in the Church. When these events were announced to the God-fearing Emperor Theodosius, it is said that he lifted his hands toward Heaven and spoke with great joy: "I thank you, O Christ, that this ancient error has been destroyed and extinguished without hindrance to the great City."

### Of Theodosius's victory against Eugenius, which was obtained more through prayer than through strength.

### The 33rd Chapter.

Thus Theodosius prepared himself for war, not only with weapons and missiles, but much more with prayer and fasting; for he himself went personally at night with the Priests and the people, wearing a haircloth <note>A garment made of coarse animal hair worn against the skin as a sign of penance and humility.</note>, before the reliquaries <note>original: "casse"; the chests or shrines containing the remains of saints.</note> of the Apostles and martyrs, and desired faithful help through the prayer of the Saints. <margin>Flavianus, a Judge.</margin>

The others set their ranks to await the battle on the slope of the mountain, but had laid ambushes on top of the mountain. And when the first had risen against the righteous Prince, a very fierce battle was fought with those who had set their ranks below in the valley, so that it was doubted with whom the victory would remain. The soldiers who were with Theodosius were beaten and took flight. Which happened not so that Theodosius should be defeated, but so it would not seem that he was winning through the power of those soldiers. And when Theodosius saw that his ranks had turned their backs to flee, standing atop a stone cliff where he could see the soldiers of both parties and also be seen, he threw his weapons from him and turned to his usual certain help, and fell down before the face of God, saying:

<margin>Theodosius to God.</margin>
> O Almighty God, you know that in the Name of Jesus Christ your Son, I have begun this war to take righteous vengeance, as I believe; and if it be otherwise, then take vengeance upon me yourself. <meta>Following the conclusion of the eleventh book of the Ecclesiastical History, which detailed the victory of Theodosius over Eugenius, this page presents a concluding or commendatory sonnet. It reflects on the power of writing to preserve history against the forgetfulness of time, serving as a philosophical coda to the historical narrative.</meta>

# SONNET.

Oh! Truly the desire for writing is a worthy desire,
That which shows us ancient Time, as if our Time were new;
Whereby, through Time passed, Mankind dwells once more
In mother Earth’s womb, through *Atropos* <note>In Greek mythology, Atropos was the eldest of the three Fates, the one who cut the thread of life.</note> being stripped of life.

So too, swift Time has no permanent stay here,
And even with his *Fame*, he would not be spared from *Lethe* <note>original: *Lethis*; the river of forgetfulness in the Greek underworld.</note>
If the pen of *Memory* had not elegantly crowned him
With gray-white hair and beard—yes, and even the deeds of his Time.

Quite rightly *Cicero* <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the Roman statesman. This refers to his famous definition of history in *De Oratore*.</note> says: that *Histories* are
The ancient record of Time, the very light of Truth,
The youth of *Memory*, the mistress of discipline <note>term: *Tucht-vrouw'* (Mistress of Discipline); a personification of history as a teacher of moral conduct.</note> of our life:

At once; also a messenger who brings Antiquity to our knowledge,
That we all, being made as an Image, do not forget our Creator:
Thus, that which is worthily written is well worth praising.

->Pure Love shown.<- <note>original: *Reyn Liefd' bethoont*; This is a "remigre" or motto, likely belonging to the author or a specific Chamber of Rhetoric (Rederijkerskamer).</note>

# The Second Part.

<note>A decorative woodcut border with scrollwork, floral motifs, and small figures surrounds a circular emblem. The emblem depicts the biblical scene of Moses and the burning bush. # OF CASSIODORUS THE COUNCILOR
## SERVANT OF THE LORD GOD, IN THE CHRONI-
### CLE OF THE ANCIENT CHRISTIAN CHURCHES, CALLED THE
### Tripartite Ecclesiastical History, drawn from the three Greek Historians,
### Sozomen, Socrates, and Theodoret: translated into Latin by Epiphanius
### Scholasticus, and abridged and most concisely
### compiled by Cassiodorus.

->*Preface* of Cassiodorus *the Councilor*, in which
he gives the *reason for his work*.<-

<margin>Theodoret</margin>
<margin>Sozomen</margin>
<margin>Socrates</margin>
<margin>Epiphanius Scholasticus, translator.</margin>
<margin>From Constantine to Theodosius the Younger, comprising approximately 425 years from the birth of Christ until this time.</margin>
With great benefit it was customary to place the Preface at the beginning of Books, from which one might know and see the form and beauty of the coming work. What is more useful to learn first, beloved Reader, than the Preface, so that no vain words in the preceding Book might disturb you in the future? Therefore, this Ecclesiastical History, which of necessity should be testified to all Christians, has been wonderfully compiled from the three Greek writers: namely, one named THEODORET, who was a venerable Bishop; and the other two eloquent men, SOZOMEN and SOCRATES. After Epiphanius Scholasticus <note>Epiphanius Scholasticus (6th century) was a translator who worked under the direction of Cassiodorus to bring Greek texts into Latin.</note> had set these into Latin, we deemed it necessary to collect all the elegant words and sayings together into one Book (with the help of the Lord) and from the three Authors and Greek Historians to make one volume <note>original: *fagret*; likely a variant or error for a term meaning a bundle or treatise.</note> and Book. It is also well to know that the aforementioned writers described what occurred from the time of the highly praised memory of Emperor Constantine, to the time of the highly famous memory of Theodosius the Younger. 

However, we have left their work and books in such a way that we have grasped each writing with a good understanding, finding that they do not all explain all dealings and matters with equal clarity and subtlety, nor decorate them as promptly and beautifully; sometimes one and sometimes the other brings the matters or histories more beautifully to light. Therefore, we have found it good that we might usefully gather the most prominent sayings from each writer and set them in order under the names of the Authors. Therefore, whichever person comes to read these Books with the help of the Lord, let them read without fear: for they may gain great benefit and knowledge therefrom, if they diligently pull together their memory with a careful mind and gather the things contained in these 12 books. Furthermore, let the order of things disturb no one, for it should be known that throughout the entire text of this work, Titles are placed, with which one may recognize and seek what is required for each place, as indicated beforehand by a suitable number.

### ¶ Preface and address of Sozomen, to the Emperor Theodosius. <note>Theodosius II (reigned 408–450 AD), known for his piety and for commissioning the Theodosian Code.</note>

#### The First Chapter.

<margin>A</margin> It is said that among the ancient Emperors and Princes, there was such diligence and practice that they equipped their admirers with elegant things, such as purple, Royal Scepters and Crowns, and whatever other such 

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Everyone has his desire for some profit.</margin> things there were: those who placed their intent in Books: they concerned themselves with fables <note>In this context, "fables" refers to secular myths or poetic inventions.</note> and in capturing them in Writing, wherewith they stirred and made willing the desires in the hearts of the listeners.

To those who manage matters of war, it is told how they should use the engines of war <note>original: "tgheschut," referring here to siege engines or artillery of the period.</note> in the most fitting manner. To fell beasts and wild animals, to carry spears and lances correctly, to

<margin>C</margin> mount horses correctly. In these things, everyone has exerted himself to observe Royal matters, so that what would be most useful to the Lords and Rulers might come to him. One brought a precious noble stone, which was difficult to obtain: another brought well-dyed clear purple: many

<margin>D</margin> brought *Poems*, that is, Verses, and other Writings: another presented and brought good Knightly Belts, or

<column-break/>

<margin>E</margin> discovered how one should use good Weapons correctly. Now, that to which the Admirers inclined themselves, the Superiors and the common man's understanding have considered the very best and most Imperial: But of Godliness <note>original: "Godsalicheydt," meaning piety or religious devotion.</note> and Religion, which is the principal ornament of the Empire, almost no one

<margin>F</margin> has made mention.

Yet you, most powerful Emperor Theodosius (to say it in a word): You have, through the help of God, surpassed all virtues. The Purple and Crown (which are signs of your Majesty) and with which you are draped, and are seen by the onlookers—these increase and plant within you

<margin>G</margin> everywhere an internal Godliness and generosity <note>original: "miltheydt," meaning both mercy and liberality.</note>. Therefore the Historians, Officials, and other subjects, for that reason and for the sake of your deeds, remain in practice and labor: You, who are a true Hero and a Judge of books, do not let yourself be caught with veiled

<margin>H</margin> words, or let the truth be bypassed through an appearance or figurative reasoning:

<margin>The judgment of Theodosius.</margin> But weighing both perfectly, so that every action has its appropriate Reason, Figure, and form: You distinguish the order and fittingness—whether they agree—the speech, the composition and joining together, the sense and History; all this you weigh diligently

<margin>I</margin> and deeply. You also reward those who Recite and speak before you (as well befits your understanding and grace), granting them golden images, gifts, and all kinds of honor, just as you hold yourself toward the Translators <note>original: "Tael-mannen," literally "language-men."</note>, and

In the same way, some judges in times past behaved toward the sweet-speaking **Homer**, or **Aleuas** toward **Simonides**, **Dionysius**, a Tyrant of Sicily, toward **Plato** (a "young Socrates"), or **Philip**, the King of Macedonia, toward the historian **Theopompus**. The Emperor **Severus** toward
<margin>Oppian described the nature of all kinds of fish.</margin>
**Oppian**, who in verse described the various kinds of fish and their natures, and how they should be caught. The Cretans compared 1,000 coins to the Homeric poems; and as one who boasts of a rich expenditure, they had this gift inscribed upon a public statue. **Aleuas**, **Dionysius**, and **Philip** were no more exceptional than
the Cretans, but they boasted of an extraordinary common utility and of philosophy, which they also might have followed in their likeness; these in deed were not lesser in their gift-giving. **Severus**, however, because he compared and rewarded **Oppian** with a gold coin for every verse, gave cause for a wonderful saying concerning his richness, which has lasted among many even until now: that the verses of **Oppian** are called "Golden Verses."
<margin>The Emperor Severus gave Oppian a gold piece for every verse.</margin>
Such gifts were given in former times by those who loved art and learning.

<margin>The Greatness of Theodosius.</margin>
But you, most mighty Emperor, you are found to be no less than those aforementioned: for you have shown yourself most rich toward the arts and learning, and it seems to me that you do not handle these things without feeling; since you surpass them all in virtue, you do well to direct and advance all your affairs toward increase and improvement. For you are sufficiently 
informed of the Histories or accounts that have preceded among the Romans and Greeks. It is said that by day you exercise with weapons and you yourself proclaim and judge the affairs and dealings of your subjects; and alone, you handle and deliberate what is to be done with others. At night,
<margin>The Lamp of Theodosius.</margin>
you lay the books open. It is also said that a lamp <note>The original Dutch uses "Luchter" (candelabrum) and mentions the "Olpe" (a Greek oil flask). The story illustrates the Emperor's self-reliance; he supposedly invented a lamp that fed itself or refilled it himself to avoid waking his servants.</note> was made for you of a precious nature, and you even pour the oil flask into the lamp yourself, so that no one of your court should be troubled with these things. Thus you are also mild and gentle toward your neighbors and all people: in this following the Heavenly King, your Patron, who graciously lets it rain upon the righteous and the unrighteous, and
lets the sun shine, and accomplishes other things without hate or envy. I also hear
that through much reading you know the nature of precious stones, and the power of roots, and what power they have for healing, no less than **Solomon**, the son of David.

<column-break/>

<margin>Gentleness is a sign of better things.</margin>
Yet you surpass him in virtues, for he became a servant of pleasures, and did not observe the godliness and fear of God until the end, through which he might have obtained much good in wisdom as well. But you, O most mighty Emperor, as one who has set the intellect against neglect, it is seen that you do not only stand before men for all justice, but that you also rule over all passions of the body and the soul. If I were also to say this, I hear that you
surpass all desire for food and drink, and that you delight in nothing at all—neither sweet apples, nor anything else that is beautiful to look upon is desired, as far as the taste is concerned—and how before all things, you praise and thank the Creator of all things. Thirst, 
heat, and cold you are accustomed to endure. It is also noted how you, through daily abstinence, have brought your nature to this same restraint. For before this time, when you were in Pontus at the city of **Heraclea** (so named after Hercules),
<margin>Heraclas.</margin>
hurrying to assist those who had suffered need for a long time, you traveled through Bithynia in the greatest heat. While the sun burned so fiercely at hot midday, someone
saw how you went along in much sweat and were full of dust; he, as one who wished to refresh you, ran toward you and brought you a lovely drink of cold water in a translucent beaker, shining as if from the sun, taken from the flowing stream.

->But, O most mighty Emperor,<-
you took the drinking beaker and praised the man for his deed, and endowed him with Imperial riches. When all the soldiers and servants enjoyed something from this beautiful beaker, and thought that he who should drink from it would be blessed, you gave the drinking beaker back to him, and said that he might handle it according to his will. For which I am grateful, that you have entirely surpassed **Alexander**
<margin>Alexander.</margin>
with your virtues, of whom those who marvel at his works speak. When he hurried with the Macedonians through a parched place, a quick soldier, having found water, scooped it up with his helmet and brought it forth; **Alexander** did not drink it, but poured it over his body <note>This refers to a famous incident during Alexander the Great's march through the Gedrosian Desert; by refusing the water, he shared the suffering of his troops.</note>. So that I may then make an end or conclusion to my speech, and as **Homer** says, call you a *Prince of Princes* <note>original: "Principem Principum"</note> (if it is permitted to speak otherwise), that is, a Prince before all Princes.

<margin>Nine parts of this book.</margin>

F The fifth and sixth parts: what happened under Julian, who were cousins with the children of Constantine the Great. Likewise, what happened under Jovian, Valentinian, and Valens. G -pire—together with the God-fearing brother of your father, Honorius, took up the rule of the Roman Empire. # Why the Gentiles more easily than the Jews accepted the faith of Christ.

### The 2nd Chapter.

I have sometimes had thoughts as to how it comes to pass that some recognize faith in the Lord’s Word sooner than others, and

<margin>Hebrews.</margin>
the Hebrews remain unbelieving, who nonetheless H from the beginning received the commandments of God, I and the presence of Christ, K and how things would be fulfilled, having been taught by the Prophets before they happened.

<margin>Abraham.</margin>
L Abraham, a Prince of their tribes and the beginner of circumcision, loved Him so much that he was permitted to be an observer and host of the Son of God <note>A reference to the hospitality of Abraham at Mamre, often interpreted by Church Fathers as an early appearance of Christ.</note>.

<margin>Isaac.</margin>
Isaac his son was honored as a significance of the true sacrifice; who, when he was bound by the Father and laid upon the Altar, was a figure of the Cross, just as later happened in the suffering of Christ, as they say who have read the Holy Scriptures together in their entirety.

<margin>Gen. 49. Jacob.</margin>
M Jacob foretold that the Gentiles <note>original: "Heydenen" (Heathens)</note> would wait for him, and also the time in which he would come, when he speaks: "Then shall the leaders of the Hebrews from the lineage of Judah their Prince cease,"

<margin>Herod.</margin>
by which he signifies the Kingdom of Herod; who, since he was an Edomite from his father and an Arab from his mother, was entrusted with the Jewish people by the Council at Rome and by the Emperor.

<margin>Isaiah 7.</margin>
There other Prophets also quite clearly foretold the birth of Christ, and this His Holy unspeakable conception, and how his mother would remain a Virgin <note>original: "Maeght"</note> even after the conception.

¶ Likewise/ regarding lineage and fatherland.
Some have also diligently studied the suffering and resurrection from the dead/ and the ascension into Heaven/ which Holy Scripture now records/ so that it shall be sufficiently understood/ that such things can no longer be hidden from the Jews.

<margin>Josephus.</margin>
Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian whose works provide crucial non-Biblical accounts of first-century Judea.</note> however/ a son of Matthias/ and a priest/ and a nobleman among the Jews/ and also among the Romans a firmly worthy witness of the truth of Christ. He did not dare to call him merely a man/ but a miracle-worker/ and a master of true reason: but he calls him the Christ, the well-beloved Son of God/ and describes how he was judged to the pain of the Cross/ and how he appeared alive on the third day/ and many other wonderful works/ which the Holy Prophets foresaw and wrote of in the Scriptures/ as Josephus reports. <note>The author is referring to the 'Testimonium Flavianum,' a famous but controversial passage in Josephus's 'Antiquities of the Jews' regarding Jesus.</note>

¶ He also testifies that there were many then among the Jews and Greeks/ whom he had chosen and who remained in his love/ and how the people named Christians after him/ have not entirely fallen away from him/ and it seems to me/ while he says such things/ that it is as much as crying out/ how it truly stands with the works of Christ. Because he is astonished and marveled at his miraculous works / and Josephus having said this/ he continues in his writing/ yet he contradicts those who believe in Christ in nothing/ but rather holds with them. Now that I have considered these things / I have wondered greatly/ how it happened/ that the Lords <note>The Dutch 'Heeren' here likely refers to the Gentiles or the ruling classes of the pagan world; the original Greek text of Sozomen discusses why the Gentiles converted more readily than the Jews.</note> were not converted to the Christian faith before other men? For even though the Sibyls <note>Ancient prophetesses whose oracles were often cited by early Christian apologists as pagan witnesses to Christ.</note>/ and other prophets among the Pagans/ predicted those things which were to happen/ yet for this reason not all Greeks shall be punished for their unbelief: For few who seemed to be the most learned/ understood these prophecies/ which were commonly described in verses and rhymes/ and spoken to the people with heavy and bold words. Therefore, as it seems to me/ it signifies a Divine foresight/ that the future prophets were not only commended to the Jewish people/ as his own people/ but also to the Pagans. Just as a musician <note>original: "melodyspeler"</note>, for the sake of the pleasure of a foreign tune, grips or strikes other strings/ or draws in others alongside those he already has. So the Pagans have used many public prophecies: yet they were found much smaller in the presence of Christ than the Pagans <note>The text suggests that those who had the prophecies were less receptive than those who did not.</note>. It is also not without cause described/ why the Church alone from among other nations

<column-break/>

<margin>God's works are wonderful.</margin>
has believed. First/ that it pleases God that a change happens through miraculous works/ in Divine and great matters/ thereafter although the Christian Faith at first/ not with simple, vain virtues of the most prominent/ seemed lost/ yet the arguments used were found: So they have been/ and still spoke with figurative words/ or used philosophical arguments: Thus they have nonetheless applied themselves to addressing the people for their good. They have left their trade and livelihood/ are as if naked/ yes, those who loved others/ have gone about here and there/ and have suffered many great and hard martyrdoms. They were not subject to the people of the cities/ nor moved by the fair speaking of the Judges/ the threats did not frighten them/ but they made it manifest before everyone/ how they suffered this struggle for the sake of a great reward. Therefore it did not require many embellished words then/ since the matter and the deeds/ which had occurred in the houses and cities/ so drove them forward/ that one had to give them belief.

<margin>Maxentius.</margin>
In the first year of the 271st Olympiad, on the 27th day of July. In Rome, Maxentius, a son of Maximian Herculius <note>Maximianus Herculius was co-emperor with Diocletian and father to Maxentius.</note>, was elevated by the Praetorian soldiers, acting more as a tyrant than as an Emperor. Then it happened that Herculinus, his father, being inclined to rule, violently stripped his son of the government, which he could not accomplish without the support of the army. Afterward, he died in the city of Tarsus in Cilicia <note>The Dutch text says "Sicilien" (Sicily), but historical records place this event in Tarsus, Cilicia.</note>.

<margin>Severus defeated.</margin>
The Emperor Severus was sent to Rome by Galerius Maximianus; arriving there against Maxentius, he was slain by a treacherous soldier. Finally, Galerius Maximianus also died, after he had previously arranged all matters and made Licinius Emperor; they had long before experienced war together and were good friends, born in Dacia <note>The Dutch text says "Denemercken" (Denmark), a common early modern confusion with the ancient Roman province of Dacia.</note>. Furthermore, Maxentius was held as a tyrant in Rome: for, as a shameless man, he broke the bond of marriage with wives and struck their husbands dead. When Constantine wished to subdue him and deliver the pious from his slaughter, he considered which God he should have as a helper in the war; for he knew that the gods whom Diocletian honored were of no use to him: But that his father, Constantius, though he had disregarded the religion of the Heathens, had enjoyed luck and prosperity.

# Sozomenus.

<margin>Christ appears to Constantine.</margin>
While he stood in this anxiety and deliberation, he saw in a dream the sign of the Cross, placed quite visibly in the Heavens; and as he marveled at this vision, angels stood by him and said: "O Constantine, in this, conquer." <note>original: "in desen overwint," translating the Latin phrase "In hoc vince."</note> It is also said that Christ appeared to him and spoke of the sign of the Cross, commanding him to have a similar figure made to have as an aid in the war, with which he would win the battle.

Eusebius Pamphili writes <note>original: "seyt met een veeren," literally "says with a quill."</note> how he heard from the Emperor himself that at noon, as the sun was descending, a sign of the Cross formed from its brilliance, and around it was woven this writing, which said to him: "In this, conquer." The Emperor himself saw this, as did his soldiers who were then together with him.

<margin>In this, conquer.</margin>

this might be, night came upon him; and while he slept, Christ appeared to him with the sign he had seen in the heavens, and commanded him to fashion that sign, so that he might have help when he wished to strike the enemies. Since there was no longer need for interpretation, the Emperor having been openly shown what he should believe concerning God, as soon as it became day, he called the priest of Christ to him and asked for counsel regarding this teaching. And confirming their words with the Prophetic Scriptures, they said that this sign which had appeared to him was a sign of triumph from the battle of the war against Hell, which victory Christ achieved and obtained by ascending to Heaven, after He had been crucified and died, and risen again on the third day. Therefore it is to be hoped, they said: That at the end of this present world, after the term or end of this life, all people shall rise again and become immortal. Some who have lived well to reward; those who have lived poorly to pain and punishment. Yet regarding the work of the forgiveness of sins unto life: that whoever was not yet baptized should let himself be baptized according to the institution of the Church; and then for the baptized and the accepted, that they should guard themselves against sin. Since there were few to handle all this, and they were of the holiest men, they taught another cleansing

# Ecclesiastical History

<margin>Constantine’s plan to test the Christians’ steadfastness.</margin>
¶ Wishing to live freely in religion, yet wanting for a time to record and examine several members of his court to see if they were good, steadfast Christians, Constantine commanded that they should come and offer sacrifices and honor his gods. If they did so, he would keep them in honor before him; but if they refused, they would no longer remain at Court, nor depart with his thanks. Indeed, on the contrary, they would not escape without punishment.

¶ When both kinds of people were found there—some who renounced their religion, and others who placed divine things before temporal things—he took those who remained steadfast in the good into his Council. The other fickle <note>The original Dutch "wyvische lieden" literally translates to "wife-like" or "womanish," a period term used here to mean weak, wavering, or lacking in resolve.</note> people he permitted to leave, as he no longer wished to speak with them: for he did not consider those to be faithful who so easily forsake their God. And while Constantine was still alive, it was not against his command, nor considered unjust, that being a Christian, one could hold the Christian faith in Italy, France, Britain, and even as far as the Pyrenees mountains and the great Western Sea <note>The Atlantic Ocean.</note>.

¶ Now, when Constantine succeeded his father <note>Constantius Chlorus.</note> in the Empire, the affairs of the Church greatly increased and flourished. After Maxentius, a son of Herculius <note>Referring to Maximian Herculius.</note>, was killed and his portion of the empire fell to Constantine, those living by the Tiber and the Eridanus (which the country folk call the Po) <note>term: <term>Eridanus</term> is the ancient Greek name for the River Po in northern Italy.</note> enjoyed freedom in their faith.

<margin>Otherwise, when they fled the heat.</margin>
¶ Likewise, those who remained near the waters of Aquila, of which it is said that the ship of Argo <note>The legendary ship of Jason and the Argonauts.</note> came, and was later carried to the Tiberian Lake. For those Argonauts, when they wished to avoid a great wind, did not take the same route on their return. Instead, they sailed through the Sea of the Argonauts, which is above the Syrtes <note>The Syrtes are two large gulfs on the coast of Libya, known in antiquity for dangerous shallows.</note>, and through those same waters reached the borders of Italy. Wintering there, they held a city called Emona. When summer came, the local people helped them, and with great skill and mastery, they pulled the ship *Argo* for a distance of 400 <term>stadia</term> <note>A stadium was an ancient unit of length, roughly 185 meters; 400 stadia is approximately 74 kilometers.</note> until they reached the waters of Aquila, which joins with the Eridanus. The Eridanus, however, pours its flood into the Italian Sea. Now after the war waged at Cibalae, the Dardanians, Macedonians, and those living around the Ister <note>The Danube River.</note>, as well as those in Hellas and the people in Illyricum, all came under Emperor Constantine.

### The 7th Chapter.

<margin>Licinius’s cruelty against the Christians.</margin>
However, Licinius, who had formerly been a lover of Christian teaching, changed his will and most miserably martyred many priests in his realm, as well as others of the prominent knighthood. Because Constantine had made war upon him, he became a total enemy to the Christians; he also thought that if the Christians fared badly, Constantine would grieve on account of their religion. For the Christians, with prayer and all manner of diligence, strove to be only under the power of Constantine. Furthermore, when Licinius wished to fight Constantine again, he sought hope for his victory in soothsaying and sacrifices, and was led astray by some who promised him that he would overcome Constantine in the war. Thus he became entirely a pagan and fell into unbelief. The Greeks also say that at that time he had the priests at Miletus, of the Order of Apollo, prophesy; and when he asked advice regarding the war, the devil answered him with this verse from Homer:

> O old man, in truth the young warriors greatly exhaust you,

# Tripartite Ecclesiastical History.

<margin>Sunday, the Lord's Day.</margin>
From that day forward, the Romans have formed cohorts and legions—which are called <term>Numeros<note>Original Latin: *Numeros*. In a military context, this refers to specific units or divisions of the Roman army.</note></term>—each having their own particular tent, and for this purpose they have appointed ordained Priests and Deacons. On Sunday, the Lord's Day, which the Hebrews call the first day, and the Greeks call the day of the Sun (Sunday).

<margin>Constantine abolished the method of death by the cross.</margin>
Likewise, on that day, which comes before the seventh, he commanded everyone to cease from all business and to rest from all dealings, and to occupy themselves only with prayer. He honored Sunday for this reason: because Christ had risen from the dead on that day. He honored the other day because the Lord was crucified upon it. He held the holy Cross in special honor because through it, much good fortune had come to him, and with it, he had achieved victory over his enemies; also because through this same Cross, many signs of Divine help had been shown. Furthermore, he prohibited by law the practice of crucifying criminals, which was common among the Romans, and ordered it to cease. Only on the coinage did he allow this Cross to remain as a sign, as is well known.

<margin>Venus forbidden.</margin>
In all things, he applied himself to obeying God. It is also known that the willful, foolish waste in unchastity—which was previously permitted—was forbidden under him, as can be found in his ordinances. We also wish to note further what he instituted for the honor and welfare of religion, for such a part of history is necessary for the Christian Churches.

<margin>Punishment of unmarried persons.</margin>
Among the Romans, there had long been a law that whoever had not married by the age of twenty-five should be deprived of the privileges of married people, and also could in no way benefit from a testament <note>A "testament" here refers to a last will and testament regarding inheritance.</note>, even if they were close friends or heirs; and those who had no children lost half of their goods. The ancients allowed these institutions to arise because they desired the city of Rome to become populous and rich in people, and to make all lands subject to it; for they had also lost many soldiers in the civil wars before these institutions were made.

When the Emperor saw that those who desired to be chaste and without children for God's sake were being mistreated by this, he considered it a foolish notion to believe that the human race is increased by human effort or will, since human nature increases or decreases through Divine distribution.

Therefore, he gave a command to all peo-

<column-break/>

<margin>Unmarried people may make testaments.</margin>
-ples that those who had neither wife nor child should have equal privileges and freedoms; both men and women should enjoy this freedom. He also ordained that those who lived in chastity and in the state of virginity had the power—whether they were men or women—to make their testaments, and this was against no law. He judged everyone worthy of all good who desired to please God and to serve the <term>true Philosophy<note>In early Christian writings, "philosophy" often referred to the ascetic or monastic life of devotion to God.</note></term>. For this reason, the Romans also recognized that the young women named <term>Vestals<note>Original: *Vestalis*. The Vestal Virgins were priestesses of Vesta in Roman religion who took vows of chastity; Constantine uses their existing legal exemptions as a precedent for Christian celibates.</note></term> could make testaments at age twenty-five, as could those who were sixty years old.

<margin>He permitted appeals to the bishops.</margin>
This pious Emperor possessed such great judgment and understanding in divine matters that he also willed that wherever imperfect sentences were given in court, one could appeal to the Bishops. If anyone wished to set aside civil law or felt burdened by it, the Emperor regarded the Bishop's sentence as so powerful and excellent that it was to be accepted by everyone just as if the Emperor himself had spoken it. He also willed that whatever the Bishops ordained or decided in Synods <note>A Synod is a council or assembly of church officials convened to decide on matters of doctrine or administration.</note> should be kept unchangeable. And this was also not omitted: he instituted for the common good that those who were <term>manumitted<note>Manumission is the formal act of freeing a slave.</note></term> and set free in the church—due to the subtlety of the law regarding unwilling owners who suffered some unfair burden in the pursuit of the better freedom called <term>Roman Citizenship<note>Original: *Civitatum Roman* (Roman Citizenship). <margin>Freedom is given under the testimony of the Priest.</margin>

## ¶ Regarding Spiridion the Bishop.

### The 1st Chapter.

<margin>Spiridion</margin>

**C** Spiridion was a man of the countryside who had a wife and children, yet he was not lacking in divine matters. It is said that at one time, wicked men came to his sheepfold, and when these thieves intended to steal from him, they were suddenly bound fast without anyone touching them. When day broke and Spiridion came to the sheep, he found these men thus bound; he released them from their invisible bonds, rebuking them and saying: "Brothers, if it suited you to take what you wanted, why did you prefer to steal it and thus spend the night so miserably?" Yet, taking pity on them, he instructed them toward better things, saying: "Go hence, and take this ram with you, for you have labored in your watch, and it is right that you leave my sheep without complaint." This is a deed at which everyone might rightly marvel.

**D** No less wonderful is what happened with his daughter Irene (a daughter so named), to whom a good friend had given something for safekeeping. She took it and buried it in the earth, where she thought it would be kept secure. It then happened that this daughter died without telling or confessing this to her father. **E** After some time, the man who had given these things to the daughter for safekeeping came and asked for them back. Spiridion did not know what he was asking for and searched the entire house; having found nothing, the man departed and Spiridion went out of the house, lamenting so terribly that he nearly died of grief. **F** Spiridion, seeing what had happened, ran quickly to the grave and called the daughter by her name; she, answering him, was asked where she had laid those things. When she made it known to him, he returned and found the items exactly as the girl had indicated, and he gave the man back what he desired.

<column-break/>

<margin>Spiridion’s custom regarding the distribution to the poor.</margin>

**G** Since I have come to this topic, it is not unfitting that I add this here as well. This Spiridion had a custom of sharing a portion of his harvested crops with the poor, while setting another portion aside to give to those who wished to borrow from him. However, he did not give it out himself, nor did he receive the returns himself; instead, he placed it in a bed-chamber. To those who desired something, he pointed them to that room so they might take as much as they needed, and afterward bring back as much as they had taken.

**H** Once, one of those who had borrowed came back to return what he had received. Spiridion, according to his custom, told him to put the borrowed goods back into the little chamber. But this man, through dishonesty, kept the goods for himself, thinking that Spiridion would not know of it. He did not give back what he owed, but took what he owed as if he had returned it, and went his way.

**I** But this could not remain hidden for long. After a certain time, this man returned again, wishing to borrow from Spiridion, who sent him to the granary so that he might measure out as much as he needed. Finding the place empty and testifying to this as an eyewitness, he told Spiridion, who said to him: **K** "O man, it is a wonder what you say. In what way do you think the granary could lack the most necessary things? Consider within yourself whether you have perhaps not returned what you borrowed, which should have been paid first. If that were not the case, you would undoubtedly not be deprived of what you lack; go back there again, and you shall find it." **L** Thus the man was caught and confessed before him that he had sinned. It is worthy that we admire the purity of this holy man and preserve it within the <term>Ecclesiastical Order<note>Refers to the structured life and traditions of the Church.</note></term>.
