->Concerning the lives of the ancient Monks, and what moved them to become Monks.<-

### The 11th Chapter.

<note>A woodcut illustration depicts a bearded man in robes (a saint or prophet) sitting at a desk and writing or reading in an open book. Behind him is a landscape view through an opening. Below this image is a decorative historiated initial 'O' depicting a seated figure.</note>

<margin>The Monks, that is, the Christian Philosophy.</margin>
About this time many pious Monks arose, who led a disciplined, righteous, and godly life, waiting for the revelation of the children of God.

<margin>Philo, a Hebrew.</margin>
It is said that Elijah the Prophet and John the Baptist were the beginners of such a Philosophy <note>Early church historians often used the term "Philosophy" to describe the ascetic and contemplative life of monks.</note>. Thus Philo the Jew writes how, in former times, the most prominent of the Jews gathered themselves together by a sea called Maria <note>Referring to Lake Mareotis in Egypt.</note>, in a valley, and there they "philosophized": their houses, their food, and their conduct were like that of the Egyptian Monks. And all those who devoted themselves to this Philosophy departed from all their possessions, dwelt within no walls, but lived in the fields, gardens, and wildernesses.

<column-break/>

Their dwellings were called *Semnia* <note>From the Greek 'semneion,' meaning a sanctuary or a private room for prayer.</note>, that is, minsters or cloisters, in which they led a completely honorable and godly life, praising God with Psalms and songs of praise. Before the setting of the sun, they ate no food. Wine and anything containing blood they did not have. Their food was bread, salt, and hyssop; their drink was water. Women and aged virgins lived among them out of love for Philosophy, who also
<margin>The cause of this way of life.</margin>
voluntarily abstained from marriage. Some believe that the cause of this way of life arose because of the persecutions, when people were driven away for their faith; while they fled into the mountains and valleys, they adopted this way of living wherever they went. Thus it is clear that Anthony, who was the greatest and most prominent Monk in Egypt, lived in this manner. The Emperor Constantine received him as a friend, writing to him and requesting an answer from him.

**E** This man was born in Egypt, in a famous place called Heraclea, and while he was still a child, he became an orphan. He shared his paternal inheritance with the poor and was brought up by pious men, whose virtues he followed, saying: "A pious life is nourished by habit, though it is somewhat difficult at first." He lived in great abstinence; his food was bread and salt, his drink water, and the time of his meal was the setting of the sun. Often he remained for two days without eating, diligent in vigils and prayers. He did not anoint or wash himself, saying that by doing so one brought the body into a soft weakness. He could not read, nor did he value it, holding a pious mind to be more noble than the art of letters, although he rightly praised the inventor of those arts. He was entirely mild, chaste, and strong, pleasant to those who spoke with him, and that without any sadness. "True happiness," he said, "is to honor God and observe His commandments." He was very diligent in
<margin>Monks shall wander or go about in the cities.</margin>
comforting the distressed. For this reason, he often came into the cities, yet having performed his business, he removed himself from there; for he said that just as a fish perishes if it is not in the water, so the honor of the Monks was laid waste if they were in the cities. Many pious and famous men were his disciples and listeners in Egypt, Libya, Palestine, Syria, and Arabia, who, like their teacher, instructed and taught others.

## How Satan brought schism and 
## discord into the Church 
## through Arius.

### The 12th Chapter.

And although the churches everywhere were then in good standing, Satan could not endure this; for the delusion of the heathens having been uncovered, and men no longer worshipping the creatures but rather the Creator and Maker, he did not wish to fight openly against our God and Savior. <note>original: "Heplant," an archaic Dutch term for Savior or Healer.</note> But through some who held only the title and name, who boasted of being Christians, yet were corrupted into servitude by the love of temporal honor and vain glory, he used these as instruments through which he sought to return many to the old error. Not by commanding them to worship creatures again, but by teaching that the Creator and Maker of the world and the creature were equal, and to be compared with one another. Where these things had their beginning, and what wicked man sowed these weeds therein, I shall relate.

<margin>Alexandria</margin>
Alexandria is a great city, and very populous, which is not only in Egypt but also surrounds Egypt, and is a capital city of the Thebans and Libyans.

But Alexander, following the Divine Scripture, said: That the Father and Son were one, and of one substance and nature; yet Arius fought against this word and said: That the Son was a created being and a creature. This he said not only in the churches, but in other places and gatherings which he also held in houses, and he seduced to his error all whom he could.

## How Alexander of Alexandria wrote to the Bishops and warned them of the error of Arius.

### The 13th Chapter.

->To the beloved and dear fellow-servants of the Christian Churches, Alexander wishes salvation in the LORD.<-

Since the Christian community is one common body, and it is commanded in Holy Scripture that the bonds and unity of peace should be maintained, we have found it necessary to write to you regarding what has occurred here, so that we, as members of one body, may share joy and sorrow with one another. Now, there have arisen in our province wicked men, rebellious against Christ, who teach such an apostasy as one might well imagine precedes the Antichrist.

<margin>Eusebius of Nicomedia.</margin>
And although I intended to remain silent about this, so that this evil might fade away among the apostates and not be heard of in other places to the offense of the simple-minded, yet Eusebius of Nicomedia (who believes that the affairs of the Church rest upon him alone: since he left the city of Berytus <note>Ancient Beirut.</note> and placed himself in the Church of Nicomedia, and no punishment followed) has sought to champion these apostates. He has justified this opinion in his writings, so that some ignorant people might see this destructive and Christ-opposing heresy.

Therefore, necessity compels us to record these things, so that you may know who these defectors are, and know to guard yourselves against their cunning words. Therefore, even if Eusebius should write to Your Graces, you should not receive it; for his old cunning, which he has long kept hidden, now wishes to bring this forth through these men. While he acts as if he writes on their behalf, he proves by his deeds that he takes this up for his own sake.

The apostates then are these: Arius, Achilles, Aitales, Corponus, another Arius, Sarmatus, Euzoius, Lucius, Julianus, Menas, Helladius, Caius, and with these Secundus and Thenas, who were at times called Bishops. And this is the sum

<column-break/>

<margin>Arius's error.</margin>
of their error: that God was not always a Father. That the Word of God did not always exist, and that God was not a Father; that God's Word was created out of things that did not exist. For the essential God did not have that essence which was not, so that it was made essential out of nothing. Therefore, he was at some time what he was not, for the Son is a creature and made; he is also not like the Father in essence, nor is he truly God, nor truly His own Wisdom, nor is the Father's Word true by nature, but is a creature and made. Through an incorrect usage he is called the "Word" and "Wisdom," having been made by the Wisdom and Word that is in God, by which God made all things and the Son. In this, he is also by nature changeable, just as all rational creatures are, to whom that Word is foreign, being separated and alienated from the substance of the Father. And the Son is invisible to the Father, for the Son does not entirely and perfectly know the Father, and thus he cannot see Him perfectly; for the Son does not perfectly know his own substance and essence as it is. Rather, he was made for our sake, so that God might create us as if through an instrument. He would not have existed if God had not wished to create us. Therefore, some have asked whether God's Word can change, as the Devil turned himself away? And they have not been afraid to say: "Yes, it can change," as if that Word were of a changeable nature. For they say, "he is created, therefore he is changeable." This is what they say.

<margin>Synod of 100 Bishops.</margin>
Since Arius and his company pour this out so shamelessly and persist in it, our Bishops of Egypt and Libya, one hundred in number, have come together and have excommunicated them. Those who now gather with Eusebius to mingle lies with truth shall accomplish nothing, for the truth shall prevail. For light has no fellowship with darkness, nor Christ with Belial; for who can hear such words without fear, or without stopping his ears so that his hearing is not deafened by hearing words that defile him?

<margin>John 1.</margin>

murderers of souls. We shall also not share a greeting with them, so that we may not be regarded as if we had fellowship with them, just as the blessed John says: *Greet the brothers who*
<margin>2 John 1.</margin>
*are with you; the brothers who are with us greet your loves.*

<margin>L</margin>
# Theodoretus.

<margin>M</margin>
Yet not only this letter, but also that which he has written to Alexander, the Bishop of Constantinople, we wish to place here; also the letter of Arius, and not omit the others either, and what serves the History and may be beneficial to the Truth, so that no one may think that I write any things which I have devised from myself. 
Now, the Bishop of Alexandria writes thus to Alexander, Bishop of Constantinople.

Tripartite Ecclesiastical History.

# ¶ The Letter which Alexander of Alexandria wrote to Alexander of Constantinople.

## The 14th Chapter.

### ¶ To the beloved and like-minded Brother Alexander, Alexander wishes salvation in the Lord.

The desire and power of wicked men, and the pursuit of ambition, are always accustomed to attack the truth, using various means by which ecclesiastical godliness <note>original: "Godsalicheyt" — refers to the proper practice and piety of the Church.</note> is resisted. Some malicious people, driven by the Devil’s prompting, have gone so far as to trample even the fear of God’s judgment under their feet.

Therefore, necessity has compelled me to write to your patient obedience, so that you may guard yourself against such people. Let none of them slip into your Church, either by themselves or through others; for they are rogues and strange people who, with all sorts of feigned and false letters, defile and confuse the simplicity of the faith.

<margin>Arius, Achilles, and Coluthus exceeded in wickedness.</margin>
Just as Arius and Achilles recently conspired together and followed the pride of Coluthus, they have even exceeded him in wickedness. For these men have refused to be subject to the Church; instead, they have made for themselves dens of murderers <note>original: "moortcuylen" — likely an allusion to the "den of thieves" in the Gospels, implying a place of spiritual corruption.</note> in which they gather day and night to act against Christ and us. In a Jewish and Heathen manner, they speak of Christ, saying: That He is not God. They confirm the opinions of the Jews and the godless Heathen regarding Christ, seeking their own glory in this, as is their custom. They also occupy themselves daily with how they might mock and ridicule us, in order to bring riot and persecution upon us.

<margin>Unrest in the church through women.</margin>
They incite literal strife and quarreling through the instigation of certain shameless women whom they lead astray, to speak evil against the whole of Christendom, while their young women run about everywhere through the villages and market towns. Beyond this, they also dare to tear the seamless robe of Christ <note>A reference to John 19:23-24; the "seamless robe" was a traditional symbol for the unity of the Church that heretics were accused of "tearing."</note>—which even the soldiers would not divide—among themselves.

Therefore, although their shameful lives and unholy purpose were long hidden and only lately became known, we have now, by the general decree of the Church—which holds Christ to be God—

<column-break/>

driven and banished them. Yet they have still presumed to run here and there, plotting against us, and presenting themselves to our people—who are peaceful ministers—as if they were concerned for peace and unity. That this is the truth is evident, for some of them, drawn away by flattering words, have been thrust into final ruin; they have requested public and unquestioned letters from these ministers, so that they might read them to the deceived persons and give them cause to persist in their blasphemy, as if they were right in this and were of one mind with the Bishops. However, they do not confess the wicked deeds they have learned and committed among us, nor the things for which they were banished by us; but they pass over them in silence or mix them with certain feigned causes. They sneak about and promote <note>original: "bootsen" — to fashion, model, or push forward a specific idea.</note> their harmful teaching with haughty words, to make it somewhat resemble the truth, so that they might better lead the ignorant astray. They do not cease to speak ill of everyone in our Religion; from this, it has come to pass that some have signed their letters and been received into the Church, and this with great difficulty. It should be considered that the Church ministers have acted presumptuously in this, since no Apostolic Rule allows it, and they thus pour out their Devilish poison or venom against Christ.

Therefore, O most beloved, I have wished to warn your Love <note>A formal address to a fellow bishop.</note> with all diligence and faithfulness of such a one of your unbelief: for they say, "He was once something when He was not the Son of God," and "He was made afterward, who previously was not such," and "He once became something, just as happens with all men." But they say: "God made all things out of that which was nothing," wishing thus to confuse and mix the Son of God among all rational and irrational creatures.

<margin>A divine saying concerning Christ.</margin>
With these words, they further suggest that He has a nature that is changeable, and that He is capable of good and evil, since it is said that He is of those things which formerly were not a Son. Thus they do violence to and lay waste to God’s holy Scriptures, which testify that He is eternal. In these Scriptures, the unchangeability of the Word, and the wisdom, and the divinity—which is Christ—is made clearly manifest.

Therefore, we might say: these impure ones also become children of God, just as He is. For it is written: *I have brought forth and exalted children, but...* <note>Referring to Isaiah 1:2.</note>

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence with the catchword "maer" (but), which will be the first word of the next page.</meta>

For they say that Christ by nature had nothing more excellent than other children, because he is not the natural Son of God, nor does he have divine properties like God. Rather, they say that God—to him who was of a changeable nature—on account of his discipline, **B** steadfastness, and virtue, and not having changed into evil, he was chosen. **C** And when Paul and Peter had come so far, they could not differ from this sonship <note>original: "kintschept" — referring here to the state of being a child or son, specifically the Arian view of Christ's adopted status.</note>.

> You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.

Since nothing was made of God's Son from that which was not made, there was also nothing that he was not. John shall be sufficient to instruct us in this, who writes of him, <margin>John 1:18.</margin> **D** the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father. For God provided this, that John would note how the Father and Son are undivided; and therefore he named the Father and the Son, who is in the bosom of the Father. Because regarding that Word **E** of God, and the things that are made, since they were not, they are not counted at all with him; but he says: All things were made through that Word, and without <margin>John 1.</margin> it, nothing was made. So John has noted his own being where he says: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. All things were made through the same, and without the same was nothing made **F** [of] that which is made.

<margin>The Word is the Creator of all creatures.</margin>
If then all things were made through it, how was he at some time not? He who granted and gave to all creatures that they might exist? And there is no reason or cause to note that he who makes a thing must be of a like nature with that which he makes.

<column-break/>

**G** If the Son of God was in the beginning, and all that is created was made through him, then he did not create it out of that which was not? This, then, where that is, has a great distinction from the things that are made out of nothing. Yet between the Father and the Holy Spirit, one cannot grasp such a coarse distinction with any thoughts. Thus the world is created out of that which was not, and has, as it were, a new birth from the Father through the Son. **H** This is why the worthy John exalts the divinity of the Word above all creatures, and did not wish to call the eternal birth of the Son of God from the Father a "created" thing, nor to call the unbegotten one a Maker of elemental letters <note>original: "Elementischen letteren" — likely referring to the basic components or elements of the physical world, which Alexander distinguishes from the divine nature.</note>. For there is one unbegotten: namely, the Father.

But since this high dealing regarding the unspeakable being of the Son of God surpasses not only the Evangelists, but **I** also the understanding of the Angels, I consider that all those who strive for godliness should not undertake to fathom this. Because it is said: Strive not after that which is too high for you, and that which is too heavy for you, do not seek to fathom it. For this and other things more are hidden from human understanding. Just as Paul also says: Things which no <margin>Isaiah 64:4. 1 Cor. 2:9.</margin> eyes have seen, nor ears heard, nor have entered into the heart of any man, which God has prepared for those who love him. Yea, also the stars (says God **K** to Abraham) you cannot count, nor the sand of the sea, and the drops of rain—who shall count them? Who then is he who dares to undertake to fathom the being of the Divine Word, unless he be out of his mind? Therefore the voice of the Prophet <margin>Isaiah 53.</margin> says: Who will declare his generation? For Christ our Savior himself has taken such a burden from the most prominent men **L** of this world, and given it to be known that this mystery belongs to the Father alone. Therefore he says: No one knows the Son <margin>Matthew 11:27.</margin> but the Father alone, and no one knows the Father but the Son.

I consider them wise who understand how senseless a thing it is for those who think that the **M** Son is made from things which were not, since that which is so made has a temporal beginning. So it is also a foolish thing, and full of sin, to wish to say that he who is the <margin>Coloss. 1. For according to this opinion, the wisdom of God proceeds, which has created it all: this distinction and this span <note>original: "spatium"</note> in which they say that the Son was not made by the Father; and thus the...

# Tripartite Ecclesiastical History

<margin>A</margin>
It is right to heed this saying: "our knowledge is partial," <note>original: "onse bekennen is stuckwerck"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 13:9, meaning human understanding is incomplete</note> whether they cease or not, it is manifest that they shall be deceived in their own hope. <margin>1 Cor. 13.</margin>
<margin>The dignity of God the Father.</margin>

Of Him we may well say, He was before all time, before the world; and we wish to speak of His Divinity thus: He is the image of the Father, and in all things like the Father, yet that which is unbegotten is properly to be attributed to the Father alone.

<margin>B</margin>
Since our Savior Himself says: "The Father is greater than I." <note>John 14:28, though the margin notes John 10. <margin>The Church is invincible.</margin>

He who became the <term>firstfruits</term> <note>The first of the harvest; here meaning the first to be resurrected into eternal life</note> is our Lord Jesus Christ, born a true Man from Mary the Virgin. Who in the latter time, for the destruction of sin, was crucified and died for the salvation of mankind; but in His Divinity, He did not die. He rose from the dead. He ascended into Heaven and sits at the right hand of the Majesty of God.

<margin>C</margin>
This I have wished to record in brief, because I know that these things were not hidden from your diligence. These things we teach and preach: these are the teachings and ordinances of the Apostolic Church, for which we would die and fear nothing at all—all those who attempt to oppress us—and even if they wished to compel us with blows, yet we shall not fall away from our hope.

<margin>1 Cor. 12:16, 1 Tim. 1:10, Gal. 1:8.</margin>
<margin>S</margin>

For this reason we are persecuted / because we have said: The Son has his beginning / yet God is without beginning. And because we have said / the Son is out of that which was not / just as we have previously said / that the Son is no part of God. Therefore we are persecuted / the rest you know well. Therefore, he wrote to Arius and Alexander, accusing and rebuking them, because they could well have kept these questions hidden, whereas now they had come into the open and were stirred up with great agitation and strife; and they had arranged no counsel therein, whereas they should have stilled the matter when it first arose.

<margin>L</margin>

However, it did not seem unfitting to me to set a portion of his letters here. For the entire letter is found in the books of Eusebius, in the *Life of Constantine*.

<meta>This page continues from Folio 239, where Emperor Constantine the Great has begun his intervention in the dispute between Bishop Alexander of Alexandria and the presbyter Arius. # Tripartite Ecclesiastical History

<margin>A</margin> You (Arius), you who ought not to have contemplated such a beginning—or rather, should have kept your thoughts silent—have imprudently cast this out first and brought it into the open, you who instead should have established such things with all diligence. Therefore, this dispute has arisen among you, and thus the high Mysteries have been brought into contempt, and the holy, pious people have divided themselves into two camps, and the bodily fellowship of one body has been severed. <note>The "bodily fellowship" refers to the organic unity of the Church as the 'Body of Christ.'</note>

<margin>B</margin> Therefore, you shall both be admonished on both sides to now be willing to apply yourselves with diligence, and to rightfully admonish your fellow servants to be obedient.

<margin>Curious questions</margin> For to bring forth many questions about those things, or to wish to answer the one questioned in such a manner, we consider to be nothing other than a useless waste of time. <note>In this context, "curious questions" refers to 'curiositas'—the prohibited or dangerous prying into the hidden nature of God that exceeds human understanding.</note>

<margin>C</margin> And although those things might happen to exercise the natural intellect, we should nonetheless keep them locked within our understanding and not speak of them openly before every man, nor unwisely bring them to everyone's ears. For it undoubtedly requires a high understanding for one who wishes to fully investigate these things, or who could explain them truly (as is proper). And even if someone were capable of that which is difficult, which part of the common people could be advised therein? Or who would want to undertake such a subtle question without great peril to himself?

<margin>D</margin> Therefore, such talk is to be fled, lest by chance a coarse understanding should be stunned by such a high question, and because of its weak nature and the sluggishness of its understanding, not grasp at all that which is proposed; or because of the ambiguity of the meaning, the listeners be found imperfect in achieving a perfect understanding of the question, and fall into blasphemy or the division of the people; or that one must forgive both sides because of these questions and answers.

<margin>E</margin> Therefore, since you have a sign of fellowship, you shall—according to the intent of the Most High God—not be embittered against one or the other, nor exalt yourselves, but be of like mind.

<margin>The sign of fellowship</margin> For if you dispute among yourselves over small things, what else do you do but tear and divide the people of God—whom you should rightly rule with your prayer and understanding—more than is believable? I shall admonish you with a small example.

<margin>F</margin> The Philosophers, because they are at one in the main matters of their trade, even if they cannot agree in some part of their sentence, and although they differ in discipline, yet they all hold themselves together as one Body. How much more should you

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin> people, as servants of the Most High God, agree in Divine matters? Think then for a moment, as those of high understanding, whether it is right: that because of a dispute over a trivial, useless word, one brother shall be so inflamed against the other, and that the honorable Council should be devastated through your godless bickering? While you people dispute and bicker over such a small matter, are you not children and fools? For this does not befit wise and sensible people in the matters of God.

<margin>H</margin> Therefore, let us flee from the devil's temptation. Our great God, the Savior of all things, has let a common light shine for all through His providence; let me, a servant of God, come to work with the highest diligence, so that I may—through my addressing you, my admonition, and earnest diligence—bring you to a Synodal unity. <note>A "Synod" is a formal council of church leaders gathered to decide on points of doctrine or administration.</note>

<margin>I Constantine re-addresses a Synodal right.</margin> For as I have said, so is there one faith in you, and your understanding is directed entirely toward one single thing, and the wish for one thing with its fine parts is set forth before His will. Therefore, because the dispute has confused you, while it does not concern the entire force of the Law: you ought not to create any insurrection or division among yourselves. I do not say this because I want to force you to fall to this or that question. But let the dignity of the Council be well and fully preserved among you, and let it be kept in fellowship among you all, even if a small dispute arises among you in particular matters.

<margin>Note</margin> For we are indeed not at one in all things. Nature does not give [this]; regarding what concerns God, the Divine providence, and the faith, one will is made known, just as through Divine Providence there is one faith in you, and so one mind through that Providence in one God.

<margin>K L M N O P Q R S T V W X Y Z</margin>

<margin>Useless questions</margin> Therefore, regarding what is disputed among you from idle questions, or if you cannot agree with one another: remember that you should keep fellowship and love as the greatest good and Sacrament. And keep the truth of the faith, and the honor before G O D, and the Law of Religion unbroken in your mind.

Therefore, return together in all friendship and Love, receive your people from the heart, take one another up again as your own souls; for friendships tend to be much sweeter when one comes to unity again after a dispute. Be willing to obey me in this, so that I may be all the more certain and peaceful day and night; for it is now time that I [bring] the peoples of God...

<header>The Second Part. | The II. Book.</header>

<margin>A</margin> ...gather my servants together again, who have been so harmfully and unjustly divided by your dispute. So that you may also feel and understand the greatness of my sadness, hear: When I recently came to the city of Nicomedia, I wished to travel quickly into the East, to the lands of the Morning. <note>Nicomedia was the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire under Diocletian; the "Morning-lands" refers to the Levant and Orient.</note> As I had now come to you and was with you for a time, the <margin>B</margin> news of your dispute hindered me; therefore, open for me the way to the East through your unity, which you have closed to me through your dispute, and allow me this quickly, so that I may see you yourselves and all other peoples rejoicing, and may give thanks and praise to God the Lord for widespread peace and unity.

### ✠ Discord concerning Easter Day, for which Hosius was sent in the manner of a messenger to Egypt.

### The XXI. Chapter.

<margin>Discord over the Easter feast.</margin>
<margin>D</margin> Thus Constantine has written to Alexander and Arius, sometimes punishing them, sometimes admonishing them, taking it very poorly when he heard that some held the Easter Day feast against

<column-break/>

<margin>E</margin> the general ordinance. For until that time, people in the Eastern cities disputed one against another for that reason. Yet one part in the brotherhood, without causing a schism, held the Easter feast in the Jewish manner. <note>original: "Jodischer wijse"; this refers to the 'Quartodeciman' practice of celebrating Easter on the 14th of Nisan, regardless of which day of the week it fell upon.</note> And with this division (as was the custom), they desecrated the *Collect*, that is, the gathering of the believers. <term>Collect</term> <note>From the Latin 'collecta', referring to the formal assembly of the church for worship.</note> Therefore, so that the Church might have rest and peace on both sides, <margin>F</margin> Constantine hastens, wishing to prevent this evil in time before it eats deeper; he has thus sent a faithful man, pious in faith and life, who had been well-tested in this teaching during the preceding persecution, to those in Egypt, to pacify those who love this teaching. And to the Easterners, who were discordant concerning Easter Day.

<margin>Bishop Hosius is sent by Constantine to Egypt.</margin>
<margin>G</margin> This Hosius was a Bishop in the city of Corduba; <note>Hosius of Corduba was a veteran of the Great Persecution and became Constantine's chief ecclesiastical advisor.</note> though he was sent out for the sake of peace in the church, he achieved nothing beyond hope. And upon his return, the Emperor’s earnestness brought about that famous Council of Nicaea. <margin>H</margin> He rode there publicly with donkeys, mules, horses, and wagons; the Bishops and those who were with them were commanded to come together in the Synod with haste and without delay.

<margin>Antioch. Alexander. Rome.</margin>

Some were exceptionally gifted in understanding and reason, well-versed in the Divine Scriptures, and renowned for a life of reasonable courage. Some were proven men in both their manner of living and their learning, whose names (as I judge) are useful for me to remember and mention here.

# Sozomen

<margin>An old and pious Christian overcomes the Philosopher.</margin>
It is also said: That when one among them <note>one of the pagan philosophers</note> raised his voice with great arrogance to mock the Priests, an old, pious, and simple Christian—an unlearned man—addressed a learned Philosopher in this manner: "O Philosopher, in the Name of Jesus Christ, listen to the teaching of truth: There is one God of Heaven and earth, a creator of things visible and invisible, who made all these things by the power of His Word, and confirmed them with the glory of His Spirit." <margin>C</margin> "This Word, whom we call a Son of God," (he said) "has had mercy upon mankind, and has delivered them from all error and ruined religion; He became man and lived among men, died for them, and shall come again to judge the life of all. This is so; this we believe. Do not then labor frivolously, seeking to destroy that which we have received through faith." <margin>D</margin> "Do not seek after the 'how' of this, or how it might not be. Do you believe me? Give me an answer on this." This reasoning of the old man fell upon the Philosopher; wondering, he said: "I believe," and said to his followers that they should be simple like him. For he testified to them that he was compelled to Christianity not by chance, but by divine power.

When he wrote to the Africans, he said it was fitting that the bishops had gathered to condemn and cast out the godless doctrine devised by Arius, namely the words "From things that do not exist" <note>Original Latin: *Ex non existentibus*—a core Arian claim that the Son was created out of nothing rather than eternally begotten.</note> and also those who make the Son of God a creature and a created thing.

<margin>From things that do not exist.</margin> Likewise, [they claimed] that he was something at a time when he [previously] was not, and that he is of a changeable nature. Against this, the true Christian believers spoke openly from the word of Divine Scripture, saying that the natural Son of God, who is from God, is the only-begotten, the <margin>Proverbs 8; John 1; Hebrews 1.</margin> Word, Power, and eternal Wisdom of the Father, true God—as John and Paul say—a radiance of His glory and a mirror of His essence, being the Son of the Father.

Those who were of the sect of Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Nicomedia and his followers, who supported Arius.</note>, driven by their own stubbornness, spoke to one another, saying: "We are also from God, for there is one God from whom all things are. And also: the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new from God." They also considered the things written in the book of the Shepherd <margin>The Book of the Shepherd, which is not at hand.</margin> <note>Referring to *The Shepherd of Hermas*, a 2nd-century Christian literary work popular in the early church.</note>, believing above all things that there is one God who created, completed, and ordained everything from nothing, that they might exist.

But the other bishops saw their malice and understood their evil, false craft, and said clearly and openly: "From God" means that the Son of God is of the substance of the Father's essence. <margin>1 Corinthians 8. From God—that is, from the true essence of God.</margin> Just as creatures do not have from themselves that which they are, but rather have a beginning to their existence—for it is said of them that they are "from God"—of the Son it is believed that he alone is from the essence of the Father. For this is the property of the only-begotten and of the true Word of the Father. That was also the reason why it was spoken: "The Son was from the essence of the Father."

Now when the bishops questioned some among them who were considered Arians, asking if they said the Son of God was not a creature, but rather the only power and wisdom of the Father, an eternal image, like the Father in every way, and a true God, those who

<column-break/>

stood on the side of Eusebius, making their views known to the others, were overcome and said: "Yes, these things apply <margin>Genesis 1:26 and 5:5; 1 Corinthians 11:7.</margin> to us as well. For of us it is also said, and always said: That we are the image and glory of God. And it is said: We who live there, so there are also many powers, for all the powers of God marched out of Egypt. Also, the locusts and beetles <margin>Exodus 12; Deuteronomy 28; Leviticus 26; Psalm 16.</margin> <note>The Arians argued that if the Son is called a "power" of God, it does not prove divinity, as even the plague-insects in the Old Testament were called God's "great army" or "powers."</note> are called God's great host. And further: The Lord of Hosts is with us. Therefore, we are also God’s own, and we have not said this simply, but he also calls us brothers. If they say the Son is the true God, that does not grieve us; for since he is made, he is truly so." This is the corrupt mind of the Arians.

When the bishops saw their deception, they also concluded and proved from Holy <margin>Hebrews 1; John 7. Words / Radiance / Fountain. Psalm 36; John 10.</margin> Scripture that the words Word, Radiance, Fountain, Flood, and Figure belong to that substance. And this: "In your light shall we see light," and "I and the Father are [one]." They also described more clearly and briefly how the Son is of one essence <term>Homoousios</term> <note>Greek: *Homoousios*, meaning "of the same substance" or "consubstantial." This was the pivotal word used to exclude Arian interpretation.</note> with the Father. And as said before, all these things have their proper meaning.

Thus it appears sufficiently that their murmuring—that these words were not brought forth with the authority of Holy Scripture—is entirely groundless. Rather, theirs is a godless doctrine based on what is *not* written, driving at what is found nowhere: <margin>The Articles claimed that the word *Homoousion*—that is, of the same essence—is nowhere to be found in Scripture.</margin> "From things that do not exist," and "There was a time when he was not." Because of these and other errors, they were condemned by the right-thinking for written reasons. Thus, the bishops did not invent these words of themselves, but the ancient Fathers who were before them prescribed these testimonies for them.

For the ancient priests who lived before them, nearly 130 in number <note>Likely referring to a Council in Rome under Pope Dionysius around 262 AD, where the term was used against Sabellianism and Subordinationism.</note>, had all accused those in our great city of Rome who said that the Son is a creature or was made, and [upheld he was] of one essence with the Father. And Eusebius, the Bishop of Caesarea, who first protected the sect of the Arians, knew this.

Finally, it was signed at the Council of Nicaea. He [Eusebius] also wrote to his <margin>Arians sign only with the hand, but have something else in mind.</margin> citizens and confirmed it for them, because he was the oldest, most prominent, and most learned bishop, and was known as a writer, saying: That the name *Homoousios*—of one essence—and the Godhead of the Father and the Son...

<margin>318 men in the Council of Nicaea.</margin>

<margin>F</margin>

<margin>H</margin>

<margin>I The word Homousion, Consubstantialis.</margin>

<margin>K Concerning the substance.</margin>
regarding the substance and essence of the Father, that it signifies He was from the Father, yet not as a part of the Father.

<margin>L</margin>

Therefore we also feel with heart and mind, nor do we refute with voice, that word *Consubstantialis*: For we look toward peace, and yet have not wished to deviate from the right understanding.

<margin>M</margin>
According to this rule, *begotten and not made* <note>original: "natum & non factum." <margin>A</margin> Therefore, we also do not say that he is a creature, he of whom it is said that all things were made through him. <margin>B</margin> And let this be enough said regarding the exposition of the faith, to which we have all consented and agreed, not without great deliberation. We have believed that whatever is not included in this confession shall be regarded as an *Anathema* <note>A formal curse or decree of excommunication against a specific doctrine or person.</note>, just as the counter-argument clearly shows. Namely, that one shall not use certain words that do not appear in the Scriptures—from which all the destruction and disorder in the Church has come. For no Scripture inspired by God says: "From things that did not exist" <note>original: "Ex non existentibus"</note>, or "There was once a time when he was not" <note>original: "fuit aliquando, quando non fuit"</note>, and more such irrational words that they brought forth, which are sorrowful to say and to teach. <margin>C</margin> This, most beloved, is what we had to write and share with you out of necessity: the judgment of our inquiry and to show you our concurring mind, and this not without sensible causes. For some writings have moved us. Therefore, we have weighed the indubitable sense of the Scripture, just as they agree, and as the confession stands in the exposition of the faith.

# Sozomenus.

¶ Regarding Priestly Marriage, and how Paphnutius stands against the commands of chastity.

->The 14th Chapter.<-

<margin>Institutions of the Council of Nicaea.</margin>
The Synod, wishing to reform the lives of men and those who dwell in the Church, made Laws which we call Canons. And it pleased some that these be introduced: that Bishops, Priests, Deacons, and Subdeacons should not sleep with their wives whom they had taken before their ordination. Thereupon Paphnutius <note>A famous Egyptian monk and bishop who had been mutilated during the persecutions; he was highly respected as a "confessor" of the faith.</note>, a confessor, stood up in the midst and spoke against this, contradicting it, and declared that marriage was an honorable state. He said that it is also a form of chastity for a man and wife to live well in marriage, and he advised the Council that they should not institute such laws. He said these were heavy burdens which might give cause for fornication, either to the men or their wives. Paphnutius spoke this even though he was himself unmarried; he expressed it thus, and the Synod praised his judgment. They did not issue a command in this matter, but instead left it to each person's will, so that no one would be forced into it.

¶ On Constantinople and Helenopolis; on the three Crosses, the Title, and their discovery.

### Chapter 6.

<margin>Constantine raises up temples.</margin>
After the Council was held, the Emperor lived in great joy, and having celebrated the *Vicennalia* <note>The Vicennalia was a grand festival marking the twentieth anniversary of a Roman Emperor's reign.</note>, he set his mind to building churches; and this in all cities, including Constantinople, which takes its name from Constantine.

## Sozomenus.

<margin>He intends to build a city.</margin>
¶ Because he was successful in all things, he desired a city of his own. Coming from the field, he encamped before the city of Ilium <note>Ilium is the classical name for the ancient city of Troy.</note>, by the Hellespont, at the grave of Ajax, where the Greeks fought against the Trojans and had their camp. There he marked out the place to build the city. He constructed the gates, which from that time until now are seen by sailors; and while he was doing this,

<column-break/>

God appeared to him in a night and warned him to seek another place, and showed him Byzantium in the land of Thrace, and commanded him to dwell there. This city was first called Byzantium, but was enlarged by Constantine and enclosed with wide walls. Being adorned with many kinds of buildings, equal to the Imperial City, he named it Constantinople and gave a law that it should be called the "Second Rome," as is well known. This was carved into a marble stone, and nearby Constantine was depicted in the form of a supreme warlord.
<margin>Constantinople (New Rome)</margin>

<margin>Irene. Church of the Apostles.</margin>
And in this city he also built two churches, one of which he named Irene <note>Meaning "Holy Peace" (Hagia Irene).</note> and the other the Church of the Apostles. And as I have said, he not only increased the Christian teaching but also forbade the temples of the heathens, taking their statues from them and decorating them finely, placing them openly throughout the city of Constantinople. He even gave the tripod table of the Delphic Apollo <note>A famous bronze sacrificial tripod originally from the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, known as the Serpent Column.</note> to the circus as a public spectacle; and when the heathens saw this, they took it very badly.
<margin>He destroys paganism.</margin>

<margin>Gladiatorial combat.</margin>
<margin>The Nilometer.</margin>
Thereafter, the Emperor, showing great concern for the Christians, cast out the superstitions of the pagans. Likewise, he abolished the combat known as *Monomachia* <note>original: "Monomachia" — a fight to the death between two men, or gladiatorial combat.</note> and ordered that his own image be placed in the Temple. # Sozomen

<margin>Praise for the city of Constantinople due to its religion.</margin>
In every way, his intention was to make Constantinople the equal of Rome, and he did not fail, for Constantinople grew greater in people and wealth. This I believe happened for the sake of the love of God, which the city showed toward the poor and needy inhabitants, providing help in their necessity. The Christian faith increased so much in Constantinople that many Jews and pagans who were citizens there were converted to the Christian faith. In this city, neither altar nor pagan temple nor sacrifice was offered until the time of Julian <note>Emperor Julian the Apostate, who briefly attempted to restore paganism.</note>, whose reign did not last long but soon passed away. This newly-built city of Christ was named by Constantine after himself, and he adorned it with many great and beautiful churches. God assisted the Emperor’s wishes and desires, revealing to him through many visions that the churches built there were holy and wholesome.

<margin>Helena encloses her Son in nails. Helmet.</margin>
$\P$ Thus the Emperor’s mother, having obtained what she desired, had the nails with which the hands of Christ were pierced fashioned into a helmet for the Emperor’s son and sent it to him. She did this out of care for her son’s head, so that he might be protected from any projectiles or blows in battle.

<margin>Bridle.</margin>
The other nails she had fashioned into the horse’s bridle, thus showing her care for the Emperor. Herewith the old prophecy was fulfilled, which Zechariah wrote of in former times, saying: "The harness of the horses shall be holy to the Almighty Lord." She also ordered a portion of the Holy Cross to be set aside as part of the Imperial Regalia.

# Socrates.

<margin>Constantine placed a part of the cross in his statue.</margin>
$\P$ Constantine, having taken this portion, had it encased in silver. Believing that the city where this piece was kept would be protected, he had it (so it is said) built into his own statue, which stands in the Forum of Constantine upon a column called Porphyry <note>original: "Prophiricam"; referring to the monumental red stone column that still stands in Istanbul today.</note>, and it is preserved there with great devotion.

# Theodoretus.

<margin>He hands over a portion to the Bishop of Jerusalem.</margin>
$\P$ The other portion he had encased in silver and delivered to the Bishop of the city of Jerusalem. Having gathered all the skilled craftsmen, he built very costly and beautiful churches there. ->Socrates.<-

After this, the Emperor, carrying great concern for the Christians, cast out the superstitions of the Heathens. Likewise, he abolished the struggle where two fight for their lives, called <term>Monomachia<note>From the Greek for "single combat"; referring specifically to gladiatorial combat.</note></term>, and commanded that his image be placed in the Temple. He also commanded that the measure called the <term>Nilometrion<note>A "Nile-measure" used to track the height of the Nile's annual flood, which was crucial for Egyptian agriculture.</note></term>, with which the waters of the Nile were measured, should henceforth not be carried every year into the pagan Temple of Serapis, but into the Church.

->Sozomenus.<-

<margin>Praise of the city of religion, Constantinople.</margin>
$\P$ In every way, his intention was to make Constantinople equal to Rome; and he did not fail, for Constantinople grew greater in people and wealth. This I believe happened for the sake of the love of God, which the city showed toward the poor and needy inhabitants, providing help in times of necessity. And the Christian faith increased in Constantinople to such an extent that many Jews and Heathens who were residents in the city were converted to the Christian faith. In this city, neither Altar nor Heathen Church nor sacrifice was offered until the time of Julian <note>referring to Julian the Apostate, the last pagan emperor.</note>, which also did not last long, but perished. This newly built city of Christ, Constantine named with his own name and adorned with many great and beautiful churches. God helped the Emperor’s wishes and desires, and revealed to him through many visions that the churches built there were holy and wholesome.

The Second Part. The Second Book.

<margin>Appearance of the Archangel of God, Michael.</margin>
A place then received the name it still holds, because the Archangel of God, Michael, openly appeared and was seen there, which I also confirm as true. And that it is so, is made manifest through Divine power to many who have experienced this: some who fell into grave matters and insurmountable terrors, and others into unknown great sicknesses, who, by praying to God, were delivered.

<margin>Aquilinius, a learned man mentioned by Sozomenus.</margin>
B In particular, things occurred and were permitted to happen as miracles, which would be too long to recount here. Yet, concerning what befell our known companion Aquilinius in worldly affairs and trade—since I have heard part of it from him myself and part was proclaimed—I must, out of necessity, record it. When a very high fever, caused by bad humors <note>original: "quade vochtichept"; referring to the ancient medical theory that health was governed by four bodily fluids or "humors."</note>, had seized him, the physicians gave him a hot drink, which he threw back up; immediately thereafter, bile <note>original: "Cholera"; in this context, it refers to yellow bile, one of the four humors, rather than the modern bacterial disease.</note> spread from it over his entire face, so that it took on the same color. Therefore, whatever he later ate or drank, he vomited back up. After he had suffered this for a long time, so that food gave him no nourishment and medicines were too weak for him, and as death drew near, he commanded his kin to carry him to that same place <note>the Michaelion shrine</note>; for he intended either to die there or to be delivered from the sickness. As he lay there during the night, the Divine power appeared to him and commanded him what he should eat, and to drink a certain beverage mixed with Pepper, Wine, and Honey. When he had done so, he was delivered from the sickness.

<margin>Concerning pepper, wine, and honey.</margin>
C Although, according to the rules of medicine, it was contrary to give a hot drink to those of a choleric temperament <note>original: "Colericis"; people believed to have an excess of yellow bile, making them "hot" and "dry."</note>.

<margin>Probanus</margin>
D I have also heard how Probanus, a court steward, had a man who lay there with gout <note>original: "Podagra"; a painful form of inflammatory arthritis.</note>, and that this man was healed of his pains at that place, and that a holy vision appeared to him in a wondrous way. And though he had long been a Heathen, he afterwards became a Christian and followed the teachings to a great extent.

<margin>Of the Holy Cross.</margin>
E Yet the cause of the whole matter—that is, the Holy Cross—he did not wish to worship. This Divine judgment, revealing itself with power, showed him the sign of the Cross which was placed there upon the altar of his Church. It was openly shown that since Christ was crucified, all things that happen for the benefit of the human race (however they may come to pass), whether through the holy Angel or a pious man, do not 

<column-break/>

occur without the power of the Holy Cross.

### How the idols were melted and the money turned to the common good.

### The 16th Chapter.

<margin>Priests of the heathens go out of business, deprived of temples and idols.</margin>
E And when the people and the city came to the Christian faith, and the priests and others—who out of care for their children had previously resisted—found they were at peace and no harm befell them, they brought forth their idols. The idols that were known only to certain priests were now made public and despised by everyone. Those made of precious materials, such as silver and gold, were melted in the fire and made into money for the common good.

<margin>Those named after Jason were costly idols. Also at the Hippodrome, etc.</margin>
But those which were works of art from the temples were taken to Constantinople to serve as decoration, and placed here and there along the streets and squares, and in the Circus <note>the Hippodrome</note>, and in the Royal Court and the Hall. Namely, those such as the Pythian priestess of the soothsayer Apollo, the Heliconian Muses, the Delphic Tripods <note>original: "Tripodes"; three-legged sacrificial altars or vessels from the Oracle at Delphi.</note>, and the famous common god Pan, which Pausanias the Lacedaemonian and the Greek cities set up after the wars begun against the Medes <note>original: "Meden"; referring to the Persian Wars.</note>.

<margin>Apollo, Pythius, Heliconian Muses, Tripods, Delphic Apollo.</margin>
Thus were the temple doors despoiled, the idolatrous images stripped and hung up; some were destroyed and overturned, held in contempt, and fell into nothingness. These included the Temple of Asclepius at Aegae in Cilicia, and at Aphaca near Mount Lebanon and the stream of Adonis <note>original: "Achone", likely a transcription error for the Adonis river.</note>, the house of Venus. Both of these are the treasures that the people of Aegae boast of, as if the sicknesses of the body were healed there; for in the night the Devil appears and heals them.

<margin>Temple of Asclepius, Venus, Aphaca.</margin>
But at Aphaca, because on a certain prominent day an invocation is made from the heights of Mount Lebanon, a burning fire like a falling star <note>original: "ghesteente", literally "stonework" or "gemstone", used here to describe the meteor-like appearance.</note> quickly descended into the nearby stream, which they say was Urania <note>original: "Vrauia", a likely typo for "Urania"; the "Heavenly" aspect of Venus/Aphrodite.</note>; for that is what they call Venus.

### Chapter 22.

<margin>The Migadi.</margin>
<margin>The Barbarians are converted.</margin>
In the meantime, a great number of the heathen Migadi <note>The "Migadi" likely refers to the Maedi or a related Thracian/Gothic tribe.</note> moved from Thrace into Asia. While these barbarians were contending against the Romans, many Christian priests were taken captive among them. When these priests began to heal the sick and cast out devils <note>original: "Duyvelen"</note> through the name of Christ, the Son of God—and moreover led blameless and virtuous lives—the barbarians were filled with wonder at their works and way of living. They thought that God would be more merciful to them if they followed these people. Thus, just as they honored God, they chose teachers from among those they had captured and were received into the Christian community.

## Theodoretus.

¶ How Eusebius violated the decrees of the Council and sought after another Bishopric.

### Chapter 23.

<margin>Eusebius a transgressor of the decrees.</margin>
the followers of Arius <note>Arius was the priest whose teachings—Arianism—denied the full divinity of Christ, leading to the Council of Nicaea.</note> would not abandon their wicked counsel; for although they had consented to the confession of faith, they afterwards acted like wolves. For when the holy Alexander, the Bishop of Constantinople, had died, Eusebius—a protector of unjust causes—disregarded the Canons <term>Canons: the official laws or rules of the Church governing conduct and administration.</term> and rules that he had previously made and signed with the other bishops. He abandoned Nicomedia and came to the seat of the deceased Bishop of Constantinople. This was done despite the Canons being against it, which state that bishops and priests shall not change their positions or run from one church to another. It is no wonder that those who are so stubborn against the Divinity of the Only-Begotten <note>Referring to Christ as the only-begotten Son of God, a central point of the Arian controversy.</note> would also violate other decrees. For he had previously done the 

<column-break/>

And when his godless teachings were discovered there, he was driven away from there after the Council, along with Theogonius of Nicaea, which the Emperor made public through letters. I wish to place a part of that letter (as he wrote it to the people of Nicomedia) here at the end of this work. Who is he who has thus taught these innocent people? Truly, it is Eusebius, a planter of tyrannical cruelty.

<margin>A part of the Epistle of Constantine to the Nicomedians regarding Eusebius of Nicomedia.</margin>
That he is a tyrannical teacher of the school is evident from many things, as the downfall of many godly and true bishops sufficiently testifies; indeed, the cruel persecution of Christians breeds murder here. I shall now remain silent about the insults I myself have suffered from him, and his fellow-helpers who secretly lurked, laid snares, and earnestly pursued me. This alone failed him and hindered him: that he did not leap forth with an armed hand like the tyrants. And let no one think that I lack proof of these things, for that judgment is public and easily brought to light: for I have caused the priests and deacons who followed Eusebius to be captured. Yet this I will pass over and not speak out of anger, but rather defend my innocence to their shame. I care for this alone, I consider this: that I see to it that you are not introduced to slander, as if you had part or commonality in it. For because of the crooked and perverted Eusebius, you have well perceived how his conscience has strayed from the truth. But regarding this matter, counsel shall still be found in time, if you still seek a faithful and pious Bishop and look solely to God. As far as the present is concerned, it has long stood in your judgment, and regarding the aforementioned Eusebius, I wish to write this to you: if your Council will listen with patience as is fitting, how a Council was held in the city of Nicaea, in which I, according to my conscience, agreed, and desired nothing else than that concord and unity might be achieved in all things. I also, above all things, wished to punish and see the cause that gave rise to this beginning.

<margin>Deut. 19. Heb 10. 2. Tim. 5.</margin>

## ¶ Concerning the riot at Antioch, which arose over the Arians.

### The 26th Chapter.

<margin>Riot at Antioch.</margin>
**A**t that time, a great riot broke out in Antioch when Eustathius was removed from his office. Afterward, during the election of a new Bishop, a fire was kindled like a flame that put almost the entire city in danger. The people were divided into two factions: one group wanted Eusebius (the Bishop of Palestine), while the other wanted to keep Eustathius. Both sides of the city were armed against each other to fight, just as if they were going to war against an enemy. Had the fear of God and of the Emperor not prevented it, it would have come to bloodshed. But the Emperor forced them by letters to cease their rioting. Eusebius 
<margin>Eusebius is praised by the emperor.</margin> 
of Palestine, however, did not wish to accept the Bishopric of Antioch. The Emperor, marveling at this, wrote to him, praising his resolution and calling him blessed, for he was worthy of being a Bishop not just for one city, but for the entire world. It is said that at this time the church at Antioch stood vacant without a Bishop for eight years. 
<margin>Euphronius becomes Bishop at Antioch.</margin> 
Finally, Euphronius was ordained there, though only at the request and insistence of the enemies of the Nicene faith. Now that we have orderly recorded the events mentioned in this book, one after the other, we shall proceed, as it is time to begin another book.

# The Third Book of the Tripartite Ecclesiastical History, from Sozomen, Socrates, and Theodoret, etc.

<note>The "Tripartite" history is a famous medieval and Renaissance textbook that wove together three different 5th-century Greek sources—Sozomen, Socrates Scholasticus, and Theodoret—into a single Latin narrative.</note>

<margin>K</margin>
## Theodoretus,

<column-break/>

<margin>E</margin>
### Of the conversion to the faith of the Indians and Persians.

#### The First Chapter.

<margin>F</margin>
<note>A decorated initial letter 'I' showing a man standing in a landscape with trees.</note>
<margin>Indians/ Persians.</margin>
In the times of the pious Prince Constantine, the nations of India and Iberia <note>This refers to Caucasian Iberia, modern-day Georgia, not the Spanish peninsula.</note> came to the Christian faith. But even then (as has been said) those of Armenia first became Christians: for their King Tiridates, due to a wondrous vision from God which
<margin>Armenians/ King Tiridates.</margin>

<column-break/>

occurred in his house, became a Christian and commanded his subjects by a mandate that they also should be subjected to the yoke of Christ. From there, the Christian teaching reached the surrounding places and was spread among many people.

# The 2nd Chapter.

**A**nd as they began to increase in number over time, they also began to have churches, priests, and other ministers.

<margin>Magi, the priests of the Persians.</margin>
Doing this troubled the Magi <note>The Magi were Zoroastrian priests who held significant religious and political influence in the Sassanid Persian Empire.</note> not a little, who held the priesthood among the Persians one after the other. This also vexed the Jews, who are natural enemies of the Christian doctrine.

<margin>Shapur, King of the Persians.</margin>
<margin>Simeon, Archbishop of Seleucia and Ctesiphon.</margin>
Therefore, they complained to the King of the Persians, named Shapur <note>original: "Sapores"; specifically Shapur II (r. 309–379), who viewed Christians as potential Roman spies.</note>, against Simeon, the Archbishop of the royal cities of Seleucia and Ctesiphon in Persia, as if he were a friend of the Roman Emperor and had revealed their dealings to him. Now, when Shapur had heard these accusers, he burdened the Christians with heavy taxation and tribute; and because he knew there were many who loved poverty more, he appointed certain men as tax collectors who were tyrants, so that through poverty and the compulsion of these plunderers, scrapers, and collectors, they would become despondent and abandon their Christian religion.

After this, he had the priests and servants of God executed with the sword. The churches were torn down, and all their vessels plundered and given as booty. And he had Simeon brought before him as a traitor to his kingdom and to the religion of the Persians.

<margin>S.</margin>
For the Magi, with the help of the Jews, hastened to destroy the churches. Yet Simeon, having been bound with chains, was led before the King, for he was a man of pious mind and magnificent strength.

<margin>Simeon is led to Shapur.</margin>
And when Shapur commanded him to be brought forward, he was not afraid, nor did he kneel before the King. Therefore, the King became even more enraged and asked him why he had not worshiped him as he had done before? Simeon answered him: "Previously, I was not led here in chains to forsake God and the religion of the Word of my true God: and I did not doubt

<column-break/>

that I then fulfilled the King's honor in the courtly manner; but now it is not fitting for me to do so, for I have now come to fight for our Lord and Truth." When he had said this, the King commanded that he should worship the Sun; if he did, he would give him great gifts and show him honor. If he did not do so, he threatened him and all Christians with death. And when he could not move Simeon with threats, nor entice him with promises, he ordered him to be led away, to see if he might be changed by long imprisonment.

<margin>Ustazares, a Eunuch.</margin>
As he was now being led to the prison, he was seen by Ustazares, an old <term>eunuch|A castrated official who often held high-ranking positions of trust in ancient royal courts.</term> who had been a tutor to Shapur and was the most prominent in the royal court. This man stood up and showed him honor, for he sat before the King's door; Simeon rebuked him severely with earnest words and turned his face away from him in contempt. For this Ustazares, not long before, though he had been a Christian, had worshiped the Sun.

This moved the eunuch to grievous lamentation and weeping; stripping off his costly clothes, he put on mourning garments, and sitting before the royal hall, he spoke with sobbing and weeping: "Oh, how God must be against me, whom I have denied. Therefore Simeon, who has been my dearest friend for a long time, would not speak to me: and is so against me that he passed by me without a kind word?"

And when Shapur heard this, he called Ustazares to him, asking what the cause of his weeping was.

<margin>U.</margin>
Ustazares answered: "O King, I have suffered no loss in the houses of this world. Oh, that God would grant that every misery had befallen me instead of this which has happened to me. I weep, for why do I live? I ought to have been dead long ago. I see the Sun, which I worshiped at your desire against my will. Therefore, for these two things I must rightly die: because I have become a traitor to Christ, and I have also deceived you." And having said this, he swore by the God of Heaven and earth that he would no longer change his mind.

Shapur then, although he greatly wondered at the eunuch's great steadfastness, finally became much angrier against the Christians, as if they brought such things about with evil sorcerous acts.

Usthazares had desired this so that the cause of his death would be announced. **I** Since Simeon was present there, he comforted them all together, speaking of the resurrection and godliness, and of the faith that the Scripture handled, and said: "To die thus is our true life; but the manifest death is to deny the true God." **K** But after this, it shall not happen the same way in eternity, for all men must give an account of all their lives: and those who have done well shall receive a reward, and the evil shall, without any <margin>Romans 8.</margin> doubt, receive punishment. <margin>Miles, carrying nothing but a pouch containing a Gospel book.</margin> But Miles, the Bishop <note>Miles, or Milles, was the Bishop of Susa in Persia, known for his ascetic lifestyle and travels.</note>, carrying nothing else with him but a pouch, and in it nothing but a Gospel book, went to Jerusalem to worship there; and from there he went to Egypt, so that he might see the lifestyle and conversation of the monks.

<margin>B</margin> What kind of man this Miles was, and with what piety and holiness he was adorned, is testified by the historians who have described his works and life. It is said that the number of men and women who were killed under King <margin>About 16,000 martyrs in Persia.</margin> Shapur <note>original: "Saporis"; referring to Shapur II, the Sasanian King of Persia.</note> amounted to about sixteen thousand.

# THEODORET <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 AD), a prominent theologian and church historian whose work "Ecclesiastical History" is a primary source for this text.</note>

->The Letter of Constantine, which he wrote to the King of Persia on behalf of the Christians.<-

### The III. Chapter.

<margin>D</margin> The Emperor Constantine Augustus <note>Constantine the Great, the first Roman Emperor to convert to Christianity.</note>, considering within himself how he might be of service to the Christians in Persia—who were being miserably oppressed by the godless and were suffering greatly because of their King’s cruel ignorance—wrote to him through his legates with divine exhortations, praying that he would uphold the servants and worshipers of God with proper honor.

<margin>E</margin> But the Emperor's diligence will be better understood from the letter which he himself wrote.

->The Letter of Emperor Constantine to Shapur, King of Persia, regarding the providence of God toward mankind.<-

<margin>F</margin> Since the Light of Truth has been shared with me, through which I have come to the recognition of the true faith,

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin> which I also guard and preserve as the most holy thing, I have sufficiently and clearly recognized, and do recognize (as the matter truly is), that I possess the right faith in the Son of God, which has powerfully helped me. For just as I, beginning from one end of the Ocean Sea <note>The Atlantic Ocean, then considered the edge of the world.</note>, have obtained the whole earth with firm hope of salvation and victory—so that all those who, in every place, were brought low by many tyrannical defeats and daily killings, had almost <margin>H</margin> fallen into oblivion, yet received the common divine cause again and have risen up as if alive from the dead—this is the God whom I worship. His sign, dedicated to God, my soldiers carry upon their shoulders <note>A reference to the Chi-Rho or the Cross, the Christian symbols Constantine’s soldiers wore on their shields and standards.</note>: which God also gives to the righteous that which they desire. From these glorious benefits of the manifestation of victory shown to me, I have quickly realized this, and I worship this immortal <margin>I</margin> God without ceasing. I also believe with a full heart that He is over all things. Him I invoke with bowed knees, and I flee from all abominable blood and horrible sacrifices, with which all heathens, in great and unspeakable error, have struck down many and various peoples and cast them into Hell. <margin>The providence of God toward the human race.</margin> For the things which God the Lord created out of providence for the benefit of the human race, He does not wish that <margin>K</margin> each person should appropriate according to their own lust: but He desires from men only a pure and undefiled mind, and He loves virtue and the faith of men, and He takes pleasure in gentleness and works of mercy. He hates the rebellious, loves faith, hates unbelief, and despises all pride, and punishes the bold. He humbles the puffed-up people, and rewards the lowly and patient; thus He also maintains a great Empire through His power, and He <margin>L</margin> preserves kingly wisdom in quiet peace. Therefore, my brother, I consider that I do not err when I confess that this is the one God and Prince, whom some in times past, moved by insane error, have dared to deny. But all these have come to an evil end. So much so that their destruction seems to be an example of a curse upon them. One of these is Valerian <note>original: "Valerianus"; Roman Emperor Valerian (reigned 253–260 AD) who was captured by the Persian King Shapur I and died in captivity, cited here as a warning of divine judgment.</note>, who, being driven out of our land like a rod of <margin>Valerius.</margin> divine wrath, was sent <margin>M</margin> so that he might be punished in your land. And this served him well, that he was punished in this time, and it is manifest to all.

¶ Thus I have also seen the end of those who, afterward with shameful commands, troubled the people of God. Therefore, I give great thanks to the Lord God that, through His Divine providence, He grants peace and joy to those who honor His divine commandments. He will also grant us (as I believe) that we shall live in pure faith and religion, and in unity with GOD. Since I then speak with you on behalf of the Christians, know that I rejoice in nothing more than that the most prominent places in Persia are adorned with them. And then you shall rule well, if you were like them, and held in common what they have: For thus would you have the Lord of all Lords, merciful and favorable.

¶ Since you are then in great high regard, I wish to leave these people commended to you; hold them dear and worthy, and show them mercy. And herewith keep yourself and us all bound in all faithfulness, one to another.

This the pious, God-fearing Emperor did; and he not only cared for his own subjects but also for those who stood under another's command. Therefore God gave him assistance, and subjected all of Europe and Libya to him, and moreover that great part of Asia, and made them obedient. But some of the Barbarians <note>original: "Barbarij"; used here in the classical sense to refer to non-Roman or non-Greek peoples.</note> served him willingly, others were conquered: everywhere one saw victory and triumph, and the Emperor remained supreme in all things.

# Sozomenus <note>Salminius Hermias Sozomenus (c. 400–450 AD), a historian of the Christian Church whose work is one of the three sources for this "Tripartite" history.</note>

¶ Athanasius becomes Bishop at Alexandria.

### The IV. Chapter.

<margin>Athanasius becomes Bishop at Alexandria.</margin>
In the meantime, the wonderful old man Alexander—who had denounced the heresy of Arius <note>Arius (c. 256–336 AD) was a priest in Alexandria whose teachings on the nature of Christ led to the Arian controversy and the Council of Nicaea.</note>—has died, five months after the Council of Nicaea <note>original: "Concilio Niceno"; the first ecumenical council held in 325 AD.</note>. And the Church of Alexandria has received Athanasius as its Bishop. Of these persecutions, flights, and anxious terrors, Ruffinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410 AD), a monk and historian who translated and expanded Eusebius’s Ecclesiastical History.</note> has written, of which we shall now leave it at that.

# Sozomenus.

¶ How Athanasius came to the Emperor, and regarding the gathering of the Arians at Mareotis <note>original: "Mareotten"; referring to Lake Mareotis near Alexandria, a center of Arian activity and regional church politics.</note>.

### The V. Chapter.

<sig>D</sig>
<margin>Athanasius goes to the Emperor.</margin>
After many tumultuous Councils were held with sedition and uproar, and the accusers with great clamor demanded that Athanasius—as if he were a great defiler and unworthy of the Priesthood—be condemned and deposed. Some were sent by the Emperor, fearing that he might be killed in the assault, and they led him secretly away from the Council. When Athanasius well knew that he was not able to act against so many accusers, and as the judges were all against him, he left the Synod and hurried to come to the Emperor.

# Theodoretus <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 AD), another primary source for this compilation of church history.</note>

When Athanasius had now come to the Emperor, he told him what intentions the Bishops had against him. These [Bishops] coming together at Mareotis, <margin>The gathering of the Arians at Mareotis.</margin> sent some Priests who held with them to the Emperor—that is, Theogonius of Nicaea, and Theodotus of Perinthus, Maris of Chalcedon, and Narcissus of Cilicia, and others like them—and they devised nothing there but falsehood and sheer lies; having done which, they came into the city of Aelia. <margin>Aelia, that is, Jerusalem <note>The Roman city built over the ruins of Jerusalem was called Aelia Capitolina.</note>.</margin> For the Emperor commanded that the entire Council of Tyre should come to Aelia; he also commanded others from other places to gather, so that they might hallow the newly built Temple <note>Refers to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, commissioned by Constantine.</note>. To that end, he appointed and sent the most prominent and God-fearing among the judges, commanding that all things should be widely provided for and considered—yes, not only Bishops and Priests, but also all the poor and needy who flocked here from all places. Furthermore, he also decorated the Altar, spreading his Royal robe over it and honoring it with golden vessels and precious stones.

# Sozomenus.

¶ Concerning the faith of Arius, and how the Emperor sent them to Jerusalem to be examined.

## The 6th Chapter.

<margin>
Arius is recalled.
</margin>

In the meantime, the Emperor summoned Arius back from his exile and commanded that he should present from the Scriptures what he believed concerning God. There, Arius immediately changed his tone and found a new name <note>This refers to Arius using more orthodox-sounding language to disguise his controversial teachings, a common tactic described by contemporary historians like Sozomen.</note> and wove together a different explanation than he had first given. This he confirmed with simple words and with the Holy Divine Scripture, swearing an oath that he believed thus, and that he understood it so in his heart, and intended nothing else. The text of his exposition was as follows:

->To the pious and God-beloved our Lord, Emperor Constantine: Arius and Euzonius, Priests.<-

The Faith of Arius, which he presented as a confession before the Emperor.
