Just as God has commanded your God-fearing love, O Lord Emperor, so we declare our faith and confess it in writing before God, that we believe thus—indeed, all who are with us—just as follows here.
We believe in one God the Father Almighty, and in one Lord Jesus Christ His Son, who was born of Him before all times; God the Word, through whom all things were created, on earth as in Heaven; who lives and has taken on flesh. And He suffered, and rose again, and ascended into Heaven, and He shall come again to judge the living and the dead. And in one Holy Spirit, and the resurrection of the flesh, and the life of the world to come, and the Kingdom of HEAVEN, and in one holy Apostolic universal <note>original: "alghemeyne"; here meaning the Catholic or universal church.</note> Church of GOD, which exists from the beginning to the end.

<margin>
Mat. 28, Mark 16.
</margin>

This Faith, then, we have received from the holy Evangelists, just as the LORD said to His disciples: Go forth and teach all nations, baptizing them in the Name of the Father, and of the Son, and

<column-break/>

of the Holy Spirit.
If we do not believe and accept these things thus—the true Father, SON, and Holy SPIRIT—as the Holy Scripture teaches, which we all follow, then GOD shall be our witness and Judge, now and in the coming day of Judgment. Therefore, O Emperor beloved of GOD, we pray you—since we belong to the church and hold the understanding of the Church and the holy Scripture—that you would arrange for us to be received back into it. Since you are a peacemaker and a servant of GOD, let all questions and whatever is not useful to that cause be taken away, so that we, being reconciled together with the Holy Church, may offer earnest prayers whereby your Godly KINGDOM and all that belongs to it may be kept in Peace.

This exposition of faith, some said, was framed with a subtle nature so that the Emperor would seem to be reconciled by it. And in considering the doctrine of Arius, which had a double meaning, they brought an assurance to the Emperor. Since the Emperor thought that Arius and Euzonius held to what had been decided in the Council of Nicaea <note>The Council of Nicaea (325 AD) was the first ecumenical council, which had originally condemned Arius’s teachings as heresy.</note>, he rejoiced greatly. However, he did not wish to let them come into the communion of the Church except through the judgment and testing of qualified persons, according to the institution of the Church. But he directed them to the Bishops who were then in Jerusalem, and wrote to them that they should examine them, the Faith they had set forth, and give a merciful sentence upon it. If they believed rightly, and if their previous wrong had come from envy—or if they did not have that with which they might be justly accused before the judges—then they should be taken back through doing penance.

<margin>
Constantine sends Arius’s confession to the Clergy to be examined.
</margin>

Here, those who were well-disposed toward Arius took the opportunity from the Emperor’s writings to receive him back into their communion. And when they had done this, they wrote back to the Emperor, and to the churches in Alexandria, and to the Bishops in Egypt, the Thebaid, and Libya, before all the Clergy <note>original: "Clericos"</note>, and commanded them that they should receive them in peace.

For the Emperor also testified that their Faith was right, just as his own epistle shows, placed here; and these things took place in Jerusalem.

Tripartite Ecclesiastical History.

### ¶ The letter of Emperor Constantine to the Synod assembled at Tyre, from the History of Theodoret.

<margin>
The irreproachability of the church ministers.
</margin>
**Constantine** Augustus to the Holy Council assembled at Tyre: It would indeed be fitting, and necessitated by the circumstances of the times, that the Christian Church (as indeed it ought to be) were entirely without uproar and discord, and that the servants of Jesus Christ conducted themselves so that they could be scolded or slandered by no one. Yet, because there are some who, out of desire, are very heated toward strife (I would almost say they live for it) and undertake to make all things restless—which does not become them—it seems to me to provide a cause for various needs, anxieties, and temptations to break into the Church.

<margin>
Proverb: Running feet without power. <note>This likely refers to the "useless haste" or "aimless wandering" of those who act without divine authority or proper purpose.</note>
</margin>
¶ Therefore, on this account, I have wished to admonish you (who have indeed run there without purpose, as the proverb goes) that you come together without any disorder, and hold that Synod, and protect those who lack help, heal the brothers who are wounded, and bring to unity those members who are at odds among themselves.

<margin>
Pride is a harmful spark.
</margin>
To the end that where there is lack and where one has erred, you should improve it according to the circumstances of the time: For in this way you shall be able to win back such and so many Provinces where this occurs to unity. Which unity (O wicked slander!) the pride of certain worthless men has corrupted.

¶ For this is, before all things, pleasing to the Lord alone, and to Your Graces <note>Original: "V. L.", likely standing for "Uwe Liefden," a formal honorific meaning "Your Loves" or "Your Graces."</note> it is before all things to be desired; yes, for yourselves, if you otherwise desire peace, it would lead to great praise and glory, if all people confessed the faith with one mind. Therefore, seek to shorten this business, and apply yourselves with the highest diligence, so that this present matter may be set right with all simplicity and faith, just as the Savior whom we serve expects of us everywhere with a clear voice. It is true, you shall desire nothing of those things from us which do not belong to our office. For I have accomplished all things that you commanded me to do through your writing.

<margin>
Dionysius the Consul.
</margin>
I have written to the Bishops, as you wished, that they should come and unite themselves with their teaching and with Your Graces. I have also sent Dionysius the Councilor <note>Dionysius was a "consularis" or former consul, acting as the Emperor's representative to oversee the secular order of the council.</note> as a friend, who shall travel with Your Graces to the Synod

<column-break/>

to record the names and write down those things which shall occur among Your Graces.

¶ Primarily, however, he shall be a protector and a listener, so that all things may occur with good order. For if anyone (whom we do not expect) shall disregard your admonition at this time and undertake not to come, we will quickly send out a message which, according to Imperial command, shall banish him and show him indeed how it is entirely unbecoming to resist Imperial ordinances issued for the investigation of the Truth. Furthermore, it is the duty of your holiness that you unite yourselves, also not acting out of envy or favor, but according to the contents of the Christian and Apostolic ordinances, to heal those who have fallen into sin with suitable medicine with the greatest diligence; whereby the church may be delivered from all reproach with which she has been burdened for a time, and by this your diligence, my care may be partly lightened. Also so that the grace-filled peace, having been accepted, may win more praise from those who now act uproariously. May God preserve you, dear brothers.

No one knows what things have been decided in your rebellious and restless Councils, for it seems that the truth has been suppressed by rebellious discord, since you are not thinking of things that please God for the sake of unity—which you have hated against your neighbor—and because no one has been able to overcome you in your intent. <margin>B</margin> But it shall be a work of Divine providence if this matter, being rightly observed, may be settled and become manifest to us: whatever you (being gathered there) have handled, whether it happened through favor or disfavor. Therefore, it is my opinion that you all join yourselves with great haste to my presence, so that what has occurred may be shown by your own selves through your actions. Why I have written these things to you, and why I have not summoned letters to me instead, you shall know through the following events. <margin>C</margin> <margin>The deeds of Athanasius before the Emperor.</margin> When I was riding in the city of our fatherland, Constantinople, and dismounted from my horse, Athanasius the bishop, being in the middle of the streets with some Priests accompanying him, approached me without hesitation. ### How the Bishops who were favorable to Arius made Athanasius appear so wicked that he was banished from the land.

### The VIII. Chapter.

<margin>I</margin>
<margin>The mildness and liberality of Constantine, who [provided] from Alexandria to Constantinople 80,000 [measures of grain]. It was as if the bishops had been the overseers of the people.</margin>
These letters caused a great uproar among those who were gathered in the Council, for many returned to their own cities. Those who were with Eusebius, Theogonus, Maris, Patrophilus, Ursacius, and Valens, when they arrived at Constantinople, allowed no questions regarding the dead Arsenius <note>Arsenius was a bishop whom Athanasius was falsely accused of murdering; the accusers even produced a severed hand they claimed was his.</note>, the broken chalice, or the overturning of the Altar, which they had arranged in the Council. They claimed <margin>K</margin> <margin>Accusation is powerful when the accuser is held to be trustworthy. <note>original: "Potent delatio quando fide dignus habetur qui accusat."</note></margin> they had heard him say this to Amantius, Arbatius, and Peter the Bishops. Therefore, gossip is very powerful if the gossiper is held in high regard and deemed worthy of belief. With these and similar slanders, they provoked the Emperor to such anger <margin>L</margin> that he sent Athanasius out of the land into exile, commanding him to live in the Gauls <note>Specifically the city of Trier in modern-day Germany.</note>. It is said the Emperor did this so that the churches might be united thereby; for Athanasius, refusing to have communion with the Arians, went to live in Trier in Gaul. <margin>M</margin>

## Sozomenus

### ¶ Concerning Marcellus of Ancyra and Asterius, and how they were deposed.

### The IX. Chapter.

<margin>Marcellus of Ancyra is deposed. Asterius. Keto:.</margin>
**W**hen the Bishops were gathered at Constantinople, they deposed Marcellus from the city of Ancyra in Galatia for these reasons: Asterius, who was a Sophist <note>A teacher of rhetoric or philosophy; here used to imply one who uses clever but fallacious reasoning.</note> in Cappadocia, abandoned that profession and promised to become a Christian. He then took it upon himself to write books, which are still in circulation, through which the teachings of Arius <note>Arianism taught that Jesus Christ was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> are confirmed. He said that Christ was a "power of God" in the same way it is written by Moses regarding the locusts and caterpillars and many such things. <margin>House arranged. Leviticus 26:16, Deuteronomy 27:28.</margin> Now, this Asterius frequently visited the Bishops who did not particularly shun the Arian heresy; therefore, he also ran to the Councils to see if he might obtain a Bishopric in some city. However, he was stripped of his priestly status because he had offered sacrifices to idols during the time of the persecutions. As he traveled throughout the cities of Syria, he sold his books as was his custom. Marcellus, knowing this and wishing to write against him, overstepped the bounds in his rebuttal. For he became like Paul of Samosata, <note>A 3rd-century bishop whose views were condemned for suggesting Christ was a mere man who achieved divinity through his moral excellence.</note> saying that Christ the Lord was a mere man. Those who had come to Jerusalem recognized this, but they had no argument with him at all at that time, for he was not among the number of the Priests.

They brought charges against Marcellus because of his book. When they found that it was stained with the teachings of Paul of Samosata, they told him that he should renounce these teachings. When he was corrected, he promised to have that book burned. But when this desire [to repent] ceased, the Bishop’s council came to the Royal City <note>Constantinople.</note> by order of the Emperor. There, before Eusebius and the other <margin>Marcellus is investigated.</margin> Bishops who were with him, they again inquired into and investigated Marcellus. And when

<column-break/>

Marcellus would not burn his faithless writings as he had promised, they deposed him from his Bishopric and sent Basil to Ancyra in his place.

However, Eusebius destroyed Marcellus's writings with three books of his own, earnestly refuting his lack of faith and his errors. After this, Marcellus <margin>Marcellus receives his bishopric again.</margin> accepted his Bishopric again at the Council of Sardica, saying that they had not understood his book, and that he had been deposed as a follower of Paul of Samosata [unfairly].

### How Arius came to Constantinople, and how he died miserably in a secret latrine.

### The X. Chapter.

<margin>Arius is brought to Constantinople.</margin>
**A**fter the Council held at Jerusalem, Arius found that those in Alexandria, Egypt, would have no fellowship with him. He thus traveled back to Constantinople to the members of his sect and those who were subject to Eusebius, the Bishop of Nicomedia. They desired to hold a Council. Alexander, being then the Bishop of Constantinople, knew of their intentions and took it upon himself to prevent such a thing. When he was unable to do so, he spoke against them openly and forbade Arius’s business, saying: "It is not fitting for those who are not of the Church." He argued that it was not right for them to diminish the opinion of the Bishops of nearly the entire world, who had united in the city of Nicaea regarding the Christian faith. But Eusebius and those with him, when they could not bend Alexander’s mind with earnest words, began to threaten him: unless he accepted Arius, he would be banished from the land on a set day, and Arius would nonetheless be accepted into the communion of the church. After this, they separated from one another and waited for the appointed day on which they might fulfill their desperate plans. Alexander, however, prayed that they would not be able to perfectly fulfill the words of Eusebius. <margin>Alexander is distressed.</margin> For he was afraid, because they had nearly persuaded the Emperor to do whatever they wanted.

During this day, Alexander offered himself in prayer to God, kneeling for an entire night, asking that He might hinder the counsel of his enemies and preserve [the church] in innocence.

# Socrates

Alexander prayed for these things from God. Meanwhile, the Emperor summoned Arius to his Royal Hall and asked whether he held to the confession of the Council of Nicaea. Without hesitating, Arius immediately signed the Nicene Creed, though he did so by wandering through cold and subtle tricks. Because of this, the Emperor demanded more of him and imposed an oath upon him, which he also performed deceitfully. Regarding how he kept the oath only as a mocking trick, I will write here what I have heard of this event.

<margin>The Emperor commands that Arius shall be received back into communion.</margin>

It is said that Arius had written his own heresy on a piece of paper and carried it under his arm. Therefore, he believed that he had sworn rightly, saying that he believed as he had written—referring to what he had on his person. <note>original: "hem soo te ghevoelen als hy ghewozen hadde". This is a famous anecdote where Arius supposedly hid a copy of his own heretical creed in his cloak and swore he believed "what I have here," tricking the Emperor into thinking he meant the Nicene Creed.</note> I have heard that this is how it happened, and it is also written in the Emperor’s letter. Therefore, the Emperor, believing him, commanded Bishop Alexander at Constantinople that he should receive Arius back into communion. It was then the Sabbath <note>In the early Church, "Sabbath" referred to Saturday, while the following day mentioned is Sunday, the day of the Eucharist.</note>, and the Emperor expected that they would join one another in communion the following day. But now the judgments of God followed upon the intentions of Arius; for when he had left the King’s hall, the servants of Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Nicomedia, a powerful supporter of Arius.</note> showed him great honor, and he walked through the middle of the city as an esteemed man. When he came to the place called the Market of Constantine, where the Porphyry Column <note>A famous monumental column in Constantinople made of purple porphyry stone, which still stands today as the "Burnt Column."</note> stood, a terror seized him, springing from the secrets of his conscience, and with that fear came a violent movement of the bowels. Having asked if there were a private toilet nearby, and being told yes, he went inside. There a hemorrhage came upon him, so that his liver, lungs, and all his intestines were voided into the seat, and he died. This private toilet where this occurred is still shown in the city of Constantinople, behind the Market of Constantine, not far from the food market; all those who pass by point at it with their fingers, always remembering the wretched death of Arius.

<margin>The death of Arius.</margin>

# Sozomenus

Not long after this, a powerful rich man, who was a follower of Arius and loved his deceitful teaching,

<column-break/>

tore down the aforementioned building and set a new house upon the spot, so that the matter might be forgotten. However, it did no good, for the fame of it ran through the whole city, and the ends of the world have spread the news of Arius's death.

->¶ How the Arians, not yet being separated, held communion with the others, using the Sacraments, and how they were deprived of their churches through the Emperor's help.<-

# The XI. Chapter.

<margin>Arius's sect not yet separated.</margin>

Although the teaching of Arius was elevated by many through disputation, up to this time it had not yet driven a specific group of people together who existed under the name of its author. Instead, they all came together in the churches and held communion of the Sacraments with one another—except for the Novatians, and those called the Phrygians, Valentinians, Marcionists, and Paulianists, <note>These were various "heretical" groups from the 2nd and 3rd centuries that had already established separate structures from the main imperial church.</note> and those who followed other heresies.

<margin>The heretics are deprived of the churches by imperial command.</margin>

Against all of these, the Emperor issued a decree, commanding that their houses of prayer should be torn down and turned into churches. The Emperor judged that they should not be allowed to gather either in private or in public, but rather that they should come together in the general Catholic Church, to which he exhorted every person. I consider this mandate to have been the cause for the ceasing of these heresies. For in the earlier times of the preceding Emperors, although they were divided into various sects, they were still regarded as Christians by the pagans and were subject to the same pains. Because of their shared suffering and persecution, they could not examine one another, and therefore they easily came together and were united in differing matters to celebrate the service of God. And although they were few, they were not regarded as divided. But now, after this law, they were not allowed to come into the church either secretly or openly, while the Bishops of the cities and the clergy kept a close watch with great crowds and prevented them. This fear caused many of them to join the Church. The others remained hardened in their opinions, yet no one followed them further in their error.

### ¶ Concerning Marcellus of Ancyra and Asterius; how they were deposed.

## Chapter 9.

<margin>Marcellus of Ancyra is deposed. Asterius the Rhetorician.</margin>
When the Bishops were now gathered at Constantinople, they deposed Marcellus in the city of Ancyra in Galatia for these reasons: Asterius, being a Sophist <term>Sophist: in this context, a professional teacher of rhetoric and philosophy</term> from Cappadocia, abandoned that profession and promised to become a Christian. He then undertook to write books—which are still in circulation—through which the teachings <margin>House settled. Lev. 26, 16; Deut. 27, 28.</margin> of Arius were confirmed. He said that Christ was a "power of God" only in the same way that Moses spoke of the locusts and the gnats and many such things. <note>Asterius argued that because the Bible calls even swarming insects the "power of God," the title does not prove Christ's unique divinity. This was a core argument of the Arian heresy.</note> Now this Asterius often visited the Bishops, especially those who favored the Arian heresy; therefore, he also ran to the Council in hopes that he might obtain a Bishopric in some city. However, he was deprived of the Priesthood because he had offered sacrifices to idols during the time of the persecution. As he traveled throughout the cities of Syria, he sold his books as was his custom. Marcellus, knowing this and wishing to write against him, exceeded all bounds in his contradiction. For he was like Paul of Samosata <note>Paul of Samosata was a 3rd-century bishop condemned for teaching "Monarchianism"—the idea that Jesus was a mere human who became divine, rather than God from the beginning.</note>, saying that Christ the Lord was a mere man. Those who had then come together at Jerusalem took no account of Asterius at all, because he was not among the number of the Priests.

They drove Marcellus out because of his book. When they found that it was stained with the teachings of Paul of Samosata, they told him that he must renounce this doctrine. When he was rebuked, he promised to have the book burned. But when this desire faded, the Episcopal council came to the Royal City <note>Constantinople</note> by order of the Emperor. There, before Eusebius and other <margin>Marcellus is investigated.</margin> Bishops who were with him, they again inquired into and examined Marcellus at Constantinople. And when—

<column-break/>

<margin>Marcellus receives his bishopric again.</margin>
Marcellus would not burn his unbelieving writings as he had promised, they deposed him from his Bishopric and sent Basil to Ancyra in his place.

But Eusebius destroyed his writings with three books, earnestly refuting his lack of faith and his errors. However, Marcellus later accepted the Bishopric again at the Council of Sardica, saying that they had not understood his book, and for that reason he had been deposed as a follower of Paul of Samosata.

## Chapter 10.

<margin>Arius to Constantinople because of a new council.</margin>
When Arius, after the Council held at Jerusalem, arrived in Egypt, the Church at Alexandria would have no communion with him. Thus, he traveled back to Constantinople to the members of his sect and those who were subject to Eusebius, the bishop of Nicomedia, and they desired to hold a Council. Alexander, being then the Bishop of Constantinople, knew of their intentions and undertook to prevent them. When he was unable to do so, he openly contradicted them and forbade the business of Arius, saying: "It is not fitting for those who are not of the Church." He also argued that it was not their place to diminish the opinion of the Bishops of nearly the entire world, who had united in the city of Nicaea regarding the Christian faith. But Eusebius and those with him, when they could not bend Alexander’s mind with earnest words, began to threaten him: unless he accepted Arius, he would be banished from the land on a set day, and Arius would nevertheless be received into the communion of the churches. After this they parted from one another and waited for the appointed day on which they might fulfill their threats. Alexander prayed to them that they would not seek to carry out the words of Eusebius perfectly. <margin>Alexander is afraid.</margin> For he was afraid, since they had almost convinced the Emperor to do whatever they wished.

Before this day, Alexander spent an entire night kneeling in prayer, offering himself to God, that He might hinder the counsel of his enemies and preserve him in innocence.

# Socrates.

<margin>Arius is questioned as to whether he holds to the Nicene confession before Constantine.</margin>
Alexander sought these things from God. But the Emperor summoned Arius to his Royal Hall and asked him whether he held to the confession of the Council of Nicaea? Without delay, he immediately subscribed to the Nicene Creed, circumventing it with cold and subtle artifice. Because of this, the Emperor proceeded to require an oath from him, which he also performed deceitfully. Regarding the oath—which he treated merely as a mocking trick—I write here what I have heard of this event.

It is said that Arius wrote his heresy on a piece of paper and carried it under his arm. Therefore, he believed he had sworn rightly, saying he felt as he had sworn <note>Arius reportedly swore that he believed "what he had written," secretly referring to the heretical document under his arm rather than the Nicene Creed he had just signed.</note>; I have heard that it happened thus, and it is so written. That he took the oath, I have from the Letter of the Emperor. This private privy where this occurred is shown in the city of Constantinople, behind the Market of Constantine, not far from the food market; and all who passed by pointed at it with their fingers, always remembering the miserable death of Arius.

### Chapter 11.

<margin>The sect of Arius not yet separated.</margin>
The teaching of Arius, although it was elevated by many with disputations, had until this time not yet driven a particular people together who stood under the name of the author. Instead, they all came together in the church and had communion of the Sacraments with one another, except for the Novatians <note>A rigorist schismatic group named after Novatian.</note>, and those called Phrygians, Valentinians, Marcionists, and Paulianists, and those who followed other heresies. <margin>The heretics are deprived of the church by imperial command.</margin> Against all of these, the Emperor allowed an edict to go out, commanding that their houses of prayer should be torn down and made into churches. The Emperor judged that they should not be allowed to gather, neither in private nor in public; but rather to come together in the general Catholic Church, to which he exhorted everyone. I consider this Mandate to have been the reason that the heresies ceased. For in the early times of the preceding Emperors in the time of Christ, although they were divided into various sects, they were still considered Christians by the Pagans and were subject to equal punishment. Because of the fellowship of suffering and persecution, they could not examine one another, and therefore they easily came together and were united in differing matters, and the service of God was upheld. And although they were few, they were not considered divided. Now, after this law, they could not come into the churches either secretly or publicly, while the Bishops of the cities and the clerics kept watch with great crowds and hindered them. This fear caused many to betake themselves to the church. Others remained hardened in their opinion, yet no one followed them in their error.

### The Seventh Chapter.

<margin>Constantine Augustus appoints his sons as Kings.</margin>
Now when the Christian Emperor <note>Constantine the Great.</note> received great joy from the welfare of the Christians, and truly recognized how, through the testimony of God, the faith had been strengthened at Nicaea, he received no small joy from the events that had occurred regarding Arius. As the Emperor Constantine now had three sons, whom he appointed as Caesars (or Kings), and each of them was set to rule for ten-year 
<margin>Constantine in his 10th year. Constantius in his 20th year.</margin>
periods of the Empire; that is: the first son, who was named Constantine like his father, he appointed as Emperor in the West on his *Decennalia* <note>original: "Decennali"; the tenth anniversary of his reign.</note>. The second, who was named Constantius like his grandfather, he appointed as Emperor in the East on his *Vicennalia* <note>original: "Vicennali"; the twentieth anniversary.</note>; and the youngest, Constans, 
<margin>Constans in his 30th year.</margin>
he appointed as Emperor on his *Tricennalia* <note>original: "Tricennali"; the thirtieth anniversary.</note>. And one year later, when he was sixty-five years old, he became ill, wherefore he traveled out of Constantinople to a warm bath.

# Theodoretus.

<margin>Constantine Augustus is baptized. Athanasius is commanded to return to Alexandria.</margin>
While he remained at Nicomedia, he grew increasingly ill; and being uncertain of the length of his life, he became a partaker of the grace of Holy Baptism. For he had delayed this until this time, desiring to be baptized in the river Jordan. He then left behind his three sons, whom he left as heirs to his Empire. And he commanded that Athanasius the Great <note>The Bishop of Alexandria and staunch defender of the Nicene Creed against Arianism.</note> should return again to Alexandria, even though Eusebius was present and advised against it.

<column-break/>

# Sozomenus.

He was baptized in the suburbs of Nicomedia.

# Socrates.

When he had now made a testament, and ordained his three sons as heirs, he died; and his body was laid in a golden sarcophagus and carried to Constantinople, and placed in the highest part of the palace until Constantius, his son from the East, had arrived, and with Imperial pomp committed the body to the earth in the church at Constantinople called the *Apostolorum* <note>original: "Apostolorum"; the Church of the Holy Apostles.</note>. The Emperor had built this Church of the Apostles so that the Emperor and the Priests would not be deprived of the 
<margin>Constantine Augustus dies.</margin>
relics of the Apostles. In the second year of the 278th Olympiad.

# The Fourth Book of the History called the Tripartite Ecclesiastical History, compiled from Sozomen, Socrates, and Theodoret, etc.

## Sozomen.

$\P$ How the Arian teaching was revived by a priest who was the Emperor's executor <note>original: "Testamentarius"; a legal term for one who holds or executes a last will and testament.</note>.

### The First Chapter.

<margin>
30
The Council of Nicaea comes into dispute again.
</margin>
These things occurred within the church under the reign of Constantine; upon his death, the teaching of the Council of Nicaea <note>The Council of Nicaea (325 AD) established the orthodox Christian creed against Arianism.</note> came once more into dispute. For although many did not accept this while Constantine was still living, they were not so bold as to openly set themselves against it. <margin>23</margin> Now that he has died, there were many, without doubt, who withdrew themselves from the Council. But these were people who had been held as suspects from the beginning; the primary followers of Arius <note>Arius (c. 250–336) taught that Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father.</note> were Eusebius and Theogonius, who strongly confirmed his teaching and used every effort to ensure that Athanasius did not return, and to help their own followers gain the right to the bishopric in Egypt.

<column-break/>

And they handled this through the service and assistance of the priest by whom Eusebius had restored Arius during the time of Constantine. For this priest was very pleasing to Constantine because he guarded the testament <note>The last will and testament.</note> of his father, and therefore he had access to the Emperor and to the most powerful men of the court. Furthermore, Eusebius was held in such high regard at court that he raised his followers to high positions. For this reason, people began to dispute and bring forward this rejected doctrine again, both privately and openly. Through this, much hatred and envy arose, as usually happens from such things.

### Emperor Constantinus, to the people of the Christian Church at Alexandria.

<margin>The Letter of Constantine the Younger to the Alexandrians on behalf of Athanasius.</margin>
I do not know if you are aware—though your pious hearts surely know—that Athanasius is a preacher and interpreter of the divine law who should be held in honor. For this reason, he was sent to Gaul for a time, because the terrible fury of his enemies was so great that it threatened to destroy his life, so that by chance no injustice should befall him through their cunning. Therefore, to avoid such things, he departed; and at my desire, he was provided with all the goods he needed in the city where he resided. Furthermore, he is such a virtuous man, so comforted in God, that all the sorrow, narrow persecutions, and adversity could not hinder him. Therefore, although our dear father of blessed memory, Constantine Augustus, my godly father, intended to restore this same bishop to his place before he died—which God prevented through death—I am willing and ready to fulfill this promise of my father. And when he comes to you, you shall recognize in what honor he has been held by me; for it is not to be wondered at that we behave toward him as is proper, for my mind shall be an example for your desires, and the sight of this man moves and compels me to this. May Divine Providence preserve you, dear brothers.

### How Athanasius, being accused before the Emperor, withdrew to Italy.

### The 5th Chapter.

<margin>The Priest-Executor brings the Arian cause before the emperor.</margin>
Now when Constantinus had departed from this temporal Kingdom into eternal life, and his children had divided this temporal Kingdom by Testament (though none of them were present at the time), the Priest to whom his sister had entrusted him was given the Testament. He was commanded to give it to Constantinus, who was the nearest among the others and likely to arrive first. Through this, the priest became known to Constantius, delivering this Testament to him, and thus gained trust and access to him. This Priest, having noticed the Emperor's wavering mind and that he was moved here and there like a reed, resolved to start a war against the truth of the Gospel and began to stir up a great storm against the Holy Church. He said that those who had set down the word *Homoousion* <note>original: "Homoousion"; a Greek term meaning "of one substance," used in the Nicene Creed to describe the relationship between God the Father and God the Son.</note>—that is, "of one essence"—were to be punished.

¶ [They] had placed in the doctrine of the faith things which are not found in the Holy Scripture: from which strife and discord among the Priests was born. From this, the accusation against Athanasius and his followers arose, and snares were laid for him. His helpers were Eusebius, Theogonius, and Theodotus of Perinthus, who was the most eloquent among them. He wrote explanations on the Gospels, which many call the Heracleotes. But these, while they were often with the Emperor, mocked how the return of Athanasius had been a cause of much evil, and said: "How not only in the land of Egypt, but also Palestine and Phoenicia, and the surrounding lands have been stirred up by him." Therefore, with these words, they approached the Emperor and advised him that he should drive Athanasius out of the church again. But Athanasius, noticing their trickery, traveled to the western lands <note>original: "Hisperias," a poetic term for the West, usually referring to Italy or the Iberian peninsula.</note>.

### ¶ How Athanasius was supported by Julius, the Roman Bishop.

<margin>Athanasius comes to Italy.</margin>

## Chapter VI.

<margin>Julius, Bishop at Rome, summons Athanasius and his adversaries.</margin>
And indeed, Eusebius and his companions made those accusations against Athanasius and sent them to Julius, the Bishop at Rome, who, following ecclesiastical customs, also commanded him to come to Rome. He also, according to the regulations, summoned the worthy man Athanasius to judgment; having received his summons, Athanasius traveled thither. But the accusers did not come to Rome, knowing that they would easily be caught in their lies. But seeing the sheep desolate without a Shepherd, they placed a Wolf as shepherd over them, that is Gregory, who for six years ruled cruelly over the cattle <note>The author uses "cattle" metaphorically to describe the congregation under Gregory's harsh rule.</note>; at last, he received the punishment for his wickedness, for he was miserably torn to pieces by all.

<margin>Gregory, an evil Bishop at Alexandria.</margin>

### ¶ How the Emperor Constans is favorable to Athanasius.

## Chapter VII.

<margin>Athanasius complains to the Emperor about the Arians.</margin>
Now when Athanasius came to Constans <note>The Dutch text says "Constantium," but historical context confirms he visited the Western Emperor, Constans.</note>, after the younger

<column-break/>

Constantine was slain in the war, he told him with great lamentation the intent of the Arians, and how they waged war against those who maintained the faith of the Apostles. He also reminded him of his father's name and especially the Council held by him <note>The Council of Nicaea, convened by Constantine the Great in 325 AD.</note>, and that this was established and confirmed by the general Synod. Telling him this with tears moved the Emperor to fatherly zeal. Having heard this, he commanded and exhorted his brother that he should keep his fatherly piety unblemished, as he had ruled with godliness, overcome the Roman tyranny, and made the surrounding peoples obedient to him.

### ¶ Of the death of Alexander, bishop at Constantinople. And how Paul was ordained by the Christians, and Macedonius by the Arians.

## Chapter VIII.

<margin>Alexander dies at Constantinople.</margin>
At this time, a disturbance arose in Constantinople, greater than the first, for these reasons: Alexander, after he had ended the strife with Arius, died in the 33rd year of his Bishopric and in the 98th year of his age. He appointed no one in his place but commanded them to choose one of two whom he would designate. For if they wanted to regard life and quality of teaching, they should take Paul, who had been ordained a Priest by him, of good witness, who, though he is young, is excellent in wisdom. But if they wanted to choose by appearance alone, they should take Macedonius, who was then a Deacon but of great age.

<margin>Macedonius.</margin>

# The Second Part. The Fourth Book.

### ¶ How Eusebius of Nicomedia attacked the See of Constantinople after Paul was driven out. And of the Council of the 90 Bishops at Antioch.

### The IX. Chapter.

<margin>Eusebius of Nicomedia becomes Bishop at Constantinople.</margin>
A short time later, when the Emperor <note>Constantius II, son of Constantine the Great.</note> arrived at Constantinople, he was very ill-pleased by the election made by the Arians <note>Arianism was a theological movement that taught that Jesus Christ was not co-eternal with God the Father, but a created being.</note>. And when he had called a Council of the Bishops, he ensured that Paul was deposed again, and he summoned and appointed Eusebius of Nicomedia to Constantinople to be Bishop there. This having been done, the Emperor traveled to Antioch. Meanwhile, Eusebius, being never at rest, stirred up all things to achieve his purpose. He arranged that under the pretext of a church dedication in Antioch, a Synod should be held. This was for the church which Constantine had begun to build, and which Constantius completed ten years after its beginning. Truly, to look upon this Synod is to see the disturbance and corruption of the Nicene Council <note>The Council of Nicaea (325 AD), which established the orthodox creed against Arianism.</note>. More than 90 Bishops from many cities came to this Synod. However, Maximus, a Bishop of Jerusalem and a successor of Macarius, did not come <note>The text likely means he stayed away or was cautious</note>, considering that they would try to persuade him to subscribe to the condemnation of Athanasius. Likewise, Julius, the Bishop at Rome <note>Pope Julius I.</note>, was not present, nor did he send anyone in his stead, even though it is a rule of the Church that no Council shall be held against the will of the Roman Bishop.

<margin>Council at Antioch where 90 Bishops were present.</margin>
Thus this Synod was held at Antioch in the presence of Emperor Constantius, while Marcellus and Probinus were the chief Consuls. <margin>Flacillus.</margin>

¶ How Gregory arrived at Alexandria and Athanasius fled from there, and what wicked deeds he committed.

### The IX. Chapter.

<margin>Gregory is brought to Alexandria with the help of the Captain.</margin>
In the meantime, Biriamus <note>Likely Syrianus, the military commander in Egypt</note> the Captain led Gregory to Alexandria, accompanied by 5,000 armed soldiers; among them were also the followers of Arius living there.

But regarding the manner in which Athanasius was pushed out of the Church and how he fled without being captured, I think it right to speak here: for it was evening, and the people were holding vigils <note>original: "vigilias", night-time prayer services</note>, and the people hoped a gathering would take place. Meanwhile, the Captain arrived and stationed his soldiers with fleets <note>original: "flotten", likely meaning ranks or companies in this context</note> all around the Church. Athanasius, seeing what was happening and considering that his people might be harmed for his sake, ordered the Deacon to finish the prayer and had a Psalm sung to prevent this. And as they sang together with one heart, they all went out through one door (though there were many doors). As this happened, the soldiers kept still without commotion, and <margin>Athanasius flees to Rome.</margin> Athanasius went out unharmed from the midst of the singers and, thus fleeing, he came to Rome. At that time, Gregory was the leader of the church in Alexandria. However, the Alexandrians, having no pleasure in what had occurred, set fire to the church named Dionysius.

¶ How, after the death of Eusebius, Paul returned to the church and Macedonius was accepted by the Arians.

### The XII. Chapter.

<margin>Julius, the Bishop of Rome, judges the case of Athanasius. Eusebius dies.</margin>
Eusebius sent a legate to Julius, the Bishop at Rome, and requested that he act as judge against Athanasius. But he did not inform Julius of what he had decided regarding Athanasius, because he died shortly after the Council; therefore, the people of Constantinople brought Paul back into the Church. At the same time, the Arians appointed Macedonius

<column-break/>

to Paul's church. This was done by the successors and lovers of Eusebius and his associates, <margin>Paul meets resistance from the Arians.</margin> namely Theogonius of Nicaea, Maris of Chalcedon, Theodore of Heraclea in Thrace, and Ursacius of Singidunum from Moesia; also Valens <margin>Valens.</margin> of Mursa from Upper Pannonia. However, Ursacius and Valens eventually repented and later gave a written statement <note>original: "Libel", a formal document or petition</note> of their conversion to Bishop Julius. And because they also agreed with that word *Homoousion* <note>original: "Homoulion", meaning "of the same substance," the core orthodox term defining Christ's divinity</note>, they were received into the fellowship.

¶ How Hermogenes the Captain tried to drive Paul out of the church and was slain by the people. And what counsel followed after this.

### The XIV. Chapter.

<margin>Civil war is stirred up by Constantine's captain.</margin>
In the meantime, a great war arose on account of the Macedonians, and a civil strife was ignited, which was the cause of much Christian blood being spilled. When Emperor Constantius heard of this—who was then at Antioch—he commanded Hermogenes the Captain to travel to the land of Thrace and drive Paul out of the Church. When he arrived at Constantinople, a riot broke out; the people were ready for revenge because Hermogenes attempted to drive Paul out with an armed hand. The people rushed together (as commonly happens in such things) and resisted him without reason; setting his house on fire, they dragged him around and strangled him. These things happened when Constantine was chief Councilor <note>Consul</note> for the third time and Constans for the second. At this time, Constans subjected the power of the Franks to the Romans. But Constantius, wishing to deal with the death of Hermogenes, <margin>The grain of Constantinople.</margin> came from Antioch to Constantinople and banished Paul from the city. He punished the city by taking away 40,000 measures of grain <note>original: "Cozens", likely referring to the grain dole</note> which his father had given them; for his father used to send 80,000 measures from the city of Alexandria daily to be distributed there.

<margin>Constantius's anger at Macedonius.</margin>
After this happened, he delayed making Macedonius the Bishop of the city: for he was angry with him, not only because he had been ordained Bishop without his will, but also because so many had died in the riot that broke out between Paul and Macedonius.

## ¶ How Gregory of Alexandria was cast out, and Gregory the Cappadocian was accepted by the Arians.

When the Arians had driven Gregory away from Alexandria as a despised man—since an uprising had occurred on his account—nonetheless, those who did not support him chose this Gregory of Cappadocia <note>Gregory of Cappadocia was an Arian installed as Bishop of Alexandria to replace the exiled Athanasius.</note>, poisoned with that Arian venom, to be a Bishop.

## ¶ How the deposed Bishops came to Rome, and how Julius wrote to the Easterners on their behalf.

### The XV. Chapter.

<margin>The bishops, robbed of their churches, come to Rome.</margin>
Now that Athanasius had left Alexandria, he came to Rome. It so happened at the same time that Paul, Bishop of Constantinople, also arrived there, as did Marcellus of Ancyra and Asclepas of Gaza. Because they were opposed to the Arians, they had to endure accusations from them—such as the claim that they had broken the altar—and they were condemned. Therefore, the church of the Gazans was entrusted to Quintianus. But Lucian, Bishop of Adrianople, was accused for another reason and, having left his church, he stayed in Rome. When the Bishop of Rome <note>Pope Julius I, who served from 337 to 352 AD.</note> learned of each man's accusation and found that they all agreed with the Nicene Council <note>The Council of Nicaea (325 AD) which established the orthodox creed against Arianism.</note>, he received them back into communion. And as he cared above all for the dignity of the see <note>original: "stoels digniteyt", referring to the authority of the Apostolic See of Rome</note>, he restored all their churches to them and wrote to the bishops in the East, rebuking them for not having acted rightly against these blameless men by taking away their churches, and for not correctly upholding the decrees of the Nicene Council. He commanded some of them to appear before him on a set day

<column-break/>

to appear, whereby he indicated that he had done nothing unjust against them regarding these matters. He also threatened that he would no longer tolerate it unless they ceased from such commotion and innovation. Thus the Bishop of Rome wrote; but Athanasius and Paul sent the letter of Julius to the Bishops in the East, and so each returned to his own seat.

## ¶ Concerning the answer of the Eastern Bishops.

### The XVI. Chapter.

<margin>The Eastern Bishops write back to the Bishop of Rome.</margin>
<margin>As a school of Apostolic piety and a metropolis.</margin> <note>original Latin: "Tanquam Phronisterium Apostolicorum pietatis metropolis"</note>
<margin>The Easterners believe Athanasius is supported by the Roman Bishop.</margin>
This greatly annoyed the Bishops in the East, and gathering at Antioch, they wrote a letter back to Julius, adorned with an elaborate style of writing—ironic, flattering, and threatening. For they all acknowledged how the Roman Church was honorable above all churches, as the one that held Apostolic care and was a mother and guardian of godly antiquity. Although the preachers of this doctrine had come from the East, they thought they were not inferior for that reason, even if they did not have as many or as great churches, since they were no less in their upright life. They also rebuked Julius for having communion with the followers of Arius, as if he despised their Council and had nullified their opinion, ruining their work as if it were unrighteous and unlike his own holiness. Having written this, they condemned his actions as unjust and contrary to the institutions of the Church. They further added that if Julius accepted their condemned Bishops and established and confirmed the ordained Bishops in the place of the condemned ones, then they would have peace and communion with him. But if he acted against their confession, they would do the opposite, although the Eastern Bishops did not resist him. When Novatus was driven from the Roman church, they did not wish to write to him about what they had done beyond the common consent of the Nicene Council.

Antioch, a city which was shaken by an earthquake for an entire year.

¶ How Gregory arrived at Alexandria, and Athanasius fled from there, and what evil deeds he committed.

### The IX. Chapter.

<margin>Gregory is brought to Alexandria with the help of the captain.</margin>
In the meantime, Syrianus the captain led Gregory to Alexandria, accompanied by 5,000 armed soldiers; with him also were the followers of Arius living there.

But in what manner Athanasius was pushed out of the Church, and how he fled without being captured, I think should be told here: for it was evening, and the people held *vigilias*, that is, vigils <note>original: "vigilias, dat is operavondt." These were overnight prayer services.</note>, and the people hoped an assembly would take place. Meanwhile, the Captain arrived and stationed his soldiers in ranks around the Church. Athanasius, seeing what was happening and considering that his people should not suffer any injury on his account, and wanting to prevent this, ordered the Deacon to conclude the prayer and had a Psalm sung. And as they sang together with one accord, they all went out through a single door (even though there were many doors). As this was happening, the soldiers kept still without any commotion, and Athanasius went out unhurt in the midst of the singers, and thus fleeing, he came to Rome. So it was that Gregory was at that time the leader of the Church at Alexandria; but the Alexandrians, having no pleasure in what had occurred, set fire to the church named after Dionysius.
<margin>Athanasius flees to Rome.</margin>

¶ How after the death of Eusebius, Paul came back into the church, and Macedonius was accepted by the Arians.

### The XII. Chapter.

<margin>Julius the pontiff chose to be Judge over the case of Athanasius. Eusebius’s death.</margin>
Now Eusebius had sent a Legate to Julius, the Bishop of Rome, and prayed that he would act as judge against Athanasius; but what he had decided regarding Athanasius he did not make known to Julius, as he died shortly after the Council. Therefore, the people of Constantinople led Paul back into the Church. And the Arians at the same time presented Mace-

<column-break/>

-donius to the Church of Paul. This was done by the followers and admirers of Eusebius and his associates, namely: Theogonius of Nicaea, Maris of Chalcedon, Theodorus of Heraclea in Thrace, Ursatius of Singidunum in Moesia, and Valens of Mursa in Upper Pannonia. However, Ursatius and Valens repented at last, and afterwards gave a *libel* <note>A formal written petition or statement of faith.</note> of their conversion to Bishop Julius. And since they shared the belief in that word *Homousion* <note>original: "Homousion." A Greek theological term meaning "of the same substance," used to define the relationship between God the Father and God the Son as established at the Council of Nicaea.</note>, they were accepted into communion.
<margin>Paul returns to Constantinople: Arians elect Macedonius.</margin>

¶ How Hermogenes the Captain wanted to drive Paul out of the church, and was slain by the people. And what counsel followed after this.

### The XIII. Chapter.

<margin>Civil war between the citizens of Constantinople. Hermogenes the captain is slain by the citizens.</margin>
In the meantime, for the sake of the Macedonians, a great war arose and a civil strife was ignited, which was the cause of shedding much Christian blood. When the Emperor Constantius heard of this—who was then at Antioch—he commanded the Captain Hermogenes to travel into the land of Thrace and drive Paul out of the church. Upon arriving at Constantinople, an uprising occurred; the people were ready for revenge, while Hermogenes attempted to drive Paul out with an armed hand. The people rushed together (as commonly happens in such things) and resisted him without reason; setting his house on fire, they dragged him about and killed him. These things happened when Constantine <note>Constantine II</note> was consul for the third time and Constans for the second time. At this time, Constans subjected the violence of the Franks to the Romans. But Constantius, when he wished to deal with the death of Hermogenes, came from Antioch to Constantinople and drove Paul out of the city. He punished the city by taking away 40,000 measures of corn which his father <note>Constantine the Great</note> had granted them; for he usually sent the city 80,000 measures daily from Alexandria to be distributed.
<margin>Constantius robs the Constantinopolitans of corn.</margin>

<margin>Constantius is angry at Macedonius.</margin>
This having been done, he delayed making Macedonius Bishop in the City: for he was angry at him, not only because he was ordained Bishop without his consent, but also because in the uprising that arose between Paul and Macedonius, very many people were killed.

### ¶ How the deposed Bishops come to Rome, and how Julius writes to the Easterners on their behalf.

## The XV. Chapter.

<margin>The Bishops, robbed of their churches, come to Rome.</margin>
When Athanasius had now left Alexandria, he came to Rome. It happened that at the same time, Paul, Bishop of Constantinople, also arrived there, as did Marcellus of Ancyra and Asclepas of Gaza. These men, because the Arians were against them, had to suffer accusations from them—such as that they had broken the altar—and were condemned. Therefore, the church of the Gazans was entrusted to Quintinianus; but Lucianus, Bishop of Adrianople, who was accused for another reason and had left his Church, stayed in Rome. When the Roman Bishop <note>Pope Julius I, who reigned from 337 to 352 AD.</note> examined every accusation and found that they all agreed with the Nicene Council, he received them back into communion. And as he, above all, cared for the dignity of his see, he restored all their churches to them and wrote to the bishops in the East and rebuked them, saying they had not acted rightly against these blameless men by taking the Churches from them, and how they did not rightly uphold the decrees of the Nicene Council. He commanded some of them to appear before him on a set day

<column-break/>

to appear, whereby he made it known that he had not acted unjustly against them regarding these matters. He also threatened them that he would suffer it no longer, unless they ceased from such turmoil and innovation. Thus the bishop of Rome wrote; but Athanasius and Paul sent the letter of Julius to the Bishops in the East, and so each returned to his own seat.

### ¶ Regarding the answer of the Eastern Bishops.

## The XVI. Chapter.

<margin>The Eastern Bishops assembled at Antioch write back to the Bishop of Rome.</margin>
This greatly vexed the Bishops in the East, and assembling at Antioch, they wrote a letter back to Julius, decorated with an artful style of writing, in an ironic, flattering, and threatening manner. For they all acknowledged how the Roman Church was preeminent <note>original: "cost-vry", here meaning privileged or held in high honor</note> among all Churches, as the one which had the Apostolic care, and was a mother and guardian of godly antiquity—although the preachers of this doctrine had come from the East—thinking they were therefore not inferior, even if they did not have so many and such great churches. <margin>As if it were a house of study <note>original: "Phrontisterium", a place for meditation or study</note> of Apostolic piety, a metropolis.</margin> Since they were also not more wretched in their upright life. They also rebuked Julius for having held communion with the followers of Arius, as if he despised their Council and had annulled their opinion and ruined their work as unjust, and unlike him in holiness. Having written this, they punished his fine handling as unjust and contrary to the institutions of the Churches. They further added that if Julius would accept the condemned Bishops and would place and confirm the ordained Bishops in the place of the condemned, then they would have peace and communion with him. <margin>The Easterners think that Athanasius was deprived of his ban and made better by the Roman Bishop.</margin> But if he were against their confession, then they would do the opposite, although the Eastern Bishops did not withstand him. When Novatus was driven from the Roman church, regarding what they had acted beyond the common consent of the Nicene Council, they did not wish to write to him about that.

### The XVII. Chapter.

**A**ccordingly, the Bishops in the East wrote of these matters to Bishop Julius in Rome. When Athanasius arrived in Alexandria, there was a great commotion because of George’s <note>George of Cappadocia, an Arian bishop installed by the Emperor to replace Athanasius.</note> people and followers, who had been ordained Bishop in that same place. <margin>Sabinus slanders Athanasius.</margin>
And for this reason, Sabinus, bishop of the Macedonian heresy <note>The Macedonians, also known as Pneumatomachians, denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note>, frequently laid snares for him. ## ¶ How Paul was again driven from Constantinople, what murder was committed there, and how Macedonius returned.

### The XVIII. Chapter.

<margin>Paul is driven out of Constantinople. Philip the Judge, a patron of the Arians. The Baths of Zeuxippus in the other part of the city.</margin>
**S**o then, the Emperor Constantius, residing in Antioch and having heard that Paul had again regained the seat at Constantinople, was enraged. He sent an earnest letter to Philip (the Marshal of Constantinople) <note>Philippus was the Praetorian Prefect, a high-ranking civil administrator.</note> ordering him to drive Paul out of the church and to install Macedonius therein. Whereupon Philip the Marshal, fearing a riot of the people, used a cunning artifice against Paul, hiding the Imperial command and feigning that he was there to act for the common welfare. He went out to the warm Baths of Zeuxippus, which is a large and famous bathhouse, and there he summoned Paul with all honor, as if the necessity required it.

<margin>Paul is condemned to Thessalonica, as if in exile.</margin>
And when Paul arrived there, the Judge Philip immediately showed him the Emperor’s letter. Thus the Judge, fearing the riot of the people, commanded a window near the palace to be opened, and through it had him carried out onto the water, placed in a ship, and sent to Thessalonica, where Paul was born. He punished him by sending him into exile, decreeing that he should not come into the Eastern lands at all.

<column-break/>

However, he was permitted to travel into the lands of Illyricum <note>A Roman province encompassing parts of the modern-day Balkans.</note> and further. Thus Paul was unexpectedly cast out of his Church; and Philip hurried from the bath toward the Church, with Macedonius being carried together with him in the wagon, escorted by soldiers.

<margin>Macedonius is led into the church.</margin>
From this occurrence, a great terror came upon the people, and they all ran together into the church, both the Homoousians and the Arians. When the powerful Marshal Philip arrived at the church with Macedonius, a great dread fell upon the people and the soldiers, for the multitude was so vast that Philip could not pass through. There, the soldiers began to force the people to give way by violence; yet because they could not move due to the narrowness of the space, the soldiers drew their swords and struck into the crowd. At that time, it is said that three thousand and one hundred and fifty people were slain without mercy.

<margin>More than three thousand were slain.</margin>
Some were slaughtered, others were trampled, and others died in the crush. In this manner, Macedonius regained that Bishopric, like one who has done nothing wrong and is pure and innocent, though it was more through the Marshal than by the ordinances of the Church. With such a murder, the Arians and Macedonians came to the Church. At this time, the Emperor built the Great Church, which is now called Sophia <note>The Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, originally commissioned by Constantine and rebuilt/expanded by his successors.</note>, which stands firmly by the church called Irene <note>The Hagia Irene (Holy Peace), one of the oldest churches in Constantinople.</note>, which the father of the Emperor enlarged because it was previously small; now they are joined in one complex.

## ¶ How Athanasius was accused of theft.

### The XIX. Chapter.

<margin>Accusation against Athanasius regarding how he allegedly stole grain.</margin>
**I**n the meantime, another plot was undertaken against Athanasius. For the Emperor’s Father <note>Emperor Constantine the Great.</note> had given certain quantities of grain as a gift to the Church at Alexandria to be distributed to the poor. They alleged that Athanasius had sold this grain and kept the money for his own benefit.

Believing this, the Emperor commanded Athanasius to be put to death. Athanasius, perceiving this, fled secretly. Whereupon Julius, Bishop of Rome, recognizing the snares laid by the Arians against Athanasius after he had received the letter of Eusebius, recalled Athanasius when he knew where he was hidden. In the meantime, he also received letters from the Bishops in Egypt.

## ¶ Concerning the death of Paul, Bishop of Constantinople.

### The XXII. Chapter.

And persecuting Paul, Bishop of Constantinople, and finding him in Cucusus, Cappadocia, they openly confessed and admitted that he should be strangled; to which end Philip the Prefect assisted, who was a patron of their heresies and a promoter of their mischievous, wicked reasoning. ## ¶ Concerning the assembly of the Bishops at the Council of Sardica.

### The XXIII. Chapter.

<margin>In the Western regions. <note>original: "Hisperijs Partibus"</note></margin>
It was the eleventh year after the death of the father of these two Emperors <note>Constantine the Great.</note>. And when Ruffinus and Eusebius were the chief Councilors <note>referring to the Roman Consuls for the year 347 AD, though the council date is debated.</note>, the Council of Sardica was held. From the Western lands, about 300 Bishops came to the Council, as Athanasius writes. From the Northern/Eastern lands, there were 76, as Sabinus says, among whom Ischyras was also counted—a Bishop of Mareotis, whom the condemners of Athanasius had made a bishop of that province.

<column-break/>

Some excused themselves by reason of bodily illness. Others claimed the shortness of time and therefore blamed Julius, Bishop of Rome.
<margin>Synod held 43 years after the Council [of Nicaea] was proposed. <note>The margin is partially unclear, but refers to the chronological distance from the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.</note></margin>

Yet the Synod had been announced a year and six weeks beforehand, and Athanasius lived in Rome, <unclear>awaiting</unclear> the judgment of the Council. When the people of Sardica and the Orientals had <unclear>gathered</unclear>, they did not wish to face the Orientals, saying that they would not enter into speech with them unless they first drove the friends and supporters of Athanasius and Paul away from their fellowship. When Protogenes, a Bishop of Sardica, and Hosius of Córdoba, Spain—as protectors of Paul and Athanasius—refused to be cast out from the Council, they <note>the Eastern bishops</note> turned back and departed in haste.
<margin>Protogenes and Hosius. The others depart and come to Philippopolis to strengthen their heresy.</margin>

And they came to Philippopolis, a city in Thrace, and held a separate Council there, openly condemning those who spoke of the "Consubstantiality"—that is, of the "same essence" <note><term>Consubstantiality</term>: The doctrine that the Father and the Son are of the same substance/essence (Greek: *Homoousios*).</note>—and they put their error into a document and sent it everywhere. Those who had come to Sardica first condemned this deceit; thereafter, they stripped the accusers of Athanasius of their honors. And when they had confirmed the Article of the Nicene Faith and rejected the libel of the "dissimilarity of the Divine Being," they publicly testified to the Consubstantiality: that is, how the Father and Son are of one essence. Having contained this in a document, they sent it everywhere. Both sides thought that they had sufficiently settled the matter: the Orientals, because they took back those who had been condemned by them; the Westerners, because they held to the Nicene faith and because they <note>the Easterners</note> withdrew before the condemners had acknowledged them, they considered that this faith was being burdened by them, and thus they restored Paul and Athanasius to their places. Likewise, they restored Marcellus of Ancyra in Galatia, who had for a long time (as has just been said) been condemned.

<meta>catchword: the</meta>

<margin>The Letter of the Council of Sardica.</margin>

**A** The Synod at Sardica, gathered by the grace of God from the cities of Rome, Spain, Gaul <note>original: "Vranckrijc"</note>, Italy, Campania, Pannonia, Mysia, Dacia, Dardania, Calabria, the other Dacia, Macedonia, Thessaly, Achaia, Epirus, Thrace, Rhodope, Asia, Caria, Bithynia, the Hellespont, Phrygia, Pisidia, Cappadocia, Pontus, Cilicia, the other Phrygia, Pamphylia, Lydia, from the islands of the Cyclades, Egypt, Thebaid, Libya, Galatia, Palestine, and Arabia—all being Bishops and fellow-servants of the Holy Apostolic Church, to our most beloved brethren: Salvation in the Lord.

**B** The followers of the <term>Arian madness</term> <note>Arianism was the belief that Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father; the author views this as a "madness" or heresy.</note> have often sought to attack and defile the servants of God and those who preserve the true faith. Because they put forward a false teaching, they also endeavored to oppress the true Christian believers, and thus they set themselves against the faith so that the matter eventually came before the pious and God-loving Emperor. **C** Therefore, the cooperating grace of God, which through the pious Prince has gathered us from all provinces and cities, has commanded that the Holy Council be held in the city of Sardica, so that once all discord and unbelief are removed, the Christian faith alone may remain whole and unblemished for every person.

<margin>Athanasius. Marcellus. Asclepas.</margin>
<margin>Julius, Bishop at Rome.</margin>

**D** The Eastern Bishops, summoned by the pious Emperor, have also arrived, primarily because of the fame and reputation spread by our dear and godly fellow-servants and beloved brothers: namely, Athanasius of Alexandria, Marcellus, Bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, and Asclepas of Gaza. It may happen that their detractors have come to you, attempting to make these innocent men look loathsome in your eyes, so that they might better hide the wicked intent of their heresy. **E** However, they are no longer permitted to carry this out; for the rightful Bishop of the Church, the Lord Jesus—who suffered death for these and others and won Heaven for us—would no longer suffer such things. Previously, Eusebius, Maris, Theodorus, Theogonius, Ursacius, Valens, Menophantus, and Stephanus wrote to our fellow-servant <term>Julius, the Bishop at Rome</term> <note>Pope Julius I, a supporter of the Nicene Creed and Athanasius.</note>, against our aforementioned fellow-priests: Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria; Marcellus, Bishop of Ancyra in Galatia; and Asclepas of Gaza. **F** Bishops from other places also wrote, giving testimony to the innocence of Athanasius, our fellow-priest, saying that everything Eusebius and his party had done was nothing but a pack of lies and slander.

<column-break/>

<margin>Julius, Roman Bishop.</margin>

**G** For when our beloved fellow-brother, Bishop Julius, summoned them to Rome to appear before him—as is noted in his writings—they refused to appear. From this, it is clearly evident that they deal in lies and are false accusers, should one recount the events that transpired with them. **H** Their falsehood is also clearly revealed by what they did in this Holy and Great Council; for having arrived in the city of Sardica and seeing our brothers Athanasius, Marcellus, Asclepas, and others there, they were afraid to come before the court. Even though they were called many times, they refused to come. <margin>Osius.</margin> **I** Also present was the elderly and venerable <term>Osius</term> <note>Hosius of Corduba, a highly respected advisor to Constantine and a leading figure at the Council of Nicaea.</note>, who by reason of his great age, his labors, and his public confession of faith, was rightly held in high esteem. He and others bore with them and urged them to enter into judgment, so that they might prove in the presence of their brothers the slanders they had written against them in their absence. **J** But as has been said, they did not come, even though they were summoned. By this, they themselves brought their accusations and secret intentions to light; **K** for, beloved brothers, those who trust in their cause do not flee from proving it face-to-face. Since they do not come forward, who can doubt—even if they still try to accuse their fellow brothers and servants in their absence—that they would have to confess and make it right if they were present? They have fled (beloved brothers) not only because of the evidence <note>original: "wapenen," literally "weapons," here meaning the rhetorical or legal tools used against them.</note> prepared against their slander, but truly also because they saw that their own followers were joining the accusers in various counts of guilt. **L** There, bonds and chains were also produced as evidence. Priests and other acquaintances and friends came out of <term>exile</term> <note>Many orthodox bishops had been banished by the pro-Arian emperors.</note>, as did those who had died for their cause. And what is most astonishing: bishops arrived there, one of whom carried a chain and bonds with which he had been bound for their sake. **M** Others recounted how, because of the plots laid against them, they had often been in peril of death. For they [the Arians] have grown in such pride and insanity that they endeavored to kill the bishops, had they not been delivered by flight. <margin>Theodulus.</margin> The pious Theodulus also came there, whose intent they had also exposed, as they had ordered him to be killed.

Some showed the wounds from swords; others sighed, telling how they had been held by them for a long time without food...

### Tripartite Ecclesiastical History

<page-num>Fol. 284.</page-num>

<margin>The letters of Theogonius against Athanasius.</margin>
...they had been there, and all the churches spoke of it, announcing and making known the destructive violence. The arming of the soldiers, the people with clubs <note>original: "Colven"; likely refers to maces or heavy staves used by guards</note>, the fear of the judges, and the presentation of forged letters; also, the letters of Theogonius were read, which he had written against our brothers and fellow-priests Athanasius, Marcellus, and Asclepas. These letters moved the Emperor and turned him against us—letters which had come by way of the Deacon Theogonius. Meanwhile, it was told how they had stripped virgins naked, set fire to churches, and imprisoned fellow priests. All this conflict they had stirred up solely for the sake of the accursed heresy of Arius.

Those who refused his communion and despised their [Arian] regulations were forced to suffer such insults and injustice. When they were thus cornered by their own evil deeds and put to shame, they fled. And when they could no longer hide these things, they came to the city of Sardica so that they might appear as if they were innocent in this matter. But when they saw those whom they had wronged and oppressed, who were also their accusers—indeed, when the accusation itself was now before their eyes—even though they were summoned, they refused to enter the court. But Athanasius, Marcellus, and Asclepas, our fellow-brothers, held their ground bravely and with good courage, making themselves heard and demonstrating how they were prepared to prove the slander against them: yes, and even how these others had sinned against their own churches. At this, the accusers were so terrified and stricken in their consciences that they fled, and by their flight, they revealed their guilt and wrongdoing.

And although their wickedness was made manifest not only by the past but by the present, we wish to take up and recount their dealings, which are contrary to the truth, so that they may have no cause for further evil through their flight. First, we noted their deceit in what happened there: that they are false accusers against one of our fellow priests, namely Arsenius, whom they said had been killed by Athanasius; yet he lives, and it is known that he is among the living. From this, one can clearly see how the other things said against him were fabricated. They also argued a case regarding how Macarius, a priest of Athanasius, supposedly broke a chalice <note>original: "drincker"; referring to a sacramental cup used in the Eucharist</note>; this is also not true, as has been testified by those who came from Alexandria and Mareotis.
<margin>Arsenius.</margin>

<column-break/>

So also the Bishops of Egypt wrote to our fellow priest Julius <note>original: "Julio"; refers to Pope Julius I</note>, assuring him that there was not an evil thought to be found there.
<margin>Julius, High Priest at Rome.</margin>

Furthermore, they said that they had performed many secret signs. Heathens and <term>catechumens</term> <note>Those receiving instruction in the faith but not yet baptized; they were traditionally excluded from certain parts of the liturgy.</note> were brought forward for this, one of whom, being a guard, said he was present when Macarius arrived. Another said that the famous Ischyras was then lying sick in a cell. From this, one may see that nothing was done in secret, since the catechumens were there, and Ischyras was not present but lay ill. This wicked Ischyras invented a lie that Athanasius had burned certain books, even though it is clear that he lay sick at the time Macarius was there; from this, it is evident that he is a false accuser. But for this slander, they rewarded Ischyras by naming him a Bishop, though he had never even been a priest. For the two priests who formerly lived with <term>Meletius</term> <note>original: "Militio"; referring to Meletius of Lycopolis, who caused a schism in the Egyptian church.</note>, and were later received by the blessed Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, and stationed with Athanasius, have testified that he was never a priest. Nor did Meletius ever have a church or a servant in Mareotis, and there was no priest there. Out of this man [Ischyras], they have now made a Bishop, using these titles to terrify their listeners with their slanders. Also read were the letters of our fellow priest Marcellus, and it was found that they [the accusers] are at one with the wickedness of Eusebius. On the contrary, the faith of Marcellus was found to be right; for God did not give the beginning of the Word in Mary, as they say. Nor did he say that his dominion has an end, but wrote that his kingdom is without beginning and without end. But Asclepas, our fellow servant, brought old writings from Antioch, made in the presence of the accusers and Eusebius of Caesarea, and signed by the judgment of the Bishops, declaring him innocent. It is rightly done (dear brethren) that they have fled; for being called, they would not obey or appear; their conscience accused them, and by their flight, they have confessed their guilt and proved the charges brought against them.
<margin>Ischyras</margin>

<margin>Asclepas.</margin>
