# The Second Part. The Fourth Book.

<margin>The Arians present their declarations to great lords.</margin>
A ¶ Furthermore, those who were accused of the heresy of Arius <note>Arianism was the belief that Jesus Christ was a created being, not co-eternal or of the same substance as God the Father.</note> have not only been taken in, but have been allowed to become great lords; they have made Deacons into Priests and Priests into Bishops. This was done for the sole reason that they might spread their godless teaching far and wide and hinder the true faith.

B ¶ These, then, are their champions: Eusebius, Theognis of Heraclea, Narcissus of Neronias in Cilicia, Stephen of Antioch, George <note>Original: "Gregorius"</note> of Laodicea, Acacius of Caesarea in Palestine, Menophantus of Ephesus, Ursacius of Mygdonia, and Valens of Mysia in Pannonia. These men came together but would join neither with the Easterners at the Council nor with the Church of God. When they arrived at Sardica, they organized their own separate councils and assemblies in various places, weaving together "Acts" <note>Records or decrees of their own meeting</note> with boasting, whereby no reasonable business was handled, and the holy and useful Council was hindered.

<margin>Arian coercion.</margin>
C ¶ We have understood all these things from our fellow brothers Macarius of Palestine and Asterius of Arabia, who came with them but then abandoned their unbelief. For once they had come into the holy Council, they made known what violence they had suffered at their hands, saying that nothing was handled rightly among them; indeed, they added: when anyone was on the path of the true faith, they hindered them from reaching it and threatened them so that they could only escape from them with great difficulty.

D ¶ For these reasons they came to Sardica and all remained together, unable to part from one another even for a short time, since one could not remain silent and allow this slander to pass without harm. The exiles, the killings, the wounds, the robbery of forged letters, the scourgings, the stripping of virgins, the banishments, the destruction of churches, the fires, the relocation from small towns into great churches—and above all things, the Arian madness against the true Christian faith—were the reasons why our dear brothers and fellow servants, Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, Marcellus of Ancyra in Galatia, and Asclepas of Gaza, the servants of Christ, were recognized as pure and innocent. It has been written to everyone so that the people may know that they have innocent and godly Bishops.

F ¶ But those who have forced themselves into the churches like wolves are Gregory in Alexandria, Basil in Ancyra, and Quintianus in Gaza. These men shall be held neither as Bishops nor as Christians—

<column-break/>

<margin>Therefore, do not deal with the re-excommunicated heretics.</margin>
G —and one shall have no communion at all with them; their letters shall not be received, nor shall any answer be given to them. Regarding Theodore of Heraclea in Europe, Narcissus of Nerona in Cilicia, Acacius of Caesarea in Palestine, Stephen of Antioch, Ursacius of Mysia, Valens of Mysia in Pannonia, Menophantus of Ephesus, and George of Laodicea: although they did not come from the East out of fear, yet because they were banned by Alexander of blessed memory, the former Bishop of Alexandria, for harboring the Arians, the holy Council has deposed them from their bishoprics by a common vote.

<margin>The Decree <note>Original: "Syndamus"</note></margin>
H We have also declared that they shall not only cease to be Bishops, but all communion with the faithful shall be stripped from them. For those who say that the Word of God is not GOD shall be banished from the Christian Church—yes, even from the Christian name—since they have despised the Word of God.

<margin>Galatians 1:8.</margin>
I For this is a command of the Apostle Paul: Even if we, or an angel from heaven, preached to you otherwise than what we have preached to you, let him be cursed.

<margin>2 Cor. 6:14.</margin>
<margin>Sirach 13:1.</margin>
<margin>2 Thess. 3:6</margin>
<margin>1 Cor. 5:8.</margin>
K Wishing also to proclaim: Let no one have communion with such people; just as there is no communion of light with darkness. Drive these far from you, for Christ has no communion with Belial. Guard yourselves, dear brothers, that you do not write to them nor receive their writings. Be diligent, dear brothers and fellow servants, as those who agree with our Council everywhere through the Holy Spirit, and testify with your signature so that it may be maintained with one mind by all fellow servants everywhere.

L ¶ Let us have no communion with those who say: CHRIST is GOD, but not true GOD; He is a Son, but not a true Son, etc., and let us drive them far from the Church. To Christ, who is from eternity, they have given a beginning and an end, which He did not have in time, but before all time; therefore, two serpents have emerged from the Arian pit.

M ¶ Valens and Ursacius, who, although they boast of being Christians, nevertheless confess that the Word and the Spirit were wounded and killed, died and rose again. Like the "Rot-heretics" <note>A derogatory term for radical sectarian groups, possibly referring here to the Sabellians or a similar faction</note>, these also say that the essence <term>substance|The underlying "stuff" of God's being</term> of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is a divided essence.

<sig>G</sig>

<margin>The holy catholic faith.</margin>
¶ Furthermore, we understand and are taught by the Apostolic faith how it rests upon a single essence <note>Original: "wesen", referring to the Greek "ousia" or substance</note> of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And if they ask what is the nature of the essence of the Son, we say that it is the very same essence of the Father; never was the Father without his Son, nor the Son without the Father, which is neither believable nor possible. This is the testimony of His Son: <margin>John 14.</margin> "I am in the Father, and the Father is in me; I and the Father are one." Let no one among us deny that he was born; but he was born before all things, visible and invisible, and he is the Master-worker <note>Original: "Werckmeester", a translation of the Greek "demiurgos", the divine craftsman of the universe</note> of the Angels, of the world, and of the entire human <margin>Heb. 1. Col. 1:17. Prov. 8:22. Wisd. 7:21. John 1:3.</margin> race: for thus it is written, "the Master-worker of all things has taught it to me," and "all things were made through him." Now, how could he have been eternal if he had a beginning? For since the Word which is eternal has no beginning, so God has no end.

¶ In summary, we believe, speak, and understand just as Holy Scripture speaks of it: "I and the Father are one." We believe in and find the Comforter, the <margin>Isa. 54:5. John 10:30 and 14:9. John 14:16.</margin> Holy Spirit, whom the LORD promised and ordained for us, and we believe that he was sent. But this one did not suffer; rather, the man who was conceived from the Virgin Mary, he was able to suffer as a mortal man, but GOD is immortal. We believe that on the third day he rose again from the dead; not God within the man, but the man rose within God, whom he also offered as a gift to GOD his Father, which man he also redeemed. We believe also that at the appointed time, he shall judge all people and all things, just as their foolishness and darkened understanding have blinded them. Thus they have not been able to see the Light of truth, nor understand it, as it is written, <margin>John 17.</margin> "that they may be one." It is clear why he said this: for the Apostles received the Holy Spirit, yet they were not Spirits themselves; none of them was the Word, the Wisdom, the Power, or the only-begotten Son. "Just as I and you are one" (he says), so are these one. Therefore, <margin>Concerning the unity of God, Christ, and his disciples.</margin> Holy Scripture has certainly distinguished this and said: "That they may be one in us, just as we are one." I, the Father, and the Disciples are one in knowledge, in the grace and power of God the Father; and through the grace and godliness of the Father of our dear Lord and Savior, they may be one.

From this letter, the accusation of these accusers and the unjust judgment of the unjust judges is well known and understood, as is

<column-break/>

the sound and true Teaching. For the dear fathers have not only given us a good report of the Divine nature, but have also declared how God became man.

## Concerning the Legate from Sardica to Constantius, and the wicked deed of Stephen, Bishop of Antioch.

### The 25th Chapter.

<margin>Silvanus the captain, Legate of Constantius for Athanasius. Stephen, a deceitful man.</margin>
Constans, recognizing this, was very sorrowful, seeing the fickleness of his brother <note>His brother was Emperor Constantius II, who supported the Arian faction.</note>, and he became angry against the authors of this evil deed. He chose two Bishops from the Council of Sardica and sent them with letters to his brother, and with them Silvanus the Captain, a pious and godly man. These letters contained not only admonitions and advice, but also instructions on how pious Princes ought to act, and sometimes even threats. For first, he announced to his brother how he wished the Bishops to be heard, to recognize what villainy had been undertaken by Stephen and others previously, and since the slanders and the shameful deeds of the previous judges and their grimness were now revealed to him, he should rightly allow Athanasius back to his Church. And he made it known that if he [Constantius] would not do what was right, he [Constans] would travel to Alexandria himself to restore Athanasius to his longing Church and drive the enemies away with hope. Constantius, receiving this letter in Antioch, promised that he would do as the letter demanded. When the opposers of the truth were greatly vexed by this, they undertook a shameful deed: for the two Bishops whom the Council <margin>Arians by deceit undermine the Christian teachers. Onager, a leader of rascals.</margin> had sent were turned into a house located on a mountain. But the leader Stephen, who was then a bishop in Antioch, along with his other helpers—great scoundrels—prepared to bring about "shipwreck" <note>Metaphorical for total ruin or destruction of faith/reputation</note> so that they might stifle the true confessors of Christian teaching altogether. To this end, he was helped by a young guide named Onager <note>Latin for "Wild Ass," a nickname for a violent and unruly person.</note>, who practiced much wantonness and rejoiced in doing evil; he not only did much evil in the streets, beating people with sticks, but also broke into houses and dragged out men and women, dealing with them according to his own pleasure.

<margin>Euphrates and Vincentius Licentianus are sought to be entrapped by the Arians using harlots.</margin>

A ¶ This man named Onager <note>Original: "Onager," meaning "Wild Ass," a nickname for a certain Arian accomplice</note> made an arrangement with a harlot and told her that some strangers had arrived who required a woman for the night. He took with him fifteen riotous knaves and hid them near the inn where these Bishops were resting. He went with the harlot to the door where these men were sleeping and, unfastening it, he gave money to a servant, deceiving him into thinking he wished to lead the woman inside to the place he would point out—where the two priests were sleeping. He told the woman to go in, while he went away to call his companions. It so happened that one of the two Bishops, named Euphrates, lay in the outer part of the chamber, while Vincentius lay in the inner room.

<margin>Bishop Euphrates calls upon the Lord Christ for help. Onager is confounded.</margin>

B When the harlot came in, Euphrates heard the rustling of feet—C for it was dark—and asked who went there. The harlot began to speak, and Euphrates was terrified, thinking it was a Devil who had taken the form of a woman’s voice, and he very hastily called upon Christ the Lord for help. At this, Onager entered with his companions and made a great outcry about the "wicked men" whom the Judge should punish. When a great commotion arose and the servants D and the household came running, Vincentius stood up and locked the house doors, managing to catch five of the accusers. But Onager fled with the others, and the harlot was kept there with them. When morning came, they woke the Captain <note>A military commander or high-ranking official acting as an escort</note> who had come with them and went to the Palace, openly decrying the schemes of Stephen <note>Stephen was the Arian Bishop of Antioch who orchestrated the frame-up</note>: how one should use neither E judgment, nor blows, nor coercion to prove his wickedness. The Captain also publicly proclaimed that they should not act as was customary in a Synod, but proceed legally against them. He said that he wished first to deliver the clerics and servants of the Bishops to justice, and thereafter deal likewise with the servants of Stephen. But when that shameless man spoke against this, saying it was not fitting to hear the matter in the Palace, F they first questioned the woman as to who had led her into the Bishops’ inn. Yet that church was not entirely delivered from that Arian poison, for Leontius from Phrygia—a great fox—became Bishop after him. When Constantius knew through experience what schemes had been carried out against the Bishops, he wrote to the great Athanasius once, twice, and three times, that he should return, as his letters show.

### ¶ What Athanasius requested from Constantius, and how the heretics were driven out when the Christian Bishops returned to their Churches.

### The XXX. Chapter.

<margin>H</margin>
Being comforted by this letter, Athanasius came into the Eastern lands. The Emperor Constantius did not then take this poorly, but undertook to judge him and to preempt what had been left behind by the Arian teaching; he said to him: "Through the confession of the Council you have regained your seat, and are satisfied through our consent."

<margin>K The Arians request a church.</margin>
"But since there are some people in the city of Alexandria who do not wish to have communion with you, allow them a Church in the city." Thereupon Athanasius answered: "O Emperor, you have the power to command and to do what pleases you. But I also desire a favor from Your Lordship; <note>original: "W. L." - Uwe Liecheit/Lust, a formal address to a sovereign.</note> I pray that you will not refuse me." The Emperor immediately promising to grant it, Athanasius said: "I desire, just like the Emperor,

<margin>L Requested for the right Christian believers.</margin>
that in all cities a Church be allowed for those who have no communion with the Arians." The Arians, recognizing that Athanasius's proposal would be disadvantageous to them, said the matter should be looked into, and they would do what seemed good to the Emperor. Whereupon the Emperor restored to Paul, Athanasius, Marcellus, Asclepas of Gaza, and Lucius of Adrianople their own seats and Bishoprics, just as the Council of Sardica had confirmed.

<margin>M The Prince's Letter.</margin>
Then the Emperor's letters were sent into all cities, commanding them how they should receive the Bishops back again.

<margin>Marcellus in Ancyra not without unrest.</margin>
When Basilius was driven out of Ancyra and Marcellus was accepted, there was no small commotion among those who felt otherwise. Those of Gaza received Asclepas. Those of Constantinople, after Paul, accepted Macedonius for a short time, and he established a separate Church for himself.

**B**ut the opponents of Athanasius, thinking they had a favorable time, prepared themselves again to calumniate him <note>To calumniate is to make false and defamatory statements.</note>, and suggested to Emperor Constantius how he had supposedly devastated all Egypt and Libya, and it weighed heavily upon him that he had established order in other churches.

<meta>This page continues the history of the mid-4th century church, transitioning from the return of Athanasius to a renewed period of Arian persecution under Emperor Constantius II following the death of his brother Constans.</meta>

# The Second Part. The Fourth Book. Folio 293.

<margin>A. *Constantius* becomes *Arian* again.</margin>
When *Athanasius* arrived at *Alexandria*, he gathered a *Synod* of the *Egyptian* Bishops, who all unanimously reached the same conclusions as the *Councils* of *Sardica* and *Jerusalem*. However, the Emperor *Constantius*, who had previously leaned toward the *Arian* sect, changed everything that had previously pleased him to the contrary. First, he sent Bishop *Paul* of *Constantinople* into exile, whose companions were killed in *Cusa, Armenia*. 
And when *Marcellus* was driven out again, *Basil* once more took over the Church at *Ancyra*.
<margin>B. Bishop *Paul* killed. *Marcellus* driven out.</margin>
<margin>C. *Lucius* died in the dungeon. *Athanasius* driven out again by *Constantius*.</margin>
*Lucius*, then a Bishop at *Adrianople*, was bound with iron and died in the dungeon. And so much weight did the Emperor give to everything said against *Athanasius* that he became enraged and commanded that wherever he was found, he should be put to death, and with him also *Theodolus* and *Olympus*, bishops of the churches of *Thrace*.
<margin>D.</margin>
*Athanasius*, not unmindful of the Emperor’s will and intentions but observing everything closely, fled from there and escaped the emperor’s threats. The *Arians* also made much of *Athanasius’s* flight, especially *Narcissus*, bishop of *Neroniadis*, *George* of *Laodicea*, and *Leontius*, Bishop of the Church at *Antioch*.
<margin>E. *Leontius* is removed from the priestly order. He castrates himself.</margin>
For this man <note>Leontius of Antioch</note>, when he was a Priest, was stripped of his office because he lived with a woman named *Eustolia*; and to avoid evil suspicion, he cut out his own genitalia so that he might thereafter live with the woman more securely. <note>Self-castration was strictly forbidden by the first canon of the Council of Nicaea; Leontius did this to circumvent accusations of "subintroductae," or women living with clergy.</note>
<margin>F.</margin>
This man, through the diligence of the Emperor, was afterward ordained Bishop at *Antioch* and placed in the position of *Stephen*, who had first

<column-break/>

come after *Placitus*. But enough has now been said of this.

->¶ Concerning *Macedonius* and his Tyranny.<-

### The XXIX. Chapter.

<margin>G. *Macedonius*, an *Arian*, and a destroyer of the church.</margin>
Up until this time, *Macedonius* was the bishop at *Constantinople*. But although *Paul*, as has been said, was also there, *Macedonius*—boasting of the Emperor's favor—waged a war against the *Christians* <note>meaning the Nicene Christians</note> and did no less than the tyrants of that same time, advising the Emperor to grant him aid to lay waste and destroy the Churches.
<margin>H. Stirs up a destructive war against the Christians.</margin>
He also brought it about that all his evil deeds were protected by law, arming himself in many monasteries which he founded of his own will in the city of *Constantinople*. With the alliance of the Bishops around him, he inflicted much suffering upon those who followed the teaching of *Paul* <note>the Nicene Bishop Paul</note>, first casting them out of the Churches and then forcing them to hold communion with him, so that many fell away because of the persecutions. Some had their goods seized, others were forbidden from civic life, and others were branded on the forehead so that they might be marked.
<margin>I. *Excommunication* involves the seizure of goods, outlawing, and branding.</margin>
This occurred throughout all the cities in the East, and especially in *Constantinople*. This persecution was at first bearable, but Bishop *Macedonius* greatly increased it; however, the cities of *Greece*, *Illyria*, and the places in the West remained unshaken.
<margin>K.</margin>

# Theodoret.

<margin>
The Arians persuade Emperor Constantius that Athanasius was the cause of the conflict between him and his brother.
</margin>
#### ¶ How, after the death of Constans, the Arians incited Constantius against Athanasius.

##### The First Chapter.

Not long after the Emperor Constans died in the Western lands, the Arians—those who sided with Arius—pressured the Emperor [Constantius] and planted the idea in his memory that it was Athanasius who had incited his brother against him. They suggested that Athanasius had nearly caused the brothers to tear the bonds of nature and destroy one another through war.

<margin>
Sebastian was sent to kill Athanasius.
</margin>
¶ With this provocation, they made Constantius so agitated that he commanded not only that Athanasius be driven out, but also that he be killed. He dispatched a captain named Sebastian with a great army, commanding him not only to expel Athanasius but to kill him like a fugitive. How Sebastian arrived with his army, what Athanasius suffered, and how wonderfully he was delivered, Athanasius himself tells best in his defense of his flight, writing as follows:

#### ¶ What Athanasius noted in his *Apologia* <note>original: "Apologia"; a formal written defense of one's opinions or conduct.</note> regarding his flight.

<column-break/>

##### The Second Chapter.

Truly, the wise will seek the reasons for my withdrawal, and they shall acknowledge that the Arians joined themselves to the soldiers so that they might lead them and betray me (of whom they knew nothing) and reveal exactly where I was staying.

<margin>
The early arrival of Christians for the Vigils and watches.
</margin>
And although there is no compassion in them, yet upon hearing this, they shall be put to shame and rest in confusion. It was night, and some of the people had come for the <term>Vigils</term> <note>Nighttime prayer services held before a major feast day.</note> and watches, and they were waiting for the <term>Collect</term> <note>The general gathering or assembly of the congregation for prayer the following day.</note> or assembly of the next day. Suddenly, the <term>Duke</term> <note>A military commander, likely Syrianus, though here referred to by his title.</note> was there with more than five thousand soldiers. These were armed with naked swords, bows, arrows, and clubs, and the captain surrounded the church with them so that not a single person might escape his hand.

<margin>
Psalm 136. The response of the people to the reading of the Psalm.
</margin>
Amidst such confusion of the unruly people, I judged it best to leave that same people so that I would not fall into greater danger. Therefore, I commanded the deacon to read a Psalm, and the people were to respond to it: *For his mercy endureth forever.* <note>Psalm 136, a traditional song of thanksgiving.</note> And after that, they were to depart.

Now when the captain had entered, and the soldiers surrounded the <term>sacrarium</term> <note>The sanctuary or most holy part of the church building.</note> and the choir so that they might capture us, the clergy and the common people cried out and desired that we should make our escape with the crowd. To this, I answered that I would not withdraw until they all went out...

...suffered immeasurably great martyrdom / and / says thus: ¶ Therefore no one among you ought to be mournful / if the ungodly deny you burial / and the like / such as being carried out to the grave / because the Arian malice has gone so far / that they have even closed the gates / and they sit upon the churchyards like Devils / so that no one of the dear right-believing <note>The term "recht-gheloovighe" refers to the Orthodox/Nicene Christians as opposed to the Arians.</note> people may be buried there: This / and the like George did in Alexandria.

The Holy Athanasius could not consider himself safe in any place / since the Emperor commanded that he be brought before him alive or dead / or beheaded / just as he promised a great reward / to whoever should bring him such news.

# Socrates.

### ¶ How Vetranio was deprived of the Empire.

### The 4th Chapter.

<margin>Constantius moves with his army into Illyricum.</margin>
In the meantime, common necessity forced the Emperor to station himself in Illyricum <note>A region in the western Balkans.</note> / because the soldiery had made Vetranio <note>original: "Britavionem"</note> Emperor / and when he came to Sirmium / he saw Vetranio / and made a treaty with him. And it happened / that the soldiers who proclaimed Vetranio Emperor and stood with him / afterwards defected to Constantius / therefore they later cried out / that Constantius alone should be *Imperator Augustus*, that is / Emperor. When no mention was made of Vetranio / he saw / that he was betrayed / and fell at the Emperor’s feet / there the Emperor Constantius took the Crown and the purple <note>The purple robe was the primary symbol of imperial office.</note> from him / and spoke mercifully with him / warning him / since he was deprived of his power / that he should now keep quiet / and rather live for himself (as befits his old age) than to have a title that was burdened with great care and labor / and ordered that he should be given a reasonable livelihood and maintenance from the public treasury. When he now lived in Prusa, Bithynia <note>original: "Prusia Betinie Britanio"</note> / he wrote to the Emperor and showed him / that he had been a cause of many good things / and that he had delivered him from great evils. Yet the Emperor did not do right / since he himself did not lead such a good life / as he had granted to Vetranio.
<margin>Vetranio in Bithynia and Prusa is a small town.</margin>

<column-break/>

### ¶ Of the Emperor Gallus.

### The 5th Chapter.

Then the Emperor made Gallus, his sister’s son, Emperor / and gave him his name and sent him into Syria to Antioch / so that the Eastern Lands might be protected by him. When he had come to Antioch / then that sign of the Savior, the Holy Cross, appeared in the East / for a Column in the form of the Cross was seen in the Sky / as a sign of great wonder.
<margin>Crosses appeared in the sky.</margin>
Others of his courtiers / he sent out with a great army against Magnentius <note>original: "Magentium", a rival usurper.</note>: but he, then living in Sirmium / waited for the outcome of the business. Then Photinus came forward with his doctrine.
<margin>Constantius against Magnentius.</margin>

He said / God the Almighty is one / who created everything through his own word: But to say that the Son had existed from eternity / and his essence was always without beginning / that he shunned. But he taught how Christ was born of Mary.
<margin>Photinus the heretic.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the theological definitions of the Council of Sirmium (351 AD), concluding the defense of the Father’s superiority in rank while maintaining the divinity of the Son. -># The Tripartite Church History<-

<margin>John 14</margin>
¶ <unclear>truth</unclear> possesses; and only the Son knows how he was born of his Father. There is also no doubt that the Father is greater in honor, dignity, and divinity, just as the Son also testifies: *He who has sent me, the Father, is greater than I.* <note>original: "De Vader is meerder dan ick" — a reference to John 14:28, frequently cited in Arian and semi-Arian debates to argue for the subordination of the Son to the Father.</note> So it is also Christian and well-spoken to say that there are two persons, of the Father and of the Son, and that the Father is greater, and the Son is subject to the Father along with all other things. Furthermore, the Father has no beginning and is invisible, immortal, and impassible <note>meaning "unable to suffer" or "unchanging," a technical term in early theology</note>. But the Son is born of the Father, God from God, Light from Light; and just as no one knows his birth except the Father, so the Son, our Lord and God, took on flesh or a Body, that is, humanity. As the holy Angel also announced, and the Scriptures and the Teacher Paul (servant of the Gentiles) teach everywhere, Christ Jesus took humanity from the Virgin Mary, through which he suffered. Now the foundation of our faith is firm, that the <term>Trinity</term> <note>original: "dryvuldicheyt"</note> of the faith be maintained, as we read in the Gospel: *Go forth and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.* This is a whole and perfect number; and the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, sent through his Son, has come according to the promise, with which he helped the Apostles and all believers.

<margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin>
<margin>Psalm 2 and 110</margin>
<margin>Philippians 2</margin>
<margin>Matthew 1</margin>
<margin>Matthew 28, Mark 16</margin>

<margin>Photinus is warned that he should sign the Council of Sirmium.</margin>
Photinus was willing to approve and sign this interpretation; they even advised him to do so after he was condemned, promising to restore his Bishopric to him if he reformed himself, condemned his own teaching, and agreed to their sentence. However, he did not accept this proposal, but instead offered to engage in a disputation. Therefore, on a set day, with the Emperor’s consent, many Bishops gathered together, as well as several of the Emperor's counselors whom the Emperor had appointed. Among those opposing him was Sabinus, a Bishop of the city of Ancyra, who stood against Photinus. The <term>notaries</term> <note>original: "Notarien" — professional scribes who recorded the verbatim arguments of ecclesiastical debates.</note> recorded their arguments and counter-arguments, and there was much word-strife on both sides. Photinus, being defeated, was condemned. While in exile, he later wrote books in both languages <note>original: "beyderley sprake" — likely referring to Greek and Latin, the academic languages of the era.</note>, for he was not unskilled in Latin. He also wrote against all heresies, seeking to confirm his own teaching. But let this be enough said concerning Photinus.

<margin>Notaries record the notes.</margin>
It is also to be known that the Bishops—

<column-break/>

<margin>The Holy Scriptures: that the faith should be kept by the pen.</margin>
—gathered at Sirmium regretted that they had set forth the Faith in the Latin language. For after it was issued, they judged that it worked against them, and they desperately wanted the Bishops who had signed that creed to return that faith and confession to them. While this was kept hidden from many, the Emperor issued a mandate that the aforementioned Latin copies of the Creed should be brought in; and whoever hid them would be severely punished. But whatever the demand was, the Emperor could not nullify it with any threats, as it had already reached many people. Of these things, enough has now been said.

### ¶ Of Hosius of Cordoba, a Spaniard.

#### The 9th Chapter.

<margin>Hosius is brought out of exile so that he might voluntarily confirm the Sirmian writing of faith.</margin>
Since we have made mention of Hosius from Spain, who came there against his will, we wish to speak a little further of him in brief. A short time before this, he had been cast into exile through Arian schemes. The Emperor, at the request of those gathered at Sirmium, had him recalled, attempting to make Hosius agree with the other Bishops through either reason or force. If this happened as they intended, they believed it would be a great testimony for their faith. Therefore, as I have said, it came about through necessity and compulsion, and not from free will. And when he refused to believe as they did, he had to suffer much pain and <term>martyrdom</term> <note>original: "Martelisatie"</note>. Because of this, he finally had to consent. With this, the things that happened then at Sirmium came to an end. Emperor Constantius, however, resided at Sirmium and waited to see how the war against Magnentius would end.

### ¶ Of the Tyrant Magnentius, and of the Tyranny of Silvanus.

#### The 10th Chapter.

<margin>Magnentius is in Rome; flees into Gaul.</margin>
During this time, Magnentius, having arrived in the Imperial City of Rome, put many of the Senators and common people to death. Having learned that the army of Constantius was not far from him, he broke camp and marched into Gaul.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the mid-4th century, transitioning from the theological debates at Sirmium to the civil wars and political instability under Emperor Constantius II. It details the downfall of the usurper Magnentius and the subsequent rise and fall of Caesar Gallus.</meta>

Fol. 301
The Second Part. The Fifth Book.
<columns>2</columns>

<margin>A</margin> In the regions of the Western lands, many skirmishes occurred; now one side held the advantage, now the other. At last, Magnentius was defeated and fled to Mursa <note>original: "Mirtsam"; the Battle of Mursa Major (351 AD) was one of the bloodiest in Roman history</note>, which is a fortress in France <note>original: "Vranckrijc"; here referring broadly to the Gallic territories</note>. His soldiers, seeing themselves cast down from their high state and being sorrowful, hoped that according to their old custom they might yet become miraculously strong.

<margin>B</margin> When Magnentius saw that his servants were sorrowful because fortune would not favor them, he stood upon a high place and began to strengthen and exhort them, as was his custom. Then they wished to honor Magnentius in the usual manner, but—though unintentional—they all cried out together: "Constantius Augustus, you shall have victory!" <note>original: "Constanti Augusti, gy sult victorie hebben"</note> This prophecy was 
<margin>C</margin> <margin>Mount Seleucus.</margin> taken by Magnentius upon himself as a sign that he was not permitted by God to hold the empire. Therefore, abandoning the army, he retreated further. As the soldiers of Constantius now pursued him, and the two sides clashed at Mount Seleucus, he fled alone and came to Lyons. There, he caught his own mother and killed her; thereafter, he strangled his brother whom he had made Caesar. Finally, he stabbed himself to death. This happened in the sixth year that Constantius was consul <note>original: "overkaet sheere"; a reference to the Roman dating system by consulships</note>, and in the following year of Gallus, on the 25th day of August.

<margin>D</margin> <margin>Death of Magnentius: he murdered his brother and finally himself.</margin> Not long after, Decentius, the brother of Magnentius, hanged himself. Yet common peace did not come through this, for not long after, a tyrant arose in Gaul
<margin>E</margin> <margin>Sylvanus a tyrant.</margin> whose name was Sylvanus; the commanders of Constantius immediately slew him.

### ¶ Of the uprising of the Jews, and the tyranny of the Caesar Gallus, and of his death.

### The XI. Chapter.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>The Jews revolt.</margin> <margin>Gallus the Caesar in the West <note>original: "oxidanté"</note> suppresses the Jews.</margin> Above all this, the Jews who lived in Diocaesarea in Palestine attacked the nearest neighboring places and took them by force, intending to set themselves against the Romans. But the Caesar Gallus, residing in Antioch, gathered an army, captured the Jews, and destroyed their city of Diocaesarea. And as he began to think he had done all things successfully, he could not 

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin> <margin>Domitianus regent in the East.</margin> conduct himself well, and fell into tyranny against those who had made him Caesar. Without revealing his intentions to the Emperor, he killed Domitianus, the Regent and Great General in the East. For this reason, Constantius became enraged and summoned him. Since Gallus could not refuse, he traveled to the Emperor, and when he reached the island of Flanona <note>original: "Flas-nona"; likely refers to a location near Pola in Istria</note>, Constantius commanded that he be killed at that same place.

### ¶ Of the Caesar Julian, and how Liberius succeeded Julius.

### The XII. Chapter.

<margin>H</margin> <margin>Julian is sent as Caesar to Gaul.</margin> Not long after, he made Julian, a brother of Gallus, Caesar and sent him against the Barbarians in Gaul. But Gallus, whom Constantius had also sent, had been slain in the 17th year that Constantius was High Consul, in the 3rd year of his reign. Julian became Caesar in the following year, during the consulship of Arbetio and Lollianus, on the 7th day of November; but more shall be said of Julian hereafter.

<margin>I</margin>
<margin>K</margin>

# Sozomenus.

<margin>L</margin> <margin>Constantius at Rome.</margin> <margin>Julius, Pope at Rome.</margin> <margin>Liberius successor.</margin> Now that the tyrants were slain, Constantius seemed to have rest from wicked men. Thus, it was his intention to put aside all strife and discord in the Church. Leaving Sirmium, he came to old Rome, wishing to hold a triumph there for the spoils taken from the enemies. As he had promised to unite the Bishops of both sides in doctrine, he again ordered a Synod to be held in Italy. Meanwhile, after Pope Julius had governed the Roman Church for 15 years, he died, and Liberius came in his place.

### ¶ Of the Heretic Aetius.

### The XIII. Chapter.

<margin>M</margin> Besides this, another master of heresy arose in Antioch, whose name was Aetius, and his surname was "Atheos," which is to say, "The Godless" or "he who is without God."

<meta>This page continues the ecclesiastical history of the 4th century, specifically following the political fallout of Magnentius’s defeat mentioned on Fol. 301. It shifts focus from civil war to the theological conflicts involving Aetius of Antioch and the renewed efforts by Emperor Constantius II to suppress Athanasius of Alexandria in favor of Arian doctrines.</meta>

Fol. 302.
Header: Tripartite Ecclesiastical History <note>original: "Historia Ecclesiastica Tripartita"; a standard medieval and Renaissance history of the early Church compiled from the works of Socrates Scholasticus, Sozomen, and Theodoret.</note>

<columns>
...[Aetius]. He held the same opinion as Arius, yet he separated himself from Arius because they allowed Arius into their communion. Arius, as mentioned, had a different mind than what he expressed in words. For while he accepted and subscribed to the words of the Nicene Council, he did not wish to agree with the Emperor, and therefore Aetius envied the Arians.

<margin>Aetius of Antioch was ordained as a Deacon by Leontius.</margin>
Now this Aetius had previously been a heretic and conducted himself as if he were most earnestly defending the teaching of Arius. After he had studied and returned to Alexandria, and from there to Antioch in Syria (where he was a citizen), he was ordained as a Deacon by Leontius, who was then Bishop of Antioch.

<margin>Aristotle wrote Sophistry not for use, but to counter those who approach us with it.</margin>
When people came to him to hold discourse, he mocked them with sophistical words. He did this by misusing the books of Aristotle, speaking much of the *Categories* <note>original: "Categorice"; a work by Aristotle on how entities are classified</note>, which he himself did not understand. This could not have been Aristotle's intention, who did not write Sophistry for the sake of misuse, but to counter those who use it.

<margin>Aetius the Sophist.</margin>
Because Aetius was preoccupied with Sophistry, he could not understand the mysteries of divine things. Thus, he was also inexperienced in godly matters, being ready only for dispute—which any peasant is capable of doing.

<margin>Clement Africanus. Origen.</margin>
And although he had not read much of the Ancients <note>Referring to the early Church Fathers</note> who explained Christian speech, he yet claimed to take great joy in the books of Clement, Africanus, and Origen, though these men were adorned with divine virtue and wisdom. This Aetius wrote some letters to Emperor Constantius and to others, in which he put forward nothing but contentious and fabricated opinions.

<margin>Aetius the Atheist.</margin>
Therefore he was called *Atheos*, that is, Godless or without God.

And although he held the exact same opinion as Arius (yet they could not understand his subtle syllogisms and regarded him as a heretic), he was therefore cast out of their community. Their rejection of him is considered true because he also wished to have no communion with them.

<margin>Aetians, later called Eunomians. Eunomius was the Scribe of Aetius.</margin>
Now those who come from him were first called Aetians, and are now called Eunomians, after Eunomius, the scribe of Aetius. He was instructed by him and brought this heresy to light and spread it.

<column-break/>

# Sozomenus <note>Salminius Hermias Sozomenus, a 5th-century historian of the Christian Church.</note>

->Concerning the enemies of Athanasius.<-

### Chapter 14.

<margin>The Arians labor with the Emperor.</margin>
The enemies of the faith, believing they had now found the right time to act against the defenders of the faith, persistently urged the Emperor that all those they had deposed—who followed a different faith—should be cast out of the Church and driven away, specifically those who had resisted Emperor Constantius while he was still living.

<margin>Athanasius always has dealings with the Arians; the gathering at Antioch.</margin>
Primarily, they accused Athanasius out of great envy and hatred; indeed, it nearly came to war. Constantius knew well how his affection for Athanasius had held back their harassment. But at Antioch, Narcissus of Cilicia, Theodorus of Thrace, Theogonius of Nicaea, Patrophilus of Scythopolis, Menophantus of Ephesus, and about thirty other bishops gathered. These all wrote to every bishop, claiming that Athanasius had come to Alexandria against the ordinances of the Church. Furthermore, they claimed he had not appeared at the Council as an innocent man, and they commanded that no one should have communion with him or write any letter to him. But regarding Gregory <note>Gregory of Cappadocia, the Arian-appointed candidate for the bishopric</note>, who was ordained by them as a true replacement for Athanasius, no mention was made of this.

->Concerning the Synod assembled at Milan.<-

### Chapter 15.

<margin>The Emperor wants the Western bishops to agree with the Eastern ones and the Arians, who are against Athanasius.</margin>
Now that Magnentius was defeated and Constantius ruled alone, he spared no effort to persuade the bishops of the Western lands to consent with those who deny that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance <note>original: "substãtie"; referring to the Nicene doctrine of *homoousios*</note>. He did this because he did not want to use force against them at first, but advised them with cunning that they should consent to the decision made against Athanasius by the Eastern bishops. He hoped that if they condemned Athanasius by common consent, he could then easily achieve his goals.

Fol. 303.
The Second Part. The Fifth Book.

<margin>G</margin>
# Socrates.

Then they came together with many bishops from the East into Italy, for many had been prevented from attending by old age and the length of the journey. From the Western lands, there were about 300 present. The Council, gathered by the command of the Emperor in Milan, <margin>Council of Milan; the Easterners; Athanasius; Paulinus at Trier; Dionysius at Alba; Eusebius of Vercelli.</margin> where the Easterners also assembled, first of all demanded that everyone should speak against Athanasius. Once this was done, the way was entirely closed to him, and his access to Alexandria was blocked. When Paulinus, a priest of Gaul at Trier, and Dionysius at Alba <note>Dionysius was actually the Bishop of Milan; the reference to "Alba" likely refers to the "white" or "metropolitan" capital of Italy at the time.</note>, in the capital of Italy, and Eusebius of Vercelli saw how the Easterners intended to act against Athanasius to the detriment of the faith, they stood up and cried out with loud voices. They declared that one should not act with such deceit against Christian teaching, and said that the accusers of Athanasius were liars and would be brought to shame if they were forced to prove their allegations. Because of this outcry from the bishops of the Western lands, the Council was divided.

# Theodoretus.

->¶ Regarding the expulsion of the orthodox bishops.<-

### The 16th Chapter.

<margin>The Arians were driven out.</margin> Now that Athanasius had been deposed, the heretics <note>The "heretics" refers here to the Arians, who believed that Jesus Christ was a created being and not of the same substance as God the Father.</note> attempted to make a different interpretation of the faith. However, they were unable to bring it to pass, because in the presence of the Emperor, it was cried out that they were acting unjustly and godlessly. When this was done, they were cast out of the Church and commanded to live outside the borders of the land. Athanasius describes this wonderfully in his *Apologia* <note>original: "Apologia"; Athanasius's formal defense of his actions and theology.</note> in this manner: Who can indeed tell what these men <margin>The true Christian believers are driven out.</margin> have done? For while the Church was at peace and the people prayed in the assembly, the Bishop of Rome, Liberius, and Paulinus, the Gallic Bishop of Trier, and Dionysius of Italy, and Lucifer, Bishop of Sardi-

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin> nia, and Eusebius from Italy—all these, as good bishops and preachers of the truth, were hunted and driven away for no other reason than that they would not consent to the Arian madness, nor would they subscribe to their deeds. What shall I say of the good old confessor Hosius? <margin>Hosius of Corduba banished.</margin> For everyone knows well that they also sent this man into exile, a very widely famous man. How did he conduct himself in <margin>H</margin> the Synod? Did he not preside? Or who is there that he did not satisfy with his good reasoning? Or what church does not keep in memory <margin>Praise of Hosius.</margin> this man’s diligent service? Where has a grieving person ever come to him who did not go away with joy and gladness? Where has any needy person come to him, desiring something, who did not receive it? Disregarding all of this, they acted so tyrannically against him that he, understanding their godless undertaking, would not confirm it with his signature. <margin>I</margin>

# Socrates.

<margin>Council of Ariminum by the Easterners.</margin> Thus, the Emperor having sent these men into exile, he planned a general Council, by which he might unite all the bishops of the East with those of the West, if it were possible. <margin>H</margin> Because this seemed difficult due to the length of the journey, he resolved to hold two Synods, so that the Italian bishops came together at Ariminum <note>original: "Armino"; modern-day Rimini in Italy.</note>, but the Easterners in Nicomedia, a city of Bithynia. Although the Emperor <margin>Council at Nicomedia by the Westerners.</margin> acted in this way, it did not reach the effect he desired. He could not unite one Council with the other, but each remained divided. For those gathered in Ariminum could not agree <margin>L</margin> among themselves, and those who were gathered in the East in Seleucia, Isauria, had another schism or division, as we shall say in its proper place.

# Sozomenus.

## ¶ Regarding the enemies of Athanasius.

### The 14th Chapter.

<margin>The Arians work upon the Emperor.</margin>

The enemies of the faith, thinking they had now found the right time to move against the defenders of the faith, strongly urged the Emperor to depose all those who were of a different faith. They sought to push out of the Church and drive away those who still resisted Emperor Constantius during his lifetime. 

<margin>Athanasius always faced their gatherings at Antioch.</margin>

Principally, they targeted Athanasius out of great envy and hatred; indeed, it had nearly come to a state of war. Constantius knew well how, out of love for Athanasius, he had previously avoided their harassment. But there gathered at Antioch: Marcus of Arethusa, Theodosius of Thrace, Theognis of Nicaea, Patrophilus of Scythopolis, Menophantus of Ephesus, and thirty other bishops. All these men wrote to all other bishops, claiming that Athanasius had returned to Alexandria against the ordinances of the Church. Furthermore, they claimed he had not appeared at the Council as an innocent man, and they commanded that no one should hold communion with him or write any letters to him. But for Gregory, who was ordained by them as a "true" Athanasius <note>This refers to Gregory of Cappadocia, the Arian candidate installed to replace the orthodox Athanasius.</note>, no mention was made of his own illegitimacy.

## ¶ Regarding the Synod gathered at Milan.

### The 15th Chapter.

<margin>The Emperor wants the Western bishops to agree with the Easterners (the Arians) against Athanasius.</margin>

Now that Magnentius <note>A usurper defeated by Constantius II in 353 AD.</note> was conquered and Constantius ruled over everything, the Emperor spared no effort to persuade the bishops from the Western lands to agree with those who denied that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance. He did this because he did not want to use force against them at first. Instead, he craftily advised them to consent to the decision made by the Eastern bishops against Athanasius. He hoped that if they condemned Athanasius by common consent, he could then easily fulfill his own objectives.

# Theodoretus.

<margin>B</margin>
¶ On the driving out of the orthodox bishops.

## Chapter 16.

<margin>The Arians were expelled.</margin>
Now that Athanasius had been deposed, the heretics attempted to create a different interpretation of the faith; however, they could not bring it to pass, because in the presence of the Emperor it was cried out that they were acting unjustly and godlessly. When this was done, they were cast out of the Church and commanded to live outside the borders of the land. 

<margin>The true Christian believers are expelled.</margin>
Athanasius describes this wonderfully in his *Apologia* <note>The *Apologia ad Constantium* or *Apologia de Fuga*, works written by Athanasius to defend his actions and the orthodox faith.</note> in this manner:

> Who can tell what these men have done? For while the Church was at peace and the people were praying in the assembly, Liberius, the Bishop of Rome, Paulinus, the Gallic Bishop of Trier, Dionysius of Italy, Lucifer, Bishop of Sardinia, and Eusebius from Italy—all these, being good bishops and preachers of the truth, were exiled and driven away for no other reason than that they would not consent to the Arian rebellion and would not sign their documents.

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin>
What shall I say of the good old confessor Hosius? <note>Hosius of Corduba was one of the most respected bishops of the 4th century and a key figure at the Council of Nicaea.</note> Everyone knows well that they also sent this man into exile, a man of very wide renown.

<margin>Hosius of Corduba banished.</margin>
How did he conduct himself in the Synod? Did he not preside? Or who is there whom he did not satisfy with his good reasoning?

<margin>Praise for Hosius.</margin>
Or which church does not hold in memory the diligent service of this man? Where has anyone in mourning come to him and not left him with joy and gladness? Where has any needy person come to him seeking help and not received it? Disregarding all of this, they acted so tyrannically against him that, understanding their godless undertaking, he refused to confirm it with his signature.

# Socrates.

<margin>The Council of Ariminum by the Easterners.</margin>
After the Emperor had sent these men into exile, he planned a general Council, through which he might unite all the bishops of the East with those of the West, if it could be achieved. Because the distance made this seem difficult, he decided to hold two Synods: one where the Italian bishops gathered together at Ariminum <note>Modern-day Rimini, Italy.</note>, and another for the Easterners in Nicomedia, a city of Bithynia.

<margin>Council of Nicomedia by the Easterners.</margin>
Although the Emperor managed this, it did not achieve the effect he desired. He could not bring the one Council to agree with the other, but each remained divided. For those gathered in Ariminum could not reach an agreement among themselves, and those gathered in the East at Seleucia in Isauria <note>The venue was changed from Nicomedia to Seleucia after an earthquake.</note> had another schism or division, as we shall say in its proper place.

# Theodoretus.

<margin>M</margin>
I will also tell you of the conversation that the highly renowned Liberius had with Constantius in defense of the truth, as it was described by the orthodox of that time. This Liberius came after Sylvester and Bishop Julius, and was Bishop of Rome and governed the Church.

# Tripartite Ecclesiastical History.

<margin>Conversation between Constantius and Liberius.</margin>
## ¶ Conversation between Emperor Constantius and Bishop Liberius of Rome, and how Liberius is quickly cast into exile.

### The 18th Chapter.

Emperor Constantius said: "It has seemed good to us, since you, Liberius, are a Christian and a Bishop of our City, that we have rightly judged to call you to us and to admonish you, without any delay, to leave and renounce the communion of the shamefully bold Athanasius. For the whole circuit of the world has acknowledged this as good, and the Synodical sentence of the Holy Church has so decided, that such a man is worthy to be deprived of communion."

<margin>Liberius's opinion: to condemn no one unheard.</margin>
Liberius answering, said: "O Emperor, it is fitting that the judgment of the Church be spoken with great justice. Therefore, if it pleases your grace, arrange a disputation; and if it be found that Athanasius is worthy of condemnation, then that condemnation and sentence shall pass over him according to the rule of the church. For it is not a thing to be done, to condemn someone whom one has not heard."

Constantius answered: "The whole world has condemned his evil deeds; yet he (as from the beginning) cares nothing for it."

Liberius: "All those who have signed <note>referring to the bishops who signed the condemnation of Athanasius</note> did not know what was happening, but have done it for the sake of glory and fear, and have consented to it so that they might not suffer harm from you, O Emperor."

Constantius: "What is glory, fear, and shame?"

Liberius: "All those who do not love the honor, fear, and love of God, and prefer your gifts instead. Now those Bishops have condemned Athanasius, whom they have neither seen nor heard; that is entirely far from being Christian."

Constantius: "He was condemned in his presence at the Council of Trier, and then all the Bishops of the world testified against him."

Liberius: "Athanasius was not present there where they condemned him. For all those who condemned him together spoke the sentence against him in his absence, while he was away."

<margin>Eusebius, a castrated chamberlain <note>The term "gesneden camerlinck" refers to a eunuch, a common official in the Byzantine-style court of Constantius.</note>.</margin>
Eusebius the Eunuch said: "It was judged in the Council of Nicaea to be a friend of

<column-break/>

<margin>E</margin>
the Catholic faith, that which Athanasius has brought forth."

<margin>B</margin>
Liberius: "Only those judged him among those who came to a schism with him in Mareotis <note>original: "Marioten," a region in Egypt near Alexandria where Athanasius was accused of breaking a chalice</note>, whom they sent to complain against him and to create a plot against him. Two of these are dead: Theogonius and Theodorus. The others are still living: Maris, Valens, and Ursacius. From among those who were sent to Sardica <note>The Council of Sardica (modern Sofia, Bulgaria), c. 343 AD</note>, for whose sake that Council was held, they have delivered their petition of conversion in this Synod and begged for forgiveness, since they had slandered Athanasius in Mareotis with fabricated certainties. We have their petition and book now at hand."

"Now, O Emperor: to which of these shall we give belief? Or with which shall we have communion? With those who first condemned and afterwards begged for forgiveness, or those who still accuse such things?"

<margin>D</margin>
Bishop Epictetus said: "O Emperor, Liberius speaks of nothing but the faith; thus he does not even fit a discourse where a Christian judgment is noted. But only that Liberius, Bishop of Rome, may boast among the heretics <note>original: "Kaettsheeren," likely referring to the Novatians or other factions in Rome</note> in Rome that he has overcome the Emperor."

Emperor Constantius said to Liberius: "What kind of part of the whole world are you? Why do you make so much of yourself, that you advocate for a rogue man and tear apart the peace of the whole world and of the Church?"

<margin>Y</margin>
<margin>Matthew <note>likely a reference to the resistance of the faithful</note> to contradict the command of the King.</margin>
Liberius: "Not because I am alone shall the matter of faith be diminished. For among the ancients there were no more than three found, being abandoned by other men, who contradicted the command of the King."

<margin>Dan. 3.</margin>
Eusebius said: "Do you wish to make our Emperor like unto a Nebuchadnezzar?"

Liberius: "No, but it is not the truth to condemn one who is unheard. I desire first that a general subscription take place, which is firmly understood according to the Council held at Nicaea. That thus our brothers be called back from their exile and placed in their own positions; and that those who now seem to stir up a commotion in the Church be found to agree with the Apostolic faith. That they all come together at Alexandria—the accuser and the accused—and after the cause has been examined in a hearing, thereafter they may speak the sentence further."

<margin>Z</margin>
Bishop Epictetus said: "It is not enough to carry the Bishops away with the postal wagon <note>The "postwagen" refers to the *cursus publicus*, the imperial transport system which Constantius used to force bishops to attend his councils.</note>."

<margin>H</margin>
Liberius said: "The affairs of the church do not require a great wagon and equipment."

# Part Two. The Fifth Book.

<margin>An arrangement, because every Church may well lead her Bishop by the hand.</margin>
<margin>The church leads her Bishop to the water.</margin>
<margin>A</margin> The Emperor says: "The customs which have been held for a long time must be examined, for the judgment of many Bishops shall be valid. You are the only one who defends the friendship of this villainous Athanasius <note>original: Athanasij; referring to the Bishop of Alexandria, the chief opponent of Arianism</note>."

Liberius says: "We have not heard that a Judge has passed sentence over an absent party; this suggests a particular hatred."

<margin>B</margin> The Emperor says: "He has caused a general injury, and to no one more than to me; for he was not even dismayed by the death of my eldest brother <note>Constantine II, who died in 340 AD</note>. He also sought to incite Constans <note>original: Constantem</note> of blessed memory against me, even though we had been friendly toward one another. Therefore, I can hope for no victory, neither against Magnentius nor Silvanus <note>Magnentius and Silvanus were usurpers who rebelled against Constantius's authority</note>, unless I first drive this rogue from the Church."

<margin>C</margin> Liberius said: "You should not avenge your private enmity through the Bishops; for the hands of the Church's friends must attend to holiness. Therefore, if it pleases you, let the Priests be called to a specific place; and if they are found to be in agreement with what we defend—according to the content of the Christian faith decided in the Synod of Nicaea <note>original: Nicea; the first ecumenical council of 325 AD</note>—then when they come together, they shall consider what serves the cause of peace, so that a man who has not sinned is not undeservedly rejected."

<margin>D</margin> The Emperor says: "One thing is sought: that I may send you back into the communion of the Churches at Rome. Therefore, consider the peace, sign the document <note>referring to the condemnation of Athanasius</note>, and return to Rome."

Liberius says: "I have already blessed the brothers at Rome; for the Churches <margin>E</margin> are of greater concern to me, and more depends upon them, than that I should merely have my dwelling in Rome."

The Emperor says: "Take three days to deliberate whether you will sign and return to Rome, or consider in what place you wish to be led?"

Liberius said: "Within three days my understanding will not change; therefore, send me where you will."

<margin>F</margin> Then the Emperor, after he had examined him for two days and could not move Liberius from his conviction, commanded that he be taken away and led into exile in Beroea <note>modern-day Veria, Greece</note> in the land of Thrace.

As Liberius was departing, the Emperor ordered the sum of 500 shillings <note>referring to gold solidi</note> for his travel expenses.

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin> Liberius said to the one who gave him the money: "Go hence and give it back to the Emperor, for he certainly needs it to maintain his soldiers." Likewise, the Empress <note>original: Augusta; referring to Empress Eusebia</note> also offered him money, but Liberius answered and refused: "Give it back to the Emperor so that he has it to give to his warriors; and if the Emperor has no need of it, he may give it to Auxentius <note>original: Aureutio</note> and Epictetus <note>original: Epicto; both were Arian-aligned bishops favored by the court</note>, for <margin>H</margin> they have need of it." When he would not receive anything from them, Eusebius the Eunuch <note>the powerful court chamberlain</note> brought him other money <margin>Year of Christ 354</margin>, to whom Liberius spoke: "You have devastated and emptied the Churches of the entire world, and do you now bring this to me as if I were a condemned man? Go hence and first learn to be a Christian." After these things happened, and when he would not take the money after three days, he was sent away into exile.

### How Liberius was recalled from his exile by Roman Matrons.

## The 8th Chapter.

<margin>I</margin> <margin>Liberius in exile at Beroea.</margin> Thus the champion of truth and the conqueror (as he was called) arrived in Thrace. And two years later, when Constantius came to Rome, the Senators <margin>K</margin> and the prominent women begged their husbands to petition Constantius to give back Liberius and restore the Shepherd to his sheep. For they said: if their husbands did not change the mind of the Emperor, they would leave the husbands themselves and join that great shepherd and Bishop. To which <margin>L</margin> the husbands said: "We fear the wrath of the Emperor and are concerned about bringing disfavor upon ourselves; but it is better that you <margin>Roman Matrons petition the Emperor for the return of Liberius.</margin> women approach him; perhaps he will spare you, and one of two things will happen: either he will grant your prayers, or if he does not, he will dismiss you without any injury." These women, greatly praising this advice, dressed themselves most magnificently so that the Emperor would see they were the wives of noble Senators and the most excellent of the city, and seeing their splendor <margin>M</margin> he might receive them more kindly. And so <margin>The women beg Emperor Constantius for the return of Bishop Liberius.</margin> going to the Emperor, they cried out with such a voice: "Have mercy on such a city, which is unprovided with a Shepherd, whereby the door stands open to the visit of the wolf." To which the Emperor answered: "The city has no need of another Shepherd, for there was a Bishop who took care of them." For after the great Liberius, one of his Deacons...

#### Tripartite Ecclesiastical History.

<margin>Felix nominated as Pope in place of Liberius.</margin>
<margin>Constantius wants to have two bishops in Rome.</margin>
<margin>A twofold cry of the people in Rome: one Christ, one Bishop.</margin>
¶ A deacon, whose name was Felix, was ordained. This man had fearlessly held to the faith decided in the Council of Nicaea <note>original: Concilio van Niceno; the first ecumenical council of 325 AD which defined the divinity of Christ</note>, yet he also maintained communion with those who sought to undermine that faith. But no one who lived in Rome was willing to enter the church while this Felix was inside; the noble Matrons <note>high-ranking Roman women who exerted significant social and religious influence</note> also made this known to the Emperor. This moved the Emperor so that he commanded that Liberius, that most famous man, should be recalled, and that Liberius and Felix should govern the church together. When these letters were read at the theater <note>likely the Circus Maximus or a similar public arena</note>, the people cried out that the Emperor’s sentence was just. But just as the spectators of the games were dressed in two different colors, so would these two be bishops, one for one side and one for the other. And though they first seemed to agree with the Emperor's letter, they afterwards cried out with one voice: "One Christ, one Bishop!" I have judged it right to record this cry of theirs here. Following this Christian desire of the people, the holy Liberius returned. But Felix withdrew and went to live in another city.

# • Socrates. •
<note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century Christian historian whose work is a primary source for this text.</note>

¶ How Eudoxius came to the Church of Antioch.

### Chapter 19.

<margin>Eudoxius, bishop of Syria, aspires to the seat of the Bishopric at Antioch.</margin>
<margin>Through the help of the Chamberlains, Eudoxius seeks to reinstate Aetius.</margin>
In these turbulent times, Leontius died, who had made the heretic Aetius <note>a radical Arian who taught that the Son was "unlike" the Father</note> a deacon. Eudoxius, Bishop of Germanicia (a city in Syria), being present in Rome at the time, feigned that he had urgent business with the Emperor. By positioning himself near the Emperor, he spoke craftily to him, as if the city of Germanicia had need of his provident warning, and therefore he desired to return to his own place. The Emperor, seeing no further into the matter, let him go. But having secured the help of the Emperor’s chamberlains <note>original: Camerlings; powerful court officials often sympathetic to Arianism</note>, and intending to exalt Aetius, he abandoned his own city and seized the Bishopric at Antioch. Therefore, he wished to gather a Council of Priests to reinstate Aetius in the office of deacon. This, however, by no means occurred, because the hatred against-

<column-break/>

-against Aetius was greater than Eudoxius's desire for him. But of this, enough has been said.

---

¶ Concerning the Council of Ariminum, and what discord occurred there.

### Chapter 20.

<margin>Bishops at Ariminum.</margin>
<margin>Ursacius, Valens.</margin>
<margin>Germinius, etc.</margin>
Now, those who gathered at the Council of Ariminum <note>modern-day Rimini, 359 AD</note>, some of whom were Easterners, remained silent regarding the matters handled on behalf of Athanasius. They said they had come to the Council gladly, and their leaders and followers were Ursacius and Valens. Although these two had been Arians in the beginning, they had afterwards sided with the *homoousians* <note>those who believed the Son is of the "same substance" as the Father</note>. Because of this, they had presented a petition <note>original: Libel</note> to the Bishop of Rome, as has been said. For the Easterners always tended to side with whoever was most powerful at the time. Their helpers were Germinius, Auxentius, Demophilus, and Gaius.

<margin>Bishops.</margin>
When they attempted to bring matters forward in the Council against one another, Ursacius and Valens said: "All things that have been said concerning the faith shall be suspended. And we shall adopt the most recent explanation contained in the assembly of Sirmium <note>a series of councils held in Sirmium (modern Serbia) that produced compromise creeds</note>." Saying this, and holding a paper in his hand, he commanded it to be read—the faith according to the explanation issued in Sirmium, which some (as I have said) had hidden there. But they held and signed such an explanation at Ariminum, of which this is the copy.

The Tripartite Ecclesiastical History.

### The letter of the Council of Ariminum to Constantius.

#### The 22nd Chapter.

<margin>A</margin> By Divine prayer and the command of your grace, Emperor, we believe just as was taught in times past. For we bishops, all together from the cities of the Western Lands, have come to Ariminum, so that the Christian faith of the Christian Church might be confirmed, and those who are against it made manifest. For after much dispute and discord that arose among us, it is now found nearest and best that one should remain by the old <margin>B</margin> faith, which the Prophets, Evangelists, and the Apostles preached to our LORD (who is also a protector of your Realm, and a helper of your salvation), so that we accept that faith and hold it fast until the end. For it would be unjust, indeed shameful, if one were to change anything from the things that have once been recognized as right and reasonable, namely, the things that were commonly ordained and decided at Nicaea <note>The Council of Nicaea (325 AD) established the core orthodox doctrine that the Son is of the same substance as the Father.</note> with the highly praised Emperor Constantine, your father. Which teaching and meaning has been preached and has reached the ears of all men. This teaching and faith alone has contested and overcome the Arian teaching <note>Arianism: The belief that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father, which the orthodox Church condemned as heresy.</note>. Through which not only these, but all other heresies have been condemned.

Now, whoever wishes to add anything here is not secure, and it is dangerous to diminish it: for if either occurs, the enemies will have the opportunity to do what they will. Therefore Ursacius and <margin>Ursacius, Valens.</margin> Valens, while they have had communion and unity with the Arian teaching, have been separated from our communion. <margin>Perform penance, flee from relapse.</margin> And in order that they might be received back, they must confess their sins and perform penance, and improve, just as their writings testify in all places. Through which they have obtained forgiveness of their sins.

<margin>C</margin> And these things occurred when the Council was held at Milan <note>The Council of Milan (355 AD) was a previous gathering where tensions between Arian and Nicene factions were high.</note> in the presence of the Priests of the Roman Church. <margin>Priests of the Roman church.</margin> We also acknowledge how Constantine, of highly praiseworthy memory, with all diligence and industry caused this faith to be proclaimed and written down, who

<column-break/>

after receiving Baptism, departed from this world to eternal rest: We deem it unjust to allow any innovation, and to despise such Holy Confessors and Martyrs who brought forth and wrote down this teaching.

God has widely expanded this faith during the time of your <margin>D</margin> reign, through our Lord Jesus Christ, before whom such an Empire has been given to you, which you possess, encompassing the circuit of our lands. Therefore they are wretched and senseless people, who with intent and evil thoughts preach and proclaim themselves, and pretend to change the commands of the truth. For when the Council was held according to your command, they revealed the counsel of their hearts. For they have stood to introduce some innovation with a trick and an uprising, just as we have found them. That Germinius <note>original: "Germanius"</note>, Auxentius, and Gaius have been tainted with wickedness, inclined to incite heresy and discord. And although their teaching was singular, it has nevertheless surpassed all blasphemy.

When they now saw that we are not <margin>E</margin> of their opinion, nor wish to feel with their wickedness, they separated themselves from our Council, as if they intended to assemble and write another [creed]. But it has become a short time [ago]: But so that the matters of the Church would not always be in motion (for trouble and uprising throw all other things <margin>F</margin> into confusion), it has seemed good and steadfast to us that the things which have long been known and decided should be held firmly and strictly.

But we have excluded the aforementioned persons from our communion, and concerning these matters we have sent legates and letters to the height of your grace, that they shall declare our opinion of the writing from the Council, and we have commanded them above all things that they should declare and testify to the Truth from old and righteous causes, with which also the fear <margin>Z</margin> of GOD is entrusted, to instruct you. For there is no peace (as Ursacius and Valens say) if the Laws and Institutions are changed. <margin>What good is to be expected henceforth from those who overturn the right.</margin> But what peace is to be believed from them, who overturn the right of peace? Indeed, much more dispute and uprising shall arise in other cities, and all the more abundantly in the Roman church: Therefore we, your humble servants, pray your grace that you [receive] our messages kindly and graciously...

Fol. 309.
The Fifth Book.

<margin>A</margin> Nobly please hear and receive our plea, and do not allow anything to be changed to our contempt or scorn. But let us remain in the things that were known and established by our forefathers. <margin>B</margin> For we hope that they established all things with diligent consideration, wisdom, and through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. For things that are changed now bring a lack of faith to the believers and a righteous anger to the unbelievers.

Furthermore, we pray you to command that those who are imprisoned here and there, and who have been weakened by old age and poverty, may return to their own people, so that the Churches standing empty without Bishops do not remain without hope. Beyond this, we pray further <margin>C</margin> that regarding what has been decided, nothing be added or taken away: But that all things, just as they were decided, shall remain unhindered, even as they were established by godly, holy men and have come down to be maintained in your times.

Do not weary us, nor let us be alienated from our Churches and peoples, so that the Bishops may remain in peace with their own people to serve and observe the Divine Service, being always ready and attentive, praying to God the Lord for the peace and prosperity of your Realm and Empire—which may God worthily preserve. Also, our Envoys bring the transcript and names of the Bishops, who may sufficiently instruct your Piety and faith, as you are well-versed in the Divine Scriptures.

# Socrates.

<margin>Constantius Augustus rejects the fathers of the Synod of Ariminum because they had not accepted what the Arians at Sirmium had set out.</margin> The Synod <note>The Council of Ariminum, consisting of about 400 Western bishops.</note> wrote this and sent it through certain Bishops to the Emperor. However, Ursatius and Valens <note>Ursatius of Singidunum and Valens of Mursa were influential Arian bishops and advisors to Constantius II; they sought to undermine the Nicene faith.</note>, anticipating this, spoke poorly of the Council to the Emperor, showing him the interpretation of the faith that they had brought with them. The Emperor, being favorable to the Arian teaching, became very angry against the Synod. He held Ursatius and Valens and their followers in great honor. Consequently, the Envoys of the Council were delayed a long time and could obtain no answer. Yet long after, Constantius sent this answer to the Synod through the Bishops, as follows.

<column-break/>

# Constantius, Victorious Triumphant Augustus, to all Bishops gathered at Ariminum, Greetings.

<margin>20 Bishops sent.</margin> Beloved, you are not unaware how we always and before all things have a care regarding the Holy Covenant of God. Now, we have not been able to see the twenty Bishops whom you sent to us as messengers, as we were necessarily required to march against the Barbarians. <margin>D</margin> And you well know that Divine matters should be handled with a pure mind and sufficient investigation. Therefore, we have commanded that the Bishops should wait for us at Adrianople <note>Modern-day Edirne, Turkey.</note> until we arrive, so that once the common welfare is entirely brought to peace, we ourselves may hear what has occurred there. It shall not burden your venerable holiness to wait so long until my return. For when they return, they shall bring you our answer, so that you may fulfill what you judge to be for the benefit of your churches. The Bishops received this letter and answered again in this manner.

# The letter of the Synod at Ariminum to the Emperor Constantius.

### The 22nd Chapter.

<margin>Letter of the Synodal Council at Sirmium.</margin> <note>original: "Sirmino" — likely a scribal error for Ariminum, as the text refers to the council currently gathered there.</note> Godly, dear Lord Emperor, we have received your grace’s letter, in which it is noted how, because of the management of common public affairs, you have not been able to let our Envoys come before you, and that you command us to wait for their return. From them, your grace may understand what has been decided by us, and whether our decisions agree with the sayings of our forefathers. Therefore, we now testify and confess with this our Letter never to deviate from our purpose, just as we have also commanded our Envoys.

Therefore, we pray you to let our peaceful and modest Letter be read to you with a quiet mind, and to gladly hear what we have commanded our Legates. May your grace also consider and weigh with us what a sadness and heartache it is at this time that, under your blessed reign, so many excellent Churches should be deprived of their Bishops.

<margin>Q</margin>
By divine prayer and the command of your grace, O Emperor, we believe as was taught in times past.
