## The letter of Constantius to the Council of Ariminum.
<note>While the heading in the original Dutch says "to the Council," the text below is actually the letter sent *from* the Council to Emperor Constantius II.</note>

### The 22nd Chapter.

By Divine prayer and the command of your grace, as was taught in times past. For we Bishops, gathered together from the cities of the Western lands, have come to Ariminum <note>Modern-day Rimini, Italy; the site of a major church council in 359 AD</note> so that the Christian faith of the Christian Church might be confirmed, and those who are against it might be made manifest. For after much dispute and discord that arose among us, it was found to be the closest and best path that we should remain by that ancient faith which the Prophets, Evangelists, and the Apostles preached of our LORD (who is also a protector of your realm and a helper of your salvation), so that we accept that faith and hold it fast until the end. For it would be unjust, even shameful, to change anything from those things which have once been recognized as right and reasonable; namely, the things that were commonly ordained and decided at Nicaea with the highly praised Emperor Constantine, your father. This doctrine and meaning he preached and believed before the eyes of all men. This doctrine and faith alone has fought against and overcome the <term>Arian Teaching</term> <note>Arianism was a 4th-century belief that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father; it was declared heretical at the Council of Nicaea.</note>. By this, not only this one, but all other heresies have been condemned.

Now, anyone who wishes to add anything here is uncertain, and it is dangerous to diminish anything: for if either of these occurs, the enemies will have the opportunity to do whatever they wish.

<margin>Ursatius and Valens.</margin>
Therefore, Ursatius and Valens, because they had fellowship and unity with the Arian doctrine, have been separated from our communion.

<margin>Repentance brings return.</margin>
And in order that they may be accepted again, they must confess their sins and perform penance and improve themselves, just as their own writings testify in all places. Through this, they have obtained the forgiveness of their sins.

And these things happened when the Council was held at Milan in the presence of the Priests of the Roman Church.

<margin>Priests of the Roman church.</margin>
We also acknowledge how Constantine, of highly praised memory, caused this faith to be proclaimed with all diligence and industry, and caused this faith to be recorded; he who,

<column-break/>

after receiving Baptism, departed from this world to eternal rest. We deem it unjust to allow any innovation, and to despise such Holy Confessors and Martyrs who brought forth and wrote down this doctrine.

God has spread this faith far and wide during the time of your reign through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom such an Empire was given to you, which you also possess, holding the circuit of our lands. Therefore, they are miserable and foolish people who, with premeditation and evil thoughts, preach and proclaim themselves and offer to change the commandments of the truth. For when the Council was held according to your command, they revealed the counsel of their hearts. For they stood to bring in some innovation with a trick and an uprising, just as we found them out. That Germanus, Auxentius, and Gaius have been tainted with malice, inclined to stir up heresy and discord. And though their doctrine was one, yet it surpassed all blasphemy.

When they saw now that we were not of their opinion nor wished to endure their malice, they separated themselves from our Council, as if they intended to gather and record another. But it lasted only a short time: But so that the affairs of the Church should not always be in motion (for trouble and uprising confuse all things one through the other), it seemed good and steadfast to us that the things which have been known and decided for the longest time should be held fast and firmly.

But we have excluded the aforementioned persons from our communion, and regarding these matters, we have sent legates and letters to your Grace’s highness, who shall explain our meaning of the writing of the Council; and we have commanded them above all things that they shall explain and testify to the Truth from ancient and right causes, with which also the fear of GOD is entrusted, to instruct you. For there is no peace (as Ursatius and Valens say) if the Rights and Institutions are changed.

<margin>What good is to be expected from those who overturn what is right?</margin>
But what peace is to be believed from them who pervert the right of peace? Yea, much more discord and uprising shall arise in other cities, and all the more abundantly in the Roman church: Therefore we, your humble servants, pray your Grace that you may receive our messages kindly and graciously.

Fol. 309.
The Fifth Book.

## The Second Part.

...wholly desire to hear and accept, and not allow anything to be changed to the point of contempt or scorn. But let us remain in the things that were known and established by our forefathers.

For we hope that they established all things with diligent consideration, wisdom, and by the Holy Spirit. For the things that are now being changed bring a lack of faith to the believers and a sense of wrath to the unbelievers.

Furthermore, we pray you that you would command that those who are imprisoned here and there, and weakened by old age and poverty, may return to their own people, so that the Churches—standing empty without Bishops—do not remain without hope. Beyond this, we pray further that regarding what has been decided, nothing be added or taken away; but that all things, just as they were decided, shall remain unhindered, as they were established and handed down by the godly holy men and maintained until your own times. Do not reject us, nor allow us to be alienated from our Churches and peoples, so that the Bishops may remain in peace with their own people and be always ready and watchful to serve the Divine Office, always praying to God the Lord for the peace and prosperity of your Realm and Empire, which may God—worthy of praise—preserve. Our envoys also bring the transcript and names of the Bishops, who may sufficiently instruct your Piety and faith, as you are well-versed in the Divine Scriptures.

# Socrates.

<margin>Constantius Augustus <note>Emperor Constantius II, son of Constantine the Great</note> was displeased with the fathers of the Council at Ariminum because they had not accepted what the Arians at Sirmium <note>A city in Pannonia, modern-day Serbia, where several Arian creeds were drafted</note> had set forth.</margin>
The Council wrote this and sent it to the Emperor by certain Bishops. But Ursatius and Valens <note>Two influential Arian bishops who served as advisors to the Emperor</note>, anticipating this, spoke ill of the Council, showing the Emperor the interpretation of the faith which they brought with them. The Emperor, being favorable to the Arian doctrine, became very upset with the Council and held Ursatius and Valens and their followers in great honor. Therefore, the envoys of the Council were delayed for a long time and could obtain no answer. However, a long time later, Constantius sent this answer to the Council through the Bishops, as follows.

<column-break/>

->Constantius, Victorious Triumphant Augustus, to all Bishops assembled at Ariminum, Greetings.<-

<margin>20 Bishops sent.</margin>
You beloved are not ignorant of how we always, and before all things, have a concern regarding the Holy Covenant of God. We have not been able to see the twenty Bishops whom you sent to us as messengers, as we were necessarily required to march against the Barbarians; and you well know that Divine matters must be handled with a pure mind and sufficient investigation. Therefore, we have commanded that the Bishops should wait for us at Adrianople <note>Modern-day Edirne, Turkey</note> until we arrive, so that when the common good is fully brought to peace, we may then hear for ourselves what has occurred there. It shall not burden your venerable holiness to wait so long until my return. For when they return, they shall bring you our answer, with which you may fulfill what you deem to be for the good of your churches. The Bishops received this letter and replied again in this manner.

->The letter of the Council at Ariminum to Emperor Constantius.<-

### The 22nd Chapter.

<margin>Letter of the Synodical Council at Sirmium <note>Though the margin says Sirmium, the context remains the response of the Council at Ariminum to the Emperor's delay.</note>.</margin>
Godly and dear Lord Emperor, we have received your Grace's letter, in which it is noted how you, because of necessity, have not been able to let our envoys come before you, and that you command us to wait for their return. Thereby your Grace may understand from them what we have decided, and whether they agree with the sayings of our forefathers. Therefore, we now testify and confess by this our letter that we shall never deviate from our purpose, just as we have commanded our envoys.

Therefore, we pray you that with a quiet mind, you allow our peaceful and modest letter to be read to you, and gladly hear what we have commanded our legates. Your Grace should also consider and weigh with us what a sadness and heartache it is at this time that, under your prosperous reign, so many excellent Churches shall be deprived of their Bishops...

---

¶ How the Emperor became angry at the departure of the Bishops.

#### The xxiii. Chapter.

When they had written this and waited a short time, and the Emperor gave them no answer, each man returned to his own city. But the Emperor, while he busied himself with sowing the Arian sect <note>Arianism was a fourth-century theological belief that denied the full divinity of Jesus Christ, asserting he was a created being.</note> through all the churches, took occasion to be angry with them because they had separated from one another so quickly, saying: That they had shown him contempt, because the Council had dissolved without his permission. For that reason, he gave Ursacius and those who were with him the power to act against those churches according to his pleasure. And the interpretation of the faith read at Ariminum having been presented, he sent it to the Churches of Italy and commanded that those who would not subscribe to it should be driven out of their Churches, and others should be accepted and installed in their places.

### Socrates.

¶ Of the Synod assembled in Nicea in Thrace.

#### The xxv. Chapter.

<margin>Nicea in Thrace.</margin>
But Ursacius and those who held with him departed from Italy and came to that city in Thrace called Nicea; there, residing for a short time, they held another Council

<column-break/>

and, reading the interpretation of the faith from Ariminum, they translated it into the Greek language, proclaimed it, and confirmed it. Thereafter they said that it was the faith of the general Council established and issued at Nicea, so that by using the same name, "Nicene," they might deceive simple people with their scheme. <margin>Arian deceit.</margin> So that people would think it was the faith made at Nicea in Bithynia <note>The Council of Nicaea in 325 AD was the first ecumenical council; the Arians held a smaller meeting in a different city also named Nicea in Thrace to trick people into thinking their new creed was the original, famous one.</note>. Yet this deceit did not help them, for not long afterward they were mocked and put to shame.

---

¶ How Athanasius once again escaped the wrath of Constantius.

#### The xxvi. Chapter.

<margin>Athanasius not heard by the Emperor.</margin>
Meanwhile, Athanasius, sensing that the Emperor began to lay snares for him, did not wish to come before the Emperor. But the Emperor chose five Bishops from Egypt—among these was Serapion of Thmuis, an exceptionally holy man and well-spoken. These he sent to the Emperor, who was at that time residing in the West, and with him three more Priests, with whom he wished to reconcile the Emperor, and so that they might answer the accusations of the enemies and do what was necessary for him and the churches.

<margin>Athanasius summoned to the Emperor.</margin>
When they had departed, not long afterward the Emperor's letters arrived and summoned Athanasius, which caused Athanasius and the people to be greatly troubled, as it was not found advisable to be obedient to a heretical Emperor, yet dangerous to oppose the Emperor. Thus Athanasius held back from going; and with this, the messenger arrived with the letter and achieved nothing.

<margin>Hilarius, the Emperor's messenger.</margin>
When it became summer time, another messenger from the Emperor arrived, named Hilarius, with the governors; they wished to persuade Athanasius with their threats, and spoke very harshly to the Clergy. Seeing that the people were prepared for a struggle, this messenger also returned. Not long after that, the Legates from Egypt and Libya were assembled; and when it was shown to them how Athanasius lay hidden in the church which is called Theonas, taking with him soldiers and their Captain, and Hilarius having the Emperor's command, he unexpectedly broke open the church doors and entered, and

# Sozomenus <note>Salamanes Hermias Sozomenus was a 5th-century historian of the Christian Church.</note>

¶ How Athanasius foretold the misfortune of the pagans.

### The xxvii. Chapter.

<margin>Athanasius was mocked for practicing the black arts.</margin>
From these and similar dealings which happened to him from God, the pagans branded Athanasius a sorcerer. For it is said that once, as he passed through a city, a raven flew before him and croaked. And as many pagans were present and spoke ill of him as a sorcerer, some desired that he should make known to them what this bird’s cry signified.

<margin>*Cras*, the prophecy of Athanasius.</margin>
It is said that Athanasius laughed quietly and said: *Cras*, in the Latin tongue <note>original: "Cras, in Latijnscher sprake"</note>, which means as much as "the coming day" <note>In Latin, *cras* means "tomorrow." To the Roman ear, the croaking of a raven sounds like the word *cras*. Athanasius used this wordplay to predict their coming downfall.</note>. While the bird cries thus, he makes known that tomorrow you shall have a day of mourning, and that by the Emperor's command. And so it happened, though Athanasius's reasoning seemed laughable, it was nonetheless fulfilled. For on the next day, the Emperor’s letters came to the judges, and it was commanded that the pagans should not be allowed into their temples, nor hold their festivals in unbelief; then all their high feast days were destroyed and brought to nothing.

# Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus, another 5th-century church historian who wrote a continuation of the history of the early Church.</note>

¶ What evil George brought about in Alexandria.

### The xxviii. Chapter.

Now when, as has been said, Athanasius had generally escaped these perils and dangers, the people and the clergy, being 

<column-break/>

<margin>G George is bishop at Alexandria after Athanasius was driven out.</margin>
favorable to him, held the churches until the Governor of Egypt and the Captain drove them out and gave them over to George <note>original: "Georgio"; referring to George of Cappadocia, an Arian bishop installed to replace the orthodox Athanasius.</note>. He arrived not long after and took possession of the churches with their rights. He conducted himself more like a tyrant than a priest, especially toward those who held Athanasius in high regard. For he inflicted great violence upon both men and women with bonds and beatings. So much so that the people, becoming incensed against him, would have killed him had he not fled to the Emperor. This having happened, the followers of Athanasius held the churches again for a long time.

<margin>H George is forced to flee.</margin>
But the Captain returning from Egypt, he gave them back to the followers of George. Thereafter, the Emperor’s secretary arrived, and many of the Alexandrians were killed.

<margin>Secretary of the Emperor.</margin>
<margin>I</margin>
After him came George, much more terrifying than he had been in earlier times when he was greatly hated; he so moved the Emperor that many were murdered and put to death. The Egyptian monks spoke out against George’s wickedness, and the multitude of the people followed them, as they gave true witness and were of a fine, pious, and virtuous life.

<margin>K Monks of Egypt.</margin>

# Theodoretus <note>Theodoret of Cyrus, a theologian and historian known for his role in the 5th-century Christological debates.</note>

I have omitted the names of these men for many reasons. But this is the content of the letter.

# Tripartite Church History <note>The *Historia Ecclesiastica Tripartita* is a famous 6th-century compilation of three earlier church histories—those of Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret—translated into Latin by Epiphanius Scholasticus and edited by Cassiodorus.</note>

¶ Damasius, Valerian, and the other
Bishops, to the beloved brethren,
the Bishops in Illyricum <note>Illyricum was a Roman province spanning much of the modern-day Balkans.</note>,
joy and salvation in the
Lord.

<margin>Letter of the Roman Synod sent to Illyricum.</margin>
**W**e believe that you hold fast to our holy faith, grounded in the Apostolic teaching, and that you present this to all peoples, for it does not agree with the institutions of the fathers that many others should be instructed otherwise than is right. But we have heard from the Gallic <note>original: "Gallicanen," referring to Gaul (modern France).</note> and Venetian <note>original: "Benedischen," referring to the region of Venetia in northern Italy.</note> Brothers how some are adhering to the heretics. For such an evil, not only shall the Bishops provide oversight, but they shall also set themselves against it; for it happens through simplicity and lack of understanding that some are misled by false teaching. Therefore, no one shall let himself be led astray with false teaching, but much rather shall the meaning of our Fathers be confirmed among you. And it has been written to us how Auxentius <note>original: "Aurentius." Auxentius was the Arian Bishop of Milan and a major opponent of the Nicene faith before the time of St. Ambrose.</note> of Milan has been condemned specifically in this matter. Therefore it is right that all Bishops in the Roman Empire, and those who are of this Law’s Teaching, should well understand the content, and not defile the Faith with various Teachings. Therefore, as soon as the Heretics had vomited out their malice—just as now the godless blasphemy of the shameful Arians <note>Arians followed the teachings of Arius, who argued that Jesus Christ was a created being and not of the same substance as God the Father.</note> is brought to light—our fathers, numbering 318, gathered themselves together
<margin>318 Fathers at Nicaea.</margin>
in the city of Nicaea and held the first proceeding. They set this confession as a firm wall against the Devil’s weapons, and with these Medicines, all deadly poisons were driven away: namely, that the Father and the Son shall be believed to be of one Divine essence, one power, and one greatness, of one being and substance, as likewise also the Holy Spirit. And whosoever confesses otherwise shall be excluded from our communion. This soul-saving and well-considered confession and conclusion, some have undertaken to cruelly destroy. But at first, their cause was driven back in the gathering
<margin>Retraction at Ariminum.</margin>
at Ariminum <note>Also known as the Council of Rimini (359 AD), where many bishops were pressured into accepting a pro-Arian creed.</note>, where they were forced to recant what they had once rightly acknowledged, claiming they had been deceived or that they did not understand the meaning of the Fathers gathered in Nicaea was against them. For that number assembled at Ariminum could not establish any judgment, since it is manifest that

<column-break/>

<margin>Authority of the Roman Bishop.</margin>
neither the Roman Bishop (whose judgment one should have expected above all) nor Vincentius <note>Vincentius of Capua, a prominent bishop of the time.</note>, who for so many years governed that Bishopric entirely blamelessly, nor others like them, gave their consent therein. Especially since (as I have said) they themselves seemed to have been misled by deception, so that they afterwards considered a better Council; thereby they make it known that those things [at Ariminum] displeased them. Therefore, your piety sees clearly enough that only the faith founded at Nicaea upon Apostolic authority and standing shall henceforth be held for eternity. And this the Easterners shall do likewise with us, who also acknowledge themselves as common Christians. Those in the West shall also rejoice in this. We hold that those who are slow in this resolution shall very soon be cast out of our communion, and the Episcopal titles taken from them, so that their subjects, delivered from their error, may turn back. For
<margin>Error cannot help the erring.</margin>
those who are bound with the snares of deception cannot in any way deliver the people therefrom. Therefore, may your Love be united with all the Priests of God, just as we trust that your Love will persevere, firm and immovable. Thus we must believe rightly with your Love, and you with us. Please also gladden us with a Letter of your love. God keep you, dear brothers.

Moreover, the great Athanasius <note>Athanasius of Alexandria, the chief defender of Trinitarianism against Arianism.</note>, in the Letter he wrote to the Africans, also disputed concerning the Synod of Ariminum in such a manner.

**N**ow that all things have been heard and brought forth, Dearly beloved, who would accept those who propose the Council of Ariminum, or any other besides that Council of Nicaea, in practice? Or who would not hate those who destroy the institutions of the Fathers, or who hold in high regard those things that were recently established at Ariminum through strife and force? Who would unite himself with those men who even [reject] their own things...

<margin>Jeremiah 2:13 and 17:13. John 4:10</margin>
waters, have dug for themselves stinking pits <note>In Jeremiah 2:13, these are "broken cisterns"; the Dutch text uses "stinckende putten" (stinking pits/wells) to emphasize their corruption.</note> that can hold no water, as it is written by the Prophet Jeremiah. <margin>Macedonius, persecutor of the churches. Eleusius.</margin>

## Theodoretus

<margin>K</margin>
These are the dealings, practices, murders, anxieties, and internal wars
<margin>Macedonius oppresses the spirit.</margin>
which Macedonius incited against the Christians. Therefore, he was not only greatly hated by those who were injured, but also by his friends; likewise,
<margin>L</margin>

Tripartite Ecclesiastical History.

<margin>Those who said that the Son was of one essence with the Father.</margin>

¶ **The Homoousians** <note>original: "Homousij"; those who held to the Nicene Creed, believing the Son to be of the same substance as the Father.</note>, However, Macedonius did not turn back for those who spoke against him, and he removed the body of the Emperor <note>Constantine the Great</note> into the Church where the body of the martyr Acacius lies buried. Having left a Governor and Ruler in the Western Lands, the Emperor Julianus <note>referring here to Julian the Apostate before his full accession</note> traveled from there toward the Orient.

# Theodoretus.

## ¶ Of Leontius the Bishop at Antioch, and of Aetius the master of Eunomius.

### The 27th Chapter.

<margin>Two Clerics and many people.</margin>
But Leontius, a Bishop at Antioch, as he was an Arian, sought to hide his defect. And when he saw that the Priests and the people were divided among themselves, and one said: "Glory be to God the Father and the Son," and the other, "Glory be to the Father through the Son and the Holy Spirit," he said his prayer silently, so that the bystanders could hear nothing else but when he said: *In secula seculorum*, that is, **forever and ever**. And so that it might not seem to be done out of a wicked mind, it should be said that he did it for the peace and unity of the people. But since he set himself against the servants of the Lord and the Knights of Truth, and advanced the heretics, he gave sufficient sign that he kept his poison hidden so that he might retain the love of the people, and also that the fear of the Emperor weighed upon him, who had commanded that one should not say that the Son was unlike the Father.

<margin>Aetius, a heretic and deacon at Antioch.</margin>
At this time Aetius—a master of Eunomius (who increased the blasphemy of Arius with his own opinion)—was in the office of the Diaconate.

<column-break/>

But Flavianus and Diodorus began a monastic life and labored diligently for the **Apostolic Doctrine**, vehemently rebuking the Bishop of Antioch because he had set himself against Christian teaching. For they said that he had disturbed a wicked human life in order to advance blasphemy to a high level, and had received the name of Deacon to the destruction of the Church.

<margin>First how they were forbidden to be.</margin>
They also threatened to suspend him from Apostolic communion and, traveling to the Western lands, to discover the things he had handled craftily. Leontius, fearing this, suspended Aetius from his office, though in other things he remained favorable to him. But these two wonderful companions, Flavianus and Diodorus, although they were not yet Priests, were nevertheless held in great regard by the people, exhorting the people night and day to live a godly life for God's salvation.

<margin>At that time: Flavian and Diodorus sing psalms at the graves of the Martyrs outside the church.</margin>
For these two first divided the people into two choirs to sing praise to God the LORD, and taught them to sing the Psalms of David in an orderly fashion. And this first happened at Antioch, and afterwards spread and came into the whole circuit of the world <note>This refers to the origin of antiphonal psalmody—singing in alternating choirs—which is a cornerstone of Christian liturgy.</note>.

These men called the friends of God to the graves of the Martyrs, held Vigils, and therein praised God one with another.

<margin>Thus they were joined to the church.</margin>
Leontius, seeing this, judged that it would not be advisable to forbid such things, for he saw that many pious men followed them. But using sweet words instead, he kindly requested them that they should rather hold these high annual Feasts in the Church. They, well-noting his craftiness, did as they were commanded and gathered those who loved them in the Church, so that they might give praise to GOD the LORD joyfully and with one mind and spirit. But Leontius could not be turned from his wicked mind toward moderation.

<margin>Stephanus and Placitus.</margin>
For wearing a mild countenance, he covered the rogueishness of Stephanus and Placitus beneath it. For these men, while they were against the right doctrine and of a base life, he nevertheless accepted as Priests and Deacons.

But those who were rich in virtue and defended the Apostolic doctrine, those he left without any honor.

<margin>Cause of heresy.</margin>
From this cause, the Clergy had many heretics. But the people fought bravely for the right Doctrine.

# Sozomenus.
<note>Salminius Hermias Sozomenus was a 5th-century Christian historian; this text translates his "Ecclesiastical History."</note>

## The 33rd Chapter.

---

<margin>Eudoxius was accused before the Emperor.</margin>
Germanica is a city situated in Cappadocia, bordering the frontiers of Cilicia and Syria, in which city Eudoxius was Bishop. This man, when Leontius had died, seized the Bishopric of Antioch for himself, and presumed with his carnal life to lay waste to the Vineyard of the LORD. He did not hide his malice as Leontius had: but openly set himself against the Apostolic teaching and persecuted the true Christian believers with many kinds of oppression.

At this time, after Marcellus, Basilius was Bishop at Ancyra, and Eustachius at Sebastia in Armenia. These men, recognizing the injustice and raging cruelty of Eudoxius, made such things known by letters to the Emperor Constantius, who was then in the Western Lands; for they were well known to the Emperor, and the Emperor loved them for the sake of their pious lives. This being made known to the Emperor Constantius, he wrote back to them, stating that he had not given the Bishopric to Eudoxius as he claimed; and he commanded that he be driven out and that he should be punished in Nicaea, Bithynia.

<margin>Another Council in Nicaea, Bithynia.</margin>
Commanding that a Council be held there, for Eudoxius himself had petitioned the powerful members of the Court so that a Council might be gathered in Nicaea. But God, foreseeing all things, hindered that Council with a terrible earthquake—as if the events were orchestrated—for a large part of the city was cast down by the earthquake, and many inhabitants were killed.

<margin>An earthquake prevents the gathering of the Council at Nicaea.</margin>
When those who had already arrived there learned of this, they returned again to their churches. But I truly believe that this was so arranged by the wisdom of God: for in this city, the Apostolic faith of the holy Fathers was 

<column-break/>

confessed and brought forth against Arius <note>referring to the First Council of Nicaea in 325 AD</note>, and by chance, the second gathering might have established something else that would have been contrary to the former. Thereby the Arians would have had cause to better trap the simple-minded with the name "Council of Nicaea," as if it were the most ancient one. But GOD, a protector of the churches, prevented this and dispersed the Council.

<margin>Vysatius from Persia predicts the earthquake.</margin>
But in a moment's time, the city shook so violently that no one could escape, but they were immediately killed in the quaking. It is said that before this disaster occurred, one named Vysatius <note>likely Arsacius the Persian, a soldier turned hermit</note>, formerly a Knight from the land of Persia, having foreseen this, became a Christian. He was under the Jovian Line <note>original: "Jupterse Linie"; likely referring to the Jovian legion of the Roman army</note>, which he left, and went to live in the city of Nicomedia <note>text says "Durin," likely a corruption of the location near the tower</note>, and exercised himself in Divine Philosophy <note>a common historical term for the monastic or ascetic life</note>. This man then, through divine revelations shown from Heaven, knew what would shortly come upon the city, and commanded by divine warning to go out of the city. Which having been done, he ran with all haste to the Church and told the Clergy that they should pray to the Lord, that it might please Him to deliver them from the approaching peril. But when they mocked him for it, he returned again to his tower <note>original: "Turing/Turri"</note>, and falling down there, began to weep.

<margin>Vysatius dies in the earthquake.</margin>
In the meantime, the earthquake coming, many died, and the rest were buried through mountain and valley. But Vysatius was found lying dead in the tower on his face, just as he was accustomed to pray. Indeed, there is reason to believe that when he began to die, he prayed to GOD that he might first end his life before he saw the destruction of the City. In which city he had first known Christ through foresight, and was regarded as one who had attained Christian Philosophy. For with his good conduct, he also drove out devils. Once, when someone was tormented by the devil, he drew his sword and ran with it through the whole city, making all those he met bleed:

<margin>Vysatius, a holy man, performs miracles.</margin>
so Vysatius met him alone, and naming Christ, he made the man healthy with a single word, so that he was immediately calmed from his madness. Because of which virtuous works

With these words, Eleusius countered the opinion of Acacius. He claimed the "Faith of the Fathers" was that which was declared at Antioch. Yet this was easy to anticipate, for one might have said: "Why do you take these for the Fathers, while you refuse to accept the [original] Fathers?" For those meeting at Nicaea agreed upon that word *of the same substance* <note>original: "Homousion," the foundational term of the Nicene Creed asserting the divinity of Christ</note>, and it was rightly established. Therefore, these should properly be called the true Fathers, because they lived in those first times. And those who later gathered at Antioch received their priesthood from them.

</margin>
If those gathered at Antioch then deny their own Fathers, then their followers have indeed followed betrayers of the fathers <note>original: "vader schenders," meaning those who dishonor or violate the legacy of their predecessors</note>. How does this rhyme together? These despise that faith as unjust. Do these others take it up as good and right? If those [at Nicaea] did not have the Holy Spirit, which is received through the laying on of hands, then these others have not received the priesthood either.

But how could they receive from those who do not have what was to be given? This may well be thrown back against Eleusius.

M They also said, if the name "substance" were suppressed, then one might also—to avoid further dispute—leave out and rewrite the term *Homoousion* <note>original: "Homousion," meaning "of the same substance," the key term of the Nicene Creed</note>, which many priests from the West (out of reverence for the Nicene Council) accepted from their hearts.

### The XXXVI. Chapter.

<margin>Acacius summons the Bishops from Bithynia to the Synod at Constantinople.</margin>
But Acacius and those who had lived with him for a long time at Constantinople summoned the Bishops from Bithynia, among whom were Marcarius, Macedonius, and Ulphilas, Bishop of the Goths. <margin>Aetius is deprived of his office as Deacon.</margin>
When this was done, they deposed Aetius from his office as Deacon, as one holding heretical views, and as one who wrote certain treatises according to human wisdom against the Order of the Church, and made *Dialogues* <note>original: *Dialogos*; likely referring to Aetius's work 'The Syntagma'</note>—mocking books full of all kinds of blasphemy—and thus acting as a disturber of the churches and a cause of much dispute and discord. It was said by some that they did not depose him from the heart, but only to do the Emperor a service. For it was said of them that they were of the same mind as Aetius.

Seeing now how the Emperor had become

<column-break/>

And as they could not agree in doctrine, they made no mention of their faith until the time of their separation, but instead imposed a particular punishment on each, according to how they had acted against the ordinances of the church.

**If** he held this opinion, he denied it and said that it was the understanding of Aetius <note>original: "Etij"; Aetius of Antioch was a radical Arian who argued the Son was "unlike" the Father.</note>, whom the Emperor commanded to be brought before him and questioned; although it was not his own opinion, he nevertheless stated that it was his. Following this, he demanded of him that he should condemn the *Homoousion* <note>original: "Homousion"; the Nicene creed's term meaning "of the same substance," which was the central point of theological conflict.</note>, which is not to be found in the scriptures. Indeed, we waited for them, in case they might change their minds, hear, and understand. When we had waited a long time and they would not renounce their opinion, we considered it much more honorable for the Church to proceed with the previously mentioned sentence than to look to the friendship of such men.

<margin>6 months for better ordination.</margin>
Therefore, we have pronounced the ban over them, giving them six months for judgment to perform penance. So that if they repent in this time and agree to the confession of their brothers, they might be received into the church and enjoy their faith and love.

But if they remained without penance and sought the friendship of men more than the order and unity of the Church, then we must consider that they were entirely unworthy of the bishop's office; and if they were deposed, others would be accepted in their places, so that the holy Christian Church might [keep] its beautiful...

# ¶ Concerning Eunomius and his sect.

## The 44th Chapter.

Now Eunomius greatly praises this Aetius <note>Aetius of Antioch (d. 367 AD) was the founder of the Anomoean sect of Arianism, which argued the Son was "unlike" the Father.</note> in his books, calling him a man of God, and has attributed great praise to him. On the other hand, at that time he was among the number of those who had been deposed, yet he received the Episcopal Office from them. Now Eudoxius and Acacius, with their companions, agreed and gave their consent to the proceedings that occurred in Nicea in Thrace <note>Referring to the Council of Nike in 359 AD, where a pro-Arian creed was established.</note>, and instead of Basil and Eleusius, they ordained other Bishops, which I now deem unnecessary to speak of.

<margin>Eunomius, Bishop of Cyzicus.</margin>
I wish to speak of Eunomius: When Eunomius had taken over the Church at Cyzicus, and while Eleusius was still alive, Eudoxius observed the true understanding of the people. He also saw how the Emperor was so enraged against those who said that the only-begotten Son of God was a creature. He therefore forced Eunomius to conceal this opinion and not to reveal it, even if he were provoked by accusers, saying: "We shall preach Eunomius at a more convenient time, whom we now hide; and we wish to teach those who are ignorant, and we shall bend, force, or punish the dissenters." With this promise, Eunomius was persuaded and presented his ungodly doctrine in the most obscure terms.

<margin>Eudoxius commands Eunomius to restrain his teaching for a time.</margin>
Now those who were skilled in the Divine Scriptures and saw the craftiness of his words took it very poorly, openly contradicting him and judging that it was merely a work of levity and not Wisdom. And feigning [interest], they went into his house, praying that he would prove the truth

<column-break/>

<margin>Eunomius reveals his teaching.</margin>
of his doctrine, and that he should not allow himself to be tossed here and there by various teachings. Then he became bolder, and the doctrine he had hidden, he then revealed. And when they said to him that it was false and unjust that those who were under him should not enjoy the truth, being misled by these and similar words, he revealed his blasphemous teaching in the assembly. These men then, having become zealous and heated, traveled to Constantinople and first accused Eunomius before Eudoxius. When he would not receive them, they went to the Emperor, complaining to him of the deception of these revelations, saying: "How this seduction was much more harmful than the ungodly doctrine of Arius."

<margin>A</margin>
Therefore, the troubled Emperor commanded Eudoxius to lead him away, and if he were overcome [convicted], he should be deposed from his priesthood. **Left Column**

<margin>Aetius is sent into exile.</margin>
Although he <note>Eudoxius, the Bishop of Constantinople.</note> was of this same opinion, he denied it and joked that it was the understanding of Aetius. When the Emperor ordered Aetius to be brought before him and questioned him—even though it was not his [Eudoxius's] true intention—he nevertheless mocked him, saying it was his own view. For this reason, Aetius was sent away into exile and driven out. Eustachius, however, cried out with a loud voice that Eudoxius was also of this opinion, demanding that he condemn the writings of Aetius. This he did, though slowly, condemning that which he had preached before and after. Following this, he hoped that he [Silvanus] would condemn the <term>Homousion<note>original: "Homousion"; a Greek term meaning "of the same substance," used by the orthodox to describe the relationship between the Father and the Son.</note></term>, which is not to be found in the Scriptures. To this Silvanus replied that the little word "<term>Creature<note>The Arians argued that the Son was a created being, rather than being of the same essence as the Father.</note></term>," and "from non-existent things," and "of another substance," are also not in the Scriptures. Therefore, by right, these words should also be nullified. Then

<margin>Silvanus: a creature from non-existent things, of another substance.</margin>
he said further (in the manner of a dispute): "Truly Silvanus, if God the Word is not from non-existent things, then He is also not a creature; and if God the Word is not of another substance, it follows that the Son is of one essence with the Father, just as God is from God, Light from Light, and possesses one nature with the Father." Then the Emperor was moved to anger and threatened to drive Silvanus into exile; to which Silvanus answered:

<margin>Disputation concerning God the Word.</margin>
"O Emperor, you have the power to inflict suffering, but we do not have the power to break the ordinances of the fathers." Then the Emperor commanded them to be driven out of the Church and to ordain others in their place. But Eudoxius, as he held the Church at Constantinople in a tyrannical manner, drove out Eleusius of Cyzicus and made Eunomius the Bishop. And they deposed Aetius with writings, even though they were thought to be on his side, and they wrote to Gregory all that had occurred.

<margin>The Mygdonius flood.</margin>
A ¶ For after that, the Persians divided the flow of the water of the Mygdonius, which runs through the middle of the city, holding it back from afar and raising it up near the city, so that the water, rising greatly on both sides and gathering, might better overwhelm the city with this great torrent.

B When he saw that the <term>water-trenches<note>These were likely dikes or embankments used to dam the river for a sudden release.</note></term> he had made began to be full, he immediately removed the gates he had constructed and let the force and power of the water run against the walls, which were broken and collapsed by it. When this happened, the water ran with great force and violence against the other parts of the walls where the water used to flow, and it overthrew them with great destruction.

<margin>Sapor sees a vision.</margin>
C ¶ Seeing this, Sapor hoped to win the city without a fight. But on that same day, it became so calm that one could bathe and walk therein. The next day, when he intended to march through the broken walls into the city with all his army, he saw how the walls on both sides were beautifully repaired. For this holy man, the Bishop <note>Jacob of Nisibis, a prominent figure at the Council of Nicaea, known for his defense of the city during the Persian sieges.</note>, armed the army and the other common inhabitants of the city with prayer; which being done, the walls were restored again. And he prepared <term>bulwarks<note>Defensive fortifications or earthworks.</note></term> and artillery to drive him away if he approached. And this he did, and Sapor did not reach the walls, but the Bishop called upon **GOD** in the Temple and fulfilled all things. At this, the King of the Persians was not only terrified by the rebuilt walls, but another vision also frightened him. For he saw one standing upon the walls who was adorned with imperial clothing, shining as much with purple as with an imperial crown.

D ¶ As he now thought that it was the Roman Emperor, he threatened those with death who said that the Emperor was not present there. When they confirmed this—that they were telling the truth, that the Emperor Constantius lived at Antioch—he understood from their faces that their words were true, and said: "That God fights the war for the Romans."

E ¶ Since he was very displeased by this, this miserable King shot an arrow into the air; and when he saw that he could not hit that body which he had seen in imperial clothing, he

F

<column-break/>

G yet did not cease from his madness. Then Ephrem—a wondrous man and a glorious writer, <term>Ephrem the Syrian<note>Ephrem of Edessa (c. 306–373 AD), a prominent Christian theologian and hymnwriter.</note></term>—commanded the holy man, Bishop Jacob, that he should come upon the walls; and seeing the barbarians, that he should then curse them and shoot the arrow of malediction against them.

<margin>The curse of Jacob against the Persians.</margin>
H ¶ Therefore, this venerable man had himself brought there and went up onto a tower. Seeing many thousands of soldiers, he wished no other curse upon them than <term>gnats and flies<note>original: "ghewimte ende vlieghen"; this refers to a plague of biting insects that famously disrupted Sapor's elephants and cavalry.</note></term>, so that through these small animals they might learn to acknowledge God’s power. Thus, after his prayer, it immediately rained and misted gnats and flies, so that the trunks of the elephants, the ears and noses of the horses and other animals, were filled. Since the beasts could not endure the filth of these vermin, they threw off their riders, broke the order of the army, and finally fled from there.

I ¶ In this way, the poor, wretched King acknowledged that God cares for the souls who fear Him, and that He punishes mildly and mercifully. And so he retreated with his army, gaining mockery and shame, and receiving no victory from the siege of the city.

At first, they said: that **GOD** the Word <note>The "Word" or *Logos*, referring to the Second Person of the Trinity.</note>, in taking on the human race, had not taken on a soul. Afterward, appearing to repent and to better themselves, they added to this and said: that he had indeed taken on a soul, but one that had no mind <term>Gemoet<note>Original: "gemoet." Fol. 327.
->The Second Part. The Fifth Book.<-

<margin>Nisibis delivered.</margin>
**A** For after that, the Persians divided the flow of the water of the Mygdonius <note>The Mygdonius is a river in Mesopotamia that flows through the ancient city of Nisibis (modern-day Nusaybin, Turkey).</note>, which runs through the middle of the city, holding it back from afar and raising it higher near the city, so that the water, rising greatly on both sides and gathering, might better overflow the city with this great pressure.

**B** When he <note>Sapor II, the King of the Sassanid Persian Empire.</note> now saw that the water-trenches he had made began to be full, he immediately removed the gates he had constructed, and let the force and power of the water run against the walls, which were bent and collapsed therefrom. This occurring, the water ran with great force and turbulence against the other parts of the walls, where the water usually had its flow, and overthrew them with great destruction.

**C** Seeing this, Sapor hoped to win the city without a fight: But it became calm on that same day, so that one could bathe and walk therein. The next day, when he intended to pull into the city through the broken walls with all his men of war, he saw that the walls on both sides were beautifully repaired. For this holy man, the Bishop <note>St. Jacob of Nisibis (died c. 338 AD), a famous ascetic and bishop known for his presence at the Council of Nicaea.</note>, had armed the soldiers and other common inhabitants of the city with prayer: whereby it happened that the walls were restored again. And he prepared bulwarks and artillery to drive him away should he approach. And this he did, and did not come to the walls, but he called upon GOD in the Temple and fulfilled all things: But the King of the Persians was not only terrified by the rebuilt walls, but another vision also frightened him.

<margin>Sapor sees a vision.</margin>
**D** For he saw one standing upon the walls who was adorned with Imperial clothing, glistening as much with Purple as with an Imperial Crown.

**E** When he now thought that it was the Roman Emperor, he threatened those who said that the Emperor was not present there with death. When they now confirmed this, that they spoke the truth—that the Emperor Constantius was staying at Antioch—he understood from their faces that their words were true, and said: That God waged the war for the Romans.

**F** As he was very displeased by this, this miserable King shot an arrow into the air, and when he saw that he could not hit that body which he had seen in Imperial clothing, he

<column-break/>

**G** nevertheless did not cease from his madness. Then Ephrem <note>St. Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373 AD), a prominent Syriac Christian deacon, hymnographer, and theologian.</note>, a wonderful man and a magnificent writer among the Syrians, commanded the holy man Bishop Jacob that he should come upon the walls: and seeing the Barbarians, that he should then curse them and shoot the arrow of malediction against them.

<margin>Ephrem, the Bishop, Sapor.</margin>
**H** So this venerable man had himself brought there and went upon a tower, and seeing many thousands of soldiers there, he wished no other curse upon them but of vermin and flies, so that through these small creatures they might learn to acknowledge God’s power.

<margin>Jacob’s prayer against the Persians.</margin>
Thus it happened, after his prayer, that it immediately rained vermin and little flies and they nested there, so that the trunks of the elephants, the ears and noses of the horses and other animals were then filled. But as the beasts could not endure the filth of these vermin, they threw off their riders, broke the order of the soldiers, and finally fled from there.

**I** In this manner the poor, miserable King acknowledged that God takes care of the souls who fear Him, and who punishes mildly and mercifully. And he thus retreated with his army, receiving mockery and shame, and receiving no victory from the siege of the city.

## ¶ On the explanation of this passage: The Lord created me in the beginning of his ways.

### The 47th Chapter.

<margin>Meletius is desired by all</margin>
At this time, the holy man Meletius governed a city in Armenia and preached there to the barbarians; he was regarded as a man of tranquil character. But because the Arians <note>Arians followed the teachings of Arius, who believed that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> believed that he sided with them, they petitioned Emperor Constantius to make him Bishop of Antioch. The faithful Christians consented to this because of the holiness of his life and the greatness of his teaching, and they signed his confession of faith and the decree of both parties. They entrusted and handed over Meletius to Eusebius of Samosata, the Bishop. But when the great Meletius arrived there, the people from both sides flocked to him, along with Jews and Heathens, all desiring to see the highly-renowned Meletius. Then the Emperor and others who were with him commanded that whoever could interpret the Scriptures should explain this passage to the people: *The Lord created me in the beginning of his ways,* etc. <note>original: "De Heere heeft my geschapen int beginsel sijner wegē." This refers to Proverbs 8:22, a central text in the Arian controversy. Arians used it to argue that the Son was "created."</note> And he ordered that the notaries should record everything. Immediately, George of Laodicea spat out the stench of his poisonous heresy. After this, Acacius of Caesarea tried to present a middle way and departed from this blasphemous teaching, yet he did not entirely preserve the Apostolic teaching. Thirdly, the great Meletius stood up and, with holy explanation, pointed out the right Rule and the firm path. For he used the truth as a weight, thereby avoiding what was too much or too little. And as the entire multitude was favorable toward him, praying that he would give a brief explanation of his doctrine, he signaled with three fingers in a symbolic manner, then drew back two and extended one, and spoke these praiseworthy words: "Three are understood, but we dispute and speak as of only one." <note>This gesture was a famous defense of the Trinity: three distinct Persons (fingers), but one unified Substance or Godhead (the single finger and the closing of the hand).</note>

# Sozomenus.

## ¶ On the unity of those three persons.

### The 48th Chapter.

<margin>Meletius is silenced</margin>
It is said that at this time, while Meletius was still speaking, the chief deacon in his church stretched out his hand and held it over Meletius's mouth. But Meletius indicated his meaning with his hand even more clearly than with words. For by stretching out three fingers, then pulling them back and closing them, he wished to give the people to understand by this figure that the three are one. After the chief deacon had stopped holding his mouth with his hands, Meletius cried out with a full voice: "One must and ought to hold to that Council of Nicaea." <note>The Council of Nicaea (325 AD) established the orthodox Christian doctrine of the Trinity against Arianism.</note>

# Theodoretus.

<margin>Meletius in exile</margin>
Against this teaching, the Arians finally sharpened their tongues, saying: "The holy Meletius is a Sabellian." <note>Sabellianism was the opposite heresy to Arianism; it taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were merely different "modes" or masks of one person, rather than three distinct persons.</note> Therefore, they advised the Emperor to send Meletius into exile to one of his provinces. Then Euzoius, of whom mention was made above, openly praised the doctrine of Arius. For the great Alexander <note>Bishop Alexander of Alexandria, who first deposed Arius.</note> had stripped this Euzoius and Arius of the office of deacon. After this had happened, the people who were not yet poisoned by the heresies were divided, and they came together in the Apostolic Church located in the old city. For thirty years after the great Eustathius <note>Eustathius of Antioch, an early champion of Nicene orthodoxy who was deposed by Arians around 330 AD.</note> had been driven out, the true Christians had to suffer the burden of the Arians and endure the changing of things as best they could.

# Sozomenus.

For the followers of Meletius did not want to have communion with those who had held the Nicene faith from the beginning, saying: "Meletius was ordained based on an Arian confession, and his followers were baptized by him." Because of these things, the Church at Antioch was divided into another part. <note>This refers to the "Meletian Schism," a complex division in Antioch where multiple groups all claimed to be the true orthodox church.</note>

# The Second Part. The Fifth Book.

<margin>Meletius gives answer by word of mouth</margin>
¶ As we have seen before, the godlessness of the heresies increased from day to day, and the protectors of the Apostolic Doctrine were openly attacked. After the holy Meletius <note>original: "Militius," the Bishop of Antioch who was a key figure in the Trinitarian disputes.</note> was driven out and the heretic Euzoius was accepted in his place, the faithful thought upon the answers given to Lot:
<margin>Genesis 19. Matthew 18. Matthew 5. Mark 9.</margin>
Save your lives. <note>original: "Helpt uwer zielen," a reference to Genesis 19:17 where Lot is told to flee for his life.</note> Furthermore, they looked to the words of the Gospel, saying: If your right eye offends you, pluck it out and cast it from you. Likewise, the Lord says of hands and feet: It is better that one of your hands or feet perish than that the whole body be cast into the damnation of hell.

## ¶ Concerning the Manly Courage of Eusebius; a noteworthy Chapter.

### The 49th Chapter.

<margin>The decree of the Antiochians remained at Meletius’s request with Eusebius [against] the Samosatene Arians.</margin>
But the wonderful Eusebius, of whom we have spoken, when he was given the charge—and seeing that they began to contemplate and maintain a compromise with Meletius—he returned again to his city. But the Arians, fearing the written testimonies, advised Constantius <note>Emperor Constantius II, who favored Arianism.</note> that he should send someone to demand back from Eusebius the testimonies concerning Meletius. Then, very quickly, a courier was dispatched to manage these matters with care. Having arrived and proclaimed the Emperor’s command, the wonderful Eusebius answered: "That which has been entrusted to me in confidence, I will not give up, unless all those who gave it to me agree to it." When the one who had been sent reported this to the Emperor, he became highly enraged and wrote again to Eusebius, ordering him to return what he had received. He added in his writing that if he refused to return it, the courier was to chop off Eusebius's right hand. Yet the Emperor gave this messenger a verbal command not to actually do what the letter contained.

<margin>The manly courage of Eusebius.</margin>
¶ And when Eusebius read the letter and discovered the penalty the Emperor had set upon it, he stretched out both his right and his left hand, desiring that both should be cut off. And he said: "I shall not give up that Decree and confession, which is a sufficient record

<column-break/>

of the Arian pestilential heresy." When Constantius saw this steadfastness, he praised him greatly; for even the ungodly admire those who speak so bravely against them, and they laud and praise them when they are heroically overcome by such great and wonderful deeds.

## ¶ How Julian fought against the Germans near Strasbourg.

### The 50th Chapter.

<margin>Occurred in the times against the Germans.</margin>
These things were being handled by the Western churches. In the meantime, the Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate, who attempted to restore Roman paganism.</note> made war against the barbarian people living along the Rhine and overcame them, slaying some and taking others prisoner. And as he returned with a glorious victory, the soldiers—restless because of his peaceful and modest way of life—proclaimed him Augustus. <note>A title signifying he was now an Emperor, rivaling Constantius.</note> Once this had happened, he thought nothing of Constantius. He distressed the judges who had been appointed by him, and to their spite, he brought forth letters in which he revealed how, on account of the war he had against Magnentius, he had led the barbarians into Italy. Whereas men had previously considered him a Christian, he very suddenly changed and abandoned the Religion; he called himself a *Pontifex* <note>original: "Pontificem," meaning a High Priest of the Roman pagan religion.</note> and <margin>Calls himself Emperor and Pontifex.</margin> entered the Temple of the Heathens, where he offered sacrifices and commanded his subjects to serve such idols.

He claimed he had taken the islands of the Rhine not by his own will, but at the urging of the soldiers. It is said that when he reached these furthest borders, although it was autumn and all the harvest was gathered, other drops were nevertheless found. Moreover, the air from above rained upon him and others, and every little drop formed the shape <margin>Note. The sign of the cross on the clothing.</margin> of a cross. When this occurred, he and others thought that the wine-drops at the end were a sign of the beginning of good things. Where the falling rain landed, it seemed to strengthen the garment it fell upon. <margin>The droplets signify the incurable reign of Julian.</margin>
The out-of-season droplets signified the ruin of the Emperor, who would perish just as those droplets quickly vanish, and that his imperial reign would endure for but a short time. # The Sixth Book of the History called Ecclesiastica Tripartita, drawn from Sozomen, Socrates, and Theodoret, etc.

## Socrates.

### ¶ Concerning the descent and life of Julian, and how he attained the Imperial Throne.

->The First Chapter.<-

<note>A decorative woodcut initial 'N' contains an illustration of a man in classical or academic robes seated at a desk or lectern, possibly writing or reading.</note>

<margin>B</margin>
Now we wish to recount briefly about Julian, his birth, his education, and how he came to the Imperial Throne. Constantius <note>The text likely refers to Constantine the Great here, as he was the one who named the city, though the Dutch OCR reads "Constantius."</note>, who named Constantinople almost after his own name, had two brothers from one father, but not from the same mother; one of whom was named Dalmatius, and the other Constantius. Dalmatius had a son, also named the same, but Constantius had two: Gallus and Julian, who built up the city of Constantinople after his death. When the soldiers had killed the young Dalmatius, these two [Gallus and Julian] also came into nearly mortal peril along with Dalmatius after their father had died, had it not been that a sickness—which then appeared to be
<margin>D</margin>
fatal—helped Gallus; but Julian was helped by his youth, for he was then only eight years old.

<margin>Gallus studies at Ephesus.</margin>
Now when the Emperor's anger against them diminished, Gallus lived at Ephesus among the teachers, where he had been placed by his ancestors; but Julian, as he grew, was placed in the school at Constantinople, where the learned men were,

<column-break/>

to exercise himself. He went about in the common fashion of dress, and he had a master and a tutor, a eunuch <note>original: "een gesneden," literally "one who is cut," a common term for a eunuch in older Dutch.</note> named Mardonius. He who taught him Grammar was Nicocles the Laconian <note>original: "Nicolaum Laconem." Nicocles was a famous grammarian of the 4th century.</note>. He learned Rhetoric from a Sophist <note>A Sophist was a specific type of teacher of rhetoric and philosophy in the Greek world.</note> who was a Christian, named Hecebolius <note>original: "Ecbolus." Hecebolius was known for changing his religion to match that of the reigning emperor.</note>. This happened through the foresight of Constantius, so that he would not be taught by any Pagan Sophist, lest he might fall into Pagan superstition; for Julian was a Christian from the beginning. But as he made progress in his studies and increased in knowledge, a rumor spread among the people that he might one day serve and rule the Roman commonweal. When this came before the Emperor Constantius, he became incensed against Julian and drove him out of the Imperial city, sending him to Nicomedia, and commanding him not to attend the lectures of the Sophist Libanius the Syrian. For at that same time, Libanius lived at Nicomedia, having been driven from the schools at Constantinople by the teachers there; therefore Julian was forbidden from hearing the lessons of Libanius because he was a Pagan, yet he nevertheless did not neglect to read his books. And when he had made further progress in Rhetoric, Maximus the Philosopher came to Nicomedia—not the one from Byzantium who was the father of Euclid, but the one from Ephesus, who afterwards practiced all kinds of sorcery <note>original: "tooverije," referring to theurgy or magic which Maximus was famous for.</note>, and whom the Emperor Valentinian later ordered to be put to death. This philosopher came to Nicomedia at that time for no other reason than because he heard so much being said of Julian, whom...

<margin>A</margin> A certain philosopher, once Julian had understood his art, also began to follow his teacher's religion, which also pressed a desire into Julian’s heart to attain the Imperial throne.

<margin>B</margin> <margin>Julian begins to pretend to be a Christian.</margin> <margin>Was ordained as a Reader at Nicomedia.</margin> But as these things were not hidden from the Emperor, Julian lived in hope and worry; wishing to avoid all suspicion (for he who was previously a Christian later became the betrayer of Christians), he had his hair shorn <note>Shaving the head or receiving a tonsure was a mark of entering the monastic or clerical life.</note> and took up the life of a monk. Secretly he read the books of the Pagans, and openly he read the books of the Christians. Beyond this, he was ordained as a Reader <note>term: Reader (Lector) <gloss>A minor office in the early church responsible for reading the scriptures during services.</gloss></note> in the church at Nicomedia: through this outward piety, he escaped the Emperor's wrath. He did these things out of fear, in no way abandoning the hope he had conceived in his heart. And he also said to many of his friends that they would see a fortunate time as soon as he attained the Imperial throne.

<margin>C</margin> While these things were being handled against him, his brother Gallus became Emperor <note>Gallus was actually appointed Caesar, a junior emperor, by Constantius II.</note> and came to Nicomedia to visit his brother as he traveled to the East. A little time thereafter, Gallus having been killed, Julian immediately came under great suspicion by the Emperor, who ordered him to be kept under guard; and though he escaped through flight, he was watched wherever he went.

<margin>D</margin> <margin>Flight.</margin> <margin>Eusebia, wife of Constantius.</margin> But at last, having been found in hiding by the Emperor’s wife, named Eusebia, she petitioned the Emperor on his behalf that no harm should come to him, but rather that he should be sent to Athens to philosophize and study.

## Theodoretus.

<margin>E</margin> <margin>Consults the soothsayers for advice.</margin> Thus Julian began to desire the Imperial Scepter to rule. And for that reason, he traveled through the entire land of Greece <note>original: "Hellada"</note> and sought out soothsayers who could give him answers, asking them if he would come to his kingdom. And he found a man who spoke to him according to his desire, bringing him to a place of idols; having led him into secret, he called forth the deceptive demons from therein.

<margin>F</margin> <margin>A miracle of the demon fleeing before the sign of the cross.</margin> When they appeared very magnificently, Julian was terrified and made the sign of the cross on his forehead. But the demons, having recognized that sign of the cross—of the victory of Christ—they

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin> thought of that victory and fled in an instant. Seeing this, the Sorcerer rebuked Julian. Julian answered him that he had been terrified and was amazed by the power of the cross, seeing which the demons had fled so quickly. To this, the Sorcerer answered him: "O my friend, do not think or believe that they fear it, as you say; but rather that they find such a sign an abomination to behold, and so they vanished." And thus, taking this wretched Julian captive in mind, he was filled with hatred against that Christian sign.

## Socrates.

<margin>H</margin> After this, the Emperor recalled Julian and ordained him as Caesar <note>term: Caesar <gloss>In this period, 'Caesar' referred to a junior emperor or heir-apparent, while 'Augustus' was the senior ruler.</gloss></note>, and gave him his sister Constantia as a wife, sending him out against the Barbarians in France <note>The text uses "Vranckrijck" (France), referring to the Roman province of Gaul.</note>. For the Barbarians, whose help Emperor Constantius had requested against Magnentius, began to destroy the Roman cities when they could not prevail against those tyrants.

<margin>I</margin> <margin>Constantia, Julian's wife.</margin> When Julian was still a youth, the Emperor commanded him that he should undertake nothing without the advice of the generals. When the generals, after receiving power, acted poorly—whereby the Barbarians were victorious—Julian nevertheless allowed the generals to practice every luxury.

<margin>K</margin> But taking the soldiers and promising them the loot of the slain enemy, he thus made a beginning of defeating the Barbarians, and so he made himself beloved and worthy in the eyes of his army.

<margin>L</margin> It is said that as he rode into a city, a laurel crown—with which they used to decorate the cities—hanging between two columns, fell upon his head when the rope broke, and he decorated and crowned himself with it. This having happened, they all cried out that this was a sign of the future Imperial rule. Some also believe that Constantius sent him against the Barbarians for the reason that he might be killed there. But I do not know if this suspicion is true: for since the Emperor gave him his own biological sister as a wife, he would have only laid more snares against himself.

<margin>M</margin> But when Julian complained to the Emperor about the negligence of the generals, another master was [sent] to him...

He was sent into the war, which was highly necessary for his needs; with this help, he bravely attacked the Barbarians. And when they, through ambassadors, had shown the Emperor’s letter in which he called upon the provinces to come, Julian took the messengers under the pretense of being prisoners and, attacking those Barbarians, defeated them: so much so that he captured the King and sent him to the Emperor Constantius. As this went so fortunately for him, he was named **Augustus** by the soldiers. and as he had no Imperial crown, a standard-bearer from among the troops took a chain from his neck and wound it around Julian’s head. In this manner, Julian became Emperor.

What this Philosopher did thereafter, the listeners shall judge. Firstly, sending no letters to the Emperor, and also having no regard for the good the Emperor had done for him, he did what seemed good to him. Now also changing and dismissing the Judges and Officials in the land: he also spoke ill of the Emperor Constantius, and through all the cities he read the letters that the Barbarians had written of him. Therefore many, departing from Constantius, followed him. Indeed, then he also threw away the pretense he had of *Christianity* <note>original: "Christenheyt"</note>, and in many cities, he opened the idol Temples and offered sacrifices, and called himself *Pontificem* <note>original: "Pontificem"</note>, that is, a Bishop of the Heathens. And while he handled such things, he inwardly prepared a cause for war against Constantius, as much as he was in any way able. For this was what Julian studied, whose *Philosophy* could not be fulfilled without great bloodshed, unless God, who is a lighter of human designs, had taken the one before the other had come. #### The Second Part. The Sixth Book.

<margin>He openly writes books for the Council.</margin>
When he entered the council, those were read openly. This Julian was the first since the Emperor Julius <note>referring to Julius Caesar</note> who delivered a formal speech or oration before the council. He also greatly loved the arts, in which he studied, and highly honored those who practiced *Philosophy* <note>Julian's devotion to Neoplatonism was central to his identity, earning him the nickname "The Philosopher."</note>. 
<margin>The Philosophers come to Julian's court.</margin>
Therefore, because of the fame of such people, many folk gathered about the Emperor’s Court who, dressed in cloaks <note>the traditional philosopher's mantle</note>, became known more for their appearance than for their mastery. They were a heavy burden to all Christians—seductive men who were constantly attached to the Emperor's religion or worship. 
<margin>Julian's *The Caesars* begins with Augustus.</margin>
As Julian was thus inflamed and inclined toward vain glory, he slandered all the Emperors who had been before him in the book that he wrote concerning the Emperors <note>original: "Cesares", a satirical work titled *The Caesars* or *The Banquet*.</note>. This pride also so possessed him that he wrote books against the Christians. Furthermore, in dismissing the cook and the barber <note>Julian abolished the lavish court of Constantius II to live a more austere, ascetic life</note>, he did not perform the work of an Emperor, but rather that of a Philosopher. That he also stripped the Emperors of their honor and spoke ill of them was truly against the duty of both an Emperor and a Philosopher.

# Sozomenus.

## How Julian, leaving the Christian faith, became a Heathen.

### The 2nd Chapter.

<margin>Julian Augustus washes his baptism from him with the blood of the Sacrifice.</margin>
It is said that Julian, right at the beginning, so openly and shamelessly renounced the Christian faith that he undertook certain sacrifices and incantations (which the Heathens called <term>averting rites</term> <note>original: "Expeditiones depulsivas", rituals intended to ward off or drive away spiritual influences</note>) through which one drives something away or prays it off, and with the blood of the sacrifice sought to wash away our baptism and to revoke the Christian confession.
From that time on, Julian both secretly and openly permitted the Heathens to offer sacrifices in their temples with great insolence. It is also said that once, when a sacrifice was made, there appeared in the entrails of the sacrificed beast a sign of the cross with a crown around it. At this 
<margin>Miraculous sign in the crowned cross.</margin>
occurrence, the ministers of the sacrifice were terrified and believed that this testified to a power of the Christian faith and some dignity

<column-break/>

of the Christian teaching. For the crown that was around the cross is a sign of victory; and because the circuit of the circle, returning into itself, has no end. And as others were now marvelling at this, the Emperor—acting as a master of this science—strengthened and said that these things signified good fortune and prosperity for him. For he claimed the circle enclosing the cross signified that the Christian teaching would be cut off and would not expand further according to their will, as shown by the encircling ring.

# Theodoretus.

<margin>Julian is chosen as a lector.</margin>
But Julian, fearing Constantius—especially since the Emperor had killed Julian's nearest friends because of his systematic Tyranny <note>original: "schickelijcker Tyrannye", referring to the purge of Julian's family after Constantine the Great's death</note>—became a <term>Lector</term> <note>original: "Leesmeester", a minor clerical rank responsible for reading scripture in church</note>, and he read the books of Holy Scripture in the church in the presence of the people. He even built a church for a Martyr, which Divine Providence did not accept from him.
