¶ **Julian, friend of the pagans and enemy of the Christians. And how the Church was formerly wealthy, and the Clergy were forced to march.**

### The 4th Chapter.

<margin>Julian, friend of the pagans and enemy of the Christians.</margin> Now when Julian held the Empire alone, and had opened the Temples again and set all other things aright, he also showed honor to the temple servants <note>original: "Tempelknechten," referring to pagan priests and attendants</note> with all devotion and reverence. He also frequently wrote to the citizens in all cities in general, saying that if they would return to the old customs of the Pagans, he would bestow gifts and honors upon them. He also made himself known as an enemy of the Christians, indeed, he did not want them to come to him or write to him, nor did he receive any messages from them. When the people of Nisibis <note>a fortress city on the border of the Roman and Sassanid Persian empires</note>, who were all Christians, expected a Persian war and sent messengers to the Emperor to obtain help from him, he would neither open the temples nor allow them to go to Holy Service. Instead, he rejected them, saying he would not help them, nor receive a message from a defiled city. He would not come to them now unless he understood that they had entirely given themselves over to Paganism. He also lamented this in Palestine, regarding the people of Constantia, and refused to help them. <margin>Maiuma Constantia.</margin> For this port is at Gaza and is called Maiuma, a place where many Christians lived together; they had obtained from Constantius <note>Emperor Constantius II</note> that it should be called a city, and it was named Constantia after the name of his son. For Constantius considered it unjust that Constantia, being a Christian place, should be subject to the people of Gaza, who were Pagans.

When Julian was in the Empire, the Gazans began to wage war against the Constantians. Julian, now

<column-break/>

acting as Judge, made them subjects of the Gazans again, although they were situated about 20 stadia <note>approximately 2.3 miles</note> from them. Retaining its previous name from that time, it was now called Gaza-by-the-Sea. It had common governors and judges. Only the church law seemed to indicate as if they were two cities. For each part had its own Bishop and Churches, as well as Vigils and Gatherings of the Martyrs, each separately. Each diocese also had its own boundaries and limits. It also happened that when Bishop Ammonius died, the Bishop of Gaza attempted to subject both groups of clergy to his rule, saying: That it was unseemly for two Bishops to be in one city. The people of Maiuma resisted this, and the Provincial Synod decided to give each of them their own Bishop. Believing that this was proper for those who, under Constantius, because of the merit of their faith, were worthy to have obtained this freedom and privilege; and though this was revoked by the judgment of a Pagan Prince, they should by no means be deprived of the anciently granted honor in the Priesthood and Church ordinances. At this time, Julian also forbade that the great and blessed city of Caesarea in Cappadocia should be called by that name anymore. And the old Imperial name, which it had received from the Emperor Claudius, he wished should no longer be remembered; in previous times it was called Mazaca. <margin>Caesarea in Cappadocia is deprived of its name.</margin> From olden times, he had a hatred against this city, because all the people of this city were Christians.

And because the Christians had destroyed and broken the Temple of Jupiter and Apollo therein. For also during the time of his reign, the Chapel of Fortune (that is, of Luck) which had remained from the Christians, was destroyed; therefore he was entirely against the city. He punished the pagans severely because they had not avenged themselves on the Christians and had not endured all things for Fortune. <margin>Temple of Jupiter and Apollo.</margin> He commanded all the goods of the Church in Caesarea to be gathered into a heap, forced by beatings, and he took 300 pounds of gold from it and placed it in the public treasury. <margin>The wealth of the churches was taken from the Caesareans. formerly.</margin> He commanded all Clergy to be gathered among the military folk. They had to serve the Governor of the Province, which was heavy and hard enough. He commanded the Christian people to be registered, with wife and child, and... <margin>Clergy forced into the military.</margin>

¶ **How in the beginning of his Reign, he spared the Christians more and treated them with kindness.**

## The 5th Chapter.

<margin>Julian judges it better to win over the Christians with sweetness than with severity.</margin>
C In the beginning, he excused the Christians and was generous toward them; for he knew that previous persecutors had gained nothing in terms of increasing Paganism by martyring Christians. Instead, the Christians grew more numerous and became more glorious because they died for the Christian Doctrine. Therefore, begrudging them their glory, he desisted from punishment and martyrdom, judging it more necessary to bring the people to Paganism through reason and exhortations. For this reason, he also wished to be considered more merciful. D

¶ **Of Bishop Maris of Chalcedon, and how he rebuked Julian to his face.**

## The 6th Chapter.

<margin>Julian is rebuked by Maris, the Bishop at Chalcedon.</margin>
E It is said that when he offered sacrifices to the goddess Fortune at Constantinople, Maris, a Bishop of Chalcedon, went to him and publicly called him an *Atheos* <note>original: "Atheos," meaning godless or an apostate who has abandoned the true God.</note>, that is, a godless man and an apostate. To this, Julian only mocked his blindness; for Maris was very old, and because of a disease of the eyes, he had to be led by another. Desiring to blaspheme God further, the Emperor said, as was his custom: "Your Galilean God cannot help you now."
F Maris answered him, saying: "I thank my God for my blindness, which was given to me so that I would not have to look upon you, Julian (who are naked and stripped

<column-break/>

of all godliness)." G
To this, the Emperor did not reply and went his way, thinking he could better confirm his Paganism if he showed himself patient and meek toward the Christian people.

¶ **Of the feigned friendship and love of Julian toward the Christians.** H

## The 7th Chapter.

<margin>On the purification of the Christians who wished to serve idols.</margin>
I While doing these things, he recalled all those who had been exiled by Constantius for the sake of the faith. He restored the property that had been taken from them and commanded the people that they should not harm any Christians, nor force anyone to sacrifice. However, those who came voluntarily to the altar of the Idols had to first be "purified" by demons <note>A reference to pagan lustration rituals intended to wash away the "taint" of Christian baptism.</note> and prepared with the customary sacrifices.
<margin>Privileges of the Clergy are taken away.</margin>
But from the Clergy, he took away all privileges, honors, and customary rights. He abolished the laws that had been granted for their sake and forced them to serve in the Imperial Court. Likewise, regarding the Virgins and Widows (who were supported among the Clergy because of their poverty), he commanded that they must return everything they had enjoyed from public funds. For when the Emperor Constantine distributed
<margin>Priests and Clergy were sufficiently provided for by Constantine.</margin>
wealth to the Church, he did so for every individual, so that the Clergy would have sufficient necessities. K This Constantine confirmed with his decree, which was also upheld after the death of Julian. This repayment (so it is said) was very heavy and difficult; for Julian frequently seized money, jewels, and ornaments from them. He also demanded back the money given for the construction of the Temples <note>Referring here to Christian churches, which Julian viewed as illegal use of state funds.</note> built under Constantine and Constantius, which were now entirely destroyed. In this manner, the Priests, Clergy, and the common Christian people were most cruelly vexed and burdened. L

### The 4th Chapter

<margin>Julian, friend of the heathens and enemy of the Christians.</margin>
**A**s Julian now held the Empire alone, and having reopened the Temples and restored all other things to their former state, he also showed honor to the temple servants with all devotion and reverence. He also frequently wrote to the citizens of all cities in general, urging them to return to the ancient customs of the heathens, promising that he would then bestow gifts and honors upon them. He also made himself known as a "friend" of the Christians, yet he did not wish for them to come to him or write to him, nor did he receive any messages from them. When those who expected the Persian War, and the people of Nisibis—who were all Christians—sent word to the Emperor to obtain help from him, he neither opened the temples nor desired that they should go to the holy service <note>original: "h. Godts-dienst"; likely referring to pagan rites Julian demanded in exchange for aid.</note>. He would not come to them now unless he understood that they had entirely surrendered themselves to Heathenism. <margin>Maiuma Constantia.</margin>
this gate is at Gaza and is called Maiuma, a place where many Christians dwelt together; they had obtained from Constantius that it be called a city, and it was named Constantia after the name of his son. When Julian was now in the Empire, the people of Gaza began to wage war against those of Constantia. Julian, now

acting as Judge, made them subject to the Gazans again, although they were situated about twenty stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters; twenty stadia is approximately 2.3 miles.</note> from them; losing their previous name, they are now called 
<margin>Gaza</margin>
Gaza-by-the-Sea. It had common Chieftains and Judges. Only the ecclesiastical right seems to indicate that they were two cities. **The Second Part. The Sixth Book.**

<margin>Julian calls the Christians Galileans.</margin>
<sig>A</sig> they must give him all tribute and taxes. With great threats he swore to them that if they did not quickly rebuild the temple, he would make the city suffer miserably and would not allow the Galileans <note>Julian used the term "Galileans" as a pejorative to imply Christianity was merely a provincial sect from Galilee.</note> to have their own rulers and heads. For this was what he used to call the Christians; and perhaps, had it not happened that he met a swift death, he would have carried out these threats.

<sig>B</sig>

¶ How in the beginning of his reign he spared the Christians more and proceeded with kindness.

### The 5th Chapter.

<sig>C</sig> <margin>Julian judges it better to win over the Christians with sweetness than with severity.</margin>
In the beginning, he excused the Christians and was mild toward them, for he knew that previous persecutors had gained nothing by trying to increase paganism through the martyrdom of Christians. Instead, the Christians grew more numerous and became more glorious because they died for the Christian teachings. Therefore, begrudging them their glory, he refrained from pain and martyrdom, judging it more necessary to bring the people to paganism through reason and admonition. In this, he also wished to be regarded as more merciful.
<sig>D</sig>

¶ Of the Bishop Maris of Chalcedon, and how he rebuked Julian to his face.

### The 6th Chapter.

<sig>E</sig> <margin>Julian is rebuked by Maris, the Bishop at Chalcedon.</margin>
It is said that when he was in Constantinople offering sacrifices to the fortune of the goddesses, Maris, a Bishop of Chalcedon, went to him and publicly called him an *Atheos* <note>original: "Atheos"; at this time, the term was used to mean "godless" or one who had abandoned the true religion (an apostate).</note>, that is, a godless and apostate man. To this, Julian only mocked him for his blindness, for Maris was very old and, because of an eye disease, had to be led by another. Furthermore, wishing to blaspheme God, Julian said, as was his custom: "Your Galilean God cannot help you."
<sig>F</sig> Maris answered him, saying: "I thank my God for my blindness, which was given to me so that I might not see you, Julian (stripped and bare

<column-break/>

of all godliness)."
<sig>G</sig> To this, the Emperor did not answer and went away, thinking to further confirm his paganism if he showed himself patient and gentle toward the Christian people.

¶ Of the feigned friendship and love of Julian toward the Christians.

### The 7th Chapter.

<sig>H</sig> <margin>Of the cleansing of the Christians who wished to serve the idols.</margin>
While doing these things, he recalled all those who had been exiled by Constantius for the sake of the faith, and he restored the property that had been taken from them. He commanded the people that they should not harm any Christians and force no one to sacrifice. However, those who came voluntarily to the altar of the idols were first to be "cleansed" by demons <note>This likely refers to pagan lustration or purification rites intended to "wash away" the Christian baptism.</note> and prepared and incited with the customary sacrifices.
<sig>I</sig> <margin>Privileges of the clergy are taken away.</margin>
But from the clergy, he took away all privileges, honors, and customs, and he nullified the laws given for their sake, ordering them into imperial service. Similarly, regarding the virgins and widows (who were supported among the clergy because of their poverty), he commanded that they should pay back what they appeared to have enjoyed from public funds.
<sig>K</sig> <margin>Priests and clergy were sufficiently provided for by Constantine.</margin>
For when the Emperor Constantine distributed wealth to the churches, he provided for each one so that the clergy had sufficient necessities. This he had confirmed with his command, which was also kept after the death of Julian. This taxation (as they say) was very cruel and heavy, for he often took away money, jewelry, and ornaments all at once.
<sig>L</sig> And the temples <note>In this context, "tempelen" likely refers to Christian churches or basilicas.</note> that were built under Constantine and Constantius he completely destroyed, and he demanded back the money that had been given for their construction. In this manner, the priests, clergy, and the common Christian people were most cruelly vexed and troubled.

## The 8th Chapter.

<margin>The conflict between the Christians and Pagans in Alexandria.</margin>
**A**t that same time, a great riot occurred in the great city of Alexandria, arising from the following cause. There was in the city an ancient, desolate, and ruined place where in former times all manner of impurity had occurred. In this place, the Pagans had offered sacrifices to the goddess Mithras <note>Mithras was actually a male deity in a popular Roman mystery cult, though the text here refers to the site as belonging to a "goddess." These sites, called Mithraea, were often underground.</note> and performed human sacrifices. Constantius and the Church in Alexandria had been granted permission to leave this site empty.

Gregory, wishing to build an Oratory <note>A small chapel or place of prayer.</note> on the site, ordered that the place be cleansed. While this was being done, a hidden, deep place was discovered where the Pagans held their "Pagan Mysteries" <note>original: "Mysteria Paganorum"</note> or secrets. For there were many human skulls—small and large, young and old—who had been killed there so that the Pagans could practice all sorts of black arts and sorcery with them.

When the Christians found these things at the entrance of the Mithraic shrine, they made an effort to mock the Pagans by revealing all these shameful things, and they spread a rumor or outcry regarding these discovered skull bones. The Pagans of Alexandria saw this, and as they could not bear the insult, they were moved to rage. They took up whatever came to hand as a weapon and, attacking the Christians, killed many of them—some with swords, others by beating them with sticks and stones.

<margin>Great riot concerning the idolatry of Mithras in Alexandria.</margin>
Some they hanged with ropes; others they hung upon crosses to show contempt for the Holy Cross. Many others were maimed and damaged with wounds, and it reached the point that even neighbors were not spared. Thus, one philosopher struck another dead, brother killed brother, and parents killed their children, and so they pitifully murdered one another. Because of this, the Christians ceased their efforts to cleanse the aforementioned site.

### Of the death of George of Alexandria.

## The 9th Chapter.

**M**eanwhile, when the judges announced that Constantius was dead and Julian had become Emperor, the Pagan

<column-break/>

<margin>George of Alexandria captured in the riot.</margin>
people of Alexandria started a riot. Rising up against George <note>George of Alexandria was an Arian bishop who was deeply unpopular with both the local Pagans and the Orthodox Christians (followers of Athanasius).</note>, they took him prisoner. Not long after, they came to him in the prison and killed him there. Loading his dead body onto a camel, they paraded it through the city from evening until morning, and finally burned it. Many of the Arians said that this was done by the supporters of Athanasius. But I consider it certain that the Pagans did this, as they had complaints against him regarding the destruction of the temple of their goddess and the prevention of their feasts and festivals, just as Julian himself testifies in his letter written to the Alexandrians. In this letter, he scolds them very harshly but waives the penalty and punishment for the sake of the honor of Serapis—whom he calls a protector of the city—and of Alexander who founded it, and for the sake of Julian's uncle, who was very earnest in paganism and hated the Christians beyond measure.

At that same time, a great riot occurred in the great city of Alexandria, and it arose from these causes. There was in the city an ancient, desolate, and ruined place where in former times all manner of impurity had occurred. In this place, the Pagans offered sacrifices and human victims to their gods <note>original: "Afgodinnen"</note> of Mithras <note>Mithras was a Persian sun god whose mystery cult was popular among Roman soldiers; his "mysteries" were often rumored by Christians to involve human sacrifice.</note>. George <note>original: "Gregorius," though historical records and the following text identify him as George of Cappadocia, the Arian bishop of Alexandria.</note>, wishing to build an **Oratory** <note>A small chapel or place for prayer.</note> on the site, ordered that the place be cleansed. Within it were found many human skulls—large and small, young and old—of those who had been killed there so that the Pagans might perform all kinds of black arts and sorceries.

The Pagans in Alexandria saw this, and as they could not bear the insult, they were moved to rage. They took up whatever came to hand as weapons and, attacking the Christians, killed many of them—some with swords, others with clubs and stones. <margin>Cruelty of the Heliopolitans against the virgins.</margin>
At this time, the people of Gaza and Alexandria greatly persecuted the Christians. And so also did the Heliopolitans and the Arethusians who live in Syria fall into such cruelty (as has been made known to us by the people who were there at that time) that they took the holy virgins—whom it was not customary to see in public—and stripped them entirely naked and exposed them. Thus forced to stand in the theater, the people first mocked them and then shaved them. Finally, they cut them open across the middle and set the swine upon them to devour them.

<margin>At Heliopolis before the time of Constantine, they used to expose virgins to harlotry.</margin>
The reason why the people of Heliopolis fell into such a fierce rage as to act in this way against these pious, innocent virgins is this: they had been forbidden from their old ancestral custom, which they once had, where their virgins were exposed to harlotry before they were married.

Now, Constantine had destroyed the Temple of Venus in their city and established a church there. He also, by a given law, forbade them to continue this aforementioned customary harlotry. But those of Arethusa brought Marcus, the Bishop of their city—an old, pious, and honorable man—to a wonderful <note>In 17th-century Dutch, "wonderbaerlicken" often meant "extraordinary" or "singular," even in a terrible sense.</note> death. They had hated him for a long time and were great enemies of his because, during the time of Constantius, he had conducted the pagans to the Christian faith and had very thoroughly destroyed their costly temples. When Julian began to reign, he was ignited with rage against Marcus and commanded that he should either pay back the price of the temple or rebuild it anew. Since this was impossible for the people as well as the priest, Marcus at first fled, according to the Gospel text.

<margin>Matthew 10</margin>
But when he saw that many were coming into danger and hardship for his sake, he returned from his flight and voluntarily surrendered himself to the people, for them to do with him as they willed. And they, when—

<column-break/>

<margin>Marcus is treated poorly by his subjects.</margin>
—they ought to have praised such a Christian Philosopher, instead mocked him more than the mockers. Falling upon him, they dragged him through all the streets, pulling his hair and breaking all his limbs; both men and women were against him, and they tore off his ears with sharp ropes. The schoolboys and servants also mocked him and struck him in the face. They hung him over stinking pits, and while he was still alive and catching his breath, they smeared him with honey and hung him up in the air in a basket. There, as he was being stung and tormented by wasps and bees, he said to the Arethusians that he was on high while he looked down at them in the depths, and that they would also suffer hereafter.

# Theodoretus.

By this treatment, they wanted to force him to rebuild the temple or pay the costs. But when he would not do so, considering himself poor, they asked for half the amount from him, and finally just a small pittance. To this he answered: "I will not give you a single penny for everything." Thus being defeated, they ceased tormenting him.

# Sozomenus.

<margin>The Pagan governor <term>Praefectus</term> waits with suffering.</margin> <note>The margin note likely refers to the Governor's observation of Marcus's endurance.</note>
It is said that the Governor at that time, being a pagan, greatly wondered at the steadfastness of Marcus and went to the Emperor, complaining and saying: "How one should be ashamed to inflict so much suffering and martyrdom on an old man." He noted how the more the Christians love such things, the more glorious they become, while those who inflict it upon them shall be put to shame. Yet Marcus was not reconciled without this suffering.

<margin>A Macedonius. Theodulus. Tatianus</margin>
At the same time, Macedonius, Theodulus, and Tatianus the Phrygians received the crown of martyrs. For when the Governor <note>Dutch: "Lant-richter," a regional magistrate or judge.</note> in the city of Meröe located in Phrygia had opened a temple in that same province—which had lain full of uncleanness for a long time—and after it was purified, these men entered therein by night and ground that idol to pieces. When many were seized and imprisoned on account of this matter and led to martyrdom, these three presented themselves. The Judge did not wish to condemn them to death because they inclined toward making excuses for themselves <note>The judge seemingly offered them a way out if they showed remorse or blamed their actions on youthful folly.</note>. But the people crying out over this, he punished them with many kinds of pain and martyrdom, and at last he ordered them to be laid upon the gridiron and to be burned and roasted. And as they were roasting, they said to the Judge: "O Amachius (for that was his name), if you have a desire for roasted meat, then turn the other side to the fire as well, so that when you begin to eat, you do not find raw meat." Thus these men triumphed through a pious and manly struggle.

<margin>Amatius the Judge.</margin>
<margin>Busirus the martyr. That is, abstinence.</margin>
It is also said that Busirus at Ancyra in Galatia gave a most clear confession when he was in the sect of the Encratites <note>The Encratites were an ascetic Christian sect that practiced "encrateia" or self-control, often strictly forbidding marriage and the eating of meat.</note>. For when the Judge had captured him as one who mocked paganism, he wished to torture him publicly and commanded that he should be hung upon a beam of wood. Then this Busirus stretched out his hands above his head and, baring his side, said: That it was not necessary; that the servants should not weary themselves in hanging him up and taking him down again, as he himself was ready to suffer the pain they wished to inflict upon him; and he bared his side for the torture.

The Judge, being astonished by this, was all the more unsettled by this experience. For when the iron hooks were frequently driven into his body, he suffered such things with outstretched arms for as long as it pleased the Judge, and thus he took the struggle upon himself with joy and a cheerful heart.

<margin>Hebrews 11.</margin>
But he was led back again into the damp prison and rested. Not long thereafter, the death of Julian was announced, and being thus delivered, he lived until the reign of Emperor Theodosius. Having done penance for his previous error <note>Referring to his time with the Encratite sect, which the mainstream church considered heretical despite their shared resistance to paganism.</note>, he

<column-break/>

remained for the rest of his time in the Christian Church.

# Of Basil the Martyr and Eupsychius.

## The 14th Chapter.

<margin>B Basil of Ancyra.</margin>
In this time, it is said, Basil, a priest at Ancyra, ended his life for the sake of the Faith and suffered martyrdom; as did Eupsychius, a priest <note>The text calls him a priest, though other traditions identify him as a layman of noble birth.</note> of Caesarea in Cappadocia, one of the nobility, who had recently taken a woman in marriage and was still a bridegroom.

<margin>C Eupsychius of Caesarea.</margin>
But Eupsychius was put to death because of the Temple of Fortune which (as has been said) was destroyed a little while before. Therefore, those of Caesarea in general had brought the Emperor's wrath upon themselves, and some were therefore killed and driven away. But Basil, a zealous and well-learned man, had resisted the Arians as long as Constantius lived. By the decree of Eudoxius, he was cast out from the order of the Church.

<margin>K Basil the admonisher of the Christians.</margin>
Now when Julian was Emperor, he publicly exhorted the Christians that they should adhere to their own doctrine and not be defiled by the superstition of the heathens. Also, that they should consider the honor and dignity which the Emperor would give them for it as nothing, being things which are perishable and which hasten eternal damnation. For this reason, then, he came under the suspicion and hatred of the heathens. For when he saw them sacrificing to the idols, sighing and praying, he cried out that no Christian should mingle himself in this error.

<margin>L</margin>
When he was now captured and delivered to the Governor, he inflicted great martyrdom and pain upon him, which he nevertheless suffered steadfastly; and at last, he died a martyr.

<margin>M Was killed.</margin>
I have spoken of these two together, although they were not killed in the same year or on the same day.

# Theodoret.

¶ Concerning the tyrannical treatment of the Christians in Gaza, Sebastia, and Phoenicia.

### Chapter 15.

<margin>The martyrs of Ascalon and Gaza.</margin>
But regarding what those lost in idolatry did at this time, though they are many and would require an entire book, I will nevertheless relate a few instances from the many. For in Ascalon, as also in Gaza, they stripped the pious wives of priests and also the virgins, sliced open their bodies, filled them with barley, and threw them to the swine to be eaten.

<margin>The Tomb of John the Baptist.</margin>
In Sebastia, which is a city in the same province, they opened the tomb of John the Baptist, burned his bones, and scattered the ashes. The blasphemy that occurred in Phoenicia—who can speak or hear of it without mourning? In Heliopolis, a city near Lebanon, there was a deacon named Cyril. When Constantius reigned, he became filled with divine zeal and broke and burned many idols that were worshipped there.

<margin>Cyril, Deacon of Jerusalem, a martyr.</margin>
The godless did not forget this deed of his, and they not only killed him but also sliced open his belly and ate of his liver. Yet they could not escape Him who sees all things. Rather, in due time, they received their worthy and earned reward. For all who were guilty of this deed had their teeth fall out, and their tongues rotted away and perished. Indeed, they also lost their sight, and their pain and punishment demonstrated the power of a godly life.

<margin>Emilian, a martyr.</margin>

<margin>Sabellians <note>Followers of Sabellius, who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons but merely three modes or faces of a single God.</note></margin>
Called ambiguity. And because the Church has been made restless by the question of *Usia* <note>original: "Usia," from the Greek "Ousia," meaning essence or substance</note> and *subsistentia* <note>original: "subsistentia," or "Hypostasis," referring to the distinct persons of the Trinity</note>, it is wisely resolved that this name shall be used only against the Sabellians, so that the terms are not used for two different concepts. And that subsistence is not considered to be the same as substance.

# Socrates.

## Instruction of Evagrius on how one shall speak of God.

### The 21st Chapter.

<margin>P</margin>
**T**his, then, is what was handled in the Synod at that time. But as for what we feel concerning *Usia* <note>original: "Usia," that is, substance or being</note> and *Hypostasis* <note>original: "Hypostasij," that is, self-standing personhood</note>, let no one be offended that I briefly make it known here. For those experienced in the Greek language have described and interpreted the little word *Usia* differently than the little word *Hypostasis*. Indeed, they have made a great confusion regarding that word *Hypostasis*. Erineus the Grammarian <note>A 1st-century grammarian, not to be confused with Irenaeus of Lyons</note>, in the book where he gathered words according to their letters, calls this word a barbaric term, and says that no ancients have used it in this sense, although it was used by Sophocles, Menander, and others in a different meaning. And if we wished to give a description of God’s substance, how could we do so—we who cannot grasp Him with any words of our own?
<margin>Erineus</margin>
<margin>G</margin>
<margin>Evagrius in the book on the life of Monks or Fathers.</margin>
<margin>Evagrius’s contention against those who speak of God in a dialectical manner.</margin>
<margin>S</margin>
Evagrius, in the book of the Monks, forbids one from disputing about God lightheartedly or without reflection. He has also entirely forbidden speaking of God with definitions in a <term>dialectical manner</term> <note>Using formal logic and categorization to define the divine.</note>. For that which is said in <term>deep-scenticheyt</term> <note>Likely referring to metaphysics or the deep probing of God’s nature</note> cannot be understood in this way. For he says thus: Every proposition has its genus, or that which is said of it, or its species, or difference, or its property, or <term>accidens</term> <note>Accident: a philosophical term for a non-essential quality</note>, from which the reasoning consists. Therefore, what is unspeakable we shall worship and honor with the reason of our quiet silence. This is the opinion of Evagrius.

## A Part of the Book of Athanasius, in which he makes known the cause of his flight.

### The 22nd Chapter.

<column-break/>

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Apologia Athanasij <note>The "Apology for his Flight" by Athanasius of Alexandria</note></margin>
**B**ut Athanasius, having previously written a book in which he gives an account of his flight, read it in the presence of those who were there. And because it contains much usefulness within it, I will briefly set a little of it here, praying the reader to read through the entire book if possible. For he says: "See, these are the intentions of the godless; thus they act and are not ashamed. Thus they have acted against us from the beginning until now, and have committed evil things against us. They slay us because we have escaped their murderous hands, and it causes them bitter pain that they have not been able to bring us entirely to death, and they cry out against us because of our fear, and do not know that in this intention they draw more guilt upon themselves."
<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Athanasius excuses himself for his flight. The attackers' great portion becomes small and weak.</margin>
For if fleeing is evil, then it is much worse to pursue one to flight. For the one hides himself so that he does not die, but the other pursues so that he may kill. And that one may flee is found in the <term>Scripture</term>; but the one who kills transgresses the Law of God and gives cause for the flight. Therefore, those who cause others to flee should much rather be ashamed of themselves for giving cause through their persecution. And if they cease to lay snares, then those who flee will also cease.

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>Matthew 10, Acts 8 and 12</margin>
But they do not cease from their wickedness, and they do not stop grasping for the virtuous; for they know that the persecution of the persecutors works a <term>patience</term> <note>steadfast endurance</note> in the persecuted, and is a sign especially in flight of long-suffering. For one does not flee from anyone who is mild and merciful; rather, one flees much more from the angry and the crafty. All the sighing and honored men of Saul fled and came to David. But these men wish to bring down those who are hidden, so that they may not punish their wickedness; therefore, they also act blindly in this.
<margin>F</margin>
<margin>Judges 17, 1 Samuel 21, Psalm 57</margin>
<margin>G</margin>
<margin>Twofold fruit of the godless.</margin>
<margin>Z</margin>
<margin>Persecutors leave a bad memory.</margin>
For the more publicly the flight occurs, the more their murder, persecution, exile, and other evils—which are attached to their craft and deceit—become manifest. For if they kill, then death cries out against them everywhere; if they condemn and drive into exile, then it is known that they leave a bad memory of themselves everywhere. And if they had a healthy mind, they would confess that they entangle themselves in this, and how greatly they wound themselves in this counsel. But since they are deprived of right understanding, they are deceived in their persecution, and in that which they have desired to kill; therein they have not [hidden] their godlessness...

When he lay hidden in the cave and changed his countenance <note>original: "aenghesicht verstelde"; referring to David feigning madness to escape capture</note> until he had escaped Abimelech <note>Likely a reference to King Achish of Gath; in the title of Psalm 34, he is referred to as Abimelech.</note>. Acts 9.</margin> While also the disciples withdrew for fear of the Jews and hid themselves. And Paul at Damascus was sought by the Prince of that same people, and was let down over the walls in a basket and escaped the hands of those seeking him.

Now since Holy Scripture says this of these pious, dear men, what do you think these [critics] will bring forward for their own defense? For if <margin>D</margin> they speak of fear, they speak against themselves like senseless people. For if they say that this happens against the will of God, they thereby show that they are without understanding of the Divine Scripture. For in the Law it is commanded that cities of refuge should be ordained <margin>Exod. 2. Num. 35. Deut. 4. Joshua 20.</margin> to flee into, so that those who were sought might be protected in some manner.

At the last time, when the Word of the Father came—who spoke with Moses—he gave this <margin>E Acts 7. Matt. 10. Matt. 24. Dan. 9. Mark 13.</margin> command again, saying: "If they persecute you in one city, flee into the other." And in another place: "When you shall see the abomination of desolation, of which the prophet Daniel speaks, standing in the holy place (let him who reads it understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains; and those who are on the roof, let them not come down to take anything from the house; and he who <margin>F</margin> is in the field, let him not return to fetch his clothes." For the Saints, knowing this, conducted their lives in such a manner. And what the Holy Spirit has commanded you, that he also commanded before he became man; and he did not speak [only] presently here to his Saints...

...but this is a term and <margin>G John 12:36.</margin> the end leading men to perfection: that what God commands, he also does. And for that reason, Christ also became man for our sake. When he was sought (just as we are), he also hid himself; and when he was persecuted, he fled and escaped the ambushers. It was also fitting that just as he hungered and thirsted, so also he suffered this by fleeing, thereby proving himself to be a true human. For first, when <margin>H Matt. 2.</margin> he was born as man and was still small, he commanded through the Angel to Joseph: "Arise, and take the child and his mother and flee into Egypt, for Herod will seek the little child to kill him." <margin>Eusebius of Vercelli grieved. Schism at Antioch.</margin>
AS MEANWHILE Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, came with all haste from Alexandria to Antioch, he found Paulinus had been ordained by Lucifer <note>Lucifer of Cagliari, a bishop known for his rigid stance against those who had even briefly associated with Arians</note>, and that the people were divided. But Eusebius, like a good physician <note>original: "Mederijn"</note>, traveled through the Eastern lands and strengthened those weak in the faith, teaching them with Christian preaching. And departing from there, he came to Illyricum, and traveling further into Italy, he proclaimed this to them.

### ¶ Of the Macedonians.

### The xxv. Chapter.

<margin>The Macedonians, being brought forth, give reasons for their heresies.</margin>
<margin>B</margin> **A**T this time there arose the followers of Macedonius and Eleusius, Eustathius and Sophronius, all named after one man, Macedonius. They very earnestly and frequently held synods; and having called together those who had followed them in Seleucia, they excommunicated the bishops of the other faction. These were those who sided with Acacius and who despised the faith of the Council of Ariminum <note>The Council of Ariminum (359 AD) was a key meeting regarding the Arian controversy.</note>; and thus they confirmed those matters all the more. But when they were addressed by some who said: "You who are now called Macedonians, if you are of a different opinion than the followers of Acacius, why have you until now held communion with them, as if you were of one mind with them?"

<margin>C</margin> To this they gave a brief answer through Sophronius, Bishop of Pompeiopolis in Paphlagonia, speaking thus: "The Bishops of the Western lands have spoken weakly regarding the name *homousion* <note>original: "homousion" — a Greek term meaning 'of one substance,' used to describe the relationship between God the Father and God the Son.</note>, that is, 'of one essence.' But Aetius, throughout the Eastern lands, has said: 'That both the essence and substance should be unlike,' and so both of these have been in error, and the reasoning of neither has brought any benefit. Therefore, we choose the middle way, as it is godly and consistent with the truth, satisfying those who question us, and so it pleases us."

# The Second Part. The Sixth Book.

<margin>A</margin>
In the cities, sacrifices were held in the pagan manner, according to the will of Emperor Julian. He was also very anxious that his intentions should not be hindered by the great number of Christians. It caused him much grief to hear that many pagan priests, along with their wives, children, and entire households, were Christians. Since he noticed that Christianity was sustained by a reasonable and upright way of life, he exerted himself to reform the temples of the pagans according to the order and manner of the Christian religion. He introduced altars and magnificent displays with pagan exhortations, and according to his own superstition <note>The author uses "superstition" here in the contemporary 16th-century sense to describe non-Christian rites.</note>, he appointed teachers as if they were Clergy, so that at appointed times, hours, and days, they would fulfill his commands. He also commanded that care should be taken for men and women who practiced the art of philosophy. Furthermore, he established dwellings for strangers and the poor.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Julian undertakes certain practices to make the pagan faith prestigious.</margin>
By these means, he intended to restore the pagan idol-worship so that he might gain the reputation of being a religious man. Whoever committed a sin, whether intentionally or unintentionally, was ordered to perform penance according to Christian institutions, and after such penitence, they were to receive a fitting punishment.

<margin>C</margin>
It is also said that he particularly applied himself to assisting the poor through a system modeled on the "epistolae formatae" <note>Letters of recommendation or "canonical letters" used by the early church to authenticate travelers and clergy moving between dioceses.</note> of the Bishops. For the Bishops used to have a special signet for letters, with which they wrote and responded to one another to recommend strangers—stating where they came from and where they intended to go—so that they would be received kindly, like friends and acquaintances, with every kind of testimony sent and sealed.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Of this formation, there is a Canon which they call "formare."</margin>
Recognizing this, he took great pains to see that the pagans practiced the same works as the Christians. But while many did not believe that he intended to imitate the practices of the Christians, it is clearly proven through the Emperor’s own reasoning and writings. For he sent such writings to Arsacius, the High Priest <note>Though the Dutch text says "Bisschop" (Bishop), Arsacius was the pagan High Priest of Galatia in Asia Minor. Julian was using Christian titles for his new pagan hierarchy.</note> of Galatia.

Therefore, we should believe—and it shall suffice us—not to look at how that Christian faith has increased through their care for the poor, their humane services shown at graves and toward the dead, and the feigned appearance of their honorable lives. You must exhort these men, or sway them with reason; or, if they do not follow you, you shall very quickly cast them out of the priestly office, unless they subject themselves to the Gods with their wives, children, and households. They shall no longer endure or suffer that their servants or children, who will not bow their necks and obey our command, [remain in service]. Or those Galileans <note>original: "Galileen" — Julian’s disparaging term for Christians, intended to make them sound like a local sect rather than a world religion.</note> who act wickedly against the Gods and prefer godlessness to piety. Those who are obedient you shall honor, but those who are disobedient you shall drive out.

### ¶ In what manner he set about restoring Paganism, and influencing the soldiers to offer worship to the idols.

### The XXX. Chapter.

<margin>Julian abolishes the cross in the standard, which they called the Labarum.</margin>
In order to root out the Christians, the Emperor acted in this way; although he could not advise his subjects of this directly, and was ashamed to use open violence, he meanwhile—in order to accustom his soldiers to that Paganism—under-

<column-break/>

took to begin reforming the figures on the Roman military standards according to the old fashion. These standards, which Constantius (as has been said) had changed into the form of the Cross <note>The *Labarum* was the military standard displaying the Chi-Rho (the first two letters of Christ in Greek), adopted by Constantine the Great.</note>, he openly had painted with an image of Jupiter, as if he were bringing him a crown and purple robe from Heaven. Likewise, he added images of Mercury and Mars, both looking at him as if testifying that he was a valiant and wise man. He wished to establish these images so that, under the guise and name of the Roman Empire, the Gods might be worshipped, and thereby the subjects might be secretly led astray. For he believed that if he presented this to the willing, he would later fulfill his purpose even better. And if he found them contradictory, he could punish them without mercy as those who sinned against the Roman glory, the common good, and the Roman Empire. But few indeed <unclear>gupt</unclear> <note>This word in the OCR is unclear; likely "perceived" or "understood."</note> him; when they were tormented, they recognized this deceit, for they did not wish to worship as was the custom. But the common people (as often happens) simply worshipped these images out of ignorance. This, however, did not help the Emperor. And as he considered many ways to exalt Paganism, he found a method that brought many Christian knights to the crown of a glorious virtue. For when the time had come that the soldiers were accustomed to receive the Imperial gifts—which usually happened on the Calends of January <note>New Year's Day.</note> and on the birthday of the Emperor, and the anniversary of the founding of Imperial cities—Julian applied himself to see how he might deceive them through their simplicity and established custom.
<margin>The soldiers nearly fallen.</margin>

He thus commanded that every individual who came to the hands of the Emperor to receive a gift should be admonished by the officials and first offer an incense sacrifice. For before the Emperor, incense and a brazier were placed, according to ancient Roman custom. Then some let their manly courage and piety be seen, and would neither cast incense into the fire nor take a gift from the Emperor. Others, on account of the law and old custom, did not realize in their minds what sin they had committed therein. Some were caught for the sake of profit, or went there out of fear, or were confused or troubled by the unusual command; and even if they understood it well, they nonetheless could not escape the Pagan works. <margin>A</margin> At the table, where they ate and drank (according to custom), while they were calling upon Christ among themselves, one said to them: "Why do you call upon Christ, whom you renounced a short while ago when you took the Emperor’s gifts and cast incense into the fire?" <note>Julian the Apostate often required soldiers to throw a grain of incense into a fire—a pagan act of worship—in order to receive their military pay or "donativum." Many Christians did so unthinkingly, not realizing it was a religious rite.</note>

<margin>B</margin> <margin>The soldiers who were Christians return their gifts.</margin> When the soldiers heard this and recognized what they had done, they quickly stood up and ran into the crowd of people, crying out to their GOD with great emotion, and openly testified to all men that they were Christians. They declared that they remained in that name and that what had happened there was done in ignorance. They said (if one may believe such a phrasing) that the hand alone was Pagan; the conscience had played no part in it. And when they came before the Emperor, they threw down the gold they had received, and prayed with loud voices that he should take back what he had given them and that he should put them to death. For they confessed with sorrow that their right hands had sinned in this matter, and that they were now minded to surrender their entire bodies to martyrdom for the sake of CHRIST.

## Theodoretus.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>E</margin> <margin>Romanus, a soldier.</margin> These things provoked the Emperor to rage. He first commanded that their heads be struck off. Then the young man, who was now delivered from death, said: "I have been cheated of death; Romanus was not worthy to be called a martyr of Christ."

### The 31st Chapter.

<margin>I</margin> <margin>Pythian Apollo of Daphne</margin> <margin>Pythian Apollo complains that his power of prophecy is taken away by the body of Babylas.</margin> After Julian had sought an answer from the idol Pythian Apollo of Daphne <note>Daphne was a famous sacred grove and temple site near Antioch.</note> regarding the victory in the war against the Persians, the idol complained to him that the body of the martyr Babylas <note>Babylas was a 3rd-century Bishop of Antioch who died in prison; his remains were moved to Daphne by Julian's cousin Gallus to sanctify the pagan site.</note> lay nearby. Because of this, the Emperor commanded that the body should be removed. For this reason, the Christians carried the body of the martyr Babylas to another place, praising God with psalms and great joy. At this, the Emperor became utterly enraged and subjected a young man named Theodorus to various tortures. In doing this, the deceiving devil only increased the honor of the martyr, and his lie was made public and known; for a bolt of lightning descending from Heaven set the entire Temple on fire and reduced the idol of Pythian Apollo completely to ashes. For though it was gilded on the outside, it was made of wood.

<margin>L</margin> <margin>Julianus, the Emperor’s Nephew.</margin> Julianus, the governor of the East and a blood-relative of the Emperor, having heard of this during the night, came with all haste to Daphne, wishing to help the God who was honored there. And when he saw that the idol had been turned to ashes, he severely beat the temple-servants and sacristans, believing that this had been done by some Christian. These men, although they were greatly tormented, would not lie, but said and cried out that this fire had its beginning not from below, but from above.

<margin>M</margin> Furthermore, the peasants from the nearby places, coming there, said they had seen that this bolt of fire had fallen there from Heaven.

### ¶ In what manner he set about to bring up Paganism, and to move the soldiers to perform worship to the idols.

### The 30th Chapter.

<margin>
Julian does away with the cross in the banner, which they call Labarum.
</margin>

To call out the Christians <note>meaning to identify or provoke them</note>, the Emperor thought thus—though his subjects could not advise this, and he was ashamed to do it with open violence—but in the meantime, so that he might turn his military folk toward Paganism, he under-

<column-break/>

took to begin reforming the Roman Banners <note>original: "Vaenteechen" — referring to military standards</note> according to the ancient way. These, which Constantius (as has been said) had changed into the form of the Cross, he had openly painted with the image of Jupiter, as if he were bringing him a Crown and a purple garment from Heaven. Likewise, he added Mercury and Mars, who both looked upon him as if testifying that he was a strong and wise man. He wished to set up these images so that under the appearance and name of the Roman Empire, the Gods might be worshipped, and thereby the subjects might be secretly led astray. For he intended that if he imposed this upon the willing, he would later better fulfill his purpose. And if he found them to be contradictors, he might punish them without mercy as those acting against Roman glory, and as those who sinned against the common utility and the Roman Empire. But few of them, when they were pressured, recognized this deceit; for as was the custom, they did not wish to worship them. But the common people (as often happens) simply ignored that these images were being worshipped. Which, however, did not help the Emperor. And as he considered much how he might exalt Paganism, he found a way that served to bring many Christian Knights to the crown of a glorious virtue. For when the time had come that the soldiers were accustomed to receive the imperial gifts—which commonly happened on the Calends of January, and on the birthday of the Emperor, and at the beginning and origin of the Imperial state—Julian applied himself to how he might deceive them out of their simplicity and through established custom.

## Chapter XXXII.

<margin>The treasures of the Temple are plundered.</margin>
**I**n the meantime, a command was issued that the jewels and the chalices of the churches should be confiscated and brought into the public treasury. Also, the doors of the Great Church—which Constantius had built—were hewn down so that anyone might enter into the holy place.

<margin>The Temples of the Christians are desecrated.</margin>
For when Julianus <note>This refers to Julianus, the Count of the East and uncle of the Emperor, often called "Julian the Apostate's Uncle" to distinguish him from the Emperor.</note>, Governor in the Orient, entered the Church, there entered with him Felix, the Royal Treasurer, and with them Elpidius, an official. It is said that Felix and Elpidius had previously been Christians and had apostatized only to gain the favor of the godless Emperor. And thus Julianus shamelessly urinated upon the altar; and when Euzoius <note>Euzoius was the Arian Bishop of Antioch at the time.</note> tried to prevent him, Julianus struck him in the head. It is said he remarked that the Christians were not without heavenly assistance.

<margin>Q</margin>
But Felix, seeing the precious vessels which Constantine and Constantius had so richly given to the churches, said: "See, with what drinking vessels is the Son of Mary served?" But for this shameless, godless, and raging madness, they received their punishment not long thereafter.

<margin>Excrement passing through the mouth of Julianus.</margin>
For Julianus very quickly fell into a heavy sickness, such that his entrails rotted within him, and he died therefrom; and his excrement did not pass from him according to the course of nature, but through his blasphemous mouth.

<margin>R</margin>
It is also said that the wife of this Julianus was a renowned Christian, and that she said to him: "Husband, it befits you to praise Christ the Savior, as he makes known to you the greatness of his power through this punishment; for you do not know him against whom you strive, though you would not have come into this punishment were it not for Divine long-suffering." From these words, and from his suffering, he recognized the cause of his misery. And having begged the Emperor <note>Emperor Julian the Apostate.</note> to return to the churches what he had taken from them, he could neither move nor soften the Emperor's heart, and so he died.

<column-break/>

### ¶ How the son of a Pagan Priest was converted at Antioch.

## Chapter XXXIII.

<margin>V A Priest’s son converts to the faith.</margin>
**A**fter these things had occurred, a youth, the son of a Pagan priest, came to the assembly of the Christian congregation. At that time, there was an honorable and sensible woman, a Deaconess; she had been friends and companions with the mother of this son, and as they frequently met together, she received this youth and invited him to the Christian religion. Now, when the mother died, the lad came to this Deaconess and received good instruction from her. And as he grew firm in her counsel, he asked her, as his schoolmistress, by what means he might escape the superstition of his father and attain the preaching of the truth? To which she answered: that he should flee from his father and rather convert to God his Father and his Creator, and betake himself to another city, in which he might remain hidden and flee the violence of the godless Emperor; promising him that she would take all care for him.

<margin>W</margin>

Also, this young man and his brothers were in the Emperor's court, having the office of setting the Emperor’s food before him.

<margin>Z</margin>
It was the custom to hold high festivals and feasts at Daphne for seven days. ### How Julian polluted all things with idolatrous water, and how Juventius and Maximus resisted him.

<margin>F</margin> ### The 24th Chapter.

In the meantime, Julian, like a shameless man, prepared a war against the right faith, though his face <column-break/> feigned as if he were mild and good. <margin>G</margin> But with this, he laid snares so that he might lead the innocent astray. First, he polluted the water fountains of the <margin>Julian pollutes food and drink with idolatrous offerings at Antioch.</margin> city and those at Daphne with the offerings of idols, so that whoever drank any water would participate in the abomination. He filled the food that was sold openly in the market with this slander; for he ordered that everything people ate—bread, meat, apples, herbs—be sprinkled with it. <margin>H</margin> Seeing this, those who were obedient to the saving Name of Christ sighed and wept over such an abomination. Yet they ate it according to the teaching of <margin>1 Cor. 8:1; 1 Cor. 10:25.</margin> Paul: "Eat whatever is sold in the market, <margin>I</margin> asking no questions for conscience's sake." But two brave, manly warriors, the Emperor's own guards, when they sat at the table at one time, became greatly incensed by this abomination. Between themselves, they used the words of the miraculous youths in Babylon <margin>Daniel.</margin> <note>A reference to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the Book of Daniel, who refused to eat the King's meat.</note> and said: "O LORD, <margin>K</margin> you have given us an unjust King, who has departed from you more than all the peoples on earth."

One of those sitting nearby reported this speech to the Emperor, who then called these brave men to him, asking them what they had said. Then, taking the Emperor's question as an opportunity to reveal their zeal, they spoke thus, uplifted in godliness: "O Emperor, we have <margin>L</margin> served you until now in the praiseworthy ordinances which Constantius and his children established."

"But now we see and notice that you have filled all things with abomination, and how food and drink are prepared and polluted. This we have lamented in our houses, and we complain of it also in your presence: for that displeases us in your Empire." When he heard this, the "Mild and Philosophical" Emperor (as he was called by his followers) <margin>L</margin> showed his true self. His tyrannical, godless heart soon revealed itself, and he commanded that they be very harshly tortured. He also had them killed—mostly because he felt he had to protect his imperial majesty's crown from insult—and he had this proclaimed as the reason for their execution, envying that these warriors <margin>M</margin> for the truth might be placed in the name of the Martyrs and <margin>Juventius and Maximus; John Chrysostom gave a glorious sermon regarding these two.</margin> crowned with honor.

The names of these men were Juventius and Maximianus, who, as dear witnesses of the truth, were honorably buried in the city of Antioch. And even to this day, their yearly memorial is observed.

#### ¶ How Valentinian, who reigned after him, struck the servant in the church on account of the sprinkling of pagan holy water.

### Chapter 35

<margin>Valentinian, a commander of the Lancers.</margin>
Valentinian, who later became Emperor, was at that time still a high captain over the Emperor’s guards <note>The original Dutch uses *Trawanten*, referring to the *protectores* or imperial bodyguards.</note>. He did not hide the zeal he had for godliness. For at the time when Julian (who would soon be struck by hail <note>A metaphorical reference to Julian's impending downfall or perhaps a specific historical omen of judgment.</note>) went leaping into the Temple of Fortune, temple servants stood on both sides of the temple doors, sprinkling with water—so they said—all who entered there to purify them.

Valentinian entered before the Emperor, and when he saw a droplet fall upon his cloak from this sprinkling-water, he became very enraged and struck the servant of the temple with his fist, saying: "That defiles more than it purifies." Seeing this, the Emperor ordered that he be taken into exile and sent away into the desert. But he, after a year and a few months had passed, obtained the Imperial throne as a reward for his confession. For the Lord God is not only honored in the lives of those who love Him, but He also frequently rewards their good work in this present life, and with present compensation He confirms the things for which we hope.

<margin>Artemio.</margin>
But Artemio, who had been a leader in Egypt during the time of Constantius,

They sang primarily this song in which the vanity of idols is mentioned, saying with David: "The gods of the heathens are silver and gold, the work of human hands; they have eyes and see not, ears and hear not," etc. Also: "Those who make them are like them, and everyone who trusts in them."

Becoming furious at this, he ordered that the choir mistress be brought to him. Although he saw that she was old and entirely grey, he had no mercy upon her. Instead, he ordered some of the guards to strike her on the cheeks, which she accepted with patience, considering it a high honor, and went homeward. But just as David the Psalmist drove away the evil spirit from Saul, so was this man like Saul: for Julian, yielding himself to a devilish spirit, raged and raved against the gifts of all godly life.

Likewise, there were many other eloquent Christian men, some of whom sought rightful honor. And some were driven mad by the <term>Arian heresy</term> <note>Arianism was a major theological dispute in the early Church that claimed Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father.</note>. <margin>Homer.</margin>

In this work, he showed how they were deceived, and that he possessed the true understanding of God. To this, the Emperor wrote to the famous bishops of that time: <term>I have read, I have understood, I have condemned</term> <note>original Latin: "Legi, intellexi, condemnaui"</note>. 
<margin>C</margin>

### The xxxix. Chapter.

<margin>The Christians were deprived of their goods.</margin>
When Emperor Julian set out against the Persians, he wished to take revenge on them because, under Constantius, they had attacked the furthest borders of the Romans. Knowing how it usually happens in war—that much misery occurs and much money is needed—he found a means to gather that money from the Christians. Therefore, upon those who did not wish to sacrifice to idols, he imposed the payment of great sums of money, and the true Christians were harshly taxed; for everyone gave as much as he had. Thus, this disorderly Emperor prepared himself for war for the sake of unrighteous treasures. Where there was no money, he sent out this command. But where there was, he used it for himself. During this time, the pagans severely oppressed the Christians; indeed, they sometimes tormented them with great physical martyrdom.
<margin>The answer Julian gave to the Christians. Matthew 10.</margin>

### The xl. Chapter.

<margin>Julian lowers the price of all things for sale in Antioch.</margin>
When Emperor Julian wished to fight against the Persians, he came to Antioch. And when the people complained to him that there was enough to sell but that everything should be sold at a better price, Julian—to show the greatness of his mercy to the people—ordered these things on the market to be sold at a lower price than they were worth. And when the sellers, traders, and many others departed because they could not afford to sell at those prices, a great shortage of necessary things arose. The people of Antioch, taking this very poorly, spoke very ill of the Emperor.

¶ How Julian incited the Jews against the Christians, and how they rebuilt the Temple in Jerusalem.

### Chapter 43.

<margin>Julian favored the Jews for the sake of rebuilding the Temple in Jerusalem.</margin>
C **J**ulian also incited the Jews against the Christians. First, calling them together, he asked them why they did not offer sacrifices, since God’s Law commands sacrificing? And when they gave the answer that God had commanded them to sacrifice only in one specific place <note>The Temple in Jerusalem was the only site where the Law of Moses permitted sacrificial offerings.</note>, the enemy of God quickly commanded them to rebuild the broken Temple.
D These miserable people thought that by doing so they could nullify the word of God <note>Julian hoped that by rebuilding the Temple, he would disprove Jesus’ prophecy in Matthew 24:2 that "not one stone here will be left on another."</note>. The Jews accepted this gladly and commanded their people throughout the entire land to give money from all sides for this building. The Emperor drove them to it, not out of mercy, but so that he might suppress the truth through it. He also appointed officials for them so that such a command would be carried out eagerly and with joy.
E But God turned and destroyed their intentions. It is said that the Jews had silver instruments for this construction, such as hooks, ropes, and shovels. And when they began to dig, a great multitude of people gathered on a set day; but at night, the earth fell back in of its own accord, as if the workmen had leveled it. Leaving the old foundations, they began an entirely new one. When they had gathered a portion of stone,
F lime, and many thousands of measures of other materials, a great wind came with a storm and quickly scattered what they had gathered. But these Jews, being entirely frantic and unconcerned with Divine patience, were immediately met with an earthquake, the Divine mysteries of which they did not understand.

<column-break/>

G Those who were not terrified by this were met with fire that burst forth from the excavated foundations, which burned many of the workers and damaged many of their limbs. <margin>A wonder of God.</margin> And also at night, while many were sleeping in the shelters of their property, these structures suddenly collapsed and killed those who lay beneath them. On the following day, the sign of the Holy Cross appeared. Also, the clothes of the Jews were filled with many
H crosses, which were not shining but were marked with black color. <margin>The sign of the cross appears on the clothes of the Jews.</margin> These God-rebelling Jews, recognizing this and being terrified by these Divine scourges, returned to their homes, confessing that He who was crucified on the wood by their ancestors was indeed God.
I When Julian heard of this, he hardened his heart like a Pharaoh and feared God not at all.

¶ Of the Persian war against the Romans.

### Chapter 44.

<margin>Persians against the Romans.</margin>
K **W**hen the Persians understood that Constantius was dead, they became bold and defied the Romans, invading their borders. For these reasons, Julian, having gathered a great army, immediately turned to his idols in Delphi, Delos, and Dodona to receive answers from them as to whether he would have victory in the war. Then all the soothsayers, <margin>The gods promise Julian victory.</margin> relying firmly on the war, gave him the promise of victory; but so that one may have an example of the deceit of idols and of lies, it shall not grieve me to bring it forth here, and it is this: *Nunc omnes aggredimur dij victorie trophaea referentes circa fluvium Thiren: horum ego dux ero belligerator Mars.* <note>Original Latin: "Now we all gods proceed, bringing trophies of victory around the river Thiris: of these I shall be the leader, Mars the warrior."</note> That is: Now all the gods march
L there with triumphant signs by the stream Triars: among whom I shall be the captain, the gruesome Mars. To recount this verse must be a mockery to him whom they call the wise God, the Prince of Pythia and of songs <note>A reference to Apollo, the god of prophecy and music.</note>. For I sigh over the lie therein, because Thiris and Tigris are similar names: for Tigris is the water that comes from the mountains of Armenia <margin>Tigris.</margin>
M and flows through the fields of the Assyrians and enters the Persian sea. Thus was the unfortunate man deceived by this answer, and he dreamed of victory in his mind. And after the Parthian war, he prepared himself to combat the "Galileans": for so he called the Christians.

### ¶ Concerning the Schoolmaster at Antioch, and the Sophist Libanius, and how Julian Saba foretold the death of Emperor Julian.

### Chapter 41.

<margin>
Concerning the schoolmaster and the Sophist Libanius.
</margin>
At Antioch there lived a pious, godly man, a schoolmaster of the youth. And there was also the famous Sophist Libanius <note>A famous pagan rhetorician and friend of Emperor Julian</note>, that godless man, hoping for the victory of Julian and having his threats before his eyes. This man mocked and rejected the schoolmaster because of our religion, saying: "What do you think the Carpenter's son is doing now?" <note>A common pagan slur referring to Jesus’s humble origins</note> Then he answered, by Divine grace—which happened shortly thereafter—speaking from Divine prophecy thus: "O you Sophist, you who call the Creator of all things a Carpenter’s son—He is making Julian a dead tree <note>original: "doode boom"; in historical accounts of this exchange, the schoolmaster's punchline is "He is making a coffin" for the Emperor</note>." And after a few days, the erring Julian was said to be dead; and being placed in a state of death, his arched pride was taken away and all his threats vanished.

### Concerning Julian Saba.

<margin>
Julian Saba in his prayer recognizes the death of Julian.
</margin>
At this same time, when that pious, godly Julian Saba—who lived an angelic life here on earth in his holy wandering (whose life we have also written of at length)—heard of the threats of the Emperor Julian, he immediately betook himself inwardly to God in prayer. And although he was far from Julian, he nevertheless, in the same hour that Julian was struck down, knew of it through Divine revelation in his prayer. He set his face to cheerfulness and was filled with joy. His servants, observing this—namely, the joy and gladness of his heart—asked him the cause of his cheerfulness, saying: "You shall no longer be bothered with his terror and threats." Acknowledging this, they all became cheerful and thanked God and offered up praise. But afterward, it became manifest through messengers that it was the same day and hour of Julian’s death that the same holy old man had known and foretold.

### The 49th Chapter.

After his death, his sorcery <note>The term "Tooverije" here refers to Julian's return to pagan rituals and alleged necromancy, which Christian chroniclers viewed as dark magic.</note> became known, for in the city of Carrhae <note>Modern-day Haran.</note> there have been seen until now the remains of his godless and perverted life. Not only did they dance in the churches and at the graves of the Martyrs, but even in the theaters they shouted of the **VICTORY OF THE CROSS OF CHRIST**, and held the sorcery of Julian in contempt.

### What the Sophist Libanius wrote against the Christians, and how Socrates the historian refuted his reasoning.

## The 2nd Chapter.

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>Libanius wrote a book on the death of Julian.</margin>
At the same time, Libanius the Sophist wrote a book of lamentation regarding Julian, of whom he said that he was enchanted by his own honor; and he mentions in the same book the works which Julian had published against the Christians. If this Sophist had only recounted the honor and the praise of the

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin>
Emperor in his writing, I would have remained silent and continued with the history. But because he, like a cunning or rather malicious Rhetorician, through the memory and recounting of Julian’s books, seems to target and damage the Christian Religion, we must therefore contradict his words a little.

<margin>The words of Libanius regarding Julian</margin>
First, setting forth the lengthening of the winter nights, he says: "The Emperor, studying the books which the Palestinian <term>man</term> <note>original: "missche" — likely a corruption of "mensche" (man), referring to Jesus.</note> brought as God and the Son of God, strongly contested them, and also overcame them in contradiction, in order to show the folly and vanity of those who honor such a person. In which labor he was found to be more diligent than the elder Tyrian <note>Referring to Porphyry of Tyre, a famous Neoplatonist critic of Christianity.</note>."

<margin>H</margin>
"But the Tyrian will surely be merciful to us and take our words in good part, just as he was surpassed and conquered by his son." These are the words of the Sophist Libanius.

<margin>I</margin>
<margin>Libanius's words.</margin>
But I know that this man is a true Sophist; even if he were not of the same religion as the Emperor, he would still say everything that the Christians say of Julian; indeed, perhaps as a true Rhetorician, he would have greatly embellished it.

<margin>Porphyry.</margin>
For while Constantine still lived, he praised him, but when he was dead, he slandered him with heavy spears of reproach.

<margin>Libanius praised Constantine while he lived, but after he was dead, he disparaged him.</margin>
And if the old man Porphyry had been Emperor, he [Libanius] would have esteemed his books more than Julian’s works. And if Julian had been a Sophist, he would also have said that he was evil, like Erebolus. Therefore, because this man, being of the same sect and a Sophist and friend of the emperor, has said what he wished and what seemed good to him, we shall refute and contradict him as much as we are able.

<margin>K</margin>
First then, he said that he studied during the winter nights: "To study," then, signifies that he intended to write a work of contempt, as the sophists are accustomed to do. For he knew the books beforehand, and then he studied them and contested them with great boldness.

<margin>L</margin>
From this it is clearly to be noted that he did not (as Libanius thinks) win in disputation or contradiction; but that because of the weakness of the truth that was on his side, he was entirely furious; and that which was well and wisely set down there, a true slanderer sought to mock and blaspheme.

<margin>M</margin>

# The Second Part. The Seventh Book.

**A** A true and Godly Faith in the LORD Jesus Christ alone is known, and drawn and chosen from the word of God. In this faith, the Holy Martyrs died in the LORD and, now resting, they stand before the Lord through that same faith. This faith would indeed have always remained unpolluted and inviolate, were it not that through the cunning of certain heretics it was sought to be violated and defiled.

<margin>Blasphemous words against the Holy Spirit, who call him a Creature.</margin>
**B** For one Arius <note>Arius (c. 250–336 AD) was a priest in Alexandria who taught that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father, a view known as Arianism.</note> and his followers sought and attempted to break the same, and in its place sought to introduce godlessness, saying: That God’s Son is a creature or a making of a thing that does not exist in nature, and that the same is also changeable: and they have thus misled many people, so that even those who seemed to be something of importance have fallen into such a blasphemous error.

**C** But the holy (our Ancient Fathers) coming together at Nicaea, as we have related above, banished the shameful Sect of the Arians in the Council <note>original: "Concilio"</note> there, and also confessed that general Christian faith being confirmed with Holy Scripture. And through the preaching of the same faith, the heresy was destroyed and rooted out, which then seemed to have been ignited everywhere.

**D** Thus this Faith was taught, preached, and read in all congregations.

<margin>E</margin>
But since some who have a desire to set up the heresy of the Arians again, they have undertaken to damn the faith that was confessed by the Ancient Fathers in the Council at Nicaea. <margin>Earnest request of Valentinian to the Bishops.</margin>
The Emperor, calling the Bishops together after the death of Auxentius <note>Auxentius (died 374) was an Arian bishop of Milan who had been condemned by several orthodox councils but remained in power under imperial protection until his death.</note>—who had been Bishop of Milan and deposed in many Councils—spoke to them in such a manner: "It is very well known to you, since you are taught through the Divine Scripture, what sort of man a Bishop ought to be, and how it is fitting that he should govern his subjects not only with words but also with his life; and that he should show and prove himself a follower of the true Doctrine and of all virtue, and that he should have an honest and good conduct and conversation as a testimony to his teaching. When the Emperor had said this, the Synod prayed and desired that the Emperor, as he was Godly and learned, should choose the Bishop himself. But the Emperor said: "Such an election is beyond us; you who are graced with the grace of God, and so honored, shall much better accomplish such a matter and choose one." And the Priests having gone out, they deliberated concerning the Episcopal throne. But the inhabitants of the city (as commonly happens) became riotous, some seeking this man, others that man, to be appointed as Bishop. For those who were of the sect of the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who believed that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> under Auxentius wanted one to be appointed who was like them. Conversely, the true Christians also wanted one appointed from their own doctrine. Now when Ambrose, who was then president <note>Ambrose was the consular governor (Consularis) of Liguria and Emilia, based in Milan.</note>, heard and understood this riot, fearing that some sedition or assault would occur, he went to the Church with great haste. But the people (once the sedition was stilled) gave their voice with one accord, desiring that Ambrose (who
