was not yet baptized) should be appointed as the shepherd of the flock. The Emperor, understanding this, immediately had him baptized and ordained as a Bishop, for he was a worthy man; for he knew that the judgment was much more right and better than any scale, and that those votes or voices were much more certain than any rule.

<margin>Song of praise of the Emperor Valentinian.</margin>
For he held it to be as a decree or conclusion of God, that his opponents also agreed and accorded with them in the election. Having then been made a partaker of the gift of holy baptism, he also received the Bishopric. It is said that the Emperor sang this song of praise to God when this had happened, saying: "I thank you, Almighty LORD and our Savior, for I have entrusted the bodies to this man, but you, LORD, have entrusted the souls; and you have shown that my choice agrees with your righteousness." And when Ambrose, a few days later, complained to the Emperor with great boldness that the Judges were not acting rightly, the Emperor said: "I have known this boldness of yours for a long time; and praising it, I did not resist it, but was a companion in the election of your ordination. Therefore, be diligent and hasten to heal the defects of our Souls." This, then, the Emperor said and did in Milan.

# ¶ The great, mighty, godly, and victorious Emperors, expanders of the Empire: Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian, to the Bishops of the provinces of Asia, Phrygia, Caria, and Phrygia Pacatiana—

->salvation in the **L O R D**.<-

A Council of such great importance having been held in Illyricum <note>Illyricum was a large Roman province covering much of the modern-day Balkans.</note>—and the question or matter concerning the saving Word having been subtly disputed there—the most holy Bishops have proven the Trinity to consist of the same Substance: of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Never forsaking this substantiality, they have practiced it as the service of their upright Religion. We have ordained by our power that this Consubstantiality <term>Consubstantiality: From the Latin *consubstantialis* (Greek: *homoousios*), meaning "of one and the same substance." This was the core of the Nicene Creed, asserting that Jesus is of the same divine essence as God the Father.</term> shall be preached. However, let no one say that we simply follow the faith of our Emperor who governs this land, rather than obeying Him who gave us the commands of salvation.

<margin>Matthew 17. Luke 20. Romans 13.</margin>
For the Gospel of our **L O R D** Jesus Christ says thus: Render unto Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and unto God what belongs to God. What do you say then, you bishops and overseers of the saving Word? If you approve of this, then cease to misuse the Imperial dignity or worthiness; love one another, and do not seek to persecute those who serve God rightly and perfectly. Through their prayers, even temporal and earthly wars are stilled, and the assault of the fleeing Devil is resisted and put to shame. Do not refuse to pay taxes or tribute according to the legal ordinances, nor resist the Royal power; but with an upright and good will, keep the commandments of the Supreme God, and also be obedient to our laws and orders.

A council of such great size having been held in Illyricum, and the question or matter of the saving Word <note>The "Saving Word" refers to the Logos, or the nature of Christ as the Word of God.</note> having been subtly disputed there: the most holy Bishops have proved the Consubstantiality <term>Consubstantiality: From the Greek "Homoousios," meaning that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit share the exact same divine essence or being.</term> of the Substance of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Never forsaking this substantiality, they have exercised themselves in it as the service of their upright Religion. We have ordained by our power that this Consubstantiality shall be preached; yet in such a way that no one may say we follow the faith of our Emperor who governs this land, rather than being obedient to Him who gave us the commands of salvation. For the Gospel of our **LORD** Jesus Christ says: Render unto Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God. What say you then, bishops and leaders of the Saving Word? If you approve of this, then cease to misuse the Imperial dignity or worthiness; love one another, and do not persecute those who serve God rightly and perfectly. Through their prayers, even temporal and earthly wars are stilled, and the assault of the fleeing Devil is resisted and put to shame. Do not refuse to give tribute or taxes according to the legal ordinances, nor resist the Royal power; but with a right and good will, keep the commandments of the supreme God, and also be obedient to our laws and commands. But you are proven to be disobedient. We are subject to Him who is the First and the Last, yet you exalt yourselves. # ¶ Of the error and heresy
# of the Arians.

### The 11th Chapter.

<margin>Audens the Heretic.</margin>
So then the highly renowned Emperor <note>Valentinian I, previously discussed as a defender of Nicene orthodoxy.</note> has sought and maintained the holy Apostolic [faith] with all diligence and earnestness. In this same time, one named Audens <note>Also known as Audius, a 4th-century Syrian priest.</note>—a discoverer of new teachings, born in Syria, and appearing from that same language—had begun to make wicked plans long before, which then became known. He very foolishly <margin>Genesis 1.</margin> did not understand that which is written: Let us make Man after our Image and likeness. Thinking that GOD had a Human form, and encompassing God within a Body, not at all understanding the sense of Holy Scripture, which often attributes Divine limbs <note>Referring to anthropomorphism, where the Bible describes God having "hands" or "eyes" metaphorically.</note> [to God]. This is for the sake of those who cannot easily understand profound things, <margin>Q</margin> to better grasp the foresight of God. To this godlessness, he added even more other [errors] (not much different). For being infected with the obstinacy of Manes <note>The founder of Manichaeism, a dualistic religion.</note>, he taught that God is not a Creator of fire and darkness. These and similar things this Audens preached, which are nonetheless kept silent by the followers of Manes. It is said that <margin>R</margin> these were excluded from the Church assembly, because among them were found those who practiced cursed usury, and also those who lived improperly with Women without lawful Marriage, leading a scandalous life, and saying that they live alone for that purpose, meanwhile concealing their Blasphemous teaching. This cloak is full of puffed-up pride, and a true rooting <margin>S</margin> of the Pharisaic Doctrine. For they also accused the Physician of the Body and the Soul, saying in the Temple to the Disciples: Why does your Master eat with Publicans and Sinners? And through the Prophet, GOD speaks of such who say: I am pure and touch me not / they shall be a smoke <column-break/> in my anger, and a fire that burns the whole day. But it is not convenient for us at this time to refute the folly of such Men: Therefore we will proceed in the narration of matters. At that time, <margin>M</margin> the heresy of the Massalians <note>original: "Massalianorum". A sect that believed in perpetual prayer as the only way to expel demons.</note> came forth, who are called Euchites <note>original: "Euchitæ", meaning "those who pray".</note>—that is, Bidders <note>In this context, "Bidders" refers to those who pray (from the Dutch 'bidden').</note>—who are also called by another name, Enthusiasts <note>original: "Enthusiastæ".</note>, <margin>E</margin> that is to say: Offerers. These wait for the workings of the Devil, and mean that it is the presence of the holy Spirit.

<margin>D</margin> But those who are entirely rooted in this sect reject the labor of hands as an evil thing, giving themselves entirely to sleep, saying that the fantasies of dreams are Prophecies. The leaders or Princes of this heresy were Dadoes, Sabas, Adelphius, Hermas, and Simeones, and some others, who had departed from the communion of the churches, teaching and saying that the Divine food <note>The Eucharist.</note> neither harms <margin>F</margin> nor is beneficial, regarding that of which the Lord Christ said: *He who eats my flesh, and drinks my blood, shall have eternal life.* And as they would gladly hide this weakness, they renounce it very harmlessly, even if they are convicted, and reject others of the same feeling that they carry in their hearts.

<margin>Litoius</margin>
Litoius <note>Letoius, Bishop of Melitene.</note> then, the Bishop at Melitene, being properly ignited with a Godly zeal, seeing that this infirmity had corrupted many Monasteries or rather Murder-dens (so to speak), has banished them and separated the Wolves from the sheep. Likewise, <margin>Amphilochius</margin> the well-famed Amphilochius, a Bishop of Lycaonia, has also done the same. When this plague grew and increased there, he resisted it very heartily, and the sheep who were tormented with such an infection, he plucked out from there. But Flavianus—worthy of being praised on all accounts—Bishop at Antioch, when he heard that these [heretics] lived in Edessa, and that they began to spit their own poison into the nearby cities, led the multitude of Monks to Antioch; and those who would not accept such a <margin>Z</margin> Plague, he rebuked in this manner, saying: That the accusers, slanderers, and the witnesses were liars. Hoping thus to bring Adelphius, who was a very old man, to him with gentleness, he commanded him to sit by him, and said: We, O old Man, who have now lived a great part of our lives, have learned the nature of man well enough and know the plots and the counsels of...

<margin>The cunning counsel of Flavian.</margin>
...other partisan Devils / and we ourselves are sufficiently instructed through experience to help ourselves with the grace of God: But these / while they are yet young / having no complete knowledge of these things / cannot hear spiritual words. <note>Flavian, Bishop of Antioch, is here using a "pious fraud" to trick the leader of the Messalian sect into revealing their secret doctrines by pretending to agree with them.</note>

<margin>The heresy of those who deny that grace is received through baptism.</margin>
Therefore tell me / how do you believe that the adversarial or contrary Spirit departs / and the grace of the Holy Spirit arrives? The old man, having been drawn out by these words, spat out all his hidden poison / and said: That no benefit came to the baptized through baptism: but that fervent prayer alone drives out the indwelling devil.

Furthermore, that all who are born / just as they receive their nature from their fathers or progenitors / they also receive the Servitude of the Devils. So much so that he has no more need / neither to fast in his body / nor any teaching to tame him or teach him to proceed in the right life.

Those who have now obtained such things (he said) are not only free from all temptations of the Body / but also clearly foresee future things / and see the Holy Trinity with their own eyes. <note>This group, the Messalians or "Praying People," believed that an indwelling demon possessed every person from birth and could only be expelled by intense, perpetual prayer, leading to a state of "apathy" or passionlessness.</note>

Flavian then / like a man digging at a foul Fountain to let all the stagnant Water flow out / answered the old man / saying: O you old Rogue of evil days / your own mouth has punished you / and not I: for your lips give testimony against you. And when this malady was made known to all / they were driven out of Syria / and went to Pamphylia / and filled that land with their pestilence.

# Sozomen, <note>Salaminius Hermias Sozomenus, a 5th-century Christian historian.</note>

### Of the Council at Lampsacus.

<column-break/>

### The 12th Chapter.

<margin>The bishops send a legate to the Emperor Valentinian Augustus.</margin>
Since then Valentinian <note>Emperor Valentinian I, who ruled the Western Empire (364–375 AD).</note> was of the same mind / as the fathers at Nicaea / so he was helpful to those who were likewise minded: But to those who felt otherwise, he was also not burdensome. When the Emperor, in the beginning of his Reign, wished to travel from Constantinople through Thrace toward Rome / the Bishops of Hellespont, Bithynia / and all those there who Preached / that the Son was of the same substance of which the Father is / sent a Legate named Hypatian, the Bishop of Heraclea Perinthi / praying him / that he would deign to appear for the improvement of the doctrine. When he had now come to the Emperor / and made the cause of his coming known to the Emperor / Valentinian answered / saying: Since I am one of the people <note>original: "vanden volcke" – likely translating the Latin "laicus" or layman.</note> / it is not permitted for me to investigate such a matter: But the Priests to whom this is commanded / they may gather by themselves where it pleases them.

<margin>Synod at Lampsacus.</margin>
Now when the Emperor had answered this / the Bishops gathered together at Lampsacus. When they had deliberated for two Months / they resolved / that what had been done at Constantinople by Eudoxius and Acacius / should be nullified. <note>Eudoxius and Acacius were leaders of the Arian/Homoian faction; the Council of Lampsacus (364 AD) sought to overturn their previous pro-Arian decisions.</note>

They would also bring to nothing / the explanation of the Faith / which they had put forward / as if it were the opinion of the Western Bishops / and had thus induced some to subscribe to it / on the condition / That that which was therein / regarding the dissimilarity of substance <note>original: "onghelyckheydt der substantie" – referring to Anomoeanism, the belief that the Son is unlike the Father.</note> should be omitted / all of which happened with lies.

They said / That the Son was like the Father through Substance / saying: That it was necessary [that "like"] should be said therewith / for the significance of the substances.

They would also cause to be proclaimed in all Churches / the Faith that was preached at Seleucia / during the Dedication of the Churches of Antioch.

They also resolved / that those who had been deposed by them / (because they taught / that the Son was not like the Father) should come again into their possession or holdings: But if there were anyone who wished to accuse them / they resolved / that it should be done with common peril...

<header>The Tripartite Ecclesiastical History <note>original: "Historia Ecclesiastica Tripartita"; a famous 6th-century history of the early Church compiled by Cassiodorus</note>.</header>

Sighing and sobbing broke out: for when the aforementioned servant of the Bishop had revealed what had been commanded of him to his closest friends, and they traveled up with him, and saw what books he had taken with him, they were all filled with sorrow because they were being robbed of their Shepherd. Consequently, the water was filled with following ships and people pursuing him.

<margin>Eusebius to Istrum <note>original: "ypstrū"; modern-day Silistra, Bulgaria, then a frontier town on the Danube</note></margin>
And when they arrived there and saw their longed-for Shepherd, they sobbed all the more, seeking with many tears and cries to keep him, so that the Wolf <note>a common metaphor for heretics or those who threaten the "flock" of the faithful</note> would not fall upon his sheep. But when they could not move Eusebius, they heard from him the Apostolic Law, which says: That one shall be obedient to Princes and those in power. This having been done, some brought gold, some silver, others clothes, and finally some servants, as one would for someone who wishes to travel to another land. But he accepted only a little, and that only from those he knew very well; and arming them with teaching and prayers, and also commanding that they should fight for the Apostolic Doctrine, he hurried to Istrum. And they, traveling back to their own city, exhorted and gave courage to one another to behave wisely against the cunning of the Wolves.

Now we wish to recount the true zeal and purity of the faith of these people. For I think that I would sin by keeping silent about it, if I did not make their actions always praiseworthy. When the followers of Arius <note>Arianism was a theological movement that denied the full divinity of Christ, which the Nicene Christians—like those in Samosata—viewed as heresy</note> had brought it about that the flock was robbed of its glorious Shepherd, and they had made a man named Eunomius Bishop in his place, not one person joined the usual gathering of the churches—neither rich nor poor, neither master nor servant, neither craftsman, nor tenant farmer, nor gardener, nor virgin, nor woman, young or old.

<margin>Eunomius, the imposed bishop, is shunned by the Samosatenes.</margin>
Thus the Bishop remained alone, and was called upon or spoken to by no one. Notwithstanding that it is said of him that he was a very gentle man, which one might notice from this: At one time, when he wished to bathe and his servants closed the door of the bath and forbade those who desired to enter with him, he, seeing the people standing before the door, had the doors opened and gladly allowed those who pleased to

<column-break/>

<margin>The Samosatenes do not wish to wash in the water against the heresy.</margin>
bathe with him, and he did the same in the bath. For he said to those who stood there and watched, that they should also use the warm water with him in the same way; yet they stood and watched in silence.

<margin>To avoid showing Eunomius honor, they had another bath made.</margin>
But as this Eunomius thought that this was done in his honor, he immediately went out. But those people, because he was tainted with heresy, considered the water itself unclean where the Bishop had washed himself, and they had another bath prepared and tempered for themselves. When he understood this, he departed from the city, considering it foolishness to live in a city where he was opposed and shunned.

<margin>Eunomius leaves Samosata. Lucius is brought in.</margin>
When this man had departed from Samosata, they were given Lucius, who was an overt Wolf and very hostile to the sheep. But the little sheep, though they were robbed of their Shepherd, did what a shepherd ought to do: for they remained pure in the Apostolic Doctrine. And how greatly they hated this Lucius, I shall recount in another place.

The boys were playing in the streets, throwing the hoop <note>original: "beugel"; referring to a ball or hoop used in the traditional Dutch game of beugelen</note> to one another, and it happened that when the hoop fell down, it passed between the legs of Lucius's donkey. Then the boys began to cry out loudly, thinking that the hoop was entirely defiled.

But as soon as he [Lucius] became aware of this, he commanded a following guard to wait there and see what end it would take.

<margin>Note the purification by fire.</margin>
The boys then, making a fire, threw the hoop through the fire, thinking that it would thus be made pure and reconciled. Now, this is quite a novelty from children, yet it remains a custom; but it is a glorious piece of evidence by which one can prove how great a hatred the City of Samosata had for the folly of Arius.

This Lucius did not follow Eunomius in his long-suffering, but had many priests banned by the court to foreign lands, especially those who fought manfully for the Apostolic doctrine, even to the furthest borders of the Roman Empire.

<margin>Euolius and Antiochus the exiled.</margin>
He also advised that Euolius, who was a Deacon, should be banished to the desert of Gasim. And Antiochus, who was the nephew <note>literally "sister's son"</note> of the great Eusebius, a man full of all virtue and also a Priest, he advised to be taken to Armenia. Who could ever sufficiently praise the works of this man, which he performed for the Divine doctrine!

When at last the holy man Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Samosata, a staunch defender of the Nicene faith against Arianism</note>, after many struggles and victories, had finally received the martyr’s crown, a Provincial Synod was held according to the ancient custom. He then thrust the hand away, saying that it was not fitting for him to suffer a hand to be laid upon him which had formerly handled or served the Sacraments with blasphemy <note>This refers to the "unclean" hands of a bishop who had practiced Arian rites, which were considered blasphemous by the orthodox party</note>.

### The XVII. Chapter.

Valens <note>original: "Vlens"</note> then commanded that Barses—of whom there is much praise—should not only be forbidden from living in Edessa, but also, forbidding him residence in Phoenicia, Egypt, and the Thebaid, had him transported to the Island of Aradus. ### The XVIII. Chapter.

<margin>I</margin>
Now when the Emperor had killed Procopius <note>Procopius was a usurper who revolted against Valens in 365 AD</note> and was uplifted by his good fortune, he began once more to war against the Christians, desiring that all religion should be united with the Arian doctrine. Yet he was principally moved to anger by the Council of Lampsacus, because they had not only deposed the Arian bishops, but also because they had banned the expansion of the faith established by the Synod of Ariminum <note>original: "Ariminis"; the Council of Rimini (359 AD), which had produced a compromise formula favored by Arians</note>. Coming then to Nicomedia in Bithynia, he summoned Eleusius; though this man followed the Arian sect, as we have said before, the Emperor, having formed a council of Arian bishops, compelled him to agree with them in doctrine. Eleusius initially refused, but when he was told he would be banished, he accepted the Arian teaching.

<margin>K</margin>
Once this was done, he very quickly felt regret over it and came to Cyzicus, where he complained of the violence done to him before the multitude, saying: That he had indeed consented, but not without being forced to it by violence. And he earnestly exhorted them to seek another Bishop, since he had forsaken his own doctrine out of necessity. But the people of Cyzicus, because of the love they bore him, would not submit themselves to any other Bishop. And so they remained under him, but they did not cease their error <note>a reference to their continued adherence to the Semi-Arian or "Macedonian" views prevalent in that region</note>. When the Bishop of Constantinople heard this, he ordained Eunomius as Bishop of Cyzicus—one whom he believed could draw the people to his view with the passion of his reasoning. So it happened: Eunomius departed, and it was strictly commanded that Eleusius should be driven out and Eunomius set in his place upon the Episcopal Throne. This occurred...

Fol. 380.

<header>Tripartite Ecclesiastical History.</header>

¶ Having been cast out, the followers of Eleusius <note>Eleusius was the Bishop of Cyzicus, deposed for his adherence to the Semi-Arian or Macedonian view, which differed from the Emperor's strict Arianism.</note> prepared a house suitable for prayer outside the City, and there they held their collections or assemblies. And let this suffice concerning Eleusius. Now we must say something of Eunomius.

#### ¶ Of Eunomius the Heretic.

### The 19th Chapter.

<margin>Eunomius.</margin>
Eunomius was a secretary <note>original: "Notarius"</note> to Aetius—who was called *Atheos*, that is, "without God," of whom we have spoken before. While he lived with Aetius, he followed his sophistical manner, paying attention only to certain arguments and creating sophistical reasonings for himself. He did not notice that through this he fell into certain blasphemies, being puffed up as he followed the teachings of Arius <note>Arianism taught that Jesus Christ was a created being, not equal to God the Father.</note> and strove in many ways against the doctrine of truth. For truly, since he was not very learned in the Holy Scriptures and could not understand them well, he often became hung up on words, always twisting them, and was never able to fulfill the purpose of his intentions. This is well-attested by the seven or ten volumes 
<margin>The volume of Eunomius on the Epistle to the Romans.</margin>
which he produced with much useless and vain labor concerning the Epistle to the Romans; for while making many words there, he was unable to hit upon the meaning of the letter. There are also other similar books of his, which anyone who wishes to read them will find quite contemptible. Thus, Eudoxius <note>The Arian Bishop of Constantinople.</note> appointed this Eunomius as Bishop of Cyzicus, attempting and seeking thereby to kick Eleusius out. And when he arrived there and used dialectics <note>A method of logical argumentation used here to challenge traditional faith.</note> according to his custom, 
<margin>The people of Cyzicus drove Eunomius out of the city for speaking too much Dialectics.</margin>
he seemed to be bringing forth something new to the hearers. Therefore, a riot also arose in Cyzicus, and they drove him out of the city, as they could not endure the arrogance and parade of his words. Coming to Constantinople, being without a bishopric, he lived with Eudoxius. But so that we do not seem to be slandering him, hear the voice or words of Eunomius himself, where he intends to speak against God with sophistry:
> <note>original Latin: "Deus de substantia sua, nihil amplius novit quam uos, neque est illi magis, nobis autē agnita minus, sed quodcunque novimus nos, hoc modis orbis etiā ille novit, Quod autem rursus ille hoc iuvenes inmutabiliter in nobis..."</note>
"God knows no more of His own essence than we do, nor is it more known to Him and less to us; but whatever we know, that same thing He also knows in every way; and again, what He knows, you shall find that in us."

<column-break/>

That is to say: God knows no more of His being than we do, and it is not more known to Him nor less known to us; but everything that we know of it, He also knows in all ways; and conversely, what He knows, that you shall find in us. By making these and other such sophisms or evasions, this sophist Eunomius did not understand that he was walking in error. But how he later departed from the Arians, we shall relate in the proper place.

## Sozomen.

#### ¶ Of the anger or wrath of Valens against the orthodox in Constantinople.

### The 20th Chapter.

<margin>Valens the Novatian... Agelius was the bishop in Constantinople.</margin>
Those who lived in Constantinople and confessed the Nicene doctrine <note>The orthodox belief in the Trinity established at the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.</note> were also tormented; the Emperor had them all driven out of the city together. He also had the churches of the Novatians <note>A rigorist Christian sect that refused to readmit those who had lapsed during persecutions; though schismatic, they held the same view of the Trinity as the Nicene Christians.</note> closed. It was not necessary to close the churches of the other heretics, for they had been barred long before under Constantine. He also banished Agelius (a Bishop of the Novatians who had been established in the church at Constantinople). It was said of him that he lived wonderfully according to the ecclesiastical commandments. His life was entirely philosophical <note>In this context, "philosophical" refers to a life of asceticism, discipline, and simplicity.</note> and divorced from the possession of money, which his conduct clearly proved; for he wore no more than a single garment and always went barefoot. 
<margin>Agelius returns to his bishopric.</margin>
He was called back from his exile not long after he had been banished and received his churches back again. 
<margin>Marcianus, [teacher of] Anastasia, daughter of the Emperor Valens the Constantinopolitan.</margin>
This recall was brought about by one Marcianus, who had learned from him and was a wonderful man. For previously he had served in the Imperial courts, but now he had become a Novatian priest. He taught the Emperor's daughters, Anastasia and Carosa, the art of grammar; from their names, the public baths in Constantinople are called the Anastasian and Carosan baths to this day.

The Second Part. The Seventh Book. Folio 381.

<margin>Augustus Valens razes the walls of Chalcedon.</margin>
## The 21st Chapter.

**S**o then the Emperor Valens commanded that the walls of the city of Chalcedon, situated opposite Byzantium <note>Byzantium is the ancient name for Constantinople.</note>, should be razed and cast to the ground. For he had confirmed with an oath that he would do this once he had overcome the Tyrant <note>This refers to the usurper Procopius, who rebelled against Valens in 365 AD.</note>, because the people of Chalcedon had done the Emperor much shameful insult out of favor for the Tyrant, and they had closed the gates of the city against him. Thus, the razing of the walls of this city was carried out by order of the Emperor, and the stones taken from there were transported to Constantinople, <margin>The Constantian Bidders.</margin> **B** to be used in the building of the house of the Bidders <note>original: "Bidderssen." This likely refers to the *Constantianae*, a famous set of public baths in Constantinople named after Constantius II.</note>, which are called the Constantianae.

**C** Among these stones, one was found upon which an answer <note>original: "antwoorde," referring to a prophetic oracle or inscription.</note> was carved; this answer had been hidden in former times but was now made manifest. For this stone gave it to be known that when an abundance of water should come, the wall of the city would then serve as a bath. And when countless barbarian nations should occupy the Roman borders and destroy them with great cruelty, **D** they also would finally die and perish. <margin>Valens builds an aqueduct.</margin> It then happened a short time later that Valens also constructed a watercourse <note>The Aqueduct of Valens, a major engineering feat of the city.</note> and gave Constantinople much water. Then the barbarian nations also rose up. It happened in yet another way that this prophecy was fulfilled. For when the watercourse was led into the city, the Regent of the city, named Clearchus, built a very large <margin>A bathhouse is built by Clearchus.</margin> **E** Bathhouse <note>original: "Byplosthuys," likely a corruption of a term for a cistern or nymphaeum; Clearchus built the *Nymphaeum Majus* in Constantinople.</note> in the street now called the Street of Theodosius, where the water flowed in, which gave the people great joy. But the prophecy was further fulfilled thereafter; for as they were firmly tearing down the city wall, the people of Constantinople prayed to the Emperor that he might stop the breaking down of the city walls. With these, the inhabitants of Bithynia, Nicomedia, and Heraclea also pleaded. But the Emperor, full of wrath, would hardly even hear their prayer. <margin>F</margin> Instead, wishing to fulfill his oath, the Emperor had the walls entirely broken down, and immediately thereafter gradually rebuilt them with smaller stones—which can still be found today in some parts of the walls, so that one can see that where great and wonderful stones once were, now only common masonry is set up.

## The 22nd Chapter.

**S**uch things then happened at this time. But one must know that this war against the Tyrant Procopius was conducted when Gratian and Dagalaiphus were Consuls <note>original: "opper Raets-heeren," the highest councilors or consuls.</note>, toward the end of the month of May. Very shortly thereafter, while they were still Consuls, **I** when Valentinian was stationed in the regions of the West <note>original: "Occidentis."</note>, a son was born to him, bearing the name of his father. But Gratian had been born before his assumption of the empire. And in the following consular year, when Lupicinus and Jovinianus were Consuls: then, on <margin>Hail at Constantinople.</margin> **K** the second day of the month of June, in the city of Constantinople, a great amount of hail fell, indeed, such that hailstones fell which were as large as very great stones. Many said that this happened because the Emperor had banished so many priests who would have no communion with Eudoxius <note>Eudoxius of Constantinople was a prominent Arian bishop.</note>. A short time later, during that same consulate, Valentinian made his son Emperor, named Gratian, on the 24th day of August. **L** In the following consular year, in the second year of Valens and also of Valentinian, <margin>Earthquake.</margin> a very great earthquake occurred near Bithynia, which also overthrew the city of Nicaea, on the 11th day of the month of October; it was in the 12th year <margin>Nicomedia fell.</margin> after the fall of Nicomedia. Not long after, through another earthquake, many <margin>Germa.</margin> parts of the city of Germa, situated in the Hellespont, were ruined and overthrown. And even though all this happened, neither Eudoxius the Bishop of the Arians <note>original: "Arrianen."</note> nor the Emperor Valens were moved in any way. **M** For they did not cease from persecuting. But these earthquakes seemed to be messengers of churchly strife. While many priests were then being banished, only Gregory and Basil <note>Gregory of Nazianzus and Basil the Great, two of the "Cappadocian Fathers."</note> were not banished, through God's providence, on account of the great reverence shown to these men of God; of whom one was Bishop at Caesarea in Cappadocia.

### How the Arians persecuted the Macedonians, and how these joined themselves to Liberius.

### The 23rd Chapter.

<margin>The Macedonians take their refuge in Valentinian and Liberius.</margin>

As those who confessed and championed the doctrine of Consubstantiality <note>original: "Consubstantialiteyt," referring to the *Homoousion*, the belief that the Son is of the same substance as the Father.</note> were being sorely tormented at that time, the persecutors also set themselves against the Macedonians. These, then, being driven by fear and force, sent legates <note>Legates are official diplomatic representatives, in this case, representing church factions.</note> to one another. They considered it best that, being compelled by necessity, they should seek refuge with the Emperor's brother <note>Valentinian I, who ruled the Western Roman Empire and was generally more supportive of the Nicene faith than his brother Valens in the East.</note> and with Liberius, who was a Bishop in Rome. They would rather accept his faith than have communion with Eudoxius <note>Eudoxius of Antioch, an influential Arian bishop.</note>. Thus they sent out Eustathius of Sebaste (who had been deposed many times), Silvanus of Tarsus in Cilicia, and Theophilus, commanding them that they should not avoid Liberius for the sake of the faith, but that they should establish communion with the Roman Church and confirm the faith of Consubstantiality. They then came into Italy with the letters that had been prepared in Seleucia; however, they were not able to see the Emperor, for he was busy in Gaul,

## The Subscription.

D I, Eustachius, a Bishop in the city of Sebastia, and Theophilus and Silvanus, legates or envoys of the Council at Lampsacus, Smyrna, and others: We have voluntarily signed this confession with our own hands. E Thus Liberius received the legates, having bound them with this writing, and giving them similar letters in return, he commanded them to depart.

# Fol. 384. Tripartite Ecclesiastical History.

¶ ...all the power and schemes of the Arians, standing like a well-fortified and invincible Castle against the arrows and onslaught of the enemies. At that time, when the Bishops of the West were gathered together in Ariminum <note>original: "Arrimino"; a reference to the Council of Ariminum in 359 AD, where many bishops were pressured into accepting an Arian-leaning formula</note>—where they were then won over to the madness of Arius through flattery or, what is more truthful, through temporary pressure—they wished to remove and craftily forsake that which had been wisely established in the faith. But thereafter, their cunning was not

¶ successful. For nearly all those who were gathered in Ariminum, having been misled or overcome by fear, have now understood the trickery. They have condemned all those who were gathered there in Ariminum and who wrote against the faith that was confirmed in the city of Nicaea. Now, having communion with us, they are ignited with much more fervor against Arius and his followers. This, the Legates of your

¶ city noticed very well, and they have added your names to their signatures. They banish Arius and all that was sent by his followers to Ariminum against the faith confirmed in the city of Nicaea, which you people—also being deceived by perjury—had signed. # Fol. 386.
# Tripartite Ecclesiastical History.

<margin>80 men sent as legates to the Emperor.</margin>
¶ When the eighty men from the church assembly (over whom Urbanus, Theodorus, and Menedemus were appointed) had arrived in Nicomedia, they presented the violence they had suffered to the Emperor and, having demonstrated what they had endured, petitioned the Emperor to provide a remedy.

¶ How eighty pious Christians were drowned in a ship by Valens.

### The xxx. Chapter.

<margin>Modestus the Governor</margin>
The Emperor, being filled with wrath, did not openly show his anger, but secretly commanded Modestus the Governor <note>Modestus was the Praetorian Prefect of the East, a high-ranking official under Valens.</note> to seize them and put them to death. The manner of this death was somewhat strange, which is why it has been kept in memory: for the Governor, fearing that an uprising might occur if he put them to death publicly, feigned that he was sending these men away into exile. And as they, in all simplicity, were obedient to him, the Governor commanded that they be placed upon a ship, as if they were to be carried to their place of exile, while ordering the sailors to drown them in the middle of the sea, so that they would die in that manner. This being done, when they had reached the middle of the sea near the place called the harbor of Astacus, that which the Emperor’s Governor had commanded was fulfilled; for the sailors, having transferred to a smaller boat that followed them, set the ship on fire. And it happened that the East wind blew strongly, and the ship was ignited all the sooner; the wreckage or remains of the ship came to a place called Daciziza, where it was entirely consumed by fire along with the godly men. It is said, however, that this did not occur without retribution, for immediately afterward a great dearth and famine arose in Phrygia, such that the inhabitants of the land were forced to leave their country and travel in all haste to Constantinople and various other provinces.

<margin>80 men drowned by a burning ship.</margin>

<margin>Punishment.</margin>

# Sozomenus.

¶ What Valens did in Antioch and Cappadocia.

<column-break/>

### The xxxi. Chapter.

<margin>Basil</margin>
So Valens, leaving Nicomedia, traveled toward Antioch; meanwhile, when he arrived in Cappadocia, he disturbed the churches there according to his old custom, wishing to hand them over to the Arians <note>Arianism was a theological movement that claimed Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father, which the Council of Nicea declared heretical.</note>. He thought this would be very easily accomplished because Basil <note>Saint Basil the Great, Bishop of Caesarea.</note> was angry with Eusebius (on account of some enmity), who at that time ruled the church of Caesarea; and Basil had thus departed for Pontus to live with the monks who practiced philosophy <note>The term "philosophy" here refers to the ascetic, contemplative life of early Christian monasticism.</note> there. But the people, and especially the noble and wise, held Eusebius in suspicion, as if he were the cause of the departure of that philosophical man who was perfect in both speech and life; they wished to abandon him and hold their own assemblies by themselves. But so that no riot would arise through the agitation of the heretics, Basil remained quietly in Pontus with his bishops who were with him daily. Thus it happened that the hatred of the people was kindled against Eusebius. When it was announced to Basil that Valens was coming to Cappadocia, he left Pontus and came to Caesarea; having made a pact with Eusebius, he strengthened the church for a certain time with his admonitions. But when Valens saw that he could not fulfill his intentions, he departed with the bishops who were with him.

# Socrates.

The Emperor Valens (not regarding the great famine that had come upon the land) then came to Antioch for food. And while he lived there, he oppressed the preachers of Consubstantiality or *Homoousios* <note>original: "Homousij"; from the Greek *homoousios*, meaning "of the same substance," the core doctrine of the Nicene Creed.</note>, who did not agree with the Arians. And although he had driven these men out of almost all the eastern cities, that was not enough for him; he also tormented them with various martyrdoms and put them to death in many ways, also drowning many of them in the water.

We must also recount here that which is said to have happened in Edessa, Mesopotamia. In this city, there is a church of the Apostle Thomas, widely renowned and also greatly honored, in which, out of reverence for the holy places, assemblies were frequently held.

<margin>son</margin> <note>original: "filius"</note>
**B** Now, when the Emperor wished to inspect this church and understood that all those whom he utterly hated were gathering there, he struck the Governor (so it is said) with his own hand, for the reason that he had not driven all the Christians out of that place. <margin>The Christians are greatly emboldened.</margin>
**C** secretly commanded that no one should remain within the Church. But there was no one who heeded his advice or his threat; for the next day, they all came together to the place of prayer. At this, the Governor, being angered, had the woman brought before him, saying: "O you miserable woman, where are you running so improperly?" Then the woman said: "There also, so that he too might be martyred." When he had heard this, he considered the steadfast spirit of those who gathered there, and quickly returning, he informed the Emperor

**F** that they were all ready to die for their faith, saying further that it would be unreasonable to put such a great multitude to death in so short a time.

And when one of the youths became sick, he came to the house and took the young man by his right hand, and through prayers, he drove away the illness. # Theodoretus.

## Concerning Basil, a Bishop in Cappadocia, and how he escaped the threats of exile.

### The 36th Chapter.

<margin>

Basilius.

Now that the Emperor Valens had deprived nearly all churches of their Shepherds, he came to Caesarea in Cappadocia, where at that time Basil was Bishop—a light of the world. And the Emperor sent his Governor or lieutenant ahead, commanding him to persuade Basil to accept the teaching of Eudoxius <note>Eudoxius of Constantinople was a prominent Arian bishop who denied that Christ was of the same substance as God the Father.</note>, or, if he refused, to drive him away. For the Emperor, having heard of the honor and glory of Basil, did not wish to attack him first, lest Basil, manfully turning back the Emperor’s arrows, should become all the more clearly an example of virtue for others. But all his schemes were nothing more than spiderwebs <note>original: "coppegeispin". This metaphor suggests the Emperor's plots were fragile and easily brushed aside.</note>. For it was enough for the other priests to follow the reasonings of the old fathers, and they held the wall of faith without wavering, as if it were a tower. But the Governor, having arrived in Caesarea, called the great Basil to him, honored him, and spoke sweetly with him, admonishing

<column-break/>

<margin>
G
</margin>
that he should adapt himself to the times, and not allow so many churches to be so greatly troubled for the sake of a small subtlety of doctrine. The Governor also promised Basil the friendship of the Emperor and many benefits that he could bestow on many people. However, the Holy Man mocked this, saying that such words pleased and served young men; these (he said) and their like were accustomed to looking upon such promises. But those who are nourished and experienced in the Holy Scripture do not allow a single syllable of the Holy Scripture to be corrupted or changed. But if it should so happen, they would rather die all kinds of deaths. "I regard the Emperor’s friendship as very great," he said, "if it can exist alongside godliness; but otherwise, I consider it to be more of a destruction." But when the Governor began to grow angry again, calling him a fool, Basil answered that he always desired to keep such foolishness. It is said that when the Governor told him to go away, so that he might consider what he should do, and that he should declare his sentence the next day, this worthy man spoke: "I will come to you again tomorrow, if you have not otherwise changed your mind, and if you remain by your threats." Thereafter, the Governor returned to the Emperor, recounting to him what had happened there, and the virtue, as well as the steadfastness and boldness, of the man. So the Emperor came into the city, remaining silent. Afterward, it happened that he saw he was being punished by God; for his son, being very sick, lay at his last gasp, and furthermore, his wife suffered various passions <note>Likely referring to physical or emotional distress/afflictions.</note>. The Dukes brought this message. Now when the great Basil came to the court and saw that the Emperor’s son was sick unto death, he said that he would become healthy again if he were baptized by a godly man. This being done, the child died immediately. But when Valens repented and understood the shameful deed of his oath, he came to the Temple and allowed himself to be taught by Basil the Great, offering upon the Altar.

## Socrates.

It must be known that while Athanasius lived, the Bishop of Alexandria, through the providence of God, the Emperor refrained from disturbing Alexandria or Egypt, hearing that Athanasius was greatly beloved by all the people and fearing that he 

<column-break/>

might risk some riot or that the Republic and the community would also be tormented. But Athanasius passed away in the second year of the Consuls Gratian and Probus <note>This occurred in 373 AD.</note> after much struggle for the state of the church in this world, having governed the Episcopal see for 46 years through many perils.

## Theodoretus.

### The 37th Chapter.

<margin>Peter over the community</margin>
Now that Athanasius, after much struggle and victory, had reached the end of his life and departed for the reward of his labor, a good man named Peter took up the Bishopric. He had been chosen long before by Athanasius, with the consent of all the priests, nobles, and the entire community, who showed by their favor that it was their own will. # Part Two. Book VII.

<margin>A</margin>
## ¶ With what cruelty Lucius arrived in Alexandria.

<margin>B</margin>
### Chapter XXXVIII.

<margin>Lucius is forced upon the people of Alexandria.</margin>
Not many days thereafter, Euzoius came from Antioch with Lucius and handed the churches over to him. It is said that the people of Samosata had already sufficiently tasted Lucius's godlessness. <note>Lucius was an Arian bishop, considered a heretic by the author. Samosata was a city in modern-day Turkey where Lucius had previously caused conflict.</note> But the people who followed the teachings of Athanasius, being well-fed on true doctrine and loathing the "contrary food" <note>A metaphor for Arian theology, which the author considers spiritual poison.</note> now being offered to them, no longer attended any church assemblies. However, since Lucius had armed idol-worshippers <note>pagan soldiers or mercenaries</note> with him, he struck some, hanged others, and forced many to flee. Into other houses, he burst as if the inhabitants were barbarians, robbing and <margin>C</margin> plundering them. But the wonderful man Peter <note>Peter II of Alexandria, the successor to Athanasius</note> shall tell this much better in his letter; but first, before the Letter of Peter, I will recount one of the villainous acts of Lucius.

<margin>D</margin>
There were certain men in Egypt who desired to live an angelic life; avoiding the unrest of the cities, they preferred to dwell in the wilderness, making the sandy and barren earth fruitful by bringing the good fruit of their virtue to the Lord. While there seem to be many authors of this way of life, the renowned Anthony <note>Saint Anthony the Great (c. 251–356), often called the Father of All Monks.</note> grew up in it from childhood and showed the monks the power of spiritual combat.

<margin>E</margin>
## ¶ What wonders or miracles were performed by the Hermits who were banished by Lucius.

<margin>F</margin>
### Chapter XXXIX.

<margin>Lucius banishes Macarius and Isidore.</margin>
The miserable Lucius drove out the followers of Anthony who lived in that place, including their most holy bishops: the venerable Macarius, and another Macarius, and Isidore. <note>Macarius of Egypt and Macarius of Alexandria were two famous "Desert Fathers."</note> Driving them out of their caves and dens, he sent them to an island that was full of godless people, for no teacher of godliness had ever been received there. When the ship reached the shore of this island, the

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin>
Devil—who inhabited the idol honored by those people and had lived there a long time—fled. He began to possess the daughter of the pagan priest, bringing her, raving and screaming, to the place where the monks' ship had arrived. Then the Devil began to cry out (using the tongue of the young girl), just as he did through the Sibyl. <note>original: "Waerseggerinne" (soothsayer). A reference to the Oracle or Pythoness.</note> All the men and women heard the Devil cry: "O, your power! O, you servants of Christ! On all sides we are driven and hunted by you <margin>The devil complains of the holy men.</margin> from the cities and villages, from the mountains <margin>H</margin> and hills, and from the uninhabited wilderness. We had hoped that in this desert island we would be free from all your arrows, but we now confess we are robbed of that hope. You were sent here by persecutors, not so that they might torment you, but rather so that we <margin>I</margin> might be driven out by you. See, we depart from this island, for we are struck by the rays of your virtues." Having said this and similar things, and having thrown the girl to the ground, the spirits departed.

<margin>K</margin>

But those who had seen this miracle fell at their feet and begged to be instructed in the way of salvation. From the letter of Peter of Alexandria, concerning the godless deeds of the pagans against the Christians and the villainous factions of Lucius.

BUT the foul factions of his presumption shall be sufficiently made clear through the letter of the wonderful Peter <note>Peter II of Alexandria, the orthodox successor to Athanasius who was forced into exile.</note>, from which I will not omit to set down that which stands in the middle of it, so as to avoid excessive length.

"When Palladius," he says, "the Governor, was a pagan in religion and always worshipped idols, he often sought an opportunity to fight against Christ. Gathering the aforementioned people, he committed violence and an assault upon the Church, just as if he had wished to bring barbarians under his power. Thus, many cruel outrages were committed, the memory of which has distressed me beyond measure as I have sat down to write them; indeed, I have wept greatly over it, and that might have lasted long, had I not comforted myself with Divine consolation."

¶ In the church called Theonas <note>One of the oldest and most important churches in Alexandria, named after Bishop Theonas.</note>, a great crowd entered, and they rejoiced in the favors of the idols. In place of honorable words, and in place of the reading of the Holy Scripture, there was a foul clapping of hands. They spoke many ugly and shameful words of blasphemy against the virgins of Christ <note>Nuns or women dedicated to a religious life.</note>, which a man would be ashamed to speak. For all wise men, hearing such talk, stopped their ears; and what is more, they wished they were deaf so that they would not be forced to hear such things. If only they had stopped at sinning with words and had not surpassed the foulness of their speech with their deeds! This blasphemy might have been somewhat bearable to those filled with the wisdom and teaching of Christ. But these men, as vessels of wrath destined for destruction, did not only make mockery and foul noise—spewing forth a stench as if from an unclean place—but they also tore the clothes of the holy virgins of Christ, who lead an angelic life here on earth, and they

<margin>
Note: Virgins dragged naked through the city.
</margin>

dragged them as entirely naked as the day they were born through the whole city, and thus mocked and jeered at them in the most shameful manner.

¶ If anyone had tried to excuse them or forbid the others, they would have been severely wounded. Woe to this misery! For many of these maidens were violated by force; many were struck upon their heads with wooden staves so that 

<column-break/>

they died without speaking another word, and their bodies could not even be honorably buried. Also, many bodies were sought by their parents with great mourning and were not found. But why do I recount such small things compared to such great ones? Why do I not rather turn to the essential matters, of which, I know, everyone will marvel with us at the long-suffering of God—that He did not suddenly root them all out and destroy them along with their possessions. For that which has never happened, nor has been read in any of the writings of the ancient Fathers to have occurred, these godless men did upon the Altar. For as if they were at a shameful dance or play, they took a youth—who was not yet a man—dressed him in women's clothing, anointed his eyes, and painted his face. Then, as was said by the Prophet <note>A reference to the 'abomination of desolation' mentioned in the Book of Daniel and the Gospels.</note>, they placed an idol in the form of a woman upon the Altar where they used to invoke the coming of the Holy Spirit. They made him move back and forth, forced him to make strange gestures with his hands, and spoke foul words. Regarding all this as a small thing—indeed, more honorable than shameful—they brought forward one among them whom they knew to be the most disgraceful of all. They stripped him of his clothes, even to his private parts, and placed him in the Chair of the Church <note>The Bishop's throne or cathedra.</note>, hoping that he would be a shameful preacher against Christ. For in the place where he should have spoken Divine words, he brought forth nothing but villainy; instead of honor, he praised lust; instead of godliness, godlessness; instead of purity, fornication and adultery, the cohabitation of men, theft, and gluttony. He said that such a life was very profitable.

When this had thus occurred, and I had gone from the church—for I could not remain there where there was much rioting and soldiers everywhere, since the common folk had been bribed with much money to revolt, and many pagans were present through great promises—then Lucius, our successor <note>Lucius was the Arian bishop imposed by the Emperor; Peter considers him an interloper.</note>, arrived. He regarded the Bishopric as a worldly honor and conducted himself with the cunning of a wolf. He was not chosen by the counsel of the orthodox bishops, nor by the decree of the true clergy, nor by the desire of the people, as the Church ordinances require. Through him, no...

<margin>E</margin> <margin>Lucius.</margin> Lucius, who for the sake of your right faith has very often been deposed for reasonable causes by all right-believing bishops, now stands in the city. He is not only like the foolish one in the Psalm who says: <note>original: "Non est Deus verus Christus"</note> "Christ is not the true God," but he is also corrupt and disturbed in all his dealings, rejoicing in all blasphemous speeches against those who honor the Savior. For as he does not differ much from the Pagans, he intends in his error to honor a new God; for some others shouted such honors to him, saying: "You are Bishop once again, you who do not protect the Sun."
<margin>F</margin> <margin>Magus against the Christians.</margin> Others said, "Serapis <note>The Graeco-Egyptian deity whose temple, the Serapeum, was a center of pagan worship in Alexandria.</note> loves you, and has brought you here," naming the idols of the Pagans. At this same time, the aforementioned Magus (a companion in his wickedness, a bitter soldier, and a servant of his cruelty) gathered a crowd of people and captured Priests and Deacons up to eighty years of age, as if they had been found in some evil sects and were enemies of the Romans. He wished to compel them with laws; but he did not know the power of the Christian law, and that the Apostolic faith was given to us by the Fathers. He also said that it was very pleasing to the Emperor Valens <note>Valens was the Eastern Roman Emperor and a staunch supporter of Arianism.</note>, saying: "Let yourselves be moved, you poor and miserable ones, and unite yourselves with the teaching of the Arians. Let yourselves be moved; the Divinity will forgive you, even if you do it not willingly but through compulsion, for necessity is an

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin> excuse, whereas willful resistance is followed by a worthy accusation. Therefore, having such reasons before your eyes, follow quickly and subscribe to the teaching of the Arians, which teaching Lucius now preaches. Know well, if it happens that you are obedient, you shall obtain money, goods, and honor from the Emperor. But if you refuse, you shall be imprisoned, martyred, tormented, scourged, captured, and stretched <note>Likely referring to the rack or a similar engine of torture.</note>; being robbed of your money, goods, and inheritance, you shall be driven out and condemned, and must dwell in cruel places." Thus this powerful deceiver, with flattery and threats, admonished and forced them all to fall away from the true faith. But they, considering nothing worse than falling away from a godly purpose, answered with manly spirit in these words, setting little store by the deception and threats: <margin>The right-believing against the Arians.</margin> "Stop, desist from frightening or threatening us now with these reasons, and bring forth no more vain words. We worship neither the new nor the first-invented god, even if you rage and foam in vain, and behave yourself in a great roaring and shaking, like a wind. We shall remain by the godly teaching until death."
<margin>H</margin> "We also do not acknowledge an impotent, nor unwise, nor untrue God, nor one who only exists at certain times, as the godlessness of Arius preaches a temporal Son. If He is a thing made or a creature (according to his madness), the Son not being [co-eternal] with the Father, then the Father also at some time did not exist: for (according to their saying) there was a time when the Son was not. But if the Father is from eternity a Father of the Son: how could anyone not be insane who would say of the Son, 'He was [at a time] when He was not,' He through whom everything that exists was created by grace?" Our Fathers (from whom these people are falling away, and are thus rightly 'fatherless') condemned and banished the teaching of Arius at the Council of Nicaea. To which this youth now answers, saying: "Not (as you compel us) that He is of the nature of the Father, but that He is of one being with the Father." This the Fathers, understanding well and with a godly mind, said: that He is <term>Consubstantialis</term> <note>From the Latin "consubstantialis" (Greek: homoousios), meaning "of the same substance" or "of one being," the defining term of the Nicene Creed against Arianism.</note>, that is, of one being.
<margin>I</margin> When they had said this and more of the same, he [Magus] constrained them for many days, thinking that they would change their sentence. But they became daily stronger, as if in a field of battle,

When they were thus struggling and made into a spectacle—as the Apostle says <note>Referring to 1 Corinthians 4:9: "For we are made a spectacle unto the world, and to angels, and to men."</note>—to angels and men, the people of the entire city ran together to see these brave <margin>☞ Tortured Christians.</margin> men of Christ. When he now ceased to torment and torture them, and many wailed and wept for their sake, he called together the disorderly mob once again to the court or condemnation, having them brought near the gates. And when thereafter, according to the custom <margin>Heathens and Jews.</margin> of the Jews and Heathens, they had cried out against them—and they would not agree with the godlessness of Arius—he pronounced his sentence or judgment, while they all sighed before his judgment seat. Namely, that they should be led from Alexandria to Heliopolis in Phoenicia, <margin>Heliopolis.</margin> where the inhabitants do not wish to hear the Name of Christ mentioned, for they are Heathens <note>Heliopolis, modern-day Baalbek in Lebanon, was a major center of pagan worship, specifically for the triad of Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury.</note>.

This having happened, he made them board a ship, and stood at the harbor with a naked sword in hand. <margin>Palladius with the naked sword.</margin> He thought that he would thus terrify those who had often wounded the hostile devil with the two-edged sharp sword. So he let them go, without food and also without any comfort, ordering that they should board the ship, <margin>G</margin> notwithstanding that a great storm arose, so that it seemed the sea wished to testify thereby that it wanted no fellowship with the wicked and evil command in the transport of the holy men. For the entire city sighed greatly; some were beaten. Others lifted hands and eyes toward Heaven, <margin>S</margin> protesting and lamenting the violence that occurred, as if they had said: "Hear, O Heaven, and give heed, O Earth, to the injustice that is happening" <note>A reference to Isaiah 1:2.</note>; the entire city was full of noise, and there was as much weeping as might be in a house of mourning, for the people wept everywhere.

As this Judge had now commanded that they should board the ship, a great

<column-break/>

sighing of daughters and women, <margin>☞</margin> old and young, was heard with many tears. As they traveled toward Heliopolis, where a devilish unbelief and superstition prevailed, all the people gathered in the middle of the city with much sighing and complaining, but dared not reveal their mourning because of the Judge Palladius, for he was also a Heathen.

Finally, many of those <margin>T</margin> who wept were also seized, imprisoned, chastised, torn, beaten, and finally banished to the mountains to dig for iron and metal. Thus one lived with the Christian men who, for Christ’s sake, fought steadfastly in great iron [shackles]. Among these were many <margin>V</margin> monks, twenty-two in number, who lived in the desert. Shortly thereafter, a Deacon came to us and brought us letters of comfort from our dear brother Damasus <note>Pope Damasus I, Bishop of Rome (reigned 366–384 AD), a staunch defender of Nicene orthodoxy.</note>; the Bishop was in the city of Rome; he was also captured, and they bound his hands behind his back, and he was thus led by the guards as if he had been a very wicked evildoer, and as if he had well deserved to be punished as one who had committed a murder. And when they had galled his neck with lead and stone, he was led to the sea and thus, without food or drink or any comfort, also sent and banished to the iron and metal mines.

And as this Governor <margin>X</margin> tormented and plagued so many children, some dying there without the presence of their friends and parents, they were also not allowed to be buried by the same. O, great inhumanity of this judge, and greater of the condemner! Should those who have thus struggled for the sake of the faith be considered equal to murderers? For their bodies are left lying unburied, and those who have <margin>Z</margin> labored godlily are left for the beasts and birds of Heaven to tear apart. Those who had compassion for the fathers whose children were killed were punished in their bodies as evildoers. What Roman Law, what judgment of the <margin>Y</margin> Barbarians is that—that those who have compassion for the fathers should be punished with death? When has such severity toward parents ever been heard of? Pharaoh indeed commanded that everything male of the Hebrews should be killed, but hatred and fear did that. How much more polite and human was that compared to what is happening now? How desirable would that still be in the face of this cruel—

# The Eighth Book of the history named the Tripartite Ecclesiastical History, drawn from Sozomen, Socrates, and Theodoret, etc.

->Translated by Epiphanius Scholasticus, and set into a brief summary by Cassiodorus the Preserver.<- <note>original: "Cassiodorum Servatorem." This refers to Cassiodorus Senator, the famous 6th-century statesman and scholar who compiled this history.</note>

## Socrates.

Concerning the life, miracles, answers, and writings of many Monks and Bishops.

### The First Chapter.

<note>A decorative historiated woodcut initial 'T' containing a figure amidst scrolls and foliage.</note>
<margin>Arsius.</margin>
At this time, Arsius <note>Likely referring to Arsenius the Great, a famous desert father.</note> was an Abbot in a monastery. He did not excommunicate <note>The Dutch "banden" refers here to the "Ban" or formal ecclesiastical exclusion.</note> the young disciples who sinned, but much more those who had come to their full years [the elderly]. For he said: "A youth who is excommunicated becomes defiant; but an elder

<column-break/>

soon repents because of the sorrow of the Excommunication."
<margin>Pior.</margin>
Another named Pior used to eat while walking. And being asked why he ate in such a manner, he answered: "I wish to use food not as a necessity, but as something foreign."
<margin>Z</margin> <note>This marginal 'Z' likely serves as a section marker or reference to a specific source.</note>
And being asked by another concerning that same matter, he answered: "So that while I eat, my soul finds no physical or bodily rest."
<margin>Isidorus</margin>
Isidorus said that he was forty years old, and although he felt sin within his mind, he nevertheless did not consent to the desires or the power of sin.
<margin>Pambu</margin>
But Pambu, because he was unlearned, went to someone so that he might learn the Psalms. When he had heard the first verse of the thirty-first Psalm <note>This refers to Psalm 39 in modern Bibles, or Psalm 38 in the Vulgate: "I said, I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue."</note>, *I said: I will guard my ways,* etc. <note>original Latin: "Dixi custodiam vias meas, &c."</note> "I have said: I shall guard my ways, so that with my tongue I [do] not..."

<margin>B</margin>
"Because I have not yet fulfilled that little verse in deed." <note>Pambus, or Pambo, was a famous Egyptian desert father. The verse mentioned is Psalm 39:1: "I said, I will take heed to my ways, that I sin not with my tongue."</note> And when he had grown old, and was afterwards asked by an acquaintance if he had learned the verse, he said: "In forty-nine years, I have scarcely been able to fulfill it." This Pambus, at the request of Bishop Athanasius, departed from the wilderness to Alexandria. And when he saw a woman there who was dressed up for a dance, he wept; and being asked by those present why he cried, he said: "Two things move me to this: the first is her destruction; the second is that I do not apply as much labor to please God as she does to please ugly men."

<margin>D Monks must work.</margin>
<margin>Picterius.</margin>

Picterius <note>Also known as Piterion, a disciple of Anthony the Great.</note> gave many natural interpretations, and when he was asked about various things here or there, he explained them; and upon every explanation, he prayed. At that

time, there were two God-loving men among the monks, both named Macarius; one was from Upper Egypt, the other from Alexandria. These were widely known for many things: for their sobriety, conduct, manners, and the miracles that were done through their hands. Macarius of Egypt <note>Macarius the Great (c. 300–391).</note> drove out so many illnesses and caused so many devils to flee that a whole book is filled with his works; he was of

<margin>F</margin>
great standing and very strict against transgressors. name and in deed; first he was

<margin>G</margin>
a philosopher in words or name alone, and was ordained as a Deacon in the city of Constantinople by Gregory Nazianzen; and thereafter, having departed with him to Egypt and having seen the conduct of the aforementioned men, he followed their life, and so many miracles were performed by him as by his masters. And

<margin>H</margin>
he wrote very necessary books, of which one is named *The Monk* <note>original: "Monachius." This refers to his work *Monachikos*.</note>, and one is *The Practical* <note>original: "Actualis," referring to the *Praktikos*.</note>, and another *The Knower* <note>original: "Cognitionalis," referring to the *Gnostikos*.</note>, according to how one becomes worthy of knowledge; this one has fifty chapters. How wonderful and how necessary these books are is known to those who read them.

<margin>K</margin>
But I deem it appropriate to recount a little of what he wrote concerning the monks and Scripture. For he says thus: "It is necessary that one investigate the ways of the monks who have preceded us rightly and well, and that one practice according to those ways; for it is found that many things were well said and done by them." For one among them says: "That a daily measure <note>original: "dach-maet," likely referring to a monk's daily ration or spiritual portion.</note> too dry and without the moisture of tears mixed with love, easily brings the monks to vice and intolerance."

<margin>L</margin>
When he saw that a brother was tormented by fantasies <note>Often referring to spiritual delusions or impure dreams.</note> at night, he helped him in this way, commanding that he should carry things to or serve the sick while fasting. And when asked the reason for this, he answered that nothing overcomes such a sickness as much as mercy. At that time, one went to the righteous Anthony, saying: "O Father, how can you bear to be deprived of the comfort of books?" To whom Anthony

<margin>M</margin>
answered thus: "O Philosopher, my book is the nature of all creatures; it is with me when I wish, and it recounts to me the words of God." He also said that the chosen vessel Macarius the Elder of Egypt asked why we hold onto the memory of evil against men, thereby destroying and strangling the powers of the soul—yet by holding thoughts of evil against the devils, we remain 

blameless?

P When a certain monk received news that his father had died, he said to the one who brought him the news: "Cease to blaspheme or slander, for my Father is immortal." <note>Referring to God as his true Father.</note> There was also one of the brothers who possessed only a

There is an island near Alexandria across the Lake Mareotis <note>original: "Zee Maria"; likely referring to Lake Mareotis near Alexandria</note> where a monk lived who was highly praised by those who practice contemplation; he said: "That all which is done by monks is done for five causes: for God's sake,
R for nature's sake, out of habit, out of necessity, and for the sake of manual labor." The same man also said that there is but one natural virtue, and that this virtue took many forms or essences according to the condition of the soul: "For," he said, "the light of the sun is indeed of one essence and form, yet it seems to take on another appearance through the windows through which it shines."

S Another monk said: "Therefore I cut off desire or lust, so that I might take from it the cause of raging; for I know that raging always fights on behalf of lust, and that it always disturbs my mind, with which I seek nothing else but knowledge."

Another among the ancient Fathers said: "Love can store up neither money nor
<column-break/>
food," and said further: "I do not know that the devil has ever deceived [anyone] in that." This is written by Evagrius <note>Evagrius Ponticus (345–399), a monk and ascetic whose writings on prayer and the 'eight evil thoughts' influenced later Christian theology.</note> in his *Practical Book*, and in his *Contemplative Book* <note>Referring to his works 'Praktikos' and 'Gnostikos'.</note> he writes this: "We have learned from Gregory the Just <note>likely Gregory of Nazianzus</note> that there are four virtues and their contemplations: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice." And he said that the work of prudence was to contemplate according to the intellectual nature, which is shown with wisdom. The work of fortitude is to remain constant and persevere in the truth, even if one is under attack, and not to turn toward things that have no true existence. To temperance belongs, he said, to receive the seeds of the laborer as a reward, and to plant them orderly and properly. But the work of righteousness and justice is that each be dealt with according to his merit: some things kept hidden, some explained with parables, and some set forth openly for the profit of the simple.

The pillar of truth, Basil the Great <note>Bishop of Caesarea (329–379), a founding figure of communal monasticism.</note> from Cappadocia, says: "A diligent memory provides or creates human wisdom, and practice makes it better; but the art that is obtained through prayer to God increases justice, patience, and mercy. Human art can be overcome, even by those full of movement and passions; but the Divine art is mastered only by those who are without faults—yea, those who at the time of prayer behold and observe themselves by the light of their own minds." But that holiest light of Egypt, Athanasius <note>Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373), a major church leader and defender of Nicene theology.</note>, says: "Moses commanded that the table should be set against the North <note>original: "Aquilonem"</note>. Therefore, those who contemplate shall consider what wind prepares itself against them, and they shall with brave courage withstand every temptation; also, those who come to them with diligence for help, they shall sustain and nourish." The Angel of the Church of Thmuis, Serapion <note>Serapion of Thmuis (d. c. 362), a supporter of Athanasius.</note>, said: "That the mind or heart, when it has received spiritual understanding, is well purified; but love heals the members that are swollen through obstinacy, holding back evil desires and influences."

The greatest teacher of contemplation, Didymus <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398), head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria.</note>, says: "Always speak to yourself of prudence and the judgment of God, and always keep the matter of your study with you. For nearly all of us sin in this regard, and you shall also find the Cause of Judgment in that distinction of bodies <note>A reference to the Origenist idea that the variety of physical bodies reflects the prior choices/judgments of souls.</note>, in which judgment this world also exists. The cause of prudence you shall find in the manner..."
