<column-1>
A person is raised from the wickedness or ignorance of the past to virtue or wisdom. We have set this down and recounted it from the writings of Evagrius <note>Evagrius Ponticus (345–399 AD), a Christian mystic and influential thinker among the Desert Fathers.</note>.

<margin>Ammonius. Note.</margin>
B There was also another among the Monks, a wondrous man named Ammonius, who was so alienated from all worldly things that when he came to Rome with Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius of Alexandria, during his exile in the 340s.</note>, he took no notice of anything except the churches of Peter and Paul, which he went to visit. When this Ammonius was chosen to be a Bishop, he ran away and cut off his right ear, so that by this physical defect he might be released from the ordination <note>According to early Church canon law, a man with a physical mutilation or "defect of the body" could not be ordained as a bishop.</note>. And when Evagrius was later also chosen as a Bishop and he also fled <note>original: "ontbloodt"; literally "bared himself," meaning he stripped himself of the obligation by fleeing.</note>, he came to Ammonius and said jokingly that he had done wrong to cut off his ear, and that he should be blamed for it. Then Ammonius said to him: "But you, Evagrius, do you not know that you are blameworthy, because you have cut off your tongue? See, so that you would not have to boast of yourself, you do not use the grace of God, but you run away."

<margin>Palladius wrote the last of the Monks.</margin>
D At that time there were many worthy men, and if anyone wishes to know their deeds and miracles, and how the beasts were obedient to them, let him read the book of Palladius the Monk <note>The *Lausiac History* by Palladius of Galatia (c. 363–420 AD), a primary source on early Egyptian monasticism.</note>, who was a disciple of Evagrius; for he has explained it all very subtly. In there he also recounts the lives of the women, and in what ways one ought to follow them. Evagrius and Palladius flourished a little after the death of Valens <note>Valens was the Roman Emperor who died in 378 AD.</note>.

# Sozomen.

<margin>John of Egypt.</margin>
E It is now the right time for me to recount and set down, as much as I am able, who those were who at that time lived as philosophers for our Christianity <note>The author uses "philosophized" to mean living an ascetic, contemplative life.</note>. Among them was John, to whom God revealed future and uncertain things, just as He did for the old Prophets in former times, and gave him this gift: that he should heal all incurable sicknesses. This man lived from his youth in the Desert, seeking God <note>original: "pijnende Godt"; likely meaning "toiling for God" or "striving after God."</note>, ate roots and herbs, and also drank water wherever he

<column-break/>

G could find it. And when he had grown old, he traveled by God's command to Thebaid <note>A region in Upper Egypt famous for its many hermits.</note> and became a Bishop over many monasteries. With prayer alone, he drove out sicknesses and Devils. And although he was not learned, he needed no books to remember anything, for everything he had once understood, he retained in truth. In that province there also lived as a philosopher Ammon, a Bishop of the Tabennisi <note>Followers of St. Pachomius.</note>, having about 3,000 disciples; Theonas also had no fewer. These were leaders of many monks; both were masters of wondrous things, filled with Divine providence and Prophecy. It is also said that Theonas was learned in the Egyptian, Greek, and Latin languages, and that he remained silent for thirty years; but it was never seen by any man that he was angry, or that he swore, or lied, nor also that he spoke anything frivolous, bitter, or any weak speech.

<margin>Copras, Hellen, Helias.</margin>
K Up to this time there were also Copras, Hellen, and also Helias. Copras, as they say, had a Divine gift to drive away sickness, to make people healthy, and to drive out devils. But Hellen, who was raised in the monastery from youth, performed very many miracles, unusual to see, such as carrying fire in his bosom and his clothes never burned. But Helias lived at that time in a Desert, not far from the city of Antinopolis, being about 110 years old. Before that, he had lived alone in the desert for nearly 70 years, and reached this age through fasting and a manly life.

<margin>Appelles of Egypt.</margin>
L There was also one at this time named Appelles, who had been a blacksmith; and when he sometimes wanted to do that work in the night, the devil appeared to him in the form of a beautiful woman, trying to rob him of his chastity. But he pulled the iron he was working on, red-hot from the forge, and struck this phantom woman in the face with it and burned her, and so the devil ran away, angry and sighing. Among these was also Isidore, who guarded the monastery everywhere and took care that no one should go out, but that they should have everything they needed within the monastery. Also at that time was Serapion, who had about ten Monks under him, all of whom he raised or fed in such a way that through their own labor they obtained everything they needed, and they also shared with other sick and needy people.

### Tripartite Ecclesiastical History.

<margin>Dioscorus.</margin>
Divided. *Dioscorus* had no more than 100 monks under him; while he was a priest and served the holy things and offices, he applied all possible diligence and earnestness to proclaim to those who came to the holy mysteries <note>The "holy mysteries" refers to the Eucharist or the sacraments of the church.</note> that they must purify their hearts and have no bad conscience.

<margin>Eulogius the Priest.</margin>
To Eulogius the priest <note>original: "Eulogio den Priester"</note>, it was known how to tell the thoughts of those who came to him; he rebuked their faults publicly and proved that everything they had thought in secret was known to him. And those who had thought of doing evil or had held bad counsel, these he did not allow to approach the altar, revealing their sins to them; and when they were diligently purified, he received them again.

*Apollo* in the *Thebaid* <note>The region around Thebes in Egypt, famous for its early monastic settlements.</note>, who lived for forty years in the heart of the desert, having a small cave or cavern in a mountain located not far from there.

But through the abundant miracles he performed in a short time, being very renowned, he became the Bishop of many monks.

At this time, there were many pious men who "philosophized" <note>In early Christian literature, "to philosophize" often referred to living an ascetic or monastic life of contemplation rather than academic study.</note> in *Alexandria*, numbering about 2,000; some of them lived in the wilderness and others around *Mareotis* <note>Lake Mareotis near Alexandria.</note>.

<margin>Dorotheus</margin>
Among them, however, *Dorotheus* was by far the most eminent, who was a *Theban* by birth and descent. His life was such that he daily gathered stones from the sea, and every year he built a dwelling and gave it to those who were unable to build for themselves.

To support himself, he made baskets at night to sell; his food was six ounces of bread and a bundle of small herbs every day, and his drink was water. Having lived thus from his youth, he did not lack anything in his old age either.

It was also never seen that he slept on a bed or stretched out his feet to rest; nor did he ever go to sleep willingly, unless nature closed his eyes while he ate or drank, being weary from labor, so that often (having fallen asleep while eating) the food fell from his mouth.

It happened that he was occasionally overcome by sleep, so that having fallen onto a dung heap, he fell asleep. Having awakened, he said secretly with sadness: "If you can convince the angels to sleep, then you shall also bring me to it from now on." This he perhaps said to the drowsiness

<column-break/>

or to the devil, who sought to hinder him from good works. While he labored, someone said to him: "Why do you thus punish your body?" But he answered: "Because it kills me." It is said of the priest *Piammon* <note>original: "Piammonem"</note> that at one time, while he was performing a divine office, he saw the Holy Angel standing near the altar, and that he wrote the names of the monks present in a book and struck out those who were not there. It is also known that God granted *John* <note>Likely referring to John of Lycopolis, a famous desert hermit known for healing.</note> so much grace against illnesses that he healed many who were tormented with gout <note>original: "Artique ofte flerecijn"; both are archaic terms for gout or rheumatism.</note>, or who were otherwise paralyzed, of their ailments.

Among these, *Benjamin* is also very renowned; through God's grace, without medicine <note>original: "Meesterye"</note>, oil, or the laying on of hands, but by prayer alone, he healed the sick. It is said of him that he was afflicted with dropsy <note>original: "waterzucht"</note>, and that his body was so swollen that he could not be carried out through the door of the cell where he lived without breaking down the door and its posts. Thus, with great solemnity during his illness for nearly eight months before his death, sitting in a very large chair, he healed and helped the sick, not being impatient or bearing it poorly that his illness did not improve or receive help, but rather comforting those who pitied him, asking them to pray to God for his soul and not to trouble themselves with his body; for he said: "When my body was healthy, it was of no benefit to me."

It is also told of *Mark* <note>original: "Marco"</note>, who lived in *Scetis* <note>original: "Scitia"; a desert region in Egypt famous for its monasteries.</note>, that in his youth he was very humble, wise, and possessed a good memory and aptitude for the Holy Scriptures, and that he was so pleasing to God that when he went to the body of the Lord <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion.</note>, an angel reached out the Sacrament to him; and he said that he saw the hand of the angel no further than to the elbow.

To *Macarius* <note>original: "Macario"</note> was given the power to drive out devils; the cause of his conversion was a slaying he had committed. For when he was small and watched the sheep near Lake *Mareotis* <note>original: "Zee Maria"</note>, he struck dead one of his companions of the same age, and for that reason, out of fear, he fled to the desert. After he had lived for three years under the open sky, he later made himself a small dwelling where he lived for 25 years. Many said that they had seen

<margin>Moses.</margin>
Moses <note>Known as Moses the Black or Moses the Ethiopian, a notorious bandit who became a desert saint.</note>, who was once a servant and was cast out of his house for a certain debt, after he had committed many murders and killings, was finally converted and subtly attained this "Philosophy" <note>In this context, "Philosophy" refers to the ascetic, contemplative life of a monk.</note>. When he was sometimes moved to lust by his own fantasies through the heat of his life, he chastised his body with much fasting, eating only bread and performing much labor. For six years, he prayed standing throughout the entire night, neither hearing nor closing his eyes for sleep; he also went around the monks' cells at night and filled their bottles or jars with water. He had to fetch that water from ten, twenty, or thirty stadia away <note>A stadium was about 185 meters; 30 stadia is roughly 3.5 miles.</note>. And even though this man thus tamed and chastised his body, he nevertheless remained as healthy as he had been before.

<margin>Macarius</margin>

Thus he wrestled in great Philosophy, feared by the Devil, and was appointed a Priest in Scetis <note>original: "Scheti", a desert region in Egypt famous for early monasticism.</note>. <margin>Pachomius. H</margin>
At the same time, an Abbot also lived in Scetis with great prestige, named Pachomius <note>Saint Pachomius is credited with founding cenobitic (communal) monasticism.</note>, who walked well and honestly from his youth until his old age. He was never deceived by the devil in either body or soul.

<margin>Stephanus the Monk.</margin>
But Stephanus also lived at Mareotis <note>original: "Marcote", a lake region near Alexandria.</note>, not far from Marmarica; he was of a perfect and chaste life, and was an expert and tested monk for about 60 years, well known to Anthony the Great <note>Saint Anthony, often considered the father of all monks.</note>. He was gentle and wise, lovely and helpful in speech; he comforted and cheered the sorrowful, even if a heavy pressure had seized them, and in his own misfortune, as previously mentioned, he was very cheerful.

<margin>K</margin>
<margin>Sicknesses come because of sins.</margin>
And when he finally came to an incurable sickness, and the physician had removed the corrupted or rotten skin <note>original: "lederen", literally leathers, but referring to diseased skin or flesh.</note>, he nevertheless worked with his hands, weaving palm leaves, and exhorted those who were present that they should not be sad over such things, nor think of anything other than having a good end. "For," he said, "everything that God has done is good. And I know that such sicknesses come because of sins, and it is better to be punished here temporally than hereafter eternally."

<margin>Pior. L</margin>
Pior <note>original: "Pioz"</note>, when he went from his father's house to Philosophy and conversion, made a vow that from then on he would never see any of his kin again. But when his sister desired to see him after fifty years, and when she learned that he lived in the desert, she would not be satisfied until she had seen him.

When the Bishop of that place saw that the sister was old and suffered great grief and sorrow over this, he wrote to the leaders of the desert that they should send Pior there.

Among these aforementioned men there was such great abstinence and "mathematics" <note>likely referring to rigorous spiritual discipline or ascetic calculations</note> that, on account of much fasting, their teeth were cast out by decay <note>original: "vande Wozmen" (from the worms), a contemporary way of describing tooth rot caused by extreme malnutrition.</note>.

# Theodoretus.

### How the Arians imprisoned many Christians and burned them in a ship.

<margin>C</margin>

## The 2nd Chapter.

<margin>The Arians burned the Christians in a ship.</margin> During this time, the Arians <note term="Arians">Followers of a theological belief that denied the full divinity of Christ, which was at odds with the "Orthodox" or Nicene creed; at this time, they held significant political power.</note> captured many priests of the godly doctrine in Constantinople and, having placed them in a ship without rigging <note>Likely meaning a ship stripped of its oars and sails to prevent escape.</note>, they steered it out into the sea. Others, who were in a different ship, followed them and set the first ship on fire, and thus the godly men were burned. In this way, those 
<margin>D</margin> pious men, struggling against both fire and sea, obtained the martyr's crown.

### How Valens gives authority to the Heathens, Jews, and heretics to hold their festivals, and has forbidden it to the Christians everywhere. Also of the virtues of Flavian and Diodore.

<margin>E</margin>

## The 3rd Chapter.

<margin>The godlessness of Valens Augustus. Heathens at Antioch.</margin> But Valens lived for a long time in Antioch and gave all liberty in their faith to the Heathens, Jews, and also the heretics. For they held heathen festivals, serving the devils: and Valens allowed the idolatry of Julian <note>The Emperor Julian "the Apostate," who had attempted to restore paganism years earlier.</note>, which had been forbidden and abolished by Jovinian, to come back into fashion and increase. Thus they did not keep the service of Jupiter, Dionysus, and Ceres in secret, as was customary under the godly Emperors, but openly in the middle
<margin>F</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin> of the streets ran those who held the festivals of Bacchus. At that time, the Emperor was only hostile toward those who preached the Apostolic Doctrine; he first had them driven out of the churches and had a new church <note>Likely a reference to the Arians being given the official church buildings.</note> established. And when they performed their service on a mountain, praising the LORD with Psalms and delighting themselves in the Divine Word—where they often had to endure heat, cold, rain, hail, and snow—they were still not permitted to serve their God there: for having sent his soldiers, he had them chased away from that place.

<margin>H</margin> <margin>The true Christians of Antioch.</margin> Then Flavian and Diodore <note term="Flavian and Diodore">Leaders of the Orthodox community in Antioch who later became influential bishops.</note> stood like screens and shields for the Christians against the arrows of the soldiers. For when Meletius, their shepherd, was forced to retreat, these two looked after the flock, setting themselves with strength and wisdom against the wolves and tirelessly caring for the sheep. When they were driven from the mountains, they brought the sheep to a river that was located not far from there. There, they did not wish—as the Israelites did when they were imprisoned in Babylon—to hang their harps and instruments upon the willow trees. Rather, they lauded and praised God, the Creator and giver of all things, in all places where His glory extended. Yet the enemy of Christ’s servants still did not allow the pious to hold their assembly in this place.

<margin>I</margin> <margin>Psalm 137.</margin> <margin>K</margin> <margin>Diodore.</margin> But the harmony of these men, who were the fatherly disciples of the Great Shepherd, trained the holy sheep in good things and grazed them with spiritual pasture. For Diodore conducted himself very wisely and steadfastly; like a great river and flood, he watered his own sheep and washed away the blasphemies of the godless as if they were flowing away. Scorning or holding as nothing the nobility of his lineage, he very gladly suffered all insults for the sake of the faith.

<margin>L</margin> <margin>Flavian.</margin> Flavian, a very good man also of very noble descent, considered that godliness alone was the true nobility that a person could attain. ## ¶ Of the praise and prize of Aphzaates the Monk, and with what boldness he answered the Emperor Valens.

### The 4th Chapter.

<margin>Aphzaates</margin>
In this labor also worked Aphzaates, whose life and conduct we have remembered in another place. For he, putting the common welfare before his own rest, came out of his own cave; leaving it behind, he took upon himself the care of a shepherd. How virtuously and well he lived is now unnecessary to recount. I shall only relate that which serves this history very well. Near the Emperor’s palace of the East <note>The imperial palace in Antioch.</note>, flows a river called Grontes <note>The Orontes River.</note>, and toward the South or midday, there is a large courtyard or harbor with many high towers; between that Palace and the river lies a street, where one may go from the City into the Suburb.

<margin>Grontes, a river.</margin>
As Aphzaates went hastily through this street to the battle against the enemies of God, having care for his sheep, the Emperor saw him from the Palace in a very modest little cloak, hurrying as much as his great age allowed. And when someone said that this was Aphzaates, upon whom the whole city depends, the Emperor said to him: "Tell me, where are you going?" He answered wisely, saying: "I go to pray for your empire." Then the Emperor said: "You should pray at home, according to the custom of the Monks." Then the holy man answered: "You speak very well; if you were to allow it, I ought to stay at home. That I have done until now, as long as the Christian sheep were left in their former peace. But because they are now disturbed with great uproar and driven away, and because the weight of danger is at hand, it is necessary that they run about, so that they are not captured, and must thus free themselves from all peril. But tell 

<margin>Valens Augustus to Aphzaates.</margin>

<column-break/>

me then, commanding Lord Emperor: If I were a young daughter who was accustomed to sitting in her chamber spinning wool, and I saw my father’s house burning, what do you think I should be obliged to do? Should I remain sitting in the house and disregard my Father’s house that is burning? Or should I have to run out and bring water to pour out the fire? I believe that you would say that I ought to fetch the water and extinguish the fire, for that is the work of a wise maiden.

This is now also being done, O Emperor; for as you have now set the fire in our Father’s house, we all run to extinguish this fire with all haste." When he had said this, the Emperor was silenced by him, remaining quiet. But one of the Chamberlains answered the holy man very harshly, for which God also punished him; for he had to tend the bath where he went after these words to prepare the bath for the Emperor, and reflecting on the words, he was very dismayed, and fell into the hot water, and died there. The Emperor sat and waited for him to bathe, as the Chamberlain was to bring him news that the bath was prepared. When he remained away for a long time, he sent other men to see why he tarried so long; when they went there, they found him dead. When this was announced to the Emperor, they recognized the power of Aphzaates’ prayer; nevertheless, they did not depart from their godless Teachings, but their hearts were hardened like Pharaoh’s heart.

### ¶ Of Acepsimas and others.

<margin>Acepsimas</margin>

Which songs even today still delight and adorn the Feasts of the Martyrs.

### ¶ Of the evil and misery that occurred under Valens in Alexandria and throughout Egypt.

### The 7th Chapter.

Now when the Emperor had commanded by decree that the Christians in Alexandria and Egypt should be persecuted, everything there was devastated, brought to nothing, and overrun. The destruction of some was brought before the court, others were imprisoned, and some were beaten. And many torments were devised and arose against the lovers of peace. <margin>The Christians are tormented.</margin> And while all this happened according to the will of Lucius <note>Lucius was the Arian bishop of Alexandria who forcibly displaced the followers of Athanasius.</note>, and when Euzoius had returned to Antioch, the Captain of the soldiers immediately fell upon all the Egyptian monasteries with a party of armed soldiers and the Arian Lucius. When they had done much evil to the holy men and could not overcome them, the superiors or leaders of the monasteries were sent into exile at the instigation of Lucius. <margin>The two Macariuses.</margin> Among whom was one Macarius of Alexandria. When they had come to an island, and the daughter of a priest there was possessed by devils—which devils cried out: "Why have you also come to drive us out from here?"—they took the daughter to them, and having delivered her with their prayers, they gave the priest his daughter back. They immediately converted the priest and the inhabitants by teaching them Christianity. These people immediately cast away their idols and turned the temple into a church; they were baptized and very gladly learned the content of a Christian life. Thus were these wondrous men persecuted, and for the sake of <term>Consubstantiality</term> <note>The doctrine that the Father and the Son are of the same substance (Homoousion).</note> they were found much more proven. They made others healthy and confirmed and strengthened their works through their faith.

# Socrates.

<margin>Didymus.</margin>
**G**OD also brought forth at this time another faithful man, through whom He wished to give testimony of the faith: namely, Didymus, a man well-renowned for all manner of learning. This man lost his sight through a disease while he was still a youth learning his A. B. C.s. <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398) was a famous theologian in Alexandria who, despite his blindness, became the head of the Catechetical School.</note> God endowed him with eyes of understanding in place of physical sight; everything that he was unable to learn because he was blind, he understood and recognized through his quick hearing. Because he was very intelligent from his youth, he easily surpassed those of keen sight; for he very easily learned the rules of Grammar and Rhetoric. When he came to Philosophy, he miraculously learned and retained Logic, Arithmetic, Music, and other philosophical arts, so that he very quickly matched those who had learned these things with sharp vision. Indeed, he so thoroughly mastered the Old and New Testaments that he even authored and produced many books. He wrote three books on the Trinity. And the book by Origen titled *Peri Archon*—that is: *On First Principles*—he explained and interpreted very skillfully and well. <note>original: "Peri Archon"</note> It is said that Anthony, when he came to Alexandria during the time of Valens <note>Emperor Valens (reigned 364–378), who supported the Arian faction.</note> on account of the Arians, saw Didymus and said to him: <margin>Anthony to Didymus.</margin> "O Didymus, do not be troubled or burdened that you have lost your physical eyes; for you lack no eyes other than those which even flies and gnats possess. But rejoice that you have such eyes as the Angels use, through which one sees and the truth is made known."

# Theodoretus.

Didymus, having been deprived of his sight from his childhood, learned Grammar, Rhetoric, Arithmetic, Geometry, Astronomy, and the Syllogisms of Aristotle, as well as Eloquence, through his hearing. <margin>Art and learning do not teach the truth.</margin> Not that these arts themselves teach the truth, but rather that they are good weapons against lies. <note>Theodoretus of Cyrrhus (c. 393–458) was a bishop and historian; here he argues that secular education is a tool for defending the faith rather than the source of faith itself.</note>

<column-break/>

And because many are found to wander into error due to the similarity of names: <margin>Gregory of Pontus.</margin> It is necessary to note that there was another Gregory of Pontus, who was born in Caesarea, a city in Pontus, who was very old and a disciple of Origen. For much is spoken of this Gregory in Athens, in Berytus, and Pontus; indeed, so to speak, throughout the whole world. For when he had come from Athens to Berytus, he read the Laws there. <note>Berytus (modern Beirut) was famous in antiquity for its prestigious law school.</note>

And when he understood that Origen was interpreting the Holy Scriptures in Caesarea, he traveled there so that he might hear the interpretations of that eloquent man. And once he was instructed by him in the true Philosophy, he returned (by the command of his elders) to his fatherland. There, at first, when he was still a young student, he performed many signs, healing the sick and driving out devils through epistles and letters. <note>This refers to Gregory Thaumaturgus (the "Wonderworker"), who lived c. 213–270.</note> And he made the pagans subject to him through both words and deeds.

Pamphilius the martyr and Eusebius also relate these things in the books which they wrote concerning Origen. So this old Gregory was formerly a disciple or pupil of Origen, and Nazianzen was a brother of Basil. <note>The text says "Nazianzenus a brother of Basil," but historically Gregory of Nyssa was Basil's brother. Gregory of Nazianzus was Basil's close friend. ¶ How Themistius the Philosopher turned Valens away from killing the

<column-break/>

Right-believers <note>The "Right-believers" refers to the Orthodox or Nicene Christians who upheld the Trinity against Arianism.</note>.

### The 12th Chapter.

In the meantime, while Valens was living in Antioch, he would have severely persecuted the worshipers of Consubstantiality <note>original: "Consubstantialiteyt" — the Nicene doctrine that the Son is of the same substance as the Father.</note> had he not been drawn away and warned by the book of Themistius the Philosopher. In this book, Themistius pleaded with him that he ought not to be cruel because of the diversity or the difference in Christian teachings. He argued that even among the Pagans, more than 3,000 different sects were found, and that each person remained in his own teaching, contrary to the opinions and teachings of others. He suggested that such variety might even be more pleasing to God, since He cannot be easily known and is glorified in various ways, and that men fear Him all the more because they do not fundamentally know how, in what manner, or how great God is. With these reasons, Themistius somewhat softened the Emperor's heart.

<margin>Ulfilas, an inventor of the Gothic letters.</margin>

D This was the cause and the beginning of the common welfare of the Romans being subjected to much misery; for when the Barbarians had taken Thrace, they willfully devastated and overran the Roman provinces.

> O Emperor, I am not defeated, but you have lost the battle, because you wish to fight against God, and are the cause that His help is more with the Barbarians than with you; for while He is contested by you, He fights for them; and it is necessary that where God is, there is victory and triumph. # The ninth Book of the Histories called Ecclesiastica Tripartita, taken from Sozomen, Socrates, and Theodoret, etc.

## Socrates.

<margin>E</margin>
¶ How after the death of Valens, the Barbarians plundered and destroyed the suburbs of Constantinople.

### The first Chapter.

<margin>The Barbarians and the suburbs of the city of Constantinople.</margin>
<margin>Dominica Augusta <note>Dominica was the widow of Emperor Valens; "Augusta" was the title for an Empress.</note></margin>
<margin>Mavia the Queen of the Saracens.</margin>
Now that Valens had died, the Barbarians once again came up to the walls of Constantinople and destroyed the suburbs. Therefore, the citizens (taking up the weapons they found) resisted the enemies. For the wife of Valens, named Dominica, gave pay from the common domains to those who were willing to fight as soldiers; thus the Saracens came to their aid, whom Queen Mavia had sent there because they were in a treaty with one another.

## Theodoretus.

<margin>F</margin>
¶ Regarding the friendliness of Gratian, and regarding his right faith.

### The second Chapter.

<margin>Gratian Augustus</margin>
But Gratian, the son of Valentinian—who shortly before, through the death of his father, had obtained the rule of Europe

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin>
and now that Valens had died childless, had also taken up the kingdoms of Asia and Libya—immediately made the godliness <note>Dutch: "Godtsalicheydt."</note> that he held in his heart evident through his deeds, and dedicated the beginning of his reign to the **L O R D** of all things. Thus he immediately commanded that the exiled Shepherds <note>A common metaphor for Bishops.</note> should return to their sheep, and that their holy churches should be restored to them—namely, to those who held communion with Damasus.

<margin>H</margin>
<margin>The exiled bishops are recalled.</margin>
<margin>Damasus, Bishop of Rome.</margin>
<margin>I</margin>
This Damasus, Bishop of Rome, always venerable, a wonderful man, highly adorned, who was always ready to do and say all things for the Apostolic doctrine, took up the governance of the churches after Liberius. <margin>K</margin> At that time, the Emperor sent out with such a command a most highly esteemed Captain <note>Dutch: "Hopman," likely referring to Flavius Sapor.</note> named Sapor. <margin>L</margin> And he commanded the preachers of the blasphemous Arian sects to be driven out of the Divine governance like beasts, and he caused everything to be restored to the pious Shepherds of the churches. He commanded that this should be observed in all provinces.

## Socrates.

<margin>M</margin>
<margin>Freedom of Religion</margin>
Now that Gratian, along with the young Valentinian, had taken up the Empire, he recalled all those who had been banished from their exile, and commanded that every doctrine should have its free practice; only the Eunomians, Photinians, and Manicheans did he thrust out of the Church. <note>These three groups—the Eunomians (extreme Arians), Photinians (who denied the pre-existence of Christ), and Manicheans (a dualistic gnostic sect)—were excluded from the general religious tolerance Gratian initially offered.</note>

# Theodoretus.

->¶ Regarding the dispute at Antioch between Paulinus and Meletius. Also regarding Apollinaris and his sect.<-

### The 3rd Chapter.

<margin>Antioch, a capital city of the East.</margin>
<margin>Discord among the Christians.</margin>
<margin>Apollinaris of Laodicea.</margin>
At the same time, such discord arose in Antioch—which is a capital city of the Eastern lands—due to the fact that those who labored for the Apostolic teaching (as has been mentioned before) were divided among themselves. Some, after having cast much slander upon Eustathius and rejecting the Arian foolishness <note>Original: "Arriaensche dwaeshept," referring to the Arian heresy which denied the full divinity of Christ.</note>, held their meetings separately and had Paulinus as their Bishop. Others, according to the arrangement of Euzoius, held their meetings with Meletius <note>The text uses "Militio," a Dutch rendering of Meletius of Antioch.</note> and were taught by him. In addition to this, Apollinaris of Laodicea took up a bishopric of another party; although he maintained an appearance of godliness and feigned that he followed Apostolic teaching, he was nevertheless shortly thereafter found to be an open enemy of the truth. For he spoke of the divine nature with false reasons, establishing certain levels of dignity, and took it upon himself to explain the hidden mystery of the Great Work <note>The "Great Work" here refers to the Incarnation.</note>, saying: That the rational soul which governs the body is deprived of the body <note>Apollinaris taught that Christ had a human body and a sensitive soul, but that the divine *Logos* took the place of the human rational mind/soul.</note>.

For if that eternal Word of God was with God from the beginning, and that same God had not taken on a rational soul (according to his saying), then He has given no medicine, nor any honor; instead, the body (which is something else) is moved by invisible powers, while the soul created in the image of God remains excluded and burdened with the disgrace of sin. To this, he spewed out and sought to confirm many more mockeries and follies. Sometimes he confessed that the flesh was taken from the body of the Virgin. Sometimes he said it came down from Heaven with God, and at other times that God Himself became flesh and took nothing from us. And he wished to mix many other trifles into the holy promises of God, which I

<column-break/>

do not deem necessary to recount here. By teaching such things, he not only corrupted his own followers with his poison, but also made some of ours partakers in it. But a short time later, when they noticed his shameful error, nearly all returned through the clarity of the Church to be received again into the fellowship of the Church. Yet they did not entirely cast off their first defect, but rather wounded many of those who were steadfast. From this root there sprouted in the Church a confusion regarding the nature of the flesh and the Divinity, and thus the suffering of the Only-Begotten was attributed to the Divinity <note>This refers to theopaschism, the idea that the Divine nature itself suffered on the cross.</note>. Many other things were also said, from which the dispute between the people and the priests arose. But some time later, the General <margin>Sapor, a General.</margin> Sapor arrived and showed the decree of the Emperor. Then Paulinus testified that he held the same views as Damasus <note>Pope Damasus I.</note>. Apollinaris promised the same, yet he concealed his sickness <note>Metaphor for heresy.</note>; but the holy Meletius, fleeing from their quarrel, lived in peace. But Flavian, a very wise man who was then ordained a priest, first spoke thus to Paulinus when the General came to him: "My friend, if you seek fellowship with Damasus, then first let the unity of your teaching be shown; for while he confesses one Essence <margin>Subsistence.</margin> of the Trinity, he openly preaches that there are three subsistences <note>Original Latin in margin: "Subsistentia." Flavian is distinguishing between *ousia* (essence) and *hypostasis* (subsistence/personhood).</note> or individualities, but you reject the individualities <margin>Substance.</margin> of the Trinity <note>Original Latin in margin: "Sustantia." Paulinus and the Westerners were wary of the term "three hypostases," fearing it sounded like three gods.</note>. Therefore, demonstrate the equality of the Teaching, and accept the order of the Church." When he had rebuked him with these words, he turned to Apollinaris and said: "I marvel greatly, my friend, that you so shamelessly resist the truth, when you nevertheless well know that the praiseworthy Damasus says: That our nature was completely assumed by God’s Word; and you teach the contrary, for you deprive our soul of salvation. If we speak falsely, accusing or charging you lightly, then revoke the novelty that you have devised. And by accepting the teaching of Damasus, follow the path of truth." Thus Flavian rebuked their boldness. But Meletius, a very mild-mannered man, said very friendlily to Paulinus: "Because God has appointed me and commanded me to care for these sheep, and you over others, then take up this care, and let us have fellowship with one another under the teaching of truth. Let us bring the flock together in friendship, and let us nullify the dispute of our Bishopric..."

<summary>This page details the three-way schism in Antioch between the followers of Paulinus, Meletius, and the heretic Apollinaris, highlighting the arrival of General Sapor to enforce the Emperor's decree and Flavian's theological defense of Nicene orthodoxy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the Meletian schism in Antioch and the reorganization of the Eastern churches following the return of exiled bishops. It details the transition from the reign of Gratian to the rise of Theodosius the Great.</meta>

<header>The Second Part. The Fourth Book.</header>

**A** bishopric. Let us shepherd the flock with a common hand and also take care of it together. And if there is a question regarding the see <note>Original: "stoel," literally chair or throne, referring to the Episcopal see.</note>, I shall also move to settle the question. Let us place the Gospel upon the throne, and let us sit on both sides; if it happens that I die first, then you alone shall be Bishop. But if it happens that you die first, then I shall take the care of the flock upon myself.

**B** <margin>Apollinaris is deprived of his Bishopric.</margin> When Meletius had proposed this with all gentleness, Paulinus would not accept it. Therefore the magistrate <note>Original: "hopman," referring to the magister militum or a high-ranking official acting as the Emperor's representative.</note>, acting as judge for both, gave and entrusted the churches to Meletius, and Paulinus remained Bishop over another flock. But Apollinaris, having been deposed from his bishopric, shamelessly and openly preached the novelty of his teaching and showed himself to be a light-minded leader of heresies; he lived thus in Laodicea.

**C** <margin>Vitalis.</margin> In Antioch, he had previously ordained Vitalis, who led an honorable life and was raised in the Apostolic teaching, but who was afterwards also infected with this sluggishness <note>Original: "traecheyt," perhaps implying a spiritual lethargy or a slow descent into heresy.</note>.

**D** <margin>Diodorus.</margin> The Holy Meletius had appointed Diodorus (of whom we spoke before) as a shepherd in Tarsus; this Diodorus had protected the church from destruction during great misfortune and tempest; Meletius also laid upon him the care of Cilicia. To Apamea—

**E** <margin>John.</margin> —he entrusted the episcopal care to John; and although he was of noble birth, he nevertheless further adorned his lineage through his virtues. This man was honorable in life; John protected the flock of his fellow believers in tempestuous and perilous times, and for this he had a helper, <margin>Stephanus, a helper to John.</margin> the praiseworthy Stephanus, whom the Holy Meletius dispatched to other struggles. For when he perceived that Germanicia <note>The text says "Germaniæ," referring to Germanicia in Commagene, not modern Germany.</note> was corrupted by the pestilential teaching of Eudoxius, he sent him there as a wise physician, for he was well-versed in the Greek language and raised in the Holy Scriptures. Therefore, he was not disappointed in his hope; for by using the gift of spiritual teaching, he turned the wolves into sheep. And when the great Eusebius returned from his exile,

**F** <margin>Acacius.</margin> he ordained Acacius, a very famous man, as Bishop in Beroea, <margin>Theodotus.</margin> and in Hierapolis he ordained Theodotus, whose wondrous life is well-spoken of. He ordained Eusebius in Chalcis, and in our Cyrus <note>Original: "Eyzen," a Dutch rendering of Cyrrhus/Cyrus.</note>, Isidore.

It is also said that he ordained Eulogius—who had fought for the Apostolic faith and had been exiled to Antinoöpolis with Protogenes—as a Bishop in Edessa,

<column-break/>

for Barses had now died. <margin>Maris.</margin> The holy Eusebius <note>Referencing Eusebius of Samosata.</note> ordained Maris as the last Bishop in the city of Doliche, for this small town had embraced the madness of Arius. When Eusebius came there to confirm Maris in his office, a woman full of that Arian poison threw a tile from the roof onto his head, whereby his head was greatly broken and torn.

**G** And shortly thereafter, he departed from this life to a better light. And when he was about to die, he bound all who were present by oath that they should seek no punishment for the woman who had done this, thus following his Lord, who said <margin>Luke 23.</margin> for those who crucified him: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do; <margin>Acts 7.</margin> and his fellow-servant Stephen, who, after he had received many throws of stones, cried out: Lord, do not hold this sin against them. Thus the great Eusebius died; he who had escaped the barbarians in Thrace could not escape the hands of the heretics there, but received the crown of martyrdom through their cruelty. This, then, is what occurred after the return of the Bishops.

¶ Now when Theodosius had slain very many, and very few had secretly escaped across the Hystrum—that is, the Danube—he returned to the Emperor, having broken camp and placed the people in garrison in the nearest cities, so that he himself brought the news of the victories to the Emperor. <margin>The vision of Theodosius.</margin>
In the meantime, the good Commander saw a divine vision, which was shown to him by God visibly. He saw that the holy Meletius, the Bishop of the city of Antioch, clothed him with the Imperial Mantle and also adorned his head with the crown. When he had seen this during the night, he told it in the morning to one of the Clerks. And this man said that the dream was very clear, and that there was nothing hidden or obscure within it. Very few days thereafter, the Ambassadors returned who had been sent by the Emperor to go and see the victory, and they recounted that many thousands had been slain there, wherefore the Emperor,

## How the Emperor Theodosius was baptized at Thessalonica.

### The Sixth Chapter.

<margin>The Emperor Theodosius is baptized at Thessalonica while ill.</margin>
And now, when the Emperor Theodosius had defeated the barbarians in war, and they sought to have the Romans as friends and to make a treaty with them, he took hostages or sureties from them and marched to Thessalonica. There he was baptized by Acholius, the Bishop of that city, after he had fallen into a great sickness; though he had been raised by his parents in the Christian teachings and in the Nicene confession.

# Socrates.

Now, as he desired to be baptized because of his illness, he asked the Bishop of Thessalonica what faith he held. And when the bishop answered him that the plague of the Arian teaching <note>Arianism was a theological movement that claimed Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father, rather than equal to Him.</note> had not been able to reach as far as Illyricum, but that they held the faith unblemished from the beginning according to the confession of the Nicene Council, he was baptized by him, listening gladly to his reasoning; and he was also healed of his sickness.

## Theodosius's Confession of Faith

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin>
### The Seventh Chapter.

<margin>The Emperor's command regarding the Christian faith.</margin>
<margin>H</margin>
**T**he Emperor Theodosius considered that it would be best for him to declare what faith he held, so that he might not seem to do violence to anyone by forcing them into a faith. Therefore, from Thessalonica, he issued a command and established a law for the people of Constantinople. The Emperor saw fit to announce this to his subjects and the city through a decree, as if placing a high tower or castle within a city. And these are the words of the command, which follow here.

->Emperor Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius Augustus, to the people of Constantinople.<-

<margin>I</margin>
<margin>Peter.</margin>
<margin>Damasus, Bishop of Rome; Peter of Alexandria.</margin>
<margin>K</margin>
<margin>L</margin>
**W**e desire that all the people and our subjects, over whom we shall mercifully rule, shall hold the faith and live in such a faith as Peter the Apostle taught to those of Rome as a religion, and which has been in practice until now. This is also followed by Bishop Damasus <note>Pope Damasus I.</note>, as is evident, and also Peter the Bishop of Alexandria, a man of Apostolic holiness; that is, that we believe, according to Apostolic and Evangelical teaching, that there is one Godhead of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, under the gracious Majesty and the Trinity <note>original: "Dzyvuldicheyt."</note>. Following this Law, we command that the name of "Catholic Christians" <note>The text uses "rechtgeloobighe Christenen," meaning orthodox or right-believing Christians.</note> shall be adopted. We regard the others as demented and insane, and judge that they shall bear the shame and infamy of heretical teaching. First, they shall face the judgment of God, and thereafter they shall be punished by us according to God's command and ordinance. Given on the 3rd Kalends of March at Thessalonica, when Gratian (for the 5th time), Valentinian, and Theodosius were chief councillors. This he commanded, and not long thereafter he came to Constantinople.

For Arius, a priest at Alexandria, had brought forth this slander there, and after him Eusebius Patrophilus, and Aetius from Palestine, Paulinus and Gregorius the Phoenician, Theodorus of Laodicea, and with them Gregorius, and after them Athanasius and Narcissus the Cilicians, and many more others who sought to cultivate the evil seed. The co-laborers of these wicked builders were Constantius and Valens. So, for these reasons alone, Theodosius caused all the Bishops who were under his government to assemble at Constantinople.

## The 7th Chapter.

<margin>The Emperor's command regarding the Christian faith.</margin>
**G** The Emperor Theodosius, considering that it would be best for him to declare what faith he held—so that he would not seem to do violence to anyone by forcing them into a faith—issued a command and established a law from Thessalonica to the people in Constantinople. **H** The Emperor saw it as good to announce his intention in writing to his subjects and the cities, like a high tower or castle in a city. And these are the words of the decree, which follow hereafter:

->The Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius Augustus, to the people of Constantinople.<-

**I** We desire that all the people and our subjects, over whom we shall mercifully rule, shall hold the faith and live in such a faith as Peter the Apostle taught to those of Rome regarding religion, and which is in use even until now. <margin>Peter at Rome.</margin> <margin>Damasus Bishop of Rome; Peter of Alexandria.</margin> This is also followed by the Bishop Damasus, as is evident, and also Peter the Bishop of Alexandria, a man of Apostolic holiness. That is, that we believe according to Apostolic and Evangelical teaching that there is one Godhead: of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, under the merciful Majesty and Fullness. **K** Following this Law, we command that the name of "Right-believing Christians" <note>This refers to the term "Catholic Christians" as used in the original Edict of Thessalonica (Cunctos populos).</note> shall be adopted. We regard the others as foolish and insane, and judge that they shall bear the shame and the slander of heretical teaching. First, by God’s counsel, and thereafter they shall also be punished by us according to God’s command and ordinance. Given on the 3rd day before the Kalends of March <note>February 27, 380 AD.</note> at Thessalonica, when Gratian (for the 5th time), Valentinian, and Theodosius were Chief Consuls. **L** This he commanded, and not long thereafter he came to Constantinople.

<margin>Theodosius, being commander, defeats the Barbarians.</margin>
Having gained strength, they now seemed to be invincible: Thus the Emperor <note>Referring to Emperor Gratian, who ruled the Western Empire.</note> finally considered that this war could be settled if he could obtain Theodosius as a commander. And calling him out of Spain very suddenly with all diligence, he made him a General, and immediately sent him against the Barbarians; so he, armed with faith, marched toward Thrace. When he had arrived there and had the Barbarians in sight, he immediately drew up his people in battle formation for war. When they now fell upon them to strike, and the Barbarians were not powerful enough to resist, they, breaking their battle lines, abandoned the vanguard. And so the Barbarians fled, and the others followed very manfully, and many Barbarians were slain there.

<margin>For they were not only [slain] by the enemies, but even [drowned] before being killed.</margin> <note>This likely refers to the chaos of the retreat across the Danube where many perished by the river as much as by the sword.</note>
When Theodosius had now slain very many, and very few had escaped them across the stream—that is, the Danube—he returned to the Emperor, having broken up his camp and placed the people in garrison in the nearest cities, so that he himself brought the news of the victory to the Emperor. Which the Emperor, while he marveled, could hardly believe had happened, because his rivals <note>original: "afghonstighe" (envious ones/detractors).</note> said that he had run away and had lost the battle. But he, for the sake of his slanderers, prayed that they should send someone there to see the multitude of those who were slain.

By these words the Emperor was moved and sent those who should inform themselves about the matter and go see it, and make a report thereof to the Emperor.

<margin>Theodosius’s vision.</margin>
Meanwhile, the good Commander saw a divine vision, which was shown to him visibly by God. He saw that the holy Meletius, the Bishop of the city of Antioch, clothed him with the Imperial Mantle and also adorned his head with the crown. When he had seen this during the night, he told it the next morning to one of the Clerks. And he said that the dream was very clear, and that there was nothing hidden or obscure within it. Within a very few days, those who were sent by the Emperor to go see the victory returned and recounted that many thousands were slain there, wherefore the Emperor, being gladdened, made Theodosius Emperor.

# Of the Church of Saint Anastasia.

## The 9th Chapter.

<margin>Anastasia.</margin>
This church was not only large and beautiful, but because the power of God was proven there, it was also gloriously named Anastasia <note>The name "Anastasia" comes from the Greek word *anastasis*, meaning "resurrection."</note>. This was because the confession of the Nicene faith in Constantinople—which had been as if dead—was, through the explanation and teaching of Gregory in this church, as if resurrected and renewed. Others say that a pregnant woman fell dead there and, through the common prayer offered for her in that place, became alive again along with her child. For this reason, this place took or obtained the name Anastasia.

# Socrates.

## How Theodosius drives the Arians out of the Constantinopolitan churches.

### The 10th Chapter.

<margin>Gregory Nazianzen wishes to depart from Constantinople.</margin>
When Gregory, an eloquent and honorable man, understood that some were murmuring because he was from another city <note>Gregory of Nazianzus had been called from his quiet life in Cappadocia to lead the small Nicene community in Constantinople; some locals resented him as an outsider.</note>, and when the Emperor had arrived, he desired to depart from Constantinople. But the Emperor, finding the churches in such a state, considered how he might bring it about that everyone was satisfied, seeking the benefit of all the churches.

<margin>Theodosius Augustus to Demophilus, a leader of the Arians.</margin>
Thus he said to Demophilus, who at that time was the leader of the Arians: "Will you believe according to the confession of the Nicene Council? If so, let the people be united and accept peace." And when he would not accept the Emperor’s proposal, the Emperor said: "Since you will not accept peace and unity, I command you to leave the churches."

Hearing this, Demophilus—considering that it is ill to kick against one's superior—called the people together into the church and, standing in their midst, spoke these very words: "Broeders, <margin>Matthew 10.</margin> it stands written in the Gospel: 'If they persecute you in one city, flee to another.' <note>Original: Matthew 10:23.</note> Because the Emperor has need of the church, know that we shall gather outside the city tomorrow." And when he had

<column-break/>

said this, he went out. Nevertheless, those words of the Gospel were spoken in a certain sense <note>The translator suggests Demophilus used the scripture as an excuse rather than out of true piety.</note>. For there we are commanded to flee the earthly dwelling so that we might seek the heavenly Jerusalem. Having gone out of the gates, they held their assembly outside the city walls.

With them also went out Lucius, who had been driven out and banished from Alexandria, for he was living in Constantinople at that time. Thus they left the Church, which they had held by force for forty years, not wishing to accept the peace and agreement of Theodosius. They went out of the city when Gratian was High Councilor <term>Consul</term> for the fifth time, and Theodosius for the first time, in the month of November. This being done, the Christian believers took possession of the churches again.

# Sozomen.

## Of the cunning of Eunomius.

### The 11th Chapter.

<margin>Eunomius in Bithynia.</margin>
When Eunomius had been separated from his churches during the time of Valens, he lived alone in Bithynia. He was a cunning and eloquent man, and a great many people came to him—some because they wished to test the man, others because they wanted to hear what he said. This report also reached the Emperor, who therefore desired to speak with him. But Flaccilla Augusta <note>Aelia Flaccilla, the first wife of Theodosius I, was a staunch supporter of the Nicene Creed.</note> kept him back with her pleas, for she was very faithful in the faith and maintained the Nicene faith as unbreakable. Therefore, she also feared that (as commonly happens) the Emperor, being seduced by the eloquence of the man, might easily have fallen into his sect.

As the bishops entered the Emperor’s court, the Emperor, leaving all others aside, ran toward Meletius. And just as a son loves his father, whom he has not seen for a long time and now beholds, he embraced him and kissed his eyes, lips, breast, head, and the right hand that had crowned him in his dream. And he made known to him the vision which he had experienced. And when he had greeted all the others as if they were his fathers, he prayed them that they would carefully deliberate upon the present matters.

## Socrates

C And he declared that they should ordain a bishop in the city of Constantinople. Hoping that the Macedonians <note>A sect also known as the Pneumatomachi, who denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note> could be reconciled, he also called their bishops together. Thus the right-believing bishops of the faith of Constantinople were gathered: Timothy of Alexandria, Cyril of Jerusalem—who, after they had improved themselves, agreed to the faith of Constantinople—Meletius of Antioch, and Acholius of Thessalonica, and many others, so that they numbered 150 in total.

<margin>That there is one substance and being of the Father and Son.</margin>
<margin>Bishops of the Macedonians.</margin>
The leaders of the Macedonians were Eleusius of Cyzicus and Marcianus of Lampsacus, and they were about 36 in total, the majority coming from the cities of the Hellespont. These then came together in the month of May, while Eucharius and Evagrius were the chief Councilors <note>original: "opperste Raetsheeren" referring to the Consuls of the year 381.</note>. Then the Emperor and the bishops on his side labored to ensure that Eleusius

E and his following would be united with the Church of the Christians. They recounted to them the message they had sent through Eustathius to Liberius, who was at that time the Bishop of Rome, and how they had previously been willing to join in communion. They argued that it was no small shame for them to change so easily from what they had once considered good.

<margin>The obstinacy of the Macedonians.</margin>
F But these men preferred to follow the Arian sect, despising both the warning and the public correction, rather than say that the three persons in the Godhead were of one substance <note>original: "eenswesens," translating the Greek *homoousios*.</note>. Having confessed this, they departed from Constantinople and wrote to one another that no one should accept the faith of the Council of Nicaea as held by Constantinople.

<column-break/>

-> ¶ Of the ordination of Maximus the Cynic, and how he was deposed; also how Nectarius was rightly ordained, and of the rules given in the Synod. <-

### The 13th Chapter.

<margin>Gregory Nazianzen departs from Constantinople.</margin>
But Gregory, who until that time governed the Church at Constantinople, made preparations to travel to Nazianzus. In his place, while the church at Constantinople was without a bishop, Timothy of Alexandria (a follower of Peter) had ordained Maximus the Cynic, whom he had recently chosen. But this man was full of the Apollinarian madness <note>The heresy of Apollinaris, which taught that Christ had a human body but a divine mind rather than a human soul.</note>. But the holy men gathered at Constantinople would not suffer this.

And when the Egyptians had broken away because of his ordination, they held the holy offices and divine services with Gregory. He took it very poorly that a schism was occurring again and prayed that they would seek a man who was worthy and appoint him as bishop. Then they fulfilled his desire, appointing a man adorned with nobility named Nectarius as bishop of Constantinople. And Maximus, who was tainted with the sect of Apollinaris, they stripped of his episcopal honor and cast out. They also then made a rule that the Bishop of Constantinople should have privileges and glorious freedoms second only to the Roman bishop, because Constantinople is "New Rome." They confirmed the Nicene faith once again and also established Patriarchs, dividing the provinces or territories so that every bishop remained in his own church and did not go into other lands. This had previously been permitted because of the persecutions. So they assigned Nectarius the great city and Thrace; and the diocese in Pontus they assigned to Helladius, who succeeded Basil; and to Gregory of Nyssa, the brother of Basil, they assigned Caesarea of Cappadocia.

Optimus became Patriarch of Antioch in Pisidia. In Egypt, Timothy of Alexandria was appointed Patriarch. But the governance of the lands governing the East they entrusted to the bishops there: Pelagius of Laodicea and Diodorus of Tarsus.

Synod of Constantinople.

The following summer, many bishops gathered again in Constantinople regarding ecclesiastical matters. There, the bishops of the western provinces <note>original: "lantschappen regent Westen"</note> received a letter from that Synod, by which they were summoned to Rome, so that the greatest Council should be held there. ### ->The letter of the Constantinopolitan Council, sent to Pope Damasus and to the bishops in the West.<-

## ->The 14th Chapter.<-

<margin>
The letter that the Council at Constantinople sent to the bishops ruling the West.

To the venerable and godly lords, brothers, and fellow-servants, Damasus, Ambrose, Britton, Valerian, Acholius, Basil, and the other Holy Bishops gathered in the great city of Rome, the Council gathered in the great city of Constantinople wishes salvation and prosperity in the Lord.

It is first necessary to make known to your reverence and to recount the abundant troubles and miseries often inflicted upon us by the Arian <note>Followers of Arius, who held that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father.</note> power; for we do not believe that your holiness is so negligent that you should need to be taught with what

<column-break/>

members <note>The text likely refers to the "members of the Church."</note> one ought to have compassion. Nor have such injustices and tempests come upon us that they could have been hidden in any way due to their smallness. Nor is the time of persecution so recent, but it still holds the old memory and remembrance, not only in those who suffered but also in those who shared in their suffering. For yesterday and today (so to speak), having been released from the bonds of exile, they have returned to their churches after many trials and persecutions; the bodies of others who died in exile have also been brought back. Likewise, some of those returning from their exile suffered more trouble in their own property through the rage and fury of the heretics than in their exile, and were pelted with stones like the Holy Stephen <note>The first Christian martyr, as described in the Book of Acts.</note>. Others were tormented with various martyrdoms, who still bear the wounds and marks in their bodies. Who indeed could recount and tell how some were stripped of their money, deprived of their honor, and had their goods confiscated, and also what insults and bonds came upon them? For all trouble and persecutions have risen above measure over us, yet justly, for we have greatly sinned, or the merciful God wished to exercise us with much suffering. For this we thank God, who has chastened His servants through so many persecutions, and according to the multitude of His mercies has led us back again to refreshment. So we have indeed had need of time and great labor, so that the improvement of the churches might thus proceed, so that through great diligence they might gradually come back to their old health through medicines <note>A metaphor for spiritual and administrative restoration.</note>. In this manner we mean and hope to be delivered from persecution, and to restore and reform the churches that were kept from us by the heretics. But we still have great and heavy wolves, who, after being driven from the sheepfolds, still pull the sheep out of the pasture, and want to make assemblies, stir up the people, and do not cease to be harmful to the church. Thus for this work (as we have said) time was needed. But since you have written of a Council in the city of Rome, and since you, showing brotherly love toward us, have called us as your own members through the letters of the God-loving Prince <note>Emperor Theodosius I.</note>, so that we, who then alone were placed under that trouble...

**B** But because it would have deprived the churches of their rest, which had only recently begun, and because it was impossible for the great multitude; and for the sake of the letters sent to us by you, we have gathered at Constantinople. **C** Of a further journey we had no hope at all, nor did we expect it, before we arrived in Constantinople. **D** For these and other similar things hindered our coming to you. Therefore, we have chosen to undertake the second best option, and desire that your love toward us be made manifest. For that cause, we have very gladly endured persecution, grief, the deep decrees of the Emperors, the cruelties of the judges, and also all other trials or temptations of the heretics, for the sake of the Christian faith, which was confirmed in Nicaea, Bithynia, by the 318 Fathers.

**E** We hope that this faith is pleasing to you and to us,

**F** and to all those who do not overturn the truth of the faith, which we know to be the oldest, following that faith. It teaches us to believe in the Name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We believe in one Godhead, one power, and one essence of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and also equal honor, dignity, and eternal command, in three most perfect <term>hypostases</term> <note>original: "selfstandicheden". A technical theological term referring to the distinct individual existence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit within the one Godhead.</note>,

**I** So this is a short summary or account of that which is most clearly taught and preached by us,

Also, how the congregation of God is provided with pastors, and how each person in particular shall be served. That is an old custom (as you well know) that has been in the Church, and also in the confession of the ancient fathers who were gathered in Nicaea, issued as such: that in every land or province, the bishops may, with their neighbors, for the sake of profit, undertake ordinances and dealings. ### The xv. Chapter.

WHEN you gave the Apostolic See its due honor, you also did yourselves much profit, most dear children. For although the holy place in which the Apostle <note>Refers to Saint Peter, whose "chair" or residency is the basis for the authority of the Roman See.</note> had his residence <margin>☜</margin> teaches enough how we shall rule the church in which we have received the governance, we nevertheless freely confess that we are small in comparison to such honor. Therefore, we hasten greatly that we might come to the glory of such happiness. Know then, that we here be-

<column-break/>

<margin>p</margin>
fore have condemned the unlearned and wicked Timothy, who is a disciple of the heretic Apollinaris, and also with him his godless teaching. We also will not suffer that in future times his remnants or relics shall in any manner prevail or be held of value. But as that old serpent <note>A common biblical metaphor for the Devil or persistent evil.</note>, being struck once or twice, becomes alive again to its own punishment, and he who is a stranger to the church does not cease to attack some of the faithful with his deadly venom. Guard yourself from that as from a pestilential destruction or poison, so that you may thus persist steadfastly and unmovably in the Apostolic faith, which the fathers in the Council at Nicaea <note>The first Ecumenical Council (325 AD) which established the foundational creed of Christianity.</note> confessed in their writings. And you shall not allow your Clergy or the common people to hear from him idle reasons and questions. For we have now given this as a rule: that everyone who has confessed himself to be a Christian should observe that which was taught and delivered to us <margin>p</margin> by the Apostles. As Paul says: "If anyone teaches you something else than what you have received, let him be accursed" <note>original: "So pemāt u liedē pet anders leert dan dat ghy ontfangen hebt / dat hy vervloect sy." A translation of Galatians 1:8.</note>. For Christ the Son of God our Lord has bestowed and given to the human race, through His suffering, most perfect salvation, so that He might free the human being, who lay entirely bound in sin, from all his sins. And if anyone says that this person has too little of either the Godhead or the manhood, he is full of the devilish spirit and testifies that he is a son of hell. Why then do you desire again the condemnation or banishment of Timothy, who is already condemned here in the presence of Peter, the Bishop of Alexandria <note>Peter II of Alexandria (died 381 AD), the successor to Athanasius.</note>, along with his master-<margin>r. c. i. 1.</margin> teacher Apollinaris? And who on the day of judgment shall suffer due punishment and plague. But if this man counsels any simple love, as if he had any hope—while he has changed the true hope consisting in the Christian confession—they shall know that they also shall perish as they <margin>u z</margin> fight against the Christian teaching. Dear children, may God keep you healthy and prosperous.

<meta>This page continues the specific condemnations (anathemas) issued following the Council of Constantinople in 381 AD. These articles define the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity against various fourth-century groups that the Church deemed heretical.</meta>

# The Second Part. The IV. Book.

<margin>A</margin>
1. Since, after the Council held at Nicaea <note>The First Council of Nicaea (325 AD), which established the foundational creed of Christianity.</note>, such an error has arisen that some have shamelessly dared to say that the Holy Spirit was made by the Son: We banish those who do not say with all freedom that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one essence and of equal power.

2. Likewise, we also banish the Sabellians <note>Followers of Sabellius, who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons, but merely three different "modes" or "masks" worn by a single God.</note> and those who follow their error, who say that the Father is the same as the Son.

<margin>B</margin>
3. We banish Arius and Eunomius <note>Eunomius was a leader of the radical Arians (Anomoeans) who argued that the Son was "unlike" the Father in substance.</note>, who with equal blasphemy, although with different words, say that the Son and the Holy Spirit are creatures or created beings.

4. We also banish the Macedonians <note>Also known as "Pneumatomachi" or "Spirit-fighters," they accepted the divinity of the Son but denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note>, who come from the Arian root, having not changed the godlessness of Arius, but only the word.

<margin>C</margin>
5. We banish Photinus <note>Bishop of Sirmium, who taught that Jesus was a mere man (psilanthropism) who became "God" only through his virtuous life.</note>, who renewed the heresy of Ebion <note>The Ebionites were an early Jewish Christian sect who regarded Jesus as a prophet but not divine.</note>, and confesses that our Lord Jesus Christ is solely from Mary.

6. We also banish those who say that there are two Sons—one from eternity and the other after the Incarnation or the taking of flesh from the Virgin.

7. We also banish those who wish to maintain that the Word of God was changed into flesh in place of a rational soul; for the Son, the Word of God, did not become a body in place of a rational soul, but took upon Himself and saved our rational and intellectual soul without sin. <note>This condemns Apollinarianism, the belief that Jesus had a human body but a divine mind instead of a human soul.</note>

<margin>D</margin>
8. We also banish those who say that the Word of God is an extension or a corruption separated from the Father, and who blasphemously say that He shall have an end without independent existence. And those who have thus cast themselves from the Church to another church, we have excluded from our fellowship until they return to the cities where they were first ordained.

<margin>E</margin>
9. But if anyone should come from one place to another and be ordained in the place of the living, he shall be deprived of his priestly dignity—having abandoned his own city—until his successor rests in the Lord.

<margin>F</margin>

¶ For the name "Gods" is given and granted by God to the angels and all the Saints; but concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because of their equal divinity <note>original: "Godsalicheyt," here referring to their shared divine nature</note>, they are not called by the name "Gods," but are named or called by the Name of "our God." This is so that we may believe that we are baptized in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit alone, and not in the name of angels or archangels as the heretics are accustomed to do, or as the Jews and Heathens rage.

¶ This, then, is the salvation of Christians: that believing in the Trinity—that is, in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and being baptized in that same Name—they also believe in one Godhead and Power, one Divinity, Essence, and Substance. This, then, took place while Gratian <note>Emperor Gratian, who reigned 367–383 AD.</note> was still alive.
