Folio 425.
### The Second Part. The Fourth Book.

<margin>Dispute.</margin>
**A** This man stated that public disputes do not reconcile the strife of heresy; rather, they are much more a cause for schisms and heresy to increase and grow ever larger. Therefore, he gave such advice to Nectarius <note>Nectarius was the Archbishop of Constantinople from 381 to 397 AD.</note>, for he knew that the ancient fathers did not wish to assign a beginning of essence to the Son of God, because they understood that he was equally eternal with the Father. For that reason, his advice was that one should shun all debatable opinions and arguments, and that one should instead draw testimonies from the ancient sentences and opinions.

<margin>The advice of Sisinnius to convict the heretics.</margin>
**B** And further, that the Emperor should ask the leaders of the heretics whether they would speak according to the ancient Teachers who had taught before the schism? Or whether they rejected them as being estranged from Christianity? And if they rejected them, then they should be challenged to place those fathers under an interdict <note>An official exclusion from the church; an anathema.</note>. And if they did not dare to do so, then they would be ruined in the eyes of the people. If this were done, it would be certain that the truth would prevail.

<margin>Arcadius, son of Theodosius the Emperor.</margin>
**C** But if they did not take offense at the Emperor’s Teachers, then it is permitted to us (he said) that we bring forward the books of the Elders, through which our doctrine might be confirmed and strengthened by their testimonies.

**D** In the meantime, as Nectarius listened gladly to Sisinnius speaking, he ran very quickly to the Emperor’s court and told the Emperor what advice had been given. Then the Emperor, having very diligently weighed the opinion, called the masters of the heretics together and asked them whether they accepted the masters of the church who had lived before the times of the division.

<margin>Theodosius’s love for the pious church.</margin>
When they did not reject those who were proposed, but honored them as their masters and commanders, the Emperor asked them again whether they would accept their testimonies for the Christian Doctrine.

<margin>Nectarius. Sisinnius, Bishop of the Novatians.</margin>
**E** The leaders and debaters of the heretics, hearing this (of whom there were many sharpened for disputing), doubted greatly what and how they should answer, and a great discord arose among them. Some said that the Emperor’s proposal was good; others thought that it was not at all useful for their purpose. For some felt one way, and others another, regarding the books of the Elders. And they made no factional groupings or conspiracies <note>original: "conspiratien," meaning they failed to form a united front</note> with one another, but were divided among themselves—not only against other heresies or sects, but even those of the same sect were for a long time entirely against one another.

**F** And just as with the ancients, the ton-

<column-break/>

-gues of the Heathens <note>original: "Heusen," likely a variant of "Heidenen" (Heathens/Pagans)</note>, who were of equal wickedness, were divided, so too were these men divided, and the wrath of their purpose was utterly cast out.

**G** Now when the Emperor perceived their lack of unity, and that they relied only upon disputing and not upon the interpretations of the Ancients, he proposed to deal with them in another manner. He ordered that each Religion should set down and declare its faith in writing. Then these cunning men of every heresy, subtly and craftily weighing their words, described their own Doctrine.

<margin>Nectarius. Agelius.</margin>
**H** For a certain day had been appointed for every Bishop to come to court. Thus Nectarius and Agelius were there, who were the leaders of the doctrine of *Homousios* <note>original: "Homousios," a Greek term meaning "of the same substance." This refers to the Nicene belief that the Son is of the same essence as the Father.</note>, that is, Consubstantiality. On behalf of the Arians was Demophilus.

<margin>Demophilus. Eunomius.</margin>
For the Eunomians, Eunomius himself was there. In the name of the Macedonians was Eleusius of Cyzicus. Thus the Emperor received those who had come and the writings of each one.

<margin>Eleusius.</margin>
**I** And stepping somewhat aside, he prayed from the bottom of his heart that God would be helpful to him in choosing the truth.

<margin>Theodosius accepts the doctrine of Homousios, or Consubstantiality, and rejects all others.</margin>
**K** After that, reading through the writings of each doctrine, he accepted with praise and prize only the doctrine of *Homousios*, or Consubstantiality, tearing up the other writings very quickly as they brought about a division of the Trinity. And this was the reason that the Novatians, for the sake of this benefit, returned again into the city.

**L** For the Emperor, marvelling at their unity in the faith, commanded that they should have their own churches and houses of prayer, and that they should possess the freedom of their churches and their faith. But the Bishops and leaders of other religions and faiths, because of their mutual discord, fell into contempt among their own followers and thus departed in shame, comforting one another with letters so that they should not mourn over it, even if many fell away to the faith of *Homousios*, or Consubstantiality, saying:

<margin>Matthew 20 and 22.</margin>
**M** That many were called, but few were chosen. Which they did not say when a great multitude of people were joining them with power.

Folio 426.
### Tripartite Ecclesiastical History

<margin>Heretics were not to be ordained.</margin>
...nor allowed to go out, so that the heretics should have churches, or that they should teach anything contrary to the faith, or that they should ordain Bishops or any others. He <note>Emperor Theodosius I</note> also drove some out of the cities and declared others unworthy of any honors. Furthermore, he allowed them neither the rights of the city nor common liberty. Beyond this, he established great punishments and penalties against them in his mandate, which he nevertheless has not yet put into use; for his intention was this: that they might become unified through these threats, rather than being tormented by many actual punishments.

## Chapter 20.

<margin>The true-believers are also restless among themselves.</margin>
Those who defended the Nicene faith <note>The orthodox Christian faith established at the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.</note> were also not without sorrow, for those in Antioch condemned those who were present at the Council and had opposed them. The Egyptians, Arabians, and Cypriots said that Flavian of Antioch <note>Flavian I was a claimant to the bishopric of Antioch, whose election caused a long-standing schism.</note> ought to be driven out; but the Palestinians, Phoenicians, and Syrians defended Flavian with great labor and effort. However, we shall recount the proper conclusion of this matter in its appropriate place. Furthermore, at this time, while the Synods were being handled in Constantinople, such things occurred in the Western lands: Maximus of Britain <note>Magnus Maximus, a Roman commander in Britain who usurped the imperial title.</note> rose up against the Roman Empire and attacked Gratian himself, who at that time was waging war against the Germans.

<margin>Maximus, a tyrant.</margin>
<margin>Justina.</margin>
While Valentinian <note>Valentinian II</note> was still a child in Italy, Probus, the old High Councilor and Governor, ruled. But when he was dead, and her son was still very young, and she came to Milan, she was very angry with Ambrose the Bishop <note>Saint Ambrose, the influential Bishop of Milan.</note> and deposed him, commanding him to be banished from the land.

# Theodoretus <note>Theodoret of Cyrrhus, another 5th-century historian used in this compilation.</note>

And when Ambrose was commanded to leave the Church, he said: That he would not do so voluntarily, so that it might not appear that I have surrendered the sheep’s fold to the wolf, or to those who blaspheme God. If you wish, then strike me dead here; in this place I shall willingly die.

# Sozomenus <note>Sozomen, a historian who wrote contemporary to Socrates and Theodoret.</note>

As the people loved Ambrose dearly and resisted those who wished to drive him out of the land, the Empress Justina became even more wrathful. She called for Benevolus, who at that time was the Master of Records <note>Original: "Gentmeester." But as he refused to do this (for he was a Christian), she sought to lead him to it by offering greater offices, higher honors, and knightly titles. But Benevolus, ungirding himself, threw his belt <note>The military belt or *cingulum* was the symbol of official Roman office; throwing it down was a formal resignation.</note> at the feet of the Empress and said: That he desired neither the honor nor any other thing as a reward for unrighteousness or godlessness. And even though Benevolus refused to do it in every way, others were found who carried out the shameful command.

<margin>How Emperor Gratian perished.</margin>
¶ In great haste she went to meet her husband at Lyons in France as he was about to travel across the water. Gratian believed that his wife, whom he had married at great expense, was surely coming; thus, he did not guard himself against the traps set for him. Like a blind man walking into a ditch, he fell into the hands of his enemies.

<margin>Andragathius <note>original: "Adragatius"</note>, the murderer of Gratian.</margin>
When Gratian reached his wife's carriage, behold, Andragathius <note>A commander under the usurper Maximus.</note> suddenly leaped out of the wagon and treacherously murdered Gratian. So he died in the year when Merobaudes and Saturninus were Consuls <note>original: "Raedtsheeren"</note>, in the 15th year of his reign and the 24th year of his life. Through this deed, the anger of Justina <note>The Arian Empress-mother and regent for Valentinian II.</note> against Ambrose was stilled for a time. However, Valentinian, though unwillingly, finally consented to the Imperial rule of Maximus due to the necessity of the times. Then Probus traveled from Italy into Illyricum, fearing the power of Maximus, and resided in Thessalonica in Macedonia.

<margin>The tyrant Maximus [acting] for the Christians, to Valentinian Augustus.</margin>
When Maximus heard of the things being done again against the eloquent preacher of truth <note>Refers to Bishop Ambrose of Milan.</note>, he wrote to Valentinian that the struggle against the Christian Church should cease. He also warned him not to abandon his father’s piety. Indeed, he even threatened him with war if he would not remain peaceful, and he intended to fulfill his words with deeds. For this reason, he came to Milan, having undertaken the war, where Valentinian was living at the time. But when Valentinian learned of his arrival and invasion, he fled to Illyricum, knowing what evil would befall him through the advice of his mother.

<margin>Theodosius to Valentinian.</margin>
But when Theodosius had heard what had been done by Justina, and also what had been written by the tyrant <note>A common term in this period for a usurper, in this case, Magnus Maximus.</note>, he wrote to the fleeing Valentinian: That it was no wonder the Emperor was seized by fear and trembling while the tyrant’s power grew and increased. This was because the Emperor opposed the piety and the life of the godly, while the tyrant supported and came to the aid of the same; therefore, the Emperor was left exposed, while the tyrant armed himself against the unprotected.

## **Theodoretus** <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458 AD), a bishop and influential theologian.</note>

And when Ambrose was ordered to leave the Church, he said: That he would not do so voluntarily, so that it would not seem that I have surrendered the Sheepfold to the Wolf, or also to those who blaspheme God. If you wish, then strike me dead here; in this place I shall die willingly.

## **Sozomenus** <note>Salaminius Hermias Sozomenus (c. 400–450 AD), a historian of the Christian Church.</note>

As the people now loved Ambrose very much and resisted those who wanted to drive him from the country, Empress Justina became even more wrathful and called Benevolus, who was the Steward <note>original: "Rentmeester"</note> at that time, and commanded him to immediately issue a Law and decree, by which the faith confessed in Ariminum <note>original: "Armenio"; this refers to the Council of Ariminum (Rimini) in 359 AD, which produced an Arian-leaning creed.</note> would be confirmed. But when he refused to do this (for he was a Christian), she sought to entice him with greater offices, more honor, and knightly titles. But Benevolus, ungirding himself, threw his belt <note>The "cingulum" or belt was the official insignia of Roman administrative or military office; throwing it down was a formal act of resignation.</note> before the feet of the Empress and said: That he wanted neither the honor nor any other thing as a reward for unrighteousness or godlessness. And although Benevolus refused to do it in every way, others were nonetheless found who carried out the shameful command.

Historia Ecclesiastical Tripartite <note>original: "Historia Ecclesiastica Tripartita," a famous medieval church history manual compiled from the works of Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret.</note>

<margin>Theodosius arrives at Milan.</margin>
Afterward, he traveled toward Milan, where Maximus was staying. Meanwhile, the Arians <note>Followers of Arianism, a theological movement that argued Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father; they were often at odds with the "Orthodox" Nicene emperors.</note> who were in Constantinople, spreading various rumors, claimed that the Emperor had lost his army and had fallen into the hands of the tyrant’s commanders, among many other reports. As enemies are prone to do out of malice, they spread these stories so frequently that many began to believe they were true. Incited by these reports, the Arian people were stirred to a very ugly boldness and burned down the house of Nectarius <note>The Bishop of Constantinople from 381 to 397 AD.</note>.
<margin>The Arians burned the house of Nectarius, the Bishop of Constantinople.</margin>
This occurred when Theodosius was serving as Chief Councilor <note>original: "Raet-heer"; referring to the Roman office of Consul.</note> for the second time, alongside Cynegius. But when Theodosius moved against the tyrant, the soldiers of Maximus—seeing the presence of the Imperial power and the approach of his army and the signs of his coming—could not hold out against the mere rumor and force of his reputation. Instead, they took the tyrant prisoner, bound him, and delivered him to be executed, while the aforementioned Councilors were still in office, on the 27th day of the month of August. Meanwhile, Andragathius <note>original: "Adzagatius," the general who had murdered Emperor Gratian.</note>, who had killed Gratian, threw himself into a nearby river and thus died by drowning.
<margin>The death of Maximus the tyrant. Andragathius drowns.</margin>
Then Valentinian and Theodosius, having secured the victory, traveled to Rome. With them was Honorius <note>The son of Theodosius, then quite young, who would later become Emperor of the West.</note>, who was still very young and whom Theodosius had summoned from Constantinople after winning the war against Maximus. While they resided in the City of Rome and held a magnificent triumph to celebrate this victory, Emperor Theodosius showed his kindness toward Symmachus, an elderly former Councilor. This Symmachus was considered one of the most principal Councilors, a wonderfully learned man and highly eloquent, of whom many books are still found today.
<margin>Symmachus, accused of having praised Maximus, flees into the church and is delivered.</margin>
This man had written a speech in praise and honor of Maximus and had read it aloud; because of this, he was later accused of speaking against the Imperial Majesty. Fearing death for this reason, he fled into a church for sanctuary. However, the Emperor—being a complete Christian who honored not only the priests of his own faith but also the Novatians <note>A rigorist Christian sect that followed the Nicene creed but had stricter rules regarding the readmission of those who had lapsed during persecutions.</note> who held a belief very close to his own—listened to the intercession of Leontius, a Bishop of the Novatians in Rome, and granted Symmachus his freedom. Once Symmachus had obtained his liberty, he wrote an Apology <note>original: "Apologeticum"; a formal written defense or justification of his actions.</note> addressed to the Emperor.

# Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380 – after 439 AD), the Greek church historian whose "Ecclesiastical History" is the primary source for these events.</note>

->¶ How Theodosius abolished the murders that used to occur in the bake-houses in Rome. And regarding the law he established against adulterous women.<-

->The 24th Chapter.<-

<margin><unclear>is here on the west side the mills ...</unclear></margin>
Now, while the Emperor Theodosius was in the city of Rome, he conducted himself very profitably by skillfully abolishing certain things and reintroducing others. Two things in particular, which had brought about much disorder, he did away with. For a long time, there had been buildings in the city of Rome of massive construction in which bread was baked for the service of the entire city. These houses were called *Mancipes* <note>Latin term for the contractors or officials in charge of the public bread supply.</note> by the inhabitants. Over time, they had turned the underground mills beneath these bake-houses into dens of murder. Because the mills were placed underground or in cellars, they built dwellings, taverns, or inns on both sides of them, and kept brothels or houses of ill-repute there to deceive many people. Some came there for bread, and others came to indulge their lusts. The buildings were so designed that people would fall from the taverns directly into the mills. This happened most often to strangers, with the result that many were forced to work there until old age and were never allowed to leave, so that their closest friends often believed they were dead and gone. One of Theodosius’s own soldiers fell into such a trap. When he was locked in the mill and they would not let him out, he drew his sword and killed those who barred his way. Being greatly terrified, they let the soldier go. When the Emperor learned of this, he commanded that not only the inhabitants—specifically the *Mancipes*—should be punished, but that the entire bakery system should be torn down and rooted out.

### ¶ How the temples of the Pagans in Alexandria were destroyed and broken down.

### The xxvij. Chapter.

<margin>The temples of the pagans are destroyed in Alexandria.</margin>
At this same time, such a riot arose in Alexandria. The Emperor had commanded that through Theophilus <note>Theophilus was the Patriarch of Alexandria from 385 to 412 AD, known for his militant opposition to paganism.</note> in Alexandria, the temples of the Pagans should be destroyed. And after Theophilus had received authority, he was diligent in destroying the mysteries and idolatries of the Pagans. He thus cleansed the Temple of Mithras, but that of Serapis <note>original: "Seraphidis"; Serapis was the patron deity of Alexandria, and his temple, the Serapeum, was one of the grandest in the ancient world.</note> he completely overthrew. The secrets of Mithras, where they committed murders <note>A reference to the rumors of human sacrifice or the blood rituals associated with the Mithraic mysteries.</note>, he made entirely public, and he fully uncovered the ridiculous fantasy of Serapis. And he commanded that the male shames <note>original: "mans schamelheden"; referring to the phallic symbols often carried in Dionysian or other pagan processions.</note>, which the Pagans held in great honor, should be carried through all the streets and ways for all to see. When the Pagans saw this, and most especially the Philosophers, they could not endure this shame; for having fallen upon the Christians with all their might, they committed a very great slaughter. And as the Christians now resisted them, this murder turned into a great war. In this battle, very few of the Pagans remained, but of the Christians very many and beyond all number; on both sides, many were wounded. But the Pagans, when they were wounded, fearing the Emperor’s retribution, hid themselves here and there, and many also fled the city. Among whom also <margin>Helladius and Ammonius the Grammarians, masters of Socrates.</margin> were Helladius and Ammonius the Grammarians, under whom I learned to read while I was still a child in Constantinople <note>The author here is Socrates Scholasticus, the 5th-century historian whose work is a primary source for this "Tripartite" compilation.</note>. And it was said there that Helladius was a priest of Jupiter, and Ammonius a priest of Apollo.

When this had occurred, the Governor and the General of Alexandria assisted Theophilus in destroying the temples of the Pagans, and they melted the images of the gods into pots,

<column-break/>

and other items for the various needs of the churches in Alexandria. For they were donated to the churches by the Emperor for the benefit of the poor. Now when Theophilus had broken all the images, he kept only one image, namely of a monkey <note>original: "Simie"; likely a statue of the Egyptian god Thoth in his baboon form.</note>, and commanded that it should be publicly displayed and preserved. He did this so that the Pagans in future times would not deny that they had worshipped such gods. I know that Ammonius the Grammarian took this very poorly, saying that the Pagans had not suffered so heavily from anything as they did from the fact that this image was not also broken; but that this single image was kept only for mockery. But Helladius boasted that in the assault he had murdered nine Christians.

### Sozomenus.

Now when the Emperor heard what had happened there in Alexandria, he declared the Christians to be blessed and granted them the crown of martyrs because they had subjected themselves to so many perils for the sake of the teaching. And he forgave the Pagans, so that he might more easily win them over to Christianity. And he commanded that the temples, which were the causes of the slaughters, should be entirely uprooted.

When the Emperor's letters were publicly read and the Christians attacked the Pagans, the guards of the Temple of Serapis fled away. And it is evident that the Christians from that time forward occupied that place. The philosopher Olympus <note>original: "Olympius"</note>, as I have recently understood, heard on that day when these things were happening in the Temple of Serapis, someone singing an "Alleluia." And when he saw that the temple was closed during the time of rest, and that he saw no one, yet heard only the voice of the one singing, he recognized by a sign what was to happen there, and thus went out secretly, and having found a ship, he sailed away.

#### ¶ Of the deceit which the Pagans committed in their temples.

### The xxviij. Chapter.

# The Second Part. The Second Book.
Fol. 431.

<margin>The Emperor Theodosius gave the idols within the city of Alexandria to the poor.</margin>
Thus Theophilus cleansed the city of Alexandria of the error of the Idols, and he did not only completely overthrow the Temples of the Idols, but also revealed the fraud of the Priests who served them, by whom many were led astray and deceived. For their images were made of copper and wood, and were hollow and empty on the inside, and were fitted with their backs against the walls. There they had left certain holes in the wall, and by entering into the images through their secret or hidden passages, they spoke through their mouths whatever they wished, and thus the listeners were continually deceived.

<margin>B. Deceit of the heathens.</margin>
Coming into the Temple of Serapis <note>original: "Seraphidis"; the Serapeum was the Great Temple of Alexandria.</note>, he saw an image or idol whose size terrified those who looked upon it.

<margin>C. The image Sumie or Alpen.</margin>
It was also very deceitfully said that if anyone went near it, the earth would immediately tremble and a plague would spread everywhere.

<margin>D. Serapis is broken.</margin>
But since he considered these words to be nothing other than old wives' tales <note>original: "ouder wyvē clay"; likely a corruption of "clapperye," meaning idle chatter or gossip.</note>, he did not pay much heed to the size of the image, seeing as there was no life in it. He commanded one who had an axe to strike Serapis mightily. And when he did so, they all cried out together, fearing because of the old fable. But Serapis, being made of wood, felt no pain from it, nor did he give any voice, just like an image that is dead.

<margin>The guardians of the Temple flee. Olympius and the Philosopher.</margin>
And when they had chopped off his head, a number of dormice <note>original: "slaepmuysen"; these were likely just common mice nesting in the hollow statue.</note> ran out, for the God of the Egyptians was a mouse-nest. Then they hacked him into pieces and burned him; but the head they carried throughout the entire city.

<margin>E</margin>

form of a cross.

When the Christians and also the Heathens saw these Characters, each interpreted it according to their own Religion. The Christians said it was a sign of the salutary death of Christ. And the Heathens said that Christ and Serapis had fellowship through these signs. For this reason, the Christians exalted these all the more.

For if the mystery of the coming of the Lord has been hidden from eternity, and was unknown to the Prince of Darkness, the devil, then it was much more so to his servants, the Priests of the Egyptians.

# The Tripartite Ecclesiastical History

A. Avoid it, for the ditch of envy stands open; and if someone leaps over it, then anger is ready. Likewise, the Adversary <note>The devil or tempter.</note> lays many other traps for us, so that he might catch those who do not watch themselves well. He also uses the impulses of the body that easily serve him, so that they might kill the soul. But only the mind of the one who takes care, being occupied with divine things, overcomes and breaks the power of these plots.

As Theodosius was a man, he also had human impulses, and in a matter where anger might have been reasonable, he allowed his majesty and unjust impulses to burst forth and show themselves. It is necessary to tell this for the benefit of those who read it, and because of the notable good deeds that followed.

<margin>The Emperor’s judges were killed at Thessalonica.</margin>

B. Thessalonica is a great city with a very large population. When a riot arose there, some of the judges were stoned and killed. Because of this, Theodosius became enraged and was no longer master of his wrath. Instead, he commanded that swords should be drawn against everyone, and that both the guilty and the innocent should be put to death.

C. It is said that 7,000 people were killed without any judgment or sentence, and just as fruits are cut down in the harvest, so they were all slaughtered. When Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose, the Bishop of Milan.</note> heard of this mournful murder, and the Emperor had come to Milan and wished to enter the Temple <note>The Cathedral or church.</note> according to his custom, Ambrose went to meet him at the door of the Temple and forbade him entrance with these words, saying: "O Emperor, do you not know how great the murder is that you have committed, even after your anger has had so much time to rest? Do you not yet consider the great audacity of your deed? But perhaps the greatness and power of the Empire prevents the consideration of your sins. It is nonetheless fitting that reason should overcome power, for one must know what nature one is—that man is mortal and perishable. And that we are of the dust of our ancestors, and that we shall become dust again."

<margin>Genesis 3</margin>

"Therefore, do not rely on the purple dye of your robes, which cannot hide the infirmities of the body. O Emperor, you are a ruler and prince over people who are like you, and who are your fellow servants. For

<column-break/>

there is one LORD over all men, one King and Creator. With what eyes will you look upon the LORD’S Temple? With what feet will you tread upon that holy pavement?

Depart, and do not increase the first sin by adding others to it. Receive and accept the bond <note>The sentence of excommunication or penance.</note> with which the Lord now binds you, for it is a great medicine for your health."

<margin>Theodosius is cast out under the ban.</margin>

V. With these words, the Emperor was obedient, for he had been raised in divine teaching and knew well what the office of a Priest was, and also that of an Emperor; and so, sighing and sobbing, he returned to his court.

And when eight full months had passed, the feast of the birth of our Savior <note>Christmas.</note> drew near. The Emperor, remaining always in the Court, wept continually. When Ruffinus, a master of the court <note>The Master of Offices, a high-ranking official.</note> who was very familiar and close with the Emperor, came to him and saw the Emperor lamenting, sobbing, and weeping, he went to him and inquired after the cause of his sobbing. But the Emperor, sighing very heavily and sobbing even more, said:

Saying this, he sighed at every word. Ruffinus said: "If it pleases you, I shall run and plead with the Bishop with words, that he might unbind the bond he has tied." -> ¶ On the virtues of the wife of Theodosius. <-

### Chapter 31.

<margin>
Augusta Flacilla, also called Placilla, was a lover of the poor.

The Emperor also possessed another profitable and good circumstance through which he triumphed in good works. For his wife frequently exhorted him regarding the Divine commandments, though she first taught herself to follow them perfectly. She was not puffed up by the high status of the empire, but was much more set aflame with Divine love. For the greatness of the benefit she received awakened in her a greater love for the Benefactor. As soon as she came to the Imperial lineage, she took great care for the crippled and the weak, not employing servants or any other ministers for this purpose, but doing it herself; she even went to their dwellings, giving to each person whatever they had need of.

<margin>
The churches have hospitals <note>Original: *gasthupsen*, referring to guesthouses or infirmaries run by the early church.</note>.

She also diligently went through the hospitals of the churches and served the sick with her own hands: cleaning their pots, tasting the broth, providing spoons, breaking bread, bringing food, rinsing out the drinking cups, and performing every other service that servants and maids are accustomed to do. And she said to those who sought to forbid her from doing this: "To hoard gold is the work of the Emperor, but I do this myself on behalf of the Empire, which gives me all my goods."

To her husband she often said: "O husband, you must

Instead, you shall always govern and rule the Empire you have received well, and you shall satisfy the author and master of these things." With such reasoning, she always gave a very useful guidance to her husband, who was otherwise also inclined toward the good by his own nature.

### ¶ How Theodosius was against the Pagans. <note>original: "Heydenen"</note>

### Chapter 33.

<margin>The service of idols was forbidden by Theodosius and Constantine.</margin>
Thus did the most faithful Emperor show great diligence against the error of the Pagans, and he wrote a law or decree commanding that the temples of the idols be cast down. The great Constantine, worthy of all praise and honor—who was the first to adorn the Imperial office with <margin>Julian.</margin> piety—did indeed command that the devils should not be honored, but he did not destroy their temples, only commanding that people should not enter them. His sons followed in their father's footsteps. But Julian gave a place to <margin>Jovinian.</margin> godlessness once more and rekindled the fire of the ancient deception. But Jovinian, when he came to the Empire, <margin>Valentinian.</margin> again forbade the making of sacrifices to the idols. The elder Valentinian also used these laws and <margin>Valens.</margin> governed Europe in this way. But Valens allowed all others to act as they wished regarding their faith; he only fought against those who stood for the Apostolic teaching. For during the entire time of his reign, fire was lit upon the altars and sacrifices were offered to the idols. Indeed, they held public feasts throughout the city. And holding the Orgies of Dionysus <note>festivals of Bacchus/Dionysus involving wine and ritual madness</note>, they ran with shields, and the dogs cast out the intestines <note>likely referring to ritual disembowelment during pagan rites</note>, raging and ranting, and they did all things which bore witness to the wickedness of their own Master. The Emperor Theodosius, finding all these things, uprooted them all by the root and brought them to oblivion.

¶ The temples of his own city having been broken down, he relied not on human but on Divine power. This account is so worthy of eternal memory that I cannot refrain from telling it. When John, a Bishop of the city of Apamea <note>Apamea was a major city in Roman Syria, known for its grand architecture and religious significance.</note>, had died, the holy man Marcellus was ordained; he was a man burning with the spirit, just as the Apostle says <note>A reference to Romans 12:11: "Fervent in spirit; serving the Lord."</note>. Meanwhile, the Governor of the eastern lands came to Apamea, bringing two captains with their subordinates. When this occurred, the Governor grew fearful of the soldiers.

<margin>Jupiter’s temple, or the temple of Jove at Apamea.</margin>
¶ There was a Temple of Jupiter <note>original: "Jovis"</note> there, very beautifully decorated and widely renowned, which the Governor of the eastern lands sought to break down and destroy. But when he saw how strong the building and structure were, he judged it impossible for a human to break this Temple, or even to separate the joints and the layers of stones from one another.

¶ For they were very large stones, well joined together, and moreover fused with iron and lead. But when Marcellus saw the faint-heartedness of the Governor, he sent him away to other cities; in the meantime, he prayed to God that He would grant success in the dismantling of this Church <note>Though a pagan temple, the author here uses "Kercken" (church/temple) to refer to the religious site.</note>.

¶ During this time, a man came to him of his own accord early in the morning at daybreak; he was neither a carpenter, nor a stone-cutter, nor any other master craftsman, but simply one accustomed to carrying wood and stones on his shoulders.

¶ This man, having arrived, promised that the church could easily be broken down if he were given the wages of two laborers.

¶ And when the Bishop had promised him this, he immediately began to work. On the four sides of the Temple, there were four high Portals, and upon them were large columns or pillars as high as the Church itself; the pillars were one cubit thick <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, about 18 inches.</note>, and the stone was naturally so hard that it could not easily be broken with any iron tool.

¶ Having undermined three of these Portals, the man placed thick timbers under the foundations and set the timbers on fire.

<margin>A black Devil appeared.</margin>
¶ Yet the fire, according to the laws of nature, could not make that wood burn, for there appeared a black devil, who hindered the fire from working as best he could.

<margin>Bishop Marcellus sleeps at noon.</margin>
¶ And when they had tried this many times and could not accomplish their purpose, they made it known to the Bishop while he lay and slept at midday. He quickly ran to the church and commanded that water be brought in a small vessel, which he placed under the Altar.

<column-break/>

And having fallen on his face to the earth, he prayed to the Merciful God that He would not permit the Devil his tyranny, but that He would reveal the demon's weakness and show the sign of His own power, so that the unbelievers would have no cause to rejoice.

¶ When he had said this and made the sign of the cross in the water, he commanded one of his Deacons, armed with faith and zeal, named Equitius, to take the water and run quickly to sprinkle it with faith upon the wood where the fire lay.

<margin>Water makes the fire ignite.</margin>
¶ When this was done, the Devil fled because he could not endure the power of the water. Through this, the fire began to regain its nature within the water as if it had been oil, and the wood was seized by the fire and very quickly consumed. The Pillars, being robbed of their supports, fell down and pulled twelve others along with them; then the entire side of the Temple that hung upon them was overthrown by the force of the fall.

¶ The noise and the sound made the people run there from through the whole city, and when they openly understood the flight of the enemy—the Devil—they gave praise and honor to God the Lord. Thus the Bishop also broke down other temples. Marcellus wrote to the victors and the Martyrs, and also received letters in return from them. At last, he too was crowned through Martyrdom <note>Marcellus was eventually killed by locals who were enraged by his destruction of their traditional shrines.</note>.

### For what reasons those who were appointed over the penitents were removed again.

### The 35th Chapter.

¶ At this time, it was decided that those Priests who were appointed over the penitents <note>Those performing public penance for serious sins.</note> should be removed, and for the following reason.

<margin>After the schism of the Novatians, the priests were appointed for those doing penance.</margin>
¶ From the time that the Novatians <note>The Novatians were a rigorist sect who refused to readmit Christians who had "lapsed" or denied their faith during Roman persecutions.</note> were separated from the churches, they would not have communion with those who had sinned and denied their faith under the persecution of Emperor Decius. From that time on, the Priests, according to Ecclesiastical rule and order, appointed their Priesthood over the penitents.

<margin>A</margin>
# Sozomen <note>Salminius Hermias Sozomenus (c. 400–450 AD) was a Palestinian-born historian who wrote a comprehensive history of the Christian Church.</note>

<margin>Confession of sins.</margin>
Since not sinning at all is entirely Divine, and goes wholly beyond human nature and ability; and since God promises forgiveness of sins to those who repent for them—whereas those who do not acknowledge their sin fall into even heavier 
<margin>B</margin>
sins—therefore, the ancient Bishops saw fit that sins should be discovered through public disclosure, with the testimony of the people in the church, as if on a stage built to be seen by everyone. To this end, they ordained a Priest of good conduct, who was a secret and wise man, to whom those who had sinned would come 
<margin>Priest of Penance</margin>
and confess their sins. This man would then impose a penalty of penance upon each individual, according to 
<margin>C</margin>
the nature of the fault. This practice is still maintained today in the churches of the West, and especially in Rome, where there is a certain place for those performing penance. For they stand there themselves as the guilty ones, mourning and weeping.
<margin>The manner of public penance among the ancients.</margin>
And when the Holy Services are finished, they do not receive communion, but with cries and tears they cast themselves upon the earth. The Bishop, running toward them, falls with them there upon the 
<margin>D</margin>
ground, with spiritual sighing and tears. After this, the Bishop rises first and lifts up those who are lying upon the ground. When he has then offered a prayer suitable for conversion, he leaves the people. But these penitents punish themselves willingly with fasting, with the avoidance of baths, with the withholding of food, or through other things commanded of them, and thus they wait for the time ordained by the Bishop. And when the proper and 
<margin>E</margin>
appointed time has arrived, and they have, as it were, paid for their guilt and been cleansed of their sins through this chastisement, they are admitted to communion with the people. The Bishops in Rome have maintained this from of old until our own time.

But in Constantinople, there was a Priest over the penitents until the time when a certain very noble woman—after she had confessed her sins and had been 
<margin>F</margin>
commanded by the Priest 
<margin>Confession forbidden in Constantinople under Nectarius, who was the predecessor of John Chrysostom.</margin>
to fast and to fall at the feet of God with good works—confessed that, while she was frequently doing this, she had for a long time been involved with a Deacon in the church and had slept with him. When the people heard this, they were embittered against the Priests, as if this evil and harm to the church had been committed by them.

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin>
Then Nectarius the Bishop removed and dismissed the shameful Deacon. Upon the advice of some, he commanded that each person should examine and search himself according to his own conscience, no longer allowing the Priests to preside over the penitents. And through this, that ancient custom was taken away, even though (in my opinion) many fewer sins were committed back then because of the shame of confession and the scrutiny of the examiners.

# Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380–439 AD) was a lawyer and historian in Constantinople. His work provides a detailed account of the late Roman Empire's religious shifts.</note>

## On the division of the heretics among one another.

### The 36th Chapter.

<margin>H</margin>
<margin>Schisms of the heresies.</margin>
I thought it worthy to relate what occurred among the others—namely, the Arians, Novatians, Macedonians, and Eunomians. For the Church being divided, each gathered by themselves. How and why they were separated from one another, we shall relate in the continuation of our discourse. But this 
<margin>I</margin>
must be known: that during his reign, Emperor Theodosius persecuted no one except Eunomius <note>Eunomius of Cyzicus was a leader of an extreme Arian sect that argued the Son was unlike the Father.</note>, who held house gatherings in Constantinople and read books there that had been 
<margin>K</margin>
made by him. Therefore, the Emperor also banished him, but he did not cause any trouble to anyone else, nor did he force anyone to hold communion with him. Instead, he allowed each to gather in their own place and commanded them to maintain Religion as Christianly as possible. He permitted some to build houses of prayer outside the city, 
<margin>Novatians.</margin>
and to the Novatians <note>A rigorist sect that believed those who denied their faith under persecution should not be readmitted to the Church.</note>, who were at one with his own faith, he permitted them to have churches within the city. There 
<margin>L</margin>
is now something more to be said. Agelius was Bishop for forty years, from the time of Constantine until the sixth year of Theodosius. When he was about to die, he ordained Sisinus as Bishop, who was a very 
<margin>Sisinus, a fellow disciple of the Emperor Julian.</margin>
eloquent man and had been taught by Maximus the Philosopher along with the Emperor Julian. But when the Novatians spoke against the appointment and complained that he had not rather 
<margin>M</margin>
ordained Martianus—through 
<margin>Martianus.</margin>
whom the Novatians had lived without any persecution under Valens—Agelius, wishing to pacify the grief of the people, ordained Martianus. When he was feeling a bit better, he went into the church and said: "After me, you shall have Martianus, and after Martianus, you shall have Sisinus."

¶ So he died after a few days. During the Bishopric of Marcian, their church also became divided among themselves for these reasons.

### Concerning Sabbatius the master of heretics.

#### The 37th Chapter.

<margin>Sabbatius</margin>
There was a man named Sabbatius who had converted from Judaism to Christianity and was ordained a Priest by Marcian. Nevertheless, he continued to cling to Jewish sects and, through this terrible deed, still aspired to the Bishopric. When he had taken to himself two Priests who were aware of his desires, he began to advocate for and justify the keeping of the Easter feast <note>The "Easter feast" (Dutch: *Paeschfeest*) here refers to the Quartodeciman controversy—a debate over whether to celebrate Easter on the 14th of Nisan, the same day as Jewish Passover, or on the following Sunday.</note> during the reign of Emperor Valens in a village in Phrygia named Pazo.

And at first, he said that he spoke because of the impurity of the churches, claiming that not every man was worthy to use the Sacraments of the church. But in the course of time, he clearly revealed his intentions when he began to hold his own separate assemblies. <margin>Marcian.</margin> Through this, Marcian acknowledged his own error and the fault of his ordination, because he had ordained proud men as Priests. He said with sighing and weeping that it would have been better to have struck his hands into thorns than to have ordained Sabbatius as a Priest. For this reason, he called together a Council of the Novatian Bishops in Sangarius, Bithynia.

<margin>The Council of the Novatians in Sangarius, Bithynia.</margin>
And when they were gathered there, they summoned him so that they might place the cause of their discord before the Synod and explain it. And Sabbatius said that the discord over the Easter feast troubled him, and that it ought to be held according to the Jewish custom, just as it had been established in Pazo.

<margin>The Novatians make a rule that everyone may keep the Easter feast as they wish.</margin>
Now, when the Bishops realized that Sabbatius did this because he sought the Bishopric out of pride, they forced him to take an oath that he would never again desire the Bishopric. And when he had sworn this, they established a rule that everyone should hold the Easter feast as they wished, so that they would not tear the Church apart over the disagreement concerning the feast. For the elders and those who had been closest to the Church, even if they disagreed on the timing of feasts, had nevertheless maintained communion with one another. And the Novatians who were in the magnificent city

<column-break/>

of Constantinople <note>The OCR reads "ko mazijn," likely a corruption of "Constantinopel."</note> never followed the Jews, but always held the feast after the Equinox—that is, after the day and night were of equal length. Now, once this rule had been made by them, Sabbatius (who was constrained by his oath, even though the Easter feast caused some discord) fasted by himself and held the feast by night on the Sabbath, and then rejoined the others in the church and partook of the mysteries <note>The "mysteries" refers to the Holy Eucharist or Communion.</note>. And though he did this for many years, it could not remain hidden. Therefore, some simple people from the Phrygians and Galatians—believing that he was justified in this—followed him and kept the Easter feast with him. But later, Sabbatius also held his own private collections or assemblies alone; and making little account of the oath he had taken, he was ordained a Bishop by his followers.

### ¶ Concerning the Easter feast and the variety of institutions and observances held by various Churches.

#### The 38th Chapter.

In my opinion, those men had no just cause to dispute over the Easter feast, nor do those who currently follow Jewish customs have any reason for it; for they have not understood in their minds that since they have changed Judaism into a Christian life, how those hidden and symbolic things of the Law of Moses have ceased—which is clearly evident from this. There is no Christian people that has received a Law requiring them to adopt Judaism. But on the contrary, the Apostle Paul himself spoke, not only forbidding circumcision, but also warning us to avoid arguments for the sake of feasts. For writing to the Galatians, he says: "Tell me, you who want to be under the Law, do you not hear the Law?" and speaking a little further on, he demonstrates that the Jewish people are like a servant, but those who go to Christ are called to freedom. He also warns that one should in no way observe days, months, or seasons. And writing to the Colossians, he cries out that these things are nothing other than a shadow of things to come, saying: "Let no one judge you in food or drink, or...

<margin>A</margin> In one part of the festival, or the new moon, or the Sabbaths—which are shadows of things to come—the same Apostle says to the Lord: For since the <margin>Hebrews 7:12</margin> priesthood is changed, it is also necessary that a change occurs in the Law. <note>The author is quoting Paul's letter to the Hebrews to argue that religious ceremonies, like the priesthood, can evolve over time.</note> And therefore, neither the Apostle nor the Gospel has laid the yoke of servitude upon those who go to preach; instead, they said that the Easter feast and other <margin>B</margin> feasts should be honored. Thus, because people love such feasts where they may rest from their labor, they have established the memory of Christ’s passion throughout their lands, each according to their own preference, and maintained it through custom. For God never commanded this, nor did the Apostles preach such a thing, nor did the Apostles or Evangelists threaten us with any punishment, <margin>C</margin> death, or curse—as the Law of Moses does to the Jews. Rather, it is noted to the shame of the Jews that they committed murder during the high feast, as is proclaimed in the Gospel, saying that the Savior suffered during the time of the sweet bread <note>original: "soeten brooden"; referring to the Feast of Unleavened Bread or Passover.</note>. The intention of the <margin>Matthew 26. Mark 14. Luke 22. John 18.</margin> Apostles was not to create feast days, but to proclaim and preach the true worship of God and to teach the people a <margin>D</margin> righteous way of life. And it seems to me that just as many other things were born into the customs of the land, <margin>The intention of the Apostles.</margin> so also the Easter feast was maintained through custom, because none of the Apostles had commanded anything regarding it. For many throughout Asia Minor have from ancient times kept the fourteenth day, regardless of the Sabbath. And even though they did so, they were not separated from those who kept it differently, <margin>Victor.</margin> until Victor, a Bishop of Rome, excommunicated those in Asia who <margin>E</margin> kept the Easter feast on the fourteenth day. <note>This refers to the "Quartodeciman" controversy, where Victor I excommunicated churches that celebrated Easter on the 14th of Nisan (the Jewish Passover) rather than the following Sunday.</note>

<margin>

Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius, Book 5.
</margin>
When this occurred, Irenaeus, a Bishop of Lyons in France, rebuked Victor with a letter, saying that it had been held that way since ancient times. He noted that Polycarp, a Bishop in the city of Smyrna—who was later martyred under the Emperor Gordian—held fellowship <margin>F</margin> with Anicetus, a Bishop in Rome, without making any distinction regarding the Easter feast, despite the fact that Polycarp was one of those who kept the Easter feast on the fourteenth day, <margin>Colossians 2:16, 17 as seen.</margin> as Eusebius testifies in the fifth book of his *Ecclesiastical Histories*.

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin> Therefore, as I have said, there were some in Asia Minor who kept the Easter feast on the fourteenth day, and some toward the East observed the Sabbath, but they did not agree on the months: for some said they ought to follow it even if it was not observed well everywhere. Others held it after the Equinox (that is, when day and night <margin>H</margin> are of equal length), not wishing to follow the Jews, and saying that the Easter feast should be held when the Sun was in the heavenly sign named Aries, that is, the Ram. But those of Antioch held it in the month of *Xanticho*, and according to the Romans, in April. And they did this not because they wanted to follow the modern Jews—whom they knew to be in error everywhere—but much more because they wanted to follow the ancients and also Josephus. For <margin>Josephus, Antiquities Book 3.</margin> so he wrote in the third book of the *Antiquities*.

<margin>I</margin> Now, while these people were thus disputing, we found that all those toward the West, as far as the Ocean sea, have kept the Easter feast after the Equinox according to ancient custom—that is, after the night and day were of equal length—and we do not find that they have ever disagreed about that time. For the Council held under Constantine did not change the Easter feast, as some say: For <margin>Constantine Augustus concerning the Easter feast.</margin> Constantine himself, writing to the <margin>K</margin> disputants, exhorted them—since they were few—to understand and follow the many. I did not wish to omit setting down a part of his writing, for he said among other things: "It is a fine ordinance which all churches of the world located toward the West, South, and North observe, and also some toward the East. Therefore, all churches consider that it goes well for them, and I myself have spoken for the sake of your wisdom. So that everything held and preserved in the <margin>L</margin> city of Rome, in Italy, Africa, and all of Egypt, Spain, France, Britain, Libya, all of Greece, Hellas, Asia, Pontus, and Cilicia, should be diligently accepted by your wisdom under one accord. Not so much regarding the number of places presented, but much more that you ought all to maintain this harmoniously together, as subtle reason demands such diligence. <margin>M</margin> And to have no fellowship with the perjury of the Jews." Thus writes Constantine. But they say that the <margin>N</margin> <margin>Quartodecimans, that is, those who keep the Easter feast on the 14th day.</margin> "Fourteenthers" <note>original: "Quarto deciani"; Christians who insisted on celebrating Easter on the 14th of Nisan.</note> were commanded such observance of Easter by the Apostle John. Others say that Peter and Paul, the Apostles, gave that Easter feast to the Romans.

### Tripartite Ecclesiastical History

<margin>Take good note.</margin>
¶ ...and other churches and lands situated to the West have been commanded: But there is found no written proof of these things; rather, that Easter was held by the provinces through custom. This comes, in my opinion, from the fact that no religion used to keep identical feasts. For although many are of one faith, they nonetheless do not agree in the ordering of how to keep Easter <note>original: "Paesschen"</note>, of which we must also say a little, for we find that fasting also proceeds differently in one place than in another.

<margin>Various ways of fasting.</margin>
Those of Rome fast three whole weeks in succession before Easter, except for Sunday and the Sabbath.

<margin>Lent.</margin>
¶ Those in Illyricum and throughout all of Greece, and no less in Alexandria, fast six whole weeks, and call the fast days *Quadragesima* <note>original: "Quadragesimam," the Latin term for a forty-day period, from which the word "Lent" is derived.</note>. Others begin to fast six weeks before Easter, but only for three weeks—that is, six days in total, omitting the other two weeks—and they also call it *Quadragesima*. I marvel at this, since they do not have the actual number of forty days, yet they still call it *Quadragesima*. They also do not have one single way of abstaining from food; for some abstain entirely from eating anything that has lived <note>meaning meat or animal products</note>. Some eat only fish from all that has lived. Others eat, besides those fish, also all kinds of poultry, saying that these things (according to Moses) have their substance from the water. Some also eat neither eggs nor any herbs. Others eat only dry bread. Some fast until noon, eating without distinction of food, and there are a countless multitude of diverse customs found.

¶ And since no ancient writings are found regarding this, I consider that the Apostles left each person free in their own opinion, so that each should do what is good and right, and not out of fear or out of necessity or compulsion.

<margin>Diversity in the Last Supper.</margin>
¶ Regarding the *Synaxis* <term>Synaxis: A Greek term meaning "assembly" or "gathering," specifically referring to the early Christian gathering for the Eucharist or Holy Communion.</term> or Lord's Supper, a great distinction is also found; for although through all churches in the world, every week on the Sabbath, the Mysteries and Sacraments are held, nonetheless such is not done in Rome nor in Alexandria, according to old custom.

<margin>Note. The Egyptians communicate toward evening after eating.</margin>
¶ The Egyptians who live somewhat closer to Alexandria, and also the inhabitants of the Thebaid, do hold their gatherings on the Sabbaths, but they do not receive the Sacraments according to the usual custom: For after they have eaten and are full of all food, they come together toward evening, and make their offering, and commu-

<column-break/>

-nicate in that manner. Conversely, in Alexandria, the Holy Scripture was read on the fourth and sixth day of the week, and the Doctors or Teachers interpret the same. And there all things happened that belonged to the *Synaxis*, that glorious use of the offering. And it seems that Origen taught much on these days, and this was an old custom in the Church at Alexandria: For since he was a wise Master, and considered how the impossibility of the Mosaic Law was very weak according to the letter, he drew the meaning of the Easter feast into a spiritual contemplation, saying that there was only one Easter feast truly kept, which the Savior kept against the opposing Powers, when He took the Cross upon Himself and won the victory against the devil.

In the same land of Alexandria, there has also been the custom that Lectors or Readers, and Psalm-singers were accepted without distinction, whether they be Catechumens <term>Catechumens: Individuals who were receiving instruction in the Christian faith but had not yet been baptized.</term> or Christians. It seems as if all Christian-believing churches maintain this ordinance.

I have also known another custom in Thessaly: if a cleric, before he became a cleric, had taken a lawful wife, and because he had known her <note>meaning he had consummated the marriage</note>, he was deposed; whereas nonetheless all the Priests in the East, without any compulsion, have their bedfellows [wives], according to their own choice in how they carry themselves: Yea, even the Bishops, for many of them have had children by their lawful wives, even during the time that they were Bishops. I have also known that this was maintained in Thessaly: that they baptized only on Easter day, for which reason also many among them died without Baptism.

In Antioch of Syria, they do not have their Altars toward the East, but more toward the West. In Greece, in Jerusalem, and in Thessaly, they hold their prayers in the evening, like the Novatians who live in Constantinople. In Caesarea of Cappadocia on the Sabbath and Sunday, when it is evening, the Bishops and Priests explain the Holy Scripture with lanterns.

In Alexandria, the Priest does not preach, and this began from the time that Arius so disturbed the church. In Rome, they fast every Sabbath. In Caesarea of Cappadocia, they exclude all those from fellowship who sin after Baptism. This is just as the Novatians and Macedonians do in the Hellespont, and also in Asia the Fourteen-dayers <term>Fourteen-dayers: Also known as Quartodecimans, these were early Christians who insisted on celebrating Easter on the 14th day of the Hebrew month of Nisan, the date of Passover, regardless of what day of the week it fell on.</term>.

# Sozomen

->¶ On the Easter Feast of the Montanists.<-

### Chapter 39

<margin>The Montanists.</margin>
But the Montanists <note>A prophetic Christian movement beginning in the 2nd century, also called the "Phrygian heresy."</note>, whom people call Phrygians, introducing a strange invention, observe Easter in their own particular way. For they rebuke those who pay attention to the cycles of the Moon, saying that one should observe the circles of the Sun alone. They say that every month consists of 30 days, and that one should begin in the Spring when the day and night are of equal length <note>The vernal equinox.</note>, which is, according to the Roman calculation, on the 8th of the Calends of April, which is the 25th of March.

At that time (they say) the two lights <note>The sun and moon.</note> were created, through which time and the year are revealed. Also, that this is revealed by the fact that the Moon runs with the Sun for 8 years, and that they both have a new month because the cycle of the Moon is fulfilled or completed in eight years, just like the beginning of the first month. Therefore, they maintain that the aforementioned day is the fourteenth day mentioned in the Scripture. And they say that this falls on the 8th of the Ides of April, which is the sixth day of the month of April. After which day they always hold the Easter feast.

<margin>The fourteenth day.</margin>
If it then happens that the day of the resurrection falls on that same day—that is, the day

<margin>Exodus 12. John 18.</margin>
of the LORD—they then hold it on the Sunday thereafter; for it is written (they say) that one shall keep it from the 14th to the 21st day.

->¶ On the Schism of the Arians.<-

### Chapter 40

3

<margin>Schism of the Arians.</margin>
There were also schisms among the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who believed that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> arising from such causes, and they conducted all their disputes with senseless arguments. For as it was believed in their church that God is a Father of the Son, furthermore, this question or issue arose among them: whether it was possible that God was also called "Father" before the Son existed. For among the Arians it is believed that the Word <note>The Son/Christ.</note> is not naturally from the Father, but took his being from things that were not.

Now then, as they failed in the first chapter, they fell into an improper battle of words simply for the sake of a bare name. For

<margin>Dorotheus.</margin>
Dorotheus, who had been called from Antioch, said that the Father could not be Father, nor be called such, when the Son did not exist. But

<margin>Marinus.</margin>
Marinus, whom they had summoned from Thrace before Dorotheus, finding a good opportunity (for he was an enemy to Dorotheus), spoke an argument to the contrary that was entirely against this question. And therefore, schisms or divisions occurred among them. And having been divided from one another for this reason, they each performed and held their offices by themselves. For some followed

<margin>Psathyriani from Psathyropolia.</margin>
Dorotheus. Others followed Marinus, saying that the Father was always Father, even when the Son was not; and these were called <term>Psathyriani<gloss>A sect of Arians nicknamed after "psathyropolia" (pastry sellers), because one of their prominent members, Theoctistus, was associated with that trade.</gloss></term>, because one named Theoctistus from Syria, of the trade of the pastry-sellers, drove this question very earnestly. The Eunomians <margin>The schism of the Eunomians</margin> also did not remain without division, for Eunomius himself was for a long time separated from Eudoxius (who had made him Bishop of Cyzicus), because he would not accept his teacher Aetius, who had been driven out. Others were separated from them through various schisms. Before that, <margin>Theophronius.</margin> a certain Theophronius from Cappadocia (who had been well-instructed by Eunomius in how to stir up disputes, and who also had some understanding of Aristotle's books called *Categories* and *On Interpretation*) wrote books to which he gave the title *De exercitio mentis*, that is, *On the Exercise of the Mind*. Now, when he had scattered these [teachings] among his followers, and they later turned away from him, he was driven out; and while he lived apart or alone, he abandoned that heresy which bore his name. But in Constantinople there was one named Eutychius; he separated from the Eunomians over a very simple question and henceforth held his assembly by himself. And some were called <margin>Eunomian-Theophronians. Eunomian-Eutychians. Note.</margin> Eunomian-Theophronians, others Eunomian-Eutychians. But these people defiled Baptism, for they did not baptize in the name of the Trinity, but only into the death of Christ.

# ->Sozomen<-

#### ->¶ Concerning the recession of the Nile, and of its return.<-

### ->Chapter 42.<-

<margin>The Nile recedes.</margin>
It is said that at that time the flood of the Egyptian Nile, as soon as the water had first increased, was drawn back. This having happened, the Egyptians became angry because they were not allowed to perform the customary sacrifices to the Nile flood. When the Judge <note>A Roman administrative official.</note> heard that a riot was starting, he made this known to the Emperor. But the Emperor judged it better to serve the Divine faith than the "pots of the Nile" <note>A disparaging reference to Egyptian idols or ritual vessels.</note>, and to place godliness above such blasphemy, saying: "God grant that the flood runs no more, rather than that the water of Holy Paradise should be defiled with sorcery and bloodshed." This being done, the flood then gave so much abundant water that it flowed and spread much higher than it was accustomed to do. When it had now flowed to its usual level and even higher, the Egyptians were exceedingly terrified, fearing that the water would destroy Alexandria and the borders of Libya. It is said that the pagans in Alexandria shouted from the race-chariots that the Nile had become old and senseless. Therefore, many of the Egyptians, leaving their ancestral religion, turned themselves to the Christian life.

### How Flavian took the Bishopric of Antioch for himself alone.

### The 44th Chapter.

<margin>Flavian, a follower of Meletius in Antioch.</margin> Flavian then followed Meletius Maximus <note>Meletius was the Bishop of Antioch whose death in 381 AD sparked a long-running succession crisis known as the Meletian Schism.</note> in Antioch, who, along with Theodotus, had suffered much conflict everywhere with his flock. Paulinus wished to take up the Bishopric of that church, but the multitude of bishops set themselves against it, saying that it was not proper that he who had not accepted the counsel of Meletius should come to sit in his place after his death. Rather, it was argued that the office belonged much more to one who was well-known and respected for having endured much trouble and great labor through many perils for the flock.

Because of this, the Romans and the Egyptians were very heated and angry against those who lived in the East. Indeed, the enmity has not yet ceased, even though Paulinus has died. For when Evagrius occupied his throne after him, they remained steadfast in that position and were hostile to Flavian, despite the fact that Evagrius had been ordained contrary to ecclesiastical ordinance. For Paulinus alone had made him Bishop, against all the rules of church ordinances. For the Church ordinance does not allow any individual to ordain for himself; rather, one must call together all the bishops or priests of the land, and it strictly forbids any ordination from taking place without three bishops.

Despite all this, they accepted the communion of Evagrius and turned the Emperor's ears against Flavian. Being very often moved by this, the Emperor called him to Constantinople and commanded him to travel to Rome. But when Flavian excused himself because it was winter, he traveled home <note>original: "naae suyp," likely a typo for "naar huys" (home).</note> after first promising that he would travel to Rome at the first opportunity. And as the Roman bishops—not only the wonderful Damasius, but also after him Siricius and Anastasius—urged the Emperor diligently, telling him how he could well fight the tyrants who opposed him, but that the Christian laws were being contradicted because he left them unpunished. Therefore, he summoned him again and commanded that he should travel to Rome.

->Concerning the Tyrant Eugenius, and how he was overcome.<-

### The 45th Chapter.

<margin>Eugenius, from schoolmaster to Tyrant.</margin> **T**he public benefit and the land for this reason was entirely disturbed in the Western lands. A Grammarian <note>A teacher of Latin literature and grammar.</note> named Eugenius, who was a Doctor or teacher of the Latin language, left his school and came into the Emperor’s Court, and became the Emperor’s Chancellor, and was honored by many for the sake of his eloquence. At that time (as is said), he took as an assistant with good deliberation Arbogast, who was of Frankish descent, and who was also a commander among the soldiers—a cruel man and very prone to homicide.

As soon as Eugenius learned of this, he became Emperor in the Western lands and did everything just as a Tyrant does. But when Emperor Theodosius heard of this, he was again burdened with care and prepared for a second battle after [the defeat of] Maximus. And when he had gathered the force of war and had made his son <margin>Honorius.</margin> Honorius Emperor, and while he and Abundantius were high commanders, on the 10th day of January, he set out again in all haste toward the Western lands.

## Theodoretus <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458 AD), a bishop and influential theologian of the Church.</note>

<margin>The dream of Theodosius.</margin>
When he found a house of prayer standing on a mountain, he prayed there to the Lord through the night. Around the time of the cockcrow, being overcome by a deep and heavy sleep, he saw in a dream as if he were lying in a field, and two men dressed in white clothes stood beside him, sitting upon very white horses. They commanded him to trust God and to have good courage, and that at dawn he should prepare his soldiers for victory and triumph, saying they were sent to his aid. These men also said that one was John the Evangelist and the other was Philip the Apostle. When he had seen this vision, he did not cease from prayer but shed many tears. This vision was also shown to a soldier, who reported it to the Emperor through various channels. To this, the Emperor replied: "This did not appear to him for my sake, but so that no one would think I invented what I saw; therefore it was shown to him as well, for the Lord revealed it to me first."

# Socrates.

<margin>The first attack.</margin>
Thus the Emperor and Eugenius engaged each other at the river called the Frigidus <note>The "Cold River," located in modern-day Slovenia.</note>. On the side where the Romans fought against the Romans, the battle was very even. But on the side where the Barbarians were who came to the Emperor's aid, the army of Eugenius seemed to be stronger. When the Emperor saw the Barbarians who helped him being defeated, he was greatly afraid; he threw himself upon the earth and prayed to God for help, and his prayer was not in vain.
<margin>Bacurius, a cavalry commander.</margin>
For one of his cavalry commanders named Bacurius <note>A prince of Caucasian Iberia who served as a Roman general.</note> was suddenly so strengthened that he moved with the principal captains to where the Barbarians were most distressed. When this was done, he very quickly broke the battle lines and put the tyrant to flight. At that same time, another great miracle occurred: a strong wind arose, and the missiles shot from the Eugenian side toward the Emperor's army were blown back, while the Emperor's weapons hit their marks perfectly—so powerful was the Emperor's prayer.
<margin>Eugenius the Tyrant falls at the Emperor’s feet.</margin>
When the war and battle ended in this way, the Tyrant fell at the Emperor’s feet and begged for safety or mercy. He was then beheaded by the soldiers at the Emperor’s feet.
<margin>Arbogastes by his own hand.</margin>
This occurred on the 7th of September, when Arcadius was consul for the third time and Honorius for the second. Arbogastes <note>The Frankish general who was the true power behind the usurper Eugenius.</note>, who was the author and master of all this evil, fled for two days after the battle; but when he realized he would not be able to survive, he killed himself with his own sword.

### ¶ Of Theotimus, a Bishop in Tomitana.

#### The 47th Chapter.

<margin>
Theotimus, a bishop.
</margin>
At the same time, **Theotimus** was Bishop of the church in **Scythia** <note>An ancient region covering parts of modern-day Romania and Bulgaria along the Black Sea.</note> and **Tomitana** <note>Tomis, the capital of Scythia Minor.</note>. The Barbarians loved his power so much—those who lived across the Ister or Danube—that they called him the "God of the Romans." This man was well-versed in Philosophy, and it was often found that he possessed divine qualities. Once, while he was traveling through the countryside, the Barbarians came upon him. When they were near him, they were so struck down that they appeared to have died instantly. He dismounted his horse and prayed, but the Barbarians saw neither him, his followers, nor even the horses

Scythia.

from which they had dismounted, and so they passed them by. And as he often passed by the Scythians, who are cruel by nature, he sought to make them gentle and friendly with food and gifts. Thus, one of the Barbarians thought he was entirely made of riches and set out to lay a trap to capture him. But as he intended to do this and reached out his hand to ensnare him, his hand was immediately bound in the air, and that Barbarian was held captive by invisible bonds. And when others pleaded for him, **Theotimus** prayed to God that he might be freed from the bonds.

### ¶ Of Epiphanius, Bishop to Cyprus.

#### The 48th Chapter.

<column-break/>

¶ In this time, **Epiphanius** was bishop in **Cyprus**, at whose grave demons are driven out even to this day. As he distributed his goods to the needy with great generosity, using what was given to him by others, it happened that the steward of the church murmured against him when money was lacking. When this occurred, it happened that one stood in the steward's house who gave him a bag with much money and then vanished, so that no one knew who had given it or who had sent it; this was held by all to be a divine act. I wish also to relate another miracle or wonder. Certain poor men sought to deceive **Epiphanius** so that he might give them something. As he traveled across the field, one poor man lay down on the ground on his back as if he were dead, and the other stood over him as if he were weeping for the deceased, claiming he had nothing with which to bury him. When **Epiphanius** came upon them, the man pleaded with him to share something to help bury the dead. Then **Epiphanius** shared with him as much as was needed for the burial of the dead and comforted the mourner, saying: "Son, cease your weeping. For he cannot be awakened by crying, for what has happened to him cannot be avoided." Now when **Epiphanius** had passed by, the man began to nudge his companion to stand up; and when he had done this once or twice, saying, "Stand up, so that we may eat from your labor today," and the other felt nothing at all, he realized that he was truly dead. So he ran weeping to **Epiphanius**, begging him to wake his companion. **Epiphanius** comforted him and said he should not take poorly what had happened; but he did not bring the dead man back to life. This happened, in my opinion, so that God's servants should not be mocked.
