### The Second Part.
### The 49th Chapter.

<margin>
The bodies of the Prophets Habakkuk and Micah found.
</margin>

Such things have not only made religion famous and renowned, but as I have understood, the bodies of the Prophets Habakkuk and Micah became known through divine revelation when Zebennus <note>original: "Hebenus"; historically identified as Zebennus, the Bishop of Eleutheropolis in the late 4th century.</note> governed the church at Eleutheropolis. This occurred in the city of Cela—previously called Ceila—where Habakkuk was found, and in Berathslatia, which is not far from the city, about 10 stadia away <note>A stadium was an ancient Greek unit of distance, approximately 185 meters or 600 feet.</note>.

At this place, the burial site of Micah was found. The inhabitants, not knowing what to call it, named it: *The faithful memory* <note>original Latin: "O fidelem memoriam"</note>, which is to say: O blessed remembrance. And in their ancestral tongue, *Mephsameemana*.

### ¶ Of the End of Emperor Theodosius.
### The 50th Chapter.

->The end of the ninth book of the Ecclesiastical Histories, translated by Epiphanius Scholasticum.<-

<column-break/>

<margin>
Theodosius Augustus becomes ill.
</margin>

Now when Theodosius, being worn out by great labor in the wars, became ill, he hoped that he would not die of the sickness. Thus, he carefully considered the common profit and reflected on what usually happens to people when an Emperor dies. He had his son Honorius fetched very quickly from Constantinople and wished to entrust him with the lands to the West. And when his son had come to Milan <note>original: "Melanen"</note>, the Emperor was somewhat relieved of his illness and held the horse races <note>original: "Kidderspel"; likely referring to the chariot races or circus games traditionally held to celebrate a military triumph.</note> as a celebration of his victory. Before noon, he behaved as if he were healthy and watched the games. After noon, however (on account of his severe illness), he could not endure the games but commanded his son to watch them. But when night came, he died, while Olybrius and Probinus were the chief Councilors <note>The Consuls of the year 395 AD.</note>, on the 17th day of January, in the first year of the 290th Olympiad. Emperor Theodosius lived 60 years and had been Emperor for 16 years.

...raised / as if she wanted to tear him apart, then he made a sign of the Cross in the air before his face, and thus spat into the dragon’s mouth <note>original: "bachuys," an archaic Dutch term for a beast's mouth or maw</note>; and the beast, as soon as she had received that spittle in her mouth, died. This beast was dragged into a nearby field by eight pairs of oxen and burned there, so that her stench would not poison the air. The burial of this Donatus is very grand, in a house of prayer named after him. There is also a magnificent water fountain there, which it is said he obtained through his prayers. For while it was a parched and dry place, it happened that those traveling with him, being weary from the journey, pleaded with him for water; and through his prayer, the rain came forth, and so that water has remained until this day.

### ¶ Of Theotimus, a Bishop in Tomis.

## The xlvij. Chapter.

<margin>Theotimus a bishop.</margin>
At the same time, Theotimus was Bishop of the churches in Scythia. And Tomis <note>original: "Tomitana," the ancient capital of Scythia Minor on the Black Sea</note> was of such power that the Barbarians living across the Ister <note>The ancient name for the lower Danube River</note> or Danube called him the God of the Romans. This man was well-versed in Philosophy, and divine things were often found in him. Once, while he was traveling through the fields, he was encountered by Barbarians. And when they were near him, they were so struck down that they immediately appeared to have died: so he dismounted his horse and prayed, but the Barbarians saw neither him, nor his followers, nor even the horses from which they had dismounted, and so they passed by. And when he frequently passed by the Scythians <margin>Scythians.</margin>—who are cruel by nature—he sought to make them gentle and friendly with food and gifts. Thus, one of the Barbarians thought he was entirely rich and set about laying snares to capture him. And as he intended to do this and reached out his hand to entangle him, his hand was immediately bound in the air, and that Barbarian was caught in invisible bonds. And when others pleaded for him, Theotimus prayed to God that he might be freed from the bonds.

### ¶ Of Epiphanius, Bishop in Cyprus.

## The xlviij. Chapter.

<column-break/>

<margin>Epiphanius bishop in Cyprus.</margin>
In this time, Epiphanius was bishop in Cyprus, at whose grave demons are driven out even unto this day. As he distributed his goods to the needy with generosity—even that which was given to him by others—it happened that the Steward of the church murmured because money was lacking. When this occurred, it happened that one stood in the house of the Steward who gave him a bag with much money, and then vanished again, so that no one knew who had given it or who had sent it to him; this was held by all to be a divine act. I also wish to relate another miracle or wonder-work. Some poor men sought to deceive Epiphanius so that he would give them something. And as he traveled across the fields, one of the poor men laid himself down on the ground on his back as if he were dead, and the other stood as if he were mourning the deceased, claiming he had nothing with which to bury him. When Epiphanius came upon them, he was entreated to share something to bury the dead. Then Epiphanius shared as much as was necessary for the burial of the dead and comforted the mourner, saying: "Son, cease your tears. For he shall not be restored by ships <note>original: "schepen," likely a reference to worldly commerce or wealth</note>, for what has happened to him cannot be avoided." When Epiphanius had passed by, the man began to nudge his companion to stand up; and when he had done this once or twice, saying: "Stand up, so that we may eat today from your labor," and the other felt nothing at all, he realized that he was in truth dead. So he ran weeping to Epiphanius, begging him to revive his companion. Epiphanius comforted him and said that he should not take ill what had happened: But he did not bring the dead man back to life. This happened, in my opinion, so that God's servants should not be mocked.

<margin>Here the Dutch copy of Chapter 48 begins.</margin>
At that time, Eas and Zeno were philosophers in Gaza, Palestine. It is said of Eas that when he had married a beautiful woman, he knew her no more than three times, and that three children were born to him; thereafter, he devoted himself to a monk’s life. Zeno the Bishop, even when he was a hundred years old, never rested nor was idle in the customary holy ministries.

### The 49th Chapter.

<margin>Here both manuscripts agree again in the chapters.</margin>
<margin>The bodies of the Prophets Habakkuk and Micah found.</margin>
Such things have not only made religion famous and renowned, but as I have understood, the bodies of the Prophets Habakkuk and Micah were made known through Divine revelation, when Hevenus ruled the church at Eleutheropolis <note>An ancient city in Roman Palestine, also known as Beth Gubrin.</note> in the City of Cela—previously named Keilah—where Habakkuk was found; and at Berathfatia, which is not far from the city, about 10 stadia <note>A stadium was roughly 185 meters; 10 stadia is approximately 1.1 miles.</note>.

By this place, the burial of Micah was found, which the inhabitants—not knowing what they should call it—named: *O fidelem memoriam*, that is to say: O faithful memory <note>original: "O fidelem memoriam" / "O salige gedachtenisse."</note>. And in their ancestral tongue, *Mephsameemana*.

### Of the end of Emperor Theodosius.

### The 50th Chapter.

<column-break/>

<margin>Theodosius Augustus becomes ill.</margin>
Now when Theodosius was exhausted from great labor in the war, he became ill, yet he hoped that he would not die from the sickness. Thus, he was very concerned for the common profit, and reflected upon what usually happens to men when the Emperor dies. Therefore, he very quickly had his son Honorius brought from Constantinople, wishing to entrust him with the regency of the Western lands. And when his son arrived at Milan, the Emperor was somewhat relieved of his illness, and he held the knightly games <note>The "Kidderspel" refers to the circensian games or chariot races held to celebrate a victory.</note> as a triumph for the victory. Before noon, he conducted himself as if he were healthy and watched the games. After noon, he could not watch the spectacle (due to severe illness), but commanded his son to watch it. But when night came, he died, when Olympius and Probinus were the supreme Councilors <note>The Consuls for the year 395 AD.</note>, on the 17th day of January, in the first year of the 290th Olympiad. The Emperor Theodosius lived 60 years and had been Emperor for 16 years.
<margin>Theodosius dies.</margin>

# Theodoretus

¶ How Honorius abolished the gladiatorial games.

## Chapter 2

<margin>C</margin> Now when Honorius assumed the empire in the Western lands, he abolished the combats where one fights against another, called <term>Monomachias<note>Original: "Monomachias," from the Greek for "single combat," referring here to gladiatorial games.</note></term>, which had previously been customary in Rome, for the following reason. 
<margin>D Telemachus a monk.</margin> There was a monk named Telemachus who had come from the Eastern lands for this purpose. And when the shameful display began, he also entered the <term>arena<note>Original: "Bailie," the enclosure or lists where combat took place.</note></term> and attempted to separate those who were fighting against each other with swords. But when the spectators, who thirsted for bloodshed, grew enraged against the <term>monk<note>Original: "papmaker," a term for a priest or religious figure, often used dismissively in this period.</note></term>, they stoned him to death. 
<margin>E Monomachia or combat was abolished by Honorius Augustus.</margin> When the wonderful Emperor learned of this, he counted him among the number of the martyrs and completely abolished that shameful spectacle.

<margin>F Nectarius Bishop of Constantinople dies.</margin> But a short time later, Nectarius the Bishop of Constantinople also died, when Caesarius and Atticus were <term>Consuls<note>Original: "opper-Raetsheeren," referring to the Roman officials who served as the year's namesake; the text uses a Dutch equivalent for high councilors.</note></term>, on the 27th day of the month of September. Thus Emperor Arcadius, with the common consent of the teachers and the clergy, called him in a very short time. And for the sake of the dignity of the ordination, as many bishops were present by Imperial ordinance and command, 
<margin>H Theophilus of Alexandria against Chrysostom.</margin> Theophilus of Alexandria also came, who intended to make some <term>objection<note>Original: "rug-sprake," meaning a legal challenge or opposition meant to stall an appointment.</note></term> against John, and thus to place his priest Isidorus there; for he loved him because he had once suffered great danger on his account. When the Emperor Theodosius fought against the tyrant Maximus, Theophilus sent gifts to the Emperor through Isidorus and gave him two kinds of letters, commanding him that he should give one letter 
<margin>I The cunning of Theophilus.</margin> to the one who did not win, but the other he should give to the victor along with the gift. For one of the <term>Readers<note>Original: "Lesers," referring to the Lector, a specific minor order in the early church.</note></term> who lived with him took the letters and showed them to the Emperor. Therefore, Isidorus being terrified, fled to Alexandria, wishing thus to hide what had been commanded of him. 
<margin>K</margin> For this reason, Theophilus loved Isidorus. But the judges of the Emperor’s court proposed John. And as many accused Theophilus,

Then the <term>Chamberlain<note>Original: "Hofmeester," the Grand Chamberlain Eutropius, a powerful advisor to Emperor Arcadius.</note></term>, named Eutropius, took the written accusations and showed them to Theophilus, saying: "Either ordain John as a Bishop, or these charges shall be brought to light."

Theophilus, being struck by this, ordained John as a Bishop. He assumed the bishopric on the 16th day of the month of February, when Honorius the Emperor was Consul and Eutychianus was Governor. That John was an outstanding man is sufficiently proven by the books he left behind. Fol. 450.
# Tripartite Ecclesiastical History.

<margin>John Chrysostom would have become an Advocate.</margin>
❧ A student of Libanius the <term>Sophist<note>A teacher of rhetoric and philosophy, highly prestigious in the Greek world.</note></term> and a hearer of the Philosopher Andragathius. And as he prepared himself to become an <term>Advocate<note>A lawyer or legal representative.</note></term>, and considered the toil and the grief of disputes and the unjust undertakings of that life, he chose instead to prefer rest. And he did this by following Evagrius, for he too, when he was being raised for such studies, preferred to have that rest.

<margin>Takes up the Christian life.</margin>
❧ John changed his life and his purpose, and listened to the Holy Scripture, and frequently came into the Temple. Doing this, he also exhorted his fellow-disciples Theodore and Marinus—who had also heard Libanius the Sophist—that they should leave that proud and pompous life of the world and should take up a simple life. From this, Theodore later became Bishop in the church of Mopsuestia, and Maximus at Seleucia in Isauria. And then these

<margin>John becomes a reader in the church at Antioch.</margin>
❧ became disciples and pupils of Diodorus and Carterius in the Holy Scripture, who at that time were the leaders of the monasteries. But Diodorus later became Bishop in Tarsus and wrote many books; by insisting upon the <term>plain letter of the Scripture<note>This refers to the "Antiochene school" of interpretation, which favored historical and literal meaning over the allegorical methods favored in Alexandria.</note></term>, he understood the meaning of it all the less. Furthermore, Bishop Flavian <note>The text reads "Sano," likely a corruption or variant for Flavianus of Antioch.</note>, when he returned from Jerusalem, appointed John—who lived with Basil and was then made a Deacon by Meletius, and later became Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia—to be a <term>Reader<note>An ecclesiastical rank responsible for reading the scriptures during the liturgy.</note></term> in the church at Antioch. And while he was still in that office, he wrote a book against the Jews.

<margin>Becomes a Deacon.</margin>
Not long after that, when he was chosen as a Deacon by Meletius, he wrote another book, *On the Priesthood* <note>Original: "De Sacerdotio"</note>, and others. Likewise the Books to Stagirius. Likewise on the incomprehensible nature of God. Likewise how one shall instruct or <term>catechize<note>To teach the fundamental principles of the Christian faith.</note></term> young children in the Scripture. After that, when

<margin>John becomes a Priest.</margin>
<margin>Chrysostom was an eloquent speaker.</margin>
❧ Meletius had died in the city of Constantinople, John, leaving the Meletians and having no communion with Paulinus, lived those years one after another in rest. But when Paulinus was dead, he was ordained as a Priest by Evagrius, his successor. Before his <term>consecration<note>Original: "Wijsdon" (Wisdom/Ordination)</note></term>, he lived in such a manner. As they say of him, he was a stern man for the sake of the zeal of chastity. And he was held in great regard more for his youth than for his age, for men feared him more than they honored him. Because of his righteous life, he was not <term>cunning<note>Original: "schalck," meaning deceptive or crafty.</note></term> and did not think on what might follow. And because he was upright and plain-spoken, he had very many words with those with whom he spoke. In teaching he was the foremost, and very useful for correcting the 

<column-break/>

manners of his hearers. In conversation, he was held by the ignorant to be a puffed-up or proud man. Being of such a character, when he came to the Bishopric, he used much more splendor and pride than he ought to have, wishing in that way to punish the life of the Clerics. Thus he was immediately hated by many, because he seemed to be very harsh on the Clergy of the church, and each fled from him as from an angry man.

<margin>Ser-</margin>
For his Deacon Serapion—so that he might enrage them all—on a certain occasion in the presence of all the Clerics, cried out loudly: "O Bishop, you shall never better these men unless you strike them all together with a staff!" By which reasoning the hatred against him became even greater. Not long after that, he punished many Clerics for various reasons.

<margin>co-</margin>
<margin>nspi-</margin>
Then these men made a <term>riot<note>Original: "rottinghe," a gathering or forming of a gang.</note></term> and a conspiracy against him, robbing him of his honor among the people. Which things they made the people believe because he let no one eat with him. And also that he, being invited to <term>feasts<note>Original: "pewers genoot," likely referring to social drinking or dining invitations.</note></term>, did not go out to eat.

<margin>eat</margin>
Some say that he would eat with no one for the reason that he ate so unpleasantly and handled the food poorly. Others say that he did it because of his great sobriety in food.

But the people loved him for the sake of the Sermons he gave in the Church, not caring much for the reasons given by the speakers against him. What kind of books his are is not necessary to relate now; those who can read them may judge for themselves.

And many things were said, and many of his hearers took offense as despisers.

The second Part. The II. Book. Fol. 451.

## ¶ How Eutropius, the Emperor's chamberlain, was put to death,

### The 4th Chapter.

<margin>...punished [...] recognize,</margin>
<margin>...Eruption of Chrysostom.</margin>
<margin>...unspeakable [...] of the praise against Chrysostom.</margin>
<margin>...ostom alone</margin>
Eutropius was the Emperor's chief Chamberlain / a Chamberlain of the Emperor.
The reason that people spoke so poorly of Chrysostom was the homily <note>A sermon or discourse on a religious theme.</note> he wrote against Eutropius. For Eutropius the Eunuch <note>original: "Ghesnedene"</note> was the Emperor's chief Chamberlain and was endowed with the dignity of a Chief Councilor. Seeking to punish certain customs that were established in the Church, he insisted that an order should be issued by the Emperor that no one should flee to the Church <note>This refers to the "right of sanctuary," where a fugitive could not be arrested while inside a church.</note>. Indeed, even those who had already fled there for some time, he insisted they should be forced out. But God's judgment followed very quickly thereafter, though the Emperor's command was fulfilled. A few days later, when Eutropius had angered the Emperor, he himself was found among those taking refuge in the church.

<margin>John Chrysostom's sermon regarding Eutropius.</margin>
Then the Bishop—while Eutropius lay under the altar, greatly terrified—delivered from the pulpit where he usually preached a very stern, punishing sermon against Eutropius. With this, he angered many people even more, because he not only showed no mercy to a man in great distress, but also did not refrain from publicly rebuking him.

<margin>Eutropius is ordered to be beheaded.</margin>
Therefore, the Emperor, on account of certain crimes, ordered that Eutropius’s head should be cut off, notwithstanding that he had been placed in the dignity of a Chief Councilor; and his name was entirely erased from the roll of the Councilors.

<margin>Only the Councilor of Theodosius was recorded.</margin>
Therefore, only the one from the time of Theodosius who was Chief Councilor with him was recorded. For various reasons, Eutropius had severely punished several people and thus became hated by many.

<margin>Theophilus seeks a reason to depose John.</margin>
It is said that John Chrysostom rebuked Gainas, a commander of the military, with his usual zeal and severity because he had desired that one of the churches in the city be granted to the Arians <note>A Christian sect that disagreed with the mainstream Church regarding the nature of the Trinity; they were often considered heretics by the state church.</note>. Therefore, Theophilus, the Bishop of the city of Alexandria, immediately after John's ordination, sought a cause to depose or dismiss him. And if any were present who opposed John, he stirred up secret rumors through them and also wrote to many who were situated far away. For he was displeased with him, not only because of this

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin>
zeal, but also because he had not been able to make Arsatius, his priest, the Bishop at Constantinople.

# Theodoretus.

<margin>John Chrysostom, a reformer of the Clergy.</margin>
Then John the Bishop exhorted the priests to live according to the ecclesiastical ordinances; and whoever did not wish to live by them, he forbade from coming into the church. For he said they were unworthy of priestly honors if they did not wish to follow them in their lives. But he had not only the city of Constantinople to govern, but also all of Thrace—which is divided into six high-provinces—and also all of Asia, where eleven governors were ruling, and which was greatly adorned with these laws and ordinances. Also the province of Pontus, where many judges govern. When he understood that in Phoenicia people still served the devils, he selected monks armed with imperial commands and sent them out against the devil-worshippers and idolaters. He gave them money to reward the laborers who would break down the idol temples—not from the public treasury, but from what had been very generously given to him by faithful women who had been advised by him to do so.

<margin>John Chrysostom was helped by the generosity of rich women.</margin>
## ¶ Of the conversion of the Celts by John Chrysostom.

### The 5th Chapter.

<margin>He speaks of the Celts, that is the Germans, who received war from the Emperor Honorius.</margin>
When he also saw that the Celtic military force was entangled in Arian laws, and considered how they might also be won for salvation, he found this plan of action. He appointed priests, deacons, and readers who spoke their language and gave them a church. Through this opportunity, he won many of them over, as he also went there very often himself and, through a Celtic interpreter, explained the Scriptures to them. By doing this often in the city, he won many of that people from the Arian sect to the Apostolic teaching. Among the Scythians <note>The original Dutch says "Scrypten," likely a typographical error for "Scythen."</note> were some who had a desire for salvation but could not attain it. But when John learned this, he sought out men who were inflamed with Apostolic zeal and sent them out,

¶ And he arranged for those who had a desire for salvation. ¶ Of Gainas and his disobedience.

### The 6th Chapter.

<margin>Gainas, a commander, a Celt or German.</margin>
<note>The text begins with a decorative initial letter G.</note> Gainas was one of the Celts <note>The term "Celt" was often used broadly by contemporary historians to describe various Germanic tribes, in this case, the Goths.</note>, who was of a barbarian mind, and very proud and bold in his tyrannical intentions. Since he was a commander at that time, he caused great fear to many of his own people and to the Romans who were under him; indeed, even to the Emperor himself because of his tyrannical designs—and he was an Arian <note>Arianism was a Christian doctrine that denied the full divinity of Christ, which the Orthodox church, including Chrysostom, opposed.</note>. Thus, he requested of the Emperor that he might be given a church within the city. Then the Emperor promised to satisfy him. And the Emperor called John to him, and explained and presented Gainas's request and his tyrannical intentions, and desired that by allowing him a church, his plans might be entirely thwarted. But then this faithful man spoke: "O Emperor, do not make such a promise, nor cast that which is holy to the dogs <note>A reference to the biblical warning in Matthew 7:6.</note>. For I will not be able to drive those who praise the Lord out of the Church and wrongly surrender it to the blasphemers. And do not fear this barbarian, O Emperor, but have us both called, and listen alone to what we shall speak between us. I shall so stop his mouth that he will not presume to desire that which could not be profitably or usefully given." When the Emperor <margin>John Chrysostom to Honorius Augustus <note>Honorius was the Western Roman Emperor, though the events usually involve the Eastern Emperor Arcadius; the margin likely refers to the imperial authority.</note> regarding Gainas.</margin> <margin>John Chrysostom to Gainas, and Gainas to Chrysostom, speaking before the Emperor.</margin> heard that, he was pleased, and called them both the following day. Then Gainas set forth his desire. But John spoke against it, saying: "It does not befit a God-fearing Emperor to act against God’s command at the outset." And when Gainas told him that he also must have a house of prayer,

<column-break/>

John answered him: "The house of God stands open to you everywhere, and there is no one who forbids you to pray." Then he said: "But I am of another sect, and I desire to have a church with them, for I have had much labor and trouble for the common welfare of Rome, and therefore my request must not be despised." Then John said to him: "You have received many rewards—yea, even greater than your labor—for you have become a commander, and also a chief councilor; and you must remember what you once were, and what you are now held to be; what poverty you once had, and now on the contrary, how much wealth; how you were clothed before you came across the Hellespont or the Danube, and how it is now. Consider then that for a little trouble and labor, much profit and reward has been brought to you, and do not be found ungrateful toward the one who honors you." With these words this teacher stopped Gainas's mouth and forced him to be silent.

## Socrates.

¶ While Gainas then aspired to the empire and intended to seize it—having formerly made a promise to the Emperor Arcadius for the sake of his faith, at Chalcedon by the holy martyr Euphemia—he pondered many schemes within himself and always remained fixed in his opinion. And because he was not able to achieve his goals in the city of Constantinople by day, he attempted to send the barbarians into the palace by night so that they might set it on fire. And then it became manifest that the LORD watches over the city; for when the barbarians were sent by him to start the fire and to plunder, there appeared a great host of armed angels, having very large bodies. When they thought it was the army, they turned back. And when this was told to Gainas, it seemed impossible to him, for he knew that all the soldiers were stationed throughout the city. Therefore, on the following night, he sent others again.

And when he was warned of the same thing again (for those angels showed themselves to the barbarians once more), he finally marched out himself with the army and found this miracle or wonder-work to be true.

# Theodoretus

<margin>The open tyranny of Gainas.</margin>
Now, after some time had passed, Gainas revealed his long-meditated tyranny; for having gathered his people, he overran all of Thrace. When the judges and the people heard of this, they were greatly afraid, yet no one dared to stand against him in battle, nor did anyone dare to send an envoy to him, for they feared his barbarian cruelty. Of such great authority was John that he caused those who were greatly feared and respected to fear and humble themselves.

### <margin>E</margin> Concerning the question that arose among the Egyptian Monks, whether God has a body or not.

## The 7th Chapter.

<margin>Whether God is physical.</margin>
At that time, a question was posed: whether God was physical and had a human form, or whether He was entirely and completely foreign to the physical form of man. With this question, a great deal of strife and discord arose, as one side held one view and the other held another. <margin>F</margin> The simple and plain among the monks held that God was physical and had the form of a man. And there were many who refuted them, saying: That God had no body, nor any physi-

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin>
<margin>Theophilus the bishop of Alexandria.</margin>
cal shape or essence. Theophilus, the Bishop of Alexandria, also agreed with these, so that he taught and disputed in the Church before the people against those who said that God had the form of a man, and he taught that God had no body. When the Egyptian monks heard this, they came to Alexandria and created an uprising against Theophilus, as if against an impious man, so that they attempted to kill him. <margin>D</margin> <margin>The Egyptian Monks attempt to kill Theophilus.</margin> Theophilus, hearing of this, devised how he might avoid death. Thus, he received the monks with friendly words and said to them: "I see you as if I see God's face." <note>This was a clever, albeit deceptive, use of the phrase Jacob used to Esau in Genesis 33:10, which the monks interpreted as an admission that God looked like them.</note> With these words, he hindered the monks in their purpose, and they said to him: "If it is true what you say, that God's face is like ours, then ban the <margin>H</margin> <margin>The books of Origen.</margin> books of Origen <note>Origen was an early Christian scholar who argued for the incorporeal, non-physical nature of God; his writings were often the center of these theological battles.</note>, for some believe contrary to us because of them. If you do not do that which happens to the impious and those who resist God, you shall also receive the same from us, and that without any doubt."

<margin>I</margin>
Then Theophilus said: "I will do what pleases you; but do not be so cruel toward me, for I am also an enemy of the books of Origen, and I accuse those who accept them." Thus he escaped from the monks, and by chance, this question was suspended from that time on. Afterward, <margin>K</margin> such a thing occurred: Over the Egyptian monasteries were appointed four worthy <margin>Dioscorus, Ammonius, Eusebius, Euthymius.</margin> men: Dioscorus, Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius, who were all brothers, and because of their great stature were called the *Longi* <note>original: "de Longi"; Latin for "the Tall Ones."</note>, who were well-spoken and widely famed for their lives, and therefore highly esteemed by those of Alexandria; indeed, Theophilus the Bishop also honored them greatly. And <margin>L</margin> therefore he made Dioscorus—who had been called by force to Hermopolis—a Bishop, and he requested of two of them that they should live with him; they were reluctant to accept that he should command them as a Bishop, but he made them clerics and appointed them as church stewards.

<margin>M</margin>
Now, when these men were distressed because they could not fulfill their intended way of life, and realized over time that their souls were also being harmed—and because the Bishop <margin>N</margin> <margin>The Bishop's greed.</margin> had much money and a very greedy desire—they renounced him and would not stay with him, preferring to live alone in the desert.

<meta>This page continues the account of theological and social unrest during the late 4th century, specifically the conflict between Patriarch Theophilus of Alexandria and the Egyptian monks, and the liturgical innovations of John Chrysostom in Constantinople.</meta>

### Tripartite Ecclesiastical History.

<margin>Theophilus is a man of a bold spirit.</margin>
¶ And when he, without knowing their will, desired that they should be with him, and noticed that he was displeasing to them, he became angry and spited them. But they, thinking little of this, went away. Since Theophilus was of such a wrathful spirit, he sought to trouble those men in whatever way God might allow. In the meantime, he greatly hated their brother Dioscorus <note>Dioscorus was one of the "Tall Brothers," a group of four prominent Egyptian monks known for their learning and asceticism.</note>, for he was distressed that the monks loved and honored them, and he knew he could not harm them unless he first attacked the monks. He had well tested this, since he had often spoken with them, and they confessed that God was incorporeal <note>original: "onlichamelijck"; without a physical body</note> and not of any human shape, so that from the necessity of human form, human passion or movement would not also follow. And although Theophilus was also of this same opinion, yet so that he might take his revenge, he turned against what he had previously praised and even taught.

<margin>The deceit of Theophilus, who speaks differently than he believes.</margin>
For sending word to the desert, he trapped many of the simple monks—who were not well-versed in spiritual exercises—with such practices, saying: That one ought not to follow Dioscorus nor his brothers, who say that God is incorporeal; for God, according to the Scriptures, has eyes, ears, hands, and feet, just like men. But Dioscorus and his followers, following Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253) was an early Christian scholar whose complex allegorical interpretations of the Bible later became a source of intense controversy.</note>, introduce a blasphemous doctrine, as if God had no eyes, ears, hands, or feet. With this deception, a great many of the monks were misled, and a very hot riot broke out among them. But the well-practiced men were not deceived, and the unpracticed ones, through their zeal for the faith, rose up very subtly against the brothers. When the riot had occurred, they attacked one another; one part called the other godless followers and false brothers, while the other part called the followers of 

<margin>Theophilus takes the field with armed force.</margin>
Theophilus "Anthropomorphites" <note>original: "Antropomorphiamos"; those who attribute a human form to God.</note> or "Humaniformians," that is, those who attribute a human being to God. Because of this cause, a great and inhumane riot having arisen, Theophilus came to Nitria <note>A major monastic center in the Egyptian desert.</note> with a great multitude of armed folk against Dioscorus and his brothers. These men could hardly escape the danger by flight.

## ¶ How John began the night-hymns.

### The 8th Chapter.

<column-break/>

While this was happening in Egypt, John the Bishop <note>John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> was in great esteem in Constantinople because of his teaching, and was very dearly loved by everyone. He was the first to add prayers to the night-hymns <note>original: "nachtghesanghen"; nocturnal vigils or matins.</note> for the following reasons. The Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who held that Jesus Christ was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note>, as we have seen, held their gatherings outside the city. On the Sabbath and Sunday, having gathered between the gates and the harbor, they sang their songs of praise and antiphons. Doing this for most of the night, they would go through the middle of the city out of the gates at dawn with their antiphons, running together toward their church. And as they often did this as a way to show contempt for the orthodox believers, they very often sang: "Where are those who say that three things are one in power?" Then John, fearing that the simple folk would be led astray by such songs, instructed his people that they should also be busy with night-hymns, so that in this way the work of the Arians would be suppressed or overshadowed, and the faith and confession of the Christians would be confirmed. Thus, this profitable diligence was brought to an end amidst unrest and danger. For when the songs of the Homoousians <note>original: "Homousianen"; those who believe the Father and Son are of the "same substance," the orthodox Nicene position.</note> appeared much clearer by night (for he had also made silver crosses, and silver candlesticks with wax candles were carried there, the costs of which were paid by Eudoxia Augusta the Empress), the Arians became so angry that they were stirred up to the point of murder. When they were gathered one night, Brison—who was the Empress’s eunuch <note>original: "Brison die gesneden Auguste"; Brison was a chamberlain to Empress Eudoxia.</note>—was struck in the forehead with a stone while he was there ordered to lead the singing. Some people on both sides also perished. The Emperor, being moved by this, forbade the Arians from singing any more hymns.

Ignatius, who was there in Antioch in Syria, the third Bishop after the Apostle Peter, who also lived in the time of the Apostles, or with the Apostle

# Sozomenus.

### ¶ Of the enemies of John Chrysostom.

#### The 10th Chapter.

<margin>How John fell into the hatred of the Empress.</margin>
**I**t is said that, among other things, John also fell into the hatred of the Empress <note>The "Augusta" refers to Empress Eudoxia, who initially supported John but became his fiercest rival.</note> because of Severian, the Bishop of Gabala. Both this Severian and Antiochus of Ptolemais were very eloquent and well-instructed in teaching before the people in the churches. However, Antiochus had a particularly clear and intelligent voice, such that he was called "Chrysostom" <note>Meaning "Golden-mouthed," the same epithet usually reserved for John.</note> by some. But Severian, although he excelled in the understanding of the Scriptures, spoke with the character of the coarse Syrian tongue.

<margin>Sion the circumcised Empress.</margin>
When Antiochus first came to Constantinople, being heard for his eloquence, he gathered much money and returned to his city. Severian followed after him and also came there. Being admitted through the favor of John, he was held in great esteem by many of the principal citizens due to his earnest preaching, and even by the Emperor and Empress themselves. Now, when John traveled into Asia, he entrusted the church to him; for he believed his flattering words and thought that he loved him in deed and truth, though Severian commended himself more to the listeners. When John heard of this, and Serapion <note>Serapion was John's archdeacon, known for his sternness.</note> told him of it, he was very displeased. When John returned from Asia, it happened that Serapion intentionally did not stand up to honor Severian as he passed by. Then Severian began to cry out, being greatly embittered: "If Serapion dies a Christian, then Christ did not become man." Because of this matter, he was accused by Serapion as a wrongdoer and a blasphemer, and was thus driven out of the city by John.

<margin>Severian is driven out of Constantinople.</margin>
When the Empress learned of this through Severian's friends, she immediately had him called back from Chalcedon; but John did not wish to see him, notwithstanding

<column-break/>

that he was entreated by many for that reason, until the Empress, in the Church of the Apostles, laid her son Theodosius <note>The future Emperor Theodosius II, then an infant.</note> upon John's knees, praying and testifying that he should, for her sake, maintain good friendship with Severian. This John finally did, though with much difficulty.

# Socrates.

In the meantime, the monks came to Constantinople with Dioscorus and his brothers, along with Isidore, who had previously been a good friend to Theophilus, but had now become his complete enemy because of such matters. Peter had been the Archpriest in Alexandria. Theophilus had driven him out of the Church out of hatred, accusing him of having admitted a Manichean woman to the holy communion before she had renounced her heresy.

<margin>Isidore is excluded from the church for the testimony of truth.</margin>
And when Peter said that he had accepted her by the command of Theophilus, and Theophilus denied this, Peter called upon the testimony of Isidore, saying that the Bishop well knew it had happened so. At that time, Isidore was dwelling in Damascus, sent by Theophilus to reconcile Bishop Flavian of Antioch with him. But when Isidore returned, he testified that Peter's answer was true, saying: "That the Manichean woman was accepted by the command of the bishop." At this, Theophilus became enraged and drove them both out of the Church.

<margin>John Chrysostom receives Peter and Isidore.</margin>
For these reasons, Isidore came to Constantinople with Dioscorus and the others to tell the Emperor and John of his deeds. When John learned of this, he at first honored the men and joined in their prayers; but he did not wish to enter into holy communion with them until he understood the matter rightly. This having happened, a false report reached Theophilus, as if John had held communion with them to help them. Thus he sought not only to avenge himself on Dioscorus and Isidore but also to thrust John from his Bishopric. So he sent letters to all the Bishops of every city, concealing his true intention.

<margin>
Theophilus uses praise to send Epiphanius to ban the books of Origen.

...had been his enemy, as one who did not have a proper understanding of God and who believed that He possessed a human nature <note>This refers to the "Anthropomorphite" controversy, where some monks believed God had a physical human form; Theophilus used this debate politically to attack his rivals.</note>; and he acted as if he had reformed himself, acknowledging that he would accept his teaching and sect. He arranged for a Synod to be held in Cyprus, and finally decreed that the books of Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD) was a prolific early Christian theologian whose complex ideas later became the subject of intense controversy.</note> should be forbidden. But Epiphanius, because he held him in high regard and was deceived by cunning due to his own simplicity, forbade the reading of Origen’s books at that ordained Synod. He also wrote letters to John <note>John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> stating that he should cease reading Origen’s books and that he should also confirm what had been found favorable in the Synod.

Theophilus, thus deceiving the widely renowned Epiphanius and seeing that his plan was proceeding according to his wishes, also gathered the bishops and forbade the reading of Origen’s books—though Origen had died 200 years earlier. He did this not because he truly held such a conviction, but because he sought to cause harm to Dioscorus and his followers <note>Dioscorus was one of the "Tall Brothers," a group of monks who had fled Theophilus's persecution in Egypt to seek refuge with John Chrysostom.</note>. But John thought little of what had been done by Epiphanius and Theophilus, continuing to labor in Christian teaching, for which he possessed a celebrated name. He gave no thought to the fact that they were often plotting against him. When it was publicly observed that Theophilus sought to depose John from his Bishopric, many of John’s enemies aligned themselves with Theophilus. Many of the clerics and prominent figures in the court, seizing the opportune time, labored to ensure that a Synod would be held in Constantinople against John. They commanded this for themselves through both letters and words. Thus, through the dealings of the bishops Severian and Antiochus, the hatred against John was increased, as we have spoken of above.

### How Epiphanius in Cyprus became an enemy to John.

### The 11th Chapter.

<margin>
Epiphanius, the bishop in Cyprus, comes to Constantinople.
</margin>
Not long thereafter, Epiphanius the Bishop came to Constantinople, bringing with him the condemnation of Origen’s books. With these, they did not wish to have Origen himself condemned, but only to have his works diminished and rejected. When he arrived at the Church of St. John, located seven miles from the city, and held assemblies there,

<column-break/>

<margin>Downcast</margin>
he ordained a deacon; and so he returned again to the City. He feared, for the sake of Theophilus, that John would invite him, and preferred to remain in his own lodging. Calling together the bishops who were then present, he read to them the ban on Origen’s books. Those who held Epiphanius in great honor subscribed to it, but some refused to do so. Among these was one named Theotimus, a Bishop in Scythia, who answered him thus: "O Epiphanius, I do not wish to speak any injury against him who has long been at rest in good peace, nor do I intend to undertake such a slanderous thing as to condemn that which our ancestors were neither able nor willing to reject. Furthermore, I find no evil teaching in the books of Origen." And so he brought forth the books of Origen and read from them, demonstrating a Christian interpretation. Afterward, he came forward and mocked: "Those who do this shame do not know themselves." It is said that the irreproachable Theotimus gave this answer to Epiphanius in his dealings. But since many backbiters have rejected Origen as a blasphemer, it will not be in vain to speak a little of this. Despicable men, and those who cannot come to any honor through their own merits, think they prove themselves to be something when they despise someone who is better than they. This was first done by Methodius <margin>Methodius.</margin>, the bishop in Olympus, which is a city in Lycia; after him by Eustathius, a Bishop for a short time in Antioch; and after him Apollinaris <margin>Apollinaris.</margin>; and finally Theophilus.

These all spoke evil of Origen, and complained about Origen, one for some reasons and another for others. This was reported to John.

### ¶ Why the Empress was so hostile toward John, through whom, and how he was led into exile.

## The 14th Chapter.

<margin>John Chrysostom against Eudoxia Augusta.</margin>
When Epiphanius had departed, word was sent to John that Eudoxia the Empress had armed herself against him. Being incensed by this, he preached a sermon to the people which was entirely full of contempt for all women. This speech was taken by all the people as if it were directed against the Empress, and so it came to the ears of the Emperor. When the Empress heard of it, she related it to the Emperor as a personal shame to him, saying that his shame was greater than hers, since it was done to his wife.

Therefore, it happened that Theophilus very quickly held a Synod against John, which Severianus also joined with him, for he was still an enemy. In the meantime, Theophilus arrived, swaying many of the bishops, so that a great many of John’s enemies gathered together. There were also those whom he had deposed from the office of Bishop; thus they gathered together in unity at Chalcedon, <margin>Council of Chalcedon against John Chrysostom.</margin> where at that time one Cyrmus was Bishop, who spoke much against John, calling him godless and proud. ...had been his enemy, as one who did not have a correct understanding of God, and who believed that He had a human form <note>This refers to the Anthropomorphite heresy, the belief that God possesses a physical human body, a view Theophilus falsely attributed to his opponents to stir up the simple-minded monks against Origen’s more allegorical teachings.</note>; and he acted as if he had corrected himself, acknowledging that he would accept his teaching and sect, and arranged for a Synod to be held in Cyprus where, finally, the books of Origen were forbidden. And he wrote letters to John <note>John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> that he should cease reading the books of Origen and that he should also confirm what had been settled at the Synod.

<margin>The craftiness of Theophilus, with which he sends the good Epiphanius to ban Origen's books.</margin>
Theophilus, thus deceiving the renowned Epiphanius and seeing that his purpose was proceeding according to his wish, also gathered the bishops and forbade the reading of the books of Origen, who had died 200 years before: not that he truly held such a conviction, but because he sought to do harm to Dioscorus <note>One of the "Tall Brothers," a group of monks who were targets of Theophilus’s wrath.</note> and his followers. But John, making little of what had been done by Epiphanius and Theophilus, labored in Christian teaching and was of a renowned name in the same. And he did not care that many things were thought against him. And when it was now publicly noticed that Theophilus sought to depose John from his Bishopric, then many of John’s enemies joined with Theophilus; and many of the clergy and of the prominent men in the court, waiting for an opportune time, labored so that a Synod might be held in Constantinople against John. And they commanded this themselves through letters and words. Thus, through the dealings of the bishops Severian and Antiochus, the hatred against John was increased, of which we have spoken above.

### How Epiphanius in Cyprus became an enemy to John.

### The 11th Chapter.

<margin>Epiphanius, the bishop in Cyprus, comes to Constantinople.</margin>

When he had gone out to the church of St. John, located seven miles from the city, and had held assemblies there,

he ordained a deacon; and he thus returned to the city, and feared for Theophilus’s sake that John might invite him, and preferred to remain in his own residence. And calling the bishops who were then present, he read to them the banishment of the books of Origen. And those who held Epiphanius in great honor signed it, but some would not do so. Among whom was one named Theotimus, a Bishop in Scythia <note>A region corresponding to modern-day Romania and Bulgaria; Theotimus was known for his long hair and his missionary work among the Huns.</note>, who answered thus: 
> O Epiphanius, I do not wish to speak any injury now against him who has long been at rest in peace, nor do I intend to begin so slanderous a thing as to forbid that which our ancestors were neither able nor willing to reject. And furthermore, I find no evil teaching in the books of Origen. 

And so he brought forth the books of Origen and read from them, and pointed out Christian interpretations. And after that, he came forward and mocked: 
> Those who do this shame do not know themselves. 

It is said that the blameless-in-conduct Theotimus gave this answer to Epiphanius. But since many backbiters rejected Origen as a blasphemer, it will not be in vain to speak a little of it. Despicable men, and those who cannot reach any honor through themselves, think to prove they are something when they despise someone who is better than they. This was done first by Methodius, the bishop in Olympus (which is a city in Lycia), thereafter by Eustathius, a Bishop for a short time at Antioch, and after him Apollinaris, and finally Theophilus.

All these spoke evil of Origen, and complained of Origen, some for one reason and some for others. But when Methodius had spoken much evil of Origen, he afterwards, as one who had changed his mind, spoke with wonder of the man in his dialogue which he titled *Xenon*; but why should I speak much of their complaints which they make against Origen? For while they accuse him for certain causes they imagine, and do not find that he felt anything evil against the Holy Trinity, there are instead proven in him testimonies of godliness and uprightness. ### The XV. Chapter.

<margin>Serapion.</margin>
So then John was busy preaching and teaching, and he ordained Serapion as a Bishop of Heraclea in Thrace, by which even more hatred was stirred up against him, for shortly thereafter this occurred, as is well known. There was a silver statue or image of the Empress Augusta <note>Empress Eudoxia</note> erected upon a Porphyry Column, dressed in a mantle, and it was not far from the Church of Sophia <note>The Hagia Sophia</note>, with only a street between the two. There was now commonly a public game or spectacle held there; but John thought that such things resulted in great disparagement of the church, and he armed his tongue again with his usual freedom of speech. And though he was asked to stop: he nevertheless did not do so, but with all possible eloquence rebuked those who ordered such things to be done. The Empress again considered this to have been spoken as a slander against her, and sought again that a Synod of the Bishops should be held against him. When John understood this, he delivered the highly famous homily in the church, of which the beginning is: <note>original: "Rursus Herodias insanit"</note> "Again Herodias rages," that is: "Herodias has become insane again, and is troubled again; she dances again, and desires to receive the head of John in a dish," which provoked the Empress much more to anger and wrath.

# Sozomen,

### The xvi. Chapter.

<margin>Assassins prepared to kill Chrysostom.</margin>

After that, the servant of the Priest Elpidius ran up to the Bishop <note>John Chrysostom.</note> and intended to slay him. And as he was held back by one person, he quickly wounded him, and immediately another who stood nearby, and then a third. Then a great cry went up, and as many people gathered together, he sought to harm many more; finally, he was captured and delivered up. From 그at time on, the people guarded John night and day, surrounding his house.

¶ Concerning the second deposition of John, and of the schism that occurred for his sake.

### The xvii. Chapter.

<margin>Another Synod on Chrysostom's account.</margin>
Not long thereafter, the Bishops were gathered together: Leontius of Ancyra in Galatia, Ammonius of Laodicea, Brison of Philippi in Thrace, Acacius of Beroea in Syria, and some others. When this occurred, the first accusers became rebellious again; since John now had good confidence in such matters, he desired that his accusation should be properly conducted. And when the feast of the birth of our Savior <note>Christmas.</note> arrived, the Emperor did not come to the Church according to his custom, but sent word to him that he would not communicate with him unless he were cleared of the accusations. And since the accusers greatly feared the safety of John, the present Bishops did not bring forward

<column-break/>

anything further, except that after his deposition, he had sat again in the episcopal chair without the ordinance of a Council. And when he said in answer that sixty-seven Bishops who held communion with him had so decided and ordained, Leontius and others cried out against this, saying: "But, O John, many more have deposed you." To this John spoke again and said: "That it was not a Christian rule, but a rule of the Arians <note>The Arians were a group whose theological views on the nature of Christ were condemned at the Council of Nicaea; John is arguing that his enemies are using illegal canons created by heretics.</note>." Which they, when they were gathered in Antioch to condemn the Christian doctrine of <note>original: "Homousios"</note> *Homoousios* <note>A Greek term meaning 'of the same substance,' referring to the divinity of Christ.</note> or Consubstantiality, had established out of hatred and envy against Athanasius.

Then they condemned him, stating that he had not done enough to satisfy them, not understanding that they also used this rule when they deposed Athanasius. This occurred around the feast of Easter. And the Emperor sent word to John and commanded him not to come into the church, because two Synods had condemned him: So John ceased his duties and did not enter the church at all. Immediately, all those who adhered to John departed from the Church and held their Easter feast in the Baths of Constantinople <note>original: "Thermis"</note>. Along with whom Bishops, Priests, and also Clerics broke away, and they held their assembly here and there alone, and were therefore also called Johannites. But John did not appear anywhere for two months, until the Emperor commanded him to be led again into exile.

<margin>John is led out.</margin>
And as he was taken out of the church, he was led away. But some who held with John set the church on fire that day, and the wind also carried the fire into the House of the Senators. This happened on the 11th of January <note>Historical sources usually date this to June, but the text specifies January.</note>, when Honorius for the 6th year and Aristaenetus for the first were supreme Councilors <note>Consuls.</note>; for which cause the Governor Optatus, since he was a Heathen, killed many of the Johannites with various torments out of hatred for the Christians.

### ¶ Of the Reader Eutropius, who was cast into prison for John's sake.

### The 21st Chapter.

<margin>Eutropius the Reader captured</margin>
At this time, a Reader <note>A "Reader" or Lector was a member of the minor orders of the clergy responsible for reading the scriptures during the liturgy.</note> named Eutropius was also imprisoned, being suspected of having set the fire in the church. After he had endured many 

<column-break/>

torments, he died after being cast into the prison. But what happened concerning him, I believe deserves to be told. Someone saw in a dream a tall, beautiful man standing by the Altar, as if he stood there in honor of the Martyr Stephen <note>Saint Stephen was the first Christian martyr; the implication is that Eutropius was a martyr of similar character.</note>; this man lamented that no good men could now be found anywhere. And going through the entire city, he had found none greater than Eutropius alone. And when he who had seen the vision awoke, he told the dream to the faithful. Afterward, he inquired about those who had been imprisoned by the Governor and severely afflicted with blows; thus he found Eutropius, and he told him the vision, and begged him with weeping eyes that he would pray for him.

When the Governor <note>Optatus, the Prefect of Constantinople, who was a pagan and harshly persecuted the supporters of Chrysostom.</note> tortured and tormented many of them, yet did not find the persons who had started the fire, he also captured some women. He advised them to have communion with Bishop Arsacius <note>Arsacius was the elderly man appointed to replace Chrysostom; the "Joannites" (supporters of John) considered him a usurper.</note>, and many of them fell away. But Olympias <note>Saint Olympias was a wealthy widow and deaconess, a close friend and supporter of Chrysostom.</note>—against whom they intended to do injustice or complete their wickedness—mocked them, saying: "Speak to my tormentors, and do even greater violence to me, for it is not lawful for me to have communion with them, nor to do that which is forbidden to the godly."

When the governor could not move her to have communion with Arsacius, he let her go; but a short time later he captured her again and took much gold from her, thinking thus to break her steadfastness. At that time, Tigurius the Priest was stripped of his clothes and beaten upon his back, and so stretched out that his hands and feet were pulled out of their joints.

## ¶ How the body of John was brought to Constantinople.

### Chapter 26.

<margin>
The remains of John Chrysostom are brought to Constantinople, where he had died in exile.
</margin>
The remains of this Teacher <note>original: "Leeraers," often used for a Doctor of the Church</note> were brought to the Royal City <note>Constantinople</note> in later times. The faithful people crossed the sea in such numbers it was as if they journeyed on dry land, and they covered the waters of the Bosporus with torches and candles. The Emperor deposited this treasure within the city—the Emperor who had inherited his grandfather’s name <note>Theodosius II, grandson of Theodosius I</note>—and he preserved his own piety uninjured. When he cast his eyes and face upon the sarcophagus, he prayed for his parents, Arcadius and Eudoxia, asking that God would forgive them for what they had done wrong in their ignorance <note>Referring to their role in John Chrysostom's exile</note>. For not long before, his parents had died and left Theodosius as an orphan. But the God of his fathers and forefathers did not allow him to experience what it was to be an orphan; instead, He caused him to be raised in piety, preserved his kingdom from all the cares of unrest, and bridled the plots of his enemies.

## ¶ Of the reward and praise of the young Theodosius.

### Chapter 27.

<margin>
The praise of Theodosius the Younger.
</margin>
This man, always mindful of God’s benefits, honored the Giver of all blessings. He had sisters with him, noble maidens who sang songs of praise with him. He considered it his principal pleasure to exercise himself in Divine matters, and they held it to be an inexhaustible treasure to do good to the poor. The Emperor himself possessed many other gifts, notably generosity, gentleness, and a steadfastness of spirit that remained untroubled by any tempests <note>Political or social upheavals</note>, for he was always well-provided with an upright faith;

<column-break/>

of which we wish to give a public sign. There was a man, a monk very sharp-witted in his counsel, who went to the Emperor to petition for a certain matter. When he had done this many times and did not obtain what he desired, he excluded the Emperor from the Church's communion <note>excommunicated him</note> and, having banned him, went away. When the Emperor arrived at the Court for the noon meal, in the presence of those who were to eat with him, he declared that he would not eat until the bond of excommunication was undone. For this reason, he sent for the Bishop of the city, praying that he would command the one who had bound him to release him. The Bishop replied that the Emperor was not rightly bound by such a spiritual person and sent word that he should consider himself already released. Nevertheless, the Emperor would not accept this release until the one who had bound him was found—with great effort and labor—and restored to him the communion he had taken away. Furthermore, he ordered the remaining temples of the idols to be razed to the ground, so that the descendants of the error <note>pagans</note> would not find even a single sign of it; for he wrote this intention clearly into his command.

When Roilas <note>Rugila or Rua, a leader of the Huns</note>, the chieftain of the Scythians, had crossed the Ister <note>The ancient name for the lower Danube, here written as "Opstra"</note> or Danube with a countless multitude of soldiers and piteously overran Thrace, even threatening to besiege and overthrow the Royal City, God struck him from Heaven with thunder and lightning, consuming him and his entire army with fire.

## ¶ Of the Miracles that occurred against the Persians.

### Chapter 28.

Such help was also granted by the Lord, his comforter, in the war against the Persians. For when the Persians perceived that the Romans were occupied elsewhere, they attacked the surrounding cities and violated the peace treaty, devastating the borders and adjacent territories. At that time, no human help came to the Romans, for the Emperor, trusting in the peace, had sent his captains and soldiers to other regions.

Now, when one of the enemy’s men spoke blasphemously, spewing out the words of Rabshakeh and Sennacherib <note>Biblical figures who mocked God during the siege of Jerusalem.</note> and threatening with great madness that he would burn the Holy Temple, the Holy Man could not endure such great insanity. Then the stone struck the head of the one who had spoken blasphemy against God; it marred his entire face, crushed his head, and scattered his brains upon the earth. When the field commander who had threatened to take the city learned of this, he became silent and confessed by his actions that he was defeated; fearing greatly, he sought peace. Thus, the King preserved this Prince as his most faithful servant, while the Prince also acknowledges that he is a servant and performs due service to the Lord.

### ¶ Of the virtues of Abdas, a Bishop of the Persians.

### Chapter 40.

<margin>
Abdas, a bishop of the Persians, [destroyed] the Pyreon, that is, the fire-house.
</margin>
There was a Bishop named Abdas, who was greatly adorned with virtues. He was entirely inflamed with divine zeal and destroyed the <term>Pyreon</term> <note>A Zoroastrian fire temple, from the Greek 'pyr' meaning fire.</note> of the Persians. Now, they called their temples "Pyrea," where they guarded the fire and held the fire to be a God. When the King heard of this from the <term>Magi</term> <note>The priestly caste of ancient Persia.</note>—that is, the Sages or Sorcerers—he called Abdas to him. At first, he accused him gently, commanding him to have the Pyreon rebuilt. When Abdas refused to do so, the King threatened <margin>Abdas is commanded to be put to death.</margin> that he would tear down all the churches—which threats were indeed carried out. For after first commanding the man to be killed, he also gave the order to break down all the churches. I consider that this destruction of the Pyreon happened very unseasonably; for the Apostle, as soon as he arrived in Athens and saw the city full of idolatry, did not busy himself with breaking the altars which they honored, but rather rebuked their ignorance with reason and taught them the laws of the truth.

But that he [Abdas] would not allow the temple that had been broken to be rebuilt, but much rather chose death—at this I marvel greatly, and hold that he is worthy of much honor. For worshipping fire and building a temple in its honor is one and the same act. From this, then, this tempest or misfortune took its origin, and <margin>A free-ranging persecution by the Persians against the Christians.</margin> rose up most cruelly against the worshippers of piety; and thus for thirty continuous years, a most lamentable devastation remained, which was also driven forward greatly by the Magi, the Sages, or Sorcerers.
The Persians held the Magi, who [worshipped] the elements...

...made into gods. I have shown these fables in another description, in which we have given answers according to what their questions deserved. Gorozanes <note>Historically known as Bahram V (reigned 420–438 AD).</note>, the son of Isdegerdes <note>Yazdegerd I (reigned 399–420 AD).</note>, also undertook to combat Christian godliness upon his father’s death and his own succession to the kingdom. For they flayed the hands of some; from others, they flayed the back; and some they flayed at the head, beginning at the forehead and continuing to the neck, leaving them thus with their flesh exposed. Others they bound with split reeds <note>A torture where sharp, split reeds were tied against the body and then pulled away forcefully to tear the skin.</note> upon the bare body from head to foot with cords, pressing the sharp edges of the reeds against their naked flesh, and then they pulled the reeds up with violence so that the sharp edges cut the flesh open as they were pulled, which was a most bitter pain. They devised many other cruel torments, for they hated the Teacher of Righteousness <note>A reference to Jesus Christ.</note>. But they could not overcome the strength of the brave men, for they ran forward of their own accord so that through this death they might obtain the gifts of the incorruptible. I shall recount something of two or three of them, so that from these one may recognize the strength of the others.

## ¶ Of Hormisda, the noble confessor among the Persians.

### The 31st Chapter.

<margin>Hormisda, a Persian.</margin>
There was a nobleman among the Persians named Hormisda, whose father was a governor. Now, when the King learned that this man was a Christian, he commanded him to be brought forth and ordered him to renounce the Savior God. Then he answered: "O Emperor, you command that which is neither right nor profitable. For he who is taught to lightly despise and deny the God of all things will also very easily despise the Emperor, seeing as he shares in human nature. If a man is worthy of death, O Emperor, who despises your

<column-break/>

scepter, then he who denies the Creator of all things is worthy of many more punishments." Though the King should have praised him for his wisdom, he instead robbed him of his honors and riches and commanded that he alone, naked except for a loincloth, should be made weary by leading camels back and forth. Many days later, the King looked down from above and saw that he was greatly scorched by the sun and quite disfigured by dust and filth; and the King, remembering his father’s nobility, commanded that he should be clothed in linen and brought to him. He thought that the man might be moved by his previous distress and this present mercy. "At the very least," the King said, "now deny the Son of the Carpenter <note>A common derogatory reference to Jesus used by opponents of Christianity in this period.</note>." But he, being filled with divine zeal, tore the garment off and threw it down, saying: "Do you think that for the sake of this gift I would depart from godliness? Take back your gift along with the godlessness you possess." The King marveled at this strength and drove him naked out of his kingdom.

## ¶ Of Sannes, the confessor among the Persians.

### The 32nd Chapter.

Sannes was a lord who had a thousand servants under him; he resisted the King and would not forsake the Creator of all things. So the King dealt with him thus: The King sought out which of his servants was the most cruel. To that same servant, he gave lordship over the other servants. He also commanded that the lord himself must serve this servant, and his wife as well, thinking that by this he would move the champion of truth. But he was deceived in his hope, for this man had built his house upon a rock <note>A biblical allusion to Matthew 7:24–27.</note>.

# The eleventh Book of the Histories called *Ecclesiastica Tripartita* / from Sozomen, Socrates, and Theodoret, etc.

# Socrates.

### ¶ How Anthemius the Governor ruled the Empire of the young Theodosius.

->The first Chapter.<-

<margin>Honorius Augustus.</margin>
<note>A decorative historiated initial 'E' featuring a figure in a landscape with foliage.</note>
**A**nd now that Arcadius was dead, his brother Honorius ruled the lands to the West, but the provinces to the East remained under the sovereignty of Theodosius the Younger. But because he was no more than eight years old, the Governor <term>Anthemius</term> <note>Anthemius was a powerful Praetorian Prefect of the East who acted as regent for the young emperor.</note> managed all things; for he was a grandson of Philippus, who had driven Bishop Paul out of the Church under Constantine and had introduced Macedonius, and who also surrounded the city of Constantinople with a great wall. He was considered the wisest among men of that time, and truly he was, for he did nothing thoughtlessly; rather, whatever was to be done, he did with the advice of many. And he relied greatly on the Sophist <note>A "Sophist" here refers to a professional teacher of rhetoric and philosophy.</note> Troilus, who, besides being his good friend, also assisted Anthemius in political wisdom.
<margin>Anthemius the Governor.</margin>
<margin>Troilus the Sophist.</margin>

### ¶ Of Bishop Atticus, and his character.

->The second Chapter.<-

<column-break/>

<margin>Atticus of Constantinople.</margin>
But when the Emperor was in the eighth year of his reign, the famous, learned, venerable, and wise man Atticus was in his third year as Bishop of Constantinople. Because of him, his churches received a great increase, for he was not only liberal and generous, but he also showed his wonderful wisdom toward the heretics, not wishing to be troublesome to them in any way. But if he happened to startle them, he would afterward show them his friendliness again. Meanwhile, he did not neglect to practice his eloquence, and he showed great diligence in reading through the Ancients, even spending his nights on it; therefore, he did not care much for Sophistic or Philosophical lessons, for he was friendly to those who spoke with him, though in his speech he was grave. And excellently, according to the teaching of the Apostle, he became all things to all people.
<margin>1 Cor. 9.</margin>

When he was first a priest, he wrote books, and when he had revised them, he recited them before the Church; afterward, through his labor, he became bold and presented that praiseworthy teaching himself. Nevertheless, his sermons were not composed in such a way that they were written down by the listeners <note>original: "datse van den toehoorders gheschreven wierden"</note>. But I wish to tell what happened in his time that is worth relating.
<margin>Atticus's sermons were not written down by the listeners, as was sometimes done with those of Origen.</margin>

### ¶ Of Theodosius the Bishop of Synnada, and how the Macedonians were converted there.

->The third Chapter.<-

--- Page 623 ---
<meta>This page continues the history of the early 5th-century Church during the reign of Theodosius II, specifically focusing on the administration of Bishop Atticus of Constantinople and ecclesiastical conflicts in Phrygia.</meta>

Fol. 470.
### Tripartite Ecclesiastical History.

<margin>Theodosius, Bishop of Synnada, persecutes the Macedonians.</margin>
In the city of Synnada <note>original: "Spinnada"</note> in Phrygia Pacatiana <note>A province in the west-central part of modern-day Turkey.</note>, there was a bishop named Theodosius. He persecuted the Macedonians <note>A Christian sect, also known as Pneumatomachians, who denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note>, who were numerous there. He did not only drive them out of the city but also quite cruelly out of the countryside, even though the Church of the true believers was not accustomed to persecuting anyone. He did this not out of zeal for the true faith, but out of a love for money. He armed everyone against them, the Clergy as well as the provincial judges, and he especially unsettled Agapitus, their Bishop. And when he considered the provincial judges insufficient to carry out his persecution, he traveled to Constantinople to obtain help from the Governors.

<margin>Agapitus, the bishop of the Macedonians, accepts the *homoousios* faith with his followers and becomes Bishop of Synnada.</margin>
While Theodosius was occupied there for such reasons, Agapitus, the Bishop of the Macedonians, decided to take the better path. Along with his entire body of Clergy, and calling together all the people under his leadership, he advised them to accept the faith of <term>Homoousios</term> <note>From the Greek *homoousios*, meaning "of the same substance," the orthodox doctrine that the Son is of the exact same essence as the Father.</note>, or of Consubstantiality.

This having been done, he went very quickly with a great multitude—indeed, with nearly the entire city—to the church of the Christians. Having offered a prayer, he took the seat in which Theodosius used to sit. Then he united the people, and by teaching the doctrine of Consubstantiality, he secured the Church of Synnada.

After these things had happened, not long afterward, Theodosius returned with the help of the Governors. Unaware of what had taken place, he went quickly to the Church. Being driven out from there by everyone, he traveled back to Constantinople. He recounted to Bishop Atticus what had been done against him and how he had been unjustly driven from his bishopric. Atticus, understanding the benefit that had come to the Church through this event, comforted Theodosius with words, telling him he should endure it with patience. Placing the common welfare above private or individual interests, Atticus wrote to Agapitus telling him to keep the Bishopric and to not think of or worry about the hostilities of Theodosius.
<margin>Theodosius the bishop is not received by his own.</margin>

->#### How a Jew who was Lame was made healthy through baptism.<-

<column-break/>

### The 4th Chapter.

This is then one of the profitable things which occurred in the church during the time of Atticus. At this time, there was no lack of occasions for miracles or for making people healthy. For a certain Jew who was lame had lain in bed for many years. When he had been helped by many medicines and the prayers of all the Jews had achieved nothing, he finally fled to the grace of Christian baptism, commending himself to it as the truest medicine for his paralysis.

This was very quickly announced to the bishop. Now, when this Jew had become a <term>Catechumen</term> <note>From the Greek *katekhoumenos*, a person receiving instruction in the principles of the Christian religion with a view to baptism.</note>, or a Christian student, and had placed his hope in Christ, Bishop Atticus commanded that he should be carried in his bed to the baptismal font. But as soon as the lame Jew had received Baptism with true faith and was lifted from the font, he immediately became healthy, and his infirmity departed from him. The power of Christ demonstrated this art even in our own times, whereby many of the Pagans, believing, have also been baptized. But although the Jews call for signs, they were not yet stirred to faith by these things. This having happened among the Christians, it was disregarded by many [Jews], and they remained in their malice. And not only did the Jews set themselves against such a miracle, but their followers were of the same opinion.

->#### Of the arch-heretic Sabbatius and his followers.<-

### The 5th Chapter.

Sabbatius then (of whom we have spoken before), as he did not wish to remain in his priestly ordination, sought the Bishopric. At the same time, he departed from the church of the Novatians <note>A rigorist sect that refused to readmit those who had lapsed during persecutions.</note> because he did not want to observe the feast of Easter according to the Jewish custom. He held meetings and collections in opposition to Sisinnius, his Bishop, at a place in the city called Xerolophon, where the market of Arcadius is; and there he set a dangerous matter in motion.
