For on the feast day, during the reading of the Gospels where it is written: "And it was the Passover of the Jews," he dared to add to it something that has never been heard or written anywhere else, namely: "Cursed is he who keeps the Passover without unleavened or sweet breads." <note>Sabbatius, a former Jew turned Christian priest, was attempting to re-introduce Jewish customs into the Christian celebration of Easter.</note>

When this was heard, it spread among the people. The simple and plain laypeople among the Novatians <note>A rigorist Christian sect that followed the teachings of Novatian.</note> came to him, having been deceived; but that evil did not remain unavenged.

Indeed, this wicked deed of falsifying the Word of God came to a bad end. For not long afterward, when he wished to celebrate the Passover feast and many gathered there to keep the vigils and watches according to custom, a subtle and devilish fear fell upon them, as if Sisinius <note>The mainstream Novatian bishop of Constantinople who opposed Sabbatius.</note> had come against them with a great force. Thus, a great riot arose in the night, and as they were in a narrow place, they trampled one another and drove each other out, so that over seventy people died there.

<margin>Sabbatians.</margin>

### ¶ How Christianity was introduced among the Persians by Bishop Maruthas.

### The 8th Chapter.

<margin>Bishop Maruthas sent on a special mission to the King of the Persians.</margin>
At that time, the Christian faith was spread among the Persians for the following reasons. Many embassies were sent back and forth between the Persians and the Romans for various reasons. It then happened, for a certain cause, that Maruthas, the Bishop in Mesopotamia (whom we have mentioned before), was sent by the Roman Emperor <note>Likely Theodosius II</note> to the King of the Persians. This King, finding great honor in Maruthas, regarded him as a divine man. This greatly displeased the Magi <note>Zoroastrian priests and advisors to the Persian throne</note>, who feared he would advise the King to embrace the Christian faith. For when the King had been tormented for a long time with a severe headache and the Magi could not help him, Maruthas delivered him from the pain through his prayers. For this reason, the Magi devised a deception. Because the Persians always show divine honor to fire, the King was accustomed to humbly worshiping a perpetual burning fire in a certain house. The Magi hid a man beneath the earth at the time when the King was known to call out:

<margin>The deception of the Magi.</margin>
"Cast the King out, for he has acted impiously by wishing to hold a priest of the Christians in honor!" Hearing this, Isdegerdes <note>Yezdegerd I, King of Persia, reigned 399–420 AD</note>, the King of the Persians, although he held Maruthas in high regard, nevertheless sought to be rid of him. But Maruthas, a man who truly feared God, prayed to the LORD without ceasing, through which prayer he discovered the deception set up by the Magi. Coming to the King, he said: "O King, do not let yourself be deceived, but go out with me, and when you hear the voice, have them dig there, and you shall find the cause of the deception; for fire does not speak, but it is a human contrivance."

Being moved by this, the King of the Persians went back into the place where the fire that is never extinguished was kept. And when he heard the voice, he had the place dug up. There they found the one who was thought to have spoken the divine

<column-break/>

voice. Therefore, the King became so enraged that he ordered the lineage of the Magi to be reduced by a tenth part. This having happened, he told Maruthas that he might build churches however he wished. From that time on, Christianity grew and increased among the Persians. Then Maruthas returned from Persia to Constantinople. Not long afterward, he was sent back there again. And the Magi tried once more to prevent the King from receiving him. They created a foul stench where the Emperor <note>meaning the Persian King</note> had to pass or go by, and they blamed it on the Christians, as if they had done it. But since the King held the Magi in suspicion or distrust, he inquired into the matter diligently and understood that it had been done by them once again. He therefore punished many of them and held Maruthas even dearer, and showed more heart toward the Romans, accepting their peace. Thus, the King almost became a Christian.

There was also another miracle performed by Maruthas and Ahaathum <note>original: "Ahaathum," likely Abdas of Susa</note>, the Bishop of the Persians. For they both delivered the King's son from a troublesome devil by driving it out through prayer and fasting. Afterward, when Isdegerdes died before he had become a Christian, the kingdom came to his son, in whose time the treaty that existed between the Romans and the Persians was broken.

When he could no longer endure his prosperity and good fortune—though he did not yet strive for the Empire itself—he marched toward the lands of the West, leaving the city of Constantinople; and when he arrived in Illyricum, he turned everything upside down. # ¶ Of Celestine the Roman Bishop, and how he persecuted the Novatians, and of Sabbatius.

### The 1st Chapter.

<margin>Celestine, Bishop in Rome. Persecution of Novatians in Rome.</margin>
**M**eanwhile, Celestine was ordained Bishop in Rome, who also destroyed the churches of the Novatians <note>The Novatians were a rigorist Christian sect that refused to readmit those who had lapsed during persecutions; they were often treated as heretics by the state church.</note> and forced their Bishop, named Rusticola <note>original: "Rusticulum"</note>, to hold his assemblies in secret. <column-break/>

### ¶ How Christianity was introduced 
### among the Persians by Bishop 
### Maruthas.

->The 8th Chapter.<-

<margin>Bishop Maruthas sent by the Emperor on a mission to the King of the Persians.</margin>
At that time, the Christian faith was spread among the Persians for the following reasons. Many various embassies were sent back and forth between the Persians and the Romans. It then happened, for certain reasons, that Maruthas, a Bishop in Mesopotamia (of whom we have spoken before), was sent by the Roman Emperor to the King of the Persians. This King, finding great reverence in Maruthas, regarded him as a godly man. This greatly displeased the Magi <note>The Magi were the hereditary priests of Zoroastrianism, the state religion of Persia, who often held significant political power.</note>, who feared he would advise the King to embrace the Christian faith. For when the King had been tormented for a long time with a headache, and the Magi could not help him, Maruthas delivered him from the pain through his prayers. For this reason, the Magi performed a certain deception. Since the Persians always show divine honor to fire, the King was accustomed to humbly worship a burning fire in a house without ceasing. 
<margin>Deception of the Magi.</margin>
The Magi hid a man underground at the time when the King was wont to worship; they commanded him to cry out: "Cast the King out, for he has acted impiously by choosing to honor a priest of the Christians!" Hearing this, Isdegerdes <note>Yazdegerd I, King of the Sasanian Empire (reigned 399–420 AD).</note>, the King of the Persians, although he held Maruthas in high regard, nevertheless sought to be rid of him. But Maruthas, a man who truly feared God, prayed to the LORD without ceasing, through which prayer he discovered the deception plotted by the Magi. And having come to the King, he said: "O King, do not be deceived, but go out with me, and when you hear the voice, have them dig there, and you shall find the cause of the deception; for the fire does not speak, but it is a human invention."

Being moved by this, the King of the Persians went back into the place where the fire—which was never extinguished—was kept. And when he had heard the voice, he had the place dug up. There they found the one whom they thought had spoken with a 

<column-break/>

divine voice; therefore the King became enraged, so that he had the caste of the Magi reduced to a tenth of their number. This having happened, he told Maruthas that he should build churches however he wished. From that time on, Christianity grew and increased among the Persians. Then Maruthas returned from Persia to Constantinople. And not long after that, he was sent back there again. The Magi tried once more to prevent the King from receiving him. They created a foul stench where the Emperor <note>original: "keyser," referring here to the King/Shah of Persia</note> had to pass or go by, and they blamed it on the Christians, as if they had done it. But since the King held the Magi in suspicion or mistrust, he inquired into it diligently and understood that it had been done by them again. For this reason, he punished many of them and held Maruthas all the dearer, and became more concerned for the Romans, and accepted peace with them. Thus the King almost became a Christian.

Another miracle also occurred through Maruthas and Abdas <note>original: "Abaathum," likely Abdas of Susa</note>, the Bishop of the Persians. For they both delivered the King's son from a troublesome devil, driving it out through prayer and fasting. Thereafter, when Isdegerdes died before he had become a Christian, the Kingdom came to his son, in whose time the treaty <note>original: "tverbodt," referring to the peace treaty or covenant</note> that was between the Romans and Persians was broken.

# The Second Part. The 11th Book. Folio 473.

<margin>Alaric, prince of the Goths, arrives at Rome</margin>
...and having held a battle at the river Hemon near Nicopolis in Epirus, the Thessalians struck down nearly 3,000 of his men. They also tortured the Senate with various torments. In mockery of the Roman Empire, they made a man named Attalus <note>Priscus Attalus, a puppet emperor installed by Alaric in 409 AD.</note> Emperor, whom they made to walk as an Emperor one day and serve as a servant the next.

When Alaric had done this, he fled very subtly when a rumor arose that Theodosius <note>Theodosius II, the Eastern Roman Emperor.</note> had sent his military forces—a rumor that was not a lie, but the truth, for the soldiery arrived. It is said that when Alaric marched toward Rome, a venerable man who was a monk warned and admonished him not to attempt such a thing, and that he should not rejoice in slaughter or the shedding of blood. But he answered: "I do not travel to Rome of my own will, but there is one who troubles me every day and compels me, saying: 'Proceed and lay waste to the city of Rome.'" But let enough be said of this.

# Tripartite Ecclesiastical History <note>The *Historia Ecclesiastica Tripartita* is a famous medieval history that combined the works of three earlier Greek historians—Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret—into a single Latin narrative.</note>

### Folio 474.

<margin>The Christians are harassed not by the law, but by spectacles.</margin>
Very many of the Jewish people, when they read, were not occupied with hearing the Law: but rather with viewing the spectacles <note>original: *schouspelen*, referring to theatrical performances or public games which were often flashpoints for communal violence</note>. This day was the cause of the dispute for both sides. And although this was somewhat remedied and improved by the Governor of Alexandria,

nevertheless, the Jews of the other party remained. And since they were always hostile toward the Christians, they fought all the more strictly against their pantomimes <note>original: *Pantomimus*; these were popular masked performers who enacted silent mythological stories, often sparking intense fan rivalries</note>.

<margin>Orestes, Governor of Alexandria. They used to call the ordinances and statutes of the people "Politiam." Hierax, a schoolmaster.</margin>
At that time, the Governor of Alexandria, Orestes, established a public festival, which is called "Politiam" <note>original: *Politiam*, likely referring to civic administration or public ordinances regarding these games</note>, in the theater where some devoted friends of Cyril were also present, desiring to see the Governor's good disposition and ordinances. Among them was one named Hierax, a Doctor and Master of the Youths, a very sincere friend of Cyril, who was accustomed to making some applause and pastime during his explanations. When the Jewish people saw Hierax upon the stage-wagon, they cried out against him, saying that he had come upon the stage-wagon for no other reason than to stir up an insurrection among the people. But Orestes, having long hated Cyril’s pride, had Hierax seized and openly beaten upon the stage-wagon.

<margin>The Jews kill the Christians through false treachery.</margin>
When Cyril heard of this, he called together the principal men of the Jews and warned them, as was fitting, that they should no longer create disturbances against the Christians. But the Jewish mob, regarding this as an insult, undertook even greater things against the Christians. And having given each other a sign—that every one of them should wear a ring of palm leaf upon their finger—they fought thus against the Christians.

On a certain night, they sent out some of their own who ran through all the streets of the city, crying out that the Church of Alexandria was on fire. Therefore, the Christians ran together from everywhere to extinguish the fire. But the Jews, knowing nothing of it <note>meaning the Christians were unaware of the trap</note>, murdered them, recognizing one another by the sign of the ring, and thus spared each other. But when it became day, they could not remain hidden. Cyril, being moved by these causes, went with a very great multitude into their

<margin>The Jews driven out of Alexandria.</margin>
Nevertheless, the Jews 
were cast out of their synagogues or schools, which were torn down, and the Jews were driven out of the city; and he commanded the people that they should plunder and take their goods and property. Thus, the Jews who had lived there since the times of Alexander 

<column-break/>

the Macedonian were driven out quite naked and scattered everywhere. But when Adamantius, a renowned physician in Constantinople, arrived and promised to become a Christian, he thereafter traveled to Alexandria. The Governor of Alexandria, Orestes, was very sorrowful because he saw the city, once so populous and full of people, so suddenly become entirely empty and deserted.

<margin>Orestes and Cyril become hostile toward one another.</margin>
Therefore, he also related to the Emperor what had happened: but Cyril likewise did not keep silent before the Emperor regarding the ugly deeds of the Jews. And through the pressure of the people, he desired the friendship of Orestes. And when the Governor would not accept the words of friendship, Cyril held the Gospels before him <note>as a symbolic gesture of peace and Christian duty</note>. And when he was still not moved by this, this happened once again: some of the monks living on Mount Nitria <note>a famous center of early Christian monasticism in the Egyptian desert</note>, who were loyal to Theophilus because he had unjustly stirred them up against Dioscorus, gladly took up the struggle for Cyril. And leaving their monasteries, about 500 of them came into the city; and as the Governor was driving through the city in a wagon, they cried out after him that he was an idol-worshipper, a servant of idols, and a pagan. And as he believed that this was done by Cyril's arrangement, he cried out and said: "I am a Christian, and was baptized by Atticus in Constantinople." And as they paid no heed to these words, one of them named Ammonius threw a stone at the Governor’s head, so that he was immediately covered in blood; and as the city officials fled, avoiding the violence of the stone-throwing, he remained there alone with only a few. In the meantime, the people ran together to avenge the harm done to the Governor. And they captured Ammonius and beat him so long that he died. Very soon thereafter, this was made known to the Emperor, and Cyril took the body of Ammonius and buried him in a church, and gave him another name, "Thammasius" <note>From the Greek word for "wonderful" or "admirable"</note>, so that people would believe he had died not for his guilt, but for the name of Christ; and he had him praised and honored as a martyr. But those who well knew that he had received a just punishment for his evil deed accused Cyril greatly. But the discord between Orestes and Cyril did not rest there, for thereafter other things followed.

# The Second Part. The Sixth Book.

### ¶ Concerning Hypatia the Philosopher / how she was murdered in Alexandria.

#### The XII. Chapter.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Hypatia.</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
There was in Alexandria a woman named Hypatia, the daughter of Theon the Philosopher, who was so learned that she surpassed all the philosophers of that time. She followed Plotinus <note>original: "Platino"; Hypatia was a Neoplatonist who headed the school in Alexandria that traced its tradition back to Plotinus.</note> in the Platonic school and explained all the philosophical lessons. Therefore, everyone came running to her, because they trusted such fine teaching was to be found with her. She also appeared before the Magistrates and felt no shame in dealing with men, for everyone held her in honor because of her wisdom.

<margin>C</margin>
Then hatred was kindled against that woman: for because she went often to see Orestes <note>original: "Horestem", the Roman Governor of Alexandria</note>, the people of the Church believed that she prevented Orestes from maintaining friendship with their Bishop <note>Cyril of Alexandria</note>. Therefore, the men formed a mob and a conspiracy, being incited by anger, and they had a leader named Peter the Reader <note>original: "Petrum Lectorem"; a "lector" was a minor clerical rank responsible for reading scriptures</note>, waiting for the woman as she was returning to her home.

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>The Christians put the honorable Hypatia the philosopher to death.</margin>
And they took her from her carriage and dragged her forward to the church named Caesarea. Having stripped the clothes from the honorable woman, they stoned her to death <note>original: "met steenen dootgheworpen"; other historical accounts specify she was killed with "ostraka" or pottery shards.</note>. Afterward, they dismembered her and burned her limbs in the place called Cinaron. This matter stirred up no small hatred against Cyril and the Alexandrian Church. For among Christians, it was not the custom for murders or battles to be found.

<margin>E</margin>
This happened in the 4th year of the Bishopric of Cyril, when Honorius for the 10th year and Theodosius for the 6th time were Consuls <note>original: "opper-Raetsheeren"; the high officials used to date the Roman calendar</note>, in the month of March during Lent.

### ¶ How the Jews were punished because of their insolence.

#### The XIII. Chapter.

<margin>F</margin>
Very shortly thereafter, when the Jews again dealt very unjustly with the Christians, they were punished. In the place named Inmestar <note>original: "Imenskar"</note>, which is located between Chalcis and Antioch in Syria, the Jews used to hold frivolous games.

<column-break/>

And being inflamed with drunkenness, they began to blaspheme the Christians and even Christ himself, mocking the Cross and those who put their trust in Him who hung upon it. And having taken a Christian child, they hung him on a Cross. At first they mocked and laughed at the child, but afterward, having become insane with rage, they killed the child with blows.

<margin>G</margin>
<margin>The Jews against the Christians</margin>
Therefore, a great conflict arose between the Christians and them. And when the Governor <note>original: "Lantvooght"</note> learned of this, he ordered the Judges of the provinces that such authors and instigators should be sought out and punished. And thus they received the rightful vengeance for their evil deed.

### ¶ Of the Jew who was baptized many times / and how the water was taken away by the power of God.

#### The XIV. Chapter.

<margin>H</margin>
<margin>The Jew who is often baptized.</margin>
Until this time, there was a deceptive Jew who, pretending to be a Christian, was frequently baptized, and through this deceit gathered much money. When he had in many ways and in many places deceived the sect of the Arians and the Macedonians <note>Arianism and Macedonianism were early Christian movements deemed heretical by the mainstream church for their views on the nature of the Trinity.</note>, he finally came also to the orthodox Church.

<margin>I</margin>
<margin>Fasting before Baptism.</margin>
When he was now ordered to fast, and he still had many days to observe, he began to hurry so that he might receive the gifts of baptism with a seemingly sincere heart. Everything was prepared for the baptism, including a garment that befits the baptized.

<margin>K</margin>
And when the font <note>original: "badt", literally "bath"</note> was filled with water, the Jew was led to the baptism. Then the invisible power of God took the water away.

<margin>L</margin>
And when those who were present, not thinking of the power of God, supposed that the water had run out through the drain, they stopped the drain very diligently and filled the font again. And when the Jew was again led to the baptism, the water was taken away a second time.

<margin>M</margin>
Then the Priest said: "O man, what evil work have you done? Have you used baptism unknowingly?" And as many people of various sorts ran together because of this matter, one of them recognized the Jew, whom he had seen receiving baptism from Atticus <note>Bishop Atticus of Constantinople</note>. And thus his deceit became known to everyone.

# ¶ How Bahram, King of the Persians, persecuted the Christians / and was defeated by the Romans.

### The XV. Chapter.

<margin>Bahram, King of the Persians after Yazdegerd.</margin>
**A**fter Yazdegerd <note>original: "Isdegerdes"; refers to Yazdegerd I.</note>, the King of the Persians, had died / his son Bahram <note>original: "Barrabanes"; historically known as Bahram V or Bahram Gur.</note> succeeded him. This man, incited by the Magi <note>original: "Magos"; the priestly class of Zoroastrianism in Persia.</note>, oppressed the Christians with many torments. And when the Christians were thus oppressed by the Persians, they fled to the Romans / seeking their assistance. Atticus the bishop <note>Atticus was the Bishop of Constantinople from 406 to 425 AD.</note> accepted them very gladly / and helped them as much as was possible for him. He reported to Emperor Theodosius <note>Theodosius II, the Eastern Roman Emperor.</note> what had happened there. At that time, there was also another cause that provoked the Romans and made them embittered against the Persians. For the Persians did not wish to return the gold miners <note>original: "Goutgravers"; this refers to a diplomatic dispute over Roman laborers who had been contracted to work in Persian mines.</note> whom they had received from the Romans for pay. Also, they had taken by force the burdens and goods of the Roman merchants. Along with this incivility followed the complaint of the Christians who had taken flight to Rome. So the King of the Persians immediately sent out ambassadors / and demanded his fugitives back: But the Romans by no means wished to give back those who had come fleeing to them. Not only because they were prepared to receive and protect those who prayed so humbly: but also because they were willing to suffer everything for the sake of Christendom. And they therefore preferred to take up war / rather than give back the Christians / whom they knew would be ruined and put to death. Thus a cruel war arose / as the treaty was broken in such a way, of which it will not be unnecessary to recount a little.

<margin>Ardaburius, the commander under the Roman people.</margin>
Then the Roman Emperor sent an army there / over which the Master of the Soldiers <note>original: "Ridt-meester"; literally "riding-master," but here referring to the high military rank of Magister Militum.</note> Ardaburius <note>Ardaburius was a prominent general of Alan descent serving the Eastern Roman Empire.</note> had the principal command. He, having marched into Persia through the Armenian borders, overran the entire province of Arzanene <note>original: "Aramenisen".</note>. There, Narses <note>Narses was a Persian general under Bahram V.</note>, the captain of the Persians, met him with a small troop of people. And when they fought, he was defeated. This having happened / Narses intended to take Mesopotamia, a province of the Romans / while it was without a guard / and thus to take revenge on the

<column-break/>

Romans. But the Field-Commander of the Romans knew his counsel well. For having overrun Arzanene <note>original: "Azazenam".</note> with haste, he himself arrived in Mesopotamia. And therefore, even though Narses had a great army of soldiers / he was unable to enter the lands of the Romans. But coming to Nisibis <note>original: "Nisibim"; a vital frontier fortress city between the Roman and Persian empires.</note>, a city in Persia lying on the frontiers / he sent word to Ardaburius / that he should appoint the day and place of the battle. But he gave this as an answer to those who were sent:

Go and tell Narses / that the Roman emperors will not fight when you wish / but he has sent his army / placing his trust alone in GOD / and that by often praying to God / help comes quickly; this can be understood from what follows. For when a great commotion arose in Constantinople because of the war / the Angels of GOD allowed themselves to be seen / by those who were going through Bithynia toward Constantinople / commanding that they should pray with trust / and believe that the Romans would achieve victory / saying further that they were sent by God as mediators of the war. Hearing this / it gave good courage not only to the city / but also to the soldiers. And when the army from the land of Armenia had come into Mesopotamia / the Romans trapped and besieged the Persians at Nisibis / making towers of wood / and raising them against the old city walls, they killed many people who fought against them from the ramparts. But when Bahram, the King of the Persians, understood / that they had overrun Arzanene / and had trapped and besieged his people at Nisibis / he provided himself with a great army / and wished to go against them. And being in awe of the power of the Romans / he called for the help of the Saracens <note>original: "Sarracenen"; referring to the Arab tribes allied with the Persians, specifically the Lakhmids.</note> / over whom at that time Al-Mundhir <note>original: "Alamundarus"; Al-Mundhir I, king of the Lakhmids.</note> was king, a strong man and also a warrior. He promised victory to the King of the Persians / because he had many thousands of Saracens / and he said he would also deliver Antioch in Syria to him / but it did not happen as he intended. For God alone struck a shameful fear into the Saracens / so that they themselves thought the Romans were chasing them. And being very terrified / and not knowing where to flee / they all threw themselves armed into the river Euphrates. Where more than 100,000 men were killed and perished.

Historia Ecclesiastica Tripartita.

### How Barrabanes, King of the Persians, persecuted the Christians and was defeated by the Romans.

#### The XV Chapter.

<margin>Barrabanes, King of the Persians, after Issegerdes.</margin>
**A**s soon as Issegerdes, King of the Persians, had died, his son Barrabanes <note>Historically known as Bahram V (r. 420–438 AD).</note> succeeded him. This man, incited by the Magi <note>Zoroastrian priests who held significant influence in the Sassanid court.</note>, oppressed the Christians with many torments. And when the Christians were thus oppressed by the Persians, they fled to the Romans, seeking their assistance. Atticus, the bishop <note>Atticus was the Bishop of Constantinople from 406 to 425 AD.</note>, received them very gladly and helped them as much as was possible for him, recounting to Emperor Theodosius that which had occurred there. At that time, there was also another cause that provoked and embittered the Romans against the Persians: for the Persians would not return the gold miners <note>original: "Goutgravers"; likely referring to Roman subjects who worked in Persian mines under contract.</note> whom they had received from the Romans for payment. Also, they had taken the loads and packs of Roman merchants by force. Following this rudeness came the complaint of the Christians who took their flight to Rome <note>The author uses "Rome" here to refer to the Roman Empire/New Rome (Constantinople).</note>. Immediately, the King of the Persians sent out envoys and demanded his fugitives back; but the Romans would in no way return those who had come fleeing to them. They were prepared not only to receive and protect those who prayed most humbly, but also to suffer everything for the sake of Christendom. They therefore preferred to take up war rather than give back the Christians, whom they knew would be ruined and destroyed. Thus a cruel war arose, as the treaty was broken; of which it shall not be useless to relate a little.

The Roman Emperor then sent an army, over which the primary command was held by the Master of the Horse, Ardabur <note>original: "Ardurus"; a prominent general of Alan descent serving the Eastern Roman Empire.</note>. Having marched into Persia through the Armenian borders, he overran the province of Arzanene <note>original: "Aramenisen / Azaxenam"; a region on the frontier between the Roman and Persian empires.</note>. There, Narseus, the captain of the Persians, came against him with a small troop of people; and when they fought, he was defeated. After this happened, Narseus intended to seize Mesopotamia, a province of the Romans, while it was without a guard, and thus 

<column-break/>

<margin>Ardabur the captain under the Roman people.</margin>
avenge himself upon the Romans. But the Field-Captain of the Romans well knew his counsel. For having overrun Arzanene in haste, he himself arrived in Mesopotamia. And therefore, even though Narseus had a great army of warriors, he was unable to enter the lands of the Romans. But coming to Nisibis <note>A vital frontier fortress city in Mesopotamia.</note>, a city in Persia lying on the borders, he sent word to Ardabur that he should appoint the day and place of the battle. But he gave this as an answer to those who were sent:

"Go and tell Narseus that the Roman emperors shall not fight when you wish; for he has sent his army, placing his trust alone in GOD, and that by often praying to God, he quickly receives help; this can be understood from what follows." For when a great commotion arose in Constantinople because of the war, the Angels of GOD allowed themselves to be seen by those who were traveling through Bithynia <note>A region in modern-day Turkey, near Constantinople.</note> to Constantinople, commanding that they should pray and believe with confidence that the Romans would achieve victory, saying further that they were sent from God as mediators of the war. Having heard this, it gave a good courage not only to the city but also to the soldiers. And when the army had come from the province of Armenia into Mesopotamia, the Romans shut in and besieged the Persians at Nisibis, making towers of wood; and having repaired the old city walls, they killed many people who fought against them from the ramparts. But when Barrabanes, King of the Persians, understood that they had overrun Arzanene and had shut in and besieged his people at Nisibis, he strengthened himself with a great army and wished to come against them. And marvelling at the power of the Romans, he called upon the help of the Saracens, over whom at that time Alamundarus was king <note>al-Mundhir I, the king of the Lakhmids and a Persian ally.</note>, a strong man and also a man of war. He promised the King of the Persians the victory, since he had many thousands of Saracens, and promised he would even deliver Antioch as "food" <note>original: "Antiochiam spijse soude leveren"; likely a boastful metaphor meaning he would conquer the city easily or provide it as a prize.</note>; but it did not happen as he intended. For God cast a shameful fear into the Saracens alone, so that they themselves thought the Romans were chasing them. And being greatly terrified, and not knowing where to flee, they all threw themselves, fully armed, into the river Euphrates. There, more than 100,000 men were killed and perished.

### Of Eudoxia, the wife of Theodosius, and of the praise of Theodosius.

->The XVIII. Chapter.<-

<margin>The Panegyrics, that is, the poems of praise for the young Emperor Theodosius.</margin>
Because God had given the Romans victory and triumph, many eloquent men described the praise and glory of the Emperors. Also, the Emperor's wife made many poems in heroic verse <note>Referring to Homeric centos or epic poetry, as Eudoxia was a highly educated poet.</note>, for she was very eloquent, being the daughter of Leontius the Sophist of Athens, and trained by her father in all manner of arts. When the Emperor desired her as his wife, Atticus the bishop brought her to the Christian faith.
<margin>Athenais Eudoxia.</margin>
And in baptism (whereas she was previously named Athenais), he gave her the name Eudoxia. Thus, many desiring to be held in some regard displayed their eloquence and described imperial praise and honor. But I, not seeking to be held in any

<column-break/>

regard, nor to display any eloquence, shall seek to recount the Emperor's good deeds with truth, which it would be a shame to keep silent.

Firstly, he was born and raised in Constantinople, and there was nothing loathsome about him. But he was so wise that when he deliberated or held conversation with anyone, it seemed that he possessed the experience and proof of all things within him; he could well endure both heat and cold. He fasted often, and especially on Wednesdays and Fridays, and that out of love for the Christian life. The Court seemed to be nothing other than a monastery: for in the morning, going to his sisters, he praised God. He also knew the Holy Scriptures by heart. When the Bishops spoke, he answered them as one who had been a priest for a long time. He gathered the books of Holy Scripture and all those who had written any interpretations upon them, doing more than Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>The Pharaoh of Egypt credited with commissioning the Septuagint and expanding the Great Library of Alexandria.</note> had done. In patience and gentleness, he surpassed all men. For although the Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate, the last pagan Roman Emperor.</note> was called a Philosopher, nevertheless he could not endure the shame and injury of the people of Antioch: but he inflicted great torments in his wrath. But Theodosius, comforting himself with the Syllogisms <note>original: "Sillogismos", logical arguments</note>—that is, the methods of arguing of Aristotle—practiced philosophy in deed, conquering wrath, drunkenness, and lust, and desiring in no way to avenge himself for anything. When he was asked by one who was familiar with him and held his company why he never put to death any of those who did him wrong or injury, he said: "Oh, that I could also raise the dead." And when another asked him about the same matter, he said: "It is no great thing that one who is a man should die; but to call back to repentance one who has died through sin, that is possible for God alone." He was so long-suffering and compassionate that whenever someone had done something worthy of death, he did not reach the gate of the city to die before a pardon followed immediately after. Once when the Emperor had come to the theater <note>original: "schouhuyps" (playhouse/amphitheater)</note>, the people cried out that the Emperor should let a cruel beast fight against a certain man; but he said: "Do you not know that we are also accustomed to delay with long-suffering?" So godly was he that he honored all those who were dedicated to God, but principally those who were of a devout life. It is said that when the Bishop of the Chersonese died at Constantinople, he...

# The Second Part. The XI. Book. Fol. 477.

He sought out a very old and simple garment and clothed himself in it, hoping that he might obtain some of the fervor of the deceased <note>The text likely refers to the Emperor wearing the hair shirt or humble cloak of a deceased ascetic to channel their holiness.</note>. Once, when there was a great storm and he was waiting at the circle <note>term: circle; originally "circkel," referring to the Hippodrome or the Great Circus where public spectacles and chariot races were held.</note>, the storm intensified as the place filled with people, and a great downpour fell. When this happened, the Emperor made his will known and had a crier announce that it would be better to abandon the spectacle and that everyone should pray to God together so they would not be harmed by the present tempest.

When this was said, they all prayed to the **LORD** with great joy, singing hymns of praise in unison. The entire city sang together as if it had been a single church. In their midst stood the Emperor, dressed in simple clothes, leading the singing. And he was not disappointed in his hope: for immediately the air cleared into beautiful weather, and the year became abundantly fruitful in all crops. Whenever wars arose, he took refuge in God just as David did, knowing that God has power over war, and he conquered his enemies with prayers.

### ¶ How John the tyrant was defeated in the Western lands.

#### The XVIII. Chapter.

<margin>* This answer is given in the German edition thus: "Do you not know that I am accustomed to eating simple and human things?" and he thus brought the people to gentleness.</margin>
A very short time thereafter, when Honorius had died after the Persian war, in the year when Asclepiodotus and Marinianus were the chief councilors <note>The consuls of the year 423 AD.</note> in the month of August, I shall relate how he conquered the tyrant John <note>Joannes, a high-ranking civil servant who seized the Western throne after Honorius died.</note> (commending himself to God). For just as it happened to the Hebrews under Moses when crossing the Red Sea, so his captains found it when he sent them against the tyrant. For when the Emperor Honorius was dead (as we have said) and Theodosius knew of it, he kept it secret. By speaking of other things, he removed the suspicion and opinion of many. Meanwhile, he sent a captain to Solonas <note>Salona, an ancient city in Dalmatia.</note>, a city in Dalmatia, so that if any disturbance of war arose concerning the Western lands, he could come to the aid of those nearby.

When this was done, he made known the death of his

<column-break/>

<margin>John, the first of the Emperor's secretaries, a tyrant.</margin>
uncle. In the meantime, John, the first among the Emperor's secretaries (unable to bear his good fortune any longer), reached for the Empire and sent ambassadors to Emperor Theodosius, desiring that he should accept his emperorship. But the Emperor threw the legates into prison and sent the captain Ardaburius, who had labored much among the Persians. Coming to Salona, he traveled from there by ship toward Aquileia; and it happened that the wind was against him, so that he fell into the hands of the tyrant. When he had captured him, John hoped that Theodosius would be forced by necessity to make him Emperor if he wished to ransom and free the captain. When the Emperor heard this, he was very afraid that some harm would come to Ardaburius. But Aspar, the son of Ardaburius, when he understood that his father was captured by the tyrant and that many thousands of barbarians were ready to help the tyrant, did not know what to do. But through the Emperor’s prayer, he conquered: for an angel of the Lord, in the form of a shepherd, led Aspar and all those who were with him. And through a pool or marsh that lies by Ravenna, they came to the place where they desired to be. For the tyrant living in the city had his camp and army there, because it is said: that no one has ever passed through it. Then God made the land that was not passable so that one could go through it. For going through the dried-up pool or marsh and finding the gates of the city open, they captured the tyrant. Then the godly Emperor showed the reverence he had for God. For while he was waiting for the people at the games in the circle, the news came to him that the tyrant was slain. He then gave a speech or exhortation to the people: "Let us go, if it pleases you, to the church; and leaving this which we have before us, let us offer songs of praise and thanksgiving to the Lord, whose hand has thwarted the tyrant's purpose." Having said this and leaving the games, they collectively gave thanks and moved together toward the church, so that the whole city seemed to be nothing else but a church. And when they came to the place of prayer, they thanked the Lord the entire day.

## The twelfth Book of the History called the Tripartite Ecclesiastical History, compiled from Sozomen, Socrates, and Theodoret, etc. <note>The *Historia Ecclesiastica Tripartita* is a famous medieval textbook of church history that combined the writings of three 5th-century Greek historians: Sozomen, Socrates Scholasticus, and Theodoret of Cyrus.</note>

### On the birth of Emperor Valentinian, who was a son of Placida.

->The First Chapter.<-

And when the tyrant <note>This refers to the usurper Johannes, who had seized power in the West after the death of Honorius.</note> had been killed, Emperor Theodosius considered to whom he might entrust the governance of the land in the West. At that time, Valentinian <note>Valentinian III, who reigned as Western Roman Emperor from 425 to 455.</note> had been born quite young to Placida <note>Galla Placidia, the daughter of Theodosius the Great.</note>, his mother,

<column-break/>

and daughter of the Great Theodosius, sister of Arcadius and Honorius, and from Constantius <note>The OCR reads "Constantino," but the historical figure was Constantius III, husband of Galla Placidia.</note>, who had received the Empire from Honorius and had ruled with him for a short time.

Now, this Valentinian, his sister's son, he made Emperor, and he sent him to the regions of Italy, and he also sent his mother Placida with him, and entrusted the governance of the entire realm to her. And as he himself also wished to travel to Italy, to bring his sister's son to the Empire and to overthrow the insolence of the tyrants with his strength, while coming to Thessalonica, he was hindered by illness.

### ¶ On the noble works of Atticus, Bishop of Constantinople.

## The 2nd Chapter.

<margin>B</margin> **B**ut Atticus managed the affairs of the Church with wonderful wisdom, and stirred the people to a virtuous life through his teachings. And <margin>Chrysostomians.</margin> when he saw that the Church was divided, <margin>C</margin> because the Johannites <note>The "Johannites" were followers of John Chrysostom who refused to recognize his successors after his exile.</note> held their assemblies separately, he commanded that John should be remembered and mentioned in the Prayers, just as was done for all other Bishops who had fallen asleep. He hoped that through this he would bring many back to the Church. He was so mild and liberal that he not only provided for the needy <margin>D</margin> of his own parishes, but also sent much money to other surrounding cities for the sake of the poor; for in sending to Calliopus, the Priest of the Nicene church, three hundred gold coins, he wrote thus:

->Atticus wishes Calliopus salvation in the Lord.<-

<margin>E</margin> **I** understand that there are 10,000 needy and hungry in the city, who out of mercy ought to be helped by the godly. But when I say 10,000, I mean a great multitude, not specifying a certain number, as I now perceive that this number has been received from the hand of the generous, and he gives this with proper distribution. And it now so happens that there are some needy who are in want and are also unable to earn or obtain anything. Therefore, my most beloved head, please take these 300 gold coins and distribute them as you please, <margin>F</margin> and principally to those who are ashamed to <margin>Care for the poor, even if they are not of our faith.</margin> ask, and not to those who, for the sake of the belly, cling to the beggar's bag. And in that case, do not look at their religion, but have regard for one thing only: that you feed the needy, and do not consider whether or not they are one with us in the understanding of the faith. Such care <margin>Emperor Valentinian.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>G</margin> Atticus had for the needy who were situated far away. He also labored to take away the superstition of some. For when he heard that the Novatians <note>A rigorist Christian sect that had split from the main church in the 3rd century.</note> followed the Jewish Passover feast and had separated themselves for the sake of the Sabbath; and that also the body of [Sabbatius] from the island of <margin>Rhodes.</margin> <margin>H</margin> Rhodes, where he had died, had been brought away, and that many prayed at his grave; he ordered the body of Sabbatius to be carried to another grave and hidden.

<margin>I</margin> And when they had come there as usual to pray, and found that the grave had been dug up, they no longer frequented that place. He was very diligent regarding the names of places and cities: for when he found a harbor gate at the entrance of the sea, which is called the <term>Pontus Euxinus</term> <note>The Black Sea.</note>, which of old was named <term>Pharmacos</term> or <term>Pharmacea</term> <note>Meaning "poisonous" or "associated with sorcery."</note>, he changed the name and <margin>K</margin> called it <term>Therapia</term> <note>Meaning "healing" or "service."</note>, so that when assemblies were held and preaching occurred there, they would not be named by a slanderous name. For the same reason, he also named another gate <term>Chrysopolis</term> <note>Golden City.</note>, which is situated at the Bosporus. Many of the ancient writers mention this, of which city Xenophon says in the first book of the <term>Hellenica</term> <note>original: "Helladicorum"</note>: That Alcibiades built walls around it and established <margin>L</margin> it so that one would cross there from the Pontus, and that they should pay tithes there.

When Atticus saw the place on the other side of Chrysopolis, which was pleasant and beautiful, he said: One should call it <margin>Argyropolis.</margin> <note>Silver City.</note> And thus this place retained the name. When some said to him that the Novatians should <margin>M</margin> not hold assemblies in the city, <margin>The Novatians are not so very evil.</margin> he answered: You do not know what they suffered with us under the persecution of Constantius and Valens, who are also witnesses of our faith: for when recently the Church was divided, they did nothing new regarding the faith. And when he once came to Nicaea to ordain a Bishop, he saw Asclepiades, the bishop of the Novatians, <margin>N</margin> who was very old, and asked him how many years he had been in the Bishopric? When he answered 50 years, Atticus said: You are a blessed man, having for so long a time taken care for a good work. Furthermore, <margin>Novatus is praised, but the Novatians are not.</margin> he said: I praise Novatus, but not the Novatians. Then Asclepiades said: O Bishop, why do you say that? Then Atticus answered: [I praise the man but not the sect]. <note>The text cuts off here, but the historical sentiment is that Atticus respected the character of the founder Novatus while disagreeing with the schism of his followers.</note>

¶ Therefore I praise him, because he did not wish to maintain fellowship with those who had sacrificed <note>Refers to the "lapsi," Christians who had made sacrifices to pagan gods under threat of persecution.</note>; I would have done that very thing myself. ### ¶ Concerning the ordination of Sisinnius and his character, and how Proclus, having been ordained for Cyzicus, was not received.

### The 3rd Chapter.

<margin>The prevailing voice in the election.</margin>
But when the Emperor Theodosius returned from Thessalonica, he did not find the body of Atticus, for it had been buried a day before the Emperor entered the City. Shortly thereafter, on the 18th day of October, news reached him that Valentinian had become Emperor. But upon the death of Atticus, a great dispute arose over the ordination of a Bishop; for one man wanted this candidate, and another wanted someone else. Some wanted Philip the Priest; others wanted Proclus, who was also a Priest. But all the people desired with a single hand <note>Meaning they were unanimous in their choice.</note> to have Sisinnius ordained, who was also a Priest, but had not been ordained in any church within the city, serving only in the suburb called Oliva; this place is situated near the city, and the day of the Ascension of our Savior 

<column-break/>

is held there with great honor. All the laity chose this man because of his reputation, and principally because he performed deeds of virtue toward the poor beyond his means. Thus the voices of the Laity prevailed, and Sisinnius was ordained bishop on the 28th day of February, when Theodosius was supreme Counselor for the 12th year, and Valentinian the Younger for the 2nd year. Philip the Priest, in whose place Sisinnius was chosen, greatly slandered the ordination of Sisinnius in a book entitled *Christian History* comprising 36 books, speaking ill of the one ordained and those who had ordained him, and principally of the Laity. For this Philip had been ordained a Deacon by John <note>Referring to John Chrysostom, the famous Bishop and orator.</note>; he also wrote much against the Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate, the last pagan emperor.</note>, but it seems to me that his History does not have much order to it, and brings little profit to the readers. Now when Sisinnius was ordained, it happened that the bishop of the Cyzicenes <note>The people of Cyzicus, an ancient town in modern-day Turkey.</note> died. Then Sisinnius ordained Proclus to Cyzicus. But before Proclus could set out for Cyzicus, the citizens came and chose Dalmatius the Monk as their Bishop, paying little heed to the rule which forbids any ordination to take place without the bishop of Constantinople. The Cyzicenes neglected this because they believed this rule had been adopted only for the person of Atticus. So Proclus remained without having his own church. Yet he was very famous for his teaching in the church at Constantinople. Thus Sisinnius, after he had been in the Bishopric for 2 years, died while Hiericus and Ardaburus were supreme Counselors, on the 24th day of the month of December. He was a man of great chastity and honor, very famous for his life, who was very sociable without any deceit and a stranger to all strife; therefore he was also held by sharp-nosed <note>An idiom for critical or fastidious people.</note> and watchful men to be a heavy man <note>Meaning dull or lacking in vigor.</note>, and one who could accomplish nothing.

Since many desired Philippus, and even more desired Proclus, it was deemed best to call a stranger from Antioch. There was a man named Nestorius, a native of Germanicia <note>original: "Germanicer" — referring to the city of Germanicia in Roman Syria, rather than Germany.</note>, who possessed a fine voice and was eloquent; therefore, they called him, believing him well-suited to teach.

<column-break/>

<margin>Anthony of the Cedonians <note>The "Cedonians" likely refers to the Macedonians, a sect that denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note> slain.</margin>
Delaying no longer, they turned to a very evil deed; for they sent out a man, and had him stand behind him, as was right, and thus they killed Anthony. This event gave Nestorius cause for further persecution; for he convinced the Emperor, and advised him, that their Church should be taken away from them. Therefore, their Church in Constantinople was taken from them, which

<margin>The churches are taken from the Macedonians</margin>
was situated before the old wall of the city; and also the Church in Cyzicus, and in many other places, just as the churches in the Hellespont were, from which some who held to the faith of Consubstantiality <note>original: "Consubstantialiteyt" — the Nicene doctrine that the Son is of the same substance as the Father.</note> joined themselves to the [main] churches. But as the scripture says: A drunkard does not lack wine, nor a contentious man strife:

<margin>Anastasius the priest.</margin>
So it also went with Nestorius, who loved persecution; for it happened that he continually persecuted the Church of God. With him was ordained Anastasius, a priest from Antioch, whom he held in very great honor, and in all matters he used him as a Counselor. When Anastasius was teaching the people in the Church at one time, he said: "That your honor should not say that Mary had given birth to God, or was the Mother of God <note>original: "Gods Moeder" — a translation of the Greek 'Theotokos'.</note>,"

<margin>God has no mother</margin>
because Mary was a human being, and that God should be brought forth from a human being is entirely impossible. When this was heard, it stirred up many of the clergy and laity together; for they were taught from above that they should confess that Christ was God. And that He should in no way, according to the dispensation as a man, be separated from God; for they believed

<margin>2 Cor. 5:16</margin>
that even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know Him so no more: Therefore, leaving now the speaking of Christ [according to the flesh], let us proceed unto perfection. When there (as I have said) an uproar had arisen in the Church, Nestorius—not wishing to punish the one he held in great honor as a blasphemer, but much more confirming his reasoning—frequently taught from it in the church. And when he with great

zeal drove this reasoning or question, he rejected this phrase (Mother of God, or She who gave birth to God), from which a schism arose in the church. And as if they were in a night-battle, they now agreed with one side, now the other, forsaking their own words. Many thought and held the opinion of Nestorius: that he held that Christ was only a pure man, and that he wanted to bring the teachings of Paul of Samosata and Photinus <note>Early Christian heretics who were accused of teaching that Jesus was merely a human who became divine, rather than God incarnate.</note> into the

<column-break/>

church. But therefrom a great dispute arose, and such a great disturbance, so that a general Synod <note>The Council of Ephesus, 431 AD.</note> assembled. But as I read the books of history, I find what this man felt, and have looked into it in Truth: I also wish to speak it out, without favor to one or malice to the other. It does not seem to me that Nestorius followed Paul of Samosata, nor Photinus. Also, it does not seem to me that he held that Christ is only a pure man, but that he had a dread of this phrase, as one who was very anxious. And that this sprang from the fact that he was not properly or sufficiently learned: but he thought, because he had a natural eloquence, that he was learned, and he did not wish to read through the books of the ancient interpreters, and thought that he was better than all others. Not knowing that in the Epistle of John, which is called Catholic <note>The "General" or "Universal" Epistles.</note>, it is written in the old copies: "Every spirit that denies Christ is not of God." This meaning they have taken out of the old copies—those who wished to separate the Divinity of Christ from the Humanity. Therefore, the old Interpreters or translators noted that some have corrupted this verse, wishing to separate the Divinity from the humanity; for the humanity followed the Divinity, and they are also not two, but one.

Because of this, the ancients did not shy away from calling Mary the mother of God, or saying that God was born of Mary. For Eusebius Pamphili <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History."</note>, in the third book of the Life of Constantine, said: "That God, whom He gave to us, was willing to be born for our sake, and the place of His birth in the flesh is called Bethlehem by the Hebrews." Therefore also that friend of God, the Empress Helena, adorned the place where the Mother of God gave birth with memorable ornaments, so that the Holy Cave was very finely decorated.

Origen <note>A prolific early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) whose works were later controversial.</note> also, in the first part of the Epistle of Paul to the Romans, says: "How she is called the Mother of God, mark that more broadly." From this it is manifest that Nestorius did not know the writings of the ancients. Therefore, as I have said, he hung only upon those words, and honored and then denied the word *Deipara* <note>Latin for "God-bearer," equivalent to the Greek 'Theotokos'.</note>, and thus denied that He who was born was GOD. But we confess that He who was born of the holy Virgin and crucified is a LORD of glory and of all honors, as the Apostle says.

<margin>B</margin> the subsistence <note>original: "selfstandicheydt" — referring to the theological concept of 'hypostasis' or the distinct personhood of the Word.</note> of the Word of God anywhere: but maintains everywhere that it has a subsistence or self-standing nature, and is a being that has an essence; he does not deny it, as Photinus and Samosata do, by saying it exists nowhere. No small disturbances have arisen in the world because of these weak and reckless arguments and the disputes of Nestorius.

<margin>The servants of the barbarian lords in the churches finally kill themselves.</margin> <margin>C</margin> In the meantime, it happened that a hideous deed took place within the church. <margin>D</margin> and were ready to avenge themselves and strike back, allowing no one to come near them. When this had occurred, a man passed by who prophesied that such an evil deed boded no good for the church; and he spoke the truth, for it signified 
<margin>E</margin> the schism of the people, and the deposition of the one who was the cause of the schism.

### ¶ Of the Council of Ephesus against Nestorius.

#### The 5th Chapter.

<margin>The Council at Ephesus regarding Nestorius.</margin> <margin>F</margin> **N**ot long thereafter, the bishops from all places were required by the command of the Emperor to gather together at Ephesus.
<margin>G</margin> So then Nestorius, with a great multitude, came to Ephesus shortly after Easter. And he found that very many bishops were gathered there. But Cyril of Alexandria delayed for a time, and arrived around Pentecost. 

<column-break/>

On the fifth day after Pentecost, Juvenal, the bishop of Jerusalem, arrived; but as John <note>John, the Bishop of Antioch, who supported Nestorius.</note> delayed in coming, the bishops who were present began to consider the question. Cyril, the Bishop of Alexandria, had prepared some summaries or short accounts from the books of Nestorius, wishing to stir him up, for he was his enemy, and said: Nestorius, although many confess that Jesus is God, yet I do not confess that God is double-bodied or triple-bodied. <note>original: "tweelyvich of dyplyvich" — likely a polemical phrasing regarding the union of the two natures of Christ.</note>

<margin>Nestorius is condemned.</margin> <margin>I</margin> and therein condemned Cyril, and with him Memnon, the bishop of the city of Ephesus.

But Cyril and Juvenal, wishing to avenge themselves on John, also condemned <note>original: "verdoet" — likely meaning deposed or excommunicated.</note> him. While they were thus entangled with one another, and Nestorius noticed that this would cause great damage, he called Maria the Mother 
<margin>L</margin> of God, saying: "Let Mary be called the Mother of God, and let that which brings dispute be taken away." But no one could believe that he said this out of any true remorse: therefore he was from that time condemned and, being 
<margin>Oasis, a wilderness.</margin> <margin>M</margin> banished, he had to live in Oasis. <note>Oasis refers to the Great Oasis of Hibis in the Egyptian desert, a common place of exile for political and religious prisoners.</note> This then is the end of this Synod, which occurred when Bassus and Antiochus were the chief Councilors <note>referring to the Roman Consuls for the year 431 AD</note>, on the 28th day of June.

### ¶ How many Bishops have been moved from one church to another.

### The 8th Chapter.

<column-break/>

But since some said it was against the ordinance of the Church for Proclus to be bishop at Constantinople because he had been ordained at Cyzicus, I will therefore recount a little, for it does not seem to me that they spoke the truth about him. Rather, they prevented it either out of spite or out of ignorance of the ecclesiastical ordinances, which have often occurred in the churches. Eusebius Pamphilus <note>Also known as Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History."</note> relates in the 6th book of his *Ecclesiastical History* that Alexander was the bishop in a city in Cappadocia; when he had come to Jerusalem to pray, he was held by the citizens of that city and placed in the stead of Narcissus the Bishop. And thereafter he ruled in that church all his life long. Thus, the bishops among the ancients moved without distinction from one church to another when the profit of the church so required. One must add the rule here, so that men may see that they have not spoken the truth, but rather prevented Proclus from being installed. If a bishop is ordained to a church or parish and does not go there where he is ordained (not that it is his fault, but because the people will not receive him, or for some other reasons of great necessity), he shall only exercise himself in service and honor, and not meddle with the affairs of the Church where he keeps his assembly, and await a successor, according to what a Provincial <term>Synod<note>original: "Synood" — A council of church leaders gathered to decide on matters of doctrine or administration.</note></term> shall judge thereof. This then is the rule. But that many bishops have moved from one city to another, as the necessity of the Churches in those times required, experience teaches; I will therefore set down their names hereafter. Peregrinus was ordained bishop at Poitiers. And because his citizens would not receive him, the Bishop of Rome commanded that he should be ordained in the capital city of Corinth, as the bishop there had died; and he was there as long as he lived. Gregory Nazianzen was first bishop of the city of Sasima in Cappadocia, and thereafter he came to Nazianzus. Meletius was first the Bishop of the Sebastenes, and thereafter at Antioch. Alexander, the bishop at Antioch, appointed Dositheus, the bishop of Seleucia, to Tarsus in Cilicia. Reverentius was moved from Arcis in Phoenicia to Tyre. John of Gordo in Lydia was moved to Proconnesus and was the presiding officer or Bishop in that same church. Palladius was moved from Hellenopolis to Aspuna. Alexander of Hellenopolis was moved from his place and appointed to Alexandria. Theosebius was from Apamea

# Ecclesiastical History in Three Parts. Folio 486.

[the things] that were promised: but they, being deceived by this hope, abandoned all their work. Leaving behind their goods and inheritances, they let whoever wished take them.

And when the day had now come which the deceiver had appointed for the Jews, as he went before them, they all followed him with wives and children. He led them thus to a cliff that hung over the sea, and commanded them that they should roll themselves off one after another like balls. The first ones did so. And when they came to the rocky cliff, they died instantly, being both torn by the sharp rocks and drowned in the water. More might have died there, had God not provided for them through the arrival of certain Christian men, who were fishermen and merchants, who pulled some who were nearly dead out of the water, comforting and encouraging them. And when they perceived their own folly, they forbade the others to kill themselves by rolling off, making known to them the deaths of those who had fallen first. They also understood the deception and punished themselves for having believed so lightheartedly.

And when they wished to destroy the Deceiver, they could not catch him: for he escaped from their eyes very subtly, and there was a great suspicion that it had been a wandering Devil clothed in human form. From this great misery, many of the Cretan Jews were converted to the Christian faith. <note>This event, occurring around 431 AD, involved a man claiming to be a reincarnation of Moses who promised to lead the Jews across the sea to Israel on dry land.</note>

### ¶ Of the great fire that occurred in Constantinople upon the death of Maximianus, and of the instruction of Proclus.

### The 10th Chapter.

<margin>The fire in Constantinople.</margin>
Meanwhile, a fire so great broke out in Constantinople that the like of it had never been before; for a great part of the city burned down, so that large buildings collapsed, and the fire reached as far as the water-house called Acilleum <note>original: "Acilleum" — Likely referring to a public cistern or bathhouse named after Achilles.</note>. And thereafter it reached a place called Pelargas <note>original: "Pelargas" — Greek for "The Storks," a district in the city.</note>, so that the church of the Novatians <note>The Novatians were a rigorist Christian sect that split from the mainstream church in the 3rd century over the treatment of those who had lapsed during persecutions.</note> was also

<column-break/>

caught in it. It is said that Paulus, their bishop, stood amidst the burning of the church, and [prayed] that God would not let their church be entirely burned, and so the place was delivered. And from that time on, a gathering is held there by the Novatians on the 17th day of August; this place has been held in honor not only by Christians but also by the Heathens from that time forward.

So Maximianus died, after he had governed the church for 2 years and 6 months, while Ariobindas and Aspar were consuls <note>This identifies the year as 434 AD.</note>, on the 12th day of the month of April, in the Great Week of the Fast <note>Holy Week/Passion Week before Easter.</note>, on Thursday. Then Emperor Theodosius ensured that no more uproar should happen in the church concerning that bishopric; for while the body of Maximianus was still upon the earth, and the Bishops were present there, he had Proclus ordained as a Bishop. This was also confirmed by letters from Celestinus, the Bishop of Rome, sent to Cyril, the Bishop of Alexandria, and to John at Antioch and Rufus at Thessalonica, saying: That it did not hinder or prevent anything if someone were or became a Bishop in another city. So then Proclus was brought in and buried the body of Maximianus. It is time that we say something of this Proclus.

### ¶ Of the life and manner of Proclus.

### The 11th Chapter.

Proclus became a <term>Lector<note>original: "Lector" — A reader; one of the lower orders of the clergy responsible for reading scriptures during services.</note></term> very early on, and also studied Rhetoric. And when he reached a more mature age, he spent much time with Atticus the Bishop and wrote down his words. And as he increased [in stature], he was ordained a Deacon by Atticus, and thereafter a Priest, and was ordained Bishop of Cyzicus after Sissinius. And all this happened to him first; thereafter he obtained the chair of the church at Constantinople. He was a man of good manners, and having been well-taught by Atticus, he followed him closely: but in Atticus more long-suffering was seen. And Atticus showed himself very disciplined and formidable at the appropriate time. But this man was much more friendly to all men, and sought to move them through kindness rather than through severity. Not wishing to be troublesome to any heresy, he followed Emperor Theodosius in this regard, for he did not wish to compel the guilty with Imperial power.

# The Second Part. The Twelfth Book.

Folio 487.

<margin>Maximianus the bishop of Constantinople dies</margin>
¶ This man <note>Referring to Bishop Maximianus, who was known for his peaceful nature.</note> did not care much whether there was anyone who did not feel toward God in the same way as he did. For this reason, the Emperor also praised him, because he followed the example of the true Priests. Here I say boldly that Theodosius surpassed all men in gentleness. Therefore, he also made his enemies obedient to him without war or struggle, as is evident with the tyrant John <note>John the Usurper, who seized the Western throne in 423 AD.</note> and afterward also with the Barbarians.

<margin>Proclus follows.</margin>
### Of the victory of the Romans against the Barbarians.

#### The 12th Chapter.

<margin>The Barbarians against the Romans</margin>
After the death and downfall of the Tyrant, the Barbarians <note>Specifically the Huns.</note> whom the Tyrant had called to his aid were quite ready to seize the land of the Romans. When the Emperor understood this, he committed the care of it to GOD the LORD, according to his custom. And as he gave himself to prayer, he quickly obtained what he had prayed for. What happened to the Barbarians, I shall now tell. Their captain, named <margin>Rugas.</margin> Rugas <note>original: "Rugas" (also known as Rugila or Rua, a King of the Huns).</note>, was struck dead by lightning. And a pestilence followed, by which the greater part of his people died; and that was not enough, but fire also fell from Heaven and consumed many of those who still remained.

Which matter drove the Barbarians into great <margin>Proclus.</margin> fear, because they saw that they had not only taken up arms against the Romans—the strongest of all People—but that they were also helped by the mighty GOD.

Then the Bishop Proclus preached a sermon before the Church from the Prophecy of Ezekiel regarding how they had been helped, and he was praised by everyone. And the words of this Prophecy are these: And you, son of man, <margin>Ezekiel 39:1.</margin> prophesy against Gog, and say: Thus says the LORD: Behold, I am against you, O Gog, you who are the chief in Meshech and Tubal; for I will judge him with death, and I will rain fire and sulfur <note>original: "Solpher" (brimstone)</note> over him, and over all who are with him; and shortly thereafter: And they shall know that I am the Lord. <margin>Theodosius’s gentleness.</margin>

<column-break/>

### How the daughter of Theodosius was given to Valentinian.

#### The 13th Chapter.

<margin>Eudoxia the daughter of Theodosius marries Valentinian.</margin>
God also showed the Emperor many other benefits because of his gentleness, among which this is one. He had a daughter by Eudocia who was named Eudoxia. Valentinian—his sister’s son, who had become Emperor before him in the lands toward the west—desired her as a wife. And when Theodosius had consented to this, he thought to hold the wedding halfway <note>original: "peuers" (likely meaning midway or together)</note>, and it seemed good to him that they should both come to Thessalonica.

In the meantime, Valentinian sent word to him that he should not trouble himself, and promised to come to Constantinople. When he had well-provisioned and garrisoned the ends of the Lands toward the West, he came to Constantinople for the wedding. And when it was held in the year that Isidoris and Senator were high Councilors <note>term: "opperste Raetsheere" (Consuls). Flavius Anthemius Isidorus and Flavius Senator were consuls in 436 AD.</note>, he took his wife and returned home.

### How the Body of John the Bishop was brought to Constantinople.

#### The 14th Chapter.

<margin>The body of Chrysostom is brought to Constantinople after 35 years.</margin>
Not long afterward, Proclus brought back to the church those who had separated themselves because John <note>John Chrysostom, who was deposed and exiled in 403-404 AD.</note> had been removed. And he thus soothed their sorrow with his wisdom. By command of the Emperor, he had the body of John brought to Constantinople thirty-five years after John was deposed—which had been buried in Comana—and, having announced it everywhere, buried it with great honor in the Church of the Apostles. This happened in the year when Theodosius and Honorius were high councilors for the 16th time, on the 18th day of January.

<margin>Paulus the Bishop of the Novatians dies</margin>
Paulus, the Bishop of the Novatians <note>term: "Novatiane" (A rigorist Christian sect following Novatian, who believed that those who lapsed during persecutions should not be readmitted to the church).</note>, died in the same year on the 20th day of July. While he lay sick, he did not abandon his usual manner of living or eating, nor his customary prayer. And when he was not far from death, he called all his clergy together and said: "Remember to choose a Bishop while I live, so that our churches suffer no more disturbance henceforth." And when they entrusted the matter to him, Paulus said: "Give me the transaction in writing, that you will choose the one whom I shall ordain."

Folio 488.

# Church History in Three Parts.

¶ And as they did this and subscribed / so he wrote the name of Martianus / and signed it: And he had the first Priests also sign this / and placed the writing with Marcus the Bishop of the Novatians <note>The Novatians were a rigorist Christian sect that followed the teachings of Novatian in the 3rd century; they were still active in the 5th century.</note> in Scythia, saying: If it happens that I remain alive / then you shall give that back to me. And if it happens that I die / then you shall <margin>Martianus follows</margin> find there the name of the one who ought to be ordained: days after his death they broke open the writing / and found the name Martianus therein. And as they considered the election good / they immediately without any delay sent to Cyzicus in Phrygia where he lived at that time. And when they found him there / they brought him to Constantinople / and ordained him Bishop / on the 21st day of the aforementioned Month.

## ¶ How Eudocia the Emperor’s wife traveled to Jerusalem.

### The 15th Chapter.

<margin>Theodosius Augustus sends his wife to Jerusalem.</margin>
**S**o then Theodosius, for the benefits that God had done for him / thanked the Lord. And with much reverence made his promise to Christ / and sent his wife <note>Empress Eudocia, wife of Theodosius II, known for her pilgrimage to the Holy Land in 438 AD.</note> to Jerusalem / for she also had desired to see her daughter in the state of Matrimony <note>Her daughter, Licinia Eudoxia, married Valentinian III, the Western Roman Emperor.</note>. She honored not only the churches at Jerusalem / but also all others that were in other places / as she traveled thither / and also as she returned.

->The end of the twelfth book of the Church History in Three Parts.<-

<column-break/>

## ¶ How Proclus made Thalassius the Senator a Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia by his own authority.

### The 16th Chapter.

<margin>Thalassius, a Governor at Caesarea, given as bishop.</margin>
**B**ut Proclus the Bishop did at the same time, in the 18th year when Theodosius was the supreme Magistrate <note>original: "opperste Raedtsheer" (Consul). In the Roman calendar, years were often identified by the serving Consuls.</note> / a wonderful work / such as none of the previous Bishops had done. For when Firmius the Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia had died / those of Caesarea came / and wanted to have a Bishop. And as he <note>Bishop Proclus.</note> considered whom he ought to give them as a Bishop: It happened that on the Sabbath day the Senators came to greet him fortunately: among whom was Thalassius, who had been the Governor <note>original: "Landtvooght" (Praetorian Prefect) of Illyricum.</note> of Illyricum. And as it was about to happen (as the rumor went) that he would become Governor of the Eastern lands / Proclus held him by force / and instead of the honor of the Governorship, he imposed upon him the Bishopric of the city of Caesarea.

This happened then in the Church. But we wish to make an end of our History here. Praying that all Churches may be governed with peace: You Holy man Theodore <note>likely referring to the person who commissioned or inspired the translation, or a reference to Epiphanius the Scholastic who translated the Greek sources into Latin for Cassiodorus.</note> / we have now fulfilled your command / making an end of our History in the second year of the 305th Olympiad <note>The Olympiad was a four-year period used in ancient dating; the 2nd year of the 305th Olympiad corresponds to roughly 439-440 AD.</note> / when Theodosius the Emperor was supreme Magistrate for the seventeenth time.

# Honorable Reader / you shall know
That this is not only an Index / but also almost a Concordance <note>A "concordance" is an alphabetical list of the principal words used in a book, often used for Scripture to find every instance of a term.</note> of all the most notable Cities / persons / and Matters / which shall all lead you further to the parts of the associated things / which shall serve as a Repository for seeking and finding various matters / and for coming from one to another: and to find things easily / you shall know / that the first number signifies / the Folio <note>A folio refers to a leaf of paper, where "a" usually denotes the front (recto) and "b" the back (verso).</note> on each side of the leaf / and each leaf is marked with dividing letters A/B/C/D/E every ten lines / and if the matters do not stand in the margins / and thus are difficult to find / we have indicated them with these Letters in the Text / and thus you are led here as if by the hand to each item / to find what you seek without great labor. Receive our labor in good spirit.
