<meta>This is the first page of the Appendix, introducing the history of the Reformation from 1517. It establishes the lineage of the movement from earlier reformers like Wycliffe and Hus to the humanists like Reuchlin and Erasmus.</meta>

# APPENDIX
->OR<-
# HISTORICAL
->And<-
# True histories
### of the Church of God / what has befallen
### the same in various Provinces / and espe-
### cially in France. Beginning from the
### Year 1517 to the Year 1556.

---

<margin>1517.</margin>
<margin>
John
Wycliffe.
Jan Hus.
Jerome of
Prague.

Johannes Reuchlin.
</margin>
When the time had come that God had ordained to draw His elect out of the superstitions that had gradually been introduced into the Roman Church: as well as to rekindle the light and the radiance of His truth, even though it had been driven away with fire and sword about a hundred years earlier, when <term>John Wycliffe</term><note>An English scholastic philosopher and theologian (c. 1320s–1384) who was a precursor to the Reformation.</note>, and after him <term>Jan Hus</term> and <term>Jerome of Prague</term>, had brought it into the world and offered it to mankind. The Lord God first raised up in Germany a learned man named **Johannes Reuchlin**, born in Pforzheim in the Margraviate of Baden: who was to bring the Hebrew language (which seemed to have been banished and rejected from all of Christendom) back into the light. Against this, the theologians of Cologne and Leuven set themselves with all their might. But God so broke their purpose that Reuchlin was acquitted at Rome by public sentence, and the study of the Hebrew language was approved and confirmed: the Lord thereby showing that He knows how to use even the enemies of His Church for His service.

<margin>
Conrad
Pellicanus.
Johannes
Oecolam-
padius. Se-
bastian
Münster.
Johannes
Capito.
Paul
Fagius.
Erasmus of
Rotter-
dam.
</margin>
From this school of Reuchlin came forth many distinguished men of the High German nation: such as **Conrad Pellicanus**, **Johannes Oecolampadius**, **Sebastian Münster**, **Wolfgang Capito**, **Paul Fagius**, and a great number of other learned men.
In other places, studies also began to flourish, even at Leuven. And from there, around that time, **Erasmus of Rotterdam**, a Dutchman, came to Paris; he brought the Latin language, as if out of great darkness, into a beautiful

<column-break/>

<margin>1517.</margin>
light. And already **Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples** <note>original: "Iacobus Fabri van Stapelen"</note> in Picardy, a Doctor of the <term>Sorbonne</term><note>The theological faculty in Paris, known at this time for its fierce traditionalism and opposition to the Reformation.</note>—though worthy of better company—seeing that the University of Paris had completely turned into a terrible, barbaric ignorance and sophistry, had begun to restore the <term>liberal arts</term><note>original: "goede Consten"</note>; even laboring to show and correct the faults of the common translation of the New Testament <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> from the Greek text. This so displeased the ignorant Sorbonne Doctors, and especially two "blunt beasts" of that time, namely **Beda** <note>Noël Bède</note> and one called **de Quercu** <note>Guillaume du Chesne</note>, who were then the heads and the principals of this Faculty, that they did not cease until they had chased this distinguished man away, just as Erasmus, who had lived there for a time, also had to depart. Nevertheless, barbaric ignorance then received such a heavy blow that from then on, it declined more and more. What is more, **Pope Leo X**, who authorized Erasmus’s Latin translation of the New Testament—instead of the "dear masters" of Paris condemning the same as heretical—mostly because of certain Latin *Colloquies* (or Dialogues) <note>Erasmus's *Colloquia Familiaria*, a collection of dialogues on various subjects, often satirizing church abuses.</note> which he had written, in which he rebuked many abuses and gross superstitions, critiquing them with a wonderful, disguised cleverness. But a little while before, the House of **Medici** in Florence had received some learned men who were fugitives from Greece, just as they had also been well received in other places in Italy: such as, among others, **Argyropoulos**, **Marcus Musurus**, **Demetrius Chalcondyles**: and namely a very excellent person from the family

<margin>Leo X authorizes Erasmus’s translation</margin>

<summary>This page introduces the origins of the Reformation, crediting the revival of Hebrew and Greek studies by humanists like Reuchlin, Erasmus, and Lefèvre d'Étaples for breaking the "barbaric ignorance" of the medieval Church.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the history of the early 16th-century intellectual revival, focusing on the introduction of Greek and Hebrew studies in France as a precursor to the Reformation. It follows the previous page's discussion on German humanists like Reuchlin and Erasmus.</meta>

# Appendix, on the

<margin>
1517.
</margin>
of the Emperors of Constantinople / named **Janus Lascaris**, who had greatly advanced all knowledge of the Greek language in the high schools of Italy. Because of this, many Frenchmen also went there to study / who, having returned to Paris, each earnestly encouraged and gave heart to the study of this language. The **Sorbonne**<note>The theological faculty of the University of Paris, known for its traditionalist and often anti-humanist stance.</note> set itself against this with such fury / that if one had wished to believe the <term>Magistri Nostri</term><note>Latin for "Our Masters," a formal title for the doctors of the Sorbonne, here used to highlight their self-importance.</note>, to study Greek and Hebrew / would have been the greatest heresy in the world. But God, in turn, set against their madness men of such authority / that they / against their will / had to see the complete opposite of what they would have liked. These persons were **Stephanus Poncher**, Bishop of Paris / **Louis Ruzé**, Lieutenant in civil law / and one **Franciscus de Luines**, through whose help the study of languages began to flourish greatly / the Greek language itself being taught publicly by **Hieronymus Alexander**, an Italian / who later became a Cardinal / and by **Henricus Glareanus**, a Swiss / and another Frenchman named **Cheradamus**, being a man well-experienced in both the Hebrew and Greek languages / although he was somewhat light-minded and of little understanding. But among all the French scholars, the crown in the knowledge of the Greek and Latin languages was held by one **Guillaume Budé**—

<margin>
Guillaume Budé.
</margin>
—from one of the oldest families of Paris / who later became <term>Master of Requests</term><note>An important judicial and administrative official in the French royal court.</note>; he shone as exceptionally as a Sun among the stars / whom even the enemies of learning never dared to approach: seeing that, to tell the truth / scholars seldom troubled themselves with theology / so that it may rightly be said that they indeed prepared a path for those who followed / upon which they themselves did not wish to set a footstep. To return to Budé / he was so fortunate in his learning that he found and obtained a King of excellent and eminent understanding / who was a great lover of good letters / although he was experienced only in his mother tongue. This was **Francis the First** of that name / to whom Budé, having dedicated an excellent book / entitled *Commentaries on the Greek Language* / persuaded the King / that not only the <term>three languages</term><note>Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, considered the essential languages for biblical and classical scholarship.</note> (namely Hebrew / Greek / and Latin) and the good books written in the same / should be taught in the schools and universities of his Kingdom /

<column-break/>

but also that there should be appointed certain fine men who were named to him to teach in the Academy of Paris / provided with good wages / with the intention of founding a college of these three languages / with a good income / to maintain therein a good number of regents / and students. Nevertheless, regarding the building of such a college, it could never be brought to effect: but many good professors were indeed appointed / among whom the most prominent for the Hebrew language were **Agathius** / and **François Vatable**, to whom was also added / **Paulus Paradis**, who was a Jew by nation. For the Greek language / **Pierre Danès** / and **Jacques Toussain**; in Mathematics / **Oronce Finé**: so that in a short time thereafter the whole Kingdom found itself very well-served / the memory of this King in this matter becoming so renowned / that mostly for this reason he was given the surname of "the Great" by common accord.

All these things were but preparations of the great goodness and mercy of God / for a higher work as we shall soon hope / which appeared shortly thereafter: not that the wisdom of God revealed through His Holy Word has need of human wisdom: but because gross ignorance had entirely buried the knowledge of the languages / in which the mysteries of God are written / it was necessary either that God again in a moment gave the gifts of tongues to men / as He did to the Apostles / or that He again put into use the ordinary means to learn the languages / and to be able to read again the <term>inscription of the Cross of Christ</term><note>Referring to the 'Titulus Crucis' (INRI), which according to the Gospels was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.</note> / noting also that through the science of the three arts / many spirits were awakened / who then lay and slept.

At that time then, two persons were raised up by God / who truly were like two brave heroes to discover the abuses and superstitions of the Roman Church / the one in the land of Saxony / namely: **Martin Luther**, a Doctor in Theology / a monk of the Augustinian Order at Wittenberg, a capital city of the Duchy of Saxony: the other was **Ulrich Zwingli**, of the Canton of Zurich in Switzerland / whose deeds and writings / especially those of Luther / (who was the first who wrote) have awakened the whole world.

# iii
## Church History

<margin>1520.</margin>
...made, and that so subtly that it is almost beyond comprehension. Many were found who condemned these works; conversely, there were also those who bravely defended them with the sword of the Word of God—though this number, when compared to the opposition, was very small and almost nothing by comparison. For besides the fact that the entire Christendom of the Roman Church opposed them with all its power, the three greatest and most mighty kings of Europe—namely, **Charles V** the Emperor, **Francis I** the King of France, and **Henry VIII** the King of England—so bound themselves to the Pope that they left nothing undone that was in their power to denounce Luther and his books. But it is not my intention to recount this at great length, as **Sleidanus** and other writers have already done so fully. <note>Johannes Sleidanus (1506–1556) was the official historian of the Schmalkaldic League, famous for his detailed history of the Reformation.</note> Rather, I intend only to relate certain things that occurred especially in France to those who were afterwards called "Lutherans."

<margin>Martin Luther.</margin>
Luther, having begun to write against the Indulgences of the Crusade (as they called them) under Pope Leo X in the year 1517, later went even further, bringing to light a certain book that he titled ***On the Babylonian Captivity***. <note>original: "Vande Babylonissche gevagenisse" — referring to Luther’s *De captivitate Babylonica ecclesiae* (1520), which attacked the medieval sacramental system.</note> Because of this, the doctors of the **Sorbonne** were so agitated that they immediately condemned and declared him a heretic,

<margin>1521.</margin>
which occurred in the year 1521. They also caused a book to be published against him with the title *Anti-Luther*, or *Against Luther*, the author of which was **Josse Clichtove**, a doctor of the same Sorbonne. <note>original: "Judocus Clitoveus"</note> He had been a disciple of **Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples**, <note>original: "Iacobus Fabri"</note> but he did not follow his master's teachings well.

<margin>Ulrich Zwingli</margin>
At that time, the Bishop of Meaux was a fine man born in Paris named **Guillaume Briçonnet**. <note>original: "Guillielmus Brisanetus"</note> Notwithstanding the censures and the fury of the Sorbonnists, he was nevertheless inflamed with such zeal that he did not hesitate to use all his power to plant the teaching of the truth in his diocese, joining works of charity with the teaching of truth. He not only preached himself (which was then a very new thing), but he invited many excellent men to join him, both in godliness and learning, such as **Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples** (of whom we spoke before), **Guillaume Farel** (who was then a regent in Paris at the college named after Cardinal le Moine), **Martial Mazurier**, and **Gérard Roussel**, <note>original: "Martialis, ende Gerardus Ruffi"</note> both doctors, who bravely stood by him.

<column-break/>

<margin>1523.</margin>
However, not all stood with such steadfastness as would have been necessary. For soon thereafter, through the instigation of the **Franciscan Friars** <note>original: "Minne-broeders" (Minorites)</note> of Meaux, persecution was stirred up against them. This Martial, instead of strengthening the Bishop, caused him to lose heart. The outcome of this persecution was such that the Bishop ceased to go any further, and Martial openly retracted what he had previously so bravely stood for and defended; he later died as a Canon and Penitentiary of Paris. **Lefèvre** departed for Blois, and from there eventually to Nérac in the Duchy of Albret, through the intervention of the King’s only sister—afterwards the **Queen of Navarre**. <note>Marguerite de Navarre, a high-ranking protector of humanists and early reformers.</note> She was a princess of a wonderful and excellent spirit, who then seemed to have been raised up by God to break, as much as possible, the cruel counsel and intentions of **Antoine du Prat**, Chancellor of France, and others who violently incited the King against those they called heretics. As for **Farel**, after staying in Paris as long as he could, he later departed for Switzerland, where in time he performed wonderful service; for he was the first to gather and plant the first congregation of **Geneva**, along with many others in the surrounding country. Likewise, **Roussel** was protected by the aforementioned Queen of Navarre; he later produced some good fruit, though he never formally joined the Reformed Churches. Regarding the "sheep," it did not happen with them as it did with the "shepherds," for they all remained so steadfast that it was a great wonder. For the small congregation of Meaux (who were almost all craftsmen who earned their living with wool) not only served as an example and pattern of wonderful steadfastness to all the churches, but they also bore many others for the Lord, who were among the greatest. Indeed, she may boast that she offered up to God the firstfruits of the martyrs since this recent restoration [of the Gospel] in France.

The first martyr I speak of was **Jean Leclerc**, <note>original: "Ian de Clerck"</note> who was thrown into prison in Meaux in the year 1523 because he had posted certain writings on the gates of the great cathedral against certain indulgences; for this, he was very severely...

Jean Leclerc, the first Martyr.

There was also another named **Jacques Pavanes** of Boulogne, who had also come to Meaux at the desire of the Bishop. He was a young man, but well-learned and of great integrity. Being imprisoned, he was so misled by the aforementioned **Martialis** <note>Martial Mazurier, a doctor of the Sorbonne who initially favored reform but later recanted and pressured others to do the same.</note> that on the day after Christmas, he performed a public penance and showed regret. For this, he later felt such heartache and remorse, lamenting his instability with many tears and sighs, that he was arrested again. As a "relapsed heretic," he was burned alive in Paris with great steadfastness at the place called **La Grève** in the year 1525. <note>The Place de Grève was the principal site for public executions in Paris for centuries.</note> He was followed shortly after by one called the **Hermit of Livry**, a village on the road to Meaux. This man was burned alive with many ceremonies; for the largest bell of the city of Paris was rung with full force to stir up all the people of the entire city, who came running to the place in great crowds. To them, the Doctors cried out that he was a damned soul who was being taken to the fires of hell.

<margin>
Jacques Pavanes burned. 1525.
</margin>
All this occurred during the time that **King Francis I** lay imprisoned in Spain. <note>Francis I was captured by Emperor Charles V at the Battle of Pavia in 1525.</note> Having returned and understanding that the teaching they called "Lutheran" and "heretical" was increasing more and more (which people made him believe had brought the wrath of God upon him and his kingdom), he ordered, following the advice of the Chancellor **Antoine du Prat**, that from now on the investigation of the accusations against the Lutherans should immediately be assigned to all magistrates and judges, each in their respective places. This was because, said the Chancellor, the wickedness of blasphemy was mixed into it. For this reason,

<column-break/>

all the Parliaments <note>In France, "Parlements" were high courts of justice, not legislative bodies.</note> began to be violently inflamed, and especially that of Paris, through the petition of the Doctors **Béda** and **Quercu** <note>Noël Béda and Guillaume de Duchêne (Latinized as Quercus), staunch conservative opponents of the Reformation at the Sorbonne.</note> and their like. At that time, one named **Denis de Rieux**, born in Rieux in Muscianen, was also burned alive at Meaux because he had said that the Mass was an outright denial of the death and suffering of Jesus Christ. He remained firm in this until the last breath of his life; he was executed on July 3, 1528.

The following year, namely 1529, there was a nobleman named **Louis de Berquin**, a very learned man of good spirit. <insert>At that time, one was also [burned] alive at Meaux—</insert> <note>This insertion appears to be a repetitive fragment or a correction from the printer.</note> who had lived in Paris from the time that the land was still under the Parliament. After he had resisted the **Sorbonnists** for a long time, he was thrown into prison but released by good friends. However, the Doctors of the Sorbonne persecuted him unto death because of certain articles they had extracted from his books, so that he was finally accused anew and imprisoned. He was condemned to have his books publicly burned in his presence, and at that same place, he was to recant his heresy and be kept in eternal imprisonment for life, unless the King’s goodwill might dispense with it. Having refused to obey this, despite the representations his friends made to him, he was condemned by another decree to be hanged and strangled, and thereafter burned. He suffered this at the **Place Maubert** with such steadfastness that **Doctor Merlin**, then the Penitentiary of Paris, who had led him to the place, was forced to say aloud before all the people after his death that perhaps in a hundred years' time, no better Christian had died than Berquin.

The following night (the day before St. Martin's), God sent such a sudden frost that all the corn [withered], followed in many places by great famine and plague.

While Satan was thus playing his game in Paris, God was working throughout almost the entire Kingdom, making true that which was very well spoken by a Church Father: namely, that "the blood of the martyrs is like rich fertilizer for the Lord's vineyard," to make the same flourish more and better. <note>A paraphrase of Tertullian’s famous quote: "The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church."</note> This was demonstrated among other places in a French city called **Annonay** in Vivarais, under the government of Languedoc and the Bishopric of Viviers.

# Church History

<margin>1528.</margin> There was, in particular, a superstition in this city <note>Likely the city of Meaux, though transcribed here as "Monnap."</note> that was very prevalent at that time, which is worth noting to show posterity how much wickedness can prevail in man—and how, on the other hand, the mercy of God is abundant, especially where sin has been most abundant. One must know that in this city of Monnap there was a chest called **The Powers of the Saints**, for the people believed and esteemed it to be full of various holy relics. No one was allowed to see inside it, for it was hung so high, right up against the vault of the Temple, and the priests made the people believe that if anyone ever tried to look into it, they would be struck blind on the spot. <margin>A chest in Monnap called the Powers of the Saints.</margin> But on Ascension Day, this chest was lowered and carried in procession with many ceremonies and great solemnity. A great multitude of people—men, women, and children—came running from all sides, barefoot and in their shirts, considering themselves very fortunate if they could get near enough to kiss it or walk beneath it. Indeed, what is more, there was a time when, as the chest passed by the Castle, all the prisoners were set free, regardless of what crime they were guilty of—except for those they called "Lutherans."

In this poor city, I say, stuck in such darkness, God sent in the year 1528 a certain Doctor of Divinity, a Franciscan monk who had been in Germany and had heard Martin Luther himself, <margin>Stephanus Machopolis.</margin> named **Stephanus Machopolis** <note>Étienne Macopolis.</note>, who began to preach openly and freely against these abuses and other superstitions that were being discovered every day. He (who was immediately forced to leave) was followed by another of the same Order named **Stephanus Reineri** <note>Étienne Renier.</note>, who set himself against them even more vehemently. <margin>Stephanus Reineri.</margin> For this reason, he was also imprisoned, but remaining steadfast, he was burned alive at Vienne <note>Original: "Wiennen." Though it looks like Vienna, Austria, in this context it refers to Vienne in France, a common site for such executions.</note>, sealing the truth with his own blood. After him, the schoolmaster of the city continued, named **Jonas**, a man of great learning and godliness. Having been thrown into prison and having made a good and full confession there, he was nevertheless delivered from it by some good friends. Because of this, the Archbishop was so enraged that he had about twenty persons arrested and brought to Vienne, some of whom died of misery and ill-treatment; others were... <margin>Jonas, a schoolmaster.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>1528.</margin> ...finally released upon payment of certain fines.

At the same time, the Lord God also began to make the voice of His Word heard in **Orléans**, as well as in **Bourges** and **Toulouse**—three cities in which there were high schools and universities, and among the most prominent in France—so that these three were the fountains from which the holy little rivers flowed to all other places. As for Orléans (where **Petrus Stella** <note>Pierre de L'Estoile (1480–1537), a renowned French jurist.</note> was then Doctor and Regent in Civil Law, having a wonderfully large following and audience, for he was considered the most acute legal scholar in all of France), there were already some persons there who had knowledge of the truth. Among others were **Franciscus Danielis**, being an advocate, and **Nicolaus du Chemin**, who kept students in his lodgings. But it was of little account until **John Calvin**, born in Noyon in Picardy, arrived—then still a very young man of about 23 years, but even then chosen to be a <margin>John Calvin.</margin> precious instrument in the work of the Lord. Having come to Orléans to study law, he received this grace from God: that he spent his best time in holy Theology, in which he progressed so well in so short a time that, with knowledge joined to zeal, he wonderfully advanced the Kingdom of God. For he taught with a wonderful gravity, weighed with great learning, so that there was no one hearing him who was not brought to great wonder.

In that same time, **Andreas Alciatus** <note>Andrea Alciato (1492–1550), a famous Italian jurist who helped found the legal humanist school.</note>, a Milanese, was also Doctor and Regent at the University of Bourges. He was esteemed as the most learned and <margin>Andreas Alciatus.</margin> eloquent legal scholar of his time, so that people came running from all sides to hear him. This was the reason that Calvin also went there, finding some persons there who were instructed in the truth, among whom were some monks, Doctors of Divinity—namely, one **Johannes Chaponeau**, a monk of the Abbey of St. Ambrose, and **Johannes Michael**, of the Order of Saint Michael, who after that time preached freely enough. There also lived at Bourges a High German named **Melchior Wolmar**, a man of great learning, who, having come from Paris to Orléans, was finally <margin>Melchior Wolmar.</margin> chosen by the Queen of Navarre and Duchess of Berry to teach the Greek and Latin languages in her city. This he did with a wonderful skill, hav—

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>1528.</margin> ...having also with him some children of a high House <note>noble family</note>, whom he very successfully taught, not only the liberal arts, but also Godliness, as much as was then possible.

With these, John Calvin conferred many times; and through his encouragement, Calvin devoted himself to the study of the Greek language: something that served him very well thereafter, indeed for the benefit of the entire Church of God. During this time, Calvin not only strengthened the small number of believers who were in the City, but he also gave many Sermons in certain Castles and Villages where he was called, and especially at Ligneres, being very gladly heard and well received by the Lord and the lady of that place.

<margin>Toulouse, famous for commerce and study, but despised for superstition.</margin> Regarding the City of Toulouse, there have always been two things therein that made it very famous: namely, Commerce and the Study of Law. But the Parliament <note>The regional high court</note> there has always been held to be bloodthirsty. And the School <note>The University of Toulouse</note> cared little for the knowledge of languages; indeed, the city in general was very superstitiously filled with many kinds of Relics and other instruments of idolatry. It was enough to be condemned as a Heretic if one passed by an Image without removing one's hat, or if one did not fall upon one's knees when hearing the *Ave Maria* Bell: or even if one merely touched a piece of meat on a forbidden <note>fasting</note> day.

There was no one who had a desire for languages and good literature <note>Humanist studies</note> who was not spied upon and brought into suspicion of heresy. The arrival of that excellent Man, Julius Caesar Scaliger <margin>Julius Caesar Scaliger.</margin> (who was descended from a Noble and ancient family there named de L'Escale or Scaliger, which for a long time dominated and ruled in Verona, Vicenza, and other cities thereafter taken by the Venetians)—this excellent person, having lost all hope of being able to return to his estates, had at that time departed with Marcantonio Commeus, an Italian and the Bishop of the city of Agen. Scaliger served wonderfully well to awaken the good Spirits <note>intellectuals</note> of the land; for he had truly made his house much more Noble with his wonderfully great learning than any of his ancestors had done with Weapons. With learning also came the knowledge of the truth, as evidenced among others by one Jean de Caturce <margin>Jean de Caturce</margin>, born 

<column-break/>

of Limoux and a Licentiate in Law. He was accused of two crimes: the first, that he had given some Lutheran sermons and exhortations—as they said—in the City of Limoux on an All Saints' Day; the other, because on a Three Kings' Day <note>Epiphany</note>, in a gathering of friends, instead of the traditional shout, "The King drinks!" <note>A common folk tradition where a "king" was chosen by finding a bean in a cake</note>, he had them shout, "Christ reigns in our hearts!" Furthermore, instead of dancing and the usual wantonness of that day, he had certain passages of Holy Scripture brought forward after the meal for a Christian exercise.

Being imprisoned for this, he showed that his tongue was not imprisoned with him, answering very boldly and unabashedly to everything they asked him. Meanwhile, he had great friends who labored to release him, provided he would recant three points in a public lesson he was to give in the school. Having refused to accept this, he received the sentence of death, after he was first degraded from his tonsure <note>the ritual shaving of the head marking clerical status</note> and from his Licentiateship. This ritual lasted a full three hours, during which he had a good opportunity to defend himself openly before the people and to bring forth much good teaching to the wonderment of a great crowd, who were gathered for this spectacle in the square of Saint Stephen. During this deconsecration, a memorable thing happened: There was a Jacobin Monk <note>A Dominican friar</note> who had to give a sermon in the usual manner; he took his Text from the words of the Apostle in 1 Timothy 4: "The Spirit clearly says that in the last times some shall depart from the faith, and follow misleading spirits and the teachings of devils." And there he stopped without reading further. Caturce, hearing this, cried out loudly: "Go on in the text, go on!" At this voice, the Jacobin stood dumbfounded and stopped short; then Caturce said: "If you will not proceed, I shall do it myself," which he did immediately, adding these words of the Apostle: "Teaching these hypocrisies of lies, whose consciences are seared with a branding iron; forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from foods which God has created to be used with thanksgiving by the believers and those who know the truth." These words he also declared and explained at length before the people. From there he was led into the Palace, where he received the decree or sentence of death. And as he was led out from there to go to his death, he spoke these words very loudly in Latin: "O palace of wickedness, and seat of injustice!" <note>original: "O palatium iniquitatis, & sedes injustitiae!"</note>

<margin>1532.</margin> ...steadfastness. And so he had to suffer death, and was burned alive with a wonderful constancy, at the beginning of the month of June 1532.

At that time, some made profession of the Holy Gospel, including one called the Protonotary <note>A high-ranking official in the papal administration</note> of Armagnac. Because of this, and because of the learning he possessed, he was favored by the Queen of Navarre, who also obtained for him the Bishopric of Rodez <note>Original: "Rhodes," referring to the diocese in southern France</note>. He later became one of the great Cardinals and one of the greatest enemies of the holy Gospel. There was also at that time in Toulouse a Franciscan who preached at the place called *la Daurade* <note>The Basilica of Notre-Dame de la Daurade</note>; he was named de Nuptijs. He was well-favored by the same Queen, who also saved him in her city of Bourges when he was sought by the Parliament of Toulouse, but thereafter he did not do much good. Even worse was the raging Melchior Flavin, who also had to flee then and was a companion of de Nuptijs, though he was much younger in years. Some years after this, another monk came, also a Franciscan, named Marcij, who performed wonderful preachings at Castres and in Auvergne. For this reason, he was dragged to prison in Toulouse, where he testified and sealed with his blood the truth he had proclaimed.

<margin>A surgeon burned at Paris.</margin> In the following year, namely 1533, among others, a surgeon or master of medicine was burned in Paris. He was born in Manton near Annecy in Savoy and named Jean Pointet. He had been accused by some priests whom he was treating for the Pox <note>Syphilis, often cited by reformers as evidence of the failure of clerical celibacy</note>; he had shown them that these were the fruits of their cursed celibacy and the prohibition of marriage. For this reason he was seized, and remaining firm in his pure confession, he was condemned by sentence of the Parliament, first to be strangled and then burned. Later, because he would not fall upon his knees before an image in the chapel of the Conciergerie <note>The famous prison in Paris</note> where the prisoners were kept, he was condemned again to have his tongue cut out, and if he did not recant, to be burned alive—which he also endured with very great steadfastness.

<margin>Queen of Navarre favorable to the Christians.</margin> Meanwhile, during this tyranny, Margaret, Queen of Navarre, the only sister of King Francis I, did all she could to soften and move her brother the King; in this she did not labor in vain,

<column-break/>

<margin>1533.</margin> making use of one Guillaume Parvi, a Doctor of the Sorbonne <note>The prestigious theological faculty of the University of Paris</note>, Bishop of Senlis, and Confessor to the King. To please her—and not out of genuine zeal for Religion—he had the *Hours of Our Lady* <note>A common prayer book</note> printed in French, after he had removed from it everything that seemed to him too superstitious.

Afterward, she herself brought to light through the press a small treatise of her own work, written in French verse, with the title: **The Mirror of the Sinful Soul** <note>Original: "Den Spiegel van de sondighe Ziele"; French: "Le Miroir de l'âme pécheresse"</note>. In it were many passages that were not customary in the Roman Church, for no mention was made of the Saints, nor of merits, nor of any Purgatory other than the blood of Jesus Christ. Even the Latin prayer ordinarily called the *Salve Regina* <note>Hail Holy Queen</note>—a prayer to Mary—was adapted into French to the person of Jesus Christ. This greatly angered the Sorbonnists, and especially Béda <note>Noël Béda, a leading conservative theologian</note> and others of his temperament; so much so that they could not refrain from attacking the Queen with barbs in their sermons. <margin>Comedy played in the College of Navarre.</margin> But especially, they performed a comedy in the College of Navarre in which they depicted the good Princess as a hellish goddess; indeed, what is more, they condemned her book. She complained of this to her brother the King, which resulted in some of the performers of this comedy being imprisoned. And the King, wanting to know on what grounds the condemnation of this book was based, called upon the University, of which at that time the *Rector Magnificus* <note>The honorary head of the university</note> was one named Nicolas Cop. He revoked the condemnation of this book and the censure of the Sorbonnists, by which the fury of these masters was somewhat humbled and resisted, and the small number of believers was greatly strengthened.

<margin>John Calvin in Paris.</margin> At that time, John Calvin also came from his studies in Law and appeared in Paris, where he made great progress in the work of the Lord, not only teaching the truth, but also setting himself against the heretics whom the Devil already sought to thrust into the Church of God. 1528. having also with him some children of a noble House / whom he taught very successfully / not only in the liberal arts / but also in piety / as much as was then possible.

Regarding the City of **Toulouse** / there have always been two things therein that made it very famous / namely / Commerce / and the Study of Law: but the Parliament there / has always been considered bloodthirsty. And the School <note>The University of Toulouse</note> cared little for the knowledge of languages / and in general the whole City / was so filled with superstition and various Relics and other instruments of idolatry: that it was enough to be condemned as a Heretic / if one passed by an Image without tipping one's hat / or if one did not fall to one's knees / when hearing the *Ave Maria* <note>The Angelus bell</note> ring: Or even if one had merely touched a piece of meat on a forbidden day.

1532: Sept. And so he had to suffer death and was burned alive with a wonderful steadfastness at the beginning of the month of June 1532.

At that time, a certain man made a profession of the Holy Gospel, one called the Protonotary of Armagnac. Because of this, and due to some learning he possessed, he was favored by the Queen of Navarre, who also helped him obtain the Bishopric of Rodez. He later became one of the great Cardinals and one of the greatest enemies of the holy Gospel. There was also at that time in Toulouse a Franciscan who preached at the place named *la Daurade* <note>The Basilica of Notre-Dame de la Daurade in Toulouse</note>. This man was surnamed De Nuptijs; he was well-favored by the same Queen, who also protected him in her City of Bourges when he was sought by the parliament of Toulouse. However, he did not do much good afterward. Even worse is that raving Melchior Flavin, who also had to flee then and was the companion of De Nuptijs, though he was much younger in years. Some years after this, there came yet another monk, also a Franciscan named Marcij, who performed wonderful preachings at Castres and in Rouergue; for this, he was dragged to prison in Toulouse, where he testified to and sealed with his blood the truth he had proclaimed.

<margin>A Surgeon burned in Paris.</margin>
In the following year, namely 1533, a surgeon or master of medicine was burned in Paris, among others. He was born in Manson near Anjou in Savoy and named **Ioannes Pointet**. He had been accused by some priests whom he was curing of the "pox" <note>Syphilis</note>; he had pointed out to them that these were the fruits of their cursed celibacy and the prohibition of marriage. For this, he was seized, and remaining firm in his bold confession, he was condemned by the sentence of the parliament—first to be strangled and then burned. Later, because he would not fall on his knees before an image in the chapel of the Conciergerie <note>A prison in Paris, formerly part of the royal palace</note> where prisoners were placed, he was condemned again to have his tongue cut out and to be burned alive, which he endured with very great steadfastness.

<margin>Queen of Navarre favorable to the Christians.</margin>
Amidst this tyranny, **Marguerite, the Queen of Navarre**, the only sister of King FRANCIS, did everything she could to soften and move her brother the King. In this, she did not labor in vain,

<column-break/>

1533.
availing herself of one William Parvi, a Doctor of the Sorbonne, Bishop of Senlis, and Confessor to the King. To please her—and not out of genuine zeal for religion—he had the Hours of our Dear Lady printed in French, after he had omitted from them whatever seemed to him to be too superstitious.

Afterward, she herself brought to light through the press a small treatise of her own work, written in French verse, titled: *The Mirror of the Sinful Soul* <note>Original title: *Le Miroir de l'âme pécheresse*</note>. In it were many passages that were unusual in the Romish Church, for no mention was made of the Saints, nor of merits, nor of any Purgatory other than the blood of Jesus Christ. Even the Latin prayer commonly called the *Salve Regina* <note>Hail Holy Queen, a traditional Catholic hymn to Mary</note>—being a prayer to Mary—was adapted in French to the person of JESUS CHRIST. This greatly angered the **Sorbonne**, and especially Beda and others of his temperament, so much so that they could not restrain themselves from lashing out at the Queen in their sermons. They specifically performed a comedy in the College of Navarre in which they portrayed the good Princess as a hellish goddess; indeed, what is more, they condemned her book.
<margin>Comedy performed in the College of Navarre.</margin>
<margin>Navarre's book.</margin>

She complained of this to her brother the King, which led to some of the actors of this comedy being imprisoned. The King, wanting to know on what grounds the condemnation of this book was based, called upon the University, of which the *Rector magnificus* <note>The Title for the head of the University</note> at that time was one named **Nicolaus Cop**. He revoked the condemnation of this book and the censure of the Sorbonnists, whereby the fury of these masters was somewhat humbled and resisted, and the small number of believers was greatly strengthened. At that time also, **John Calvin** came from his law studies and was present in Paris, where he achieved great growth in the work of the Lord—not only teaching the truth but also setting himself against the heretics whom the Devil already sought to thrust into the Church of God. Especially against that unfortunate **Michael Servetus**, who denied, among other blasphemies, the Holy Trinity and the eternity of the Son of God. This man, having agreed to a dispute with Calvin, and the day and hour appointed for it having come, did not dare to appear but immediately withdrew from the assembly. It was also then that he [Calvin] bravely stood against the Libertines or "Free Spirits," through whom in our time the abominable sect has been revived...

Meanwhile, the aforementioned Queen had worked so well that the City of Paris was blessed with three good preachers who proclaimed the truth somewhat more discreetly <note>original: "hypocrielijcker," meaning here with strategic reservation or "under the rose" to avoid immediate suppression.</note> than was customary. <margin>Three good preachers in Paris.</margin>
But this did not last long because those of the Sorbonne did so much—and especially Noël Béda, with another named Picard, born in Paris, then still young but of such a fiercely driven head as ever existed (who was also afterwards held as one of the principal pillars of the Roman Church)—that the pulpit was forbidden to them. Seeing this, they changed their preaching into private lessons. The Doctors, being unable to tolerate this at all, obtained enough power that Roussel was imprisoned and Courault was held by the Bishop of Paris. 
<margin>Bertault falls away.</margin>

<margin>Roussel falls away.</margin>

<margin>Courault, a preacher in Geneva.</margin>

The outcome of this matter being thus moderated, if those whose eyes God had opened had kept themselves quiet and still for that time, there was a great appearance that the King himself would have begun to taste something of the truth little by little. For he had been brought so far by the Queen of Navarre, his sister, and by the two brothers of the house of Bellay—namely the Lord of Langey (who was then very famous because of some embassies he had performed for the King) and his brother the Bishop of Paris, both greatly beloved by the King for their courage and great learning—that they (I say) had brought the King so far that he had promised and resolved to have that great and famous man, Philipp Melanchthon, come to France to be heard speaking in person.

<margin>Articles against the Mass.</margin>

# Church History. Fol. ix.

1534. They sought every means and did not let this opportunity pass, especially the Grand Master <note>original: "grooten Hofmeester," likely referring to Anne de Montmorency, the Grand Maître de France.</note> and the Cardinal of Tournon. From that point on, they decided and resolved to destroy everything related to the new faith, had it been in their power. At that time, the Criminal Lieutenant <note>original: "Lieutenant Crimineel," the chief judicial officer for criminal cases in Paris.</note> was one Jean Morin, a very great enemy of the Religion and a man of very dissolute life. He was famous among all the judges of his time for his boldness, for he feared no one when making arrests; he was also particularly cunning in trapping prisoners in their own answers. Having received orders from the King to proceed immediately to investigate and capture all those he could catch, he applied himself with total diligence. In a short time, he filled all the holes and prisons with men and women of every quality and condition. He made use of a traitor who, being about to be burned at the stake, bought his miserable life through a promise (which he later kept) that he would lead the "deep-searchers" <note>bounty hunters or investigators</note> from house to house where the 

<margin>
The falsehood of an apostate.
</margin>

Lutherans lived. For he had been used to going secretly into the houses of the believers to announce the day and hour of the secret gatherings, where they met with one another to read from the Scriptures and pray to God. Nevertheless, many escaped his hands and were scattered here and there—especially many learned students who moved to other universities. Among those who went to Bourges were Claude des Fosses and Jacques Canaye (who later became a very famous advocate in the Parliament of Paris), and Jacques Amyot. Amyot was a man of very humble status but had studied the Greek language well by that time. Through the help of Melchior Wolmar, the Greek professor of Bourges, he was made tutor to the nephews of Jacques Colin, who was at that time the Abbot of Saint-Ambroise. Amyot later succeeded Wolmar in the Professorship of Languages, and finally, through the favor of Bouchetel, the Secretary of State, and Lord Morvillier, who had great credit with the King, he was made preceptor or master to King Charles IX. He earned great praise for his labor in translating the books of *Plutarch*. But he later greatly defiled his beautiful gifts, for he not only forgot Jesus Christ, but later became a cruel persecutor of His Gospel after he was made Abbot of Saint-Corneille and eventually Bishop of Auxerre.

<column-break/>

<margin>
1534.
</margin>

A little before these things happened in Paris, the Franciscan monks of Orléans played a tragedy <note>In the 16th century, a "tragedy" could refer to a staged deception or a scandalous event.</note> not very different from the one the Jacobins <note>Dominican monks</note> of Bern in Switzerland performed, of which history makes mention. This history is as follows: Around this time, the wife of the Provost of Orléans died. She was from a good and ancient house. Whether it was because she had some knowledge of the Religion or for some other reason, she had requested before her death that she be buried in the Cloister of the Franciscans (or Minor Brothers), in the tomb of her ancestors from the house of Saint-Mesmin, without any pomp or expense according to the usual custom. This being done by her husband, he gave the aforementioned monks no more than six gold crowns. Later, when they requested some wood from him that he had cut and sold, he refused them. Because of this, they conceived such a spite against him that they resolved to take revenge by making the whole world believe that his wife was eternally damned. The principal leaders of this business were Brother Coliman, the Provincial of the order, who was in great esteem among his monks, and Brother Stephen d’Arraen, a Doctor of Divinity who was considered a great preacher. To make a good beginning, Stephen preached several sermons with great fervor, speaking and crying out much about the state of souls in Purgatory—not forgetting to make the people believe that spirits or souls returned to this world. Afterwards, these two seduced a young monk of the kind they call *novices* <note>original: "Novitij," those in their probationary year.</note>. They took him and hid him above the vault of the Temple <note>the church ceiling</note>, where he made a great noise and racket at night while the others sang Matins. Coliman, acting as the boldest and being well-armed with all kinds of exorcisms, began to conjure the feigned spirit. But the spirit did not speak. It was ordered to make a sign if it were a mute spirit, whereupon it raged and made a great noise again. This was the sign. This beginning having been made, they went to some citizens of good standing who were most favorable to them, saying that a sad thing had happened in the Temple without telling exactly what it was. They begged them to be present at their Matins, which the citizens did. And as the Matins began, the spirit let itself be heard from above. They asked what it wanted and who it was...

Antoine du Prat, Chancellor and Legate of the Pope throughout the entire Kingdom of France, did the same. Therefore, the Franciscans, no longer being able to withdraw themselves, were brought to Paris along with the young monk who had been found on top of the vault. The young monk was brought to the house of Counselor Fumile; though he was frequently questioned, he did not want to confess, mostly because he feared the monks would kill him when he returned to their vault. But the judges, noticing this, assured him that no harm would come to him and that he would no longer be under their subjection and power. He then went on to relate the whole history and the events of the matter; and being confronted in the presence of the others, he remained steadfast and did not deviate from what he had told. Seeing they were convicted as if caught in the act, they appealed again to their privileges and refused to answer for their case before the judges. But it did not help them, for they were condemned to be brought back to Orléans and kept in prison. After that, they were to be brought before the great church, and from there to the place where criminals are executed, to confess their wickedness there. But they nevertheless found so much favor and grace that it was never possible for the execution to be put into effect; thus some of them died in prison, and others found a means to escape.

# Church History

<margin>1534.</margin> The inhabitants of this place enjoyed great freedom, partly because the Counts, who were their lords, did not reside there and seldom visited, and also because there were few priests, monks, or canons in this small town. There was only one parish, with the church standing outside the city walls, and a priory or <margin>A chapel used as a wine cellar.</margin> monastery without monks, which led to the temple being used as a wine cellar. Nevertheless, the believers there were no less threatened; but however often this occurred, it passed easily without much trouble. Even when one of the councilors of the Parliament of Paris, named Bourgoin—born in St. Pierre-le-Moûtier, one of the nearby towns—intended to persecute them, he could never succeed. Afterward, there came to Sancerre one of "our masters" <note>original: "Magistri nostri," a formal title for doctors of theology</note> named Oris, who was a renowned Inquisitor of the faith. But while he was there, he was so well-quieted with the good wine given to him to calm him down, that upon returning to Bourges, he publicly declared from the pulpit that he had found the inhabitants of Sancerre to be entirely pious and good people.

<margin>Rocheli.</margin> There was also a substitute for Oris named Rocheli, a Jacobin monk <note>a member of the Dominican Order</note> from Bourges, who was sent to persecute them; but he returned just as his master had. The Special Lieutenant <note>original: "Lieutenant particulier," a local judicial official</note> of Bourges, who was called "the Abbot"—an ignorant man and a great persecutor—complained about this, often saying that good wine and a new cap sent all the Inquisitors home well-satisfied <note>original: "gepaept," likely meaning satiated or pampered like a priest</note>, without bringing him any results. Finally, this Rocheli, who had delivered many inflammatory sermons in both Bourges and Sancerre, doing everything possible to incite the people to kill and burn, was so changed by someone who pointed out his improper behavior and his ungodly life, that he afterward sought to rebuild what he had tried to destroy. Because of this, the Archbishop of Bourges and Lord Jan Tranchant, the Archpriest of Sancerre, took up the cause so vehemently that many inhabitants were forced to flee. Among others, three were imprisoned there: two of whom were released after a long imprisonment upon paying a certain fine. And <margin>Brion.</margin> the third, named Denis Brion, a barber, after he had steadfastly confessed the 

<column-break/>

truth, was burned at <margin>1535.</margin> the festival of Angers. Notwithstanding this, the congregation maintained itself happily, waiting for a better time.

To return to the persecution in Paris, which had arisen because of the Placards <note>The "Affair of the Placards" involved the posting of anti-Catholic posters across Paris, which infuriated King Francis I</note>: the King, being very pleased with the diligence of Jean Morin <note>the Lieutenant Criminal of Paris</note>, came to Paris in the month of January at the beginning of the year 1535. On the 29th of the aforementioned month, he ordained a general procession in which he himself took part, joined by his three children, walking on foot with bare heads and holding white wax candles in their hands. During this procession, at the princi-<margin>Six persons at the procession in Paris.</margin>pal places of the city, six persons were burned alive with great cruelty, amidst such wonderful mockery and shouting from the people, who cried out like madmen at the poor souls, that they nearly tore them from the hands of the executioner to devour them themselves. Furthermore, after the King had eaten his midday meal in the great hall of the Bishopric, the entire Parliament was seen there in red robes, along with most of the clergy, the highest nobility, and the ambassadors of various nations. Before them all, the King protested with great anger that if he knew one of his own limbs was infected with this doctrine, he would immediately tear it off, so as not to be further defiled by it. But as great as his fury was, the steadfastness of the believers was even greater. Among those worthy of eternal memory are <margin>Bartholomew Milon.</margin> Bartholomew Milon; Nicholas Vale-<margin>Nicholas Valeton.</margin>ton, the Receiver of Nantes in Brittany; <margin>Jan du Bourg.</margin> Jan du Bourg, a cloth merchant in <margin>Stephen de la Forge</margin> Paris living in St. Denis Street at the sign of the Black Horse; Stephen de la Forge <margin>La Catelle. Anthony Poille.</margin> from Tournai, who had lived in Paris for a long time, a very rich man and no less charitable to the poor; a schoolmistress named La Catelle; and Anthony Poille, a poor mason from Meaux, but singularly blessed by God, as he bore the prize among all the martyrs, being treated with the utmost cruelty, as is recorded in the Book of Martyrs.

This year was uniquely bloody, not only in France, but also in the Netherlands and in England. King Henry VIII, having become an apostate through a certain spite, and not at all...

It is also very remarkable that in this same year, the **Anabaptists** <note>The Anabaptists were a radical wing of the Reformation; the "madness" refers to the Münster Rebellion where they seized the city, leading to a bloody siege.</note> instigated such a strange madness and violence in the city of **Münster** in Westphalia. Beyond those who were executed in France, there were many notable men who willingly banished themselves from the land, moved by the second persecution. Among these were **John Calvin** and with him another notable man, well-versed in the Hebrew language, named **Pierre Robert Olivétan**. The Lord God wished to make use of them, as He afterwards demonstrated in countless ways, and especially in the **French translation of the Bible** which was first printed in Neuchâtel in Switzerland, for which all good Frenchmen are indebted to him. At that time, there also left France one of the Doctors of the **Sorbonne** <note>The theological faculty of the University of Paris, known for its fierce opposition to the Reformation.</note> named **Caroli**, dragging with him the same spirit of ambition, of contradiction, and of unchastity. His behavior showed clearly enough that the Spirit of God had not sent him, but that Satan had used him to hinder the work of God, as will be related more fully in the *History of Metz*. This same tempest also first drove **Clément Marot** <note>A famous French poet who translated the Psalms into French verse.</note> out of France, who went to Italy to the **Duchess of Ferrara**. But the greatest evil was that from that time on, the highest-ranking people began to accommodate themselves to the King’s moods, gradually estranging themselves from the study of the Holy Scriptures, so that they finally became worse than the others. Even the **Queen of Navarre** <note>Marguerite de Navarre, the King's sister, who was known for protecting reformers.</note> behaved quite differently than before, giving herself over to idolatry like the others; not that she recognized such superstitions as good in her heart,

<margin>
Roussel.
</margin>
but because **Roussel** <note>Gérard Roussel, a preacher and bishop who favored a middle ground between Catholicism and the Reformation.</note> and many like him persuaded her that there were indifferent and neutral things that could be done or left undone. The end of this was that she, being blinded, allowed into her house two great **Libertines** <note>A term Calvin used for a specific sect that believed their spiritual freedom excused them from moral laws.</note>, one named **Quintin** and the other **Pocques**, whose blasphemies and errors are found in the books of John Calvin.

This persecution moved the Protestant Princes of Germany (whose friendship the King needed at that time) to complain about it, because they felt themselves condemned in the persons who were being persecuted. The King excused himself for this through the counsel of the **Lord of Langey** <note>Guillaume du Bellay, a diplomat who tried to bridge the gap between Francis I and the German Protestants.</note> (who had become more a servant of the King than a servant of God), saying that he against

<column-break/>

his will had been forced to use such severity only against certain rebels who wished to disturb the state of his kingdom under the cloak of religion. This gave **John Calvin**, who was then in Basel, the occasion to write that precious book, his ***Institutes of the Christian Religion***, dedicated to the King himself to make him understand that his faithful subjects were most falsely and slanderously burdened with the charges of heresy and rebellion. Thus, God drew a wonderful light out of a thick darkness. But notwithstanding all this, the persecution of the believers continued in many different places. Among other martyrs, one must not forget **Alexander Canus**, otherwise named **Laurentius of the Cross**, who from a **Jacobin monk** <note>A member of the Dominican Order.</note> became a Christian. He was captured at Lyons, where he had preached for a time to some goldsmiths and others of the city, from where he was led to Paris. There he was so cruelly tortured that one of his legs was broken, and finally, he was burned after he had made a glorious confession of faith. Likewise, a certain woman named **Marie Becaudelle**, having been instructed in the truth in the city of **La Rochelle**, was burned with wonderful constancy because she had privately rebuked a **Minorite** <note>A Franciscan friar.</note> who had preached at Essars in Poitou, where she was born. In other places, such as in the city of Mâcon, **Iohan Cornon** from the land of Bresse was also burned; he was a simple and plain farmer, without knowledge of letters <note>He was illiterate.</note>, but he was so practiced in the Holy Scriptures that he brought all his enemies to great wonder. Not wishing to appeal his sentence, he had to die with a wonderful constancy.

In the following years, notwithstanding the heavy war with **Emperor Charles** <note>Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor.</note>, and generally throughout the entire reign of **Francis I**, the persecutions were continued by all the Parliaments, whatever excuses were given to the Germans. And truly, it would be almost impossible to describe piece by piece the strange cruelties that were practiced; for they burned the trial records along with the persons, and they cut the **tongues** out of their mouths as they were being led out, so that one should not hear anything from their mouths, and thus prevent it being recorded as a memorial for posterity. Therefore, it shall be enough that we summarily mention some of the most particular and notable acts. Thus then, the believers of **Piedmont**...

<margin>Ieronymus Vindocinus.</margin>

<margin>1539.</margin>
...and it was also executed in the afternoon outside the city in a field by the river called **La Gravier** <note>original: "la Gravier." Likely the Promenade du Gravier in Agen, a historic public space by the Garonne river.</note>. Many people from outside the city gathered for this spectacle, as it was a new thing, and there was no one in the company who did not wish him a much worse end, though his steadfastness and certain patience brought them to great wonder. He was then burned alive, having been given four monks—one from each Order—along with a Flemish priest who taught philosophy in the city named **Guillielmus Lapidanus** <note>William Lapidanus (c. 1490–1550) was a Flemish monk and scholar.</note>. But he put them all to shame. He was the first in our time to die in Agen for the truth of the Lord’s word. His books and goods were given to one **Jan Valern**, who was afterwards well enough known for his bestiality and bitter persecution.

<margin>Andries Bertelin.</margin>
Those from **Beaune**, a city in the Duchy of Burgundy well-renowned for the good wines grown there, were persecuted at this time by the **Parlement of Dijon**, so that ten or twelve had to flee. And on the other side, in **Annonay** <note>original: "Nonnap," likely a transcription or spelling variant of Annonay in the Vivarais region.</note>, a city in Vivarais where they had long been persecuted as we have said, there was one **Andries Berthelin**, who was burned alive solely because he would not kneel before an image that stood on the road as he was going to the market in **Lyons**.

<margin>1540.</margin>
<margin>Steven de Bruyn.</margin>
The year 1540 was renowned in France for the passage of the Emperor and for the exceedingly great heat. There was a poor husbandman <note>A tenant farmer or simple countryman.</note> from **Recortier** in the land of **Dauphiné**, in the diocese of Gap, named **Steven de Bruyn**, who had never been to any school. But he received such great grace from God that he not only taught himself to read his own French language, but through diligence and industry, he progressed so far that he understood Latin and could recount many passages of the New Testament in Latin, teaching his family every day, and often boldly shaming the priests and pastors of the villages and striking them dumb. Because of this, he was captured in the year 1538 and placed in the prison of the Bishop of **Embrun**, where he was so misled that he signed a Latin recantation which he only half understood. But two years later, having been rebuked and condemned as a heretic by a <term>Friar Minor</term> <note>A member of the Franciscan Order; "Minnebroer" in the original Dutch.</note> inquisitor named **Domicelle**, he was further condemned to be burned alive, which death he also suffered with a wonderful steadfastness:

<column-break/>

for while standing at the stake in the fire, the wind was so great that the flame turned away from him, and he remained standing untouched. Because the executioner could not burn him, he struck him on his head with an iron hook, upon which the martyr said: "Since I am condemned to be burned alive, why do you want to strike me dead?" But thereupon he was stabbed through and cast to the earth very cruelly with many blows, and was thus miserably murdered and consumed by the fire. Following this, it was openly forbidden for anyone to speak of his death upon pain of similar punishment.

<margin>Claude le Peintre</margin>
Within **Paris**, in the same year, **Claude le Peintre** was burned. He was born in the suburb called **Saint-Marceau**, a goldsmith by trade; through his death, many were edified because of his great fearlessness.

<margin>1541.</margin>
<margin>Andreas Melanthon.</margin>
<margin>Andries de la Voye.</margin>
In the year 1541, at **Tonneins** in Agenois, on the river called the Garonne, was **Andreas Melanthon**, a German <note>original: "Hoogh-duytscher," referring to someone from High Germany or a German speaker.</note>, who served the school and preached, as did **Jan Calvin**, born of **Artois**, who was afterwards a Minister at **Montauban** <note>This likely refers to a local Reformer of the same name, or a confused account, as the famous John Calvin was from Noyon.</note>. The same was also done by **Aymon de la Voye**, born in Picardy in the city called **Sainte-Foy**, also located in Agenois on the river Dordogne, whose steadfast suffering is notable for several reasons. For firstly, having been well-informed that he would be captured, as he had been sentenced by the **Parlement of Bordeaux** at the insistence of the pastor there—and even when an usher had come to catch him—instead of hiding himself, seeing the weakness of his flock, he remained steadfastly waiting for what God would please. And though earnestly prayed to by good friends that he should save himself, he refused, answering that he was no **hireling** <note>A reference to John 10:12-13, contrasted with the "Good Shepherd."</note>, but that following the example of **Saint Paul**, he was ready not only to be bound at Bordeaux, but also that he wished to seal with his blood the teaching he had taught. And there, foreseeing that he would see his sheep no more, he gave three more sermons, recounting a summary of everything he had taught them, exhorting each one to remain steadfast in the same doctrine. During the third sermon, the usher, wishing to execute his commission, entered the assembly and laid hands on him; and as there were some there who wanted to rescue him from the usher's hands, he rebuked them earnest—

<margin>1542.</margin>
...earnestly, so that they left the tithes. Nevertheless, the Magistrate did not allow the Bailiff to lead him away, but took him into their own custody until around Christmas time, when they handed him over to the Parlement at Bordeaux. Once there, although a legal challenge was made against President Belcier (the first), Calvimont (the second), and Alix the Counselor: it nonetheless happened through the persistence of Counselor Riverac (who was a cruel man and a great pleader of cases, and who acted as a fierce witness for his own side, even though he had sworn that he would have the man burned even if it cost him a thousand crowns). The good man, after having suffered much contempt until the 21st of August, finally received a sentence to first betray his companions. Upon this, he was so improperly and cruelly tortured <note>The "extraordinary question" or judicial torture was often used to force prisoners to name accomplices.</note> that he was left for dead for a long time. Yet they could get nothing else from him except that all those who had the knowledge of God and sought to live by it were his companions and brothers; and sometimes he prayed to God for those who tormented him, asking that He might forgive them for the misery they caused him. Afterward, a crowd of monks was sent to him, all of whom he sent away, refusing to hear their talk, except for a young Carmelite who was of a better sort than all the others. This monk remained alone with him for a long time, and the man succeeded so well that he brought the young monk himself to the knowledge of Jesus Christ. Afterward, he was questioned again on new points of religion by the Presidents and some Counselors, especially regarding the Lord's Supper. He answered all their questions clearly and very excellently, as is described more extensively in the *Book of Martyrs* <note>original: "Martelaer-boeck." This likely refers to the famous martyrology by Jean Crespin.</note>.

<margin>Psalm 114:1</margin>
Finally, being led out of the prison, he sang the 114th Psalm: namely, *When Israel went out of Egypt*, etc. <note>This psalm, celebrating liberation from bondage, was a favorite among the Reformed during their executions.</note> and he remained in this wonderful steadfastness until he was strangled and thereafter burned.

<margin>Students are imprisoned.</margin>

But nothing came of it, except that one poor servant was placed into the hands of the Rector of the College, Andreas de Govea, a Portuguese man and Doctor of the Sorbonne (commonly called **Mustard-eater** <note>original: "Sinapivorus," from the Latin *sinapi* (mustard) and *vorare* (to devour).</note>), to be punished by him.

<margin>1542.</margin>
Andreas Melancthon was also captured and placed in the prison of the Bishop of Agen, but was afterward, at the request of the Queen of Navarre <note>Marguerite de Navarre (1492–1549), sister of King Francis I, was a known protectress of humanists and early reformers.</note>, brought to the Conciergerie or the Prison of the Palace of Bordeaux. From there he was placed in the castle named Trompette, where he suffered much; but he was finally delivered through the help of a good friend.

At that time, the Cardinal of Lorraine held the Bishopric of Agen on behalf of one of the children of Lord Cesare Fregoso, so that all things were done through him. At this time, one Jan Valeri was made Suffragan <note>An assistant bishop.</note> of this Bishopric, whose deeds are well enough known in all of Guienne. For as soon as he was in this office, he became so arrogant—because he saw that his head was mitered—that he wished to have a rule over everything to show that he was such a man.

<margin>Arrogance of Jan Valeri.</margin>
Everything that was against him, he excommunicated. If the wine was not good that was poured for him when he made the visitation of the Bishopric, he excommunicated it along with the vineyard where it had grown, and even the barrel in which it was kept. If he found a cart that hindered his way, he cursed it. But if a beautiful girl was presented to him, he took the mitre from his head and set it on her head, saying laughingly that she would be a fine "bishopess," and gave her a kiss. Otherwise, he was a great persecutor. I write nothing but what was known to everyone there, for which reason some of his own people almost made him lose his office, but they were reconciled in order to better torment those of the Reformed Religion. He was an Italian and had a bastard son who was a Counselor in the High Council of Agen, who was quiet enough, but just as ignorant as his father.

Belcier, the first President of Bordeaux, died around this time in the month of December. He was succeeded by one de Lage, a bloodthirsty man and a strong persecutor, and a great friend of the Franciscans.

Previously, the Queen of Navarre had caused President Calvimont to be removed from his position, but he was later reinstated after the death of King Francis, through the favor of the Constable <note>likely Anne de Montmorency, the Grand Master and Constable of France.</note>.

Fol. xvi.
### Appendix to the

<margin>1543.</margin>
...he spoke these notable words: "Indeed (as the Apostle says), we are the filth and the offscouring of the world <note>original: "wy zijn de vuylicheydt ende het uytvaeghsel des Werelts," a reference to 1 Corinthians 4:13.</note>, and now we stink before the men of this world; but let us rejoice, for the scent of our death shall be pleasing to God and shall edify our brothers."

This became indeed a prophetic speech, as was shown afterward. In this same year, the Parliament issued an express prohibition stating that no one should sell or possess forbidden books, and specifically the *Institutes* of <term>John Calvin</term> <note>Johannes Calvinus; his "Institutes of the Christian Religion" was the foundational text of Reformed theology and a primary target for censors.</note>. And at the request of the Inquisitor, a new mandate was given to all pastors to inform themselves of everyone who held a "bad opinion" of the Roman Church, and to report all such individuals within six days to certain appointed Doctors, namely: Henricus Gervasi, Nicolaus Clerici, Petrus Ricardi, R. Buecin, Ioannes Benot, and Franciscus Picardi, or to Ioannem Morin, the Lieutenant, under penalty of excommunication. Processions were held, and some people were burned in the meantime. Nevertheless, a very fine and good opportunity presented itself to spread the Kingdom of Christ, but it was not seized by the one who
<margin>Franciscus Landry.</margin>
seemed chosen for it. This was one Franciscus Landry, Pastor of Holy Cross <note>Sinte Cruys</note> in the city—a man of more boldness than wisdom, yet one who was driven by a certain zeal. Thus, he gave many sermons in place of the canonical hours and was called from his small parish to St. Bartholomew’s, and also preached in several other parishes on high feast days, with a great following of people. The <term>Sorbonnists</term> <note>Theologians from the University of Paris (the Sorbonne), known for their fierce defense of Catholic orthodoxy.</note> were very dissatisfied and feared that other such enemies would increase, as indeed happened when several Bachelors of Theology
<margin>Franciscū Perucel.</margin>
followed his example, such as one Franciscus Perucel, a <term>Friar Minor</term> <note>Minnebroeder; a member of the Franciscan Order.</note> and a master in the convent, who afterward died a well-renowned man and preacher of the Holy Gospel; and Beguetti, a <term>Jacobin</term> <note>Jacopiner; a common name for a Dominican friar.</note>
<margin>Beguetti.</margin>
monk who later became a Doctor, but his beautiful beginning had a "monk’s end" <note>An idiom suggesting he returned to traditional monastic life or retracted his reformist views before death.</note>.
<margin>Boucherat</margin>
And Boucherat, a monk of the Cistercian Order, who was later accused of heresy but cleared himself so well that he became a superior of his Order. To return to Landry: his reputation spread so far that it reached the ears of King Francis I, who therefore decided to hear him to see what would come of it, although those who otherwise held him in their power (especially the Cardinal of Tournon) worked hard to dissuade him from that purpose, presenting to him certain points

<column-break/>

that the Sorbonnists had noted down from his sermons. Among other things, they burdened him with the charge that he did not perform the Mass, bringing forward the excuse (as it was) that he naturally drank no wine <note>Since the Catholic Mass requires the priest to consume consecrated wine, Landry’s physical aversion to wine served as a convenient reason to avoid the ritual.</note>. In addition to this, they accused him of speaking poorly of Holy Prayer, which, if true, would bring the Roman Church into great abhorrence. But the King, who was a discreet man and a prince of great judgment, after he had heard enough discussion on the matter, said plainly that he wished to hear Landry, and that he would thereafter do what was necessary. The Romanists were very busy preparing for this same resolution of the King. The remedy was that they would make Landry so terrified through certain agents that he would not have the heart to defend his cause before the King.

And indeed, in the year 1543, when the King wished to speak with him, he was warned—supposedly by a secret friend, though by the design of the Cardinal of Tournon—that the King was so enraged with him that if he began to defend any points of Luther’s teaching in his presence, the King would immediately cast him into the fire. This so terrified this poor man that he stood entirely mute before the King and remained so, despite the friendly expression and good permission the King granted him, with all sweetness and courtesy. The end was that the King, although he was annoyed that he had found nothing less in this man than what he had heard said, nonetheless did not deal harshly with him, but commanded that since he had preached publicly, he should be made to recant, and that from then on he should perform no more service except in his own parish. Following this command, he recanted as requested, and everything they wanted, in the presence of the Parliament on April 29th—an act displeasing to both parties. Yet one thing happened at his death worthy of remembrance: fourteen years later, when there was already a secret congregation in Paris, Landry desired to see one of its ministers to speak with him. This he obtained through some of his friends who were in the Congregation. Therefore, coming to his house where one of the ministers was, namely La Roche, they spoke of a point that was then much discussed: namely, whether it was permitted at that time to dissemble <note>Nicodemism, or the practice of hiding one's true Protestant beliefs while outwardly conforming to Catholic rituals to avoid persecution.</note> and to adapt oneself somewhat to the Roman Church. Landry defended and excused the superstitions as much as he could. And after La Roche had pointed out to him that he indeed...
