<margin>1543.</margin>
<margin>543.</margin>
...he clearly saw that this invention <note>Referring to a compromise or theological "middle way" proposed to bridge Catholic and Protestant views.</note> was nothing else but an excuse for the Papacy, and that it was as the Psalm says: *That those who go through the bypasses shall eventually be dragged away with those who work iniquity,* <note>original: "Dat de gene die door de onwegen gaen, eyndelijck ghesleept worden met de ghene die d’ongherechtigheydt wercken," a paraphrasing of Psalm 125:5.</note> along with some other similar discourses through which the judgment of God was placed before the eyes of this **Landry**; he departed afterward full of unrest. But a few months later, as he had become sick and his friends visited him—including a certain honorable woman who was well-instructed in the knowledge of God—he said to her that he wished to reveal something to her that he had never told any man, and that his illness increased because he had not hurried to do that which he had promised. Finally, being urged to do so and the hour being set, the woman came to hear him. <margin>Note.</margin> But just as he began to speak, he immediately lost his speech and died shortly thereafter. Behold, this man who had not wanted to speak before the great men of this world when he was required to do so, could not utter a single word for a woman when he finally desired to. This is what befell this **Landry** at his death.

**Claudius Dispense** <note>Claude d'Espence (1511–1571), a French theologian and humanist who initially sought reform within the Catholic Church.</note>, a nobleman and Doctor of the <term>Sorbonne</term> <note>The Faculty of Theology at the University of Paris, the primary authority for defining Catholic orthodoxy in France.</note>, a well-read man but very inconsistent, was also preaching then in Paris with a great following, speaking somewhat more uniquely than others. And because he once, speaking of the **Golden Legend**, <note>A famous 13th-century collection of hagiographies (lives of saints) by Jacobus de Voragine.</note> called it the *idle legend*, he was so pressured by the Sorbonne that he publicly recanted it; after this, he never did much of any virtue.

This same year was very notable for the siege of **Perpignan**, and the sedition of the **Salines** <note>A revolt against the *gabelle* (salt tax) in southwestern France.</note>, and for the heavy war that rose up again between **Emperor Charles** and the King; nevertheless, those of the Parliament did not cease to proceed just as harshly against those of the Religion. This was the reason that many departed from the Kingdom, among whom was **Clement Marot**, who, since his return from Italy, was greatly hated by the <term>Sorbonnists</term> <note>Strict Catholic theologians of the Sorbonne.</note> because he had very skillfully and successfully translated thirty **Psalms of David** into French. He had dedicated these to the King, who found them of such good taste that they were printed. But he was forced to save himself and take refuge in **Geneva**, where he translated twenty more. But as he had always been 
<margin>Clement Marot.</margin>

<column-break/>

brought up in a very "bad school" <note>Refers to the worldly and often scandalous environment of the royal court.</note> and therefore could not subject his life to the reformation of the Gospel, he wished to spend the rest of his days in **Piedmont**, which was then under the King, where he lived in some hardship under the favor of certain Governors.

<margin>Bonpain.</margin>
In the year 1544, **Pieter Bonpain** of Meaux was forced to depart for **Aubigny** (where there was a great trade in drapery); there he greatly advanced the Kingdom of God, so that many wealthy merchants came to the gathering, where only some chapters from the Holy Scripture were read, along with prayers. But he was not allowed to do this for long, for he was captured and dragged to Paris, where he was burned alive through the persecution of the **Lord of Aubigny**, a Scotsman and a very cruel man, desiring nothing else but to make himself rich with the confiscation of the goods of the wealthiest in his city. But God punished him very quickly: for it happened that the **Earl of Lennox**, his eldest brother, being sent by the King to Scotland to secure the state of the land after the death of **King James V**, instead of performing the King's affairs, allowed himself to be misled by **Henry VIII**, King of England, taking his niece in marriage. When this treachery was revealed to the King of France, he had this Lord of Aubigny, his brother, thrown into prison, where he remained for a long time; thus giving the poor sighs <note>The persecuted Protestants</note> in his city a good relief, as they were then growing and increasing from day to day.

In the same year, a small gathering also began to emerge in **Sens**, an episcopal city, which was immediately discovered; some of them were captured, and some escaped.

<margin>Beguetti.</margin>
Among the prisoners was found a <term>Jacobin</term> <note>A term for a member of the Dominican Order in France.</note> monk named **Beguetti**, who had studied at the Sorbonne and was promoted through and at the expense of **Cardinal de Chastillon**, and who had acquired a good reputation as one who had given some of the purest sermons in Paris. But the belly misled the head: for not only did he recant some points that he had preached from the pulpit, but he also became one of the bitterest persecutors of his Order.

### Fol. xviij.
### 15
#### Appendix to the

<margin>
1544.
Guillaume Husson
</margin>
In Rouen, an apothecary from Blois named **Guillaume Husson** was burned because he had scattered certain books just as the Parliament was adjourning. He was burned alive with such great steadfastness that it moved everyone to wonder. This was the reason that many began to inquire after the **Religion** <note>In this context, "the Religion" refers specifically to the Reformed or Protestant faith.</note> and were won over to the Congregation. But it is time that we come to relate a persecution that occurred at that time, which was the most unusual and cruelest that has ever happened in the Church of God. However, we shall begin from a bit further back so that the matter may be better understood.

<margin>Waldensians</margin>
The **Waldensians**, so named for a long time, having set themselves against the abuses of the Roman Church, have been so persecuted—not with the Sword of God's word, but with all violence and cruelty, joined with thousands of slanders and false accusations—that they were forced to scatter everywhere and hide themselves, wandering through the wilderness like poor wild animals. The Lord God, however, preserved the remnant in such a way that, notwithstanding the rage of the enemies, they remained, just as they are still found today in various places far from one another: some in Calabria, others in Bohemia and the surrounding lands, and the third group in the valleys of Piedmont, through which they scattered into the districts of Provence more than three hundred years ago, and principally to **Mérindol**, **Cabrières**, **Lourmarin**, and the surrounding places. And although the places where they had fled were all wildernesses—both because of wars and the wildness of the land—God nevertheless so blessed their labor that those same lands became fruitful and abundant, both in corn and in wine, oil, honey, almonds, and great herds of livestock, so that they could feed many other lands. They acquired the reputation of being faithful people, exceptionally hospitable and charitable, paying their debts without litigation, and in short, enemies of all sin, whereby they were very well-liked by all their neighbors. Regarding Religion, they never clung to the Popish superstitions, but through the long passage of time, the pure teaching had become very corrupted among their Ministers, whom they call in their language <term>Barbes</term> <note>original: "Barbes," meaning "Uncles" in the Waldensian dialect.</note>, which is to say "Uncle," just as in the Papacy the Priests in some places were called <term>Heer-ooms</term> <note>A Dutch colloquialism for priests, literally "Lord-Uncles."</note>. For this

<column-break/>

reason, they were always troubled by the Bishops and Inquisitors, who so greatly abused the political power among them that it is a great miracle of the Lord that they have still survived. This has also frequently been evidenced by the terrifying judgments of God that have fallen upon those who persecuted them, among whom must not be forgotten a **Jacobin Monk** <note>A member of the Dominican Order.</note> named **Jean de Roma**. Beyond the robberies and the violence committed against these poor people, he went so far as to have boots filled with boiling hot oil, into which he forced the naked legs of those he wished to torture.

<margin>
The
Abomination
</margin>
When the King was informed of this—however great an enemy he was of those who held a contrary Religion—he nevertheless strictly commanded that every diligence be made to capture that cruel Monk. But having been warned in time, he saved himself within **Avignon**, where, having escaped the hands of men, he fell into the hands of the living God, who executed a terrifying justice upon him before the eyes of the whole world. For a short time later, another thief stole all the riches he had plundered, and God struck his body with such a terrifying and stinking disease that no one could come near him. Finally brought to the hospital, he ended his days in a terrifying manner, being entirely rotted while still alive in all his limbs, and gnashing his teeth; after he had unsuccessfully attempted to kill himself, he did nothing but cry out for someone to kill him. But to return to our history: the aforementioned Waldensians, having understood the grace that God had shown in Germany and Switzerland, sent on their behalf one **Georgius Morel**, from Freissinière in Dauphiné (who was a Preacher whom they themselves had supported in his studies), along with one named **Petrus Masson** from Burgundy. They very diligently conferred on all points of Religion, both in Basel with **Johannes Oecolampadius**, and in Strasbourg with **Capito** and **Martin Bucer**, and in Bern with **Berthold Haller**, the first Minister of that Church. and as they understood through the report made to the Churches that the purity of the doctrine among them had somewhat decayed over the long passage of time, they put it into good order, sending word even to their brothers in Calabria, who all together made a good reformation. Thereafter, around the year 1535, they had the first Bible printed in the French language, at their own expense, in **Neuchâtel**.

Castle in Switzerland; this Bible had been translated from the Hebrew by **Petrus Roberti Olivetan** <note>Pierre Robert Olivétan (c. 1506–1538) was a cousin of John Calvin. His 1535 translation was the first French Protestant Bible translated from the original languages.</note> with the help of **John Calvin**, who also later improved it in certain passages. For as for the French translations of the Bibles which had been printed before in the darkness of the Papacy, they were nothing but falsehoods and gross ignorance. These things wonderfully stirred the **Waldensians**, so that from that time they were in extreme peril. But since they had taken refuge at the court: the King caused the heavy legal proceedings against them to cease, doing so by Letters in the year 1535, on the 16th of July, and 1536, on the last of May, granting them grace, on the condition that six months after the publication of these, they should make an abjuration <note>A formal public renunciation of their Protestant faith.</note>; however, they did not use these same Letters for anything else than to somewhat curb the fury of their enemies. And although some of them who were summoned to the Parliament of **Aix** and appeared there were killed, others branded on the forehead with a hot iron, and others robbed of their goods, nevertheless the main body of that people was not attacked until the year 1540. In that year, the inhabitants of **Mérindol** were summoned in the person of fifteen or sixteen of the principal men; through the insistence of the King’s Prosecutor in the Parliament of Aix, and at the request of the Archbishop of **Arles** and the Bishop of Aix, and other ecclesiastical heads, a decree or sentence was decided and issued against them. It was the cruelest, most gruesome, and most inhuman ever given in any Parliament; and to say it in a word, it was truly a sentence like in every way the Edict of King **Ahasuerus** <note>original: "Assuerus"; referring to the biblical King of Persia from the Book of Esther.</note>, given at the insistence of the wicked **Haman** against the people of God, as is recounted in the History of **Esther**:
<margin>Comparison with Ahasuerus and Esther.</margin>
For besides the fact that all those who were summoned and did not appear were condemned to be burned alive, and that their children, servants, and families were to be banished and their property confiscated, the town of Mérindol itself was condemned to be <unclear>razed</unclear> and made uninhabitable. All the woods were to be cut down for two hundred paces around it: all this without even having heard their defense once. This sentence was found so strange that the First President himself, named **Barthélemy Chassannée**, and many other Councilors by no means approved of its execution. That caused the aforementioned—

<column-break/>

<margin>1544.</margin>
—Archbishop of Arles and the Bishop of Aix, with certain Abbots, Priors, and Canons, being assembled at **Avignon**, to decide to request the execution of the aforementioned sentence, offering to pay for soldiers at their own expense to go there with flying banners and heavy artillery. Following this resolution, although the aforementioned President pointed out that this Article was not properly definitive and that therefore the laws and ordinances of the Kingdom did not allow for execution without further procedure—seeing that much evil might arise from such an execution, besides the displeasure the King would have regarding it—nevertheless, by the authority of the same Court, the drum was beaten in **Provence**. Captains were appointed with a certain number of horse and foot-soldiers, who already began to march well-armed and mounted. Then the **Lord of Alenc**, provided with knowledge of divine and human law, used such lively and earnest demonstrations before the President that he immediately revoked the commission and the attempt was broken. Those poor people of Mérindol, meanwhile preparing no resistance—men, women, children, masters, and servants, expecting nothing else than to be led like poor sheep to the slaughterhouse—cried out with one accord to God. He also touched the King’s heart so that, having heard the rumor of this matter, instead of approving it, he wrote to the **Lord of Langey**, his Lieutenant in the land of **Piedmont**, that he should take diligent information on the whole case. Obeying the King in this, after he had diligently taken good information both of the manners, nature, and religion of this people, and also of the truth of what was charged against them by their enemies, he gave such a report to the King that on the 8th day of the month of February in the year 1540, he sent Letters of Grace for all who were in the land of Provence. He commanded the Parliament very expressly that they should not proceed so strictly in such things in the future; yet he commanded that the "straying" ones should, within three months after the notification of these letters, make a public abjuration of their error. These letters were held back for a long time, until by the insistence and request of many, the Parliament caused them to be published, adding to them that all suspected of being **Lutherans**—men, women, and children—should come to present themselves before the Court, except those against whom—

# Appendix to the
## Church History

<margin>1544.</margin>
...what the King’s Prosecutor intended to claim: but those of **Mérindol** <note>A village in the Luberon region of Provence, which became a stronghold for the Waldensian faith.</note> having requested through petitions and shown what a great trouble and labor it would be for everyone to appear there in person, they obtained permission to do so through an Attorney. And so eight days later, **Fransoys Chay** and **Guillaume Armant** were appointed as their Attorneys, who also appeared in their name and requested that the errors and heresies charged against them be proven, so that they might be convinced of them through the Word of God, etc. Now these good people had never been able to obtain any copy or duplicate of all the proceedings taken against them: indeed, all Clerks and Notaries had been generally forbidden from providing them with any writings or copies. Thus, they were forced to take refuge with the King, who immediately commanded that duplicates of all proceedings be given to them, with an order to all Notaries and Officers to execute all acts, notwithstanding the sentence of the Court to the contrary, which was thereby revoked.

<margin>Antiquity of the Religion of the Waldensians</margin>
Having then obtained a Notary, they had the teaching they held—and which had been left to them from generation to generation—costly described: indeed, since the Year 120 after Christ’s birth, just as they had always understood and been taught it by their parents, of which this is the sum.

<margin>Their Petition.</margin>
Very honorable Lords, the great troubles, damages, and torments that we have had to suffer in our persons, goods, and reputation, from the year 1531 until this present Year 1541, through the false accusations and complaints made against us, weary us and, as if by necessity, compel us to pray to Your Lordships again. May it please Your Lordships, for the sake of God’s honor, to kindly hear our humble and Christian petition, with certain and truthful notice, which we shall give to Your Lordships in upright conscience—taking God, who is a knower of all hearts, as witness—so that Your Lordships may stand for us in right and equity, as those who must administer Justice to the poor as well as to the rich, without favor.

<margin>Confession of their faith.</margin>
Firstly, since all the trouble and persecutions brought against us arise from the cause of Religion: So we confess before GOD and before Your Lordships and all Christian Princes, in what faith and teaching we exist and wish to live. And first, we are in all things at one and accord with the right sense of the Christian church and Religion. As for the only rule of our faith, we have the 12 Articles of the Faith <note>The Apostles' Creed, the traditional statement of Christian belief used since the early church.</note>. We are not

<column-break/>

<margin>1544.</margin>
tainted by, nor do we desire to be, any errors and heresies which were condemned by the ancient Christian church, and we hold the teaching that has been approved by the upright faith. We hold ourselves to be corrupt and lost through **Original Sin**, and that we of ourselves can do nothing but evil and sin. We confess that the first and principal foundation of all good in man is the **regeneration of the Spirit**, which God, through His goodness and grace, gives to His elect. And as all men are sinners by nature, so we hold that they lie in damnation and under the wrath of GOD, except those whom He has preserved by His grace. But the manner in which we are delivered is such: we must receive **Jesus Christ** as He is presented to us in the holy Gospel—that is, that He is our redemption, righteousness, and sanctification. Therefore we believe that we are justified only through faith which is powerful through love, mistrusting our own works and giving ourselves over entirely to the righteousness of Jesus Christ. Regarding regeneration, we hold that man from his birth is blind in his understanding and corrupt in his will: and so that he may have the true and saving knowledge of God, and of His Son Jesus Christ, he is and must be enlightened by the **Holy Spirit**, and is then also bound to good works, so that having the Law of God written in his heart, he may forsake all fleshly pleasures and desires: whereby the forgiveness of sins is always necessary for us, without which no one can stand before GOD in reconciliation. We call upon only the Father in the unique name of Jesus Christ the **Mediator**, and use no other prayer than those which stand in Holy Scripture, or agree with its meaning. We hold to no human teaching that contradicts the Holy Word of God, such as the satisfaction of sins through good works, and all commanded institutions without that Word of God, with a false opinion of obligation and merit, and all superstitious customs, such as the worship of **Images**, **Pilgrimages**, and the like. We hold the **Sacraments** in honor, and we believe that they are testimonies and signs through which the grace of God is confirmed and assured in our conscience: whereby we believe that **Baptism** is a sign through which the cleansing we obtain through the blood of JESUS CHRIST is thus strengthened in our hearts...

<meta>This page continues the formal confession of faith submitted by the Waldensians of Mérindol to the French authorities. The previous page ended as they began outlining their beliefs to prove they were not heretics but followers of ancient Christian tradition.</meta>

# Church History

<margin>1544.</margin> ...serves as the true washing of rebirth and renewal. The Lord's Supper is the sign under which the true communion of the Body and Blood of **Jesus Christ** is given to us. Regarding the Magistrate—as well as Princes and Lords, and all who administer justice—we hold them to be ordained by God, and we wish to be obedient to their laws and commands concerning property and the body. To them, we gladly wish to pay all taxes and assessments and everything that is due to them, showing them all honor and obedience in all things that are not against God.

In the remainder of this writing, they answered some specific accusations, praying that it might please the authorities to show them with friendliness if they find that they wander in any things, and that they might ensure they are not thus overwhelmed; and that they might be allowed to plow their land and work, in order to earn a living for their poor wives and children.

-> All this thus debated at **Mérindol**, the 6th of April 1541. <-

To all this, no answer was given, except that the petitioners might come in safety, up to the number of ten, to declare whether they wished to avail themselves of the King’s letters of grace <note>Letters of grace were royal pardons that usually required a formal recantation of "heretical" beliefs.</note> or not. Meanwhile, since the place of **Cabrières** <note>A neighboring village to Mérindol, also a Waldensian stronghold.</note> with its surrounding areas were also a people under the sovereignty of **Venisse** <note>original: "Venisse" refers to the Comtat Venaissin, a territory around Avignon that belonged to the Pope rather than the French King.</note> and the jurisdiction of the Pope: these same Articles were sent with a broader explanation, both to the Bishop of **Cavaillon** and to **Cardinal Sadolet**, Bishop of **Carpentras**. Because he was a very learned man and often had to acknowledge many things through his conscience, he gave a good answer—yet one that still aimed to lead them to the "softening" of the truth. For he had conceived such hope from seeing the simplicity of those people that, in the following year, when the Vice-Legate of Avignon had gathered many infantry and cavalry with the Bishop of **Cavaillon** to destroy **Cabrières**, the same **Cardinal Sadolet** thwarted and nullified the entire plot. He promised these poor people that when he returned from Rome, he would do wonders for the **Reformation** of the Church—something which, however, he did not do.

Meanwhile, the aforementioned Archbish-

<column-break/>

The Court ordered that a Councilor with a Clerk, and the Bishop of **Cavaillon** with a Doctor of Divinity, should go there to convert them. But the Bishop and his Doctor, having arrived there first, gained nothing, except that the Doctor, having seen the aforementioned Articles <note>The confession of faith written by the villagers.</note>, instead of disputing against them, admitted loudly and clearly that he had not learned as much from the Holy Scriptures in his whole life as he had done in eight days by comparing those articles with the passages and places of Scripture that were cited in them.

The same Bishop came there once more afterward, accompanied by four monks who had recently arrived from the Academy of Paris <note>The Sorbonne, the center of conservative Catholic theology.</note>. One of them, having heard the little children answer the questions of their Catechism, also openly admitted that he had never learned as much good in all the disputations he had done and heard in the **Sorbonne** as he had heard and learned from these little children.

A short time later, the Councilor and the Clerk of the Court arrived with a Doctor. In the presence of the Bishop there, after many presentations by one side and answers from the other, the people offered to abjure all the errors that could be pointed out to them. Whereupon, the Articles of their confession being read, and the Bishop not wishing to speak except according to the judgment of the Lord Commissioner, and the aforementioned Doctor refusing to speak anything but Latin <note>The villagers spoke the local dialect (Provençal/Occitan) and some French, but not the scholarly Latin used by the clergy to maintain intellectual dominance.</note>, all the Commissioners returned home entirely confused. What is more: the three Doctors who had come on three different occasions <margin>The Doctors themselves converted.</margin> later left the Roman religion and have since become Preachers of the religion they previously persecuted.

Now, after these things, the inhabitants of **Mérindol** remained in peace for a short time through a special grace of God, who had terrified their enemies with the ghastly death of **Roma** <note>Referring to a persecutor mentioned earlier in the history.</note> related above. Also by the sudden death of **President Chassannée**, who had nevertheless been much milder toward them than **President d'Oppède** <note>referred to here as Menier</note>, of whom we shall now speak.

<margin>1544.</margin> ...to buy, besides having to lose his status, it also cost him all his property, so that he left no other goods to his son, Jan Menier, than the title of the Lordship of Oppède, which was then very little. This son, a true heir to the ambition and very evil conscience of his father, worked so well that he was first made a guard of the Pope in the city of Cavaillon, the better to make the proverb true: *Like master, like servant.* From there, through certain means, he became President of the Parliament of Provence, even Governor of Provence in the absence of Lord Grignan.

<margin>Jan Menier’s wickedness.</margin>
And to improve his lordship of Oppède, he did not fail to accuse many of the wealthiest countrymen of being heretics. Keeping some in prison in a miserable wretchedness, driving away others, so as to come into their riches, without having any compassion for the women and small children. And finally, as his lordship was located only a mile from Mérindol, he decided to put that aforementioned cruel Decree <note>The "Arrest de Mérindol," a 1540 decree by the Parliament of Provence ordering the destruction of the village.</note> into effect, to completely exterminate those same poor people and to take a rich plunder from them. Those of Mérindol, being informed of this plot, went to King Francis in the year 1543, informing him of the contents of his letters given in the year 1540, and of the misery and perils into which they had fallen. The King, continuing his benevolence toward them, called that Decree stubborn before him, nullifying all the proceedings of the Parliament until a Master of Requests with a Doctor in Theology from the High School of Paris, sent to the appropriate places, should have taken good information again regarding the Faith and conduct of those of Mérindol and the surrounding places.

<margin>Morné <note>Likely a reference to Mérindol or its leaders.</note> burdened with lying slanders.</margin>

Although at Mérindol there were no more than two or three of those who had been condemned. <margin>Note the judgments of God.</margin>
Regarding these tyrants, God did not delay long in allowing His judgments to fall upon some of them during their return. For Louis de Vane, brother-in-law to the President <note>Referring to Jean Meynier d'Oppède, the President of the Parliament of Aix.</note>, as well as the brother and brother-in-law of Pierre Durant, drowned while crossing the Durance River. <note>The Durance is a swift and dangerous river in Provence; their drowning was viewed by the author as divine retribution.</note>

After these aforementioned cruelties had occurred, those of the Court sought to cover up their injustice. They sent Commissioners to conduct an inquiry into the suspicion of heresy. Seeing that the complaints had reached the King, they sent to him La Fon, who gave the King to understand that all the inhabitants who had been so treated had first been properly heard and admonished, and also condemned as heretics. He obtained letters dated August 23, 1545, in which all these executions were silently approved. But it was asserted that afterward, as the King lay on his deathbed, he had a very great unease in his conscience regarding this, and charged his son with a great protestation that he should do justice upon these murderers. <note>King Francis I died in 1547; his son, Henry II, did eventually oversee a trial regarding the massacre, though many perpetrators escaped serious punishment.</note>

<margin>Note.</margin>
While people of the Religion <note>A common historical shorthand for the Reformed or Protestant faith.</note> were being treated so cruelly, the Pope prepared a thick smoke to darken the eyes of those whose eyes were being opened clearer and clearer every day. I refer to what was later called the Council of Trent, which, having dragged on for a long time—namely from this time until the year 1563, after it had been frequently broken off and renewed—finally concluded with a confirmation of all kinds of abuses and superstitions. The King, having made peace with the Emperor, although he had often promised the Protestant Lords that he would never agree to a Council that was not entirely free and open, nevertheless agreed to it with the others. But being advised by Castellanus, his Reader and Bishop of Mâcon, that if one had to dispute with the Lutherans, one must come well-prepared or else necessarily stand ashamed; therefore, the King desired that some of the most learned French theologians should gather at Melun to confer together (as a preparation) on all the principal points being disputed, first commanding them upon their oath to keep their resolutions secret. They did indeed gather: but

there arose such a great quarrel among them that nothing was heard but insults and bickering; indeed, they sometimes came to blows, because some ignorant men who had been mixed in with the others could not endure that the abuses should be touched upon in the least. Thus, nothing more could be known of the outcome of this matter. But this much is certain: that the King, in the following year, sent among others to the Council one Petrus Danes, a man well-learned in the Greek language—for which reason he had also been made a Professor in Paris—who delivered a fine Harangue or Oration in the Council. This Danes also had a fair knowledge of the truth, but as he later became the Preceptor of King Francis and a Bishop, he became a persecutor like the others. At this time, Calvin wrote an excellent tract against the Nicodemites <note>Calvin used the term 'Nicodemite' (after Nicodemus in the Bible) to criticize Protestants who hid their true faith and continued to attend Catholic Mass to avoid persecution.</note>, as there were many then who thought one might well go to Mass if the heart did not consent to it. He refuted the slanders of the Libertines with such great power of the Spirit that it did a notable good in the Church of God; through this, some wicked tongues sought to incite the Queen of Navarre against those of the Religion, because Calvin had named in that tract two great Libertines among the principal doctors, Quintin and Pocquet, who were held in high regard by the Queen. But Calvin satisfied her so well that she never complained of it again.

<margin>1546.</margin>
In the year 1546, some believers in the city of Meaux had begun to establish the form of a Congregation, just as they had seen John Calvin had established in Strasbourg. They had chosen as their preacher one Pierre le Clerc, a wool-comber by trade, who, besides his uprightness of life, was wonderfully practiced in God’s word. And God the Lord blessed the service of this person so wonderfully that there was a gathering not only of many from the city, but also from the surrounding area for six miles around, having three or four hundred people in their assembly, whereby they could not long remain hidden. It happened then on September 8, 1546 (on which day the Papists hold the Feast Day of the Nativity of Mary, the mother of Jesus Christ), that the Lieutenant and the Provost of the city with their henchmen, being advised by some spies, raided a meeting of sixty persons. ### Ecclesiastical History
Folio 26.

<column-break/>

<margin>1546.</margin>
...they would give themselves up as prisoners; it was so far from the case that they would have offered any resistance, even though they could have very well done so and all escaped, as some help had already arrived from outside. But they allowed themselves to be bound and taken prisoner, praising God for the honor He did them. Among them was a young girl who, seeing she was being bound, said to the Lieutenant: "Sir, if you had found me elsewhere than in this holy and honorable assembly, you would not bind me so." <note>The "Lieutenant" refers to a local judicial officer representing the crown.</note>

They were then all placed in prison. After information was gathered and it was found that they had held the Lord’s Supper, they were all thrown onto carts and dragged to Paris. They were treated so severely and harshly on the way that there were many who were already maimed and broken before they even reached the rack <note>The "pijnbanc" or rack was a torture device used to extract confessions or names of accomplices.</note>; there were 61 men and 19 women in total. The outcome of the trial was that on October 4, by sentence of the Court, fourteen of them were to be extraordinarily tortured <note>original: "extraordinaerlijc gepijnight," a legal term for severe torture intended to precede execution.</note> and thereafter burned alive in a fire on the great market square of Meaux, near the house of Stephen Mangin where they had been captured, and that all their goods <margin>Peter le Clerc.</margin> were confiscated. These were Peter le Clerc, the Preacher; Francis le Clerc; Stephen Mangin; James Bouchebet; John Brisse- <margin>Names of the Martyrs.</margin> barre; Henry Hutinot; Thomas Honoré; John Baudouin; John Flesche; John and Peter Piquery; John Maresson; Philip Petit; and Michael Caillon. Regarding the others: Louis Piquery was condemned to hang on the scaffold for as long as the execution lasted, then be beaten with sticks, and finally be imprisoned forever in the Monastery of Saint Faron. Louis Coquemant and Pasquier Fouasse were to be beaten with sticks on three different days with ropes around their necks, and thereafter banished. Adrian Grognet was to be beaten with sticks once at Meaux and once again in the village of Harp. John Vincent was to be beaten once at Meaux, and thereafter all of them were banished. The rest of the men and women—except for five women who were released—were condemned to stand by the execution and thereafter perform a public penance <note>original: "eerlijc amende," a ritual of public humiliation and apology.</note>, the men in their shirts and the women with bare feet, and thus be present in a procession, a <margin>House of the Christian assembly demolished.</margin> sermon, and a solemn Mass with torches in their hands. All of this was accompanied by the public announcement of the demolition of the house where they had been captured, so that a chapel could be built on that spot where a Mass of the Holy Sacrament would be held every Thursday, funded by the money from the confiscated goods. This decree having been pronounced, the fourteen who were to be burned were

<column-break/>

brought separately into different <margin>1546.</margin> monasteries to make them waver in their faith, but it was in vain. Therefore, they were delivered into the hands of Gilles Berthelot, the Provost, and were thus led to Meaux. They had two Doctors, pillars of the Sorbonne <note>The Sorbonne was the prestigious theological faculty of the University of Paris, known for its staunch opposition to the Reformation.</note> named Picard and Maillard, at their sides and in their ears without rest. Along the way, an event occurred worthy of note: namely, as they passed through the forest of Livry, there was a man from a small village named <margin>Note.</margin> Couberon, a weaver. He began to follow the wagons and exhort the prisoners with a loud voice. And because he could not keep up with the wagons, he raised his hands high and cried out loudly: "My brothers, remember Him who is there above in Heaven!" Seeing this, the Provost’s shooters took him, bound him, and threw him onto the wagon, from which the prisoners received great comfort. Having arrived at Meaux, they were immediately placed on the rack and were treated so cruelly that it was a thing to be pitied. Yet they all remained so steadfast that they did not betray any of their brothers. Indeed, there was one in the group who cried out loudly to the executioners who were stretching him: "Courage, friends, and do not spare this miserable body which has so violently resisted the Spirit, contradicting the will of its Creator!"

On October 7, they were led to their deaths, and Stephen Mangin’s tongue was cut <margin>Miracle.</margin> out; despite this, he did not cease to say quite understandably: "Blessed be the Name of the Lord." Then he was dragged on a hurdle with William le Clerc, and the others on dung-carts to the great market square. There they were burned at fourteen stakes planted in a circle. Seeing one another face to face, they gave each other courage, praising God until their last breath, although their words were greatly hindered and could not be well understood by the people because of the priests and papists <note>A contemporary, often derogatory term for Roman Catholics.</note> who cried out like madmen against them, "O saving Victim" and "Hail, Queen." <note>original Latin: "O salutaris Hostia" and "Salve Regina," traditional Catholic hymns.</note> This being done, the next day, October 8, Doctor Picard, to complete his triumph, held a fine procession to the place where the fire was still burning. He preached under a canopy of cloth of gold and said, among other things, after he had raved enough, that it was necessary for salvation to believe that these fourteen who were burned were damned in the abyss of Hell, and that if an Angel from Heaven came to say the contrary, one should not receive or hear him; for God would not be God if He did not damn them eternally. Nevertheless, he could not make this believed by all the people...

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the persecution of early Protestants in France following the 1546 execution of the "Fourteen of Meaux." It details the spread of the Reformation despite these deaths and the specific trials of several martyrs including Jean Chapot and others in the late 1540s.</meta>

# Appendix to the [History]

Folio 72.

<margin>1546.</margin>
...these good people had recognized that they had been too virtuous and honorable for such a fate. <note>This refers to the martyrs of Meaux mentioned on the previous page, whose conduct in the face of death impressed observers.</note>

Now, although the dispersion was great, the seed of truth was not thereby extinguished in the city of Meaux. Nevertheless, the scattering was very extensive, but to the great advantage of other churches that were built with the "stones" of this destruction. <note>The author uses a metaphor here: the persecution scattered believers, who then planted new congregations elsewhere, like building a new house from the ruins of an old one.</note>

<margin>François d’Augy.</margin>
At Nonnay, one François d’Augy was seized while returning from Geneva. By a decree of the Parliament, he was burned alive, displaying such steadfastness and faith that he was heard by the bystanders in the midst of the flames crying out, "Courage, my brothers! I see the
<margin>Acts 7:56.</margin>
Heavens open, and the Son of God standing ready to receive me." <note>This is a direct reference to the biblical account of the martyrdom of St. Stephen.</note> Through this, some of the bystanders were so strengthened that they also shouted back to him whatever God gave them to speak; to put it this way, it was only up to the tyrants whether they should follow him into the fire. However, none of them were seized at that time. Likewise, in this same year of 1546, a poor man was burned who was quite simple and unlearned, named 
<margin>Anthony of St. Paul.</margin>
Anthony of St. Paul. Because the priests owed him some money and he could obtain no payment, he once entered the church, found the tabernacle open, and took the Host and the monstrance <note>The "Host" is the sacramental bread; the "monstrance" is the vessel used to display it. He took them as "collateral" for his debt.</note> to his house as a pledge until they should pay him. But the payment he received for this was that (although he had devoutly returned them when he heard the city was in an uproar) he was burned alive, having made them believe he belonged to the "Religion." <note>The "Religion" was a common contemporary shorthand for the Reformed or Protestant faith.</note>

<margin>Jean Chapot.</margin>
Around this same time, a man named Jean Chapot, from Dauphiné, was caught in Paris by Jean André, a bookseller of the Palace, with several packs of books that he had brought from Geneva. This man moved the entire Parliament through a very learned and holy remonstrance <note>A "remonstrance" is a formal protest or statement of grievances/faith.</note> which he made to them, so that the senior Doctors of the Sorbonne <note>The Sorbonne was the theological faculty of the University of Paris and a fierce opponent of the Reformation.</note>—namely Nicolaus Clerici (who was the dean of the Theological faculty), Picard, and Maillard—were called to dispute with Jean Chapot face to face, something that had never happened before. They did not dare refuse out of shame, yet they would not argue from the authority of the Holy Scriptures, but only from the constitutions and institutions of the Roman Church. Because of this, many of the Council members, upon hearing this, wanted to acquit him. However, the cruelty of some and the cowardice of others prevailed so much that he was condemned to be burned, with this "mercy": that if he would recant, his tongue would not be cut out. Nevertheless,

<column-break/>

as he was led to the Place Maubert, he was permitted to speak while standing upright, being supported by two men, for he had been so tortured—to make him reveal to whom he had sold books—that he could not stand on his own limbs. Then he made an excellent confession regarding the point of the Lord’s Supper <note>The "Lord's Supper" (Avontmael) was a central point of theological conflict; Protestants rejected the Roman Catholic doctrine of Transubstantiation.</note>; at which point he was interrupted by Doctor Maillard, causing a great murmur among the people. Because of this, he was immediately taken from the cart and bound to the stake. To make the people believe he had said the "Ave Maria," he was first strangled and then burned. But Maillard, arguing that if the others were allowed to speak so much, all would be lost, persuaded the "Fire Chamber" <note>original: "vyer-camer," likely the *Chambre Ardente*, a special court for heretics.</note> (as they called it) to decree that henceforth no one should be brought out without first having their tongue cut out. As for the aforementioned Jean André, who had long served as a spy and betrayer of the children of God, he finally received his reward, being struck by God with a sudden apoplexy <note>A "Popelsie" or stroke.</note> and died without confession, which he had made so much of for others.

At Langres, a Bishop’s city and one of the oldest in France, there was a good man named Seraphin. He had begun a good church, though with small gatherings of 15 or 16 people, which later grew to a great number. He was finally imprisoned and burned in Paris with wonderful steadfastness. In this execution, something notable occurred: Doctor Picard, being completely astonished, instead of making many spiteful and mocking remarks as he was accustomed to do, began to exhort one of the five to patience. This man, with a smiling face, spoke these words to him so loudly that he could be heard by many: "Lord, Our Master <note>original: "Domine Magister Noster," a formal academic title.</note>, God be praised that you have changed your tune; if you stood in my place, would you dare to boast that you would have such good patience as the Lord has given me?" And so the five martyrs died. In the city of Sens, Jean l’Anglois was burned (1547), a lawyer and a learned and godly man. This happened at the request and expense of his own uncle, the Archdeacon of the church of Sens, named Barville. Likewise at Issoir in Auvergne, a martyr named Jean Brugere triumphed. He was from a village named Rozmal and so effectively resisted the Inquisitor Ory on the point of the Lord’s Supper that Ory was forced to say to some of his friends that Brugere was being treated unjustly, and that if it had been possible, he would have had his sentence lightened. Nevertheless, he was very horribly and cruelly burned.

And so, the preaching was completed regardless. From this, a great disturbance arose in the city, for the priests went to complain to Matheus Ory, a cruel Inquisitor, who caused much trouble in this matter. But those of the parish defended their preacher as a Doctor of Theology sent to them by their own Pastor. Thus, Ory knew not what else to do but to come and preach himself. But it was not with such an audience [as Michel's], nor did he deserve one; for starting his sermon with a quiet and feminine voice, he suddenly began to raise it and bellow like a bull, without any sense or learning. He preached nothing else but the same old song, which he himself called the *Quinque verba Pauli*, the five words of Paul. <note>original: "Quinque verba Pauli." This refers to 1 Corinthians 14:19: "I would rather speak five words with my understanding... than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue." He became so boastful that he had it proclaimed by trumpets that he would preach in the great cathedral of St. Etienne, with a command that all heads of households must attend upon penalty of ten silver marks. What is more, he had himself brought there in state by the officers of Justice. But although he cried and shrieked like a possessed man, he could not be heard because of the great multitude and the noise made by those who had come. Thus, he left the pulpit in great shame without finishing his sermon, crying out that he would go complain to the King. This sermon was thereafter called "The Preaching of the Trumpet." Ory did not stop preaching in other churches because of this, until the official Guillaume de la Porte—having been alerted by learned men who had noted his words—noted that Ory had spoken many heretical statements himself.

This now having come into the open, this miracle became a mockery, and the good brother lost his credit, and the Master Physician lost his regular salary which he had previously drawn from the Monastery.

### 1547. 
After being brought before the image they called **Our Lady of Fourchaut**, she performed even more wonderful things, even speaking several Latin, Greek, and Hebrew words which she had certainly been taught. And as she was a shrewd and wicked woman, seeing certain people standing there and knowing "the birds by their feathers" <note>An idiom meaning she could judge people's character or social standing by their appearance.</note>, she sometimes spoke true things, by which she put them to shame. Because of this, the people cried out, **"Miracle! Miracle!"** and there was no one who did not cry out and curse the **Lutherans** <note>At this time, "Lutheran" was often used as a general slur for any Protestant reformer, regardless of their specific theology.</note>, who respected neither the Saints nor the images. But the **Official** <term>Official<note>An ecclesiastical judge or administrative officer of a bishop's court.</note></term> named **de la Porte**, noticing something was amiss, was not unsettled by the Devil, but had all three of them placed in the Bishop's prison. He examined the young priest so thoroughly—rightly thinking that he followed the young woman more than he followed the Devil—and found him inconsistent in his words. After de la Porte threatened to put him on the rack, the priest finally confessed the whole truth, to the great confusion of those who had so easily believed it.

<margin>Third miracle.</margin>
Around this time, another similar miracle occurred in the suburb, in the temple called **le Chasteau**, where it was discovered that blood was running down the face of a large image standing in the portal. When this rumor was heard, the entire city came running with great devotion and processions, and they were so moved by it—due to the incitement of the Priests—that many who were considered heretics were in great danger of being killed and massacred. But in good time, the Lieutenant General arrived, named **Françoys de l'Aubespine**, a man of great standing and excellent intellect. Having observed everything closely, he had a man climb a ladder to where the image stood, and before all the people it was discovered that a dove which had been wounded had perched on that image, for they found the feathers and blood on the head of the image. Once this was made known, it caused the Priests to turn back with their crosses and banners, quite ashamed.

During this time, the Gospel was also received in the episcopal city of **Angers**, where there was a University; the city was filled with priests and monks. At that time, the bishop there was **Ioan Oliverius** <note>Jean Olivier, Bishop of Angers from 1532 to 1540; the text here likely refers to the ongoing influence of his tenure or a slight chronological overlap.</note>, the brother of **Olivier**, the **Chancellor of Alençon**, who was afterwards Chancellor of France. Being a learned man like his brother, he somewhat favored those of "the Religion" <note>original: "die vande Religie," a common contemporary shorthand for the Reformed or Protestant faith.</note>, among whom was one named **Germain Colin**, an old friend of **Clement Marot** <note>A famous French Renaissance poet whose translations of the Psalms were central to Huguenot worship.</note>, who with many others

<column-break/>

<margin>1547.</margin>
came to the gathering for prayers, as did several preachers who powerfully advanced the cause. But this could not last long without being discovered, and some were caught—among others **Germain Colin**, who, worn down by a long imprisonment, forgot himself so far through weakness that he bought his life with a recantation. But some others did not do as he did, but rather sealed the truth with their blood: namely, **Françoys Fardeau**, **Simon le Royer**, **Iean de la Vignole**, **Denis Saureau**, and **Guillaume de Reu**, whose ashes "wonderfully fertilized the field of the Lord," as the Book of Martyrs testifies.

There also preached there a **Friar Minor** <note>A member of the Franciscan Order.</note> who had great gifts of eloquence, named **Abel Pepin**, who was later a Minister in Geneva. The other monks bore such a hatred against him as they did against des Fosses, that they did not even spare the **Queen of Navarre** <note>Marguerite de Valois, sister of Francis I, known for protecting scholars and reformers.</note> in their sermons. Once good information was gathered on this and brought to the Court, and the King was informed by his aforementioned sister, <margin>His name was Toussains Henard.</margin> the most prominent agitator among these Friars was seized and, by sentence of the King, condemned to a galley, which somewhat checked the zeal of these monks. And so, those of the Religion took new courage, especially the leading members of the judiciary, and notably the King's Prosecutor named **Arthuis**, an old man of great reputation. Such was the rise of the Christian church in France, though with much pain and torment under the reign of **Francis I**, who died at Rambouillet on March 31, 1547. He was later called "the Great," which truly might have been rightfully attributed to him had he been as great a lover of the truth as he was a lover of good letters and a good soldier. After King Francis had died, his only son **Henry II** succeeded him on April 1, 1547, but he had neither the living spirit nor the eloquence of his father, though otherwise he was of a gentle nature, and therefore the easier to deceive; for he neither judged nor saw except through the eyes, ears, and advice of those who had completely taken hold of him. Some sought to maintain or improve their status through arms; others sought only to better themselves through greed, covering themselves with the mantle of Religion, whereby they did not cease to incite the King against those they called heretics. This was the reason that his kingdom was nothing other than a constant rage against those of the Religion within, and a cruel war without. But the Lord wished to show that His church never triumphs better than under the Cross. It must then be understood that four persons in particular held all the credit with this Prince: namely, **Anne de Montmorency**, the **Constable**, whom he called his "Compere," who also, as 

<column-break/>

<margin>1547.</margin>
soon as his late father had closed his eyes <note>original: "de mont geslotē hadde," literally "had closed the mouth," an idiom for death.</note>, was summoned back to Court, from which he had been banished due to some displeasure the King's father had held against him. The others were **Charles of Lorraine**, the son of the **Duke of Guise** and a **Cardinal**, the most gifted in all virtues that could be found in that estate; along with **Diane de Poitiers**, then called the **Great Seneschal**, and later the **Duchess of Valentinois**; and **Jacques d'Albon**, later called the **Marshal of Saint André**. These four were hereditary enemies of the Religion. But the Constable alone erred here through ignorance and superstition, helping only to feed the fire that was lit by the other three. The Marshal of Saint André was a man devoted only to filling his belly, and having few means of his own, he sought all the more to enrich himself with the confiscations of those they could somehow trap. Regarding the other two: one held the King's conscience as if in his sleeve, the other possessed his body—not without great appearance of wickedness, seeing as she had already spent her time in very bad reputation, and there was nothing in her by which she should pierce the heart of so great a Prince and draw him to her. These three were always at the King's ear to make him believe two points: namely, that the Religion was an enemy of all Monarchy and lordship; and also, that the true means to cover all sins before God and men, in which they maintained themselves, was to root out the enemies of the **Roman Church**. In short, they worked so well that from the beginning of his reign, he did nothing more diligently than persecute the poor believers, seeking to root them out if he could. Following this resolution, the fire was lit more than ever before, and above all in the Chamber of Parliament, which they called the **Burning Chamber** <term>Burning Chamber<note>original: "brādende Camer," referring to the *Chambre Ardente*, a special court established to try heretics, so named because the sentence was often death by fire.</note></term>, for they threw into the fire everything that fell into their hands. **Jean Morin** was busily occupied in catching and sending people to Paris. **Pierre Lizet**, the First President, let no one escape. <margin>God's judgment upon this Morin.</margin> Until God somewhat checked this madness, shaking His fearful judgment over this Morin through a fire that broke out in parts of his legs, and his body became completely rotten, so that he died miserably. And Lizet, for a certain reason, was cast out from his service and office.

But it would be impossible to recount the number of those who were executed in the year 1548. Among others, one named **Sanctinus Nivet** is worthy of memory. <margin>Sanctinus Nivet.</margin> He was from **Meaux**, and had departed for Germany about two years prior; after the fourteen were burned <note>Referring to the "Fourteen Martyrs of Meaux" executed in 1546.</note>, he was recognized and captured, but having made an excellent confession of faith...

<meta>This page continues the account of religious persecutions in France under the reign of Henry II, following the death of Francis I. # Church History.
Fol. 31.

<column-break/>

<margin>1548.</margin> ...of the faith; he was burned at Paris with a wonderful steadfastness. Also, a very wealthy stonecutter from Tours, who had lived for a time in Lyon, named **Octavian Blondet**, was betrayed by his host at "The Crown" <note>An inn or tavern.</note> where he was staying, because he had occasionally heard him speak some Christian words. He was taken prisoner by **Gabriel de Saconex**, a master in the College of St. John at Lyon, who was a notorious adulterer (bearing the visible marks of it) and who was very hungry for a rich golden necklace that Blondet was supposed to carry to Constantinople, which he and another nobleman intended to get into their claws. In short, they did everything they could to obtain it, but Blondet had some good friends who took such care of the matter that they were cheated of their hope. 

However, Blondet was persecuted all the more severely for it, to such an extent that although he was momentarily overcome by the constant pleading and tormenting of his friends and by the terror of death—so that he had somewhat dissembled—he was nevertheless condemned to the fire and taken to Paris. There, he honorably and remarkably corrected his fault, speaking much more boldly than before. He was burned with a wonderful steadfastness, greatly mourned, especially by those he had met in prison, to whom he had shown great love; he even released some who were imprisoned for debt by paying their creditors.

<margin>Decree of the King against the murderers of the Waldensians.</margin>
In the year 1549, the Lord God began to show that he held the hearts of kings in his hands. For although the King was violently inflamed against those of <term>the Religion<note>The standard term used by contemporary writers to refer to the Reformed or Protestant faith.</note></term>, it nevertheless happened that while making a journey through Piedmont, he learned of the terrible cruelty committed against the poor **Waldensians** <note>The Waldensians were a pre-Reformation Christian movement persecuted for centuries; a major massacre of their communities in Provence occurred in 1545.</note> under the name of the Parliament of Provence. Remembering the words his late father **Francis** had said to him on his deathbed, he was so moved that he issued certain letters and a decree this year against the principal authors of this murder. He expressly commanded his Prosecutor General to bring the knowledge of this cruel execution to trial, that it should be publicly pleaded in the High Chamber of the Court of Paris, and that criminal proceedings should immediately be taken against these same executors. These letters were dated at Montereau, March 1, 1549.

Nevertheless, despite the fact that this case was pleaded at length on both sides in various hearings, nothing came of it. For almost all the judges before whom the pleading took place had their eyes, ears, and hands stained with innocent blood, and fear-

<column-break/>

<margin>1549.</margin> -ing to condemn these men, lest they should also condemn themselves, they added to this boldness by allowing only **Guerin**, the King's advocate in the Parliament of Aix, to be hanged. **Menier**, who was the principal author of all the evil, not only escaped but was even restored to his former status, in which he did not fail to return to his cruelties. 

<margin>Gauthery, Bartholomew Audouin.</margin> In retaliation, among others, he caused to be burned one **Gauthery**, a learned man, and also an advocate named **Bartholomew Audouin**, born in Bessa near Bagnols. But God surely found him when the time for his payment came; for the Lord sent him such an inflammation and burning in his secret parts, with such a terrible 

<margin>The terrible end of Menier.</margin> flux of blood through all his passages, that being burned from his navel downward, he died in a truly wretched manner, passing (as it is feared) from this fire into another.

<margin>Hubert Burré.</margin> The Parliament of Dijon at this time caused a young man of about 19 years, named **Hubert Burré**, to be burned.

This same year, as the King made his entry into Paris, he learned that many were imprisoned for the Religion and desired to speak to one of them (it seemed, as a pastime). The Cardinal, hearing this and knowing that some learned and clever men were held there, feared that if any of them came before the King, they might speak too much. He therefore brought in a poor, simple tailor, thinking that upon seeing the King’s face and the great company with him, the man would remain entirely mute and terrified. 

But he was quite mistaken; for this poor man, strengthened by the power of the Most High, spoke so well and so clearly of the Religion, answering the questions of **Castellanus**, Bishop of Macon (an apostate), that everyone was greatly amazed. But when **Madame de Seneschale** <note>Diane de Poitiers, the King's influential mistress, known for her hostility toward the Reformation.</note> also wished to say something, mostly intended as mockery, this faithful servant of God could not endure it and gave her a short answer, saying: "Madame, be content that you have infected all of France, and do not mingle your filth with so holy a matter as the Word of God." 

This speech so violently angered the King, who loved this woman more than himself, that he wished to see this poor man burned alive himself in St. Anthony's Street, at the conclusion of a general procession. Others were also burned that same day, and more shortly thereafter; but the King never wished to be present at such a spectacle again, for he was so haunted by it that, as he himself said later, he saw nothing else the following night...

They used great diligence to employ their gifts, bringing in learned and good preachers, such as a **Jacobin** <note term="Jacobin">A member of the Dominican Order.</note> named **de Bosco**, mentioned previously. There also preached a **Minnebroer** <note term="Minnebroer">A Franciscan friar, from the "Friars Minor."</note> who had a great gift for eloquence, named **Abel Pepin**, who later became a Minister in Geneva. The other monks bore such a hatred toward him, as they did toward des Fosses, that they did not even spare the **Queen of Navarre** <note>Marguerite de Navarre, sister of Francis I, known for her intellectualism and protection of Reformers.</note> in their sermons. When accurate information about this was taken and brought to the Court, and the King was informed by his aforementioned
<margin>He was named **Tousaine Henrard**.</margin> sister, the foremost instigator among these Franciscans was seized. By the King's sentence, he was condemned to the galleys, which somewhat cooled the fire of these monks. And so, those of the Religion took new courage, especially the primary officials of Justice and the King’s prominent Prosecutor named **Arthuis**, an old man of great reputation. Such was the rise of the Christian church in Macrye <note>Likely referring to Meaux, a major center of early French Protestantism.</note>, and that with much pain and torment under the reign of **Francis I**, who died at Rambouillet on March 31, 1547. He was later called "the Great," a title that truly might have been granted to him had he been as great a lover of the truth as he was a lover of fine letters and a good soldier. After King Francis died, he was succeeded on April 1, 1547, by his only son, **Henry II**. But he had neither the lively spirit nor the eloquence of his father, though he was otherwise of a gentle nature and therefore easier to deceive; for he neither judged nor saw except through the eyes, ears, and advice of those who had entirely taken him over. Some sought to maintain or improve their status through arms, while others sought only to advance themselves through ambition; these covered themselves with the cloak of religion, by which they did not cease to incite the King against those they called heretics. This was the reason that his kingdom was nothing other than a constant rage against those of the Religion within, and a cruel war without. But the Lord wished to show that His church never triumphs better than under the Cross. It must be understood that four persons in particular held all the credit with this Prince: namely **Anne de Montmorency**, the Constable, whom he called his *Compere* <note>Godfather or close companion.</note>, and whom he recalled to the Court as 

<column-break/>

soon as his late father’s mouth was closed <note>i.e., immediately after Francis I died.</note>; he had been exiled because of some displeasure the King’s father had with him. The second was **Charles of Lorraine**, the son of the Duke of Guise and a Cardinal, the most gifted in all virtues—if ever there was one in that state. Also **Diane de Poitiers**, then called the Great Seneschal and later the Duchess of Valentinois; and **Jacques d'Albon**, later called the **Marshal of Saint André**. These four were hereditary enemies of the Religion. But the Constable alone erred here through ignorance and superstition; he only helped to light the fire that was deeply stoked by the others. The Marshal of Saint André, being a man devoted only to filling his own belly and having little means of his own, sought all the more to enrich himself with the confiscations of those they could somehow trap. Regarding the other two: one [the Cardinal] held the King’s conscience as if in his sleeve; the other [Diane] possessed his body, not without a strong appearance of sorcery, seeing as she had already spent her time in very ill repute and had nothing in her by which she should strike the heart of such a great Prince and draw him to her. These four were always in the King’s ear to convince him of two points: namely, that the Religion was an enemy to all Monarchy and lordship; and second, that the true means to cover all sins before God and men—in which they themselves lived—was to root out the enemies of the Roman Church. In short, they watched so well that from the beginning of his reign, he did nothing more diligently than persecute the poor believers, and as he had resolved, to root them out. Following these resolutions, the fire was lit more than ever before, and above all in the Chamber of Parliament, which they called the **Burning Chamber** <note term="Burning Chamber">The *Chambre Ardente*, a special court established in 1547 to try heretics.</note>, for they threw into the fire everything that fell into their hands. **Jean Morin** was diligently busy capturing people and sending them to Paris. **Pierre Lizet**, the First President, let no one escape. Until God broke this madness somewhat, shaking His terrible judgment over this Morin through a fire that broke out in his legs, and his body became entirely rotten, so that he died miserably; and Lizet was cast out of his service and office for a certain cause. 

But it would be impossible to recount the number of those who were executed in the year 1548. Among others, one named **Sanctin Nivet** of Meaux is worthy of memory; having departed for Germany about two years prior, and after the fourteen were burned <note>Referring to the "Fourteen Martyrs of Meaux" burned in 1546.</note>, he was recognized and captured, but having made an excellent confession of the

Likewise, a very rich stonemason from Tours, who had lived for a long time in Lyon, named **Octavian Blondet**, was betrayed by his host at the Crown inn where he was staying, because the host had heard him engage in Christian discourse. He was imprisoned by **Gabriel de Sacones**, a master at the College of Saint John in Lyon, who was a notorious adulterer (bearing the physical marks of his lifestyle). Sacones was very hungry for a golden and very rich necklace which Blondet was meant to carry to Constantinople, and which Sacones, along with another nobleman, intended to seize for themselves. In short, they used every possible diligence to get hold of it, but Blondet had some good friends who looked into the matter so well that the conspirators were cheated of their hope. 

However, because of this, Blondet was persecuted all the more severely—to such an extent that although he was eventually overcome by the constant pleading and tormenting of his friends and by the terror of death, causing him to somewhat falter <note>original: "gebuynt," likely meaning he recanted or wavered under pressure</note>, he was nonetheless condemned to the fire and taken to Paris. There, he honorably and excellently corrected his fault, speaking much more boldly than before. He was burned with wonderful steadfastness, greatly mourned, especially by those he had met in prison, to whom he had shown great love—even releasing some who were imprisoned for debt by paying what they owed.

<margin>1549.</margin> ...and saw those people <note>The text refers back to the King's memory of the martyrs he watched burn.</note>; indeed, by day he sometimes experienced such visions and terrors that he imagined the man was following at his heels. He swore, therefore, that he would never watch another execution, so dearly had this "pleasure" cost him. Yet he would have done better had he paid more heed to the righteous cause of the poor, anxious, and oppressed believers.

And in passing, I must speak of the notable History of the aforementioned Bishop of Mâcon, serving as an eternal memory. This good bishop, named **Castellanus** <note>Pierre Duchâtel (Latinized as Castellanus), c. 1480–1552, was a French humanist and bishop.</note>, was of humble birth. He was first a Regent <note>A teacher or professor.</note> at Dijon under Master **Pieter Turreau**, who was considered one of the most esteemed prognosticators of his time. From there, he went to study law, and as he possessed a fine spirit, he was highly regarded in the time of **Alciat**. From Bourges <note>OCR: DanVourges</note> he went to study at Basel, where he grew greatly in Philosophy and in Religion while living in the house of Master **Sebastian Münster**. Finally, he returned to France and presented himself to **Jacques Colin**, who was at that time the King’s ordinary reader at the royal table. God willed that Colin present him to the King, who was eager to hear clever and bold men at his table. The King sidelined Colin and kept Castellanus by his side for the rest of his life. Eventually, the King endowed him with the bishopric of Mâcon, and later of Orleans, following many other lesser types of benefices. He was a man of fine spirit and excellent understanding, elegant in his Latin, and at first well-disposed toward the Reformed Religion; indeed, so much so that he used his authority to protect the cause of that eminent printer **Robertus Stephani** <note>Robert Estienne, the famous scholar-printer.</note>, the King’s Printer, when he was greatly tormented by the Sorbonne for having printed certain Bibles. But thereafter, he changed, even to the point of persecuting those he had previously held in high esteem. He finally became Bishop of Orleans, where God had set his limit.

<margin>Judgment of God over the Bishop of Mâcon.</margin> For on the day before his formal entry into his city, having arrived at the monastery they call Saint Puerte <note>Likely the Porte Saint-Vincent or a similar ecclesiastical gate/monastery.</note>, he went into the pulpit to preach. A great multitude had gathered, curious to hear a Bishop preach. But as he was most severely threatening those they called heretics, the Lord God struck him with such a heavy and sudden pain of colic that he was carried away. He died most miserably that following night, ending his days and making his "entry" into another place instead of Orleans.

On the 19th of July, many excellent witnesses of Jesus Christ were also executed in various places throughout the City of Paris.

<margin>Flo</margin> Among those worthy of mention are **Leonard Galunart** of Vendôme and **Florent Vernot**, born near Sedan in Brie. The latter first endured unbelievable torments in various prisons within Paris for a period of four years and nine days. During this time, he was kept for six weeks in a deep pit called *la chausse a l'hypocras* <note>Literal: "The Hypocras Strainer." A notorious funnel-shaped dungeon cell where the prisoner could neither stand, sit, nor lie down.</note>. It was so narrow at the bottom that whoever was inside could neither lie nor sit, but had to stand mostly on their toes, standing in water and foul filth. With a hunched body, he could not stand upright. According to the testimony of those who guarded the prison, no criminal had ever been able to survive there for more than fourteen days. But this faithful servant of God endured all this with unbelievable steadfastness. He also overcame the final cruelty, being burned alive in the Place Maubert.

He was followed by a very godly woman from Orleans named **Anne Audebert**, widow of **Pieter Genest**, an apothecary. > My God, what a beautiful belt my Bridegroom gives me now! I was married to my first bridegroom on a Saturday, and on this Saturday, I go to be the bride for my second marriage, to my Bridegroom Jesus Christ.

1550. possessed such a wonderful grace; nevertheless, he had such great knowledge coupled with a sincere zeal that in the beginning, he was sought out to instruct the assembly, which he did previously with much fruit. The other person was the new bishop, named **Antonio Caracciolo** <note>original: "Antonius Carraciol"</note>, (surnamed Prince of Melfi on account of his father). Having been instructed from a lower station in the knowledge of the truth, he also went forth boldly to preach against the abuses of the Roman Church, except that he did not touch upon the matter of the Mass. His sermons were of great edification, with everyone flocking to them—some out of curiosity, having never heard a bishop preach, others moved by a good zeal. However, at nearly the same time, one named **Mace Moreau**, who dealt in books, was caught and condemned by **Marc Champy**, the Criminal Lieutenant. From a Christian, he was [labeled] an atheist <note>In the 16th century, "atheist" was often used as a derogatory term for anyone departing from established Church dogma, regardless of their actual belief in God.</note>; by which condemnation the aforementioned Moreau was burned, singing Psalms until his very last breath.
