<margin>A poor Bookseller.</margin>
There was also imprisoned at Bourges a poor bookseller who possessed some books concerning the Religion <note>A common shorthand for the Reformed or Protestant faith.</note>. Upon his arrival, he brought a letter to one of the Councilors named **François Velle**, who received him well, though he knew from the letter what sort of man he was. It happened a short time later that this poor man was imprisoned and brought before the same councilor to be examined. The councilor labored greatly to turn him away from his faith, finally saying to him: "Do you wish then to die? Then you shall die." The good man could have accused the councilor on account of the letter he had delivered, but he said nothing else except to admonish him not to act against his own conscience. Nevertheless, the councilor signed his death sentence, by which he was burned. While the Councilor stood by this, he was immediately struck by the hand of God and went to lie in his bed. Although no specific sickness could be detected other than melancholy <note>At this time, "melancholy" was seen as both a physical ailment of the humors and a profound spiritual despair.</note>, he died within a few days with much crying and shouting.

<margin>Anne Aysbert.</margin>

<margin>Gabriel Berauuin. Jan Godeau.</margin>
Likewise, by a Decree of the Parliament of Chambéry, **Gabriel Berauuin** of Loudun and **Jan Godeau** of Chinon in Touraine were burned, having been imprisoned because they had rebuked a Priest who was blaspheming the Name of God.

<margin>Claude Thierry.</margin>
In the following year, 1551, the King having entered into a certain treaty with **Maurice, the Duke of Saxony and Elector**, and with **Albert, Duke of Brandenburg**—both of the **Augsburg Confession** <note>The primary confession of faith for the Lutheran Church.</note>—he thus received the title of "Protector of the Empire" against the Emperor **Charles V**. This ambition caused the zeal of the Cardinal and other officials of the Roman Church to cool slightly; therefore—

<column-break/>

1551. —no one was sent to Trent <note>The Council of Trent (1545–1563) was the Roman Catholic Church's formal response to the Protestant Reformation.</note> at that time, except for the Abbot of Belosane, surnamed **Amiot** <note>Jacques Amiot (1513–1593), a famous humanist and translator.</note>, to protest against the Council. It was also forbidden to bring any more money to Rome for the sake of benefices <note>church offices that provided an income.</note>. On the other hand, the King, wishing to remove all suspicion that he intended to show any favor to heretics, issued an Edict that was thereafter called the **Edict of Châteaubriant**. It was dated June 27, and in it all previous edicts made against them were renewed, giving all judges power to proceed against those who held wrong views of the Roman Church. By virtue of this Decree, **Pieter d'Estrades**, criminal judge of Agen, acting against his own conscience, publicly whipped a poor man of the Religion and afterwards caused another to be burned. In that season, many other kinds of cruelties were practiced, too long to recount here.

<margin>One whipped, and burned.</margin>

<margin>Claude Monier.</margin>
In Lyon, a God-fearing man named **Claude Monier** was also imprisoned and burned; he suffered death with great steadfastness.

<margin>Mauritius Secenat.</margin>
Likewise in Nîmes, another named **Mauritius Secenat**, born in Saveneys, by whose steadfastness many were edified.

<margin>Thomas of St. Paul, 18 years old.</margin>
But the wonderful steadfastness that God gave at this time to a young companion of 18 years, named **Thomas of St. Paul**, is to be marveled at. For he made his executioners entirely amazed and terrified. The cause of his imprisonment was that he had rebuked a blasphemer; the latter spied on his house, and thus he was brought to the **Châtelet** <note>A notorious prison in Paris.</note>. In that place, he was tortured as horribly as a human could endure; nevertheless, they could get no names of other persons from his mouth. He died on September 9th.

<margin>Jan Joery.</margin>
In Toulouse, a remarkable confession was also made by **Jan Joery** of Albi, aged about 22 years, together with a young servant who served him. Both of these confessed Jesus Christ and died singing a Psalm in harmony until their last breath. In Bourg-en-Bresse—being at that time under the King’s obedience and the Parliament of Chambéry—**Hugue Gravier** was burned. He was from the land of Maine and was then the schoolmaster for the Count of Neuchâtel in Switzerland. He was captured at the bridge of Mâcon while he intended to travel to his fatherland. Likewise, in Saumur in Anjou, **Renier Poyer**, the own son of **Chancellor Poyer**, died with great steadfastness.

The year 1553 is very memorable for the great persecution and the glorious triumphs of many Martyrs. First, in Lyon: where five persons arrived on the last day of April in the year 1552...

Being fastened to it, they began with one heart to sing the *Song of Simeon* <note>original: "lof-sangh Symeonis"; also known as the *Nunc Dimittis* (Luke 2:29-32), a traditional hymn of peace at the end of life.</note> and so gave up the spirit.

<margin>Nicolas Nail.</margin> named **Nicolas Nail** of **Le Mans**, was treated piteously. And as they were to lead him away, they bound (which had never been done before) a wooden gag in his mouth, fastened from behind with ropes and pulled so stiff and tight that not only did his mouth bleed on both sides, but because of the great opening of his mouth, his face was entirely hideous and terrifying. And so he was brought to the place of his suffering with a great outcry and the mockery of the maddened folk, who almost tore him from the executioner's hands to rip him to pieces. Having arrived at the place, his naked body was pulled up into the air; and to testify to their cruel tyranny and to torment the poor man, they had first smeared his whole body with grease and then coated it with resinous kindling <note>original: "Boscryt"; likely a flammable pitch or resin used to accelerate the burning and increase the victim's agony.</note>, so that as he hung over the fire, as soon as they set the coating aflame, even before the wood burned, that poor body was ignited in a gruesome manner. Nevertheless, this faithful servant of God remained steadfast until the rope of the wooden gag burned away, and with his mouth he still praised his God with a loud voice until his last breath.
